text:
A game that tells the tale of four ancient goddesses engaged in an eternal divine war for control of the world itself, and most importantly which video game console is the best, how piracy will destroy the world, and how close girls can get before it's no longer subtext.
The game is very competent, without anything that particularly lacks or stands out. The story really just boils down to "what if game companies and consoles were anime ladies", but the writing is amusing and the little jokes and nods towards the companies (the Wii girl has incredible defenses, the Xbox wears a red ring, etc.) are a nice touch. The battle system revolves around setting up combos, choosing from weak attacks that raise a meter for powerful attacks, attacks that reduce the enemy's guard, or high HP damage above all else.
The world, art, and locations look very pretty, and the music is enjoyable, but there could stand to be more variety and many dungeons are "The dungeon from before but with an extra path and area added". The enemies are standard RPG fare, with the occasional anime joke or game parody such as Mario's pipes or Pac-Man ghosts. The game also boasts crafting recipes that allow you to add items to the shops, access new dungeons, or change the items and enemies that can be found within a dungeon.
The only real concerns with the game are the grinding and fanservice. With the former, you'll often reach a boss and find yourself suddenly outgunned, and needing to go back until you've gained a few levels, with one early boss apparently enough to send people to forums, convinced that victory is impossible. Regarding fanservice, most early introductions include cutscenes where the only animation is jiggling, and certain outfits and attacks will mean upskirt city. That said, if you're looking at this game, it's probably a selling point for you.
If you play, keep in mind that the "camera reset" button lets you skip attack animations.

Bottom line:  I put hundreds of hours into the first CoH, but this one has been even more fun and addicting for me!  BEST. WWII AND STRATEGY GAME. EVER!!!!!!!!!!!
Company of Heroes 2 is one outstanding RTS game, and easily the best ever made to this point.  I'm estimating I played close to 1,000 hours of Company of Heroes 1, and I do really think they took a great leap forward from that first game (which was also incredible).  There are a number of small improvements in the interface alone that make this new entry in the series TONS more accessible and enjoyable to play.  These few interface additions even multiply the ease of command and diversify your tactical options (such as infantry now being able to hop over walls and fences).  The line of sight update, which means a building now restricts your commmand view of the other side of the building in the fog of war, adds to realistic surprise attacks and ambushes.
CoH2's biggest addition, IMO, is the new commander system.  Some people call it pay to win (which is silly--like any other game, it is simply pay to play....you had to buy the game to begin with in order to win, and why should expansions be free?), but it is really just pay to add variety and enjoyment to your game.  There are SOOOOOO many commander choices that the battles are extremely different every time.  Your enemy's commander choice will effect what special units you face on the battlefield, forcing you to adapt and craft new victory plans each time.
The new Theater of War mode is also great.  These are unique scenario challenges that really change the game's experience.  From sniper hunts to giant tank battles to wave defenses, this mode provides WWII action that is different from what you'd experience in normal multiplayer.  Quite a few of these mission are also co-op fun with friends.  They are also historically based.
The graphics are also a VERY big leap forward.  This is a gorgeous game all around.  I also appreciate the ability to choose camo paints for vehicles, adding the visuals and bringing some nice variety to the game and personalization.  The sound is also top notch, from great explosive effects to the always comical chatter among soldiers.  The men under your command have a great sense of humor.
For those new to the series, it may be a lot to learn, but success in this game is immensely rewarding.  For veterans of the first game, expect more of the same great WWII combat!
*NOTE: The new Western Front Armies expansion has made this game twice as good as it was at release!!!  New workshop features add thousands of maps to play on as well.

This is a perfect example of a very bad first impression.
Coming directly from playing the first two games in the series, this one felt out of place and did not explain the giant leap of the old west setting to the modern-day world of the Mexican cartels. If you wait it out, the connection between them appears to be there, but it is not exactly obvious.
It started as a generic, cheesy, and unbelievable story that eventually became a somewhat tolerable and almost interesting one that will end up being forgotten when compared to other story-driven first person shooters. Gameplay mechanics are nothing new and very generic. Shoot, cover, rinse and repeat with the straight forward driving sections to mix up the gameplay a bit.
If you stick with it to the end, you can see some design choices that carried over from the others in the series, which they attempted to improve upon, but ultimately ended up with mixed results.
This game was clearly made for a co-op experience and it is strongly recommended to play it that way if at first you find it really hard to have fun.
It is not a very good game, but it is also not a completely bad one either. If you give it a chance, it can grow on you. With its equal amount of shining and eye-rolling moments, it is an underrated title.

I first found out about this games existince around springtime of last year, when I randomly came across a let's play video of this game by a youtuber known as Long Pause. While the video was good for a quick laugh, the game itself didn't capture my intrest. In fact, I would've forgotten about it if it wasn't for a Splatoon Gmod video called "Squid-nanigans". In it, the main character of this game, Neptune (based on the Sega Neptune), encounters an Inkling and.....chaos ensues.
This lead me to do a little research, and eventually I had the motive to buy this game(but not at full price). Christmas comes around, I get steam money, it was on sale for 6 bucks, bought the game and.......I spent 6 hours on it and didn't touch the game for at least 2 months.
Near the end of march, I decided to give the game one last shot, to see if I can try and find a reason to keep going. Thankfully I did, as I made some serious progress, and I realized that this game is actually good. Very good. In fact, It's surprizingly good.
Pros:
-The EXE attacks are amazing.
-The regular special attacks arn't to bad either.
-Compa.
-The characters are chock-full of personallity.
-The world of Gameindustri is based on video games.
-The battle system has plenty of variety.
-Compa.
-Lots of side quests to keep one busy between major story events.
-Foruth-Wall breaks. I like those.
-Me laughing the whole way through, especailly when it comes to Neptune and her pudding.
-Did I already metion Compa? What I'm saying is that I really like Compa (and Blanc, and Nepgear, and Noire, and Neptune, and 5pb who is my real favorite character but she's not in this game so Compa will do, and...).
Cons:
-The voice acting goes up and down in quality.
-Some of the items in the shop are more expensive than they should.
-A glitch that causes enemies to become self-aware and not attack on their turn.
-The game in general can be hard without DLC or if your characters arn't at a proper level.
-The simple fact that I had to rewrite all the changes I made to this review because my laptop is literally a SELF-AWARE A$$HOLE THAT SECRETLY HATES ME!
Would I recommend this game? The box says yes but I don't really know. It depends on what kind of gamer you are. I mean, if you're the kind of gamer who's willing to look past the fanservice, likes RPG's, Video game references, fourth-wall breaks and a storyline that doesn't take itself seriously and focused more on comedy, or just really wants to see some of their favorite game consoles as godesses/anime girls, then who knows? Maybe this games for you. If you don't like any of those things, then get ready for a bad time(insert Undertale reference here).
Seriously though, I need an actual computer.

This is a really fun RTS with a lot of fun lore behind it. The gameplay, especially the unit variety, lets the game down.
I'm going to compare this to Starcraft (not Starcraft II - the first one) just as a baseline.
The lore is all there. Compelling story, memorable characters. It doesn't have the same sort of humour Starcraft does (in terms of unit quotations or in the story)
Unit variety is its weakest point. There are only about 12 unit types per side - about eight land units, three air units, plus an epic unit (think experimental units from Supreme Commander). You have a basic unit, a light armour unit, a tank, artillery, a siege unit, and a scout - and that's it. Air units consist of a fighter, a bomber, and an air scout. No special abilities, just units. It's kind of like Supreme Commander in that sense.
Upgrades...well, there are a total of 12 upgrades per side, three in four categories - and you can only pick one per category. The main thing here is that usually there's one upgrade that beats the others in terms of usability, and you'll end up picking that all the time.
That said, the sides do play considerably differently while maintaining a consistent look and feel across all of them. It's a lot like Starcraft in that sense. Unless you're playing the Goo, which plays unlike anything else I've seen in an RTS.
There is unfortunately a very small multiplayer community, but if you have a team ready to play or you like story-driven RTSes, really consider this game.
$60 CAD is a steep asking price, but if you can nab the game on sale, do so.

This is a great real-time strategy game, developed by some of the original team behind the Command & Conquer games, and it shows. Grey Goo features a similar resource system as the C&C games (a flow economy), but does away with the need to build power plants to generate energy. The latter move has been called into question in some corners and it does remove some of the nuance in the base-building aspect, but the game works fine without it.
Grey Goo is named after the eponymous Goo faction, which consist of nano machines. They are a roving faction that don't need structures to create new units. Instead, park your main unit -- the Mother Goo -- on top of a catalyst (i.e. main resource) vent and, once the Mother Goo has grown to a sufficient size, split it in two to generate another Mother Goo or a prothean (which can be split into actual units). The Goo are one of the most interesting factions to come along in an RTS game in a long while and offer a different kind of challenge regardless of whether you're controlling them or fighting against them.
The other two factions are also interesting. The humans are the most technologically advanced faction in the game, which makes for quite a nice change from most other games where humans are presented as the underdog. They field hover tanks and build bases using a system of conduits. They are ideals for those players who wish to turtle up. They can teleport structures and units around, which gives them a flexability that offsets the rigidity that building a human base initially seems to bring with it.
The last faction are the Beta (the name that the humans have given them, actually). These are aliens and perhaps the most traditional of the factions in the game. You build hubs of various sizes and attach other modules to them, such as factories. They are the only faction in the game to field any type of infantry. Most of their units consist of vaguely dinosaur-shaped mechs, which give them a character all of their own. Like the humans, they are able to erect walls. This means that they can turtle up like the humans, but are also more flexible thanks to using hubs as the centre of their bases.
Each of the factions also fields a single "epic" unit: the magnificent and deadly purger for the Goo, the Alpha for the humans (essentially a giant, floating robot with a human inside), and the Hand of Ruk (a flying fortress) for the Beta. Each faction also has five tech slots: you have to pick from three techs for every slot and they essentially serve as bonuses. The system is simple, but it works great.
One of the things that the developers specifically set out to do is create an accessible RTS that emphasizes strategy over tactics. As a result, all units do one thing and one thing only. They don't have any special abilities that you need to worry about. Just create groups and focus on the bigger picture. Units move more slowly than, for example, in Command & Conquer and they are also a bit more durable (the structures seem a lot more durable), with the epic units offering a way to avoid a late game stalemate.
Terrain is also important. The game features layered terrain with ramps in a manner similar to Starcraft and lots of other RTS games. It also includes "brush": vegetation that units can hide in and look out of. Enemy units cannot see these units unless they enter the brush, which means that the vegetation offers a place to hide from enemy aircraft or to lay an ambush. I haven't seen something like this since Praetorians, a much older RTS set in Roman times where you could hide your troops in forests. It's a great feature that more games should use.
The game includes a fifteen-mission campaign, in which you control each of the three factions in turn (Beta, humans, and finally the Goo). There's also DLC available that adds three more missions that fleshes out the story a bit more. Weta Workshop was involved in the design of the game and created the full motion videos -- the look of the game is wonderful and the cinematics are excellent. The tone of the game is great, too; serious, but not grim or dire, and with a certain joy in its execution that makes the game a delight to play.
If you get bored with the campaign or want to hone your skills, the game naturally offers a skirmish mode. If you feel inclined to compete against other humans, multiplayer is also available. All in all, Grey Goo offers a complete package and is the best "traditional" real-time strategy game to have appeared in a long while (not that it has a lot of competition!), and arguably ranks up there with the best RTS games to have ever appeared. Heartily recommended.

The turn-based combat (and the ability to strategise by holding oppnents turns back, slowing them down, and charging moves) system is deep enough to satisfy RPG fans, but shallow enough to learn easily and control without any fuss. A secondary character can be controlled by mouse (or other joypad analog stick) - allowing a second player to control your companion in battle (he's wonderful for strategising, healing, etc).
Moving around the worlds is a beautiful experience, seeing the artwork shine, and talking to characters in rhyme. The Piano and strings music is gorgeous, really emphasising the game, and drawing the player into feeling for the game's characters and situations. Frankly, the soundtrack can compare to movies and much bigger game soundtracks easily.
Controls are simple, and never leave you frustrated.
This is a gem of a game, and can sit proudly alongside other RPGs without being unfavourable viewed.

Excellent turn-based sci-fi game. Most of the time, it's tactical, squad-based combat, but there is a lovely degree of strategic decision-making when you're developing the X-COM home base, and deploying satellites and interceptors.
It has a learning curve that is a bit uncomfortably steep, but if you can get past that, there's a lot to love about this game.
I only have two real gripes about the game. One is that you, the player, can only ever play in a reactive manner. Except for the limited scenarios allowed by the linear campaign, you cannot lure aliens into ambushes, lay traps, or clear out areas proactively.
The other gripe is that the campaign is too short. Of course, this is also a compliment, since I'm essentially saying "I like the game so much, I want a longer campaign, please!"
Despite those two relatively minor issues, I can wholeheartedly recommend this game to anyone who likes turn-based games.

Black Desert Online is an interesting Korean based MMORPG with many unique contents, that cannot be compared with other MMO such as Wow and other game. It have implentmented contents such as life skill which is something you would do on a everyday basis like Fishing, Mining, Cooking, Processing, Sailing, Training (Horse), and etc. Which you can level your profession and in order decrease time taken to do that certain action. This game also doesn't have raid dungeon compared to other MMO which is a change from the MMO genre while having world bosses that spawn in certain area with a certain interval of time. Gears and equipment have no level requirement meaning that you could be equiping the best gears on a lv 1 and quickly grind up level very fast.
Combat system is very unique as you have to memorize the keys to activate a certain skill while other mmo use hotkey like Wow and this is a change and makes it more enjoyable. If you play till end game, you'll unlock awakening at lv 56 which will give you an extra weapon along with a set of new skill. Combat gets much more better than before as this show the full potential of BDO combat system.
Graphic is very realistic which makes the game even more lively and just pulls you into the game. I have nothing else to complain about the graphic as it well done.
One of my main concern of BDO is XignCode Anti Cheat which is an Anti-Cheat Program, that gets install on your pc with prior knowledge. This program monitors your PC resource usage and much more, people of the BDO community does not like this as this is a breach to our privacy. Resulting in a loss of playerbase due to this reason. When you uninstall BDO the files still remains on your pc and you have to locate it and manually delete which is very fustrating. Another slight concern of BDO is PTW as this can increase the gap between the people who just buy the game and those who pay to benefit from buff like costume which give stat and pets that auto loot with a cetain interval and also increasing inventory slot and weight limit. I've heard that BDO have decrease this gap during the time of its launch between both side making the game slightly more fairer for those who have brought the game.
But in the End, Black Desert Online is considerable game to play if you want a change in pace from the typical MMO and you should at least try the 1 week trial on their site.

Good lord, this game.
Simply, it's a twin stick shooter, where the frequency of the enemy ships and the power or your shots are powerered by your music you load into it. It has really REALLY bright lights for all the explosions and the bosses can sometimes catch you rather unawares. It's a bit of a time sink too. I was planning on just playing a couple new songs off a new album I got, and I usually end up playing like 3+ hours more.
A little LESS simply though is that there is something about the game with makes songs more emotionally investable. Soemthing about the fact that, sure, your ship is powered by the song. But in part, YOU are too. It's not really prominant in anything silly, like say Weird Al, but load up something Masterplan or Skillet and crank up the volume and youcan find yourself burning through an entire album without realizing you did so.
Online play is kinda meh to me though. You BOTH have to have the song that you want to play, Otherwise, you'll be forced to use the library provided by an internet radio station connected to Beat Hazard or some tracks that were (I beleive) made for the game it self.
Another feature that differs from when i first got this game on my Xbox360 some 5 years ago is that is has the option to change your ship. And with each ship you can unlock OTHER ships by completing "Shadow Missions". The more powerful the ship the harder the mission. I'm currently trying to finish the Shadow Mission for the DragonFire, a very powerful but really slow ship, and to finish the mission you have to beat 3 songs no less than 3 minutes, 30 seconds long on INSANE difficulty without losing a life..
Needless to say, this is INSANEly difficult. The jump from "Hardcore" difficulty to "Insane" is huge, but the difference is made up in the possibility to get rather high scores.
Be warned though, this is a possible seizure inducing game! You can reduce the intensity of the lights of the explosions, but even then they are still very bright. Even if you don't suffer from epileptic seizures, if you're not careful, the explosions will get you dead cause you can't see incoming ships or shots fired from the enemies. This is especially true when it comes to anything harder than Average, where the volley of enemies number WAY up there and can last half your song.
Personal favorite song to play in this game is Black In The Burn by Masterplan. It varies soo incredibly much, you'll get all different facets of strength from your ship.

What can I say about Civ 5 that hasn't been said?  I thoroughly enjoy this game.  It may not be the deepest strategy game, but there is enough there to keep you entertained for quite a long time.  With different civilizations, maps, and ways of winning the game, you can always find some different way to play.
If you have not played a Civilization game before, this will take a little bit of time to get the hang of.  I had never played one before this, but after the tutorials and just toying around with the game for a bit, I was hooked and understood what I was doing.  So there is a learning curve, but it is not as bad as you may fear.  Plus there are 8 different difficulty levels so you have the oppertunity to learn without much fear of losing.
If you were to pick up this game, I would recommend the complete edition as it gives you 45+ civilizations to choose from, a nice assortment of maps to play on, and around 10 scenarios to play as well if you want a break from the main game.  And with workshop support, there are a number of things you can add to make the game more entertaining for you.
Overall, a very good strategy game for new and existing strategy game fans

Pros :
- Expect the unexpected. There are a lot of WTF moments in this game.
- Memorable, likeable, HATABLE characters.
- Great voice acting & atmosphere.
- Graphics isn't much, but each character got their expressions right and that's all this game needs.
Cons :
- Sometimes, you will be forced to make a choice you don't want to. An expected flaw for a game like this.
- If you have some characters you like, be ready for "anything" that will happen to them. You have been warned.
- "Sometimes, there are a few things that you can't prevent (I won't spoil the story) no matter what choices you made. I think its normal because the story still needs a foundation." <-- that's what I thought at first. But, the ending makes me realized that the story is already planned from the start that you are going to be f*cked in the end no matter what choices you made.
That feeling when you've spent your time playing this game, thinking so hard that your choices were the right ones, all the frustations you had from watching your characters die...and all of them are for nothing. That's what this game is.

Unlike a good bit of games from Japan, NeptuniaRe;birth1 is VERY well translated, I didn't notice any major grammar nor spelling mistakes, which is always a good thing, the devs obviously put a lot of work into making sure the English Version worked perfectly, and that makes me happy
The Story itself is enjoyable and funny, the characters will often find themselves in very risqué situations for your viewing (fapping) pleasure
The story doesn't take itself seriously and smashes the fourth wall like it's the cool aid dude on laced weed, which is always enjoyable, but I would of liked a few more serious moments to see a more serious side of the characters.
Combat:8/10
Combat itself is turned based, you normally get to go first but there are exceptions, if an enemy runs up to you from behind, you are ambushed and the enemy will go first, if you run into an enemy or they run into you from in front, you get to go first (usually). If you run up to the back of an enemy and hit them with your sword/dagger/Giant Syringe of death then you get a Symbol attack, and gain a small bonus your first attack as well as going first, which is very helpful against stronger foes, but tends to leave weaker foes in the dust, after being 5+ levels higher than an enemy you can normally wipe them out in a single round
Boss Battles are a bit different, in (nearly) every dungeon there are bosses, more powerful enemies that will likely take you a while to knock down even if you’re a significantly higher level, though after a certain point they won’t even do damage to you, turning that fairly long boss fight that should be exciting, into a chore especially if you have to do it several times to fulfill a quest.
Let me be clear, your first play through is likely to be VERY grindy, so if you aren't a fan of grinding you may want to look else where
The grinding itself is actually surprisingly fun (most of the time, see reasons above), using my skills to wipe out multiple foes at once is always a satisfying feeling plus the animations are surprisingly good considering the graphics level of the game.
Overall I take a points for no counter balance to make farming low level dungeons anything but a boring chore and because after level 90 you’re basically a war god who can nearly transcend dimensions and tear the fabric of reality with your pinky
Crafting:7/10
You can find plans, either through playing through the story or defeating bosses in dungeons, which you can then use to add new items to the game (none of which are required to beat the game so it’s strictly for fun). Finding the items needed is kind of tricky since you get next to no help from the game itself, I eventually broke down and googled where to find a couple of items so I could craft a few new items into the game that I wanted, which while it was easy to google it, I would of liked if the game at least told you what dungeon and/or enemy you had to fight to get the item (note this has changed in Re;Birth3 so you can look at hints to find items in plans and quest)
Graphics:6/10
Now I don’t play games for graphics, but I know that some people do, so I’m putting this section in here to make sure people are aware of what they’re buying
Neptunia’s graphics rely more on CPU horsepower than GPU power, I would have preferred the game be housed more in GPU than CPU, but that’s just me your millage may vary
The game itself great looking, but I think the main focus should be on the artwork shown in cut scenes, and I can safely say that the artwork is a solid 9/10, no shaky edges that I can see on a 1080p monitor, but for anyone who is wondering if their PC can run this game, you probably can, I’m using a 6-core AMD CPU and I can run it @60fps will no noticeable stuttering at 1920x1080
I really don’t think graphics should play a large part in deciding if you should buy a game but I also think people should be aware
Dungeons & Quest:5/10
Probably the most annoying part of the game for me would be the fact that most dungeons are just rebranding’s of other dungeons, it’s basically the same hand full of dungeons that you see stuffed with new enemies throughout the game, I know that these lower budget games have to save wherever they can but I still would have liked more dungeons
The quests have a very similar problem
In the game there are 5 factions, that have shares, shares represent how many people pray to a certain goddess, you can affect these shares by completing quest and raising or lowering a certain factions power, and it’s difficult to balance things out (which is required for a certain ending) so you will likely end up spamming certain quest over and over again to balance everything, I would of enjoyed only being able to do a quest 2 or 3 times then being forced to do another, it would of made the entire process my more fun
Other thoughts:
The game doesn’t come with an auto-save feature which really sucks considering how it crashed on me three times in my first play through and once in my second, most of the enemies are recolored to look a bit different, and some don’t even go that far, you will see the flower enemy multiple times looking exactly the same just with a different name and higher stats. Quest are also very repetitive, once you complete a quest you can immediately pick it right back up to help change your shares
Conclusion:
Now after all that said, you might be wondering, ‘so does he recommend this game or not?’ my response to that is, don’t interrupt me while I’m talking
But seriously, I strongly recommend this game for anyone who enjoys a good bit of grinding and just wants something funny and cute to play after a rough day, if you’re into explosions guns and gore, go somewhere else, this isn’t for you.
Even with the repetitive quest, dungeons, and enemies, the combat is fun once you get into it and the grinding barely feels like grinding. The characters are cute, funny and different from one another, I often find myself in some games not memorizing people’s names because they always tend to have one of 2 or 3 personalities, in this all the main characters have their own personalities that are difficult to categorize, giving me a lasting memory of them that sticks out.
Overall Score: 7.1/10 (averaged)
8/10 (my personal score overall)

Ok, so this game is not as good as it could have been, not by far.
The Good:
1. You get a great feel for the Game of thrones world, especially initially.
2. You get to see multiple people's stories, just like the show.
3. You learn aboout more of the lore. (Not sure if it is canonical to the book or movie)
The bad:
1. Endless choices that pretend to be important, when 90% of them actually aren't important at all.
2. You can't enjoy being in the game of thrones world, because you are constantly baragged with meaningless B.S choices.
3. Every single character is a judgemental prick, nobody gives you a ♥♥♥♥ing break. It is pretty annoying after a while. Even people that are on your side, are ready to leave you out to dry for the smallest♥♥♥♥♥♥
4. The game does a bad job in some of the scenes. In one scene the controls suddenly change, with no warning. Who the ♥♥♥♥ thought that was ok. I died because of that garbage lol. Other scenes literally give you a choice and barely enough time to even ask the implications of what you are agreeing to. Then, suddenly the choice is made for you. What's up with that... I felt pretty salty.
5. A real lack of moments where you can just enjoy playing the game, there aren't enough of these. This isn't Game of Thrones, survival of the choice maker, this is a "tell" "Tale". So tell a ♥♥♥♥ing tale, don't just pack a story full of shallow choices, that constantly pretend to be important.
6. Some of the moments you choices NEED to be highlighted. In 1 situation, my only choice was to kill somebody, in the other, exact same situation, I could have spared the guy. How the ♥♥♥♥ could I have known that. This game doesn't make your choices clear at times, and it is really aggravating.
I think the idea was that the game was supposed to be harsh, just like the show. This doesn't translate to fun, nor does it translate to a meaningful ending. I was just salty as hell when the game ended.
7. The end the game tries to judge you. Hey Telltale, you can't judge your players when you hid choices, and barrage us with meaningless choices on top of that. You just can't...
That being said, if the game is 5 Dollars i.e. 75% off, I do recommend it for that price, but not for the full price. I did enjoy the first 2 parts, it took me until chapter 3 to realize though that the game wasn't going to let me enjoy it very much. Hopefully they don't ♥♥♥♥ up Season 2.
TL:DR: The game is definitely worth 5 dollars, but I hate to think how much better it could have been if it was done with proper pacing between, action, choices, and just enjoying the world. Don't buy it full price, it isn't worth that much.

So I made a very unfair review on the game straight off the bat and gave my first impressions. So I decided to remove that review since a lot of people were upset. So here is my quick breakdown of this game
Optimization: I run a GTX 970 AMD 4300 Quad Core and the game runs... Ok. Not AMAZING but Ok, I do go above 60fps and stay there for a bit of time and then the frames tend to drop to around 40-50. This is on High settings, either way I feel that it should be running a lot smoother than this but either way the port is OK.
Graphics: Awesome. Very nice to look at and very detailed. From the grass, trees, sun glare and even the character models. the only fault would be the water textures which are really odd looking. but overall it really is a beautiful game to look at.
Gameplay: Combat is instantly familier to the old Far Cry games and nothing has really changed much. There is a new beastmater mode where you can call apon a compainion to fight with you in the wild which is pretty cool. So far I have a White Wolf and I love sneaking into camps and ordering my wolf to take out 1 enemy then I jump on another.
Instead of guns its clubs and spears, And of course a bow. But combat overall in the game is fun but for anyone who is looking for something diffrent to the previous Far Cry games, you will be disappointed.
The World and Objectives: So the world is pretty big but sadly not as big as FC4 & FC3. The objectives are rather copy and paste from previous games. Bonfires act as signal towers to reveal new areas of the map, and enemy camps which you can take out and claim new land. There is a little meta game at the side which is to build your village. Pretty simplistic but still a fun little scavenge mission for you to run around and find the parts needed to build new structures.
Final Verdict: Far Cry Primal (PC) Still has the look and feel of a good Far Cry game. The combat is fun,the graphics are nice and the beastmaster system is fun to play around with and try out new beasts to fight along side you. But for some it will feel TOO familier to previous games, like a copy paste Far Cry with Spears and Clubs replacing Guns. Same with the objectives. And also to add that there is no co-op is really sad since that feature was a cool addition to FC4.
Score-7/10

I was pleased with my purchase and got many good hours out of GD but it boggles my mind how a game that, at least visually, exudes so much passion and attention to detail could have gotten the player experience just so darn WRONG.  This game is one of the best in the "dungeon crawler" genre I've seen but I feel sad saying that after tallying the number of poor design choices that went into the final product.
LIKES (in no particular order)
- KB+mouse ctrls not nerfed to be "fair" to console controls.  Controls are fully customizable but you'll be using your LMB a lot regardless.
- Graphics, art, color, themes, spaces, clutter.  Even the sourceless illumination that surrounds the PC seems oddly natural.
- I play w/o music because the ambient soundtrack is totally worth it.
- Very noticeable day-night cycle.  Detailed weather.  Different SoundFX for the type of terrain you walk upon (including puddles).
- Lore tidbits are delivered as lootable objects which give xp when read.
- Tool tips, when given (see Dislikes), are very detailed, legible, informative, and intelligently written.
- No weapon/gear durability.
- Gear buffs, mechanics, & cues are cool and powerful.  Spell/Ability VisFX are spectacular yet neither blinding nor obfuscatory.
- Your personal rift portal is persistent to wherever you last left it, until you log out.  Items left behind on the ground are still there when you come back through the rift.
- The Devotion constellations are inspiring, very reminiscent of Path of Exile and leagues cooler than Skyrim.  But it's all a bit bewildering and broad.  Could do well with some filters so the player could be astronomically guided to which constellations complement their build or combat style intentions.
- Enemies in a given area have a decent level range to try to scale to your PC's level on subsequent passes, continuing to give you xp while you execute the obligatory farming (see Dislikes).
- Crafting recipes are stupidly rare but at least they are unlocked for your entire account (incl. future characters) once found & read.
- Gear is exquisitely detailed and staggeringly varied, even junk gear, and it makes a big difference on your PC's appearance (which is best viewed from the Main Menu).
- Every class feels unique and powerful in its own way, but certain class combos work far better than others.
DISLIKES (from utterly intolerable to mildly annoying)
- Cloud saving is opt *out* rather than opt *in*; will trigger internet firewall until you assign an exception.
- No quicksave.  No Save button. No visual cue when a save is being performed; auto-saving is nerve wracking despite being reliable.
- This Dislike alone (see >>>>>) is what made me stop playing the game.  I was spending dozens of hours progressing expendable characters to level 31 (well into Act 2) so I could investigate every ability in their primary class just to try to *GUESS* at what classes I might like to turn into combos for permanent characters. >>>>> Only partial character respecs due to class Mastery points being non-refundable.  If you discover you dislike your secondary class, you better just reroll a new char.  If you decide in late game that you'd rather transfer your primary class investment to favor your secondary (or vice versa), too bad -- you better just reroll a new char.  I am trying to combat this by using local saves (not cloud) and making backups of my save files prior to spending level-up points in case I regret my allocations.
- Voice acting is horrible and only a few of the NPCs have voices - most are mutes (textual dialogue) - and even the voiced NPCs tend to only have the opening portions of their dialogue voiced; the remainder is text.  Intonations sound like low budget actors doing cold readings of a script.
- Waypoint pathing is unintelligent and simply doesn't work way too often.  Far easier to guide your PC by constantly holding LMB and aiming the cursor ahead of them as they move.  Segue:
- Ergonomic unfriendly over-reliance on the LMB, even after customizing controls.  Causes pain/cramps after play session of modest duration.
- No camera controls.  Camera auto-adjusts its angle with the ground based on zoom but your PC will frequently be obscured by terrain and foreground clutter.  The devs tried to minimize this by having roofs and treetops disappear but too often it's not enough.
- UI and tooltips:  Certain windows are poorly placed and can't be moved or rescaled.  Tooltips exist seemingly arbitrarily; many icons are not explained at all, even in the character window where info matters.  Nearly all icons are too small to discern (I was level 4 before I noticed the prompt to attend to level-up activities) and my resolution is only 1080p!  There is an icon which shows your computer's system time when you mouse over it instead of in-game time for day/night cycle immersion.  Clicking on the minimap does absolutely nothing; the buttons to adjust the minimap size are 1/3 distance across my screen from where the minimap is displayed.
- Generic items like currency, potions, etc. will be auto-looted.  Gear, however, can only be looted by clicking each individual object on the ground or by repeatedly pressing the Loot key.  There is a loot Filter button in the UI but that only filters what item labels are displayed and does *not* prevent your Loot key from picking up items beneath your filtered quality level.
- Inventory mgmt:  Game cannot intelligently sort inventory; I can usually find space for a couple extra items by manually moving items around.  When swapping items between inventory and equip slots, the formerly equipped item will find its own place in the inventory rather than trying to occupy the space you just vacated for it, thus interfering with sorting, segregation, or neighboring gear comparisons.  Starting inventory is very small and can only be expanded after doing certain quests.  Access to account storage (transfer items between char's) is granted only after completing the tutorial, by which time you're already level 6.  Some items (eg. purple background, including unique boss drops for crafting) cannot be placed into account storage, meaning you will soon find yourself using a single character to farm areas for crafting loot so he/she alone can craft.
- You are *expected* to farm.  The devs even say so, and proudly.  Any given area of the world does not grant enough xp from a single clearing for your PC to safely proceed into the next one or two areas.  Furthermore, gear stats are randomized rather than being specific to your current character's class combo.  Finding the right gear to match your PC's class combo, ability build, and your own playstyle can take a very long time indeed.  I ended up making mule characters just to hold onto gear that *might* be nominal for a current or future character.
- No PC aesthetic customization.  Male or a female: that's it.  Once your PC has some serious gear, it's hard to even distinguish gender.

Tropico 4 feels more or less like an expansion pack and patch for Tropico 3. The graphics, audio, and gameplay are almost entirely unchanged. That’s not really a bad thing though, because Tropico 3 was a great game and tempering with it too much would only result in ‘fan rage’. Tropico 4 does distinguish itself from its predecessor by bringing in lots of new ‘little’ features that can go unnoticed by those who have not played Tropico 3 in a long time. There are new building, new natural disasters, an improved diplomatic system, objectives (which get repetitive after a while), and many other little additions. Overall, if you liked Tropico 3 and are eager to build a new tropical paradise (or hell) with a host of new features and options, but want the game to feel and play very similarly, Tropico 4 is for you.

Excellent turn-based sci-fi game. Most of the time, it's tactical, squad-based combat, but there is a lovely degree of strategic decision-making when you're developing the X-COM home base, and deploying satellites and interceptors.
It has a learning curve that is a bit uncomfortably steep, but if you can get past that, there's a lot to love about this game.
I only have two real gripes about the game. One is that you, the player, can only ever play in a reactive manner. Except for the limited scenarios allowed by the linear campaign, you cannot lure aliens into ambushes, lay traps, or clear out areas proactively.
The other gripe is that the campaign is too short. Of course, this is also a compliment, since I'm essentially saying "I like the game so much, I want a longer campaign, please!"
Despite those two relatively minor issues, I can wholeheartedly recommend this game to anyone who likes turn-based games.

I waited two years to purchase Child of Light, waiting for it to be on sale. Finally I got my hands on this highly praised game, not actually really knowing exactly what it was. I only knew it had a neat art style and only recently found out it was a turn based combat RPG.
This game is surprisingly great. If you enjoy RPGs, I highly recommend it. Even at the full price of $14.99, it is well worth it.
The mechanics are both familiar and new - a very refreshing touch. I don't want to give away too much, but it is a game that makes the turn based combat even more strategic than most games of the same genre. You can interrupt enemies or be interrupted yourself, and you can use your little Firefly companion to slow enemies or aid your allies in and out of fights.
The music is fun, although for the most part you're listening to the same song over and over in different compositions. Thankfully the song is good, but I feel like I only walked away remembering the main song.
Every character in your party serves a purpose. At first I felt like I was just playing favorites, but different characters are very good against different enemies and you'll have an opportunity to utilize all of them. The example I can best give is your healer - for the most part, you won't need one if you're playing strategically well enough. But when the boss battles come around and the fights are more drawn out, you best believe you'll need one.
The characters are also all very diverse and interesting, and reasonably interesting. I wouldn't say they're terribly deep, but I have so far enjoyed them all.
My only complaint is that you can only use two characters in a fight at a time, out of your roster of 5 or 6. What's nice is that everyone benefits from the experience, which is definitely a bummer in other RPGs. But I would definitely have enjoyed fighting with three characters out at once, even if the enemies were a little tougher. However, your team is easily rotatable during a fight (much like Final Fantasy X for those that are familiar).
I would definitely give this game at least an 8 out of 10, maybe even a 9. I have yet to beat it, but wanted to give it a brief review part way through. I'll be sure to update this review once I finish the game.

A positive review yes, and a clearly positive one but not an unreservedly positive one.
So the good stuff - it's a nicely laid out game,helpful (but astoundingly brutal) tutorial, game development, new weapons as you go on and new enemy to use them on.  Unlike the old X - Com games it doesn't outstay its welcome - the original X Com in particular made you wait a very long time for the final mission.  Good ending - the final mission is very tough (particularly first time) but not unbeatable.  Graphics are good, view level is good.
The bad ?  In terms of development and kit this is a really weak game compared to earlier X Com games.  The general rule is Plasma > Lasers > Projectiles and that holds solid throughout the game.  The game also massively limits you on equipment - so you can have 1 grenade or additional armour but not both.  There is very limited variety in weapons and armour isn't hugely better.  It's turn based which is unrealistic - back when UFO Defense first came out computers couldn't handle the processing power necessary for simultaneous movement.  See the UFO series - Aftermath, Aftershock, and Afterlight for how these games play out in simultaneous action.  Your soldiers get assigned classes after their first promotion and each promotion thereafter gives a maximum choice of two for each new ability.  It also has the "we're at war so that justifies torturing the enemy to death" sensibility of a lot of American media ATM (cf "24" etc).  Are producers on a kickback from the NSA or the CIA ?
I don't want to over praise this game or over damn it.  As I write this review it's on sale at what is probably $5.00 US and at that price it's a bargain.  It's a good, competent, well produced game.  What drives my reservations is that the original game was mould breaking, memorable decades after release.  Here the producers aimed for a "B" and delivered a "B".  It's good.  But with simultaneous movement, the huge variety of weapons from the original X Com games, double the number of enemy, more complex characters and obituaries it could have been fantastic.

For years I looked at this game and was never sure whether I should buy it or not--because, judging by the screenshots, I couldn't quite tell exactly what kind of game The Banner Saga was. If you wonder the same thing, let me try to clear that up:
There are men and giants (Varls) in the game's world, and for a certain story-related reason you gotta keep moving all the time, so you spend the entire game going from one city to the next--and
You don't get to choose where you go, you just keep going where the game takes you. As you watch your caravan moving through those beautiful sceneries (and your limited supplies being consumed every day)
will pop up often. There are many of them, and the outcome of your choices include receiving new party members or losing them, same thing for supplies, getting into combat or not, gaining or losing caravaneers/fighters/varls (although they should, these don't really matter much... fighters/varls are only slightly useful during a small part of the game, and caravaneers never).
You can
during your travels to rest and regain moral (which boosts your characters' willpower in combat) or train (fight a normal combat, to get enough kills with your party members so they can level up). In cities, you can buy supply/items from the Market, and the main events will occur.
Ok, that's basically how the game goes. And then there's the
, of course.
You can choose up to 6 characters from your roster to form your party and enter combat. You position them around the battlefield before the actual fight starts, begin, kill all enemy units, win. You know how this goes. Ok. But here's what The Banner Saga does differently:
- Every unit has Strength and Armor. Strength is both your HP and Attack Power combined in a single attribute--you take damage, you cause less damage afterwards. Armor blocks damage on strength, and if the defender's Armor is higher than their attacker's Strength, only 1 point of damage can be inflicted on the defender's Strength, and the attacker gets -10% chance to hit per point of Armor the defender has above his, the attacker's, Strength. Damn, this sucks to explain in writing. Don't worry, it's not so complicated. But it
an interesting change from the usual formula.
(- To damage armor, you either need to use a skill or strike directly at it, using a separate attack/atribute, the armor-break, which never fails but is weaker than Strength/Direct Damage.)
- There are several different classes of characters, and each has only one active skill and a passive one. Some are better combined with others, some are good by themselves, some suck. But most of them involve some strategic thinking, and careful positioning.
- If one of your guys gets "killed," they are Injured afterwards, meaning you gotta Rest thrice until they're fully healed or they'll suffer (severe, I assume, because I never really tried it) penalties in combat.
Winning fights will grant you Renown points. These are used both to level up your characters (they need an X number of kills to be able to level up, and then renown points to actually upgrade) and to buy supplies/items in cities--so you gotta manage that... specially near the end of the game.
You can distribute the 2 attribute points you gain when level-upping over 5 different attributes:
- Armor: Reduces/Deflects incoming damage.
- Strength: Your HP and "Life-Damage."
- Willpower: Used for skills, adding extra damage to attacks, or moving further on the battlefield.
- "Whatever its name is:" An attribute that determines up to how many willpower-points you can use on a single movement/attack (if you have 2, you can walk +2 squares, or do +2 damage with an attack).
- Armor Break: Independent attack from your Strength one, determines how much damage you deal to an enemy's armor.
Finally, you can equip 1 item in each character, which you'll get from events or straight from the market.
Customization-wise you don't get a lot of room for maneuvre, true. 2 points per level up, fixed max-limit on each attribute, character level-cap of 5, 1 item and 1 skill on each character. It's far from being great, it could be much better, but... it's ok--other aspects of the game make up for it.
I'd say the
is where The Banner Saga really shines. It's not really
(pretty much anything imaginable has already been done by now) but it's still quite interesting, and told in an elegant way. The combat system, the role-playing aspects, the travelling, the art, the story, with their strong points and a few shortcomings all end up coming together to form a rather unique and very charming game. It is a pleasant experience, and I have no doubts about recommending it.
I just finished The Banner Saga (took me 16 hours) and I'd love to get into The Banner Saga 2 right away--I actually
to see where the story goes next, which is rather unusual for me. (But I gotta wait for a sale, because games cost twice as much where I live than they do in the US.)

tl;dr, a mediocre entry in a fairly solid franchise.
The Call of Juarez is a western based first person shooter; think cowboys, revolvers and such. This entry in the franchise took the franchise to a more modern time, centering on gangs and drugs. This upset many fans who immediately gave it a 0/100. While I personally believe the preceding and following games (Bound in Blood and Gunslinger) are far superior products, for the most part this game is  mediocre and not terrible.
Gameplay 7/10
At the heart of the game is fairly solid gameplay that plays like all the other entries in the Call of Juarez series. Weapons are powerful, but manageable, and the game ticks off all the positive points of a first person shooter. What brings the game down is driving sections or really anything that relies on your allies.
Characters/Story 2/10
Without a doubt the weakest part of this game is the characters you will be interacting with and the story you'll be interacting in. Your AI team will complain if you miss, complain if you play well, and factor into the non-sense story with secret agendas (Everyone is bad etc.). My least favorite parts of this game are the parts where you have to rely on your team mates for anything, as they are just terrible. Not only are they absolutely incompetent, but their one dimensional personalities are absolutely grating and their tacky voice acting is just awful.
Sound 8/10
Easily the strongest part of this game is the excellent sound design. Music is well written and fits the period well, with modern western metal mixing with a score. Firearms have a powerful sounding boom, and even the starter AK and pistol sounding like a cannon when it goes off.
Visuals 7/10
While I experienced no major pop-ups/glitches, the game is average for the course. Serviceable with occasional rendering delays.
Overall 24/40 or 60%. I personally would recommend skipping this game, for even with the solid sound engineering and gunplay, it's sequel (and prequel) do that without the irritating characters. If it goes on sale and you're a completion-ist, by all means go for it.

RATING (rated as if released in 2017)

V-Sync setting doesn't work, so the game performance could be as high as 200 fps before dropping to 30 fps on some scenes, making the visual looks choppy. The game requires Uplay, but I don't have problem with it. And unlike other Uplay games, this one have fully working Steam achievements.
Storytelling is good enough with good voice acting and cutscenes. There are 3 playable characters and each character have it's own story (although the missions still the same for all of them). Graphics obviously are outdated, but still look beautiful enough with every missions offers different environment. Music and sound effect are standard, nothing impressive. Control is tight, but the gameplay mechanic is just standard first-person shooter (no leaning, no parkour, etc) although it does have bullet time system. The car driving is bad though.
Beside the regular multiplayer match, this game also offers 3-players co-op campaign. But the way the game doesn't explain clearly how to do co-op campaign, so lots of people including me get confused at first. Basically, before each of the campaign mission, you will be in a "lobby mode" and this is the only place and time where you can invite friends to your game. If the connection break in the middle of a mission, you automatically enter single player mode and can't back into co-op mode until the mission is over and you're back in the "lobby mode".
The game base price is low enough these days, and with great story, co-op and multiplayer match, it definitely worth it.

As of writing this, episode 6 has yet to come out.
I went into this game with some level of apprehension due to some of its more lackluster reviews and overall not being a massive fan of the series in general. I'm glad I gave it a chance however, because it is a very good game. Not a great one, mind you, but a good game nonetheless. I'd wait for episode six to come out to judge it as a whole, but until then, here are some pros and cons.
Pros:
- Canon characters all have original voice acting and are well-written and excellently realized
- Twists and turns to match the ones seen in the show
- Pacing keeps you on your toes
- Not as grimdark as some reviewers make it seem. Yes, it's bloody and heartbreaking, but there are glimmers of hope and innocence mixed in there to balance it out
Cons:
- Watercolor style leads to some very frayed edges on both characters and objects, which can be distracting
- Some of the main characters are a little bit dull compared to others
- Dialogue has a tendency to get cut off at certain parts, but not enough to really impact the game (cut lines will still be visible as subtitles)
All in all, it's worth a look. I got invested in the main characters more easily than I'd thought, so if you have even the semblance of human empathy, you should too.

This is a really enjoyable ARPG.
There are a bunch of ways to customize what type of character you want to play. You start out with a choice between 6 classes, but you quickly gain the ability to multiclass, combining two classes into one. Each class has it's own tech tree, so there is some decision into how to best allocate points into this system. This gives weight to the choices you make in crafting a character to take on the enemies before you.
There is also this really neat secondary progression system. This involves activating shrines throughout the game and then allocating the points from that into a massive node system that gives both stat boosts and can modify your abilities. Again, since their are limited points to spend this is also another system that makes you feel like your point choices do matter. How you progress nodes and decide which routes to traverse places nodes in a loose heirarchy. This is probably one of my favorite things about this game.
Moving around the world is pretty simple. You unlock waypoints a long the way and you get a free castable waypoint. This free waypoint acts as a normal waypoint and not just a portal to town. As someone who likes to explore the whole map, I sometimes make descisions on how long to play based on going from one waypoint to another.
Overall, I feel this is a great game. I like playing ARPGs, and this is one of my go-to ones. If you enjoy ARPGs definitely check it out.

Divinity: Original Sin is a fantastic RPG set in a beautiful fantasy world. This game combines old school RPG and fantasy and wraps it with beautiful graphics and a brilliant story in such a way to create an excellent game that I have highly enjoyed. But, even though I had an amazing experience playing this game, I do think that the reviews on this game is overrated. There are some features that I disagree upon highly, and I found quite upsetting. That being said, I still recommend this game to the RPG lovers out there. Recommended, 8/10.
PROS:
-Massive content with many areas to explore and quests to do.
-Various character costumization possibilities.
-A beautiful and large explorable world. The story takes you to various places in the Rivellon, each with new areas to explore and its own side quests.
-Excellent plotline. You start your journey as Source Hunters sent to investigate a murder. But as you reveal conspiracies, your adventure turns to something far grander than you can imagine.
-Great and funny character interactions.
-Possibility to create your characters' own personality and traits.
-The ability to decide how the story will proceed.
-Brilliant combat system with tactics to imply and interactible environment.
-Challenging puzzles.
-An excellent sense of humor, with funny writing and dialogues along with various Easter Eggs.
CONS:
-As with many RPG games where you create your own character from scratch, you don't find yourself attached to your characters much, if at all. I for one, found myself more attached to the recruitable NPCs in my party (Jahan and Madora).
-Extremely repetitive NPC dialogue. NPCs that are not crucial to the plot or have no character depth repeat their dialogue
obnoxiously. Said once, fine. Twice, fine. Thrice? Okay. Fourth, please no. Fifth, no. Sixth? Fireballed.
-Almost no voice acting on the dialogue, resulting in a boring reading session of long walls of text said by the characters or NPCs.
-A part of the dialogue is negotiation. This system determines what the outcome of certain events are, based on the result of the negotiation. Now that would be awesome, if the entire thing didn't rely on a rock, paper, scissors system which involves almost no strategy. Using rock at the wrong time could cause an entire massacre or the death of your entire party. Go figure.
-The game starts out amazing, however towards the end of the game, there are considerably less side quests, or if there are any, they are related to or is a part of the main quest. Also the story started feeling a bit more rushed and slightly forced.
-The progression in this game (in my opinion) must be done in a certain order. There are places which you MUST NOT under any circumstances visit unless you are a certain level. Even though I am quite terrible at games, I can still see when a battle is utterly impossible to do, even though you are the same level as your enemies. My progress was halted at a certain part of the game, where I can't enter a single fight without being decimated. And so I had to spend too mch of my time grinding to get a level up. Once I was a single level higher than my opponents, I obliterated them easily.
OVERALL:
Loved it, liked it, hated it, furstrated by it. But still recommended. However, do get the Enchanced Edition instead. Some of the negative sides mentioned in this review is fixed or have been improved in the newer version of the game. It is far from perfect, but still an excellent and well thought out game that is rare and difficult to find these days. Worth your money, worth your time.

Cons (Although the cons are few, I have to elaborate to make my points clear... again, without spoilers.)

Writing is mediocre- I love the overall story and story elements (characters, setting, world building, character development, etc,) except, the dialogue and narrative are quite underwhelming. There's really one instance in which I thought the dialogue was pretty intense, but overall, it seems like the story is written for kids, despite the mature concepts. Short (took me about 15 hours)- Based off the size of the map I assumed it would be a relatively long game. However, I've only gotten through a small fraction of the world map before the campaign ended. I was surprised because I spent a lot of time browsing the map and was eager to discover and unravel its secrets, but I hardly discovered much of it. Left me fairly disappointed. I understand that there are various choices I could make throughout the game, and if I replay the game and make different choices, I would ended up with twice or three times the amount of hours, however, I would be trotting through the same paths on the world map. Only the narrative would branch out slightly different.

Abrupt ending- Still feels like I've only scratched the surface of what the story had to offer by the end of my fifteen hours. As if the game ended only after the first boss. The narrative begs you to purchase Banner Saga 2. A bit distasteful.
Overall, I would still recommend the game. Would be much better to pick-up the Banner Saga bundle, so you would be able to continue where you left off with part 2. At the time of writing this review, I haven't purchase Banner Saga 2, just wondering if I need to buy part 3 to further continue the segmented story, or will end with Banner Saga 2!?!... I don't want to be disappoint with an abrupt ending... again.

Banner Saga should be played for the aesthetics alone, but fortunately there's an intense and welcoming strategy RPG beneath the gorgeous 2D character artwork that graces the entire game. Set in a mythical Scandanavian-esque land where the sun has frozen in the sky and no longer sets, the gods have either destroyed themselves or left the world entirely, and an entire race of people known as the Varl are unable to reproduce and thus are slowly inching towards extinction, Banner Saga really homes in on just how overbearingly hopeless and dire the setting is. From the story (which is an escalation of bad to worse to WORST) to the setting to the dour nature of the characters to the very mechanics of the game itself, Banner Saga is an emotional slog from start to finish in the best possible manner.
Really, I mean that. Mechanically Banner Saga is a serviceable if slightly awkward grid based, turn based strategy RPG. There are classes with special abilities and you level up characters to increase their abilities. Alongside that, however, is a caravan system. As the story progresses, your main characters lead a caravan of survivors with them in hopes of escaping their impending doom from the coming of the enemy known only as the Dredge. This small bit of diet Oregon Trail where you have to make stops, placate traveler worries, stay supplied, and fight off attackers is what cements Banner Saga's harrowing aesthetic and is the real reason I love it. Every step you take and choice you decide upon can bring death or boon to these people that have turned to your main characters for help and guidance. Their struggle to survive isn't a footnote in the story, but front and center of every major movement on the world map. Now to be fair, the caravan does not do much for the combat portion of the game (something the sequel allegedly addresses), but even with that shortcoming its a brilliant way of building pathos in my opinion for your NPC followers.
So yes, in short its a good but not mind blowing strategy RPG that more than makes up for its missteps with a fantastically oppressive fantasy atmosphere and great character writing. Certainly reccommend!

This game is truly a thing of beauty. Being a long time Fire Emblem fan, this game instantly caught my eye. It falls into the same underused category of tactical RPG, and the handdrawn art is absolutely stunning.

The story is captivating and emotional, and unforgiving. The choices- though at time with random, unforseen consequences- have real effects; maybe not on the story itself but certainly on the journey through it. I would say it does an even better job at giving meaningful choices than telltale does. Rather than give the illusion of affecting the story, it surrounds you with a cast of deep and highly expendable characters.
the only complaint I have at this point is that sometimes the battlefield can get rather cluttered when there are many characters grouped together, but it has yet to cause me any real problems.
In my humble opinion, this is one of the overlooked games of the decade. If you are on the fence, do it.

This game is a very mixed bag.  It has nice graphics and sound.  I could have done without the mini-games.  They greatly exagerate the influence player decisions have over a largely linear plot.  The consequences of your decisions are largely cosmetic.  There are three main plotlines.  The Kings Landing plotline involves mostly canon characters from the series, and they captured these characters essences very well.  The need for this plotline to interweave with events from the series, also kept this plot line fairly immersive.  The Ironrath plotline, however, is the polar opposite.  The characters and plot events are predominantly their invention, and they fall terribly short of the bar set by George R. R. Martin.  The need to force things down a fairly linear path, while pretending to provide a wide range of choices, results in some incredibly immersion breaking Deus Ex Machina.  You can see how they are trying to capture the elements from the series that everyone loves--betrayal, suspense, and outright shock--but they just don't deliver.  The moment of the big reveal vis-a-vis the betrayal was so hamfisted and over-the-top that I first rolled my eyes when the cutscene drug on and on and then laughed out loud.  If you had a pulse, you knew what was coming the entire time and they took themselves way too seriously thinking there was the least bit of suspense built up.
tl;dr  The game engine is alright.  The design is alright.  The problem is their writers aren't good enough to play in George R. R. Martin's world, so unless you happen to pick specific choices, you will find yourself routine broken out of immersion and realize how very little influence you actually wield over the plot.  Considering the point of this game is supposed to be a gripping storyline and the world being reactive to player choices, I reluctantly have to give this a thumbs down.  I think their other games, where there will be a lower bar to clear, are likely to be worth checking out.

This game is a well developed asymmetric RTS game, featuring 3 vastly different factions.
The humans are network based, all the constructs are linked and the game-play is heavily advantagous for those who prefer the turtle approach thanks to the turrets and the compact design their playstyle promotes. They are also the only faction capable of teleporting 6 units at once to any spot on the map where you have visibility allowing you to quickly reinforce troops if needed. Their elite unit sends a laser beem straight forward in a line, damaging any enemy ground unit (imho. this is the weakest elite unit, but they have air-superiority anyways thanks to their airplanes and how small their storages for the airplanes are).
On the completely opposite side this this is the Goo, the playstyle of the goo focuses on aggressive hit-and-run tactics, their elite unit can cause serious havoc and is also able to climb any obstacle and destroy enemy buildings and units by simply being around them. They are very strong if coming in a pack and when lacking form they can devour an entire base by simply being there. That said, their forms (units) do have a lot of advantages such as range, ability to target airplanes and pure damage.
The goo has no structures, they are a fluid faction in every meaning of the word.
The Beta are most normal of the factions, specifically said by the Devs to be intentionally so for new players to get used to the game, but they are still very strong and definitively a force to be reckoned with. Their elite unit is a walking production facility that sends out miniature nuclear bombs and is able to attack any close-range enemies by having units mounted ontop of it. This is one of the big strengths of the Beta, some of your units can mount walls and the elite unit, allowing you to create a strong permimiter that is very hard to break through.
If you then decide to go on the offensive, the elite unit will help you take down most resistance, having what is probably the strongest of the elite units in the game.
As for the campaign, it is very well made, although, it is a bit short, allowing you to get used to each of the factions while also deliviring a great story that they have confirmed will be expanded.
Note: It will come through DLC.
Now, on a more negative note, while humans are strong, they often feel unflexible as you might not be able to expand anywhere due to it not always going so well building uphil and some areas are just blocked off for building. For the Beta, that just means you place it somewhere else, for humans, it means stop.
Also, the game, at least so far, allows for only up to 4 players, meaning you can't even have a 3v3 with one of each faction on each side.
PLAY IT

I don't usually reveiw games, but I felt obligated to to protect RTS fans from dropping $50 on the boring that is Grey Goo.  My problem with this game, in a nutshell. is the blandness.  For example, there aren't particularly few units; it's just that the units the game has all feel very generic and similar.  The beta all have walkers with guns.  The goo have spiders or blobs that fire blobs.  The humans have hover drones with guns (a couple lasers).  And the units feel very similar not jsut in appearance, but in gameplay.  It doesn't seem to make much of a difference whether I build a few tanks or mroe smaller units; they all move slowly and kill the enemy slowly.  Also, the AI is terrible.  On the hardest difficult, it's almost no challenge at all with even teams, and even with uneven teams it's not too difficult.  The campaign is bland and uninteresting, much like the units and the world.  The game has nice graphics, runs smoothly, and has polish.  But it has no character.  It's supposed to harken back to the golden age of RTS, but it's just so bland.  Command & Conquer (in its various incarnations) always had flaws, but it had plenty of character.  There were flamethrowers, machineguns, shotguns, lasers, cannons, artillery, missiles, superweapons, and unique factions.  Every unit felt cool, and varied greatly in appearance, function, speed, damage, damage type, armor, etc.  Every unit looked was unique.  Grey Goo is jsut a pile of similar units doing similar things, and if you have more units, you win.  There's only one resource that has basically no explanation or interest.  There's really no reason to come back and paly thsi game more than a few times, because every match feels exactly the same.  Not recommended.

Man, what a game.
As a title clearly inspired by classic JRPG's, this game manages to infuse the classic feel of exploring, battling, and progression into a lovely, whismical world that I couldn't get enough of.  Exploring the settings was always lovely and rewarding, since you gain the ability to fly relatively early and every location is filled to the brim with chests, loot and stat boosts. The story being told is simple and concise, but hit all the right notes for me, especially going in expecting a fairytale story (With some hidden depth if you collect the confessions and decipher their meaning from the verse). The battles were a blast, with essentially an upgraded version of Final Fantasy 7 being the main forcus, where attacks must be correctly timed to interrupt and stagger your opponent. It doesn't get old with the pace you go through enemies, and none of the bosses were insurmountable with the right strategy (The most I had to retry a boss was 4 times, I believe). The soundtrack is resonant and stunning, the characters enjoyable. The ending is a little shakey but not enough to derail the experience. This game is a must for those looking for a new spin on the classic JRPG formula.

This could be a fantastic game. So many of the elements are done really well. Research and base management are cool. The upgrade options and squad management are interesting mechanics. The pacing is really well done and everything feels like part of its own universe that's dynamic and lived in.
Unfortunately the game has two major shortcomings in my opinion. First, in a game full of choices, nothing seems particularly meaningful and you're never really introduced to the consequences of say, selling a bunch of alien corpses instead of keeping them for research. A lot of things just feel like extra buttons to press for more fluff. A lot of it is quite enjoyable and rewarding fluff, but fluff nonetheless.
The second, and much worse issue, is the tactical combat. There are a number of issues I find personally annoying and a couple that I feel really break the game to the point of unplayability. RNG plays far too big of a role in combat. Hit and miss chances don't feel at all intuitive and seem like the product of really lazy math and coding work on the part of the developers. Unloading an LMG clip at a hovering drone out of cover 5 ft away and totally missing not only seems unrealistic, but spraying all the bullets 2 ft to the left in a perfectly straight line seems really clunky in a modern game. For a game that seems to want to reward flanking, coordination, and aggressive play, the way that enemy aliens spawn and interact with the squad seems unnecessary and often bizarre. Making a good positioning decision might activate one of two alien squads and leave you totally outnumbered. The incredibly limiting 2 actions/turn instead of an action point system often means your soldiers seem totally incapable of doing anything significant during their turn. A completel overhaul of the tactical combat is what is needed to make this a truly modern, functional game.

Very worthy succesor to the original X-Com game. As in that one, your job is to save mankind from alien invaiders. You'll start with a smaller squad and train your way up to your 6 person team. Their is a good variety of skills needed to be successful: Sniper, Heavy, Assault, and Support. (Don't skimp on the Support--that's where your field medics are, and they will save many a life on the battle field. They're also not too bad for offense, but there are better options for that). You will take pride in successful missions, and scratch your head as to what went wrong with the unsuccessful ones.
Missions vary from clearing downed alien ships to saving citizens in alien abductions, to clearing alien terrorization attacks, to invading alien bases. The difficulty level ramps up as your capabilities do. The player is challenged without being overwhelmed.
There is also the game within the game of resource allocation and management. There is a constant tug of war between Research and Engineering. You'll also have to build additional facilities and satelltes.
The game is fun, but it can also be a bummer when you lose a highly experienced and trained soldier to an Elite Muton or other alien.
The game will prod you to complete it--and look forward to X-Com 2.
