Including offline time at this point i've put in about 10 hours towards the game. At first I was a little hesitant, as it wasn't what I had expected and it seemed super slow almost to the point of being turned off. But I stuck it out and i'm really glad that I did...
Negative first. Foremost I must say that this is truly the only negative thing that I have to say at all. I want more information on character building BEFORE I make my character. I was not originally aware that you must save skill points to further upgrade those skills later - this was a major mistake and i was forced to reset my game so as not to of wasted any skill points nonchalantly. Secondly, I think more emphasis should be put on how important it is to make your party varied in the elemental arts as well as the NEED for a ranged character. So far the best group i've come up with is a mage and a thief/mage (splitting elemental types between them), an archer and a high defense, high constituition knight of sorts. Variety in your skills is MANDO! And make your characters masters of ONE or TWO set of skills. Do not make jack of all trades - it will weaken your part as a whole.
COMBAT:
The turn based combat delivered on a high level and surpassed the high standards that I had for it. I truly enjoy ALL aspects of combat from ranged skills and melee / rogue type abilities to the more jaw dropping elemental magics that intertwine with the local environment. For example, I electrocuted an Orc Shaman while he was standing in a puddle. It just so happens that his two body guards were standing in the same puddle. BAM! All three instantly damaged and shocked, losing a turn. Not to mention being able to cast water spells near a teammate to do damage to your enemies but put out the flames burning your partners shoulders to a crisp.
WORLD:
I haven't explored much yet but everything that I've seen so far has been put together very well. From item placement and decorations to broad scale placement of dungeons, changing weather and variety of landscapes.
NPCS:
I normally skip through that NPC's say in other games. The usual B.S. filler type material that just get irritating - BUT in this game I've become more involved in the storyline and actually enjoy the bickering within the group as well as the diversity in NPC personalities. A lot of effort was put in to making the storyline full with a hint of sassy.
SIDE NOTE:
I am a bit OCD and a horder in games... and sometimes it ruins games for me because I spend too much time collecting things. Example would be, in Skyrim and Fallout 3. I spent hours upon hours just making sure that 'THIS' chest in my home had only Elvish equipment or Laser weapons. While 'THIS' chest had only Ebony gear or Plasma weapons. I like to seperate things so that I can easily go back and look for things later, plus it becomes a center of pride for myself in game. Odd? Maybe. But this game allows me to feed my sorter desires by giving me back packs and a "home" to store my people and valuables. I have backpacks for every different type of item and with the "pack mule" talent, its that much easier... I spent 2 out of my 10 hours just organizing and reoganizing. This may not be a selling point for some of you but for those who know what I'm saying... Yup, smile wide. :-D
10/10 - So Far.

Hyperdimension Neptunia Re;Birth 1 is an odd name for a game. But seeing as it’s a JRPG that’s been ported over to English language and to PC, I think it gets a pass. Some things simply don’t make sense in English.
Anyway, I really very much enjoyed Hyperdimension Neptunia. I found it to be a fun, light hearted, self aware game with interesting, well fleshed out, endearing characters and a interesting deep combat system. The Lore surrounding the game was especially intriguing; a world where the culture surrounds video games, and the goddesses of their respective nations battle each other to win shares in the console war. It’s an unsubtle allegory for the competition between different video game platforms and Hyperdimension Neptunia revels in this.
When I look back on this game (I finished it some months ago, only just got round to writing this), the main things that stand out to me are the characters and their interactions with one another, and the combat system. I’ll start with combat. The combat is based on classic turn based JRPG combat, if you have some familiarity with JRPG’s its not particularly difficult to pick up. The combat isn’t amazingly intuitive if  you’re new to these games, I’d say there certainly was a bit of a learning curve to understanding the different elements to combat but once you start to get it after a few fights it begins to come together. It guides you through the basic elements of combat in the first few battles. The combat is turn based and has a lot of strategic depth. Even outside of battle; Who you choose to open combat, how you choose to pair up warriors on the field, how  you position them, order of combat, which weapons you equip, armor, healing items, status effects, move sets and so much more. There really is a lot you can do to optimise combat and I loved this aspect of it. There really is a lot of substance and depth to combat and this isn’t something I expected from a game that comes across as otherwise very light hearted and almost satirical.
My first playthrough took me about 45 odd hours to complete, which I felt was great. Story is a good length, and of good depth. The story was a lot of fun to follow. The game can essentially be split into two components; the visual novel aspect (where the story/character development unfolds) and the free-roam/combat aspect (where you fight, level up and do video game-y things). Each component is very important, as it is very much a story driven game. I loved how the characters interacted and developed, and how the lore of Gameindustri was revealed. I also loved the random asides where you can see what the inhabitants of Gameindustri have to say. For the most part, these citizens don’t have anything to do with the story, but their random quips, tidbits and chatter can be amusing to read, and generally helps bring the world to life. To me, it shows that Gameindustri is a world full of other citizens just going about their business.
The different dungeons are pretty basic in terms of design, but navigation isn’t the core component of the game. You’ve just got to seek out the various monsters to battle, or item to complete your quest. Graphics wise, there’s not too much to say. They’re not amazing, but they’re good enough. I don’t think the point of the game was to be hyper realistic in looks, to me, it looks fine. I don’t think I’ve ever played a JRPG for its graphics. But if I were to say there was a clear weakness, it could look better in terms of high resolution assets.
Initial looks at this game may garner rolls of eyes at the cliché goddesses in revealing outfits, and general tropes you see in anime and JRPG’s but Hyperdimension Neptunia is very much aware of this and pokes fun at the genre every now and then. But in the light of the depth of combat and how your character progresses, I would say this is an example of ‘never judge a book by its cover’. Or perhaps I’m just biased.
I really enjoyed the game sound track, and felt it fit the game well. The voice acting is superb, and really helps in constructing personalities for each character. I think the voice actress for Mako Mankanshoku (from Kill la Kill) did the voice for Compa (or at least they sounds identitical). So production values are definitely there. I was a fan of the art direction of the game. The ideas for monsters were original, and the 2D backdrops for the various locations are gorgeous. A lot of care went into character design and world building and I can really appreciate this.
Controls wise – definitely play this with a controller. I played this title with an xbox 360 controller and it worked flawlessly. Keyboard/mouse, is fine but for games like this where combat is turn based precision isn’t key – you have the luxury of taking your time, and the comfort a controller affords can go a long way. Technically, the game worked without a hitch. As mentioned controls are fine, framerates were good (I haven’t benchmarked it, but I’m sure it wasn’t capped at 30FPS), as a PC port I would say it’s been done pretty well.
After a long day of work, lying in bed to play this was a real joy. Fun, light hearted story, strategic combat, interesting characters, replayability. The game took me by surprise by how well it was constructed and I’ll be sure to revisit it at some time in future.

This could be a fantastic game. So many of the elements are done really well. Research and base management are cool. The upgrade options and squad management are interesting mechanics. The pacing is really well done and everything feels like part of its own universe that's dynamic and lived in.
Unfortunately the game has two major shortcomings in my opinion. First, in a game full of choices, nothing seems particularly meaningful and you're never really introduced to the consequences of say, selling a bunch of alien corpses instead of keeping them for research. A lot of things just feel like extra buttons to press for more fluff. A lot of it is quite enjoyable and rewarding fluff, but fluff nonetheless.
The second, and much worse issue, is the tactical combat. There are a number of issues I find personally annoying and a couple that I feel really break the game to the point of unplayability. RNG plays far too big of a role in combat. Hit and miss chances don't feel at all intuitive and seem like the product of really lazy math and coding work on the part of the developers. Unloading an LMG clip at a hovering drone out of cover 5 ft away and totally missing not only seems unrealistic, but spraying all the bullets 2 ft to the left in a perfectly straight line seems really clunky in a modern game. For a game that seems to want to reward flanking, coordination, and aggressive play, the way that enemy aliens spawn and interact with the squad seems unnecessary and often bizarre. Making a good positioning decision might activate one of two alien squads and leave you totally outnumbered. The incredibly limiting 2 actions/turn instead of an action point system often means your soldiers seem totally incapable of doing anything significant during their turn. A completel overhaul of the tactical combat is what is needed to make this a truly modern, functional game.

Don't be fooled by the simplistic visage of Biodrone Battle.  Underneath its  surface there are a gauntlet of challenging levels and smart enemies to test your skill.
PROS:
+ The "morphing" mechanic-adds another element to the twich shooting mechanics of the typical top-down shooter, and makes into more of a tactical affair.  Tactical in the sense that you get 3 slots to fill with drones that have different strengths and weaknesses, which can be employed in different situations.  It also presents more than one way to advance through levels, as you are limited by the amount of energy and must mix fighting and morphing to survive.  Gameplay with each drone takes on a different tone, as the special powers of each as well as their speed, range, and attack power make
+ The challenge-This game will test your reflexes and ability to play offense and defense at the same time.  Many enemies are relentless (see below), and often a single mistake will prove fatal.  This in turn makes every victory immensely gratifying, as it is not simply a matter of figuring out the exploits and taking advantage, but being faster and smarter than the machine, which falls right in line with the game's narrative.
+ The A.I.--Enemy drones react like human players.  They don't sit still or wander into traps, and it takes some cleverness on the part of the player to dupe an enemy drone into a corner.  Enemies also utilize their strengths--a long range Sniper will evade and create distance where it can pick you off from offscreen, a Maintenance drone will repair its stronger comerades and skate away before you can destroy it.  Enemy drones know when they're losing--they'll retreat, recharge, regroup, and attack again with strength.
+ Classic gameplay--Underneath all the fancy bloom effects and explosions, it's still a classic shooter at its core.  The non-linear level design allows you to go to higher levels and attempt to morph into high-level bots, but this of course comes with the risk of one-shot kills.  The risk-reward factor is seen throughout the action and decision making.
CONS:
-As mentioned, the game is hard.  Unless you're of legendary hand-eye-coordination, be prepared for multiple retries of the same level.  Be prepared to destroy every enemy except one on a tough level, only to be destroyed by the last enemy because your hand slipped off the mouse, and having to do it all again.  The difficulty isn't necessarily punishing, but may scare away gamers looking for a casual experience.

Pong and Mortal Kombat combined in to the single greatest fighting game ever. There's 6 characters, a secret 7th character serving as the final boss of challenge mode, all of them with balanced movesets and the like.
RAPTOR: 15 year old baseball dude. He doesn't jump too high, but he has a smaller hitbox and can wall-jump. His special allows him to hit the ball two times in a row, completely remove or even add hit-lag (hit-lag is a mechanic where when someone hits the ball, the game pauses while the shot is being "charged up"), and change the direction of the ball to wherever he wants.
SWITCH: Robot skater dude. He can skate across the walls, leading to some interesting shenanigans. His special is confusing, as you need to perform it by pressing the jump button in the air, not while hitting the ball. It allows him to remove all hit lag, and it will automatically direct the ball to the bottom-right of the screen.
CANDYMAN: Mutated insane dude. He has no special ability related to movement, although, he has the highest base jump of any player (he is able to reach the ceiling of all maps with a single jump). His special allows the ball to pass through walls, useful for tricking the enemy.
SONATA: Chick with a giant beatbox hammer. She can double jump, but each jump is much shorter than normal. Her special allows her to "hit" the ball as it's traveling, changing the trajectory of the ball as it goes. Very useful in "Strikers" mode.
LATCH: Robot alligator dude. He can climb on the walls, and hit the ball while on the walls (balls to the wall!). His special makes him eat the ball, and spit it back out in a different direction. You can also "bunt" the ball out of your mouth by pressing the bunt button while executing the special move.
DICE: Monk with a ping-pong paddle. He has an extremely short jump, but if you crouch and then jump while crouching, your jump height can rival Candyman. His special allows him to telepathically move the ball in a different direction, and it will continue to worm it's way across the field until the ball hits a corner, at which point it will spasmatically bounce across the stage.
SPOILERS!
DOOMBOX: A giant boombox demon. Serving as the final boss of challenge mode, he has a much larger health pool than the previous challengers, but has a much larger hitbox to compensate. His special allows him to double the speed of the ball while he's hitting it, and change it's trajectory to almost any direction. Hitting the ball will also fill double the normal amount of the charge bar (meaning instead of 1 bar, it fills 2). Unlike other characters, when he gets hit, he doesn't fall off stage, and instead gets angrier and angrier until you hit him one final time.

Review Based on Episodes 1-5
Where do I start with this game? Well first off because I get into it lets go ahead and establish that if you're not up to date on HBO's Game of Thrones then you probably shouldn't play this. It will spoil a lot of things. If you don't ever plan on watching it and you want this game, watch it. You'll understand so much.
First of it's a Tell Tale Game, so of course it's story driven. And damn if it's not a good story. It's follows loyal bannermen of the Starks, House Forrester. Their lord has died, they're going through some rough times. On top of their people being hungry and them having no army they're under threat from the White Hills who want to take their precious iron wood. And the white hills are backed by the Boltons which are the Wardens of the north. The choices I had to make were making me feel all kinds of ways. And some of them were actually really hard. Don't let anyone fool you and say your choices don't matter in a Telltale game, because they do. The dialouge you get means a lot, the way the characters act means a lot. Of course some things will probably happen, but still the dialouge is what makes it.
It's like the TV Show, many things are happening at once. You'll follow Gared, Ethan, Rodrik, Mira, and Asher. All of which are the children of Lord Forrester with the exception of Gared; he was a squire. It's just astonishing how so much is going on and it all ties together. Mira is in Kings Landing pulling favors almost like Sansa Stark. Asher is in Essos, Lord Ethan and Rodrik are both in Ironrath, home of the Forresters, and Gared gets sent to the wall.
The voice acting is terrific. They even brought in actors from the show to voice their characters on the game. If that isn't great I don't know what is. The graphics are the same as Telltale's Walking Dead, nothing much but still a nice feel. Combat for me was a little tricky because I had a ported PS4 controller and I didn't know any xbox buttons, but other than that it's alright. It's not a fighting game of course so don't expect to fight and have fun.
I really don't see many flaws in this game. It's an amazing story driven game and if you enjoy Game of Thrones I would tell you to seriously consider picking it up.
tl;dr
Great story driven game, not too many flaws.

Review written after 2 hours of play. Doubt I'll finish this one.
First, the bad: it uses Uplay which means that Steam family sharing for this won't work. My wife won't be able to play this at all unless she buys a copy. That's annoying because I didn't care for the game, but she found it interesting. In that regard, it was a bit of a waste of money.
I really liked the art style - it's very well presented. The game is told in a series of rhymes, which are a little less well presented. Some of the rhymes are clumsy and forced. Many of them are forced to the extend that there are nowhere near the same amount of syllables on the rhyming lines - the rhythm and flow of the poetry is way off. It grated on me, but "A for effort" I guess. Putting that aside, the story (so far) seems interesting: something about 19th century Austria and a girl named Aurora who may (or may not) be dead. I suppose I'd have to finish the game to know what's actually going on.
But I won't be finishing because the main mechanic here is JRPG-style turn-based combat, which I loathe. I've wasted hours of my early gaming years on this, and I can think of no worse way to waste my gaming hours than repeatedly and slowly choosing what action I want to do for N characters on every battle turn. This is not for me. If it's for you, you'll probably have a great time.
So given that I hate the central gameplay mechanic, am annoyed with Uplay killing family sharing, and twitch my eye at the neat-but-flawed rhyming twist: not recommended.
All of these things are somewhat me-specific so if you don't mind them, I imagine you'll have a much more enjoyable time.

A surprisingly fun and pretty well done game. I wasn't expecting much when I heard that the devs of Dead Island were going to make Dead Island but with more parkour, but it seems like they really out-did themselves and made a fun game with lots of stuff in it. (I liked Dead Island btw)
The parkour works very well. The combat is better, though the zombies are less dismember-y than the ones from Dead Island sadly. I played through the whole game on the hardest mode (Before an even harder mode came out) which was punishing and frustrating. I tried it one difficulty lower, and it was almost too easy in comparison. Then when The Following came out, the Hardcore difficulty is even more punishing and frustrating than the hard difficulty.
The main story is meh. Kyle Crane, the main character, is a bit of a doofus. Gets himself bit, makes enemies with most powerful guy in the country, gets his friends killed, etc. At least they didn't add a Dead Rising esque time limit in which you had to get zombie medicine. The story for The Following expansion was much better in my opinion. It kind of took a lot of notes from Farcry 3/4 and made a cool mountain-y place to drive around in with your new buggy. I love the culty stuff and I enjoyed it a lot more than generic bad guy VS good guy main story.
Overall it is a very fun game that is definitely worth a play, especially if you have friends to do co-op with. Stealthing and running from super zombies at night is an awesome experience, and it's the same with driving from super zombies at night in your buggy. The devs did a good job on this game. The different costumes you can wear are fun too.

I recommend you research the game extensively before making a purchase.
If you are looking for a fast paced, tactile, flashy, rip roaring, hack and slash adventure game set in a beautiful fantasy world, this game is amazing, and cheap to boot.
If you are looking for an MMO that you can heavily invest in (both monetarily and emotionally) for years to come, this is one of the worst games you will ever lay a finger on.
If you are looking for an RPG, look elsewhere, this isn't an RPG in spite of the tags above.
Everything that makes this game an MMORPG, it utterly fails at, but if you want an incredibly pretty online Dynasty Warriors, this is your game.
Firstly, there are basically no RPG elements in this game .  An RPG means that there are play elements within the game that allow you to control the role of your character, hence the R in RPG.  These elements can be creating a build, building a party, or choosing a path in a branching story.
BDO has absolutely none of that, you can choose from one of several classes and customize their look to the umpteenth degree, but this has no inidividual effect on gameplay.  Every class plays through the exact same story and the only choices it gives you affect some alignment meter, which in the end has no effect on the completly linear storyline.
Similarly, you cannot choose build and playstyle at all, all characters of the same class have the exact same abilities once fully leveled, there are no talent trees or skill customizatoin, the only customization that affects gameplay is your choice of gear stats, and the only time you will be different from every other character is while leveling up.
Every single MMO element is done in the worst way possible, either for the sake of laziness, fault of poor game design, or most common, flat out unfiltered unending greed on part of the publisher.
PvP, isn’t PvP, it’s PvEvsPvE.  It all runs on PvE gear, and gear differentation is so massive and rigid and difficult to obtain that every matchup is decided wholly and completely by gear score.  This game has no PvP that actually tests your skill against another player, only your ability to grind and get lucky drops or amass cash.
The only group (massive) content are open world bosses that are completed by strafing and spamming like a bunch of mindless lemmings.  Any other open world is handled easily by yourself.  No dungeons or raids or anything of the sort.  There is some sort of Guild vs Guild mode but I never got in to it, but I highly doubt it alone can be the saving grace of this games horrible excuse for group content.
The economy, if you enjoy playing that end of MMOs, is in complete shambles and has been since launch.  And the developers do not care to the slightest degree because it pushes people towards the cash shop by freezing up all resources that could be used to earn anything in the game beside gold and stats.  There are also basically no rewards, you fight for a pitiful chance at higher and better stats.  All new skins since launch (over three years) have been in the cash shop, for $30-40 each, oh and they are bound to the character, not the account.  Remember what I said about greed?  Yeah...
The publisher, is in my opinion the most dishonest to ever walk the earth.  There are a million examples showing this, but I only need one.
Shortly after launch, some outfits bugged out to hide peoples names, preventing those people from being reported and subject to both support and the games karma system that discourages Pking excessively.  In response to this, the publishers put a flare in the cash shop which would reveal these players names.  That’s right, they literally put a bug fix in the store and charged people for it, and that isn’t even the only time they’ve done so.  The flare has since been moved to being purchased with in game currency, but other examples of this exact same dishonesty exist and are still only available in the cash shop.
Nonetheless, I bought the game after researching it and deciding how I would play it.  If you want a fun beat-em-up for $10 ($6 on sale, I got it on sale and I would recommend waiting), and can enjoy the game without being tempted to give these dishonest schills another dime, pick it up and enjoy yourself.
EDIT: As people have pointed out, there are RP elements in the economy, to that I say, there are still no RP elements in this game.
Why?  There is no "play" to the economy in this game.
As I already said, and as they are choosing to ignore to be nitpicky and selective with their facts: the only thing you can buy is higher and more varying stats.  Because the only outfits you can craft are locked behind mats that very rarely pass hands thanks to the games complete and utter economic freeze.  And anything else, is in the cash shop for $30-40.
There cannot be role "play" elements to what there is no "play" to in the first place.\
Technically, stuff in the cash shop can be bought for ingame currency if someone buys it with real cash and lists it on the marketplace, but the developers decide the listing price, not the player, and the developers force a listing price that isn't profitable, so that they never pass hands, and are probably one of the biggest roots of the games economic freeze.  There are cash shop items that have not been listed in literally years, and some which have been listed only a few hundred times in the three years the game has been out.  I myself have not seen a single outfit listed in the entire time I've played this game.
Or in short, no, you cannot just get whatever you want from the marketplace, that is a flat out lie.

I played this originally on the PSVita, and I like the series quite a bit in spite of its flaws (more on that shortly). Figured I'd try the PC port before HDN:Re2 came out so I could see if the port was acceptable.
It was not.

Oh my goodness, this port.... Sound glitches, graphics hiccups, crashes, freezes, save corruption..... the laundry list is extensive. And all this AFTER waiting for two patches just to get past the main menu without a CTD. I have seen some shoddy ports, but this one is in the ranking for worst without breaking a sweat. Moreover, if you experience issues at this point you're screwed, since the publisher has long since moved on to other ports. It's a very poor showing, and I think it says a lot about the publisher.
Sadly, this reflects poorly on a niche game with a hard enough time selling itself in the first place.
You play as cute anime girls in various levels of revealing clothing beating the crap out of an array of enemies based on or ripped directly from gaming and otaku culture (it took a minute to register what 2X Rainbow Man represented...). The world represents the gaming industry (it's called Gameindustri ffs), with the scantily-clad anime girls being consoles or the games and franchises played on them.
In tone and direction, this game shines. The entire thing is tongue-in-cheek and self-referential almost to a fault. This is a game targeted at a very specific demographic, and they pull no punches in delivering. The narrative is a bit weak, but the lore, dialogue and art direction are excellent and compliment each other well.
Innovative, interesting or even challenging outside of a few inexplicable difficulty spikes.
If you like grind, this is your game. If you like killing the same mob 10k+ times for a single rare drop, this is your game. If you enjoy the feeling of safety you get from only being exposed to 4-6 different maps to explore with different mob spawns and loot drops, this is your game.
HDN:Re1 is JRPG to the core. It takes all of the oldest and most tired mechanics from classic RPGs, and then makes NO ATTEMPT WHATSOEVER to put its own spin on things. This is easily its failing, and the reason I think it hasn't seen wider popularity. Simply put, the gameplay is NOT FUN. You will have to grind (not optional) for hours just to clear some bosses, and this artificial padding of the game's length hurts it further.
All in all, this is one of the few times that I would recommend cheating, if only to bypass the dozens of hours of required grind and simply get through the story. Scream blasphemy if you must, but it makes the game as a whole much more enjoyable and fresh when you aren't in the same area killing a slightly stronger, palette-swapped version of an enemy you fought 8 dungeons ago.

Far Cry: Primal is AWESOME so far! Firstly, from a technical point of view, the game is running great: a steady 60 FPS with no dips on a 970 (and on my other rig with a Titan X) at ultra preset. The graphics look good, a small upgrade over Far Cry 4, and for those with monitors in a 16:10 ratio, GOOD NEWS: they FINALLY support it correctly - no more black bars at the top and bottom!
From a gameplay perspective controls feel smooth, combat is tight, and the mission setup is very good. The game seems to focus heavily on hunting, at least so far, and that's fun to me. Getting an animal companion is fun as well. I already tamed a dire wolf and commanding him to kill an unwitting Udam is just a blast. I also appreciate that there are some animals you just don't mess with right away or you WILL die. It adds an element of "holy crap, run" to the game. The AI is spot on for the cavemen (Udam) as well. They aren't terrribly smart, but they ARE cavemen, so it works with the immersion. Crafting has been heavily refined from Far Cry 4 and it feels far more useful this time around. Building a village and raising a population also feels highly rewarding becuase as the population grows and the village becomes more complex, they will actually work for you and produce much needed goods that translate to weapon upgrades and items.
Finally, one of the most impressive aspects of the game for me so far is the use of sounds. It is completely immersive and makes me feel like I am indeed right in the middle of the wilds during the stone age. Everything from the crackling of wood as it burns, to the sounds of birds in the not-so-far distance, to the cry of a lone wolf in the far distance, to the sound of wild dogs gnawing on a fresh kill just brings you into the world and keeps you there.
Anyway, all in all, GREAT so far! Get it, play it, enjoy it! Right now I'd say it's an 8.5/10 and if the story turns out to be good: 9/10.

So since everyone is talking about the greatness that is D:OS I'd like to talk about a few of its faults. Don't get me wrong, it's a great game but even great games have problems.
The slow start:
Divinity has this problem where, after a lengthy but necessary tutorial section, the game opens up into a city with a rather tedious and laborious amount of dialogue and an underwhelming investigation sequence. Not that the dialogue isn't well written, but the pacing of the game goes from a very fast tempo to a complete and utter grinding halt. If the game had started slower this might never have been an issue, but when you begin your game with a hectic amount of combat and then suddenly stop two hours in and force the player through another two to three hours of exposition dump rather than exploring the narrative more naturally you can ease in a sense of boredom. It also hampers the replability viability. Often I've said: wow I really want to play through this game again and see what I've missed! But those first six hours are just dreadful.
The lack of direction:
An open ended story is amazing. Divinity has this ability to allow you to create your own stories by not holding your hand and directing you from point A to B. You can bypass entire story points by arriving at certain areas out of order and create your own narrative. However, this is not entirely to Divinity's credit. Due to a sincere lack of direction you can often stumble into higher level baddies than you can possibly handle that will completely murder your party, and even if you do succeed there's just more of them lying in wait around the corner. Often times quest givers will give a very vague sense of direction and this results in a very vague sense of "well I know it's around this approximate area somewhere OH GOD DEATH KNIGHTS!"
The Lack of Interesting Mechanics introduced later on:
Divinity's use of enviroments enabling combonations of certain spells is fantastic, in the early game when it still matters. By about level twelve or so it's pretty safe to ignore it due to the complete lack of spells that support this combination behavior. Often times it's just better to drop a rock and fireball the area over and over again because of how powerful that combination is against every group of enemy. It's generally completely unecessary to create fog and then electrecute it to shock enemies. The combinations that, to an experience player, could turn losing fights into landslides early on cease to have much of an impact as spells just become giant blasts rather than interesting enviromental spells.
Conclusion:
Divinity is an amazing game. It has an engaging story, interesting and challenging combat system, and phenomenal characterization. Does it have it's errors? Sure, but that doesn't mean it still isn't one of the greatest RPGs ever made. I am a huge fan of the classic isometric RPGs and Divinity was such a phenomenal take on the genre that I can't help but appreciate it. However, due to it's overwhelming awesomeness every flaw stands out like a sore thumb and jerks you out of the experience. Such is the nature of great video games.
Ultimate verdict: 9/10

Take it from an old gamer who's played all the big ARPG's.  Grim dawn nails it.  The folks at Crate definitely have their collective finger on the pulse of the ARPG fan, (and the jilted Diablo fans).
What does Grim Dawn do that's worth your hard earned money?
***Character Depth***
- With six masteries granting FIFTEEN class types, three good old fashioned stat points and TEN damage types and all corresponding defense types, Grim Dawn allows for deep customization and diversity in builds.  The well implemented dual-class system allowing you to combine two masteries into one class with all accompanying skills available to you, makes the possibilities many.  Add to that stat points granted every level and the possibilities grow.  Then, to top it off,  an extremely powerful "devotion" system granting huge, game-changing damage and/or defense bonuses and unique skills above and beyond your class selections.  You can build DPS focused killing machines, insurmountable tanks or bizarre mixed builds where your imagination is the limit.  Throw gear into the mix and it's perfection.
Graphics: 10/10 - Phenomenal when maxed out.  Nails the dark, grittiness we crave and diversifies into just stunningly beautiful landscapes with day/night changes just adding to the artful beauty.  You can literally see the effort that was put into getting everything just right.
Sound: 9/10 - Very atmospheric.  Satisfying explosions and weapon noises.  Monsters are spot on and voices are fitting.  One monster in particular sounds like he's whispering in your ear when he dies.  Just great.
Music: 8/10 - What's there is just fantastic and original.  Nevertheless, I find there are too few tracks and the game could do with just a few more.  But just a nitpick.
Game play: 10/10 - Spot on.  Slick and intuitive.
Just BUY IT NOW!

The Call of Juarez series is one I'd definitely recommend giving a go. Every game in the series is distinct and has its own identity, which is something I really appreciate. I'll avoid going into too much detail about the rest here, but they're all a good time with individual strengths and weaknesses that form a satisfying whole.
Unfortunately, the defining characteristic of game number three, The Cartel, is that it's an utter shambles. The classic Wild West setting of the previous games was ditched for a staggeringly uninspired modern-day Los Angeles/Mexico counterpart, which is exactly as appealing as it sounds (i.e. not at all). Likewise, the hole left by the entertaining and likeable cast of the first game and Bound in Blood (like legendary gunslinger Ray McCall) is filled with some of the flattest caricatures to ever spout tired one-liners. Once all the character and charm of Call of Juarez has been stripped away, what you're left with is a medicore first-person shooter that is an absolute chore in single-player and probably not much better in the new co-op mode. Solo players be warned: your AI partners are incompetent, and they will make no effort to hide it, though they will continually belittle your performance as you carry them for the game's entire duration.
Lackluster AI, boring gunplay, dull visuals and an uninteresting plot combine for eight hours of unmitigated tedium. The only saving grace is the way the game ends, which could have been a pretty cool conclusion to a much better game, but is of course held back here by being part of The Cartel. In retrospect it's good that the series had one final outing after this, though The Cartel remains a testament to how quickly good games can go bad. It's almost worth playing just for that lesson, though I'd suggest you try any of the others over this rubbish.

Double Action (created by Vino) is a spiritual successor to The Specialists, a Half-Life 1 mod which saught to recreate The Matrix in a GoldSRC environment. With the inclusion of a stunt button, you could dive, slide and flip your way around a low-res version of the one and only Lobby. After a few years of updates to the engine, it was rendered nigh unplayable, and extremely buggy. And then along came Double Action, aiming to be 'the most stylish game ever created,' and bringing about some of the most fun I've had in a video game to date.
We all love over-the-top action movies, even if some of us would never admit it. Watching somebody leap through several panes of glass firing a high caliber assault rifle is just plain exciting. Getting to act out these scenes of violence and death defying acts is a few steps from Nirvana, and Double Action is the metaphorical Buddha of this cocaine coated dream.
While it is hosted on the source engine, (meaning it has its hiccups here and there,) Double Action is a solid, crazy fast and absolutely bonkers experience. Movement is quick, whether you're jogging, sliding, or diving. The gunplay isn't the most refined you can find in a game, but feels nice and tight and translates well from first to third person. The scoring system, which is entirely based upon style, offers even more incentive to throw yourself around the environment. The pool of default maps is not massive, but quality shines brightly over quantity. Mastery of stunting is rewarded by fluid movement around arenas which are a nice mix of claustrophobic corridors and wide open deathboxes.
At the end of the day, Double Action is just a source mod. However, it is incredibly clear that years of time, effort, and care have been pumped into it. Sure, it may be a bit rough around the edges, but you
won't hear me complaining while I'm powersliding and firing two high powered handguns into the air.

, third installment into
's CoJ series, seems like the misfit child of the bunch.  It's not as good as
; it's not a game to be taken seriously or to carry any real expectations for, whether you're a fan of this developer or not.  As action shooters go, it's definitely more of the same.  It did provide me a brief bit of fun & includes a potentially decent cooperative experience.
The
series &
are by
too, so if you liked those you'll be at home with The Cartel, which looks and feels similar in a number of ways.  Level design, enemy AI, linearity of missions, visuals/art, side tasks involving item collection, gun aiming & handling, driving & playable characters with unique personalities & combat characteristics all felt familiar.  What you shouldn't expect much of in The Cartel is homage to the CoJ series itself, 'cuz there ain't much.  You do get to play as a modern day McCall, dual wield revolvers, take a brief jaunt through a familiar place & hear a schpeel from a guy who's obsessed with the treasure of Juarez.  None of that gives this a real connection to the rest of the series, however.  In my opinion it lacks the flair that makes the others entertaining.
By 2011 standards The Cartel is decent, & I'd say by today's (2015) it's mediocre but worthy of purchase on the cheap.  I got it on sale and can't imagine anyone doing otherwise, by now.  It's a very brief campaign consisting of 15 missions; took me about 7 hours to finish on Medium difficulty, with the AI companions rather than real teammates.
The AI teammates worked out well enough, although I regrettably didn't play it with anyone else & thus missed out on what looks like a fun three player co-op.  You can breach rooms together, provide covering fire allowing allies to advance & also engage in some friendly competition via the Secret Agenda feature (each law enforcement agent has an ulterior motive & they each mistrust each other, so you try to catch the other two red-handed while being sneaky & accomplishing your own hidden objective unnoticed).
I tried doing some multiplayer action online but was unable to find anyone for the Cops vs. Criminals mode or the online campaign mode.

The entire game is pretty much a sensationalized portrayal of the Mexican Drug War.  Each character & most of the dialogue was cliche.  I feel like I'm describing a Hollywood blockbuster film.
I'm not saying I wouldn't recommend
to anyone; it was okay.  It just doesn't merit recommendation unless you're looking for a quick bit of shoot-em-up action & don't have better alternatives - or if you're a big fan of this dev & just crave that experience.

Here's the deal... I really like this game. It's rare for a developer to not only make an RTS, but also a good story with it. Full of likeable characters, a great soundtrack and fun gameplay.
Some possible spoilers below.
Pros:
1.) Solid, varied gameplay. All 3 sides are very different. Humanity, The Beta, and the Goo.
2.) The Story is well thought out, with bits of backstory that really add to the experience. It leave me wanting more. I really hope there will be a sequel.
3.) Mutliplayer is fun and fast paced. Not for people who want to turtle or play defensive games however. Expect most matches to end within 30-45 minutes, or possibly faster.
4.) It's an RTS in an era that has forgotten this once great genre. I love supporting anyone willing to make a AAA RTS.
It's not without it's issues however. The Multiplayer is very limited, just 1v1 or 2v2. The reason for this given by the developer is performance, which I can believe. However, I'd rather the developer just leave multiplayer open for the future, when more players have hardware capable of running the game well. I believe this is the chief reason for the game not being more successful than it is.
Cons:
1.) Only 1v1 or 2v2. This limits the appeal of the multiplayer greatly. I really hope the dev opens up 3v3 and 4v4.
2.) Micromanagement can be excessive. This is really a problem with most RTS games however.
3.) Late game is dominated by high end units, like Epic units and heavy tank units. This tends to also be a weakness in RTS games. I would like to see tech 1 units stay useful in late game.
4.) Story ends on a cliffhanger... I'm afraid that I won't get the whole story if we don't get a sequel.
Overall, I really like this game and want more. It's easily accessible to Starcraft 2 and Command and Conquer fans, and has as enjoyable a story as SC2.
8.5/10. 9/10 if you don't care about 3v3 and 4v4 multiplayer.

I love Dying Light. Like the Dead Island series before it, this game has gameplay I adore. Crafting weapon mods! Spectacular graphics! Physics model that sends enemies flying!
But Dying Light has problems. Some severe ones. The PC controls are a simple port of the console version. Vague, squishy, and with a hell of a lag, the controls make playing on PC ridiculously imprecise.
But the gameplay! That's what made me fall in love in the first place with this game. Pasting on a parkour mechanic seemed like a great idea. Maybe, but it IS one that takes an infuriatingly long time to adapt to on PC because console port.
Where Dying Light really falls apart is in the end game. Not only is one of your primary tools removed for an absurd reason ("exhausted" yet able to climb up the outside of a 30-story building, ffs?), an entirely new game mechanic is introduced
If just one of these things had happened it might have been forgivable. But both? Frack these game design choices.
If you've already bought it, just don't play the end game and you'll be perfectly happy. If you haven't, I cannot recommend it.

After playing - and liking - Gunslinger, I wanted to get into more of the Call of Juarez series that I missed. The Cartel was the natural next entry to try because other than Gunslinger (2013) it was the most recent (2011).
It's awful.
I can only imagine that ads for this game claimed it was "high-octane" or contained "explosive firefights" and while there is the occasional fun moment, for the most part it is a boring, bland affair.
Despite some cool concepts and set pieces, the graphics are subpar, even given when it came out. The animations are choppy, textures low-res and flat. The skyboxes are particularly grainy, like they were JPG compressed.
The sound is even worse, with horribly repetitive dialogue delivered by some of the worst voice acting I've ever heard in a game.
The menus are especially painful because of a terrible font choice and the fact that the mouse speed there is not affected by the sensitivity setting. It crawls across the screen and turns anything you want to do in a menu into a belabored chore.
And the story is a jumbled mess of cliches.
Where a run-of-the-mill FPS normally shines when it falls flat in other areas is the gameplay. As you might expect, that's not the case here. The enemies are predictable and easy to outmaneuver even on the highest difficulty. The weapons and controls are very standard. And there are driving sections that are more frustrating and annoying than they have any right to be.
Unlike all the other games in the series this one takes place in modern times instead of the Wild West. The only thing it has in common with a Call of Juarez game is the name and a concentration mode. It's like they were trying to boost sales on a project they knew would fail by randomly attaching it to this pre-existing franchise.
So if you want to play a Call of Juarez game, you're better off with Gunslinger. If you want a better FPS from 2011, then go play Homefront.

This game has average ratings from many critics. To a certain extent, they're right. The Cartel doesn't add many new ingredients to the mix and the graphics engine is certainly not as advanced as Techland claimed it to be. Also, I feel that the game could have been a sandbox. The level of freedom of the game is very restricted to the story, which attempts to make players live in the moment, before it is either shattered by someone's death or a turn of events that brings down the villains involved, once and for all. In this respect, The Cartel is unfinished.
However, the level designs are very good. Both the main characters and the antagonists are foul mouthed and not the most likable people you're ever going to meet, but they make entertaining adversaries and the camaraderie between Ben and his collegues is admirable. The gun physics are a little off and the AI isn't very challenging, but the Cartel does manage to create an atmospheric adventure, with believeable environments and gaudy villains.
If only Techland had invested a little more money or taken a little more time to polish the Cartel, it would have been as notable as its predecessors. However, there is enough for fans of the series and of law enforecement to enjoy. The chance to play as the other protagonists offers some replay value, but only after leaving the game to let the memories of a somewhat caged environment have faded.

Do you love Game of Thrones/A Song of Ice and Fire? Hey, me too! Wouldn't you love to immerse yourself in the lore and roleplay as characters in said world, especially since your GoT D&D group has conflicting schedules and can never meet... damn you guys! *shakes fist* Ahem, anyway, if you want those things, this may or may not be the game for you. Telltale got the tone right and the voice actors are wonderful, but that's about it.
You play as members of House Forrester, who are basically Bargin Bin Starks. They have the potential to be interesting, but too often I catch many similarities between Forrester and Stark (Lady Forrester being the biggest offender, she's practically Carbon Copy Catelyn. Ryon is like Rickon, who is the extra kid that serves no purose. And there's Gared Tuttle, who reminds me a lot of Jon Snow.) Of them all, I enjoyed playing as Gared, Ethan, and, to a lesser extent, Mira.
My biggest issue with Mira's story is that half the time she seems smart and the other half she's made to be stupid. I get that she's no Varys or Littlefinger, but the girl has no sense of tact or wit. She discovers something and two seconds later she's forced to confront someone with said discovery and does so with complete lack of subtlety. For example,
As with any game rich in choices, sometimes I found myself wishing for better options. Like at a certain point as Mira, you can either lie or tell the truth to your friend's possible betrothed about her family, but there is no third neutral option (and the possible third option is handwaved as 'tell me the truth, no waffling', even though it IS true and you're forced to choose between honesty and duplicity). The game is littered with situations where I wondered why I didn't get an (in my opinion) obvious option that fits the world, especially having read the books/watched the show.
But what does that matter? Absolutely nothing, because your choices don't matter.
The list goes on and on. All your choices are basically window dressing and (as of episode 5) don't affect anything in the long run. It's 'the illusion of choice', not real choice. It is possible for a game to force you to play out the main story 'on rails', but still have your choices be impactful, but GoT is not one of those games.
The story has the potential to be good. Unfortunately, House Forrester is constantly shoved into the dirt again and again, no matter what you do. Everything seems hopeless and bleak and made me a bit depressed. Small victories would be nice and keep the player optimistic that House Forrester will pull through. As of right now, it seems like we're being led to a deus ex machina resolution that will be pulled out of thin air minutes before the end. I'm not cool with that.

Because of that, cars, gangs and customization feels pointless. Why would you want to drive when running is so much faster?
You also have gliding, super jump, super strength, stomp, mind-control, ice and heat attacks. It also makes the game really easy as you can one punch kill enemies although guns are still required for certain enemies. Luckily, you can play music outside of your car (like WATCH_DOGS) since the developers considered that cars will be obsolete in the game and it may feel more like an iTunes playlist rather than a radio station (like WATCH_DOGS) but there's actually a great number of songs in this game (unlike WATCH_DOGS).
The graphics isn't much of an improvement over the third game and it actually recycles the environments of its predecessor but you wouldn't care less as the game is so much fun. The voice-acting in this game is superb, especially from J. B. Blanc who plays Zinyak. The superpower gimmick is actually a great addition to the franchise and the open-world genre.
It may not replicate the gangsta root of the previous games like you might expect but how many times are we going to get a gangsta-themed open-world game (like Grand Theft Auto and Sleeping Dogs) before it gets old? I'm not sure if it'll work the second time but superpowers is the new Saints Row and I like it a lot.

Take it from an old gamer who's played all the big ARPG's.  Grim dawn nails it.  The folks at Crate definitely have their collective finger on the pulse of the ARPG fan, (and the jilted Diablo fans).
What does Grim Dawn do that's worth your hard earned money?
***Character Depth***
- With six masteries granting FIFTEEN class types, three good old fashioned stat points and TEN damage types and all corresponding defense types, Grim Dawn allows for deep customization and diversity in builds.  The well implemented dual-class system allowing you to combine two masteries into one class with all accompanying skills available to you, makes the possibilities many.  Add to that stat points granted every level and the possibilities grow.  Then, to top it off,  an extremely powerful "devotion" system granting huge, game-changing damage and/or defense bonuses and unique skills above and beyond your class selections.  You can build DPS focused killing machines, insurmountable tanks or bizarre mixed builds where your imagination is the limit.  Throw gear into the mix and it's perfection.
Graphics: 10/10 - Phenomenal when maxed out.  Nails the dark, grittiness we crave and diversifies into just stunningly beautiful landscapes with day/night changes just adding to the artful beauty.  You can literally see the effort that was put into getting everything just right.
Sound: 9/10 - Very atmospheric.  Satisfying explosions and weapon noises.  Monsters are spot on and voices are fitting.  One monster in particular sounds like he's whispering in your ear when he dies.  Just great.
Music: 8/10 - What's there is just fantastic and original.  Nevertheless, I find there are too few tracks and the game could do with just a few more.  But just a nitpick.
Game play: 10/10 - Spot on.  Slick and intuitive.
Just BUY IT NOW!

I learned about this game when I was searching for something similar to the excellent Ori and the Blind Forest. And yes, there are some similarities, but each of these two games give you quite a different experience.
The best thing on Child of Light is its artistic style. "Watercolor" graphics are beautiful, original and together with excellent soundtrack create a dark atmosphere. A dark atmosphere that can really evoke some creepy emotions... just by watching and listening... I was quite surprised.
The way how dialogues work and how the story is narrated is (again) original, but it took some time before I could get used to it. Child of light, a dark fairy tale where every text is in rhyme. Well, why not, but sometimes it seemed a little forced and "not-much-fitting", but I enjoyed it nevertheless.
The gameplay is based on constant switching between non-combat exploration mode and turn-based combat mode. Combat style reminded me of Heroes of Might and Magic series with a little real-time enhancement. At first I was worried that it will soon get repetitive and boring, but somehow I managed to complete the whole game without getting bored (well, maybe there were few locations with unnecessarily too much encounters, but nothing I couldn't handle...). Combat remained entertaining mainly because it was challenging from beginning to the end (I played on hardest difficulty) and I really had to think about my combat strategy. I would only point out the "switch party" move, which seems to be quite OP when you have more and more party members. I would appreciate some usage limit, timeline penalty, whatever to make it better balanced.
The game offers pleasing experience, although there are some things that could have been done better - like always. Also I think the game isn't for everyone. Sometimes it requires time and patience from the player, for example during exploration, searching for secrets, crafting gems and equiping them, investing skill points, etc.
Do I recommend? Well, maybe not for a full price, but when it comes to the sales. Then yes. I recommend. Because there are not many games which can give you such a unique experience like this fairy tale full of action!

Nice game, a refreshing change from SC2 (the most dominant RTS lately).
It's kinda simple, with only 1 resource type, no need to build "house"-like types (like pylons etc, you always start at 200 max) and mostly small maps, the games are short, semi-fast paced which is both positive and negative.
Also, you do not need to make typical harvesters, which, along with the reasons mentioned above, make this game kinda casual.
Each race can only make about 10 different units + 1 super unit, which is kinda low/average but like any other rts games, the weakest units will not get used.
In this game, early game is everything, since in the words of the devs: "Focuses on large scale decision making", means that snowballing is more effective, micro is less required and the person who gets the better headstart through better build order, unit splitting and tactical decision making will likely win.
The biggest upside to this game is the Goo race, which is the most unique form of RTS playstyle i have ever seen.
You do not have a typical base, instead you have a Mother Goo which can split into units or other Mother Goo, allowing for exponantial growth (until you hit the cap) allowing you to quickly take over defensive opponents.
The biggest need for change is the upgrade system. About 50% of the upgrades are typically worthless because of how specific they are. the other 50% are only sometimes taken, depending on the situation.
Overall I'd give this game a 7.5/10 hoping it will grow to have more features, more maps, more units etc etc.

This is one of the most charming and engaging games I've played in a long time. You explore the world in a sidescrolling platform style, but with some mechanics that are pretty unique to this story. (For example, you can control both the main character and a mote of light as well. Both have abilities and unique ways of interacting with the environment.)
There are simple environmental puzzles, which makes it interesting without being particularly over challenging.
When you interact with villains, the action becomes very Japanese roleplay game turn based play but with an emphasis on timing and a few other twists. I felt like I was engaging with something new, rather than simply playing in a certain known style due to these alterations. It was great!
You can collect characters for your team, explore the environment, fly, and influence character builds in meaningful ways with interesting skill trees and add on items.
The storyline is like a child's fairy tale, with all the innocent sing song quality and the underlying heavy themes.
I found the play to be pretty stress relieving, as I could take time in combat to really think through what I wanted to do. I could also go back to earlier areas and just explore with low level foes for a bit, if I wanted to game without thinking much about it. After you finish the game, that is also an option. You can go back and revisit and explore areas, just for the joy of doing it.
Visually, the game is just beyond stunning and the attention to detail (like the cursor being able to make the character's hair swish about in different ways) were suprising and charming.
The only criticism I have of the game is the somewhat abrupt and rushed feel to the end. I would have appreciated a bit smoother transition.
All in all, one of my favorite games in recent years.

In Short: If you like goofy anime stories, adorable characters, highly-energized music, and don't mind being subjected to unnecessarily bouncing breasts and the occasional panty shot, you will love this game. :3
In Long:
* The battle system is where the majority of the gameplay is and is kinda like a cross between Chrono Trigger's position-based system and Final Fantasy X's turn-based character ordering system. It works really well and is easy to understand.
* There IS grinding in the early game, but not in the later game, unless you want all of the achievements, in which case... you've got a MASSIVE amount of grinding ahead of you.
* Many of the areas you travel through are reused multiple times with slight alterations. Kinda dumb given how well everything else was done in this game. :P
* The game never outright crosses the fan-service line, but do expect to see bouncing breasts for no really good reason in several story segments, as well as panty shots from some of the playable characters when ther perform certain moves. (Or in the case of Compa, just by winning a battle with her scoring the final hit.)
* Nothing changes in New Game +. Defeating bosses you otherwise couldn't defeat before as a story point doesn't alter the story or give you anything special. In fact, certain unlockable things can be missed simply by going past the chapter they're obtained in, meaning to unlock all the areas and plans for those areas will require either a perfect and well-planned first run, or multiple runs.
* There's a TON of game mechanics to learn, but thankfully they're all very straightforward.
* Most people recommend playing with a gamepad, as many of the prompts are built around that. I play with a keyboard by setting up a dual-handed approach with one hand on the AWDS keys and the other on the numeric keypad. Works well but required a lot of tweaking of the default controls. :P

The only negative things I can write about this game are:
1. The first few hours are INCREDIBLY boring
2. Attacks can be a bit temperamental due a slight lag on the toolbar which means you can sometimes end up moving instead of attacking
3. How to use repair, craft and other skills is not always intuitive
However, these are very minor gripes.  Once you get up to about level four the game starts to blossom, and once you learn how to craft and blacksmith then then the diversity of the game really starts to shine through.
The gameworld is beautiful, but not at the expense of gameplay.  There are more than a few developers that could take a leaf out of the book of the makers of D:OS.  Combat is a joy and the difficulty is pitched really well.  The satisfaction at beating a group of enemies a couple of levels higher than you is high.  The fights are not easy and demand that you understand how the combat mechanics work and that the environment is as much a part of the battle as spells and weapons.  Role playing is pretty good and your decisions, both within the party and externally, really seem to make a difference.
The enhanced edition is coming out soon and I can't wait :)

Divinity: Original Sin is turn-based rpg with most important feature in my opinion multiplayer the game up to 4 players. And it's not pvp or some multiplayer scenario, it's the actual game played in multiplayer. It works, and it's really fun.
Game contains lots of dialogue and interactive combat. Combat is turn-based and environment matters. If it's raining, burning effects wont stay, and if there's ice on the ground, you can slip on it. Things like that make the game more tactical and can sometimes create really unfair, but often fun results.
Story is affected by the choices player(s) make, to some extent. You can deal with encounters in plenty of different ways, for example peacefully negotiate, or straight up murder everyone. Literally. You can kill almost everyone in the game if you want, town npc's and such.
You can develop your character in many ways. Be either a melee warrior, stealthy rogue, mage out of many different spell schools or ranger. You're also free to combine these stereotypes and play hybrid class.
It's great, fun game with tongue-in-cheek attitude. I wholeheartedly recommend the game to anyone wanting a turn-based rpg action.
----------------------
Then, my personal negative sides of the game:
My personal negative side of the game is that combat-wise pure damage is way stronger than any kind of tanking. While this is true in most rpg games in general, it still saddens me that there's great possibilities for some kind of tanking setup but it's much harder to play, or rather pure damage dealer party is so much more stronger that it's bit silly.
Another negativity is that stealing is way too easy. So easy that it becomes second nature to just steal everything even bit valuable, and that can break the game more or less. At least I felt that I became bit too overpowered because I could just steal everything, sell, buy things like bonus skill point books. If you get caught while stealing, you can get attacked and so on, but it's very easy to avoid that happening. Stealing doesn't affect morality of the characters in any way besides one dialogue option between the players, and even then you can say that stealing is wrong and steal stuff anyway.
Besides these two things, the game is exceptionally good and wholeheartedly recommended!

The developers have put a lot of work into the campaign and the graphics, voice actors, and concept is really interesting. That being said, the mechanics are what you'd expect from a 90's RTS.  I always enjoyed playing Red Alert and Warcraft so I thought it would be great change of pace from some of the faster paced modern ones, turns out not really. I tried to like the game, played a couple campaign missions and a skirmish. Within the two hours I had it, it really felt like I understood all that the game had to offer.

This is one of the most charming and engaging games I've played in a long time. You explore the world in a sidescrolling platform style, but with some mechanics that are pretty unique to this story. (For example, you can control both the main character and a mote of light as well. Both have abilities and unique ways of interacting with the environment.)
There are simple environmental puzzles, which makes it interesting without being particularly over challenging.
When you interact with villains, the action becomes very Japanese roleplay game turn based play but with an emphasis on timing and a few other twists. I felt like I was engaging with something new, rather than simply playing in a certain known style due to these alterations. It was great!
You can collect characters for your team, explore the environment, fly, and influence character builds in meaningful ways with interesting skill trees and add on items.
The storyline is like a child's fairy tale, with all the innocent sing song quality and the underlying heavy themes.
I found the play to be pretty stress relieving, as I could take time in combat to really think through what I wanted to do. I could also go back to earlier areas and just explore with low level foes for a bit, if I wanted to game without thinking much about it. After you finish the game, that is also an option. You can go back and revisit and explore areas, just for the joy of doing it.
Visually, the game is just beyond stunning and the attention to detail (like the cursor being able to make the character's hair swish about in different ways) were suprising and charming.
The only criticism I have of the game is the somewhat abrupt and rushed feel to the end. I would have appreciated a bit smoother transition.
All in all, one of my favorite games in recent years.

Glitchy, poorly paced, and with attrociously frustrating driving mechanics, this game really is the low point of the Call of Juarez series.
I generally try not to hate on games too hard, but in this case, they completely threw the concept of interesting, identifiable, and compelling characters right out the window. One of the player characters, Guerra, seems like he's got a bit of a story behind him (DEA agent that's a compulsive gambler and selling drugs on the side to try to pay off his debt), but it's never really fleshed out. The female characters name eludes me because she was so one dimensional it wasn't even worth remembering who she was.
The game starts out with you "meeting" all of these characters in a high speed car chase in which you have no earthly idea what you're doing or why you're shooting at these various cars. Get used to that feeling, because this game rarely stops to explain what the hell is going on. After that you're catapulted into a world of tracking down the leader of a drug cartel after a DEA building is bombed (the connection between the two is nebulous at best), and protecting a girl who is thought to have witnessed the bombing... and also one of the playable characters survived and witnessed the bombing but is somehow expendable enough to simply throw into a massive, violent war against drugs rather than being temporarily relieved of duty and examined by psychiatrists to handle the mental trauma. Also, he's suspected of being the bomber, so... send him out on police work? Sure.
What follows is a half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥attempt at making an action game that allows you to sling enough lead to supply a Chinese paint factory for a month while also tossing all of the rules of common sense straight out the window in favor of cheap "thrills". Oh, and the driving sequences... God save us all from the driving sequences... The driving mechanic is so poorly designed and implimented that it's far more frustrating than cool, and unfortunately you're almost ALWAYS the driver. And as for the guns, they all feel approximately the same, apart from different skins and rates of fire.
The storyline is approximately 6.5 hours in length, but manages to feel like it's dragging on for an eternity (see GTA V for the opposite effect, where it lasts 40+ hours and still feels like it's not enough), having overstayed its welcome within the first 45 minutes.
With all of these terrible features, there were a few redeeming qualities. Personally, I felt like the bullet time mechanic was well done and well integrated, the music was quite well directed to fit the situation, and I do like seeing games branching out and police games starting to trickle onto the market. I also feel like some of the voice acting was done competently, and the graphics were, for the time, moderately good.
Unfortunately, in my opinion, the few things it did right weren't enough to save this honker, and so I give it a thumbs down. Buy it only if it goes on sale for $2 and you need something to waste a few hours with.

I went into this game without knowing too much about it. All I knew really was that it had that "Diablo-esque" vibe to it and that's exactly what I wanted. "Why not play Diablo then?" you might be asking, and the honest truth is I didn't see it in the Steam store. That is in no way a diss to this game but I wanted an immersive world with similar gameplay elements from what I knew  Diablo would deliver.
What can I tell you about Grim Dawn? It delivers that and so much more. I'm deeply immersed in the lore and I honestly feel bad when I make a decision that leads to the deaths of folks just trying to survive in the world.
Rather then a pros and cons section I think I'll just include a "things you need to know" type deal and without any spoilers of course.
Starting off, this game is very lore heavy. You'll find tidbits about pre and post "Grim Dawn" Cairn(the game world) ALL OVER. Enemies will drop pieces of lore. You'll find journal entries throughout the landscape telling you about various aspects from character motivations to heart pulling tales about the denizens as the "Grim Dawn" is happening.
Most of all the game doesn't hold your hand with tutorials. They're always available through the Codex window and, you'll get the occasional quick tip about something you're doing in the top left corner of the game. Which is quick and you may miss if it you're not paying too close attention to that side of the screen. Which, unless you have minions, you have no need to look in that corner anyways. So pay attention to any tips the loading screen offers or you'll miss something important but I'll get into that later.
The UI is very simplified, Health and Energy(some call it Mana, MP, SP, etc. this game just calls it energy) above some quick slots. A mini-map will be at the top right(you can turn it off for more immersion or if you truly want to lose yourself in the game map. And you have an active quest list right below that. That's all thats on your screen other than, like I said earlier, if you have Minions, then their HP/Energy is on the top right. You can UI Scale as well in the options to make these even less noticeable, not to mention you can toggle the map and quests for even less on the screen.
Oh yeah I forgot to mention that the game's difficulty is in the top left as well. I suppose to let you know what difficulty you're playing on currently(you can adjust it from the main menu). This is one of those things I wish I knew about when starting the game. In games like these, I'm used to there being one difficulty and as you beat the game harder difficulties become unlocked. This game has two starting difficulties: Normal and Veteran. Me not knowing the exact difference of them I started on Normal because who wants to die on the first enemy because he's way too high level for you? But during one of the game's loading screens, I read that Normal is more geared towards players who have never played an ARPG before. I imediately switched to Veteran and IMEDIATELY noticed the difference. Enemies scale with you pretty well.     I haven't gone into an area and felt like it was just a grind(unless I was doing it on purpose) to get through the area and on to the next one. I honestly enjoy the fact that I can just die if I'm careless: from traps to the harder "boss" and "hero" monsters that spawn in randomly. And I mean random because I've fought 4 of them at a time before and that is a heart racer I tell you.

•	An exhillarating and tranquilizing mix of music.
•	A beautifully executed simple story.
•	Hand drawn art.
•	A classic blend of RPG elements in a side scroller.
•	Turn-based combat.
•	Great side-characters.
•	A delightful main lead.
•	An agape world called Lemuria with alot of adventure.
In terms of gameplay it is a good game.The combat mechanics are pretty simple. However, you need to think your actions well in order to act in the best and fastest way as possible. At the start you will play solo, but with time you will find many interesting and strong allies which will help you, by forming a party of 2 characters during the battles. You also have a firefly as an ally, which you control with the mouse. A pretty interesting mechanic but it becomes pretty repetitive during the combats. Out of combat it is an simple 2D platform game, with some puzzles, traps and tons of hidden loot. Sadly, in terms of combat, the game becomes extremely repetitive in the second half of the game because at some point, excluding boss battles, you will repeat the same tactics over and over again since the variety of enemies is pretty low. It gets so repetitive that at some point, you will start avoiding your enemies instead of attacking them to earn experience. You also have a perk system, as expected in a RPG, which is also pretty simple, yet intuitive. There is also a gem system called Oculi, that gives you the chance to upgrade certain stats of your characters.
The story in this game is told in an extremely simple way, yet that is part of the beauty of it. It is a very sad story with some unexpected plot twists, supported by excellent characters and good dialogues, except the fact that they always rhyme, something that really grinded my gears, especially during the second half of the game because the rhymes start to feel too forced. Apart from that, it is an excellent tale of the journey made by the protagonist Aurora, in her attempt to save the Kingdom of Lemuria.
Visually this is an epic game. The game art is absolutely astonishing, it really gives life to this wonderful fantasy world. Everything as an immaculate aspect, it is hard not to like the artistic work made in this game. Another highlight is the fact that this game as the "feeling" that all was hand crafted, as if the game was drawn on a canvas. Really spectacular in this category.
The biggest strength in this game is the soundtrack. Absolutely amazing! It is hard to not be immersed in this awesome world with this wonderful combo of visuals and sounds. Simply astonishing. The sound and music gives the strength and energy you need to play this game, really inspirational.
