Black Desert is indeed like no other MMORPG you have ever played. Let's start with the good things:
-Amazing immersion: next gen graphics, artistic direction that reminds of Skyrim, realism (characters collide with each other, clothes and hair have excellent physics, characters get wet under raining or in water, get stained by mud and blood when fighting, even sweat when fighting, going to de desert produces dehydration and therefore the need of drinking water periodically, etc.)
-Sandbox elements: housing, complex farming system that reacts to temperature and weather of each region, horses can be tamed in the wilds and have different skills, they can be breeding, used for racing, etc; you can trade goods from town to town, you can befriend merchants and they will give you secret quests, sell you hidden goods, etc. You can go hunting whales and other creatures with a rifle, take a nap in your home to quickly recover energy... Sandbox really is a thing in this game.
-Population all around the world: Everywhere you go in black desert, there's someone. This is achieved mainly with 4 features: 1) there's no fast travel in black desert, 2) The leveling is not quest-based, but grind-based. 3) End game content very is spread out: world bosses are very apart from each other etc. 4) Each main town has it's own advantages so people do not gather in just one place, ie one town might have the best daily quests, other town will have merchants selling stuff you won't find anywhere else, other might be coastal and very close to a profitable fishing or grinding point, etc. Also towns have their own marketplace and item warehouses, with their own taxes, etc. All this ensures people is constantly going around the world and do not stay in one place.
-More complex action combat than in any other MMORPG. Classes are therefore very difficult to master which makes for a very rewarding experience.
-No pay to win system.
-Very long lasting. Having top gear in this game takes... Forever.
-PVP content. Eg guilds do not recruit players for free but rather contract them. Guilds can conquer towns and other places that will give them weekly tax money. This kind of guild wars are truly spectacular with players building forts and towers, and other players besieging those buildings with cannons, elephants, etc.
Now the bad things:
-Poor PVE content. This aspect of the game really is in very early stages and there's no guarantee it will go much further. Main story is cliché and you won’t be paying much attention to it. Monsters lack any tactical approach (do not expect monsters with mechanics you need to learn like in TERA) and are generally very easy to kill. Bosses are sealed within scrolls and you can only acquire one scroll daily so you will only be doing 1 boss daily with a very low chance of it giving anything valuable to you, moreover the bosses are a joke meaning you can solo kill them easily in less than a minute. Another PVE element is world bosses. Those are big monsters that spawn at certain locations once/twice a day. There are only three of them and they are not soloable, they can’t be killed with a party either, they are ofc not instanced, and, in summary, they are zerg fests of 30+ characters, destroying your fps, and also you might not even reach the boss before it’s killed... There are currently two dungeons in game, both are super end game so this part of PVE will not be available to you for a LOOONG time. Drops are not worth it considering the gear you already need to have to be there, experience isn’t good either because mobs take too much time to be killed, dungeons are not instanced which is great from a PVP point of view, but we are talking about PVE now aren’t we? In summary, in BDO there’s hardly any PVE content to enjoy most of the time.
-Odd leveling and learning curve. First 50 levels are super fast, which means you will not enjoy the world since you will outlevel the region you are in very fast and feel the need to move on. This fast leveling makes difficult/impossible to learn the class properly until you are already level +50 and therefore quite advanced in the game. So you just learnt how to play but suddenly Awakening (class upgrade) comes at level 56, renders useless most of your skills and combos, and forces you to re-learn the class with a new weapon, very different mechanics, etc. It really is frustrating.
-No open world pvp. Remember TERA where you could kill anybody anytime? Age of Conan? Wow PVP servers? That’s gone. PVP doesn’t start till you are lvl 45, once you reach that level, you will have huge penalties for killing more than 3-4 people a day. Penalties will literally cost you millions, like losing enchantments on your gear, loosing durability faster, even a chance of dropping your gear! Penalties are reduced in the Valencia Desert, but nobody goes there because the area lacks any interesting incentives.
You start to see the problem here, right? No PVE, and not REALLY a PVP world.

Like its predecessor, Half-Life 2 is a single-player first-person shooter broken into several chapters, permanently casting the player as the protagonist Gordon Freeman. The sequel has nearly the same mechanics as Half-Life, including health-and-weapon systems and periodic physics puzzles, except with the newer Source Engine and improved graphics. The player also starts without items, slowly building up an arsenal over the course of the game. Despite the game's mainly linear nature, much effort was put into making exploration rewarding and interesting; many optional areas can be missed or avoided.
A diverse set of enemies is present, which usually require being approached with different tactics: some coordinate in groups to out-maneuver or out-position the player; others, like the Manhack, fly directly at the player through small openings and tight corridors; still others use predictable but powerful attacks, while others hide before swiftly attacking the player. Gordon can kill most enemies with his weapons, or make use of indirect means, exploiting environmental hazards such as explosive pressurized canisters, gas fires or improvised traps. For some portions of the game, Gordon can be joined by up to four armed Resistance soldiers and medics, and can send his team further from him or call them back.
Many of the game's new features utilize its detailed physics simulation. Two sections of the game involve driving vehicles. Instead of button-based puzzles from Half-Life, environmental puzzles are also introduced with makeshift mechanical systems, revolving around the player's new ability to pick up, move, and place objects. Solutions involve objects' physical properties, such as shape, weight, and buoyancy. For example, in Chapter 3, Route Kanal, the player is required to stack cinder blocks on a makeshift see-saw ramp to proceed over a wall. Alternatively, the player can use these to build a crude staircase, so sometimes, multiple approaches lead to the desired outcome.
Part-way through the game, Gordon acquires the Gravity Gun, which allows him to draw distant objects towards himself or forcefully push them away, as well as the ability to manipulate larger and heavier objects that he cannot manipulate without the weapon. These abilities are required to solve puzzles later in the game, and can also be used to great effect in combat, as any non-static object within proximity to the player has the potential to be used as a makeshift defense (e.g. a file cabinet) or a deadly projectile (e.g. a gasoline can or a buzzsaw blade).
The game never separates the player with pre-rendered cutscenes or events; the story proceeds via exposition from other characters and in-world events, and ensures that the player controls Gordon for the entirety of the game. Much of the backstory to the game is simply alluded to, or told through the environment.

A lot of harsh old school X-COM comments about this game out there. To be honest, I found most aspects to be at least as good as the old game (of which I have played far more than Steam knows... probably more like 800+ hours over 21 years).
*The mission interface which you use on missions, is fantastic. But honestly, the maps needed to be procedurally generated, as once you've played a map a couple of times, you pretty much know how to 'win' any mission on the map.
*The base building is pretty good, but I'd like to see multiple bases for X-COM and the aliens.
*I do like the skill system, however, I think I'd prefer that skills were not tied to rank. I thought the original X-COM nailed ranks, so you didn't have 10 Commanders and only 2 Captains.
*Weapon selection is pretty good, and inventory management is well done, though I did like in the original game, how if a mission was going badly, you could pick up items (and even corpses) from the aliens for research even if you had to abort the mission.
*Reduced number of soldiers on missions is excellent. One problem with the original game, is that you could have large numbers of soldiers on the battlefield which would make each turn exceptionally slow (but I guess you needed them, as there were no real cover options, unless you wanted to sacrifice sight, which led to many dead soldiers).
*Research and Construction are both pretty well handled in the new game, but they were handled well in the original too, so, much of a muchness.
*Needs more ships for more variation. Original had 5 different ships: Interceptor, Skyranger, Firestorm, Lightning and Avenger. Each had benefits and disadvantages (except the Avenger really, which was pretty much the ultimate) and were specific to what you needed for the mission. New X-COM removes this choice.
*Needs more variety in enemy ships too, and less variety in the type of enemy on each ship. Something original X-COM nailed was that you'd generally only face a couple of different types of enemy on a mission, showing that different aliens were focused towards different mission tasks.

This game follows the world progression that you are already very much familiar with from the HBO hit Tv show 'Game of Thrones'. The characters you play as however are unintroduced in the shows, as is your story.
Honestly the games plays out really well and I thoroughly enjoyed the story, it had me on the edge of my seat, choosing my words carefully, rewinding more than once, and also dying more often than I'd care to admit publically.
The games strongest points are its Character, its story, and just the emotion it brings. The Characters its introduces do their job really well, you care about the ones you want to save and they feel fleshed out well enough, while at the same time the 'bad guys' aren't so much bad as opposed to your own house. The story I also very much enjoyed, going through chapter by chapter and struggling alongside the strugglign Forrester House in many different situations and lands was somethign I very much enjoyed watching and being a part of. And then the emotion that I felt for all of it left me very raw once I reached the conclusion of the current Episode, I was very much involved in the tale, rooting for the good guy when something went right, sad and very much angry with my choices when something went sour, and howlign at my screen when the evil characters did something I wished to make them pay for.
Unfortunately the game isn't without drawbacks. You'll find during multiple playthroughs that your decisions don't actually affect the plotline in any significant enough margin, they mearly change the narrative and how things play out, but they always play out in fairly much the same way. At certain points this left me feeling a bit frustrated in general, but my emotional attachment to the characters drew me back in. Also there's no real control over your environment, I was rather confused as to why there needed to be an inventory system at all and my control over any situation was basically limited to conversation choices.
Overall it very much does remind me of Game of Thrones in a way, its very much enjoyable, a high replayability value, but you must have the realization that no matter how much you might wish to change something, you just can't in most cases.
While the game is nowhere perfect, and in some places its more like an interactive novel than anything, I don't consider that a con to its overall value, maybe because I love books, but I could understand that being something of a turnoff for some.
In conclusion I gave this game a solid 7.9/10, due to some of the more irritatiting moments where I wish I could've done more in the game I can't give it an 8 or higher, but I suppose its part of the GoT experience. It wouldn't be GoT unless they crapped over some of your favorite characters on a regular basis

Hyperdimension Neptunia Re;Birth1 is a good, perhaps even great game, but it does not come without significant flaws. It is a bit of a rollercoaster between good and bad, and the bad moments are just as frustrating as the good moments are amazing. Whether or not you'll be able to forgive Neptunia for its flaws and enjoy it for the good it offers seems to depend mostly on personal preference.
Unlike most modern western games that go for the lowest common denominator, this game was made with a clear target audience in mind. If you are not a fan of japanese animation in general, then you do not belong into this group and a significant part of the game will not appeal to you.
In Hyperdimension Neptunia Re;Birth1 you'll spend your time with two types of activities; dialogue in VN-style with animated sprites, and gameplay with jRPG typical turn-based combat.
The dialogue is not very interesting on its own and mainly consists of "cute girls doing cute things". If you do not like that sort of thing, then a large part of Neptunia's charm will not appeal to you. But then again, you wouldn't be here in the first place if that was true, right?
Then there's the gameplay. During missions and quests you'll be wandering around in so called "dungeons", which I'd just call "maps", as a majority of them are outside. These dungeons are filled with monsters, and upon contact, you'll face off against them in turn-based combat. The combat can be a bit hard to get into at first, but after getting used to it, it can be quite enjoyable. However, it quickly gets repetitive and killing everything in your way will soon feel like a chore. A few hours into the game, you'll probably want to avoid most of the "trashmobs" and then repeatedly kill boss-type mobs over and over again to grind some much needed levels for the upcoming event bosses. The bosses in general can be very though, they have a lot of health and whether you'll find them a pushover or unbeatable will depend a lot on your level, which makes a huge difference.
The combat is surprisingly deep with many options for combos, finishers, super moves, abilities that come either as passives or as a bonus from other party members, and hundreds of possible bonus abilities from equipment slots, particularly discs that you can configure yourself.
Easily the worst part of Hyperdimension Neptunia Re;Birth1 is the leveldesign. There are a handful of maps, like a cave, a mountain pass, a grasslands area, a warehouse, and so on. There are tons of dungeons in the game, and it just so happens that these few maps get copypasted over and over again. Many of the dungeons use literally the exact same map, along with the same enemies using a new color and name. Going through the same looking dungeons will quickly become a chore.
The game does however offer a ton of endgame content with lots of replay value. If you only play through the story once and then quit, you'll miss a significant amount of content, although doing so is certainly understandable given the copypasted nature of the dungeons and enemies. About half the dungeons are optional, and you can spawn additional bosses in every dungeon through the use of a crafting system that calls those things "plans". There are more items in Neptunia than you could ever hope for. Most of them are crafted and require specific materials, including boss drops. Getting some of them is a feat on its own, but attempting to get everything possible is extremely grindy. There are optional party members, super strong bosses, difficult dungeons and amazing weapons/armors that you can attempt to get once your party has a high enough level.
Another major gripe is the localisation. The translation is extremely liberal, seemingly in an attempt to "americanize" the game. The text box displaying something along the lines of, but still completely different from what the characters say is a frequent occurrence, to the point that it even changes the characters personalities sometimes. I did some digging around and apparently the localisation of this game is considered "good" by the community, which speaks volumes not only about the standards of the fans, but moreso about the quality of the translation of other games in the series.
In conclusion, I can recommend Hyperdimension Neptunia Re;Birth1 to people who like anime and/or turn-based gameplay. Despite doing many things wrong, it can offer an enjoyable experience if the things it does right appeal to you.

This uncompromising game does not babysit you through the campaign. Much of the mechanics too is left to you to discover, which could be frustrating to most gamers. I myself was not immune to some of the mistifying puzzles, customizations and storyline thrown at me and I had to turn to the online community to save my bacon.
There are genuine issues though, such as a cluttered interface and inventory. Many items found in the game can have contextual benefits which are a wholly blink and miss affairs. Due to the isometric view, some objects such as buttons and levers can be infuriating to find. You'll know what I mean when you play the game.
However, much of the issues do not lessen the fact that Larian has a winner here with an intriguing story, rich characters, varied landscapes and an engaging combat system. If you are a fan of Neverwinter Nights, Icewind Dale or Baldur's Gate then you'll feel right at home with Divinity.

I went into this game without knowing too much about it. All I knew really was that it had that "Diablo-esque" vibe to it and that's exactly what I wanted. "Why not play Diablo then?" you might be asking, and the honest truth is I didn't see it in the Steam store. That is in no way a diss to this game but I wanted an immersive world with similar gameplay elements from what I knew  Diablo would deliver.
What can I tell you about Grim Dawn? It delivers that and so much more. I'm deeply immersed in the lore and I honestly feel bad when I make a decision that leads to the deaths of folks just trying to survive in the world.
Rather then a pros and cons section I think I'll just include a "things you need to know" type deal and without any spoilers of course.
Starting off, this game is very lore heavy. You'll find tidbits about pre and post "Grim Dawn" Cairn(the game world) ALL OVER. Enemies will drop pieces of lore. You'll find journal entries throughout the landscape telling you about various aspects from character motivations to heart pulling tales about the denizens as the "Grim Dawn" is happening.
Most of all the game doesn't hold your hand with tutorials. They're always available through the Codex window and, you'll get the occasional quick tip about something you're doing in the top left corner of the game. Which is quick and you may miss if it you're not paying too close attention to that side of the screen. Which, unless you have minions, you have no need to look in that corner anyways. So pay attention to any tips the loading screen offers or you'll miss something important but I'll get into that later.
The UI is very simplified, Health and Energy(some call it Mana, MP, SP, etc. this game just calls it energy) above some quick slots. A mini-map will be at the top right(you can turn it off for more immersion or if you truly want to lose yourself in the game map. And you have an active quest list right below that. That's all thats on your screen other than, like I said earlier, if you have Minions, then their HP/Energy is on the top right. You can UI Scale as well in the options to make these even less noticeable, not to mention you can toggle the map and quests for even less on the screen.
Oh yeah I forgot to mention that the game's difficulty is in the top left as well. I suppose to let you know what difficulty you're playing on currently(you can adjust it from the main menu). This is one of those things I wish I knew about when starting the game. In games like these, I'm used to there being one difficulty and as you beat the game harder difficulties become unlocked. This game has two starting difficulties: Normal and Veteran. Me not knowing the exact difference of them I started on Normal because who wants to die on the first enemy because he's way too high level for you? But during one of the game's loading screens, I read that Normal is more geared towards players who have never played an ARPG before. I imediately switched to Veteran and IMEDIATELY noticed the difference. Enemies scale with you pretty well.     I haven't gone into an area and felt like it was just a grind(unless I was doing it on purpose) to get through the area and on to the next one. I honestly enjoy the fact that I can just die if I'm careless: from traps to the harder "boss" and "hero" monsters that spawn in randomly. And I mean random because I've fought 4 of them at a time before and that is a heart racer I tell you.

Like its predecessor, Half-Life 2 is a single-player first-person shooter broken into several chapters, permanently casting the player as the protagonist Gordon Freeman. The sequel has nearly the same mechanics as Half-Life, including health-and-weapon systems and periodic physics puzzles, except with the newer Source Engine and improved graphics. The player also starts without items, slowly building up an arsenal over the course of the game. Despite the game's mainly linear nature, much effort was put into making exploration rewarding and interesting; many optional areas can be missed or avoided.
A diverse set of enemies is present, which usually require being approached with different tactics: some coordinate in groups to out-maneuver or out-position the player; others, like the Manhack, fly directly at the player through small openings and tight corridors; still others use predictable but powerful attacks, while others hide before swiftly attacking the player. Gordon can kill most enemies with his weapons, or make use of indirect means, exploiting environmental hazards such as explosive pressurized canisters, gas fires or improvised traps. For some portions of the game, Gordon can be joined by up to four armed Resistance soldiers and medics, and can send his team further from him or call them back.
Many of the game's new features utilize its detailed physics simulation. Two sections of the game involve driving vehicles. Instead of button-based puzzles from Half-Life, environmental puzzles are also introduced with makeshift mechanical systems, revolving around the player's new ability to pick up, move, and place objects. Solutions involve objects' physical properties, such as shape, weight, and buoyancy. For example, in Chapter 3, Route Kanal, the player is required to stack cinder blocks on a makeshift see-saw ramp to proceed over a wall. Alternatively, the player can use these to build a crude staircase, so sometimes, multiple approaches lead to the desired outcome.
Part-way through the game, Gordon acquires the Gravity Gun, which allows him to draw distant objects towards himself or forcefully push them away, as well as the ability to manipulate larger and heavier objects that he cannot manipulate without the weapon. These abilities are required to solve puzzles later in the game, and can also be used to great effect in combat, as any non-static object within proximity to the player has the potential to be used as a makeshift defense (e.g. a file cabinet) or a deadly projectile (e.g. a gasoline can or a buzzsaw blade).
The game never separates the player with pre-rendered cutscenes or events; the story proceeds via exposition from other characters and in-world events, and ensures that the player controls Gordon for the entirety of the game. Much of the backstory to the game is simply alluded to, or told through the environment.

Call of Juarez is a western-themed FPS game series released by Ubisoft. The Cartel is the "odd one out" in this series as it is the only one taking place in a modern day setting instead of the good old Wild West. Interestingly, the concept works and it makes for a good - albeit somewhat mediocre - game that fans can feel free to pick up as it becomes, after all, an important part of the franchise.
The game is best played cooperatively. For some reason the developer decided to pick not two (remember Bound In Blood?) but 3 protagonists. When playing alone they are controlled by the A.I but they are not exactly sharpshooters; however, the upside here is that you do not need to revive any of them.
They all work for a different organisation serving their country - Ben is an LAPD cop (he wears a cowboy hat and his surname indicates he is the descendant of Ray McCall from the 1st game), Kim is from the FBI and Eddie represents the DEA. They are all after The Cartel and during gameplay each of them receives a phone call asking them to complete a secondary objective. This is pretty funny as with each player you are to pick up various things and the rest cannot know about it. If noticed, you lose the opportunity. These are all illegal activities (such as stealing money) as to a certain degree all of them are dirty.
There are some driving sequences, too. One player drives while the rest do the shooting. The mechanics are similar to the one experienced in Dead Island (another Techland game series): it is pretty easy to navigate but the camera is positioned behind the dashboard so you do not exactly have the chance to change the view. There's also levelling up that unlocks newer and more powerful weapons throughout the game but it is pretty generic. Multiplayer is also available and while it does not offer anything new it is pretty entertaining.
Like I said this is the odd one out in the series but it does not mean it is a bad game. At the time (2011) the Chrome engine already looked outdated and while there is a handful of cinematics the game's story is not exactly very original. Still, The Cartel is an entertaining game and if you liked Call of Juarez you might get fond of this, too.
Just remember: beside McCall's character and the slow-mo shootouts and the available revolvers nothing really makes you remember its predecessors. Perhaps it's best to wait for a discount so as not to be disappointed very much.

You can level these characters to suit your style, and you're not just filling spheres on a skill tree without branches.
The rhyming dialogue is interesting, bouncing between clever and annoying at times, but overall I think it's a success.  I'd recommend for anyone who enjoys RPGs with turn-based battles.  It's not a very difficult game, and there's plenty of side stuff to do if you go looking for it.

A lot of harsh old school X-COM comments about this game out there. To be honest, I found most aspects to be at least as good as the old game (of which I have played far more than Steam knows... probably more like 800+ hours over 21 years).
*The mission interface which you use on missions, is fantastic. But honestly, the maps needed to be procedurally generated, as once you've played a map a couple of times, you pretty much know how to 'win' any mission on the map.
*The base building is pretty good, but I'd like to see multiple bases for X-COM and the aliens.
*I do like the skill system, however, I think I'd prefer that skills were not tied to rank. I thought the original X-COM nailed ranks, so you didn't have 10 Commanders and only 2 Captains.
*Weapon selection is pretty good, and inventory management is well done, though I did like in the original game, how if a mission was going badly, you could pick up items (and even corpses) from the aliens for research even if you had to abort the mission.
*Reduced number of soldiers on missions is excellent. One problem with the original game, is that you could have large numbers of soldiers on the battlefield which would make each turn exceptionally slow (but I guess you needed them, as there were no real cover options, unless you wanted to sacrifice sight, which led to many dead soldiers).
*Research and Construction are both pretty well handled in the new game, but they were handled well in the original too, so, much of a muchness.
*Needs more ships for more variation. Original had 5 different ships: Interceptor, Skyranger, Firestorm, Lightning and Avenger. Each had benefits and disadvantages (except the Avenger really, which was pretty much the ultimate) and were specific to what you needed for the mission. New X-COM removes this choice.
*Needs more variety in enemy ships too, and less variety in the type of enemy on each ship. Something original X-COM nailed was that you'd generally only face a couple of different types of enemy on a mission, showing that different aliens were focused towards different mission tasks.

While XCOM is a fairly well made game, and most of its bugs were elimated shortly after release (some of which were fairly serious) it's just also extremely god damn boring.
The problem, like most titles of this sort, is just the fact that there is no content, and the content that IS there is massively uninspired.
You can discover the breadth of what this game has to offer in a single playthrough, and similarily, you will also all the tactical options available to you at the same time.
You will also discover that there is one optimal way to play and that way always yields the best results, which is fairly unforgivable in a tactical strategy game.
The game's lack of variety just spells itself out in several ways, building your base isn't really much of a thought exercise, rather just something to do that will always end out well unless you're completely brainless. Outfitting your squad, choosing perks, researching, all these things are extraordinarily linear and simple with very little deliberation involved, and that just makes the "thought-provoking" intent of this game non-existant.
There are some other things that just blatantly reveal the total lack of depth in this game, the prefab areas that are usually just four giant blocks stuck together, with little to no randomization, the extraordinarily linear enemy progression that turns the late game in 90% Mutons and nothing else, the dull combat that ultimately always plays the same, and like most low-concept tactics games simply amounts to positioning, sometimes grenade and ability use, and very little other thought applied.
This is the kind of game where your longest thought processes for a turn can take around 30 seconds and not much longer, but then you have to fight 100 battles that are essentially just as simplistic.
The game is droll, like most games that demand replay by their very concept, there's very little that actually warrants replay in this game, and that's a shame. I can go on about how uninspired the art style is, how disappointing the destruction and how totally lacking in atmosphere it is, but the most severe problem is just how little reason there is to actually finish the game, since you'll see all it has to offer after only about 10 hours.

I know this is a pretty unpopular opinion but I've never really liked this game.
I played it a bunch on Xbox360 a few years ago and then got it in the valve complete pack a few less years ago.
I love Half-Life 1 and I thought H-L:2 Episode 1 was good. But Half-Life 2 always felt like pretty much a glorified tech demo.
For it's time yeah sure the physics engine was impressive, but the amount of the times the story or action would grind to a halt so you can load a pile of bricks onto a plank or a lift or something. Like I think it's more than 3, and each one is more annoying. Like ok you want some puzzles I can dig that but don't stop the game in the middle of me fleeing for my life from an army of alien nazis to put a small crate onto a big crate so I can hop a chainlink fence. or at least don't do it more than once.
There are 2 overly long and mostly boring vehicle sections as well.
The gravity gun is cool but again it hasn't really dated well considering how much of a prominent place it has. Like again for the time I'm sure it was fine, but there are so many games where you can pick things up and throw them. It's pretty much treated like "oh look what we can do" like the dialouge when you get is pretty much "hey come here and try this new gravity gun(tm) it's so good pick up things and throw them whooo this is not a tech demo"
It probably doesn't help that aside from the bits I enjoy like most of Ravenholme, some of the Antlion parts and...other Parts I think, Pretty much everything good the game does can be recreated in Gmod in under half an hour. Not that I'm a huge fan of Gmod either really but It doesn't help a game age well when every asset and weapon is available in a sandbox mod-game with the same graphics and so much more to do than pile 4 bricks onto a beam or listen to scientist man talk at you about teleporters for 20 minutes.
To be clear I don't hate this game, I think it's a slightly dated generally solid fps, but I see so many reviews and people saying it's the best fps ever made or that there hasn't been a better game made since. Like thats your opinion and I respect that but I just can't help wondering what it is that you're seeing that I'm not.
There are parts in the game I really like, but the overall package is just way too bloated and contrived feeling.

The game itself is beautiful and interesting with lots of lore behind most of the characters. While interesting it gets very boring after a while, with my eyes numbing to read all the text. I feel sorry for people that need glasses specifically for reading. This aside the adventure itself is fun and exploring and loot is always going to appeal to people. For new players the "normal" difficulty is brutal when you have no idea what your doing and the "tutorial cave" does not even come close to a tutorial. The constant reloading of previous saves IS going to happen. Get used to that load screen....
The lack of waypoint markers is very annoying. I know i read somewhere that the devs were even against map markers, but it still would have been nice for players completely new to this style of game to have an option to turn a feature like that on. We spent ages running around doing nothing getting into fights with ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s with much higher levels than us trying to figure out what to do.

I can imagine this game would be great to people used to the genre or WoW or even LoL and dota players but for someone that generally plays fps or other types of games the start is punishing. I could talk for hours about Kickstarter and how it constantly ♥♥♥♥s people over, but Divinity is one of the few games that actually delivered on its promises.  Actually, I can’t talk for hours about Kickstarter, because I’ve never been on Kickstarter before.  But I KNOW WHAT IT IS AND THAT’S THE IMPORTANT THING.
Divinity: Original Sin is a great game for a multitude of reasons, but mostly because it actually has really good, thoughtful, funny writing.
It might seem silly, but 95% of video game scripts are ♥♥♥♥ing HORRIBLE.
Exhibit A: the GTA series.
When talking about Grand Theft Auto, people are always like: “oh my god its like im playing a AAA hollywood movie,” when in reality, the plot feels like it was written by some dude in a 1st year creative writing program who thinks that writing earnestly about a crack smoking sociopath who whips his♥♥♥♥♥♥out in public is a tour de force and hits all of the foundational cornerstones of our society’s deep-rooted problems.
It doesn’t feel like Divinity is EVER farting around with its plot or character development, and that’s all I’m asking for.  Just don’t fart around.  Or if you’re going to fart around, do it thoughtfully at least.
Divinity’s fart clouds are shaped like of all of the best PC RPG’s you’ve played, mingling together to create a fruity pungent green toxic bouquet that you can light on fire with a flame spell and roast 5 zombies when the green fart cloud explodes.
I’m going somewhere with this!
In most RPGs, fighting doesn’t really have consequences. In D&D (which almost all PC RPGs are inspired by), you can basically do whatever you want: if there’s a skeleton warrior king you could just be like, “♥♥♥♥ it, I’m going to use this lvl.9 firestorm spell and melt that skeleton king’s golden throne so it fuses to his butt and then when he tries to stand up his butt and pelvic bones will disattach from his body and then his legs will fall off and then i’m going to use this lvl. 10 summon bees spell and unleash a 1000 bees on my own group of adventurers because I’m a huge ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.”
You can never do that in PC RPGs, it’s always just “click on enemy and kill them.”
Divinity actually fixes that issue by making spells and environments interact with each other.  Your rogue is burning alive?  Cast a rain spell, my doggie.  Bunch of oil lying around leading to a keg of dynamite for some reason?  Strike it with your flaming sword and watch the fireworks.  Sure, it’s not perfect – the mechanics are still limited to the possibilities of a game engine after all, but it’s a step in the right direction because these possibilities feel organic and real.
The character building is also fantastic.  You control two main protagonists; how these protagonists interact with the world, and with each other, is entirely up to you.  If you want to make them totally agree on every single decision and be best buddies who run town complimenting each other at every turn, you can do that! Or, alternatively, you can make them disagree on everything and be working together strictly because they’re forced to.  It’s a cool dynamic, and one that refreshingly differs from most traditional RPGs where you’re forced down a straight linear path with the illusion of choice.
Not every decision has to be a “CHANGE THE FATE OF THE WORLD” consequential decision.
Sometimes it can be more immersive to be able to ask one of your characters why the just beat the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of a senile 90-year-old mayor, and to see how they respond.
There’s just so much detail in this game it’s kinda outstanding.  Everything is meticulously and lovingly put together.  The world feels alive and teeming with activity, which is a huge accomplishment for a video game.
This doesn’t happen very often, but I got the feeling of “damn, this game is ♥♥♥♥ing amazing” while playing Divinity: Original Sin.

The genius of Telltale Games lies in telling a really good story with the illusion of plot-significant choice - it's GoT offering is no exception. The story's flavor changes depending on how you play (mercifully, pragmatically, vengefully, etc.), but the broad strokes of the plot do not.
Fortunately, the plot is the rich, twisty joy GoT fans have come to expect. You play members of House Forrester, a minor yet economically important family from the North that enjoys a virtual monopoly on the growth and crafting of ironwood. Episode 1 starts off with a bang - when it's revealed your character is with Robb Stark's army the night of the Red Wedding, players familiar with GoT are treated to a delicious "Oh,♥♥♥♥♥♥quot; moment before the story starts in earnest high gear that never really lets up.
If that previous paragraph referenced events, ideas, and people you don't know anything about, this game is not for you. Working knowledge of the GoT universe up to the most recent book/season is required to enjoy the story. The gameplay alone is insufficient, as it comprises QTEs and dialogues that only carry weight if you're invested in the characters and world.
For players seeking agency, a more sandboxy RPG will probably scratch that itch. For us GoTers, Telltale has served up a pitch-perfect fifteen hours (once they release the last episode) in Westeros and Essos.

I learned of this game from the developer on the Shmups facebook page. I finally got around to it after about a year and in some aspects, it reminds me of Really Big Sky, in which I reviewed in 2013. I have revised the review at

You start by choosing a level based on a song (I suggest going in order), and you are push into a scrolling space background where your ship automatically shoots. You generally will only need to strafe left and right, but you can move freely which will be needed for a few enemies that chase you. Your gun shoots a straight bullet shot, which can be upgraded by collecting blue drops from every enemy. Killing enemies also increases your power meter and a multiplier. Some enemies drop gold squares that give you a temporary additional wide shot. They drop frequently, so the majority of the game is trying to dodge bullets to survive and and grab these squares to kill a screen filled with dozens of enemies. Some enemies like bigger ships, minibosses, and snake like enemies require alot more hits, which can more easily be dealt with your beam by pressing the fire button, which also slows your movement speed. This beam also seems to provide a shield and can destroy enemy bullets. The beam depletes from your power meter, though, I never felt like I would ever run out since by the time you need it - the drain doesn't seem heavy and you usually have enough power to deal with the amount of bullets sent to you at a time. I feel you will only loose it if you hold Fire the entire time, which is a  bad strategy since it slows you down from dodging.
I found many big budget games come with unnecessary Epilepsy warnings, but HIIIPE doesn't, which should be a crime because I can't think of a better candidate for one. Besides colorful, flashing enemies, bullets and items, some level seeds have manic rainbow patterns that I would imagine to easily trigger somebody's epilipsy. That said, I was able to handle it (since I'm not epiliptic). The game is too visually busy for me to stick with and finish, but my shmup gaming skills kept me entertained in the few levels I did complete.  Each level is based on the tempo of a techno track, though the way enemies generate are random, so this game would be near impossible to master and somewhat tough to one credit clear because of this. Many of my deaths were my fault because it is VERY EASY to cancel bullets, but often times, bullets or enemies are hard to see because of the visual noise which lead to a few semi-unfair deaths. Player deaths doesn't really stop the the action besides some invicibility frames and maybe killing some enemies, so you can still keep playing at the fast pace this game wants.

Building upon their greatest work, Company of Heroes 1, Relic created a masterpiece we now call Company of Heroes 2.
Company of Heroes 2 is by far the greatest strategy game I've ever played. The graphics are intensely beautiful when put to Maximum Settings. The explosions look realistic and captivating. The armor of all the units look very authentic. The maps have beautiful textures. Just like how Company of Heroes 1 was marvelous to the eye, Company of Heroes 2 provides the same role as one of the best looking Strategy games out there.
First of all, you need to give Relic slack for even making a sequel to their videogame. These guys were completely bankrupt by THQ, who sold them to Sega. Relic suffered through some serious financial problems, but loe and behold, they had the heart to make the next greatest game. They couldn't do everything they wanted to do, nor did they have the funds to tweak the game to the point where the community wouldn't be upset. So please, if you feel that the game is rusty, give them some time.
By now, if you're reading this. The game is already near perfection. The old days of overpowered units are over, and Relic is continuously, month after month, providing game changing balance tweaks and completely new content. I anticipate every month that they provide us with whole new maps, new units, new commanders, and balance tweaks.
If you guys got bored of this game in the past, please give it another shot. And for the people who are skeptical about buying this game, this game is totally worth it!
It's Relic, they made arguably the greatest strategy game of all time, and they are bound to do it again!
And by the way... Metascore lies. That 80 point Metascore only considers Company of Heroes 2 at day 1 of release, not where it is now. It is a completely different game from what it used to be.

The Call of Juarez: Cartel is interesting in a lot of ways.  With all the drug violence on the South Western US border, this game takes the player into the seedy and dangerous world of the drug dealers and the cops who try to stop them.  The game starts in a marijuana field in Sequoia park, and ends in a huge hacienda of a gun runner in Mexico near Juarez.  In between there are plenty of gun battles, and also an interesting plot line, as you try to follow informants and leads to  bust the bad guys.  The graphics are pretty good,  and there are a pretty good variety of guns to try.  Picking up enemy guns is a great way to try one out before it becomes available in your inventory.
Unfortunately, there are a couple of issues with the game play.  For one thing the AI of  your partners is pretty bad.   They are dumb as a post, continually stepping in the line of fire.   Fortunately, friendly fire is disabled, or they would commit suicide multiple times in every battle.
To make the weak AI situation even worse, as a side plot you are supposed to acquire items without the puppy-partners seeing.  But since they are  always stupidly right on your heels like of couple of love-starved puppies, this side agenda quickly becomes irritating rather than fun.
Another weakness of the game is the driving sequences.  These maybe wouldn't be so bad if they weren't so numerous.  Unfortunately they are in almost every level.  No matter which kind of vehicle you are in, your top speed is quite a bits slower than all the enemy vehicles.   Consequently, enemies are always swarming around shooting.  If you vary from  the predefined path even a little like a normal  human would to avoid the fusillade of gunfire,  the game warns that you are "leaving the mission" and the level ends.  I found myself yanked out of the immersion of the experience when driving, and just hoping Ii could get through it without having to repeat it.  The lack of player options made it more of a chore to  be endured, rather than fun.
In summary the game is a great idea that isn't fully realized.  If you can get it on sale, it is worth a play through.  I wouldn't recommend it a full price though.

In my opinion, this is the single most underrated first person shooter ever made.  Critics and some users have taken this one apart (for some odd reason). I mean, okay, I definitely understand some of the complaints regarding polish.  The graphics, though not ugly by any means, are outdated. A few stiff animations, a bad draw distance (only in the first level) emotionless character facial expressions, not much color to the world, and a few (non game-breaking) glitches here and there. The story also could have used some more refinement, especially the unlikeable overly foul-mouthed characters (seriously, dropping 20 f bombs in 5 minutes of gameplay makes you sound desperate, not edgy). All this aside though, the Cartel is a blast to play. The first mission is a little slow, but once you get into it, the game slowly builds and builds into this high octane corrupt cop action movie that you happen to be in control of.  The gunplay? A little floaty, but solid overall. The action? Fast paced and exciting. You'll be gunning down criminals through city streets, warehouses, alleyways, forests, strip clubs, swamps, country locales, rooftops, etc. Each of these locations is varied enough to hold your visual interest and each of them has plenty of open spaces for you to run aroud dodging bullets, taking cover, and returning fire.  It's nothing short of exciting (though the enemy AI does get a bit dumb on occassion). One particular sequence left me totally breathless: a mad dash through the streets where you have to lean out your car window and open fire on a bunch of criminal cars as they try to gun you down or ram your car off the street. Like most of the game, it was stressful, exhilirating, and adrenaline-pumping.  I have more to say about it, but it's best not to make this review too long. I'll just sum up the positives and negatives to wrap this up.
Pros:
Fast-paced, breathless combat
Varied scenarios
A few awesome set-pieces
Decent variety of weapons
Nice ambient music and sound effects
Low system requierments (I run the game on an outdated, mid-range nvidia gt 640m and it runs near perfectly at max settings)
A few somewhat visually attractive areas.
Cons:
Boring story driven by the most unlikeable and repugnant characters ever created (if you're turned off by nonstop language and insults, stay far away from this one. Even Jason Brody and his dude-bro friends from Far Cry 3 were more likeable than these characters.)
Some glitches here and there
A few bad animations (not the weapons themselves. Those animate quite nicely in my opinion)
Outdated, occasionally ugly graphics (even at max settings)
Gunplay, despite being pretty satisfying later on, feels a little floaty and awkward at first (it's hard to describe it)
Could have used a little more mission variety, though what you do get is still satisfying
First mission is a bit boring when compared to later ones
Bottom line: Its flaws are noticeable (at times glaring), but The Cartel is still an exciting, fast-paced, and rewarding shooter. For me, graphics, production values, and story aren't what make a game. The gameplay is, and this one a real winner on that front. I'm not kidding when I say this is one just joined my "favorite shooters" list. If you're looking for a deep, meaningful gaming experience with a top-notch story, mind-blowing visuals, and terrific voice-work, stay away. On the other hand, if you're just jonesing for action-movie style firefights between corrupt cops and criminals, with some of the most fast-paced action you'll ever see, car chases, and satisying fist-fights, don't hesisate to lay down the ten dollars for this one.

This is not a good game, but it is pretty ambitious, especially considering it's the sequel to 2 pretty darn good FPS's.
If the devs had just edited out some of their ideas, and focused on quality, it could have been a solid 7/10 or 8/10 type game, but they just spread themselves too thin. The idea behind the story is great, with all 3 playable characters operating with their own motives and secret objectives, but the story just doesn't hold up and gets stupid and unbelieveable fast. Kind of like one of those sitcoms where for no reason characters withold important information from each other just to create "drama". In this case, it just makes everything incomprehensible. The dialogue is also just terrible. B-movie from the 90s kind of "Gangsta" swearing bad.
Gunplay is okay, but level design is horrible. The game uses a waypoint system with giant, ugly, low-res dots on the screen every 20 meters. Sometimes it breaks and stops working and when that happens, you will get lost because the levels are so poorly constructed and repetitive.

Call of Juarez®: The Cartel is the third game in the series. It is considered to be the worst Call of Juarez game, but is it realy that bad?
I consider myself a fan of CoJ series. And I like western setting in general. So it was sad to hear that the third game of epic western shooters is actually not a western, because the action takes place in 2011 and the setting here is called...ugh, "Neo-Western". Well, whatever. I've read some reviews of this game before playing so I wasn't expecting much to begin with. But let's talk about it, there are good things and bad things, like in any other game.
First thing, the story, the setting, the atmosphere and the soundtrack. Well, those are not half bad if you ask me. Well, the story is a mess actually, there are lots of uninteresting dialogs and complicated stuff in the mood "who betrays whom", actually the story here is much worse compared to all other CoJ games (even the Gunslinger). There are 3 playable protagonists, the police officer Ben McCall (a walking tribute to Ray McCall, not as Badass as the latter, but not half bad though), the DEA agent Eddie Guerra (for some reason he remonds me of Pierce from Saints Row series, probably because of those black and purple tones in clothes) and FBI agent Kim Evans (the girl with an attitude). Each of them has their own problems and "inner demons", but in the end I can tell that only Ben McCall is interesting enough as a character. Anyway, the characters don't trust each other, there is no bond between them so you won't like them too much anyway. The heroes must find and terminate the Mendoza Drug Cartel, who is presumably responsible for some kind of bombing in which several people died. They investigate deeper into the case and it turns out to be that the culprits are also their higher ups in FBI/DEA or whatever. Anyway there are many things in story that I didn't get fully and that's quite sad, when the plot is overweight in lots of uninteresting twists. I'd say the story is really poor, well, at least there are several endings.
The graphics in the game are so-so. Not bad but not good either. They say the developers were testing the new engine, meh. The soundtrack is actually pretty good. There are many decent western-themed tracks that actually create a western-feel in the game. There will be some missions in western setting and you will even visit Juarez, so those levels come along nicely with the soundtrack.
In terms of gameplay the game is so-so. You can play as one of three characters and the other two will accompany you as AI bots (or you can play online with other people, but I couldn't find any partner via internet, looks like nobody plays this game anymore, lel), each one is good with a different type of weapons: mister McCall is good with pistols and heavy machineguns, the lady is good with sniper rifles and Eddie Guerra is decent with SMGs at medium range. There is almost no recoil from guns and it was kinda hard for me to shoot enemies at times for some reason. I just don't feel the gun and the crosshair in this game (and I didn't have this problem with other CoJ games by the way). Oh and you won't ride horses in Cartel, but there will be some car chasing missions and they are actually pretty fun.
There are some bugs in the game, like clipping issues and stucking in the walls, but nothing serious so far.
VERDICT: CoJ The Cartel is indeed the worst game in CoJ series, but it still has good things in it. And most importantly it feels like CoJ game and has a western feeling. The chars are pretty boring though (and some of them are just replicas from other games, like ben mccall and Juan mendosa), the story is not captivating and the gameplay is iffy at times. But I would still recommend this game to those who like Call of Juarez series. I think it is worth a try, at least, besides it is not very long and you can complete it within 7-8 hours. My personal rating for this game will be 6/10.

I was gifted this game by a friend, who heavily praised it. And, although I went into it worried that it might not live up to the praise, it easily did so.
It's a mix of turn-based RPG (where level-up is determined by number of kills rather than exp gained), strategy, and a little bit of Oregon Trail  (managing your caravan and making decisions that affect your clansmen, supplies, and overall morale).
The story is very fleshed out, and the choices you make at times determine which group members join you (or leave; be careful which characters you get attached to). The map showcases this; it's so thorough and detailed that, in the beginning, I spent 20+ minutes just reading the backstory to each location before even reaching it. In addition to this, the music is incredible on its own, and does a very good job of complementing the events in the story. In terms of sound, the only downside is that there doesn't appear to be a sound mixer/volume control, so you'd need to use your computer's main volume control if it's too loud. Kind of a strange, but minor oversight. Lastly, and probably most importantly, the combat is well done. It's layered with enough complexity to keep it consistently interesting, allowing for characters and abilities to synergize. It can also be exceedingly difficult at times, especially when your caravan is at a disadvantage, thereby necessitating using abilities strategically to weaken enemies or keep them from reaching your vulnerable characters.
In short, it's a lot of content and quality for the below-$20 price tag, but you have to like turn-based strategy, story-driven games in order to enjoy it.

Moderate Criticism
The short of it: The banner saga is a somewhat controllable storybook/tactical turn-based combat hybrid with a high number of probability-controlled events.  Its strengths are the mostly solid writing, making you feel the weight of every decision and some measure of unique presentation.  Its weaknesses are an endless supply of implementation and framing issues, as well as the fact that most decisions don't actually matter one iota.
The long of it:  This game is probably best described as a chapter-based visual novel with a lousy fighting system and random events.  There are some management systems, but they're both highly influenced by the random events and sorta reset after certain chapters- which means there's actually not a lot of continuity.  Sure, there are some decisions that are clearly wrong, but in a few instances like a gated city early on, it's actually slightly better to "do  it wrong" for mechanical reasons that aren't apparent at all.  On top of that, your best warrior may decide they'd like to take a flying leap off a cliff for no particular reason, which is actually fairly common.  You might miss out on a unit if you choose not to say certain things, but since you're making almost every decision in a vacuum it doesn't really matter.  The only war "strategy" that seems to reduce losses is "Have a lot of giants and then charge 90% of the time".
The combat system is really the worst part of the game in most respects.  There's a lot of fights where you can't change your fighting force, there isn't much to equip and it's either obviously incredible or very middling, and having more characters is awful and you want to keep your enemies' numbers up.  The reason for this is that it uses the "my turn-> your turn" format, but for only one character at a time.  On top of this, health is also your attack stat.  This ends up creating idiotic situations like hamstringing a giant and then tanking it with your archer since it'll waste turnshacking them for no damage as you weaken two more guys that do real damage.  It's pretty much rocket tag- whoever's damaged first does way less damage and can no longer effectively remove the others' damage-dealing capacity.
Most of the special abilities are worthless, you just want to have a two-hander giant clean house whenever possible, weakening your enemies to wet-noodle status.  You can't really set up in a lot of combats, you just play from wherever people happen to be standing.  Grinding in camp is annoying given you're surrounded and it's harder than most of the actual storyline fights.  The final battle is of some interest, but it's too little too late, and the whole thing leaves off on a cliffhanger for the sequel.
When you're not in a settlement or fighting, you're out moving on a little turning world graphic watching your food tick down wondering if the game will allow you to do anything to stop it.  Most of the time, it doesn't.  Some of the time, it gives you a choice between food and personnel or time, which all leads to more or less the same result: hemmoraging followers.  This felt like the bulk of the game, and did not hold my interest very long.
The writing in this game is reasonably competent, but you don't stay in any one place besides maybe the last one long enough to get a good feel for it.  Maybe that's the point, but it's about as at odds with itself as the idiotic combat is with the attempt to present nuanced decisions.  Every time I started to get interested, though, I was brought out of it by either an idiotic decision, forced situation or the awful tactical fighting.
I don't recommend The Banner Saga.  I didn't feel compelled to play the sequel or replay it.  It's not especially long, but it sure feels like it is.

Goes a long way to recapturing the early days of the Real Time Strategy but didn't really succeed with the new things it tried, still an interesting game though.

Gameplay: The Gameplay is a turn-based system where you and your enemies take turns beating each other up and magical or physical attacks, sometimes both at the same time. The higher your combo, the more abilities you can use. There's a shop in every city that's indentical (The shop that is) and sells gear for your Party Members. There's also plans, which are basically upgrades you can get which will change the game or different characters, but you need materials for said plans. To get plans you have to visit through dungeons and collect loot, kill enemies, and explore. There's roughly 7 or so dungeons that are all very different, but they get copy-pasted for roughly 40 or something dungeons. Same with enemies, so it can get repetitive very quickly. Some Dungeons such as the Snow-related ones are also too big and don't have enough enemies. Plus, lots of treasure can go un-noticed due to the painful amounts of white everywhere.
Characters: The characters in Neptunia are so good and likeable that there's even fans who pretend to be them, kinda odd, but kinda charming in it's own unique way. The Characters themselves are also charming, it's very silly with dialogue. You don't get to pick who you send out to talk, or the words which they say. Instead you're pretty much just watching them talk to each other, sometimes with voice to go along, other times just text. To move on to the next text box, you need to press Enter on your Keyboard. I found myself pressing Space by accident and ended up skipping tons of important dialogue, the skip is just so fast that it literally skips all of it within just 2 seconds. Kinda annoying, but it's a habbit that you can break easily.
Dungeons: The Dungeons are the classic turn-based RPG game, they look really pretty and large, but only a small portion is where you can play. Enemies are randomly strewn about in the dungeon, who will sometimes follow you and attempt to take you down, or you can sneak up on them and get the first-turn of combat, which is very useful against those stronger boss-like enemies. As I noted earlier, the dungeons are very limited and are copy-pasted a ton throughout the game, same with the enemies who are just retextured with different colours. The enemiy choice for some of the Dungeons make no sense. Like, a flower in a dystopia Tron-setting.
Enemy Design and Item Design:
Something which immediately freaked the♥♥♥♥♥♥outta me was the enemy models. THEY ARE ODD! A giant walking Flower with an angry face, a man who is part-plane, a weird flying face that shoots out steam. Pretty bizarre stuff, but it also sort of gives the game it's own style and charm. The kind of charm where a Game-Show Host shows you different Enemies from different games and asks you which one is which. You see a Part-Man, Part-Plane and immediately you know that it's from Neptunia. The items, like weapons and costumes also look wicked cool. Classic giant Japanese weapons, can never get enough of them.
I'm afraid that's really all there is to the game. It's a very simplistic game that should probably be just 10 hours long. But they manage to stretch out longer, while keeping new surprises coming towards you in terms of story and dungeons (even if those dungeons are copy-pasted, they add small changes each time).

After playing Saints Row IV for just over fifteen hours, beating the campaign, and enjoying a few side missions along the way, I have noticed vast improvements throughout the series.
Customization:
As most of you should know, customization is key in games such as Saints Row, Grand Theft Auto, and other sandbox games along these lines. Games in the Saints Row franchise have all had some sort of deep customization. Players can create exact replicas of themselves, or even turn into whatever they desire. Although in this addition to the series, we are not left disappointed. The possibilities are endless. Would you like to go around shooting people with Dual Wielded SMGs? You can do that!  Want to shoot up a store with Han Solo's signature blaster? You can do that too! Whatever you sick little mind can come up with; you can do it.
Gameplay:
Looking back at Saints Row: The Third, you'll definitely notice how many of the activities have reappeared. Some of your favorites such as Tank Mayhem and Insurance Fraud. Although, in this addition to the franchise, the activities have gotten far more challenging; giving the player a harder time and not making the game drift away so quickly. For example, when you're ragdolling your character around the city in Insurance Fraud, you'll need to gain a certain amount of money to either earn Bronze, Silver, or Gold!
City Upgrades:
If you've played any of the other Saints Row games, you've probably noticed the lack of aerial combat. That has changed completely in Saints Row IV. When the developers added the VTOL hover-jets and rocket cycles, it just makes the game feel that much more entertaining. We've also seen improvements on the vertical areas of Stilwater, it's far easier to throw yourself off the top of a building to a quick and easy death. That is, only if you don't have your superpowers activated ;)
Removal of Importance:
Remember in the previous Saints Row games when you had to earn "respect" from your crew and gang? They've removed that and simply changed it's name to XP. While this makes sense due to the scenerios and there only being about nine humans technically alive. It still makes the game feel a little less like the classic "Saints Row" style game.
Cars and Music:
Basically since this game takes place almost entirely inside a computer simulation, you can do some pretty awesome things. One of them being that you can hijack a car and then "upload" it into your virtual garage. Later on, you can simply "download" it to wherever you may be on the map. It's pretty much the same as the cars, but now you can play music wherever you may be. Yes, you read that correctly. You don't even need to be in a car! This adds a whole new level of excitement to the game, and makes it much more enjoyable.
Overall:
Overall, this game was fun to play through and gave me plenty of time driving around and killing ferocious aliens. Although it kind of seems like a let down, it feels just like a large expansion to Saints Row: The Third. It's the end of 2016 and I still recommend it, as it has a unique story and will give you many laughs along the way!

I fully admit, when I first went into it, I thought I would absolutely hate Neptunia. On the surface, it's everything I hate in one neat little package. But oh boy, was I wrong.
The story of the game is about the console war, which as the name alone might have given away, is essentially just one big spoof of the console war between different video game console owners on the internet. Each console is represented by their own goddess, which is just a cute girl version of said console. I think this alone speaks volumes for the very lighthearted and goofy tone and story the game has. The game is very self aware, and knows that it isn't a new Final Fantasy, and it never pretends to be anything else, and I appreciate this aspect quite a lot. Even if one is bothered by this, which I can fully understand why one would be, the developers were kind enough to make it possible to skip dialogue with but the push of a button. Nifty, right?
One of the first things that really struck me about the game was the surprisingly colorful and pretty environments you move around in during the gameplay segments. Enemy designs are equally cheerful and colorful, all of this goes very well with the very happy and fun tone the game is constantly aiming for. Unfortunately, it reuses these assets pretty heavily, to the point where some areas can be the same map but in reverse, and a lot of enemies are simply recolors of earlier enemies.
The flipside of the reused assets problem is that they use it to make sure there's a somewhat massive amount of things to actually do in the game, at least. You'll constantly be unlocking new sidequests, new plans that require you to gather new materials so you can unlock new items, areas or maybe even gameplay changes. There's even a coliseum asking you to fight various difficult battles in exchange for very good items.
Speaking of battles, the battle system is actually what mainly made me enjoy the game as much as I did. The combat starts out as simple turn based fights with a lot of emphasis on positioning, similar to the Legend of Heroes games. As the game goes on, more and more features are added on to the combat giving it more and more depth. It never goes so far as to become complex or particularly deep though, it adds "just enough". Some examples are special attacks, transformations and a pair system. Just enough to keep the combat fresh and entertaining, as personally I'm a sucker for the very over the top and flashy special attack animations.
To summarize things; Hyperdimension Neptunia Re;Birth is a simple and fun game that never really aims or pretends to be much more than that. If you're looking for a just solid and lighthearted JRPG then this game might be one of your best bets on Steam. Don't judge a book by it's cover, as I initially did, because you just might end up missing out on a pretty good game due to it.

The return to the isometric RPG with a modern twist has been a godsend for me. The release of Divinity Original Sin followed shortly thereafter by Pillars of Eternity, and soon following Torment: Tides of Numenera are my wettest wet dream games that I could ever imagine.
Divinity in particular is great because of its classless character development system, allowing you to customize yo' people any which way you want. A Wizard isn't limited to staves because of high intelligence/lowstrength (there will be penalties, though). Your skill points you invest improve these things, and your attributes further amplify their power-and there is no limit just because you start as a rogue that says you cant invest a skill point into the pyrokinetic school of magic!
The story leaves a little to be desired, not by its content, but by the way it's expressed, some of these issues will be fixed in the up coming Enhanced Edition, which will add a ton of voice acting, hopefully adding a little more color to spots where the going can get somewhat repetitive. However, each battle, puzzle and quest is a problem that needs solving, and there are truly so many ways to go about solving them. The turn based combat is to die for-one of the best combat systems I've ever seen-for realizies.
One tonal issue I found is that sometimes, I found humor in places where I thought levity had no place. Don't get me wrong, I love a laugh as much as anyone, but the game seems to make light of almost everything in a bordering-on-buffoonish way. I could have handled a little more darkness, considering that the main quest revolves around investigating and defeated wicked dark sourcerers.
Overall, though a fantastic game! Can't wait for Enhanced Edition and the upcoming sequel!

Freedom and plenty of options in a game are great, but sometimes a title needs to stick to a few things at a time to be engaging.

Child of Light is a beautiful children's story book brought to life with an exquisite hand-painted world. You play as a child princess, exploring and fight your way to the truth in a dream which turns proves to be more than a figment of imagination.
You move around in the game by literally flying across the world from very early in the game. There is not much of gameplay outside combat other than avoiding traps and trying to hit the enemies from behind to trigger a ‘sneak attack’. Most of the enemies are optional but you’d want to fight them as frequently as possible to gain valuable experience which will come in real handy during the game’s much tougher boss fights.
The combat is Turned-interruption-based. There is a timeline bar on the bottom of the screen and every action takes a fixed amount of time to perform. The bar is towards the right is split into ‘casting region’, which is the envelopes the time it takes for player as well as the enemies to perform their move. The idea here is to hit your enemies while they are casting so you ‘interrupted’ them.  Meaning they not only be able to perform their action, but they are also sent back a few notches behind the timeline, opening the window of opportunity for you to attack.
I was not very familiar with this type of combat mechanics as a result I died quite a few times during boss fights. I asked around and to many people they found the game very easy on the ‘advanced or normal’ difficulty I played on. I had to grind to level up in order to defeat the final boss, so again I suggest to engage in all encounters. There is no drawback to losing to an encounter, you simply start with a full health and mana at the beginning of the section or whenever there was a checkpoint.  So the difficulty really depends on how familiar you are with this type of game.
There are certain things I didn’t like about the game though. I feel the combat system doesn’t relay a lot of the vital information to the player. For example, you do not know the health of the enemies nor do you know which type of elemental stuff you have your team equipped. This means you are forced to memorize how you distributed your equipment and cannot make a well-timed final blows with no stats to look after. This especially hurts in the boss fights where the margin of error is very thin. Also the crafting is also not very well explained. You basically equip elemental attacks and defenses by equipping specific colored gems. You can also combine gems to create a different colored one. The game does not really explain which colors are possible to craft. So it is possible for a lot of players to go through half the game without knowing a certain gem color exists. I suggest you look into a guide just to make sure you get caught up with all the colors so you can equip your team with more organized attacks and defenses.
I am not a fan of Ubisoft as a whole, but this is a side of Ubisoft I really admire. In the end I feel the game could have been a more rounded experience if they had more time and budget. A lot of effort had gone into making this game visually spectacular, unfortunately it meant the core mechanics of the game suffered and stretched a bit too thin for my taste. In the end these drawbacks can be frustrating, but does not detract much from the beautiful experience this game delivers.

Amazing game, probably one of the best multiplayer experiences I've had this past year. It's a projectile fighter, so your aim is to hit the opponent with a projectile (in this case, a ball). Simple, right? Well, you have different ways to hit the ball, directions you can aim it, and specials specific to your character that make each matchup intense. Games can be over in a second once the ball starts moving fast, or even in the first ten seconds if you play right or predict your opponents' moves. There's immense satisfaction in each return, and the game really excites you with the euphoria of good returns mixed with the  rush and fear if your opponent somehow still returns the ball that you just shot at him at 10000 mph. It's sort of similar to in the projectile match between Link and Ganon in the Legend of Zelda, except you die if you screw up once. There's a few game modes that you can switch between, and there are some options to tweak your matches. The options are a little limited, but honestly, the game is so fun that you won't really even need to switch things around to have a great time. Definitely check this out sometime!
With online play: I have had some problems with online battles with friends (game freezing up after stage select, player randomly disconnecting after game), but none of these problems were fixed in under a minute and didn't occur that often. Local play is also supported and is a blast!
