Call of Juarez: The Cartel (just "Cartel" from now on) is one of those shooters that was a product of the times, or even slightly behind the times, and tried to meld a Western motif onto "modern day" (early 2000's, after 9/11) US Mexican border. This is a "modern" shooter where instead of hunting for health packs, just hide for a little while to regenerate your health (theres' not even a health meter). However, there is no cover system. It's side-strafing all the way.
The back story is the DEA office in LA got bombed, and the DOJ arranged for a DEA guy, an FBI girl, and a LAPD veteran to for an interagency task force to find out who did it, then one of the dead agent's daughter had a message from his dead father... So she's a witness... The trio each had their own agenda they try to accomplish without revealing to their two partners. As the investigation takes them from barrios of LA to border to desert to Mexican estates, they get to shoot their way through a TON of bad guys of various types, from simple gangbangers all the way up to mercenaries. And sometimes, they even have to deal with heavy enemy support... like gunships.
To do that, you get your standard arsenal, from pistols and revolvers to SMGs, assault rifles, shotguns, and even light machine guns. However, you can only keep two pistols and one long gun. To make things simple, all pistols use the same ammo, and all rifles use the same ammo, even though in real life they use different calibers. And yes, you can dual-wield the single-hand weapons like pistols and light SMGs. It's fun to do so, as you'll have two triggers (mouse left and mouse tright) for separate guns.
The "Concentration mode" (i.e. Matrix slo-mo) is back, where basically time slows down so you can kill bad guys by pumping them full of lead before they can react. There are also various "breach" scenarios where your team line up on the door and at the signal, bust in, and in slow-mo, shoot everybody that has a gun. (Yes, there are often civilians, and you get an award if you don't cause collateral damage by end of campaign).
One of the factors that sets Cartel apart are the driving sequences... where you get to drive the car, dodging traffic, and if you're not driving, you can hang out the window and shoot at bad guys. If necesary, that is. There is a mission where you need to tail another car, not too close, not too far. (And don't run over civilians)  But often, you need to chase enemy vehicle while dodging things left and right, and sometimes, you just need to get away.
Another thing that sets Cartel apart is the fact that this is a 3 player co-op shooter... In "single player" you play with two AI bots. if you have multiplayer set two buddies join you to shoot your way through bad guys. There's also competitive mode online. It's basically the same game instead of completely separate SP vs. MP map levels.
As mentioned before, each member of the team has their own personal agenda, and often will get calls or reminders about where their ultimate loyalty lies, and have "secret agenda" on missions, as well as try to sneak some evidence, money, or such "found" on various parts of the mission. And they have to do so without being seen by their partners, making it tense. This is how the character gain "XP" for levels to unlock additional weapons,  in fact. So you have to explore a little.
The story is actually better than the average shooter. There's no "foozle", just a lot of guys with guns, and each guy has their own motivation to "do the right thing", which may not be THE right thing.
The hardware requirements are strange. I can play COJ: Gunslinger with no problem, but somehow Cartel felt slower. At least the bots know how to conduct themselves.
All in all, COJ: The Cartel is a hard break from the "Western" roots of COJ. There are some tie-ins but ultimately it felt really weak. The shooters are not bad, and 15 levels ain't bad for co-op, but it's not exactly a shining sample of how shooters *should* be done. I applaud them of trying to break new ground, but the execution seems to lack that "must keep playing" feeling. It's recommended, but only if it's at bargain bin level prices.

- Unfinished: the game got released when its development wasn't finished yet. It is technically horrible, with dull graphics, many bugs and audio issues. Expect frustrating moments.
- The main menu and the first levels are dull (luckily the game gets slightly better and more interesting afterwards).
- The gunplay, the driving and grenades.
- No drop-in joining (players can only join your co-op match at the start of a level).

I fully admit, when I first went into it, I thought I would absolutely hate Neptunia. On the surface, it's everything I hate in one neat little package. But oh boy, was I wrong.
The story of the game is about the console war, which as the name alone might have given away, is essentially just one big spoof of the console war between different video game console owners on the internet. Each console is represented by their own goddess, which is just a cute girl version of said console. I think this alone speaks volumes for the very lighthearted and goofy tone and story the game has. The game is very self aware, and knows that it isn't a new Final Fantasy, and it never pretends to be anything else, and I appreciate this aspect quite a lot. Even if one is bothered by this, which I can fully understand why one would be, the developers were kind enough to make it possible to skip dialogue with but the push of a button. Nifty, right?
One of the first things that really struck me about the game was the surprisingly colorful and pretty environments you move around in during the gameplay segments. Enemy designs are equally cheerful and colorful, all of this goes very well with the very happy and fun tone the game is constantly aiming for. Unfortunately, it reuses these assets pretty heavily, to the point where some areas can be the same map but in reverse, and a lot of enemies are simply recolors of earlier enemies.
The flipside of the reused assets problem is that they use it to make sure there's a somewhat massive amount of things to actually do in the game, at least. You'll constantly be unlocking new sidequests, new plans that require you to gather new materials so you can unlock new items, areas or maybe even gameplay changes. There's even a coliseum asking you to fight various difficult battles in exchange for very good items.
Speaking of battles, the battle system is actually what mainly made me enjoy the game as much as I did. The combat starts out as simple turn based fights with a lot of emphasis on positioning, similar to the Legend of Heroes games. As the game goes on, more and more features are added on to the combat giving it more and more depth. It never goes so far as to become complex or particularly deep though, it adds "just enough". Some examples are special attacks, transformations and a pair system. Just enough to keep the combat fresh and entertaining, as personally I'm a sucker for the very over the top and flashy special attack animations.
To summarize things; Hyperdimension Neptunia Re;Birth is a simple and fun game that never really aims or pretends to be much more than that. If you're looking for a just solid and lighthearted JRPG then this game might be one of your best bets on Steam. Don't judge a book by it's cover, as I initially did, because you just might end up missing out on a pretty good game due to it.

This took me way back and I mean WAYYYY back.
Grey Goo - Thats not a name I would of expected of a old school RTS however its aptly named considering the story behind it.
Faction Gameplay - Overall you have 3 unique races, the beta's focus on expansion while the humans focus on fortification and the grey goo...well they do everything.
Overall the human faction will have you feeling most at home if you love turtling up and making impenetrable bases just like the old C&C series though expanding was an option back then im betting like me most of you turtled built up a massive force and just overwhelmed your opponent haha. Funnily enough the human faction seems more alien than human or rather far more advanced than we'd actually consider to be possible so dont be suprised if you feel less human when playing haha

The beta's will claim victory through rapid expansion their ability to maximis the use of their production through tech addons and various other extra's which allow you to spread across the map at a rapid pace will make you love them they are extremely adaptable, it will take some getting used to of couse as it might not be something you're used too however once you get the hang of it you'll enjoy every minute of it. The beta's are essentially closer to human than the human faction although obviously they are not, they use bullets, shells etc all the things you'd find in mondern day humanity but with much more advanced tech, think of them as us but within the next 200 years.
The grey goo.. well, they or rather "it" is the most interesting Faction Ive encountered in an RTS in a long time and they can do 1 thing that nobody else can...scale cliffs and mountains...you start off with the mother goo and essentially just divide, divide, divide until you have such a large force and so many reasources that you overwhelm your opponent. If you love the idea of just completely and utterly dominating your enemy through sheer numbers and doing rediculous flanking maneuvers over mountain tops where the enemy can barely touch you, you should play the as the goo. The goo are well... the most unique life forms in the game, they are many but one at the same time I suppose if you said they are legion that would be a fair and valid description. If you ever wanted to be flubber from the 90s movie this is probably the closest you'll get although you aren't green and you arent bouncing around 24/7 haha, generally if you want a unique gameplay experience then you'll have that with the goo.
Campaign - Ill try not to give any spoilers here;
You get to play as 3 factions but all bundled up into one story  you transition from one to the other learning more and more about the entire story. I actually appauled this form of story telling, simply because it allows the continuity of the story to flow quite fluently without any contradictions or plotholes though im sure there could be one or two I havent actually played through all of it so far so I wouldn't know. However overall you start off as the beta's then play as the humans then the goo so dont expect to start off as whomever you want it doesnt work like that.
you start off as the Beta's who are explorers they are simply looking for new life and new civilizations - very star trek, Im looking at you old westwood peeps.  Anywho as they were "exploring" their scientific abilities they created a "hole" (gah trying to limit my description due to spoilers is not fun), this let something through something they thought they had escaped when infact it was something far different and confusing than they had ever thought possible, from there you discover quite a bit and learn about the enemy you have been fighting and then just when you think your day couldnt possibly get worse, well... you get the picture.
I appologise wholeheartedly for the poor description of the story but im loving the game so much right now i dont want to spoil it for anyone else.
Multiplayer - I havent actually played the multiplayer yet but if you just have a glance at my description of the game play you will find a similar answer for the multiplayer. Very unique, very diverse and quite enjoyable enough said.
If I could Rate this game 10 out of 10? - I would give this game a 10, If you loved the old C&C style games, if you loved base building and expanding to get more reasources, if you loved building massive armies and decimating your opponent with them then this game is for you. Oh and the stories pretty good too :)
note to the old westwood employees: WE LOVE YOU, for the love of god go nuts with this and buy back your C&C franchise and bring back the C&C series too glory! If you can make a brand new game this good then you can do that with C&C!

****This game does not support Windows 10 & DirectX 12****
****Stay clear if you have this system****
Let me start off by saying that I enjoyed the gameplay and the game itself. It was a remarkable and entertaining game, filled with several hours of fun. That is to say, before it stopped working.
I was able to start the game back in March and played for 2 1/2 hours before stopping, thoroughly enjoying the gameplay I had. However, it was not meant to be.
This game suffers from a tremendous error associated with its files related to DirectX. After updating my PC to Ryzen and re-installing I found out about the bug as it was right around the timeframe Windows 10 released the Summer update. Essentially, the DirectX files in the game are for DirectX 10 released in 2015. Windows has now updated these files and released a newer version with DirectX 12. As such, the game will open to a blank white screen with its icon invisible in the icon tray. If you click to exit the game, it says "This Program is not Responding" and force closes. Never opening the game. I have reinstalled the Dx files from the folder, changedt he game to windowed mode, tried compatibility, reinstalled and tried numerous other troubleshooting methods prior to contatcing Konami. Upon contacting me, they emailed me back a robo-reply for 2 weeks, only once asking for followup by providing my dx data to them. Suddenly one day the replies stopped, no reason given.
I contacted Konami's chat desk after this. They told me "The issue is the game is incompatible with Widnows 10. I'm sorry, I'll forward this to the development team." And left it alone. That was a while back. This game has less than no support, they have stopped updating it so this issue will never be fixed likely.
Even worse, I have partnered with others in the forums to seek out a fix and Konami literally told one of them to uninstall DirectX 12 and keep only DirectX 9 & 10 on the computer to fix it. That is not a solution or patch to ask us to downgrade the system, nor is it even a working patch most likely.
As such, I cannot recommend this game while it has no support and stands so heavily broken without repair. If Konami actually fixes it, I'll re-evaluate. Like I said, I liked it, but if you have Windows 10, don't play. It will break at some point.

I got this game as a big Game of Thrones fan (Books and show). I also adored the first season of Telltale's Walking Dead. I expected the same level of emotional attatchment, loss and game changing plot twists as the Walking Dead product.
Not so much.
The game plays the same way the WD does. It has an artistic rendering making you feel as though you are playing through a comic book, but very quickly it begins to feel as if the decisions you make will have little influence on the overall plot. In the WD in the first episode there is a moment where you have to choose between saving one person or another and that choice will impact who you have by your side for the next three episodes. There seems to be no such choices here. There are often times where you have to pick an allegiance to one friend/lord/house or another, but by the end of the episode a third-party event occurs that seems to take precedent over all those decisions. I will give you an example, so *SPOILER*
Episode 1 a member of your family is at the capital and has to decide whether siding with Queen Cerci or siding with Margery will best give your house an opportunity to still sell your most valuable resource. You have to make some decisions that feel as though they will be game changing about who you are going to help. Yet no matter which way you go within 2 minutes of this tense situation Tyrion comes up and offers to buy your family's resource. Seriously. The game wastes no time in slapping you in the face with the knowledge that your choices really don't matter.
The characters are well developed and the voice acting is spot-on. However this is less of a decision-oriented game and more of a slightly interactive couple episodes of Game of Thrones. If you are a big GOT fan then it might be worth $10, but no more.

HBO and Telltale missed a great opportunity here. They could have considered using the decisions players made in this game to feature in later installments of their TV show. Just imagine if your choices mattered that much to the series which probably made you buy the game in the first place.
That being said, Telltale once again made me want to believe the lie they're selling. Your choices DON'T matter to how the story ends but by all the gods of narrative do they matter to YOU. It does make a difference if Ethan stands his ground against Ramsay Bolton or meekly swallows his insults in the same way as a passionate love affair or casual one night stand could still produce the same child. It is an illusion of meaningful choice but you get to chose the illusion which feels right to you and in making that choice you get a fair share of entertainment for your money.
On a technical side the game looks nice and at times even pretty but as many other commenters pointed out the movement animations are clunky and can be a major factor in breaking immersion.
All in all this leaves a game which is a must-buy to a fan of the series because if you buy into the fantasy world of Game of Thrones you will feel good about accepting the lie that is every Telltale game out there. Should you be unfamiliar with the GoT universe then you might feel left alone and many lose ends become apparent and minor plot holes widen to chasms of disorientation in a world which after all is easy to get lost in.

This game is not as bad as everyone says it is. But it is one of the worst sequels of all time.
I love the Call of Juarez franchise: the first one was good, "Bound in Blood" was great and "Gunslinger" is a fantastic FPS. But where does "The Cartel" stand?
The story starts in a very mediocre way, following a police officer, a DEA officer and a FBI agent as they try to bring down the Mexican Cartel's operations in Los Angeles. The first levels are as dull as they can get, but as time goes on, there are multiple scenarios that are quite engaging: car chases through cities, shootouts in rainy docks...
The only link to the other CoJ games are the police officer (a relative of Ray McCall) and some levels set in Juarez.
The gameplay is really mediocre: the guns are recoil-less and they feel all the same. There isn't the dynamic cover like in  "Bound In Blood", and the special ability is your typical bullet-time. The three characters are identical, if not for tiny little differences (again, unlike "Bound In Blood"): McCall has more accuracy with pistols, DEA with shotguns, FBI with rifles.
The graphics are okay, but the worst parts are the FOV that can't be changed and the Depth of Field that works like♥♥♥♥♥(and can't be turned off). The Graphic Options are♥♥♥♥♥♥poor (unlike "Bound in Blood" xD), but you will get used to these issues after a while (2 hours max).
Overall, this game is a really bad sequel, and definitely worse compared to "Bound In Blood". However, the action setpieces, great voice acting and longevity.

A great viking saga. This is one of those games that you really need to view as a sum of its parts to get the most out of it, because there isn't any one particular thing that it excels at. Rather, it's concerned with creating an engrossing, evocative experience the sucks you into its world and makes you care about the struggles of the characters you're following.
Before you get into this one, be forewarned that it opens pretty weak. The story begins by following a group of side characters rather than the main cast, and for the first half of the game the narrative is routinely interrupted by hopping back and forth between two different stories unfolding on opposite sides of the map. The Banner Saga wanders into a lot of the problematic tropes of epic fantasy early on -- too many characters, too many places, too many concepts, too many exotic names, and a narrative that jumps around rather than remaining tight and focused while the audience warms up to the setting.
That being said, once you get over the initial hurdle of these problems The Banner Saga becomes an engrossing experience with likeable, down-to-earth characters, a rich and well developed world, and player choices that carry a hefty amount of weight behind them. The combat is fun, but it's probably a good thing the game doesn't rely too heavily on it, since once you figure out the "trick" it's somewhat easy to exploit the mechanics to your advantage in a weird way that probably wasn't intended.
It's really the caravan mechanics that shine in how well they support the narrative, however, with dwindling supplies, low morale, and dying followers all putting pressure on the player to make decisions that they perhaps wouldn't were their situation less dire. This becomes exceptionally well paced toward the end of the game, where previously bountiful resources dwindle away to almost nothing as you approach the last leg of your journey.
Rough around the edges in some respects, but ultimately The Banner Saga has a lot of heart and passion that shines through despite the flaws, making for a compelling saga that always drew me in every time I sat down with it. Definitely woth a look for those who enjoy gripping narratives and turn-based tactical RPG gameplay.

First I should make it known that I have had the game prior to steam and have well over 5000 Hours logged (Albeit mostly AFK)
While it may not be for everyone this game is very immersive, my first few days were filled with a constant stream of "wow this game has ____! Thats incredible!"  My first experience was back in December and the moment it started snowing and the snow accumulated on the ground had me shocked for what I at the time was just considering a cheap B2P MMO purchased on a whim.  It has now since become my main MMO taking the throne from Guild Wars 2 as my favorite MMO to play.
The combat is varied and every class plays differently and you can find something to fill the play style you want.  It's also gorgeous and has plenty of non-combat progression with 10 Life skills to master and atleast 2 in the works, one of which being rock climbing, which after reaching the highest ranks will allow the player to scale castle walls.  Even if you never touch combat there is plenty here.  And vis a versa if you never touch life skilling there is still plenty of gameplay just bashing mobs into a pulp with a stiker or watching the world burn as a Wizard.  And if you tire of one there is always the other.
The World is also pretty massive taking a good while to cross the map from end to end even with a good horse and a fast boat.  There are so many places to see while many hidden little gems like waterfalls and calm lakes off the beaten path. If you just go out and look around you'll find some great vistas to enjoy.
It isn't without it's share of negative aspects, if you want story, at the moment it may be best to make up your own.  If thats something you prefer anyway then congrats no story to shoehorn into your charactors back story.  Currently there is no traditional Raid or Dungeon content, though "Dungeons" do exsist they are an open to all instance and have no narrative tied to them.  End game grind spots can also be limited though upcoming content could change that, currently it's best if you hate Pirates and militia because those are two of the primary enemies you will be destroying after hitting level 56 if you desire to level further.
PvP is fun from my rather limited experience and I can see it being something the more competitive would enjoy.
Currently the lag can be bad around daily check-in but on NA servers I don't notice it all that often.
The game is also NOT P2W, it's at best Pay for convenience and the Pearl shop can be avoided.  If you never spoil yourself with Value packs I feel it would be totally do able without any real life transactions.  That being said I have spent money in game.

Personally, in hindsight, I really didn't like this game too much. Why the 60+ hours then? Because I'm a farming freak. I literally spend around 30 of those 60 hours farming up lvs and items. So why did I not like it?
-Dungeons and enemies are reused. There are only around 8 unique dungeons and maybe 40 enemies. The rest are reskins.
-Hard to get started. The guide given is pretty confusing and you can't change the controls. It took me 15 minutes to figure out how to jump, half an hour to figure how to acess the menu, and I didn't firgure out until halfway through the game how to activate HDD mode.
-Acessories are basically useless. They really don't change character's apperances much. All dresses look the same physically, they're just recolorings. And even then, the recolorings aren't that noticable. I mean, from light green to dark green? not much. There are only a few that I actually noticed, like nep's carrot one. Also, IF doesn't have any dresses >:(
-Status effects don't do anything. Poision is really annoying. Oh wait, no it isn't. Why? Because none of the enemies inflict it on you. And when they do, it really doesn't do anything. And in turn, it's basically useless against enemies. Oh, 1/16th of their health right? So that would be useful against enemies with large amounts of hp right? nope, not really. Mainly because most tanks in this game have hp regens which esentially cancel out the poison. Virus and that no-sp moves one are basically useless too. I mean, I usually played with Compa, IF, and Nep, so most of the time, they were hit with somethign that didn't affect them. Maybe If you played with an all-godess loatout, virus would affect you a bit, but NONE OF THE BOSSES INFLICT VIRUS. Serously, the only time you use HDD is against a boss, so what's to point of having virus when it doesnt affect the player.
The only effect that actually affected me was pralysis. That one was good. I could use it against enemies, and they could use it against me.
-Good plot? Wtf are you talking about. The plot is not intresting in any way, shape, or form. Serously, you could get better plot out of those shovel animes they make just for money. There's no character development, one plot twist which wasnt even that intresting, and on top of all that, You don't even get to know 1/2 the playable characters. Boxer girl? ninja girl? That one with the giant ball which looks like that maurzill pokemon or whatever? Some of them met Nep before, which I'm guessing was a prequel, but we never even got to know why they're here or how they got here. (unless it was explained after the final boss battle, since I never finished that fight.)
-ehhh BGM. The BGM in this game isn't all that amazing. You coud probably hear all the songs within 30 minutes of playing the game. Also, none of it is really memorable. Zelda's theme song? can play it right here for you. Classic FF's? yep. Skyrim's? Yep. HDP's? ehhh... Not really...  The only sound I can remember is that annoying beeping sound whenever you get sneak attacked, which brings me to my next point
-Symbol attacks and sneak attacks dont really do anything. Serously, All they do is change who goes first. I mean, If you have that one add-on, you can avoid fights, but most players usually just run past the enemies anyway. Completely useless.
And here's my biggest complaint. The hardware system.
Serously. WHAT. THE. ♥♥♥♥.
There is ABSOLUTELY NO POINT AT ALL to incuding this system in the game. First of all, the connection to the godesses and computers isn't even all that clear. The most sufficent point we got was "Oh, they live in a video game world, oh wait we didn't even say that, we just said that the world they live in is called game-something (Already forgot the name)". Whenever I was playing the game, I was constantly worring about how much space I had left. "Should I get this? I only have 1256 GB left though..." I literally played through th game without getting 90% of the main upgrades. The only ones I got were the exp up, the gold up, jump height up, the colluseaum, and no dmg restriction.  In the end, I ended up having some 800 GB (or was it MB? can't remember) left. I'm just completely confused why they would implement this into the game, besides increasing playtime and frustrating the players who got everything as soon as they got the plan and ending up with no space left. The plan system was good though. I liked that.
Ok, so enough with the hating, this game does have some good points right?
Let's see....
-Cute characters! I mean, they are pretty cute. Not much else to say.
-Humor? I guess... It was kinda funny, but I can't remember any special moments where I actually laughed. Probably forgot em all.
-Oooh! I know! The battle system was pretty fun! I liked the ideas and concepts behind them, but It took me half the game to figure out all the options. I didn't know how to add the 4th move until I got to Neo-Volcano. And yes, I did read the guides, but they explained WHAT the fourth move was, but not how to add them.
-The animations were pretty good
-Oh, here's a big one. I liked the refrences they put in, like MAGES:Steins;Gate and.. there was another big one, but I forgot what it was.
-Voice acting on the japanese side was pretty good. Can't say much for the english side since I didnt use it.
Overall, If you want cute asthetics and don't care much for gameplay, buy it. If you actually care about gameplay in a game (which you should), don't buy it. It's a waste of time and money.

Black Desert Online took me by surprise. It's mmorpg - sandbox type of game, if you like to grind, grind and grind mobs for money and lvls this game is for you. Otherwise this game has a deep lifeskill system, with hunting, trading, fishing, prossessing, just to name a few, which keep you hooked to the game. You can afk and profit also, there are several ways to make money while doing nothing like afk fishing, afk trading, prossessing, etc. Which means you could take a break from the game and play another or just leave the pc running while you watch your favorite tvshow. Keep in mind this game has no proper fast travel, which means you will spend some time riding your horse/camel/elephant/donkey to your destination, but it helps with immersion and making the world feel big. If your thing is questing, this game has thousands of those, altho not voice lined.
There are rumors about this game being P2W, which is not really the case. There are ways to make money in game with real money but you would have to put thousands and thousands of euros/dollars to even compete with one/two hours of killing mobs in the best spots.
Fair warning, BDO suffers from lag on weekends and after work hours due to higher player base because of the steam players arrival. They are working on it, but it's really annoying if you can only play on weekends. Also there's a problem with steam achievements at this time, they don't really update. I should have about 15 or 20 achievements done put I only have 4. That's about the only big complaints I have about this game.
Keep in mind that this game is really complicated to learn due to lack of tutorials and how deep all the systems work. You will need hundreds of hours just to have a good feeling of it. Personally after 600hours I still havent touched a big portion of the game but that's also one of the reasons that I wanna keep playing because there's always something to learn.
I recommend new players to find a guild as fast as possible to have players to which you can ask questions to.
Hope this helped, see you in game. ;)

You are the commander of a star ship, travelling from planet to planet, while being hunted by rebels, which forces you to proceed to the next star system after a certain amount of turns.
On every planet you visit, something will happen, may it be good or bad for your progress.
On the positive side, this is one of the better developed and thought out games i have played.
Everything is well explained and learnt fast, while the game itself requires tough decisions and much planning.
Additionaly, the replayability is high, since theres lots of stuff to unlock, universes are randomly created, and with the currently released, free expansion, everything has expanded.
On the negative side, randomness plays a bigger role in this game than strategy
(which means, that no matter how hard you think and plan- you WILL lose. Not always, but too often to speak of a skill based game, and often enough, to make playing a frustrating experience, at least for me. In my personal oppinion, a good game should be always winable).
Every event, and the game relies on them, is randomly chosen, so you might as well be lucky or screwed from the beginning, which took out a lot of fun for me.
(One example: In the second star system, after careful playing and doing well so far, i got to a planet where all shields are disabled and was attacked. The enemy ship used a drone, which damaged my ships systems significantly, so that i wasnt able to charge my engines and flee, while the enemy ship fired with laser and beam weapons, which damaged my ship further and caused fire. I ended up getting destroyed, with no chance of success).
I really wished there was more room for personal influence, than no choice (being attacked) or a/b  choices, which lead to a) (move on) nothing or b) (stay) being attacked or encounter a random event, all the time, where the player doesnt even know the chances of possible outcomes. Just make a decision and hope the best.
Additionaly, the game is extremely hard, to a degree where it seriously gets frustrating. Having to fight all the time, and getting hardly anything in return is no fun. You dont even get to prepare yourself, since the difficulty begins right from the start.
All in all, a very good idea and well developed, but suffering from a lack of refinement...

Clearly a game worthy of its price, reduction or not.
Pros :
- The game is surprisingly long. With that kind of game you would usually expect about 5 hours of lifetime. This one will take you approximately 15-20 hours to reach the end, unless you rush it like an idiot. If you like to complete games to 100%, you can add another 10 hours to that already long lifetime.
- The combat system is nice. It's strongly inspired from the one from Final Fantasy but with some extra mechanisms like the possibility to interrupt or be interupting during the casting time of an action, the possibility to slow down a specific opponent using your mouse, etc.
- The graphics are really sweet, colorful and yet sober.
- There are plenty of little things hidden here and there that will push you to explore every place in order to find them. These hidden things can be gemstones or various bonuses, poems or even new hidden characters that can join your group. This is something that we used to see a lot a decade ago in games like Zelda OoT and that we see less and less in nowadays videos games where exploration is not rewarding you.
Cons :
- Sometimes you have to solve enigmas by doing some specific actions to advance in the level. These enigmas are not bad, but they are very simple to solve and are rather redundant. Must of the time it's pushing/pulling a box to the right place or using your mouse to create a shadow on a wall and aim it at something.
- The gem combination system itself is nice, but the game doesn't provide enough information about it. You can hardly know what are the possible combinations unless you look them up on wikis or find them by luck.
- You're forced to install and use Uplay to play the game. I already have enough crap on my computer, I don't really like being forced to install another privacy invading game client that sucks extra RAM on my PC just to play a game. Steam is already enough.

An in depth review from a Baldur's Gate fan.
Expecting Baldur's Gate:
The BG experience: 3/10
Expecting a fun top-view rpg:
The game experience: 7/10
---------------------------------
To explain what I see as the Baldur's Gate experience: Diverse characters with histories, life challenges, current running problems, romances and the interaction between them, challenging your course of adventure. This in a well described world, history and all, creative as life and all under its current pressure and troubles. From a major storyline in this world, all in the game's context is derived. That means all that you see and experience makes sense. The combat system and all of its components must fit this world (classes, spells, weapon types, etc. all have a history and are explained by their fit and are as diverse as the environment demands it - as in perilous times with undead swarms are bound to push some clerics to figure out some new spells ) The better it all fits together, the higher the immersion.
Divinity: Original Sin has beautiful areas, has some nice AI going for some social appearance and reactions and has some fair dialogues here and there. Yet, nothing feels really serious. It is more like a collection of story fragments, sometimes switching between ingame context and player experience context.
The layout of the world and the flow through the areas are too formulated. There's just 'stuff' to do, for the sake of the player to be active. Fortunately, they made it really good, technically and visually. The way puzzles are integrated is mostly supply driven and mechanical, using options through good programming against a strong engine. Without thinking like: 'what kind of people live in this town, to combine their efforts to scape the surrounding land into active puzzles that don't really make sense other than having travellers walk silly willy lines and make them think twice of not bringing a mage to get to that chest that is clearly visible to the world of skeletons that seem to somehow always rise in positions relatively strategic to the barrels with verious types of damage which must have been obviously placed by high strength master stealth nearby citizens who may as well be standing nearby watching me go through their torment' the puzzels are enjoyable.
The combat system is not nearly as refined as good old ADND. Next, the setup of classes and their fit in the world is heavily affected by there being many puzzles and the turn based system. There is no real balance, though there is fun in creating powerhouses of characters and that is good for the challenge. With hard to beat balance, this would have contributed alot to replayability. The game soothes a bit with harder difficulty modes, but they do not force many new situations other than restricting you further using what you know is powerful. A top quality game follows 'easy to learn, hard to master', and here the game does not deliver. They did get a high quality custom turn-based combat system going and with that a very refreshing experience. If the game were more 'worldy', I'd have loved to see this system refine to balance.
So the game is not Baldur's Gate or an equivalent. As just a fun rpg that came along, it has fair music, plenty of models, little repetition, fun little stories, clickables and dragables everywhere and looks really good on top. The playability could be higher, the interface is sometimes annoying and unpolished. I think it is worth about 20 euros.

For the game itself, the gameplay is acceptable, decent even.
As this is a take on classic space invaders, you are shooting at enemies coming from the
top of the screen. you can move left, right, forwards and backwards.
That, excluding the inspired sprites, concludes the similarities to the base material.
Instead of having a static screen, the screen scrolls upwards with enemies coming from
every side. Some enemies can shoot, too, which fills the screen with loads of
enemies and bullets. If your defensethingy touches anything, you're dead.
Your ship constantly fires, which was a bit confusing at first, but considering
the loads of enemies on screen, you would not want to stop firing anyway.
Alternatively, you can press the fire button to concentrate your fire into a red
beam. Doing so will deplete your powergauge, but is also the only way to
destroy enemy-bullets. This is the must strategic feature in the game.
Come to think of it, I wonder why they bothered to base this on "Space invaders".
This is a bullet-hell shooter. And as a lowprice game itself, this might be fun for an hour.
As a game compared to the genre, this game clearly has some flaws.
First, the game is light on content, which is compensated in the price.
However, the full retail is still a bit much for a shooter wthout alternate modes
(or local multiplayer).
The Shooter-part is solid, but unimaginative. wiggeling left and right, shooting,
trying not to get hit. Not much more to it.
Speaking of trying not to get hit.
The goal in a good bullet-hell is to see patterns in enemy attacks you can navigate through.
That might not always be easy, but managable, with a clear visual distinction between enemies and
bullets, powerups and so forth.
That being said, the graphics and audio of this game were a dealbreaker for me.
Shooting your way though the walls on enemies unleashes lightning effects close to the
pain level of getting laser eye surgery on the white hot surface of the sun.
It's hard enough already to navigate to the random waves of enemies, bullets and powerups
that all seem way to simliar, it gets ten times harder when, everytime you hit anything,
your game screams "FLASHBANG" and scorches your retina with explosions of
white, blue and red.
Hell, I played Beathazard Ultra and this is the first instance I needed to squint my eyes
to avoid agonizing pain.
Also, the technosoundtrack is a bit heavy for my taste, but whatever.
Considering all of this, I would recommend this game for the discounted price, you'll get
a fun hour out of it.
For full retail and as a shooter in general, there are far better titles you can play.
And considering this might be the last thing you see before your eyes are torched
beyond oblivion (and hyperspace, i guess), you might reconsider.

To start off, I've only finished this on nomal (both ironman and not ironman) and have played the DLC's enough to review them. This review is for the base game only.
SO. Aliens invade the Earth, and a council of many major nations get together to fund and kickstart the XCOM project. This is basically a load of elite soldiers, engineers, scientists, and comms people grouped together, with you as their commander. From the very start it looks as though the aliens have incredible technology, weapons, and abilities - far more advanced than your's. However, as the game progresses, you'll soon catch up, as you attempt to turn the tables...
The combat is turn-based, with a simple to use system to use for moving your soldiers around, and shooting bad guys. On top of this, the use of items, hunkering down, overwatching and other various things unlock as your soldiers rank up, after some missions. It really is tense as you hunt around for groups of enemies, knowing that moving up any of your troops could move up, spot some enemies, and watch them scramble for cover - ready to open fire once you've finished your turn.
As for the base building and management between missions - it's fantastic. You manage the amount of engineers and scientists, create new facilities, research into new fields of technology, and a huge amount more. With every day passing on the hologlobe map, you are constantly looking at the list of incoming events, wondering what will be done when, and what other possiblities it will open up.
- Although hints and an tutorial mission is included at the start, it leaves you to make your own choices and discover you and your enemies’ strengths and weaknesses.
- Very challenging, especially on difficulties over the normal difficulty setting.
- Extremely replayable, with fantastic mission/scenario generator. Many choices and options provide a different playthrough pretty much every time.
- Soundtrack is of great quality and is a joy to listen to. It is very fitting of the game's various circumstances.
- Bugs and glitches. Although much effort has been put in with patches, weird camera angles aren't exactly rare.
- Thin men.
To conclude, I think that XCOM: Enemy Unknown is an excellent turn based strategy game, that I thoroughly recommend to those looking for a gripping, progressive story, littered with new challenges around every corner. It is a game that will last many, many hours, and provide dozens of hours of entertainment with it's randomly generated missions and scenarios, and tremendous replay value.

If you're the kind of person who seeks the social approval of those around you in regards to what sort of games you play, you should probably turn back now, as the whole point of this game is not to be taken too seriously. Re;Birth 1 is a niche JRPG that clearly knows its audience, and the premise is extremely silly - four goddesses referencing Sega, Playstation, Xbox and Nintendo fight over a land called Gamindustri through the power of shares, and the constant video game and anime references are usually genuine and funny, although sometimes also forced and cheesy. I often found myself crumbling into laughter out of nowhere simply due to the absurdity of the overall situation I was in. Aside from its charm and humor, nothing particularly stands out about Re;Birth 1, but it's still an addicting game with decent overall mechanics.
You'll spend a fair portion of your time with the dialogue sections between the characters, all of which are fully voice acted presuming you use the Japanese voiceovers. With English however, only some scenes have voice acting and its quality is lower overall, thus I made the switch from English to Japanese about halfway through my first playthrough. You won't find anything particularly deep or engaging in this story, but it's bound to get you into a good mood with its themes and humor. The goddesses are charming with each having their own distinct traits, and some of the jokes catch you completely off guard, like one of the default equips for the Xbox referencing goddess being a ring that has a red glow to it with only three fourths lit.
The gameplay itself revolves around leveling up, gathering items and fighting various monsters in simple dungeons for easily obtainable drops to unlock items, equipment, optional dungeons and new powerful enemies as well as to modify the game mechanics. All of these actions use up points called MB, as in memory, which you can only get a limited amount of on each playthrough. However, the game has a New Game+ system that always carries over everything you've bought or unlocked except key items, letting you regain MB every time while still retaining all your unlocks. Unfortunately, many dungeons and monsters use the exact same layouts and models respectively, sometimes with slight variations, making the otherwise unique and charming game lean too much towards quantity over quality. Still as a result, the sheer amount of things to unlock and the need to gather items and drops from different places and monsters combined with the pacing of the story keeps the gameplay fairly addicting.
The battle system is turn based and relatively simple. You've got your elements, ailments, buffs and debuffs along with three types of attacks including ones that quickly build up your special meter called the EXE meter, ones that do the most damage and ones that deplete the opponent's guard meter, causing them to take more damage when its empty. You also have special moves that use dedicated points called SP, and powerful EXE drive moves that use the EXE meter mentioned earlier. You can also freely position yourself within a specific area and most of your attacks have an area of effect, being able to hit several enemies at once. At the end of the day though, you'll generally be maximizing your EXE meter build for constant EXE drive usage along with occasional buffs and debuffs, and that's about it. The combat loses a lot of its potential due to the imbalances of the system.
All in all Re;Birth 1 is an alright game. It lacks polish, and having more unique dungeon and monster designs as well as balancing out the battle system would have helped overcome that issue. Still, I can recommend this game to those RPG fans who already know they like this kind of stuff and are willing to look past these flaws, as well as people who are looking for something new and quirky since the premise of the game alone can be very refreshing.

I was wondering where all the RTS games where, starting to get depressed because maybe nobody will even try making one ever again in this mess of cruddy, half made sack of empty promises of early access games on here, but then, this game popped up! and I was like 'oh god finally someone made a RTS game that looks decent!'. I waited for a sale, got the game and ended up with a... very shallow and dull RTS game sadly. I wish I could say this game is RTS of the year but it really can't be, there are so many other RTS games that do the genre so much better, this game wears itself thin extreamly fast and offers nothing new to have fun with, its a pretty, bog standard, run of the mill, every day pair of socks RTS game. =/ And yes it's pretty, it has a great graphics style going for it and good visuals but that's sadly the only thing I can say it does well and everyone that plays games knows the game mechanics and gameplay are always more important, that's where the soul and fun of the game is.
Was I expecting something original in an RTS game? I guess not, but since ive already done the RTS grind a million times in other games, build orders, favourite units, favourite play styles to finish the enemy base off, favourite faction ect this just sadly feels like the same old RTS grind, but not in a fun way. Why tho? I believe it's becuase of variety and depth. The fact of the matter is there hardly is any, you end up using some units to your play style and not using any of the others generally cas they just plain suck, are too micro intensive, or don't fit your playstyle so what you end up with is 3 or 4 units you actually like to attack with and that... really is not that interesting is it? Sure there are technologies that add some additional cool things to your units as well, that adds depth right? No not really, most of the techs for all factions are very situational or are for very specific playstyles, it takes alot of trial and error to find ones that don't actually suck... oh and yea the tech limit only allowing you to take one out of each of the five slots, that's just annoying! if I could take all the upgrades even if it was one at a time my units might actually feel like they are getting strong enough to do something. Also their is one resource in this game that you have to manage, yes, just one, and generally it's automated once you get the harvester down leaving the player to sit back and do nothing but watch until they get enough income to actually do anything with... so engaging! yay.
Generally the stragety of this game is, build big base -> build lots of units -> attack -> lose them all to defenses -> attack with more units - > if they die just spam more units -> win. Yea it's litterly that simple that a brain dead monkey could do it, every time, that's how I won, ultimatly the only way to win is just spam units at the enemy, the good ones that is, not the weak crappy ones that would take years to kill anything. =/ And thats for -every- faction, you can be sneaky and go around to the back of the base and case chaos sure, but generally that fails or takes forever. You can try spam artillery at the base sure, that sometimes work, oh how about spamming some stealth units at the base and sneak in and take out their economy!. How about spam some air units at them that should do some damage! nope not really, air units take forever to do anything having to come all the way back to base to reload and are shot down super easily, you see where im going with this? There are ultimate end game units tho yea! you could just charge one at the enemy base and assume it will go great and you will win yay, that works too but it takes years to build one of those so you may as well just spam combat units anyway, plus it's... not even slightly fun, does it sound like fun? Just sitting there right clicking buildings again and again to make it bomb them... They dont even feel that tough and powerful, kinda just like a giant dinky unit that slowly trudges along and does stuff and they all pretty much function in the same way for all factions so don't hope for variety with the ultimates either cas their really isen't any.
Just like almost every RTS game ever starting the base up and getting the economy takes awhile too, but in this game it seems to take forever! It took me a good 10-20 minutes or more especially with the Goo faction to get things going and it just feels like the game drags on forever... probably becuase there is just so little fun to find here. Man I wished this game was more fun... but it's really not, please take my word on it or at least be aware of unfortunate downsides I took the time to point out before buying or playing this game. =( If you get immediatly bored of this game in the first 2 hours then just get a refund, it's an extreamly expensive game for how little content it has so your only doing yourself a favor. I wish the devs the best and hope they are able to make better games from this and grow but this was just so dissapointing and boring for me. I don't really think there is any way they can make this game feel like a fun, deep RTS now that it seems fully built but maybe they can if they added a butt load more mechanics, units and maybe a couple more factions, 3 factions is... again, very poor variety if you compared it to Supreme commander: Forged Alliance which is basically the ultimate RTS on steam still with how much depth it has and unit variety.
Once I finished single player I realized this game is just a really not fun waste of time, the game speed/pace is super slow by default and there is horrifyingly no way to speed up game time, why?! Every good RTS game lets you speed up time so the game goes at a pace that fits how intense you want it, the pacing could have been easily fixed with a speed setting so it's just a shame there isen't one to be found.
And for all these reasons I can't possible recommend this game for the price it's at, for as how well made and pretty it may be its a generic RTS borefest and I would highly recommend getting it at about 10-15 dollars at most or playing another RTS with more depth, they are out there just look. I rarely had any fun throughout the singleplayer campain and there is no way im going to touch mutliplayer since I hardly believe it will offer anything differant so it's already time to let this game sit in my steam libary and grow dust, such a shame. =/ Sadly is a 4.5/10 for me.

Black Desert Online took me by surprise. It's mmorpg - sandbox type of game, if you like to grind, grind and grind mobs for money and lvls this game is for you. Otherwise this game has a deep lifeskill system, with hunting, trading, fishing, prossessing, just to name a few, which keep you hooked to the game. You can afk and profit also, there are several ways to make money while doing nothing like afk fishing, afk trading, prossessing, etc. Which means you could take a break from the game and play another or just leave the pc running while you watch your favorite tvshow. Keep in mind this game has no proper fast travel, which means you will spend some time riding your horse/camel/elephant/donkey to your destination, but it helps with immersion and making the world feel big. If your thing is questing, this game has thousands of those, altho not voice lined.
There are rumors about this game being P2W, which is not really the case. There are ways to make money in game with real money but you would have to put thousands and thousands of euros/dollars to even compete with one/two hours of killing mobs in the best spots.
Fair warning, BDO suffers from lag on weekends and after work hours due to higher player base because of the steam players arrival. They are working on it, but it's really annoying if you can only play on weekends. Also there's a problem with steam achievements at this time, they don't really update. I should have about 15 or 20 achievements done put I only have 4. That's about the only big complaints I have about this game.
Keep in mind that this game is really complicated to learn due to lack of tutorials and how deep all the systems work. You will need hundreds of hours just to have a good feeling of it. Personally after 600hours I still havent touched a big portion of the game but that's also one of the reasons that I wanna keep playing because there's always something to learn.
I recommend new players to find a guild as fast as possible to have players to which you can ask questions to.

[2017]
As much as I hate on COH2, Neo-Relic and Sega's nightmarish DLC policy, COH2's multiplayer (2017) is as close to perfection of the RTS formula as I've seen.
This doesn't come easy, it took two years for Relic to finally throw off the yoke rock paper scissors that they've ruined themselves with ever since Homeworld 2 fifteen years ago (2003) Instead, they've come to grips with the community-balance solution which has adopted a more icefrog-esque system of strengthening everything instead of nerfing it to the ground. Relic's original game was rubber bullets and weather condition nonsense that made the game beautiful, but laughably slow. The reviews at the time reflect this - even mine highlighted how terrible the game was.
Two years of DLC and massive, sweeping balance patches later and we've got a fine example of engaging and often thrilling multiplayer mayhem. One of the few games that pulls off team play well (unlike Starcraft's 2v2-3v3-4v4, which is quite literally sitting in a corner and spamming battlecruisers/rays) Teamplay involves taking and holding the map, not simple economy. A system I whole-heartedly despised in games like DOW2 and COH1, the formula has been refined and the battlefields are skillfully crafted and shaped to promote interesting encounters.
Chokes are visible and valuable, but there's always chances and routes to flank and artillery options that aren't too strong, but strong enough to shake even the fortress-building Brits from digging in too heavily. Gone is the rock-paper-scissors gameplay that Relic has grown so fond of.
The battlefield changes. Trees are knocked over, walls crumble as shells impact them, explosives leave craters. A heavy enough vehicle will plow over the terrain and take everything with it, including buildings. An hour long match will look nothing like the last one simply because the map has been so flattened, so charred, so reduced to ruble that you will have to be improvising new battle lines constantly and moving your pieces in a beautiful tug of war. Very few games have made me so thrilled that I shout at my screen or hurry to type a command to an ally for reinforcements and very rarely does losing ever carry with it some bitter sting that other games do - if I lose, it's because I made a poor decision or over-reached my fragile supply lines that resulted in a costly defeat. I am bested only by better players or by mistakes of my own, and with the ability to watch replays, I can see where I went wrong if I care enough - most of the time I simply re-queue and head into the next battle to try something different.
Each faction has been through it's trial by fire over the course of two years resulting in varied playstyles that you'll have to try yourself.

I bought Saints Row 2, Saints Row the Third, and Saints Row IV all at the same time when they were on sale, and played them in order. Saints Row IV is easily my favorite of the three, despite bringing back SRtT's slightly limited character customization and the terribly designed city of Steelport (deliberately ♥♥♥♥♥♥ city-planning is still ♥♥♥♥♥♥ city-planning).
Fortunately, very early in the game you obtain super powers, and the joy and rush of power from being able to sprint faster than you can drive and leaping over buildings allowed me to quickly look past those shortcomings. The ability to access the in-game radio stations even when not in a vehicle is a nice touch as well (and necessary, as you probably won't bother with conventional automobiles, boats, or planes).
I also appreciate that this game managed to balance out Shaundi's personality. The shift from mostly useless stoner in SR2 to hardass ♥♥♥♥♥ in SRtT (who, ironically, was kidnapped more times in that game) swings back to more of a middle ground in IV when she literally comes face to face with herself. Her character arc feels as though the writers are specifically attempting to address complaints about how she was written in the past.
A potential negative to players who haven't experienced the previous installments is that the Saints Row series is loaded with callbacks and has a high degree of continuity from game to game that isn't explained. SRIV does do a little better about this than previous games, as the personal hell simulations the player has to rescue their crew from are essentially flashbacks to previous events, and one type of collectibles in this game are audio logs filling in backstory and character insight.
I've seen a lot of complaints that the increasing ridiculousness of the franchise is a betrayal of its gritty roots, but I prefer the growing absurdity and sense of fun that Saints Row IV embraces rather than a game like Saints Row 2, which might be described as "like GTA, but... with funny outfits, I guess."

Let's be straight. Call of Juarez: The Cartel is not really a good game. It take the wild west setting of the previous installments and brings them to the modern day. The game is buggy, it's incredibly linear, the gunplay is mediocre, the enemies are on the bullet sponge side and the AI is nonexistent as your partners are absolutely worthless at times. That said, I had an absolute blast playing CoJ: The Cartel. It is the video game equivalent of playing a B-Movie, and I love B-Movies. You see all the "twists & turns" in the story a mile away in a cliche ridden script filled with stereotypes and eye rolling dialogue,  But like a trainwreck I just couldn't take my eyes off of it. You play one of the individuals from different agencies (FBI, DEA & LAPD) put in a task agency meant to take down the Mendoza Cartel who is responsible for drugs, gun running, human trafficking, domestic terrorism blah blah blah and then off you go. I really liked the level variety. You from the Sequioa National Forest to the Streets of L.A. to Arizona and finally to Juarez, Mexico. All very nicely realized. Gameplay wise, you don't have much to do other than going from point A to point B while killing lots of dirtbags along the way. Sometimes you'll get a side mission but those pretty much consist of finding an item on the level somewhere. One escort mission where you are being chased through the streets of LA and up the freeway deserves special mention. An absolute blast. I also felt the voice acting was excellent. Like I said, CoJ: The Cartel is not really a good game but I enjoyed the hell out of it.  If you're looking for political correctness, mind blowing set pieces & a leap forward into the FPS genre look elsewhere. But if the positives I've mentioned are up your alley, well here you go. 7/10 from me.

Child of Light is a beautiful game that has many elements of other types of games that have before it while combining them in fantastic ways. I received this game as a gift from a close friend and immediately began to play it without hesitation. I quickly fell in love with this game due to its adorable gimmicks and lovable characters. Aurora is a cute little princess who seems too good to be true, and remains strong even though the weight of the world weighs down on her. Let's get to a little list of positives and negatives!
Positives
- As previously said, the characters are cute and lovable, while all having their own personalities.
- The ability trees are very interesting and let you build characters in many different ways to create a team as you see fit.
- The DLC is cheap if you're interested and adds in some more colorful characters, which I only recently discovered.
- The storyline is sweet with amazing cutscenes that love to show off all of the hard work put into this game.
- The quests are all very direct which makes the game a bit linear (if you enjoy that) but also allows wiggle room if you like to do side quests.
- All side quests that I've found give really good rewards while not being too easy or difficult.
- The puzzles are simple enough while still being entertaining in the few places that they show up.
Negatives
- Aurora can often be seen as too picture perfect even if it is part of her charm.
- You can bypass a lot of companions if you aren't paying careful attention.
- Although the new game plus is fun and adds to the game, it's important to take into consideration that nothing changes except for the levels, which kind of dries the game out.
- Theres no type of multiplayer unless you hand somebody your mouse so they can be your little firefly friend, which gets boring quickly.
This is a decent list of some vague things in the game that are obvious once you play it a bit, although it should give you a good enough idea of whether or not you'd like to buy it. The game is personally one of my favorites and I adore the pleasing feeling of freedom you receive when you have the ability to fly around like a fairy while looking at the picturesque landscape of the stages you go through. This game is entirely worth it if you're a fan of fairytales, books, poetry, or platformers.

I think Grey Goo is the next big RTS for me. Although some high end RTS gamers are playing the game, I believe it is targeted at the more casual player (like me), who doesn't neccessarily find it fun to give individual orders to 30 different units in every engagement. I haven't used every unit yet but they don't seem to have any micro abilities you need to trigger, for me this is a good thing as I have time to give plenty of move/attack orders during an engagement, managing my reinforcements/base, eco and tech (macro), etc. If you LOVE the micro intensiveness of Starcraft, this probably isn't for you. But if that's you... why not keep playing Starcraft?
Pros
+3 factions with unique base building methods
+base building is fun and you can do walls, which a lot of people missed from the last decade of games
+units are fun to command, respond well to orders without pathing issues.
+I think the in-game interface is great, with all units shown in categories on a single build menu, (structures and techs have separate menus). The hotkey system is good it is a 3 key grid system, eg q-q-q to choose placement for a new economy structure.
+You don't need to construct units that do your building/repairing, which I like. There are harvestor units but they take care of themselves; also nice imo. So the skill in resource management is pretty much just about occuping the areas on the map with resources and then building a collection building to claim that resource. Set it up and forget about it.
+although micro is said to be low, players like myself find plenty of clicking to be done thanks to the number of game mechanics to consider including: air/anti-air, stealth/anti-stealth, terrain: height advantage, hiding in heavy foilage.
+units and backgrounds look pretty enough for a 2015 game, if only just. Game runs at a nice fluid pace.
+campaign missions are varied and a good introduction to all the mechanics of the game
+the goo is cool
Cons
-a little expensive for the size of the game, many feel they should have worked up a substantial player base first for a new series of RTS.
-DLC is apparently 3 missions which doesn't seem worth it imo. Make it $2 and I might buy. At least you don't have to pay any extra to keep up with the multiplayer scene.
-loading screens take longer than I would have thought for the size of the maps. I'm on a SSD and its 15sec or so, which doesn't bother me but worth a mention I thought
-south african accents in the campaign, if a matter of opinion.
-campaign story is not as exciting as you might expect after watching the promo video
-map scrolling methods aren't as accessible as they should be
Go blind for only $5. Technology is amazing.

Banner Saga has really interesting story and tactical combat, as well as characters, and the decision making that affects them. The biggest failure to me lies in the caravan side of things, they don`t really matter and you can simply ignore it, suffering only a bit of consequences in fights due to the bad mood.
Story
The story and the characters are great. You get to know and play with humans and varls (giants) as you change between two different caravans, that end up joining later. There are lots of good interactions between the different characters - some you'll love, others you will hate (like that annoying prince). There are a lot of tough decisions to make along the way.
You may lose some characters due to options you choose in event, or some may not join you (Spoilerish Tip: You may not want to recruit EVERY character that comes you way, though). Some characters are really hard to keep alive: In my 1rst playthrough, Egil never left the first village, and even if he survives, he has plenty of later decisions that may end up killing him.
I usually abhor losing characters in this kind of game - i will always reset a mission in Fire Emblem if i lose someone, for exemple. But I accepted losing characters in the first playthrough, playing it without consulting any guide, and it was still pretty good. Later, playing with all of them, it was a bit easier, as I could rotate my injured men and varl out of combat.
Ps. Do unlock Triggvy, the character who was exclusive to the KS backers - the devs don`t mind, and he is useful early on. You might have to fiddle a bit with files to do that, though. Everything to unlock him is on the devs forums.
Combat
Some of the reviews say the combat is dumb, and they dislike idea that health is the same thing as strength, and you deal less damage the more injured you are. I find it quite interesting and clever, as anyone that has been battered and bleeding for a whole fight would never hit as hard as if they were fresh. And it`s quite interesting as you reflect and decide whether to hit the enemies armor in preparation for more effective blows, or chip at their health so they won`t hit your characters as hard.
People also complain about the turn order, always alternating between the player and the enemies, making it a tactical decision too when to start really killing off the enemies. Letting them live while being completely depleted in health is a quite vital tactic. It may be artificial, sure, but it does add another tactical decision to make, and it never bothered me.
Ah, another interesting tactical decision is how many men and how many varl you take to each combat. Naturally, Varl are more resilient and stronger than the puny humans and are larger, and they also block the enemies passage, keeping the backline safe, but they are bigger targets, and sometimes get in the way of their own allies.
The skills are pretty useful, and you should use them to good effect (i sometimes forgot them in the 1rst playt., and suffered for it).
Renown: Promotions, Supplies and Itens
The game`s "coin" is renown, which is primarily earned through combat, and through some decisions. I never had enough, as I was always buying supplies for the party. So, I almost never got to buy itens, that i usually only had because of one or other event. Besides that, the main use for renown is promoting your men (and varl) which is quite important. It`s understandable due to the setting the scarcity of supplies, but tying them with the promotion of troops wasn`t a good idea, IMO.
Overall, a great game.

After playing 125 hours and reaching lvl 53 Striker, lvl 20 Wizard and 5 other lvl 15s, I cannot recommend this game.
Aside from the Xign anti-cheat software, this game is made for one purpose only : to milk your wallet.
Black Desert Online is an asian fantasy role-playing mmo focused on pvp and gambling. There are some pve element but to reach end-game pve, you'll need to grind for months to reach it which relies on black stones you can either craft, grind or buy from the trading house. You will need black stones to upgrade your gear because every gear has levels and they're about the same. In-game money of 10,000,000 silver is the equivalent of 8$ USD and game store of 1000 pearls is 10$ USD. When I said this game this game is focused on gambling, it is because it works like a slot machine whenever you use a black stone to upgrade your gear. For a weapon, the first seven levels has a 100% success rate but past that, the higher you go, the lower the chances and it really falls down where you NEED to rely on failstacks which are imaginary bonuses that increases your chance to succeed. Let's say to reach end-game gear, you'll need about 150 AP, that means you're going to need about 115 black stones per gear (primary wpn, secondary wpn, shoes, gloves, armor, helmet) which is a total of 230 weapon black stones @ 300,000 silver and 460 armor black stone @ 250,000 silver.
A grand sum of 184,000,000 silver, in just upgrading your gear but then you'll also need to upgrade your accessories which is a very special case. To upgrade your accessories, you need two of a kind and if you fail, you lose both of them.
In one month @ 125 hours of gameplay, I've reached 80,00,000 silver so personally, it'll take me around 3-4 months. A lot of people manages to make millions per hour but that's if you're willing to throw away real money to buy pearls and use those pearls to buy pets (10$ each) and weight limit increase (50,100,150,200 - 1 of each).
Also, costumes costs between 20$ to 40$. You might get a costume in-game but if it says 7D, it means it'll disappear after that week of use is over.
To conclude, this game is a money pitfall and even though it is gorgeous, it is badly optimised which will force your hand to lower your graphics to be able to do world bosses but that's only after you've geared yourself to reach endgame. Levels don't matter. Your AP/DP does and depending on how much money you've spent on the shop will vary to how quickly you'll reach it. [2017]
As much as I hate on COH2, Neo-Relic and Sega's nightmarish DLC policy, COH2's multiplayer (2017) is as close to perfection of the RTS formula as I've seen.
This doesn't come easy, it took two years for Relic to finally throw off the yoke rock paper scissors that they've ruined themselves with ever since Homeworld 2 fifteen years ago (2003) Instead, they've come to grips with the community-balance solution which has adopted a more icefrog-esque system of strengthening everything instead of nerfing it to the ground. Relic's original game was rubber bullets and weather condition nonsense that made the game beautiful, but laughably slow. The reviews at the time reflect this - even mine highlighted how terrible the game was.
Two years of DLC and massive, sweeping balance patches later and we've got a fine example of engaging and often thrilling multiplayer mayhem. One of the few games that pulls off team play well (unlike Starcraft's 2v2-3v3-4v4, which is quite literally sitting in a corner and spamming battlecruisers/rays) Teamplay involves taking and holding the map, not simple economy. A system I whole-heartedly despised in games like DOW2 and COH1, the formula has been refined and the battlefields are skillfully crafted and shaped to promote interesting encounters.
Chokes are visible and valuable, but there's always chances and routes to flank and artillery options that aren't too strong, but strong enough to shake even the fortress-building Brits from digging in too heavily. Gone is the rock-paper-scissors gameplay that Relic has grown so fond of.
The battlefield changes. Trees are knocked over, walls crumble as shells impact them, explosives leave craters. A heavy enough vehicle will plow over the terrain and take everything with it, including buildings. An hour long match will look nothing like the last one simply because the map has been so flattened, so charred, so reduced to ruble that you will have to be improvising new battle lines constantly and moving your pieces in a beautiful tug of war. Very few games have made me so thrilled that I shout at my screen or hurry to type a command to an ally for reinforcements and very rarely does losing ever carry with it some bitter sting that other games do - if I lose, it's because I made a poor decision or over-reached my fragile supply lines that resulted in a costly defeat. I am bested only by better players or by mistakes of my own, and with the ability to watch replays, I can see where I went wrong if I care enough - most of the time I simply re-queue and head into the next battle to try something different.
Each faction has been through it's trial by fire over the course of two years resulting in varied playstyles that you'll have to try yourself.
