I'd love to give a deep and detailed review of this game, but I can't because, well: Xigncode.
If you don't want to read much further (I'm wordy), basically I can't play this game because a piece of software included with the game that- while it's intended to prevent cheating- probably goes WAY too far in attempting to do so- looking at installed software in your computer that has absolutely ZERO chance of ever interacting with the game.
Principally I have no issue with game devs wanting to discourage cheating, but there is a balance to be struck, and this is a bridge too far.  I can't reccomend the game as such.
If you do want to read further, I'll go into great detail about it- and in no small part because it seems hard to get much if any information out of the developers about what exactly Xigncode does.  I'm aware of the discussion posts, but even they are pretty vague and general- probably to some extent by necessity.
There's a lot of claptrap about this in the forums and such- that it's malware, a rootkit, it spies on you.  I'm not exactly a subscriber to all that (though the last one is ~kinda~ true).
The "truth" is that- like a lot of MMOs from this corner of the world, the priority is placed largely on grinding, and as such, some folks not really keen on grinding- or perhaps not too keen on doing the legwork involved at least- might feel inclined to automate tasks they feel are mindless and beneath them.
Xigncode is anti-cheat software, to put it simply.  It's intent is no more (and no less) malicious than that.
I don't get the allure myself- cheating, that is.  Why pay for a game you're not planning on experiencing?  And if the experience is grindy and that's not your thing?  Well...  the game's probably not for you.
So why then would I write to apparently call out Xigncode- if I don't principally have an issue with game devs not wanting people to cheat at their games?
The answer is... complicated.  But to sum it up: False Positives
I'm an IT guy, someone who by trade deals in- if not a lot of exotic software- then at the very least a wide variety of software- any of which might be installed on my machine at any given time.  Some of it might even be designed for the task of automating other software- and for perfectly understandable reasons.
So I fire up the game, and eventually it crashes with a message from Xigncode that very obliquely and indirectly tells me "you've been naughty".
My thoughts immediately head to the wealth of software I have on my machine- some of which might edge close to this category of "forbidden"- and I think to myself, "Gee, I'd sure like to know if that's the problem, for sure (again, IT guy, I'm used to self-diagnosing my computer issues).
And hey, the game helpfully directs me to this file (xigncode.log) where it's suggested I might find that verification.  So I go have a look, and well, it's a lot of this:
This is either unicode characters my computer can't read (the game is after all, foreign), or it's encryption.  Good news for the malware conspiracy theroists (or maybe bad news if you really WANT to believe this thing is evil incarnate), the latter possiblity would probably represent evidence that Xigncode is in fact keeping the data it collects safe on your machine from just any schmoe reading it...
But it'd be bad news for me, the guy trying to figure out exactly what tripped this thing.
They of course invite you to send this to them, so I guess they can decode that mess.  I could do it, sure.  But the truth is: I haven't done anything wrong here.
Even if there's some piece of software present on my machine that Xigncode thinks is the devil- it's not running in the background, and so there's no way it's in use on the game itself.  So exactly what measuring stick am I being evaluated against here?  Not knowing is kind of aggravating.
Going to the discussion forums on steam here for the game to ask questions seemed like a good avenue- but they appear to be locked.  So that's a one-way prospect.
They're either more interested in soapboxing than they are interacting with the community, or there's been so much hate and misinformation and frustration being vented there over this Xigncode thing that they just got sick of it all and locked the forums.
A mixture of both is also possible, of course.
In any case in the process of looking at what player posts were already there, I got the sense that Xigncode does at least marginally more than look for active background software- it seems to look for software you may have recently used, or maybe is just present on your system- and if it finds anything it doesn't care for, shuts the game down.
So you know, it could be a matter of simply having a piece of software installed that it finds objectionable.  That'd be something of a pisser because, again, I'd have to go uninstall that piece of software- which I might be using for other, perfectly legit purposes.
False Positives are funny things.  My antivirus routinely pegs several Steam games/apps I have as malware for...  whatever reason (I'm a technical sort of guy and even I can't figure it out- best I can do is: "dunno, heuristics?").  But the difference there is I can look in my AV log, find out what it's having a fit over, and then set an exception.
Hard to tell what Xigncode is having a fit over here because, yanno, encrypted log file.  And in cases like this, companies rarely want to tell you what "the rules" are.  If you were intent on breaking them, you might use that information to get around Xigncode.
And that brings me back to the principle of the thing: far as I know, I've done nothing that amounts to cheating, and if this isn't some sort of false positive, then it's probably that Xigncode is just being WAY too overzealous in it's search for even signs I might be inclined to cheat- e.g.: searching for installed or recently accessed, software, rather than stuff that's actually in the background- and actually capable of affecting the game in real-time.
I guess that's the Game Dev's prerogative- if they want to be overzealous, they can do that.
Thing is, it's my prerogative to choose NOT to get involved with that mess.  Or at the very least to choose not to play because my ability to play has been been made far too onerous.
A short cautionary tale on the anti-virtue of over-protectiveness:
One upon a time there was a little piece of Desktop Publishing Software called QuarkXpress, made by a company called Extensis.
This underdog, no-name Little Engine that Could very breifly managed to accomplish something that most people in the graphic design industry would have thought impossible: it breifly unseated the mighty Adobe (whose own flagship Desktop Publishing software was Pagemaker, at the time) as the industry standard in desktop publishing.
And it did so by being way more innovative- offering features that Pagemaker at the time sorely lacked.
But Extensis- perhaps feeling vulnerable after having taken the limelight as dramatically as it had- decided that QuarkXpress needed a metric butt-ton of Digital Rights Management Protection- to, yanno, "keep dem pirates from keelhaulin' yer software, ARR!".
In principle, I can understand the desire to not have ones' creation pirateded to infinity.  That said, there's a balance to be struck.
In a very short period of time, the DRM protection they had in play got so onerous that it wasn't uncommoon for even legitimate owners of the software to be completely unable to run the product they had purchased.  Users pretty understandably became frustrated...
...and then along comes Adobe with a nifty little product called InDesign.  And that's why no one knows the name QuarkXpress any more.

I bought Saints Row 2, Saints Row the Third, and Saints Row IV all at the same time when they were on sale, and played them in order. Saints Row IV is easily my favorite of the three, despite bringing back SRtT's slightly limited character customization and the terribly designed city of Steelport (deliberately ♥♥♥♥♥♥ city-planning is still ♥♥♥♥♥♥ city-planning).
Fortunately, very early in the game you obtain super powers, and the joy and rush of power from being able to sprint faster than you can drive and leaping over buildings allowed me to quickly look past those shortcomings. The ability to access the in-game radio stations even when not in a vehicle is a nice touch as well (and necessary, as you probably won't bother with conventional automobiles, boats, or planes).
I also appreciate that this game managed to balance out Shaundi's personality. The shift from mostly useless stoner in SR2 to hardass ♥♥♥♥♥ in SRtT (who, ironically, was kidnapped more times in that game) swings back to more of a middle ground in IV when she literally comes face to face with herself. Her character arc feels as though the writers are specifically attempting to address complaints about how she was written in the past.
A potential negative to players who haven't experienced the previous installments is that the Saints Row series is loaded with callbacks and has a high degree of continuity from game to game that isn't explained. SRIV does do a little better about this than previous games, as the personal hell simulations the player has to rescue their crew from are essentially flashbacks to previous events, and one type of collectibles in this game are audio logs filling in backstory and character insight.
I've seen a lot of complaints that the increasing ridiculousness of the franchise is a betrayal of its gritty roots, but I prefer the growing absurdity and sense of fun that Saints Row IV embraces rather than a game like Saints Row 2, which might be described as "like GTA, but... with funny outfits, I guess."

Definitely not as bad as the majority of other reviewers make it out to be. This is just like Resident Evil 5; when you take it out of the series, you have a decent game. When you compare it to the other games in the series, yeah, it's a bad game. On its own, not so.
However, is this game good? Is this game going to make you tremble with ecstacy? Is this game will the "the one"? Hell no.
The only thing keeping this game together is its incredible story. You can take this game's plot and shoot a blockbuster Hollywood movie with it. It's extremely realistic, dark, and a very good reflection of the hellhole we call politics. It becomes so complex sometimes that you need to pause the game and get all the pieces together in your mind's eye.
Soundtrack is well done. It suits the theme of the game and the environments you play in very well. It's not ♥♥♥♥♥♥ic, but it's definitely enhancing.
Voice-over is brilliant. You can feel they paid attention to quality in that department.
AI? Well, it's complicated. Sometimes they just get stuck and stare at you like some idiots. Some other time, you see them flanking you, moving from cover to cover and getting you at your most vulnerable moment. Your partners though, they are completely useless. Don't expeck anything big and you won't have a problem with them.
Gameplay mechanics? Bad. It's just plain bad. Covers don't always work, the game glitches and bugs in some missions, forcing  you to load a checkpoint, grenades are useless, weapons don't differ from each other much, playing offline really detracts from the whole gaming experience, etc. One good thing is the "Secret Agenda" system. During most missions, someone important calls you a gives you a secret mission that you must complete without being seen by your partners. It's a breeze when playing offline, but I reckon it adds a lot of excitement on online playing sessions. A very refreshing idea. More games should try something like this.
Worst thing? Sound effects. You fire a shotgun and it sounds like a tiny balloon just popped. You fire a friggin M60 and it sounds like an old man's fart. You shoot you Desert Eagle and it sounds like a kid is clapping his little hands together. It's downright terrible.
Overall, would I recommend this game? If it's below 5 bucks, yeah. It just isn't worth 10 dollars.

Hands down by GOTY 2014. Absoultely incredible game design, Original Sin is a world populated with characters, quests and enemies that you will love to explore. Further on the note of combat, I found the balance between my team's ability level and the enemies I was facing very fine-tuned- rush into an area you're not ready for and you will be crushed, but at no point is there any mundane grinding (enemies do not respawn, ever). If you are at all inclined toward RPGs, even if you feel an isometric perspective is dated (which it is), you owe it to yourself to give Divinity:OS a shot.

Main question: Should you buy this game? ABSOLUTELY.
+ Large amount of replayability, with no two runs being the same.
+ Mind-blowingly good soundtrack.
+ Great variety of ships, with about 6 or 7 classes, each having 3 to unlock and 2 secret classes to find...
+/- Interesting combat system that combines an RTS-esque (Real-Time Strategy) with the ability to pause the game and plan your next move.
+ A large amount of races to see and meet.
+ Interesting weapons and good variety of them.
+ Moddable. One of the more popular mods is the Captain's Edition (I have no idea how to get it, look up TotalBiscuit's video on it), which adds even more variety.
+/- Very high difficulty level. A turn-away if you're kind of casual and don't enjoy a high-difficulty game.
- Lacking difficulty choices and/or customization, only being Easy (150%-ish Scrap. Score is 50%), Medium (100%-ish [?] Scrap, Score is 100%), and Hard (50%-ish Scrap. Score is 150%). I'm not sure on the earnings and score, though. Look those up.
+ Backgrounds are beautiful and are of decent variety.
+ Great price-tag of $10 for the amount of content available.
+ Will keep you coming back. It's addictive, with that feeling of "Alright, just one more run, then I'm done." all the time when you're playing it.
My overall thoughts: This game is cheap and is very hardcore. Extremely difficult, but highly rewarding with new ships to unlock, races to meet, weapons to bring ruin with, and more. For $10 ($4 at the time this review was written), DO NOT IGNORE IT. It is addictive and really fun.

HyperDimension Neptunia is a series that you will either love or hate. If you are not willing to look past the fanservice and suggestive aspects of it, you will not have a very good time. However, if you are willing to look past those, you will find a series full of well-written and developed characters and a large amount of meta-humour that is hard to not get a laugh out of.
To start things off, Neptunia a JRPG. In the world of Gamindustri, there are four nations: Lastation, Lowee, Leanbox and Planeptune. Each nation is ruled over by a goddess CPU (Console Patron Unit). CPU Black Heart rules Lastation, CPU White Heart rules Lowee, CPU Green Heart rules Leanbox and CPU Purple Heart rules Planeptune. The CPUs reside in Celestia, where they are locked in battle to determine who will obtain the title of True Goddess. After hundreds of years of fighting, a strange voice suggests for Black Heart, White Heart and Green Heart to group together and defeat Purple Heart. They agree and send her careening off the edge of Celestia towards Gamindustri, during which she reverts into Neptune, her human form. After being found and tended to by an aspiring nurse named Compa, it is learned that Neptune has amnesia, and so she, Compa and a member of the Guild named IF set out across Gamindustri to restore Neptune's memories. The story is very lighthearted and rarely takes itself seriously. The characters are all well-developed and likeable, and their conversations often involve the breaking of the fourth wall to hilarious effect.
Gameplay-wise, the game is relatively solid. It uses a turn-based system where you move you characters around the battlefield before using their abilities or using combos. Combos are composed of Rush, Power and Break attacks. Rush attacks are more effective at building your EXE Gauge, which allows the use of EXE Drives. EXE Drives are very powerful attacks that can be performed alone or with other characters, depending on which character is using an EXE Drive. Power attacks deal the most raw damage out of the three, and Break attacks are better at decreasing an enemy's Guard Points. When their Guard Points reach zero, that enemy will take around double damage for a short time.
In addition to the three characters on the battlefield, you can pair them with another three who will provide passive bonuses such as more EXP or increased defences. When two characters are paired together, they have a Lily Rank that shows how much those characters like each other. As the Lily Rank increase, more bonuses become unlocked between those characters. Some characters can even perform EXE Drives together if their Lily Rank is high enough.
In conclusion, HyperDimension Neptunia Re;Birth1 is an excellent game if you are able to forgive/look beyond the sexualized aspects of it. The characters are likeable and believable, the humour is great and hard to not laugh at, and the gameplay is fun and surprisingly deep. I recommend that anyone who just wants to have a good time purchases this game.

So I'm re-writing my review now this is Free To Play, I was a paid player however the game was dying due to lack of players, I'm glad it's free because there's now over 1500 active players daily on Steam and the game is in a much better state! Firstly unlike a lot of free games here's no pay to win which will please lots of people everything is unlockable over time apart from the skins and cosmetics which you need real cash for. Paid players who bought the game before it was free get character unlocks and skins as a reward for buying the original. Block n Load in my opinion is in the top ten best free to play games on the Internet or Steam. It's primary a shooter but has some Minecraft building mechanics and 5v5 game play like a moba which I'll explain below.
This game is simple but great though you need to get through your first 20-25 matches before you start getting team mates who know how to play and want to improve and learn the meta. Early on people clearly have no idea how to play, they troll a lot and argue and make stupid decisions which lose matches quickly. Low level players think they are playing team deathmatch game and generally do stupid♥♥♥♥♥♥so expect 10 hours of frustration before the game comes into it's own.
Once you hit match 25+ or above half of those lowbies carry on playing and get better and the others leave. Things get very fun once the competitive players remain and only the core community who understand the game are left.
Matches in general can last between 10-30 minutes and some occasionally an hour when teams are very well matched on the bigger maps. I love jumping on with a friend or two and found teaching new friends to play was nice and easy as there's a tutorial video and you can make custom games. What I enjoy most about Block N Load is some games are a long tactical slog where as others are rush rush rush and lots of killing and carnage with a quick win or defeat. One match you might be dug in on a stale mate and others you push early and gain the upper hand for a quick victory.
Block N Load certainly feels like a moba mixed with shooter mechanics and Minecraft block placement. It's matches feature 5v5 gameplay, choice of loadouts, cool skins and there is a kind of meta for each champ some are attacking and others defending play styles. There isn't any minions or skill trees like you'd get in a moba but your base is effectively the nexus or objective.
As you can see from the pics and vids it uses Minecraft like voxel graphics and engine which suits it nicely. It runs very well and is stable I never experience disconnection from their servers or get lag at all I've played on a 4mb connection and my home 70mb fibre. The combat is first person shooter like where you shoot other players with a small selection of weapons and fit out your character with perks and building objects but the moba element is basically two teams attack and defend each others cubes (Nexus) trying to destroy it to win.
Just a side note I have never ever seen a hacker on this game either!
So basically to explain a match or the core game play a you get a build phase/resource gather phase which is normally 5 minutes to prepare your cube defence. After that a shield wall goes down and you battle until one team loses all their cubes (some maps have more than one).
There's not much else to say it's build then fight and then either win or lose. Games can be pretty intense and action happening all the time. My only complaint is the game should force at least one player to play an engineer or defensive class as sometimes you can lose a match in character select and build phase if no one on your team can build decent walls, traps or turrets.
The game can be won or lost in hero selection and in build phase if a player disconnects or leaves they are replaced very quickly, this is a great feature.
Block n Load is the best voxel based builder and shooter game out there!

What I didn't like about the Expert difficulty is that it sometimes feels like the only way to win nice and easy is to overlevel, since the number of characters in a fight and the moves you can make are quite limited. And that's why, the way I see it, leveling and gearing could have been improved in way to provide more strategies and different fight styles. I don't have much time to play, so maybe my experience is too limited, but it felt like either:
1) I had to fight in a very conservative way to avoid damage as much as possible, since even the tank characters could die very easily, and I would sometimes find myself fighting in long "Defend, Attack, Heal" loops; or
2) when I could fight more agressively it was just an overkill.
Maybe opening one more character slot to fight would solve this and make fighting more fluid. Even so, I enjoyed the battles a lot, especially the boss fights.

is the revival of the classic "X-Com" series of turn-based tactical games, with modern graphics, utility and design philosophy. The game takes place in the near future, and gives the player the role of commander of the "XCOM Project". The game has two distinctly different gameplay scenes: the strategic and the combat screens.
gives you a manager-like control of your base, and lets you make decisions about what to build, what to research, what to buy/sell, etc.
gives you control of the tactical, turn-based combat of your squad.
The game starts out with basic terran equipment and Xenology, and the "story" goes forward only as you achieve certain milestones, which is an interesting way of progressing a game. Such milestones can be the capture or elimination of certain aliens or artifacts, or completion of certain research projects. In the long run, you'll see your base and your soldiers evolve from being small and weak, to being big and effective.
There is too much depth and variation in this game to write a thorough declaration of features here, but rest assured; this game
challenge you, if you let it. There are however fans of the old games who state that the new game is lacking in features, compared to the classic games, and they would be right. What the game lacks in quantity, it makes up for in quality.
.
If, however, you are one who appreciates quantity over quality, I would recommend the varius DLC's for this game, especially
, as well as a community-made module called "Long War". I must warn you though: Both the DLC and
the mod will make the game
hard, so i suggest postponing the installation of "Long War" until you have clocked at least 20 hours of the game. 20 hours goes by with the blink of an eye as long as you enjoy turn-based
games.
There is also a 1v1 multiplayer mode, which is only the combat screen, and lets the player choose their units from a pool of both X-Com and alien
, but i would again recommend you to postpone that until you are more than familiar with the game.
Buy it for: Its excellent single player experience, as well as feeling like the saviour of mankind.
Pirate for: To see if it's actually something you might like, especially the DLC's.

I will tell the story, of Colonel Myles "Wolverine" Curtis, Assault, Psychic Operative.
Col. Curtis joined up with XCOM, being one of the first recruits, along with 3 friends, Colin "Vampire" Grimes, Adam "Yeti" McKeon, and Brian "Atlas" Hollenback. They made it through their first mission, each being promoted to Squaddie. Myles became the assaul, Colin, the Sniper, Adam, the Heavy, and Brian, the support. They went through their missions, becoming the commanders A-Team. Their squad increased in size, with John "Moose" Smith, Heavy, and Jacob "Gypsy" Hohmann, Support, being added. Eventually, through time, with the A-Team being outfitted with the best weaponry the commander can give them, psychic powers are discovered. With the commander testing each and every single XCOM operative, the only psychic is Myles. They train his psychic ablities, and he becomes ruthless in his ways, downing over one hundred and fifty aliens alone.
SPOILER ALERT
The time comes. The End Game. The commander willingly sends his A-Team, knowing full well, that although the risks, they will all make it back alive. Because that's what they do, his A-Team. With over 50 missions together, his A-Team works flawlessly. In and out, usually without a scratch.
But that's not what happened. Even though the team was prepared, there were just too many to handle at points. They made it through the first corridor of the Temple Ship without much damage. They took some damage in the second chamber, but made it through. They were doing good. They had killed the mutons in the chamber in front, then they proceeded into the next chamber, too cocky about their situation. "This is easy", they thought. John dashed a bit too far, and was destroyed by the 2 sectopods that layed in front of him. They became infuriated, and took down the sectopods angrily. But it was too late for John. He was killed instantly, and there was no way to save him. They knew that the aliens had to pay for this. Unfortunately though, they were flanked by 2 Muton Elites, who killed both Adam and Brian. The final 3, Myles, Colin, and Jacob were devastated by grief. They entered the final room, ready to fight. Ready to kill. Colin, the sniper, being in a good spot as usual, shot at the Uber Ethereal, dealing a critical hit, with massive damage. A whopping 18 damage was dealt to the Boss. Myles, being the assualt, who was usually past the front lines, ran up to the Ethereal, shot it with his Alloy Cannon, and ended it's life. The ship started to turn into a black hole, but Myles, saved his teammates, and the world, with his life. His last sight, was his teammates flying off into the distance. He smiled, knowing he had fulfilled his goal.

Introduction :-
Legacy of the Duelist is a Yu-Gi-Oh game that includes story mode for all Yu-Gi-Oh anime series from the Original Duel Monsters till the newest installment ARC-V.
The story mode consists mainly of the key duels that happend in the show. Some of the filler tournaments/ duels that have no significance to the story are removed, such as the KaibaCorp Grand Championship from the original Yu-Gi-Oh.
The game includes an impressive amounts of cards, at least 6500+ unique cards, all can be unlocked by playing single player campaign or multiplayer. You will be rewarded everytime you play a duel, no matter if you win or lose, but of course if you win your reward will be higher.
Unlocking the cards is very easy and reasonable. The card shop in the game includes upto 6 characters from each of the Yu-Gi-Oh series, you can unlock packs with the awarded currency you get when you play a duel and each character has at least 200+ unique cards awaiting for your unlock. Each time you unlock a pack from a character you earn 8 random cards.
The game also includes muliplayer modes, ranked matches or single duels, you can play with either your friends or strangers, and it gives you the options to set your desired limitations (LP and time limits).
Game strength points and weaknesses :-
Strength Points :-
- Captivating campaign mode, which allows you to play either using the anime decks the heroes used at the time, or your own.
- Has 6500+ unique cards.
- Recognized signature monsters have 3D animation when they attack, such as :  Dark Magician, Blue-Eyes White Dragon, Elemental Hero Neos, Stardust Dragon & Number 39: Utopia .,. etc
- Can be a nice experience if you have a friend to duel against in multiplayer mode.
- You can play reverse duel which allows you to play as the anti-hero and unlock their deck receipts.
Weakness Points :-
- Basically all of ARC-V campaign are DLCs that cost $5 each. The only included duel is the tutorial which is laughable.
- Multiplayer is basically dead, I wouldn't buy this game if this is what you are looking for only. If I got lucky and found any duelists online they are the same guys I've seen yesterday and the day before -lol- so most of the duelists in multiplayer are the players who are dedicated to the game.
- This point is a followup to the above point, so as a result of this you will only find highly skilled players online, and if you are a newbie in this game it is most likely you will get crushed.
- Most of the pre-built decks are weak or unbalanced, the decent decks are really few. The developers didn't put much effort in them. They just chose 13(+1) random cards then added three copies from each card and called it a deck.
- Not all monster cards have 3D animation like how Yu-Gi-Oh! Forbidden Memories was.
- The music is generic, repetitive and dull.
Conclusion :-
Overall, I recommend this game for single player and I totally enjoy the campaign, but I do not recommend this for multiplayer unless you have someone to play against.

Tell you what - I second-chanced it. Soon as I posted my review, and I mean within seconds, I got either two developer accounts or two fanboy accounts thumbs-downing it.
First, let's take a look at Petroglyph games I've purchased in the past:
SW: Empire at War
UAW: Earth Assault
And, I purchased most of the C&C series every time they came out with a new one, with the exception of Generals. I prefer non-symmetrical race/faction selection and long tactical battles to twitchy mass-and-slaughter games.
When much of the early C&C series became available as a Steam download, I jumped on it - it was cheap and brought back some good memories of early pay-by-the-hour LAN houses.
When I looked at the reviews for GG, I thought, "Kind of a silly name for a game, but hey - it's got a lot that I like in it". Got it on sale, downloaded, installed, played a bit of the campaign to get a feel, jumped into Skirmish. Beyond the crashing, over-bloated filesize (and unnecessary cinematics), here's what you can expect:
Graphically speaking, it's reminicsent of the art styling used in RA/CC - that is, isometric terrains with very little detail on the small units. I wouldn't be surprised if the game was structured into "doodads" and "statics". While this helps performance, especially when dealing with large groups, it feels largely unoptimized. Lighting and shadows seem about 10 years old.
But hey, it runs smoothly enough.
Now, this is the point where I really didn't like the game. I liked the return to the traditional RTS, but everything was stripped of depth. Tech trees that result in 4 technologies that are pretty underpowered? How about two of the playable races being PRETTY MUCH THE SAME in terms of building, with one being able to spread out a little more using conduits, the other being little blob bases with satellite areas? 1 basic infantry, 1 light tank, 1 heavy tank, 1 artillery, 1 stealth, 1 scout air, 1 bomber, 1 general purpose air. Turrets and flak. Walls. That's the game in a nutshell. There's no real unit variety, no real differences between the units beyond their animations and textures. ZERO depth.
Because of this, gameplay becomes the same as playing GDI in the RA series. Seriously, I played both of the non-goo races and wiped the Goo off the skirmish map using a handful of air units while turtling in a base with a couple turrets placed strategically.  The AI (on normal) has a REALLY bad habit of trying the same entry points with the same units over and over and over again, only changing the numbers it sends. Take out resource production and you're good to go.
There's nothing new here.
To be honest, I didn't even try MP. I won't even give it a shot - this game is flat and dull.
Save your money and move on. If you want good old-school RTS, get the old games. You won't find much MP, but at least you won't get a shoddy copy of gameplay from ages gone past. Looking for strategy? Look elsewhere. Looking for pretty? Not here. Looking for depth? Don't make me laugh. The problems with this game go far beyond crashes and optimization. I appreciate Developer response, but it won't be necessary.

Pretty much a lightweight mobile strategy game that has quality graphics, a great soundtrack, and repetitive and shallow gameplay.  Players looking for depth should really look elsewhere.  There isn't a heck of a lot of variety in this game.  As others describe it's a Choose Your Own Adventure book in video game form with very little voice over work and a lot of reading boring generic text.  The story is alright but a little thin and cliche.  Combat is really all its about and its pretty boring after 6 or 7 rounds.  As a budget title its not a terrible pickup but it's certainly over hyped and you can do a lot better elsewhere.
Thats the short of it.  The reasons I didn't like the title are largely because of how shallow and uninteresting the game ultimately was.  The game is a linear journey from one battle to the next broken up with camp sites or village visits that really don't offer much.  Buy some supplies, maybe buy a piece of armor, rest, repeat.  Thats it.  Combat is very simple and expected for the genre.  Maybe 4 total classes when you really break it down.  Move, attack, or use a special ability.  I never found the speciasl abilities all that wonderful for most characters.  Also the interface is sloppy.  Seems pretty clear it was a mobile game ported to PC with all the erroneous clicking and re-clicking.  Not very intuitive either.
The biggest grievance I had was the game mechanics don't make a heck of a lot of sense and it gives off this vibe that it just makes the rules up as it goes along.  For instance combat turns just always seem to be totally random and enemies just move whever they want.  In one complete round of combat some enemies will move 3 or 4 times to your single moves per character.  Gets a little annoying really and kind of cuts away the strategy element and reminds you of how shallow this title really is.  I do not believe it is deserving of the massively positive reviews it possesses.

I really like this game! It's fun to play, has a lot of fun duals from the various series to see if you can win. Thousands of cards to play with so that you can build so many decks, also the whole story can be done with custom decks so if you want to feel like you're an unstoppable card playing machine you can really get that fulfillment. As an aside, if you are used to playing the modern TCG because of the new format things are a lot faster there than they are here, so if like me you find pendulum and link summoning aggrivating and that the system has phased out slower play this is a great game to go for instead. There are also a lot of computer duals for people who dislike playing against other people and some of the challenge decks are actually pretty tough all things considered. The system also showcases if cards would be banned normally in a legit duel so if you want to be someone who uses only tournament legal cards (at least this game's version of tournament legal) you can.
The game isn't perfect however, there have been a few crash issues I've had to deal with. Certain cards like the dark magician and blue eyes also have little animations that play whenever they attack, this can slow down duals considerably so be warned if you want to go hard on a dark magician or blue eyes deck that you will tire of these animations and they can't be turned off. Also be warned that by default the game will ask if you want to activate an effect every single part of a turn once a card that can be activated any time comes into your hand. This means that mystical space typhoon and other cards like it can end up VERY aggrivating if you don't change that setting to stop notifying you in the options.
Overall a really enjoyable game with a huge slice of the card game and series I grew up with. I may be biased but I personally find this my favorite card based video game I've ever played and the satisfaction I get from trying to beat opponents who give me trouble or modifying a deck that needs a little tweak can't be beat. Try this out if you grew up with the series or if you liked whe the slower formats from the TCG were still viable.

Now that the last episode has been released, I feel I need to adjust my review. Unfortunately, this adjustment doesn't change the fact that I can't recommend this game.
Telltale's Game of Thrones starts off weak and suddenly becomes strong toward the end of episode five. Episode six carries itself very well, but this does not change the fact that the other episodes are difficult to play. I found myself bored, waiting for dull dialogue to finish, and altogether displeased with my purchase.
It is important to note that I absolutely LOVED Telltale's The Wolf Among Us and The Walking Dead. I didn't expect Telltale's Game of Thrones to be on par with either of those games, but even still I was dreadfully disappointed. I'm really hoping that when (if?) they release a second season, it will make up for this game's shortcomings. The game progressed at a painfully slow pace. I've now played the game pretty much through, done all the quests and my save said 95% completed. I must admit that it got better towards the end and I was smiling during the end credits, but shortly after that my game crashed (again).

The positives: it was mainly good fun, the quests varied a lot more towards the end, plenty of laughs to be had especially near/at the end, superpowers (yay!).

Let me start off by saying that while I don't recommend this game, it is indeed an enjoyable one.  My "thumbs down" does not mean that it is a bad game, simply that I don't think it is worth playing.
I was not a fan of Saints Row The Third, and I originally did not plan to play this one, but I got it in the Humble Bundle, so I figured I might as well see if this iteration was better.
It was.  The addition of "super powers" adds a huge amount of enjoyment to the game.  The only real downside to the powers is that it is sometimes difficult to utilize them fully.  You can't shoot while jumping or sprinting, so you generally use those sparingly in combat, and many of the powers are either on long cooldowns or just aren't strong enough to practically be used in many situations.
The downside to the game is that other than the powers, it is just like The Third, which in my opinion wasn't very good.  The shooting mechanics aren't the greatest, and they basically come down to using the pistols to headshot every grunt enemy and emptying several magazines of any weapon into the "tank" enemies.
The story is not particularly interesting, but it takes itself way too seriously.  It is a generally over-the-top game, but they seem to try to give you an emotional attachment to the story, which is not going to happen.  I'm playing this game to blow up aliens, not look deeper into myself.  Many cutscenes are skippable, but some aren't, which sucks.  The voice acting is okay, but the animations in cutscenes are sorely lacking - none of the characters' bodies move when they are talking, only their mouths.
The game's biggest sin, however, is in the collect-a-thon.  The upgrades for the super powers require a "currency" called "clusters", which are scattered around the world on rooftops, buried in walls and terrain, or stuck in floating orbs, and you must collect 500 to 1000 to fully upgrade your abilities.  That is not a small amount.  You can also upgrade your weapons, ammo, and some other stuff like health.  This, of course, requires a currency called "cache" (cash), which you get from killing enemies (and picking each individual bit of cache up off the ground afterwards), completing challenges, and doing the story missions.  It requires an obscene amount of cache to upgrade everything fully.  On top of these upgrades, there are various collectables - you can destroy small statues, of which there are 39 scattered about the world, you can collect audio logs, which there are around 30, you can "hack" all the stores, complete all the challenges, do all the activities and try to earn a "gold" rank, etc.  It's a huge grind, and some of the more interesting powers are locked behind it, such as walking on water.
Speaking of walking on water, the "activity" that you have to get a gold on to unlock that ability is just terrible.  It basically tries to rip off 3d Sonic the Hedgehog games, and does it very badly.  If you're wondering why Sonic games are being brought up in a review of an open-world 3rd person shooter, you aren't alone.
Conclusion:  Decent fun, but overall not very good.  6/10 would not replay.

Played the Game for about 25 hours, so I wanted to rewrite this since I kinda just made a brief summary.
The game is amazing and for an indie title its one of the best, easily one of my favorite games.The game has its ups and downsides which ill explain.
+Difficulty- While this might discourage some the game rewards you with accomplishment and doesnt spoon feed you info needed to win, its like Dark Souls in the fact that its mostly trial and error and you have to learn from your own mistakes, which very much appealed to me.
+Crew- In FTL one of the best features is the diversity of the races and the certain things they excel and struggle with. Add in the fact that if you dont have a clone bay when they die they're gone forever and you can get quite the attatchment to your crew.
+Story- The game has a small backstory that if you read into events that happen you cna piece together. The way the story is told is one of the best because it gives you the option of learning it if you want, but if you want to just blow everything up it wont shove it down your throat.
+Mods - The modding community is great, plenty of ship, weapon, and even story changing mods you can have a real hayday. I highly recommend the Captain's Edition mod as its a large collabaration of great mods that dont change the game, just add to it.
+Style- Im a sucker for these more retro type games, and this game really refines it making it aestetically pleasing even if you aren't a big fan of it.
+-RNG- While I do love the game when it comes down to it alot of the time your success will depend on luck. This works both ways though. you can be someone fresh into the game and beat the boss from luck or a veteran who didnt get any weapons. While these dont happen often it is still annoying when it does. Now the Plus side is that this is annoying but really helps you make the best of a pile of crap. When you find yourself barekly living but making it, it offers a small thrill.
-Repetition- The game is great. however the vanilla game will start to get repetitive since it only comes with a set amount of events to give to you. You may come across the same event 2-times a run depending on how far you get. This can be remedied with mods which can add more events and features to make those recurring empty beacons especially helpful and immersive.
-"Meta"- The one gripe i often have is that while the game offers different playstyles and crew to supplement that, there are ships inherently easier. While its not a terrible thing it kinda takes value away when you kill entire crews for the entire 8 sectors and breeze through the boss
SUMMARY: In all the game is VERY well made and seems like it was made by a triple A company in my opinion. It punishes and rewards and with the mods the community pumps out, will definitely occupy much of my spare time. I'd give the game 9/10 almost perfect, but still placing in my top 10 favorite games.

This is a very decent yugioh game with a few flaws, but is definitely worth buying.
First of all i strongly suggest going into settings and changing the prompts to simple mode, which will make the prompts a lot less annoying during gameplay.
Pros:
*Multiple Generations- This game travels through the various generations of yugioh and its pretty cool to see how each generation advances in gameplay from the very vanilla original yugioh gameplay all the way to sunchro, xyz, and pendelum monsters.
*Deck Customization/ Booster Packs- You are able to earn credits through duels which will allow you to buy booster packs to create decks. You earn credits pretty fast so earning booster packs never feels like a chore.
*Story Mode- Allows you to experience a wide variety of deck types with the story decks, while also allowing you to use your own created deck. If you're a fan of the anime it can be cool to play with familiar character decks.
Nuetral:
*Forced Tutorials- Will be repetitive for people who already know how to play, but honestly arent that long. You only have to go through a short battle and additional tutorials are available if newer players need more help.
*Story- The story for each series seems to be very abridged. It mostly consists of quick dialogue to introduce a duel.
*Animation- The animation for monsters are low quality, but only a few monsters have them and they are very short, so it isnt that big of a deal.
Cons:
DLC- It sucks that a lot of extra duels are locked behind a paywall, but it does have a good amount of base content, where the dlc isnt something that you really need to buy.
Card Packs- This is only a small gripe, but you can only open card packs one at a time which can be annoying when you have enough credits to buy thousands of packs.
It would also be nice to have packs that are non-character based, since it is hard to tell what booster pack you need to get for a specific deck.
All in all, this is a very solid yugioh game and while it does have some annoyances, the actual dueling, which is the main part of the game, is very well done and lots of fun.

Listen, there is nothing wrong with this game. I wish I could say it is a good game, but its not. It's not a bad game either. I usually dont like to be so ambiguous when voicing an opinion on a game but this one left me feeling like i was poured a glass half empty. Now I realize this is a "saga" which inherently means there will be more volumes added with time; a fact for which I am thankful. Realistically, this game lacks a certain spirit. By that I mean, it feels like it wants to be more than it is or even can be for that matter. Perhaps it's a allusion for things to come. Ultimately though, in the time between title releases, I enjoy a game with a good replayability value and, on that front, this game tanks. Maybe when there are like five or six Banner Saga titles this game will have a rewatch value like Lord of the Rings. Right now however, with only two titles, it is hard to stomach more than a one-time playthrough. This is sad because I had such high hopes for this title. I had read some great reviews and everyone I talked to seemed to enjoy it thoroughly. Would I recommend this game? ...Yes. Would I recommend you play it more than once? ...No. And hey, maybe that is the intention.
It may seem as though this is a scathing review, and I don't intend to mislead. There are many good things about this game. So many in fact, I played through the title twice just to see if I was the crazy one. I think the most striking part of this game is the art design. It has elements of Mary Blair (the artist responsible for the awe inspiring "Allice in Wonderland" and many other classic Disney movies of yore). It has giants and crazy people whose illustrations are varied and interesting. The story, albeit just a portion of a clearly more involved epic, is enticing. There are characters that you develop feelings for,  and then they die in time to awkard scenarios and dialogue. And yes, you do miss them. It is well paced. The music, although somewhat repetitive, sets a mood and is fitting given the story and environment. Long story short, many things are good!
So what's wrong? Well first and foremost, this is a story game. It is presented as a strategy game; or at least an amalgamation of the two. This is not a strategy game...not really. If you want to play a strategy game, maybe go find another title. That being said, for a story game (one wherein you are given choices) there is a preconceived notion that the choices you make have some over-arching consequence to the outcome of the story. Disappointingly, it does not. I played through this twice and chose completely different story options and, with the exception of one character not dying, the result was completely the same. Now maybe I could play through it a third or even fourth time to completely change the destiny of a couple of the dozen or so characters one will meet throughout a playthrough, but I dont see how that will change anything in terms of combat options or story line directive. On the topic of combat, it is... a bit mundane. Yes, you can equip certain items to certain characters to min/max their effectiveness on the field, but at a point you are just achievement hunting. If that is your thing this may be a good game for you, as a single playthrough is only about seven hours or so. I like achievements, but I dont think I would subject myself to 20 more hours of this game unless I was embarking from the start of a exciting epic. Which I may do when they release two or three more episodes.
I am however going to go ahead and give this game a thumbs up. Its certainly not the best title and I dont know if I would pay full price for it, but its does have some substance and therefore merit. I am intrigued to see more from these developers in the same title series. So it's not all that bad...right? I guess I'll just wrap up by saying: decide for yourself, just dont say you went into it without at least some idea of what you were buying.

This game, in my opinion, should not be criticized from a gaming perspective but from a cinematic one. And from this point of view, it's an amazing title.
For the most part, the game runs from scene to scene without any option for the player/viewer to wander around; the few scenes where you can move for yourself have very limited options, and usually work as means to enhance the dramatic effect - your character will walk slowly across a room, or around a table, in a predefined road; The camera will rotate automatically according to predefined direction orders. Having a look around will trigger an event that will carry you on to the next scene.
However, do not mistake: the design of this game requires an enormous amount of viewer involvement, which makes this unique mini-series one of the most engaging experiences I had.
First of all, you usually have a limited amount of time to choose your next line, meaning you must decide and measure the consequences of each option quickly. The game will not wait, and inaction will result with silence. The game will also not go backwards, and you will not be able to go through all dialog options. This design gives the game a fantastic pace which carries you strongly into it's world, enhancing your empathy with the characters you play and with their dilemmas, struggles, decisions and consequences.
The action scenes works very much the same: although the player controls are as basic as it gets, and even though the scenes are usually railroaded from start to end, your moves are integrated with some fantastic choreography and thrilling direction, which makes these scenes some of the best action I've got to experience.
Now, the main story arc will converge to a general pre-set story, obviously; however you do get to make a good amount of decisions, and also define the contents of most dialogue throughout the game. You get to shape the nature of your characters, to make them who they are, to walk them through a character development. The game starts with the words: "The story is tailored by your choice" - and so it does.
UPDATE: Unfortunately the game's last part pretty much messed up anything good about this game, making the majority of my review no longer viable. While the game linearity was essential to make it through its six parts, I did expect to have some influence of its end. Unfortunately, in order to prepare the ground for a second season, it ended in a total railroad that wasn't much affected by any of my decisions. And it was a frustrating ending. Not sure that I would still recommend it.

So what that Russian version is free. Support the admins! Join our community and appreciate this game!
Now, I'll keep this review honest and straight-forward will state things many players look down on, as well as the good things I look up to.
Pros:
-Minimal P2W (like, only p2w I know of is battle pets. Nothing to freak out over in my opinion. If you think this is P2W, you haven't played ArcheAge)
-Well worth the 10$ price tag (in my opinion, in my boyfriend's opinion. Keep in mind, we're former ArcheAge players. 10$ is NOTHING)
-Fun player base = they fill in the silence in roleplay chat mostly, with references to memes, open conversations and discussions e.t.c.
-Run-to-checkpoint mechanic = Busy? Select on the map with right click where you'd like your character to travel. Then press T, and sit back as it follows roads to its destination. Really nice, especially since there is no fast travel, and really nice if you want to play and are doing something else while the game runs in the background.
-Graphics and weather mechanics are STUNNING = the amount of detail put into the map, is simply breathtaking. When it rains your character and their mount is shiny with moisture, roads become drenched.
-Lots to do = Trade running, horse breeding, horse levelling, fishing, exploring, grinding and so much more.
-Amazing combat mechanics = Not your typical press 1 press 5, though it can be used optionally. Each class has a different play style and different combo shortcuts. The amount of detail put into this game left me speechless.
-Fun classes = Wanna be a ninja? Berserker with a hand cannon? Mage? Bo-staff fighter? It's all here!
-Unique world = medieval, with a fantasy tinge, though mostly strictly medieval. (unless I'm missing something here)
-Useful Mounts, can carry load= They can all carry your items in case you're under too much load. When your mount carries an item, it is equipped with load physically. Little details like that add life to the game. Donkeys and wagons have more carry slots than horses.
-Map is H U G E = Wild guess, two Skyrims?
-Changing characters / having a few characters does not affect your max energy / NPC relationships e.t.c. = Your character levels, skills and skill points and inventories are separated. Stables, warehouses and energy pool (for crafting / talking to NPCs) is the same, however each character regenerates their energy independently, which adds to gameplay if you're a person who loves each character and must play it yet wants to keep it worthwhile. I love this mechanic.
-Diving = Though I didn't get this far, it is possible to swim the ocean in this game, as well to fish.
-Guild PvP = Didn't experience it either, but guilds PvP over trading nodes, which is damn fun to watch.
-World has depth and realism = Stablehands take a break now and then and are unavailable for some time, at night monsters get aggressive and have a larger aggro range, small things that add depth.
-The map is awesome = Map can have rain, clouds, sun e.t.c. It's another small thing that makes BDO pleasant and worthwhile.
Cons:
-Servers like to disconnect you or delay certain actions = Looting, stamina regeneration e.t.c. seems to be server sided. My internet is a steady 10mb/s and it does not affect me too much, however on busy days if you're an unfortunate user with slow net, it will most likely affect you. This however, is easily countered if you switch to a non-crowded server. (BDO servers can be changed any time and are not a permanent choice)
-Horse-levelling wagons running loops through towns. Though it keeps things more lively, it certainly feels like a small turn off when the same carriage passes you five times as you wait for a friend to get to you.
-Separate Stables = Dontcha just love running back two towns to grab your favorite steed, which you've left behind in a town stable to keep it safe while grinding? Well, although it may not be an issue with most, to a new player the whole "each stable is separate" concept is quite confusing. And this is extremely annoying when you move to a new zone and feel like moving all your beloved mounts to it. However, with 3 slots per stable per town, you can have a hell load of different horsies.
-Separate warehouses = Just like the stables. But it teaches you to be organised. Temper stones in one town, junk in another. It is a realistic idea, but an average person would consider this a downside, hence why I'm putting this here.
-No mount share, no wagon share = You can't drag your friend along with you, unfortunately. Only on a tier 6 horse with a special perk(which, mind you, is costly in in-game currency). However at the moment it's not too much of a problem. Just something worthy of mention. Wagons usually make your brain automatically relate the vehicle to "Two or more" being transported on one. Not the case here!
-No proper tutorial for crafting and majority of game mechanics = Combat and movement and questing explained, but at level 37 I still haven't run into any crafting tutorial except how to make sugar lumps to tame horses.
That's all I can think of for now. As far as crafting and gear goes, I'm clueless for the time being. So I shall post this review, and consider it a first-glance from newbie point of view.

I have had my eye on this game for awhile and finally decided to pick it up while it was on sale.  I am very glad that I did.  It is a projectile-based fighting game where you attempt to smash a ball into your opponent while also avoiding getting hit, kind of like dodgeball on super steroids. Each character has their own playstyle and most will find one they like over others.
The only real flaw I've seen so far is that the single player/challenge mode is a little boring, but oh well.  Online is more fun anyways.
Overall I would strongly recommend this game.  It has great gameplay, very fun multiplayer, interesting characters and stages, and a good soundtrack.

I distinctly remember seeing this game several days ago and paying it no mind, thinking it was just a bunch of Source engine trash. First impressions were quite mediocre but I would say the game has very quickly grown on me.
First the good. it is legitiamately fun. No seriously, the floaty controls and ice rink surfaces make for an incredibly fast paced and twitchy shooter. Not for everyone but it does appeal to peopel who like the acrobactic martial arts gun-fu style of combat in movies such as Die Hard and The Matrix (Hell theres a Matrix poster in one of the levels...). The gun sounds are satisfying and the animations, while crude, get the job done. The standard deathmatch mode, with all its hilarity, are punctuated by micro-objectives such as a race from point to point or a wanted system. Completing these objectives gives buffs and bonues to the player who won these challenges, adding another dimension to gameplay. The greatest strength this title has is in its hilarity and its lack of taking itself seriously. Surprisingly enough, for a game that encourages player to run around like chickens with thier heads cut off, glitches are not very common. That may be a personal experience however.
Unfortunately the game suffers at this moment from a severe lack of content. With only three playble characters, a relatively small menagiere of weapons and limited number of maps, the game does tend to get boring playing online quickly (I could only handle 30-40 minute spurts before getting bored). Additions of more gamemodes would be welcome as while the standard deathmatch mode is fun; the boring factor does tend to set in quickly.
Weapon balance may also be taken into consideration. The persuader (shotgun) does tend to dominate and in massive battles, it quickly degenerates into a persuader fest. The vindicator (FN FAL) and the Black magic (M16) also are normally not ideal as long range in this game is basically two rooms over, still shotgun distance. The Mac Daddy (Mac 10) with its higher damage and rate of fire dominates the Undertaker (MP5K). The single pistols are useless. Enough said.
Weapon balance could be tweaked.
The frantic movement of the player models and such also may prove a heath hazard. I do not recommend playing this game if you easily suffer from any sort of motion sickness. This could prove lethal.
Despite its obvious lack of polish, I still rather like the game. Its not for everyone, fans of tactical shooters such as Insurgency, ARMA and Counter-Strike (I personally dont think thats tactical at all) will most definately not like this. Visually its choppy, laggy and uninspiring. Its disorientating, confusing and infuriating at times. Gameplay wise however, it offers something that you just dont find in F2P games these days. Did i mention it was free? The Developers obviously have put quite a bit of love into this game and I am personalyl interested in how they will take this game.

Let me start off by saying that while I don't recommend this game, it is indeed an enjoyable one.  My "thumbs down" does not mean that it is a bad game, simply that I don't think it is worth playing.
I was not a fan of Saints Row The Third, and I originally did not plan to play this one, but I got it in the Humble Bundle, so I figured I might as well see if this iteration was better.
It was.  The addition of "super powers" adds a huge amount of enjoyment to the game.  The only real downside to the powers is that it is sometimes difficult to utilize them fully.  You can't shoot while jumping or sprinting, so you generally use those sparingly in combat, and many of the powers are either on long cooldowns or just aren't strong enough to practically be used in many situations.
The downside to the game is that other than the powers, it is just like The Third, which in my opinion wasn't very good.  The shooting mechanics aren't the greatest, and they basically come down to using the pistols to headshot every grunt enemy and emptying several magazines of any weapon into the "tank" enemies.
The story is not particularly interesting, but it takes itself way too seriously.  It is a generally over-the-top game, but they seem to try to give you an emotional attachment to the story, which is not going to happen.  I'm playing this game to blow up aliens, not look deeper into myself.  Many cutscenes are skippable, but some aren't, which sucks.  The voice acting is okay, but the animations in cutscenes are sorely lacking - none of the characters' bodies move when they are talking, only their mouths.
The game's biggest sin, however, is in the collect-a-thon.  The upgrades for the super powers require a "currency" called "clusters", which are scattered around the world on rooftops, buried in walls and terrain, or stuck in floating orbs, and you must collect 500 to 1000 to fully upgrade your abilities.  That is not a small amount.  You can also upgrade your weapons, ammo, and some other stuff like health.  This, of course, requires a currency called "cache" (cash), which you get from killing enemies (and picking each individual bit of cache up off the ground afterwards), completing challenges, and doing the story missions.  It requires an obscene amount of cache to upgrade everything fully.  On top of these upgrades, there are various collectables - you can destroy small statues, of which there are 39 scattered about the world, you can collect audio logs, which there are around 30, you can "hack" all the stores, complete all the challenges, do all the activities and try to earn a "gold" rank, etc.  It's a huge grind, and some of the more interesting powers are locked behind it, such as walking on water.
Speaking of walking on water, the "activity" that you have to get a gold on to unlock that ability is just terrible.  It basically tries to rip off 3d Sonic the Hedgehog games, and does it very badly.  If you're wondering why Sonic games are being brought up in a review of an open-world 3rd person shooter, you aren't alone.
Conclusion:  Decent fun, but overall not very good.  6/10 would not replay.

Man, oh man, do I love Half-Life 2! Possibly one of the greatest games I've ever played and that's a statement I don't make lightly. But after beating the game and getting all of the achievements, I can safely say that I not only love, but completely ADORE Half-Life 2. It should be noted that I'm not an FPS fan for the most part, with the majority of my time with shooters being spent with the original Doom and it's sequel, Doom II. Another good example of an FPS I like is Devil Daggers, a game I really need to play more of. But Half-Life 2 has definitely been my favourite out of all them.
GAMEPLAY
The game holds your interest. From level to level, chapter to chapter, enemy to enemy, the game takes what it already has and makes it fresh even if you are just slaughtering Combine for the one hundredth millionth time. Never in the entirety of the game did I feel like it was a slog (OK, that's a bit of a lie, considering that *GASP* I don't think Ravenholm is that great! (More on that later)). The multitude of different weaponry, with each one having it's own "kick" and weaknesses, make you become very creative with how you use them. Use a crowbar for up-close encounters, the SMG for large quantities of enemies or the shotgun for quickly dispatching your enemies. And trust me, by the end of the game, you'll be able to snipe with the 9mm like a pro. Also, the Gravity Gun is one of the coolest weapons in any video game I've ever seen in just the concept alone; and in practice, it's incredibly fun to use.
STORY
The story, all things considered, is very simple. You, Gordon Freeman, are a badass, plain and simple. And it is up to you to lead a resistance of humans to undermine the strict and bloody regime of the alien force known as the Combine. Despite the story's simplicity, I was invested pretty much the entire time, mostly because everyone treats Gordon Freeman as the messiah. And to be honest, I can kinda see why. Not only does he have the highest level of plot armor in video game history, but he's also a beacon, the "one free man", the symbol of hope in a world torn apart by countless assaults by the Combine against the humans. It's actually quite uplifting, in all honesty. Oh by the way, there's a guy called Wallace Breen, who is your old boss from a facility known as Black Mesa; the actions of said facility basically caused this entire mess to occur in the first place. You will learn to hate and only hate this man by the end of the story. Relish it.
WORLD/DESIGN/IDK
Can I say that the way that the actual game is designed is brilliant? Unlike other first person shooters (or really any other game) where you sharply and jarringly transition from level to level, you progress, albeit linearly, through a seamless world. True, this 'seamless' world is made up of short loading screens which aren't really loading screens per se as they are just loading the next map directly in front of you, if that makes sense. To put it simply, the world never breaks. There's cohesion and connection because if you were to somehow make the entire game take place on one map, it would feel natural, as you're moving forwards constantly within the world of the game. This is what I think is sorely missing in some modern day games. And I don't mean open world, not at all. But I wish there was more linearity that has...well 'world linearity'.
THE SOURCE ENGINE OR HOW I LEARNED TO STOP CARING AND LOVE VALVE
The Source Engine is in my opinion one of the greatest game engines of all time. The level of detail that's possible, the amount of objects that can be present at once, the unbelievable lip syncing and animation especially on Alyx Vance, who will become an invaluable companion along your journey. Seriously, some of the animation is so believable and human, it could give some games made today a run for their money. And this game was released in 2004. 2004! And my jaw still drops at some of the things this versatile engine can pull off. Also, the AI is fantastic. I don't necessarily mean enemy AI (THAT can be incredibly stupid), but the AI of your allies is extremely strong and they can certainly hold their own against enemy AI. I never, ever had a complaint about the AI throughout my entire playthrough of this game. Ever. One last point about the Source Engine is that there are no traditional cutscenes. It all takes place in real time within the game. Meaning that, for the majority of the cutscenes, you can jump around like an idiot while two or more characters talk about something I'm sure is incredibly important.
COMPLAINT:
Yes, complaint. I really only have one. And that's the chapter that takes place in the 'legendary' Ravenholm. Now please, put down your torches and pitchforks and allow me to explain. First of all, the atmosphere is AMAZING. Not necessarily scary, but incredibly spooky and just absolutely dripping with macabre themes and locales. But here's the problem, for the majority of the game, the maps have been very linear, which is perfectly fine. But all of a sudden, Half-Life 2 says "Nuh-uh, buddy! Maze-like structure of a town for you!" and then after you beat it, the game never does it again. So I question as to why? Sure after the first attempt (such as if you go back to get the "Zombie Chopper" achievement), you can blast through Ravenholm with remarkable ease. But for the first time around, I spent a good hour or so scratching my head and getting frustrated, going around in circles. Maybe it was different for other people, But "We don't go to Ravenholm" was definitely the most infuriating chapter in the game.
THE WRAP-UP
Whew! Don't worry, I'll keep this short. Suffice to say-BUY IT, BUY IT, BUY IT, IT'S AMAZING, IT'S UNBELIEVABLE-Ahem, excuse my inner fanboy, but this game is certainly well worth the price of admission (a pretty cheap one, all things considered) and delivers on an extremely impressive experience that rivals and even dominates many of the tired, boring shooters of today, despite being over a decade old. If you love shooting things (while also having your brain challenged) and you haven't played Half-Life 2, play it. You're seriously missing out.

There's much less fanservice in Hyperdimension Neptunia than I expected. I mean, less than I expected, there's an absolute ton of fanservice, I just thought there'd be more. Not disappointed there.
Now, I've seen this game called a grindfest, and I think that's unfair. The first and most important thing you need to know about Nuptunia is this: the unlockable dungeons and items are not 'optional'.
Completing the hundreds of side-quests the game throws your way is crucial to making progress, but as long as you do, the difficulty curve is fair.
There is no way to run a 'low level game' in Neptunia. Even two or three levels difference can mean tripling your damage output, and damage output is extremely important seeing as strong enemies auto-heal at the end of every turn starting from the very first side-dungeon.  It's simply not possible to cheese your way through hard enemies with items or special attacks.
The game, which plays like a single-player, turnbased Phantasy Star Online, stays interesting by constantly throwing enemies your way that seem unbeatable. You walk into the fight, throw down your best offense and do... 0 damage per hit. It's okay! You don't need to grind. You'll be relieved to find that, by now, the previous 'unbeatable' enemies are total pushovers. If there aren't any previous enemies to push over, it might be time to advance the plot.
Neptunia loves to tease the player (you) by 'unlocking' items which can't be actually bought until 5+ hours later in the game, showing you what you *could* have, and it's sometimes infuriating but also a good hook to keep you playing. Other than that sense of acomplishment, there's not a lot of reason to play.
So if gratifying rushes of endorphins for doing what the game wants you to do is your thing, this is the game for you. Other than that, there's some very funny dialog aimed towards anime and gaming enthusiasts. Cute outfits which will take you 50+ hours to unlock are not much of a reason to play. There are any number of ways you could get your rocks off, and this ain't the game for that.
Review revision, after finishing the game:
It took me a week to play the first two-thirds of Hyperdimension Neptunia and several months to play the last third. The game runs out of steam in the most curiously awkward - no scatch that more like absurd - collision between gameplay and story I've ever seen.
The writing for the main cast of this game is excellent. The characters are extremely likable and deceptively deep, trading dialog mainly about Japanese etiquette that translates surprisingly well into English. The recurring joke of the game is that these characters, literal goddesses in their universe, are nerds, shut-ins, obsessive gamers, simple minded, rude, and often exchange♥♥♥♥♥♥jokes for several paragraphs on end. They get a lot of milage out of this concept, right up to the end it's pretty amusing, however...
At some point, someone thought it would be really funny to give Neptune an attack which can one-hit-kill mooost of the enemies in the game. She transforms into a fighter jet and lets loose a cluster of missiles and that's it.  Once you unlock that, the difficulty curve goes to♥♥♥♥♥♥and you can blitz to the final boss no sweat. This is when the game introduces a flurry of second-tier party members, incase you're still looking for a challange, you can take on the last 3rd of the game with severely underpowered non-goddesses.
So because it was apparently vitally important to the game that Neptune have a one-hit-kill special, these extra characters are introduced, and they're all given dialog, and all of their dialog is pointless. It shouldn't even be there. The main cast keeps getting interrupted by these nobodies, not even interesting nobodies. Take TEKKEN for example, who has no memorable dialog, and whose sole gimmick is that she looks way too frail to be in any way associated with a fighting game franchise.
I'd still recommend this game, but the best content is frontloaded. Unless you want those skimpy outfits I mentioned, those are all at the very end.
