Video Review:
The Banner Saga is a turn based strategy game where you get to live through a book basically. I feel like describing it any other way would be technically incorrect. You do a lot of reading and make a lot of choices like choose your own adventure games. Is The Banner Saga worth your time? Let’s talk our way through that.
The gameplay of the banner saga in terms of the combat is turn based as you can expect. There’s some special armor and hitpoint mechanics that make it very unique. WIth three different well-scaled difficulty settings you can find a challenge no matter your skill level. There’s many different classes you’ll find available to you too that you can use to bring into battle. It’s a lot of fun, if maybe a little repetitive over time since the goal is always the same. Kill approximately six enemies. Over and over and over. It’s fun enough though and short enough that that’s not really a problem unless you plan on replaying it for different story results. The biggest problem with the gameplay is that to level a character you need to kill the enemy with that character. Apparently warriors don’t learn by fighting, they learn by killing. And be careful who you choose to give kills because almost everyone is expendable, but we’ll get to that later
Story-wise, The Banner Saga will have you mostly reading text, kind of like a visual novel, but with some flavor choices that generally get the same response with a different word or two. There are some very important choices you can make which is a very nice thing such as whether or not to let someone into your caravan, whether or not to try to save someone, whether or not to risk your life on a bridge filled with endless monsters. There’s plenty of them and they really do have an effect which is AMAZING. However...there is a bit of walking dead syndrome here. If someone is meant to die? Then they will. Several chapters later they will be killed off. And on the rare occasion they aren’t? They will simply lack dialogue for the rest of the game. And this may be considered a slight spoiler, but you will figure it out yourself VERY shortly into the game. Almost every single character in the game is slated for death. They have very limited dialogue written and one way or another you are forced to kill them off or live with a mute for a while before they are eventually killed off anyway. Most of them don’t even stick around long enough for you to get invested in them. At first it gets you immersed and feeling like you’re constantly struggling against the evil forces in the game and then you just realize that nothing you do matters anyway in the long run because through a mixture of scripted encounters, mutinies, and occurrences they will kill off every single character they meant to kill off one way or another. These choices are amazing...until you realize the effects only matter for the first game. I can count on one hand the amount of choices that ACTUALLY matter and would need an auditorium filled with hands to count the amount of choices that are there just to fool you into thinking you ever had a say to begin with.
It really pisses me off because when I saw this game I wanted it. I wanted to like it. It was so good looking and had such positive reviews. But I have no idea what the heck anyone liked about this in the end. Did they actually play it? It’s a very short game depending on difficulty setting and how many fights you choose to get in. And by the way...if you don’t choose as many as possible then you end up with severely weakened fighters that will be at a constant disadvantage during fights as the difficulty scales over TIME. The game LOVES to take strong fighters from you and give weak ones to you all the time so that can really screw you over late-game if you’ve built up only the ones that aren’t permanent. (Pretty much everyone but a few main characters.) But then again, losing doesn’t matter either. When you lose you just lose some pointless statistics of people which I will explain later, and get some slightly different text saying someone saved your♥♥♥♥♥ There’s literally zero consequences whatsoever to losing a battle.
The caravan system itself is shallow as hell as well. You spend renown, which is also experience that you use on leveling up, to buy supplies for your caravan. Your supply need is decided by the amount of clansmen, fighters, and Varl you have in your group. What’s a Varl? I don’t know. It looks like a giant horned viking inspired beast of a man. The game never explains any of this to you though, it just starts you off playing as a Varl. All Varl are apparently fighters and them plus fighters can engage in what is called a “war” encounter.
Wars are easily the most pointless aspect of this game simply because they scale. When you enter a war you can pick how many you want to fight yourself or whether you should just run away or something. Although the enemy amounts always scale to your current fighting population and you’ll find it’s easy to kill 1000 enemies with 700 fighters even if you only kill six and only lose 20 people in the process. Seriously, what is the point of these if they scale? How many people you lose doesn’t matter. There’s no flavor text regarding it and there’s no mechanical effect either. If you lose a lot then you fight a lot less. If you lose none then you fight a lot more. They’re all numbers with literally no meaning whatsoever. The story likes to try to trick you into thinking taking on “a lot” of enemies is a bad thing. Meanwhile I ran right through “a lot”, killed all of them in the process, and only lost 30 warriors. This mechanic is pointless.
And it still really pisses me off that I can’t like this game because a lot of the writing itself behind the story is actually amazing. If this had proper production, choices that actually mattered, or at least a lack of illusion that your choices do matter then it would be such a fun game. If the war and caravan systems got more depth and meaning with less scaling then that would make the game even more strategic and enjoyable. But The Banner Saga just doesn’t do that. Maybe their dev team couldn’t handle it. But this game is filled with illusions and scripted events that love to trick you into thinking you have a choice.
The game is buggy too. Several times my game broke and it wouldn’t let me rest to heal my units. It made the days pass by, but my units never healed. I had to reload my save to fix that. And that’s another thing. Why does it tell you the time passed when time doesn’t matter? In this game you’re constantly on the run and the enemies are constantly described as being right behind you. I rested for like a week or two in a town once and nothing happened. Right behind me? Yeah right. This game is too scripted to simulate something like that. There is no dynamic feature to be seen anywhere.
The Banner Saga gets a 3/10. I really wanted to give it a 4 just to try to emphasize that I was able to have fun with it for about 3/4ths of the total chapters, but I also need to emphasize just how quickly all of these cons and problems add up. The Banner Saga COULD have been a great game. It had all the potential, but none of the execution. And I’m really just sad because I wanted to play the whole saga. But with a linear saga that picks up where one game leaves off and is heavily story-driven? With this many problems with how they move the story along? What’s the point?
Don’t buy this game unless you like being thrown around like a lab rat to try to evoke from emotional response out of you with a bunch of scripted nonsense while the game lies to your face about saying you had a choice in the matter when the wiki and gameplay videos themselves will easily prove that wrong. Avoid The Banner Saga. It’s one huge and disappointing lie.

I like videogames.  I like music.  I like having my retinas assaulted by swirls of colorful space dust.
If you enjoy treating your brain to videogames and music like I do, and are enthralled with the amalgamation of the two, then there’s a good chance you’re going to enjoy Beat Hazard as well.  The twist is that Beat Hazard uses your own music to create custom levels.
Beat Hazard uses songs from your computer, so you can choose which song you want to play and the game creates a level around it.  Levels begin like the arcade classic, Asteroids, where you reduce large hunks of space rocks into smaller pieces with your lasers before some mean old spaceships arrive to provide put up a fight.  The unique aspect of the game is that everything from  the velocity of the asteroids to the quanity of boss ships you fight is dependent upon the music.
Blasting enemy ships into space rubble provides power-ups, which increase your firepower and the volume of the  music.  Your weapons are also influenced by the tune of the music, so when a song is softer or hits a quiet spot, your firepower is greatly reduced.  It’s like the gunner on the ship is a little kid sucking down fistfulls of Pixie Sticks.  He’s running around screaming with his hands in the air one minute and the instant the song tones it down a bit, he is lulled to sleep.
In addition to determining the patterns of the enemies, the game’s visuals are also greatly affected by the song selection.   As the ship is upgraded, its firepower is transformed from simple white blips into a seizure-inducing kaleidoscope of doom.  Spots in the background that initially appear nondescript also pulsate and swirl with colors to the song’s beat.  It’s something straight out of a Hawkwind concert (or Pink Floyd, for those not in tune with their ’70s space rock).  The background effects intensify the point where it can seem like you’re trying to play a game through a late-90s Windows Media Player visualizer.
Did you ever watch those visualizers and imagine playing a game through it?  Me neither.  That’s because while the visuals are quite impressive and make the game infinitely more compelling for onlookers, they are also a serious hindrance to actually playing the game.  I frequently find myself dying thanks to something that I either didn’t see or assumed was just a part of the background.  I suppose it could be argued that the visuals are a way of increasing the game’s difficulty, particularly for longer songs.
Crazy psychedelic visuals and customizable soundtracks are about as useful as a chainsaw to a beaver if the game feels like a chore to play, and thankfully the meat of Beat Hazard is excellent.  I find twin-stick shooters to be stressful at times because of the never-ending onslaught of ever-increasing enemies, but Beat Hazard is refreshing because your targets appear in waves.  Depending on the song, you tend to have a few seconds to catch your breath before preparing for the next attack.
One of the unintended benefits of the game is that it gives me an impetus to root through my music collection and dust off some tunes I have not heard in awhile.  I love shuffling through my songs and thinking “Hmm, I wonder what this song will be like?”  I find that in general, songs tend to work better if they are more dynamic and have a lot of changes in their volume or beats.
The game does a great job of tracking your progress and keeping a tally of how many songs you have beaten, or if you have finished an entire album.  Even if you don’t complete a song, the game still awards experience and you can still gain levels which add bonuses and a feeling of persistence.  Achievements would be a fantastic addition to this game, but unfortunately are absent through no fault of Cold Beam Games.
Despite it being a little too mesmerizing for its own good, Beat Hazard is an amazing experience and quite the technical accomplishment.  It is easy to recommend laying down the $5 for gamers who are music enthusiasts.  Outside of the allure of playing your own music,  Beat Hazard is an exciting and unique shooter and a great addition to the Indie library.

Now, I'll keep this review honest and straight-forward will state things many players look down on, as well as the good things I look up to.
Pros:
-Minimal P2W (like, only p2w I know of is battle pets. Nothing to freak out over in my opinion. If you think this is P2W, you haven't played ArcheAge)
-Well worth the 10$ price tag (in my opinion, in my boyfriend's opinion. Keep in mind, we're former ArcheAge players. 10$ is NOTHING)
-Fun player base = they fill in the silence in roleplay chat mostly, with references to memes, open conversations and discussions e.t.c.
-Run-to-checkpoint mechanic = Busy? Select on the map with right click where you'd like your character to travel. Then press T, and sit back as it follows roads to its destination. Really nice, especially since there is no fast travel, and really nice if you want to play and are doing something else while the game runs in the background.
-Graphics and weather mechanics are STUNNING = the amount of detail put into the map, is simply breathtaking. When it rains your character and their mount is shiny with moisture, roads become drenched.
-Lots to do = Trade running, horse breeding, horse levelling, fishing, exploring, grinding and so much more.
-Amazing combat mechanics = Not your typical press 1 press 5, though it can be used optionally. Each class has a different play style and different combo shortcuts. The amount of detail put into this game left me speechless.
-Fun classes = Wanna be a ninja? Berserker with a hand cannon? Mage? Bo-staff fighter? It's all here!
-Unique world = medieval, with a fantasy tinge, though mostly strictly medieval. (unless I'm missing something here)
-Useful Mounts, can carry load= They can all carry your items in case you're under too much load. When your mount carries an item, it is equipped with load physically. Little details like that add life to the game. Donkeys and wagons have more carry slots than horses.
-Map is H U G E = Wild guess, two Skyrims?
-Changing characters / having a few characters does not affect your max energy / NPC relationships e.t.c. = Your character levels, skills and skill points and inventories are separated. Stables, warehouses and energy pool (for crafting / talking to NPCs) is the same, however each character regenerates their energy independently, which adds to gameplay if you're a person who loves each character and must play it yet wants to keep it worthwhile. I love this mechanic.
-Diving = Though I didn't get this far, it is possible to swim the ocean in this game, as well to fish.
-Guild PvP = Didn't experience it either, but guilds PvP over trading nodes, which is damn fun to watch.
-World has depth and realism = Stablehands take a break now and then and are unavailable for some time, at night monsters get aggressive and have a larger aggro range, small things that add depth.
-The map is awesome = Map can have rain, clouds, sun e.t.c. It's another small thing that makes BDO pleasant and worthwhile.
Cons:
-Servers like to disconnect you or delay certain actions = Looting, stamina regeneration e.t.c. seems to be server sided. My internet is a steady 10mb/s and it does not affect me too much, however on busy days if you're an unfortunate user with slow net, it will most likely affect you. This however, is easily countered if you switch to a non-crowded server. (BDO servers can be changed any time and are not a permanent choice)
-Horse-levelling wagons running loops through towns. Though it keeps things more lively, it certainly feels like a small turn off when the same carriage passes you five times as you wait for a friend to get to you.
-Separate Stables = Dontcha just love running back two towns to grab your favorite steed, which you've left behind in a town stable to keep it safe while grinding? Well, although it may not be an issue with most, to a new player the whole "each stable is separate" concept is quite confusing. And this is extremely annoying when you move to a new zone and feel like moving all your beloved mounts to it. However, with 3 slots per stable per town, you can have a hell load of different horsies.
-Separate warehouses = Just like the stables. But it teaches you to be organised. Temper stones in one town, junk in another. It is a realistic idea, but an average person would consider this a downside, hence why I'm putting this here.
-No mount share, no wagon share = You can't drag your friend along with you, unfortunately. Only on a tier 6 horse with a special perk(which, mind you, is costly in in-game currency). However at the moment it's not too much of a problem. Just something worthy of mention. Wagons usually make your brain automatically relate the vehicle to "Two or more" being transported on one. Not the case here!
-No proper tutorial for crafting and majority of game mechanics = Combat and movement and questing explained, but at level 37 I still haven't run into any crafting tutorial except how to make sugar lumps to tame horses.
That's all I can think of for now. As far as crafting and gear goes, I'm clueless for the time being. So I shall post this review, and consider it a first-glance from newbie point of view.

Okay where do I start...
:
First thing you'll probably notice about this game is the (literally) hand-drawn aesthetics, and boy is it amazing. This game is ♥♥♥♥ing beautiful, and because it doesn't rely on trying to achieve photorealism, it's still gonna be as beautiful many years from now. Everything looks so pretty and innocent that it really makes you feel like a child in a fairy tale again, very refreshing compared to the hoards of grimy brown games we get these days. On the technical side of things, my frames never dropped below 60, hence I have nothing but praise for the graphics department.
:
On to sound design, if you thought the graphics were already good enough, I'm here to say the sound design tops even that, it's the best thing about this game in my opinion. The music is always fitting, sad/epic/calm/energetic you just ♥♥♥♥ing name it, this game has the theme that fits it. Among all the sounds, Aurora's theme and it's many variations stand out the most, especially THAT DAMN FLUTE, it just gets better and better everytime it plays, and when you hear it again right before the final battle it almost made me cry. Sound design is perfect.
Now onto gameplay, here the game still does well, but not as well as the earlier 2 categories. The combat system is simple yet hides a surprising amount of depth. However that's all pretty wasted since you'll soon find yourself running battles the same optimal way over and over again, and won't really need to make use of the full cast of characters' many abilities. The game gets really easy once you understand it, and I had to intentionally gimp myself by running different sub-optimal character combinations for each battle to spice things up. And before anyone jumps on me, I played on expert mode.
In my opinion, the thing that really holds the combat system back is the 2 character limit and the fact that the game is balanced around it. Switching constantly in battle is tedious though it carries no cost, especially because the buffs only work on your current active characters (you can't buff those in the sidelines, not even with buff-all versions). It encourages not switching as often, and concentrating on just a few out of the many characters you have. And because of this, I think the enemies are balanced to accommodate sloppy play, not necessatating the use of every niche of every character so that the tedium of switching is reduced.
Exploration and "platforming" when out of combat is handled well. I put platforming in quotations because the game gives you the ability to fly VERY early on. This of course fits very well with the child like theme of the game, I absolutely adored flying around as a pretty princess, but it also means the platforming complexity is reduced to almost nothing. In addition, puzzles and quests in this game are also extremely simple.
I personally appreciate everything being simple and straightforward, it made anything outside of combat very calming, making the game more enjoyable for me during the cooldown time in between fights, but some might not like this.
All in all, gameplay is excellent, just noticeably inferior compared to the perfection of the previous 2 categories.
I must admit, Child of Light really brought out the child in me. I found the straightforward nature of the story and presentation really welcoming. It appeals to the heart more than the brain, and I found it relaxing to be able to shut the latter off (figuratively) while playing this game. If you're looking for a deep, dark and mature story with lots of twists/gray areas, and completely fleshed out characters with lots of depth. This game is NOT for you. Turn back, because what you're getting here is a textbook Good VS Evil fairy tale.
That said, the game felt EXTREMELY rushed towards the very end. I'll try to keep spoilers to a minimum, but basically you fight a very important boss in what you think is the second last dungeon, and then you get the expected plot exposition, seems good. But immediately after that, with LITERALLY no breaks (where you can control your character) in between, you're thrown into the encounter with the final boss and the final confrontation begins. No final dungeon in the form of the dark majestic castle you were flying towards before the final boss just flies out to meet you in the middle of the sky. Not sure if development time ran out or they just got lazy. The final boss itself was also very underwhelming, no multiple phases, in fact I found the fight before that slightly tougher. So besides the ending/resolution, the game does excellently in this category.
Overall, I consider Child of Light a must buy if the idea of a simple turn-based RPG with an innocent fairy tale presentation even remotely tickles your fancy. It made me feel like a kid again, and touched my heart more than many of the "deep and mature" games ever could.

A fairy tale of a game with wistful music and dreamlike environments, and an incredibly open feeling world due to being allowed to fly freeform through the entire thing.
The game tells the story of an Austrian Princess, Aurora, who ends up in a mystical fantasy world called Lemuria, told that she must save the world from the evil Queen and recover the Sun and Moon, with the help of her magical crown, magical sword, and her friends. From there begins a rhyming journey across Lemuria, meeting jesters, gnomes, beasts, and more that join your party. The game is set up in JRPG fashion, with turn based battles that are reminiscient of Grandia with the use of the timeline, and interruption skills that let you halt and delay enemy attacks, and let them do the same to you. Your party levels up constantly, and while individual levels don't offer too much, over time you accure new skills, upgrade old ones, and get a steady feed of progress across your entire party (as even inactive party members get full XP!) Equipment is handled through the use of "Oculi", colored gems that can be combined with themselves to make bigger versions with new effects, or with other colors, entirely new versions with new powers.
Party members are all useful in their own way, and I found myself using all of them except the final party member you get, a great deal. They tend to be split along usual lines, physical attackers, healers, tanks, magical attackers, and etc, along with a party member who specializes in manipulating the timelines. Each character has three separate skill trees they can go down that emphasizes particular skills and stats, and Stardust, found through the game, can be used to permanently increase  acharacter's stats, allowing you to customize them further (or just feed them all to Aurora because the main character should obviously be the best at everything.)
The game feels just long enough to tell the story it wants to tell, and the world helps it every chance it gets. The music is immersive, the art and world are watercolored and move you across lots of different environments. Honestly the only thing I felt really detracted from the game was the forced rhyming scheme. It doesn't follow any real rhythm and just focuses on trying to rhyme lines regardless of length. One party member has recurring issues finishing rhymes and it's lampshaded by another party member constantly, which might actually be the best part of the whole rhyming gimmick.
There's two major downsides to this game though:
1: It's an Ubisoft game so it comes bundled with uPlay. This is your own thing to deal with, unfortunately. It didn't bother me.
2: The DLC is straight cashgrab stuff. The Golem character's quest takes about two minutes and he is ultimately forgettable, but useful. The rest is complete cashgrab items that aren't even good - you can acquire them from the first few treasure chests to come across. To provide context: It takes dozens of lower gems to make the higher ones, in a 3 -> 1 ratio. Don't buy the DLCs unles you really want the other dresses for Aurora.... or the Heal skill unlocked for Aurora that comes from the Light Aurora pack. The healer you get in the game works perfectly fine though, and she's the first party member you meet.
Wonderful game and absolutely worth the price of admission.

If you are looking to live in a world that is beautiful, feels organic and something you can spend a year or more in before "the next best thing" comes out... Look no further.

Pros
-The combat system really is good, despite the way it's actually utilized.

-Enviormental effects add depth to the game.
Cons
-The UI is terrible in more than one way. Character inventory is particuraly bad and very messy to navigate.

This is particularly bad when using and postioning an archer, sometimes the mouse will randomly move on it's own resulting in a needless miss.
-The game is deceptively linear. Despite giving you no set objectives you have to progress in a painfully specific order. If you attempt to break from the order the game in no way displays you will either die to something more powerful than you, or the quest will not progress as you have deviated from the hidden order.
-Classes seem terribly imbalanced. The problem is you have no way to know that either one of your characters could be quite useless, or your combination just doesn't work. This is discovered hours after creation, far beyond any point of fixing the issue. I have to ask why even give me the option to create characters if the classes aren't balanced? I would've rather had fairly balanced Source Hunters, created by the developers to provide an adequeate response to the game's challenges.
-Combat relies far too much on cc. There is precisely one tactic that works, cc spam the enemy so they lose the ability to do the same to you. Which in my opinion is just lazy. This futher adds onto the problem of class imbalance, given that if one of your created characters has weak cc capability then you're screwed.
-Enemies overwhem you with numbers and stun/freeze spam as opposed to knowledge of tactics, and differing mechanics.
-You can literally fail side quests from a lost conversation dice roll between your characters. This is so laughable that I'm not sure there is much else I can even say to express just how arbitrary and ridiculous this "mechanic" results in being.
There are a few other things that have annoyed me, but I think listing anything further would take away from what I feel are the game's objective negatives.
Despite my review, I don't hate this game. This is just a title that I incorrectly assumed I would very much enjoy, instead of struggling to discover a single thing about it I may actually find somewhat tolerable.

I have been a Divinity series fan ever since I played the first game as an Action/Adventure/RPG game. When I heard they did a Strategy/RPG game, I had my doubts about this game, but after buying it and playing it, I am a huge fan. Although the game play is different from it's counter parts, it's a nice touch and a nice change from the normal game play.

Combat is pretty simple, you take turns making moves and choosing your attacks and then the enemy does the same. There's tons of quests and plenty of items to find and use throughout this game. Maps are very nice and big enough to do plenty of exploring.
Here's my outlook of this game...
PROS
====
-Plenty of character developement
-Plenty of additional characters to find and bring with you to add to the party
-Lots of spells and skills to learn and master (Your not just set with defaults, you can add more as you progress)
-Tons of maps/locations to explore
-You can reach well over Level 100+
-With added skills and abilities, you can have well over 20,000+ HP
-Gateways allow you to reach locations easily once you find them
-Elemental effects that can change the tide of combat
-Spells and skills that range from close combat attacks to the long range explosive fireball
-Lots of NPC's to interact with and gain addtional quests
CONS
====
- (When I find some I will let you know, most of the CONS I have read, I can't really fault that as part of the game itself. Some complained that there was too much dialog, and yet people always want a story. RPG's are designed to have long stories so I can't fault that to the developers nor the game, I like a good story in RPG games, otherwise there's no point in making RPG games. No story, no reason to be part of the game.)

In Half-Life 2, you once again assume the role of Gordon Freeman, the theoretical physicist and dimension-hopping commando who saved the world from an alien invasion at the end of Half-Life. Or did he? Half-Life 2 starts you off facing the infamous G-Man, the mysterious blue-suited character from the original. At the end of Half-Life, the G-Man offered you a choice: work for him or die. Since there would be no sequel if you chose the latter, Half-Life 2 assumes you chose the former, and so you start the game on a train entering City 17 for your introduction into this new world.
City 17 is a run-down urban center that's the equivalent of the Warsaw ghettos during World War II; instead of Jews being rounded up to live in City 17, it's all the remnants of a defeated humanity. Half-Life 2 takes place an untold number of years after the Black Mesa incident, but it's clear that much has changed. A mysterious enemy known as the Combine has conquered the planet and installed a human puppet government to carry out its rule. Black-clad security forces patrol the streets, while propaganda blares endlessly from omnipresent video screens. If there's one thing that Valve does extremely well, it's capturing a sense of atmosphere, as this vision of a dystopian police state is chillingly effective. But you won't spend a lot of time soaking in the scene before you're thrust into the struggle to defeat the Combine and free humanity.
As soon as the shooting begins you'll join an essentially nonstop battle that will last the remainder of the game. Like the original Half-Life, Half-Life 2 is presented as a nearly seamless experience. You play entirely from Gordon Freeman's perspective, without cutscenes, perspective changes to take you out of the moment, or narrative jumps that skip ahead in time (at least, there are none from your perspective).

THEN BOOM, Saints Row 2 comes out, and it offers MORE STUFFZ I didn't even think that was possible, I was so happy with Saints Row, and now they're giving me more? It keeps the same tones as the original, humor spread out with seriousness and continues your gang's push for dominance in the city, directly after the events of the first game. Imagine Rogue.  In space.  But without the dungeon.  But with lasers!
"Wait," you interrupt, "so how's that Rogue-like?"
Well, in every other aspect.  First, you learn by playing.  Or more specifically, by playing a few minutes, and dying after accidentally opening an airlock, causing your crew to suffocate to death.  Then starting a new game, only to assume you're in a safe battle, rush to the bathroom, only to come back and see that the enemy boarded your ship, sabotaged the life support system, causing your crew to suffocate to death.
"So, the big boss is a lack of oxygen?  Sounds lame, " you quip.
No, smartass.  I was just using that to illustrate how such a basic aspect of space travel will still get you killed in a galaxy far, far away.  There are a lot more ways you're going to die.  The big boss is just the toughest hurdle.

This is an excellent strategy RPG. My initial attraction to this game was the art style.  The visual art has a hand drawn feel to it and the story takes place in a low fantasy Norse-style mythical world.  There is some political intrigue mixed with the pressing fear of murderous humanoid death machines.
The game play is fairly simple: move your character 'x' number of squares then dish out you attack; then wait and take your servings of pain and repeat. Your characters have five stats that equate to the following: Strength/HP, defence, power points, allowed use of power points per turn and sunder. Strength is responsible for how much of a spanking you can dish out. Because your HP is tied to your strength, any damage you take diminishes the efficacy of spanking the enemy. Defence is checked against Strength; for every point of your defence that is above the enemy's strength, your character gets a 10% bonus to negate damage.  Sunder breaks down defence. You can use power points to beef up attacks or sunder.   You also get a special move which you can use for a power point or two. --Crush your enemies see them driven before you, and level up your characters.

I like videogames.  I like music.  I like having my retinas assaulted by swirls of colorful space dust.
If you enjoy treating your brain to videogames and music like I do, and are enthralled with the amalgamation of the two, then there’s a good chance you’re going to enjoy Beat Hazard as well.  The twist is that Beat Hazard uses your own music to create custom levels.
Beat Hazard uses songs from your computer, so you can choose which song you want to play and the game creates a level around it.  Levels begin like the arcade classic, Asteroids, where you reduce large hunks of space rocks into smaller pieces with your lasers before some mean old spaceships arrive to provide put up a fight.  The unique aspect of the game is that everything from  the velocity of the asteroids to the quanity of boss ships you fight is dependent upon the music.
Blasting enemy ships into space rubble provides power-ups, which increase your firepower and the volume of the  music.  Your weapons are also influenced by the tune of the music, so when a song is softer or hits a quiet spot, your firepower is greatly reduced.  It’s like the gunner on the ship is a little kid sucking down fistfulls of Pixie Sticks.  He’s running around screaming with his hands in the air one minute and the instant the song tones it down a bit, he is lulled to sleep.
In addition to determining the patterns of the enemies, the game’s visuals are also greatly affected by the song selection.   As the ship is upgraded, its firepower is transformed from simple white blips into a seizure-inducing kaleidoscope of doom.  Spots in the background that initially appear nondescript also pulsate and swirl with colors to the song’s beat.  It’s something straight out of a Hawkwind concert (or Pink Floyd, for those not in tune with their ’70s space rock).  The background effects intensify the point where it can seem like you’re trying to play a game through a late-90s Windows Media Player visualizer.
Did you ever watch those visualizers and imagine playing a game through it?  Me neither.  That’s because while the visuals are quite impressive and make the game infinitely more compelling for onlookers, they are also a serious hindrance to actually playing the game.  I frequently find myself dying thanks to something that I either didn’t see or assumed was just a part of the background.  I suppose it could be argued that the visuals are a way of increasing the game’s difficulty, particularly for longer songs.
Crazy psychedelic visuals and customizable soundtracks are about as useful as a chainsaw to a beaver if the game feels like a chore to play, and thankfully the meat of Beat Hazard is excellent.  I find twin-stick shooters to be stressful at times because of the never-ending onslaught of ever-increasing enemies, but Beat Hazard is refreshing because your targets appear in waves.  Depending on the song, you tend to have a few seconds to catch your breath before preparing for the next attack.
One of the unintended benefits of the game is that it gives me an impetus to root through my music collection and dust off some tunes I have not heard in awhile.  I love shuffling through my songs and thinking “Hmm, I wonder what this song will be like?”  I find that in general, songs tend to work better if they are more dynamic and have a lot of changes in their volume or beats.
The game does a great job of tracking your progress and keeping a tally of how many songs you have beaten, or if you have finished an entire album.  Even if you don’t complete a song, the game still awards experience and you can still gain levels which add bonuses and a feeling of persistence.  Achievements would be a fantastic addition to this game, but unfortunately are absent through no fault of Cold Beam Games.
Despite it being a little too mesmerizing for its own good, Beat Hazard is an amazing experience and quite the technical accomplishment.  It is easy to recommend laying down the $5 for gamers who are music enthusiasts.  Outside of the allure of playing your own music,  Beat Hazard is an exciting and unique shooter and a great addition to the Indie library.

“10/10 would seize again!” - The Joy of Stiqs
“A revolutionary tool.. [has been] invaluable in continued research” - National Epilepsy Diagnostics Foundation
“A true thriller that had me shaking in my boots.. and then in my chair.. followed shortly by the floor.” - PartialSandwich
Tasteless epileptic jokes aside, this game is fantastic. Beat Hazard is a twin-stick bullet-mayhem shooter very much akin to the Geometry Wars franchise. While the mechanics are quite similar, Beat Hazard makes the game your own by allowing your personal music collection to generate the levels you play.
The game comes with about 20 or 30 tracks (all of which are pretty awesome) but nothing quite compares to the screen going mental when the beat drops in your favorite song. Speaking of the screen going mental, I tend to be bemused by games that put the photo-sensitivity warning before the game begins. I don’t understand the mechanics by which a seizure is induced but typically games have that warning when the only light flickering is a lamp swinging and sparking from the ceiling. Beat Hazard on the other hand means business, I have never seen such chaos in all my life!
But here is the incredible part: the developers have masterfully balanced all the elements of the game so that even amidst all the chaos you know exactly what you’re doing. It was truly baffling to me when I played my very first game. I don’t know how they pulled it off but the design of this game is top notch. A must buy in my opinion!

Beat Hazard, or: How I Learned to Stop Worrying and Love Particle Effects.
Now before anyone reads this, I should mention that Beat Hazard IS ACTUALLY A GOOD GAME, it's  fun and well designed, I just can't reccomend it, personally.
Beat Hazard is a victim of great potential, poor execution. I'm not a huge fan of shmups, but when I do play them, being able to have the tempo of the level set to my own music was an idea I was fast enamored with. The game works as advertized, I suppose and it's relatively fun. That should be enough to get it a thumbs up... but I just can't do it. Beat Hazard suffers from a terminal case of a complete lack of gameplay clarity.
If you at any point start chatting up a games developer, there is a good chance that at some point, they'll tell you that it's generally a good idea that the player feel responsible for their own failure. If failure in a game is beyond the player's control, they will quickly start to resent the game for it. Failure is rewarding if it gives experience towards doing better next time, but failure in Beat Hazard often comes from not being able to tell if a piece of debris is a particle effect or a broken chunk of dangerous meteorite. Failure comes from being hit by a missile indistinguishable from the sparks coming from your ship, other ships, powerups and even parts of the freaking user interface, which are lit up more flamboyantly than a mardi-gras fireworks show.
EDIT: Yes, I did turn down the particle effects in the options menu. It did not help.
The biggest letdown to me though, was the fact that the music only really affected the strength of your weapon (and the intensity of the godforsaken particle effects) and not the size and tenacity of the enemy. Enemy ships will probably appear in greater numbers on a 180 bps drumstep track compared to a 40 bps suicide anthem, but the intensity of the song has little to no effect on how fast the enemy moves or what kinds of bad guy appear. The slow spots in any song do slow down the action, and buildups are often oddly quiet which is a nice touch, but it honestly doesn't feel like the track you select makes a noticable difference in the level.
In perfect honesty, short of Audio Surf, Beat Hazard is probably one of the better rhythm games out there, due mostly to the fact that it's powered entirely by your own music, and can do so competantly. That being said, I'm not going to reccommend a rotten game just because it's slightly less rotten than everything else in the fridge. Beat Hazard is a pretty standard shoot-em-up that could probably be marketted more successfully as a music visualization program. Imagine playing "Operation" while being shot in both eyes with a rapidly flashing, high intensity laser while in a moving car, with a stereo stuck at 90 dB playing dubstep and you have a pretty solid idea on what Beat Hazard is like.

TL;DR: enhanced Mirror's Edge+enhanced Dead Island=Dying Light=Awesome.
A fresh take on an old concept is always nice. With a genre that is crowded with mediocre attempts at making money, Dying Light comes in and kicks (or should I say, jump kicks) every other zombie game's♥♥♥♥♥so hard that is almost unfair.
From the same developers as the good (not great) Dead Island games comes yet another zombie game that focuses on the same idea: loot and melee your way to victory. But this time with a little added feature: parkour! Techland took the amazing gameplay from Mirror's Edge and turned it into a freerunning dream come true, enphasis on "free". You can parkour in pretty much everything in this game, there are no limitations (like there were in Mirror's Edge). Freerunning around town is so fun that you'll forget where you're going or what you're supossed to do to complete the quest, which, by the way, is cliched to the max, but the gameplay is so smooth and rewarding that not even a pretty lame storyline can mess with it.
Think of Dying Light as an enhanced Dead Island meets Mirror's Edge meets Assassin's Creed (the parkour part, not the boring stuff). Plus, you get to kill all kinds of zombies and undead in various creative ways. What's not to love?
Beware though, when the lights go out and the night hits, the real challenge begins. The aptly named "nightmares" come out to play and you are their favorite toy!
All in all, this game is extremely fun to play. The pacing and the abilities that you unlock by progressing are impeccably timed, and the DLC that have been released just add to the enjoyment of an already amazing core game. The Bozak Horde tests your skills in a brutal fight against tough enemies and the clock, but offers a reward that makes it worth the effort. The Parkour Fever challenges offer a really nice challenge for those who want to perfect their freerunning abilities to the max. The Be the Zombie mode adds a nice challenge as a competitive multiplayer mode and a chance for the player to be the nightmare! And the Following expansion pack offers some really nice new alternatives and a story that, while is better than the core game's story, still falls short.
On the negative side are the weak storyline (side quests are better than main quests) and the fact that there is little to do after you've beaten the game, outside of trying the higher difficulty levels (which are pretty hardcore for an average player), or playing in Be the Zombie.
I absolutely recommend this game. It made it to my top 10 list incredibly fast and I've no doubt that the same will happen to anyone who likes parkour and killing zombies.

Alright, this is sort of an impressions review since episode 6 (the finale) hasnt released yet, but through 5 episodes, Telltale has been able to keep track of and make relevant many divergent character arcs and tie them together superbly. Obviously, TT games offer the illusion of choice while taking you on a wild ride through whatever tale they are telling, and this is no different. Yes, some decisions will have different immediate impacts on your game, but overall, all decisions lead in the same direction. That isnt a bad thing, but I have noted that this is a common complaint, and so I thought I would comment on it.
The graphics wont blow you away, but they are well done and honest to the topic matter.
This game actually features a bit more action via QTE's than many of their other games, which makes for a more engaging experience IMO.
So far, I have thoroughly enjoyed my time with this game and look forward to the finale, after which I will revise this review to reflect the game as a whole.
For now though, I can easily recommend this game and give this 8 murdered Starks out of 10 possible (despite there only really being one Stark in this game lol).

Game of Thrones - A Telltale Game Series pits a family of good, against a world of evil. Fans of the Game of Thrones series can be certain that evil almost always triumphs over good. But unlike the books and TV series, this game offers the fans the choice to risk life and limb and act out the hero only dreams can fulfill. Because when you play the Game of Thrones, "you win, or you die." Or the story progresses and the viewer continues to enjoy the show.
Choices, conflict, and repercussions are what fuels this games story, pitting you against the moral decision and the logical outcome. Which ever path is chosen the choices feel tense and impactful. The story itself could be considered a straight to DVD movie, but the game none the less draws the player in and allows them to make decisions, as if starring as an actual character in the Game of Thrones universe.
Overall, the game offers some intense moments, both action packed and of the verbal variety often associated with Game of Thrones. The scenes in King's Landing are often more subtle and thorough, while scenes outside of the city tend to be more dramatic and brisk. This change of pace keeps up well with the TV show and keeps the player interested in all of House Forrester's problems.
While short, this game opens news stories, choice and consequence, and a good variety of characters, not offered in the books or TV series, and is a welcome addition to the GoT universe.

Hyperdimension Neptunia is one of those games with a large following for its characters. As an avid animemer, I was excited to see such a game available on steam, especially one with Visual Novel and RPG aspects.
However, after playing it for a while, I found it to not quite live up to my expectations. Gameplay-wise, it's a lazy PC port, with a clunky UI slowing it down from its already grindy game. Perhaps I'm just not used to or suited for these types of games, but it seems difficult to be entertained in a game where levels take prevalence over strategy.
The pros would be... a vivid cast of characters. There are hair, hats, and breasts of all sizes, shapes, and colors. I'll be honest, it's what brought me and probably a lot of the playerbase to this game. And for what it's worth, it does this job pretty well. In addition, it seems there is an incredible depth to customization of your characters' costumes and skills, should you reach the endgame point. Also a lot of references to a lot of games, and the "industri" in general.
TL;DR Good for memes and lewds, but not for casual or fast-paced gaming. Not my cup of tea, but certainly could be yours.

But then Gunslinger appeared and gave me that nice nostalgic feel of the 2nd one! Boy, those are a lot of "But then"s :P
Anyways, The Cartel Is an average FPS that lets you play as 1 of the 3 agents at your choice, each one with it's unique abilities (but those abilities/skills are pretty boring, like faster reload for pistols with one guy, the other reloads faster with SMGs and can Dual-Wield them and the female agent reloads rifles faster, aaaand that is it...)
Going to the graphics, they are below average, bad texture pop-ins here and there and offline lag! YES! The campaign lags when you play (framerate drops and lag, actually), when you run to be specific, same issue that I had previously with Dead Island (same engine BTW).
Character models are just awful and the dialogue is f*cking laughable.
Gameplay wise, the guns all feel pretty much the same, and they all feel bad! Except the pistols, so I just used the pistols the whole game, except during Concentration mode (slows down time and increases accuracy for a short period of time) that you get by killing people, and also used rifles and smg's during the car shootout and car chases, because pistol kind of suck in those situations. Hyperdimension Neptunia Re;Birth1 is one of those titles I had a feeling would be good, then after playing for 60 hours, it surpassed my expectations.
The graphics are not the best, but are still very nice and clean. This is a remake from the original PS3 version of the game after all, I totally enjoyed the visuals and it's anime style.
Gameplay-wise, it is turn based + tactical, tho I did not find it as tactical due to the easy difficulty the game seems to be (be warned: this does not mean the game is entirely easy). It is a lot more fun once you have more characters to choose from, extending different combinations to your preference.
The music and sound design was a mix between awesome to questionable, I have noticed that there are certain moments where the voice acting had some weird poping noises and sounded very low quality, not sure what that was about, the bg music would lower down a bit then a pop would sound off, the bg music raises up again with the rest of the dialog sounding good and clear.
The story is heart warming with all the parody you can get. The characters are pretty interesting as many represent current consoles as well as representations of certain franchises such as Ys and Tekken, I can see the love for gaming in this game which made me only love gaming more.
One thing I will say I am not a huge fan of is crafting, while the rest of the game has a ton of replay value going into New Game + to make the experience last longer, crafting would of been better being replaced with earning many of those items by defeating bosses or special mini bosses. Grinding to become strong is one thing, then there is grinding to obtain certain items that are a bit tough to follow unless you are looking at a guide.
Overall, if you enjoy JRPGs, anime, cute female protagonists, fun gameplay mechanics with replay value, and light story, I highly recommend you get a copy of this game. Thumbs up!

Imagine if someone took Oregon Trail and Final Fantasy Tactics, and then let Vikings raid the studio and make the game all about themselves. You have Banner Saga. This game is easily one of my favorites, and although I have only given it one good playthrough, I intend on returning to this game before purchasing and playing through it's sequel.
The storyline is akin to the Icelandic Sagas and old Viking Lore. The primary race are humans, and the Varl are large horned warriors who seem to coexist with humans in this world. Everyone in the land has now come under threat of the Dredge, a race of sentient armor that wage war from what appears to be a hive mind. You play as Rook, who must help guide his daughter and envoy across the land safely. The story is on point, leaving room for moving into the sequel but still giving a satisfying conclusion on it's own.
Gameplay is most choice, and is a good example of how to use your game mechanics to propel a story as opposed to just providing random challenges along the way. In the spirit of a good tactics game, you build your team and utilize their unqie strategies in tandum to defeat your enemies. The catch is that this game is a lot like Game of Thrones, in that it will not protect you from sudden and painful loss. Unlike other games, it doesn't acheive this by making your team members high value and easy to lose, but is heavily influenced by story aspects and choices made while travleing in the caravan or dealing with dialogue choices. You will miss the ones you lose, but push on... it's a great feeling, both for the challenge of the game and the pacing of the story.
The graphics work. I don't know if one could really talk it up too much, as it is a 2d game and uses almost entirely hand drawn art, at the same time that's what makes it so great and amazing. It really captures the aura of the story, and helps to make a whimsical yet tragic world to progress through. It feels like the pages of a storybook coming to life.
The storybook elements continue in the excellently executed caravan sequences, where you make choices on how to survive your harsh journey. Sometimes you are attacked by bandits, sometimes you have to take a vote on how to deal with a food shortage. There's quite a few ways this can play out, all of which lead to different outcomes in your story.
Overall, I really, really enjoyed this game. It's a lot like that Titan AE movie, but adapted into a Fantasy Game from a Sci-Fi movie. If nothing else, grab this guy during a Steam sale and give it one good playthrough. It's worth it.

I picked this up during the summer steam sale and while it does have some nice qualities, overall I feel it is lacking in depth, expected RTS features, and overall seems a bit risk averse to give it staying power. I did have some fun going through some matches, but ultimately don't anticipate this will remain in my library for long. Specifics thoughts:
-Nice keyboard shortcut scheme. You select the building or unit type with QWER+ and then it brings up a new set of choices, again QWER+ and then a final menu. So, if you need a certain unit you very quickly realize you can do EQQ or whatever... but, the game does lack some expected commands. Can't pause at any point or change the game speed, no select all units, couldn't figure out how to bring up FPS, etc.
-Has a neat cover system where you can hide in a forest and fire from it w/o being targeted... but, there's few areas on the maps and they are too large. They should've been more liberal with the placement of cover and included some smaller one-unit areas. Some other games I can recall have done this maybe a bit better.
-The two human/alien races are a bit too similar. Props to them for making the Goo race work very differently, though. I feel they put all their risk in this one race and played the rest of the game too conservatively.
-The units within those races are a bit too similar. For example, it's very obvious in a game like StarCraft how a marine, siege tank, and hellion are different. No questions about strengths and even confusing unit types. In this game, the units tend to run together once in a category. There are a few exceptions, air units and artillery are definitely different, but I found the units overall a bit bland.
-The tech is pretty cool. You have 4 tech choices each with 3 options. Once you commit to an option within those choices (eg, Tech granting Anti-Air unit ground attacks as well) you can't pick the other 2. Was easy enough to manage from the interface and understand what each bonus was. I tended to pick the same bonuses game to game, unsure if that was play style or simply balance problems but would have to play more to know for sure.
-Framerate / slowdowns - Toward the end of a longer game, the game 'stutters' while trying to compensate for what I think is low framerates (can't pull it up to determine, though). Could be network? Hard to say what it was, but I've got a solid connection and a solid i7 w/ GTX 960 and graphics actually mostly turned down.
-Building placement all have to be part of your initial set of root structures (either your HQ or hubs if you're playing Beta). They went for a smaller singular base as a game decision, okay that works. However, it is not elegantly done. Some of the ways attachments work early on (you have to attach a Tank module to a factory to allow you to build tanks) make it easy for new players to make mistakes and build useless modules. In addition, it was a bit buggy when selling structures, I'd sometimes cut power off to half my base. Okay, that's a feature, let me rebuild it to connect power again. Nope. Guess it is a bug, but ran into a few times where visually I should have power but half my buildings wouldn't.
All in all, for a 60% off steam sale this reminded me of the heyday of RTS fifteen years ago where I'd pick up a new game in the summer and nine out of ten times would see it fall flat, just as this one has.

An excellent game containing amazingly polished gameplay mechanics with a few dark spots here and there. If you like zombie survival, go for it. Just pretend there is no story.
Contents:
The main points of the game for me were the story and combat/parkour elements. I can't really speak for multiplayer as I have not explored that part very thoroughly (yet) and other aspects of gameplay I just don't find very important.
Basically, I talk about points which would be a reason to buy/skip for me.
The story was one of the most generic pieces of sh*t I've witnessed in a long time, pardon my French. The main characters (including yours) are mostly utterly unlikable arrogant badasses. Secondary and sidequest characters are supposed to be the comic relief I guess. Most of them are either abusing you, scamming you or just plain stupid. The main protagonist sometimes mumbles an irritated remark but other than that, most of the time he seems very much at peace with everyone taking advantage of him.
I have never seen so many consecutive anticlimactic quests and events in a single game world. This would not be so disasterous if it was done in moderation and/or with a meaningful background but... You basically finish a quest and the game slaps you with almost a random event that makes everything you have done meaningless. It's like you're building a house of cards right next to a person with a fan in their hands, finger on the power switch. After a few quests you see all of this coming miles away but you can't do anything about it.
What I find most hilarious is the stereotypicality of the main villain which is enormous to the grotesque degree. For example, the guy will literally send 4 waves of goons to kill you while having a perfectly planned scenario to make you feel miserable which would be absolutely pointless if you actually died at any point.
There are many moments which are there just to show you what a terrible person you are fighting against. The story is trying so hard to deliver this message to you that it actually makes the main villain look painfully stupid and inconsistent. The bad guy appears to have everything happening in the game world under full control, without you being able to do anything about it. With this in mind, he LETS you get so close just so you can do damage. If there comes a point at which you actually hurt the villain in any way, it doesn't feel like you are achieving something at all - it just feels like the guy is too bloody stupid to make a rational decision. You can basically tell how the story will end just from the way the tension between the main character and the main villain rises.
An unrelated note to finish it off: QTEs = still a thing.
This game had me pretty hooked even though the story was quite painful to follow at times. The gameplay mechanics are truly something that other developers should learn from and build upon.
I opted to keep most of my campaign private but co-op brings you a whole different way to play the game if you're into it, not to mention there is a considerable amount of on-line features that I haven't even touched yet. This adds so much value to the game which is already great and I would never advise anyone to skip it just because I think the story is terrible.
Dying Light simply manages to make most of the important things right. Big thumbs up from me and kudos to the developers.

Company of Heroes 2 is the latest installment to one of if not the best RTS series of all time. Set in the Eastern Front experience the brutal battles of Stalingrad and Leningrad.
Many of the core prinicples and mechanices still are present here. Cover, flanking, suppression, etc. are all still important concepts to master. However you not only fight the enemy but the weather as well. You constantly have to ensure your soldiers have a fire nearby or cover to protect them from the cold. Its this new dynamic that sets COH2 apart but also can lead to some of its biggest frustrations. Leave your soldiers exposed for too long and they will die from the elements. This concept makes sense from a realistic standpoint. However in practice it can make a game that already requires a significant amount of micromanagement to be awkward.
In the end Company of Heroes award winning blend of real time combat and territory control return with new features that make the harsh soviet winters just as deadly as the german war machine that you face.
**DLC**
The DLC for COH2 thus far has been ...alright. While I appreciate being able to play as the american forces and the OKW; I find it odd that these factions were released as standalone multiplayer addons when they usually would have been included in a standalone expansion with a story campaign. Perhaps even more baffling is that after OKW and US forces were launched as standalone multiplayer factions? They then did release an American campaign.
Ardennes Assault is pretty solid and offers a unique campaign that plays a bit like an actual war where your missions/battles gain you territory on a tactical map. Now the British forces are again getting their own standalone multiplayer DLC. I have a feeling that when I buy these 'campaigns' I am being charged for something I have already bought in the multiplayer DLC.

Had i written this 10 hours into the game, it would have been one, uninterrupted praise. It still kinda is but later some problems in the story telling emerge.
Pro:
It's a wonderful mixture or Assassons Creed, Far Cry and Mirrors Edge. It has a huge and interesting open world, good fighting system, reasonably dangerous zombies in impressive quantities (hello dayz). And fun tools and abilities to deal with them. Once you skilltrained™ out of the hide-and-run-away phase.
And it's not just an action/fighting/parcoury game, with an open world to play in, but very story driven and quite a lot of RPG added, to make it very nteresting and motivating and unique. Which also sets it apart from Far Cry and some of the later Assassins creeds.
Also some of the side quests are quite remarkably in style, emotional storytelling and athmosphere, and an absolute highlight of the game. Like the kindergardener with his wife... don't want to spoil it.
That makes it (for an action game) very special and unique and makes more then up for the small glitches in the main story i'm adressing now.
You could even argue that, if Fallout 4 passes for an RPG, Dying Light does as well or even more.
Con:
So what's my problems?
1. It's the tools and drive of the (main)storytelling.
Several times during the story script-events, you can not influence, put you in situations you could've easily escaped. For example you're suddenly made to surrender to 2 people with guns, you'd normally kill or beat up in a few moments,
Just to make the following boss fight more difficult and frustrating (completely artificially AND unfairly)  than it should be.
It made me so angry, i cheated back at the game at this point :-)
2. Also at times and with no explanation parts of the game mechanics, like grapple hook, the bow or special abilites, are simply... disabled to to make a situation artificially more difficult.
That's just bad game design.
3. Towards the end (?),Story and main quests feels AWFULLY strechted out.  Feels you're close to the end for FAR too long now.
The thing is: that's completely unnecessary. At this point, the game is far longer already then action games these days usually are. And it gets there in a very good, interesting and motivating way.
There would be no shame in closing the story in style to a satisfying end.
Instead they started to turn buildings into labyrinths, let you check 5 instead of 1 or 2 locations for a quest, send you in circles for them.
4. Also i feel that unlike in Far Cry, the stealthy approach, the game kinda offers, doesn't really work, too many psychic enemies, you can't hide from.
___________
It has a online mode, i don't use and therefore can't judge. The times when they got people VAC banned for single player mods are gone, i think. They got rightfully a lot of flak for this BS mechanics.
___________
Still: I edited the review, as it sounded more omplainy than the game deserves. Cause at the bottom line:
__________________________________________________________
It's VERY VERY good game for a very long time, just loses it's drive a bit later on. Rather do more side quests then rush though the main story without ever looking left and right, or you miss out badly.
It beats several well known fulll-on RPGs in this area.

Disclaimer: this is my first time playing BDO (but have played Lineage2, WoW, and many other MMO's).
First quality of life issue: LAG.  It is server-side, and they are 'working on it'.  It's not as if they knew there'd be a massive influx of people from steam, right?  ...  Loot will drop, but I am unable to pick it up.  We're talking.....the loot disappears before I am even able to pick up a 1/10th of it due to severe and continual lag.  So be warned: you may not be able to pick up loot (with or without pets, does not matter).
Second, with no loot, you're playing Farmville.  BDO has crafting, fishing, and farming galore: all of that goes into the economy to make bigger and better things, all the way up to end-game things (like top-tier upgrade stones for weapons/armor).  In addition, you can send out your workers (that you hire and board through a grindy mechanic called CP [Contribution Points]).
Third, you will level so quickly, that you run into a big problem: you can no longer damage the higher level mobs to efficiently level.  You need good gear to level at 56+.  150+ap/200dp.  If you don't powerlevel very hard and hold out for the Jarette's 6 piece jewelry (42 AP for rings/earrings/belt/neck), then you might be ok.  But to beat 42 AP from the free 20-day jewelry, you need 9ap neck, 7ap belt, 7ap ring x2, 7ap earring x2.  That's basically Pri jewelry, requiring either lots of luck or silver (10mil per piece x 2 x 6 pieces, assuming you you dont fail a single pri piece which you will fail a lot, thus meaning the jarrette's will be the best you can do for a long time).  TLDR: To continue leveling, make bank money.  Mobs are difficult to kill 56+, requiring 150ap/150dp.
Fourth, the fun: the fun doesn't exist in this game.  There are clans out there with 80/80 members (or more) who each has 100+ billion in wealth.  You start this game with about 60 million given to you for free, but beyond that, you will be starting from scratch trying to piece together a bottom tier duo set and hoping for some uber/lucky boss drops.  To have fun, would require you to be able to compete in PvP.  Getting wrecked by people at 280ap will not be fun.  Nor, can anyone reliably PvP for fun, as the entire servers are lagging because the massive influx of people.
TLDR: Servers are laggy AS ♥♥♥♥ and sometimes entirely unresponsive (loot). Do no buy. Boycott this game until the servers are fixed.  Even with the servers fixed, you are climbing an uphill battle with the vet's sitting on knowledge and wealth, much of which can be traced to the wealthiest clans owning castles/nodes.

As both a huge fan of the Game of Thrones T.V. show and the Song of Ice and Fire books, I was excited to play this game. Additionally, I played and thoroughly enjoyed both seasons of Telltale's the Walking Dead. At this point, 5 episodes in, I can safely say my expectations have not been met. Telltale's Walking Dead was strong because it put the characters in situations that had never been seen on the show - bear traps, meat lockers, frozen lakes, wolf attacks (the animal, not the cannibals - although they have those too). Going through each game felt refreshing. Additionally, the characters (especially Lee and Clementine) all had complex and interesting relationships. (mild spoiler alert ahead)
This game is a failure on most accounts. The characters aren't deep, and you don't spend enough time with any of them. The Meera story is totally irrelevant to the main plot, and is basically there to pander to show-lovers by giving Headey, Dormer, and Dinklage cameos. They completely overshadow any attempt at creating an intriguing story, because we already know whats going to happen to these characters. We know not to side with Tyrion, because we know he'll be charged with regicide, for example. Additionally, seeing characters like Cersei and Margaery makes us completely forget about Meera, which is no good if she's a protagonist. Meera's story was too disconnected, and the game would have been better off if they had devoted their time to developing the characters at ironrath and their money towards anything other than celebrity cameos (maybe work on the polygon counts?????)
Asher's story isn't much better. Shoehorning in Denaerys and the dragons was annoying for a number of reasons - one, having to play out extended action sequences taking Meereen was no fun, because that was never what made these games interesting. Quicktime events should be short if they're going to be in the game. Two, while I think Emilia Clarke is an excellent Denaerys, I thought her voice acting was very sub-par in comparison to her silver screen work. The Meereen story has so little surprise or intrigue, it has almost no place in this story. Asher's story had potential - rallying a mercenary army in Essos was an interesting concept. However, it would have been about 10x more interesting if they had used a completely new location, with a completely new set of characters - or even ones used in the books, but not really in the show. Why not go to Pentos, or Volantis?
As for Ironrath, it is basically just winterfell lite. You have Gared, who is Jon lite. You have Rodrik, who is Robb lite. You have the mother, who is Catelyn lite, and Thalia, who is Arya lite. Ethan is Bran lite - see the pattern? I'm not necessarily talking about storylines so much as characters themselves, but that is potentially worse. The characters here are all just shells - especially Gared, who exhibits virtually no independent thought throughout the entire storyline. Honestly, it baffles me that in a game that advertises choice, we are FORCED to betray the night's watch to look for the dumb North Grove. I mean I certainly wanted to tell Duncan to ♥♥♥♥ off after he told me to desert the night's watch shortly after I swore my life to them, but no, I couldn't. The ironrath story is interesting enough, but the stakes aren't fully understood. Ramsay pops at seemingly at random to remind peope Iwan Rheon is an awesome actor, but when he appears the story shakes a little - no matter what happens, we're going to have a minimal effect on the big picture. If we beat our rivals, we still have to serve the Boltons. With the game approaching it's sixth episode, it's clear that we'll be ending it with the Boltons still ruling the North.
What the hell was the point of all this then? This was a game meant to pander, and it lost a significant amount of substance in the process. The celebrity cameos overshadow the dull leading characters. The quicktime events are used too much. The plot has a few nice twists and turns, but the stakes are quite low, so it doesn't really matter overall. I think this game is worth buying on sale after a price drop. At $32.99, you're better off buying something worth your time, like dark souls or fallout or ♥♥♥♥ing E.T. for the SNES
EDIT: Just wanted to say that after playing episode 6, and sitting on the game for a few months, my opinion has not changed at all. This game is not worth $30CAD or whatever it costs elsewhere. Wait for a nice sale, and go in with low expectations so you can be surprised. As such a huge fan of the series I'm actually STILL disappointed at the missed opportunities of this game A little creativity now and then would be nice, TellTale.

While this is on sale, definitely snag this one if you've ever been into turn-based RPGs. It's an enchanting journey, albeit somewhat repetitive with combat. Still, the combat system is easy to learn but difficult to master, but above all, it's innovative. In this review I'm gonna talk strictly about how the combat system is fun, and bear in mind of course I played on the hard difficulty.
First of all, combat consists of 2 party members, and up to 3 enemies, and the flow of combat is both real-time and turn-based. There's a bar at the bottom that shows whose turn is coming up next, and towards the end of that bar is where they choose their action, and the speed changes accordingly. However, if someone is in that red zone and takes damage, their action is interrupted and they're knocked about halfway down the meter to act again (though they do get to reselect what they do).
Next thing is, the fairie that you control with your mouse. This little guy has a mana bar that regenerates slowly over time, or by using a potion, or by hovering over the blue plants and collecting the little mana bubbles they create. He has two functions: he can slowly heal a party member (even while paused), though this expends a lot of his mana. He can also, at a much lesser cost, slow down an enemy's active time bar heavily. That's where the tricky play comes in: timing your party member's action right after your enemy's so you can land an interrupt. That's pretty fun. That is, until you fight a boss that counters interrupts with something you really don't want, but that's another story.
Last thing to note is, even though you can only have two party members on the field at a time, you can, when one's turn is up, swap them out for another member, and they take their turn immediately (if said party member was up next). So, to compensate for this, as you go through the game and collect your party members, the game seems to swiftly ramp up in difficulty, forcing you to make tactical choices in your playstyle, your oculi (gems that change elemental damage, resistance, or otherwise improve your characters), and what skill tree to go down for each character.
All in all, this game's a blast for anyone who grew up with games like Pokemon or Final Fantasy. Most battles will feel like a triumph when you've won. There's nothing more satisfying than a boss fight where you win just by the skin of your teeth after having to use most of your consumables.
Beyond the combat, the game's presentation is enchanting. The OST is great, art style is enjoyable, all the dialog rhymes, everything's just plain fun. The ONLY demerits I can give this game are the repetitive combat and wonky difficulty spikes. But on the whole, I recommend it, especially at the price it's at now.

Ok, I accept this game is first decent one since original Divine Divinity, but still I say - Larian failed to make a masterwork RPG here, just as it failed with DD 10 years before.
I like this game is many aspects:
+ graphics. That's almost perfect, f/x, ambient, surfaces, perspective, etc., - everything is very attractive.
+ music. Kirill (R.I.P.) managed to make Divinity series his own orchestral playground. Hats off.
+ humor. Grotesque is everywhere, but it never becomes too annoying.
+ sandbox. I mean here a lot of possibilities to experiment with magic effects, elemental powers, crafting, etc. Not to mention sidequests or secrets, even main game story requires out-of-the-box thinking without any hints, and thus - player has many ways to achieve his goals. It makes game feel sometimes too 'weird', partially like Arcanum was, but it's still a great feature that makes player use his brain and get very excited with working solutions. The very neccessity to use these 'sandbox' features makes D:OS nicely difficult if you're not looking at playthrough every now and then.
+ tactical battles. Unbalanced, unpredictable, even extremal, but not chaotic at all - tactical part is significant.
All this tornado of magic effects and special skills feels like headache at first, but after you get used to it.. well, battles are slow and very time consuming, and also really challenging (even on 'normal' difficulty setting), so I'd say it's the most important part of the game.
BUT...
the story is.. just idle. It didn't make me empathize or even believe main characters. Ok, here is the motivation to go kill that fiend and find this artifact.. ok, I got it. next, next, next, finish, now let me fight someone already please. A lot of TOO epic stuff that becomes tedious rather quickly, like end-of-the-world-prophecies, omniscient gods and so forth. The story badly needs notable characters and catching plot.
Music, graphics are brilliant per se but the world lacks the atmospheric basis. It don't make you want to 'live' in this universe. e.g. Witcher, Skyrim or Fallout do that thing perfectly, but Larian let it to chance and failed. D:OS world just feels NOT consistent.
generally, the game is good, at least worth trying (especially for Divinity series fans).
But I beleive it's overrated, great potential (!) is wasted and Larian keeps stepping on the same rake again and again.

The best part of the Hyperdimension Neptunia games is inarguably the concept: Four goddesses, each representing a different game system, are waging a “Console War” against one another in a cutesy, high-octane anime fashion. Following this idea, Re;Birth1 is filled with meta, fourth wall-breaking humor, and a good bit of charming self-awareness. Pretty much every character and party member you encounter along the way fits into some sort of anime or gaming archetype — Neptune, who represents the fourth (imaginary) console, is the high-energy, childlike protagonist, while Iffy is a smart tsundere who can get quite flustered at times — and Re;Birth1 actually does a good job of balancing character versus caricature.
This game is a must have for any fans of the JRPG genre.
