Probably the best turn-based RPG released in the last ten years, at least mechanically. The writing isn't always perfect(though mostly because it could stand to be more present, not because it's bad), but the mechanics are just top notch. The combat's always fun, often challenging, never gets dull, and on the rare occasions where there exist more than one similar encounter, it's only been copied a few times, and will often be in a different location, and location(nearby traps, terrain features, etc.) can change everything about a fight in Divinity: Original Sin.
Literally nothing bad can be said about the actual combat mechanics, so just assume that everything else is 10/10 while I emumerate the game's few flaws.
Firstly, there's the storyline. It's simply not very there, it's not bad, it's not good, it's just present mostly in the volume necessary to make the game happen and give you an excuse to go places and solve puzzles and beat up badguys. On the subject of puzzles, sometimes your combat abilities also serve useful puzzle-solving applications outside of combat, I like this.
Secondly, there's the level-up pacing. It really feels like the game starves you for points. Not in that you're underpowered, but in the sense that it limits how many abilities you can have, which is fine for challenge purposes, but does mean that it takes a bit of planning to get maximum tactical options. And the more options, the more fun you'll be having.
Still, with an expanded-edition slated for sometime late 2015 or early 2016, it sounds like most of my few kvetches will be fixed and plenty of things I praised as 10/10 will be upped to 11/10!

In Half-Life 2, you once again assume the role of Gordon Freeman, the theoretical physicist and dimension-hopping commando who saved the world from an alien invasion at the end of Half-Life. Or did he? Half-Life 2 starts you off facing the infamous G-Man, the mysterious blue-suited character from the original. At the end of Half-Life, the G-Man offered you a choice: work for him or die. Since there would be no sequel if you chose the latter, Half-Life 2 assumes you chose the former, and so you start the game on a train entering City 17 for your introduction into this new world.
City 17 is a run-down urban center that's the equivalent of the Warsaw ghettos during World War II; instead of Jews being rounded up to live in City 17, it's all the remnants of a defeated humanity. Half-Life 2 takes place an untold number of years after the Black Mesa incident, but it's clear that much has changed. A mysterious enemy known as the Combine has conquered the planet and installed a human puppet government to carry out its rule. Black-clad security forces patrol the streets, while propaganda blares endlessly from omnipresent video screens. If there's one thing that Valve does extremely well, it's capturing a sense of atmosphere, as this vision of a dystopian police state is chillingly effective. But you won't spend a lot of time soaking in the scene before you're thrust into the struggle to defeat the Combine and free humanity.
As soon as the shooting begins you'll join an essentially nonstop battle that will last the remainder of the game. Like the original Half-Life, Half-Life 2 is presented as a nearly seamless experience. You play entirely from Gordon Freeman's perspective, without cutscenes, perspective changes to take you out of the moment, or narrative jumps that skip ahead in time (at least, there are none from your perspective).

As a single player game and as a learning tool for newcomers to the game, this is a must have. As a multiplayer battle sim... look elsewhere.
This is easily the best duel AI out there, bar none, and the duels you partake in are mostly well-balanced. There are a few difficulty spikes, but for the most part it's fairly consistent. While the tutorials in the dedicated tutorial mode are not very great, the first duel for each series teaches a game mechanic that's highlighted in that series, which each serve as a much better learning tool for those mechanics than the dedicated tuorials are. This makes it a great entry point for new players, as well as a fun game overall. Do note that this game still is using Master Rule 3, so there is no link summoning, no dedicated extra zones, and in turn there's no way to learn about that kind of stuff. That stuff can easily be taught later, so that's not much of an issue.
As for multiplayer, it's buggy, getting cards out of packs is just inconvenient, the card selection is outdated and better options exist. Don't get this if your main intent is to duel friends on a competitive level, as a lot of things are outdated, missing, and overall cumbersome. If you're ok with this being the case, actually dueling your friends isn't difficult, although there is a bug where private rooms don't work, so you gotta be fast sending and accepting those invites.
This review was written just as Master Rule 4 took effect in America, so this review will likely become outdated as this game ages and doesn't get updates. I would not be suprised if Konami makes an entirely new game rather than updating this one, but only time will tell. I will NOT be updating this review.

I bought Black Desert Online during the Summer Sale for $8. I've put in over 20 hours so far and it's been a great experience overall, even got my father playing it.The way the player is kinda thrown in the pool with only basic instruction reminds me of how Morrowind started which I really appreciated. It's left up to the player to go out and explore, learning and experimenting.
Pros:
Fantastic art direction
Fighting game style combat
Great soundtrack
Great atmosphere (dusk into full on night combat with no lantern looks  phenomenal)
Living world with lots of wild life and plant life
Incredibly deep options to do everything from commerce to alchemy to farming
Cons:
Enemy AI has been dumb as all get out (I cut down three imps on a hillside with at least 30 of them surrounding me and the rest didn't seem to care at all. This is a problem with every enemy type I've seen thus far except bosses. Regular enemies are idiot pacifists unless fighting at night when there's a slight improvement.
Lack of native support for the Steam controller is a WTF moment. BD:O is a Steam game but doesn't support the Steam controller. Yes, I'm aware there are ways to get the controller to work with the Steam overlay available (No method has worked for me thus far) but this shouldn't be necessary as the lack of native Steam controller support for a game running on Steam is borderline stupid.
Voice acting ranges from "okay" to "terrible" and lip sync is non existent.
Controller support seemed to be an afterthought. The game wants gamers to use mouse and keyboard and it shows when there are absolutely no options to show prompts using controller buttons and joystick movements. You can use a controller and do quite well (XBox One Elite in my case since the Steam controller isn't natively supported in the game) but the game doesn't accomodate you for doing so.
Character customization is limited in some ways that it shouldn't be. I understand that this is a Korean made game and that's awesome. But BD: O is a game that plays on the idea that Black people can't be heroes, can't save the world, aren't relevant and have no place in popular culture unless they're servants. I'm over 20 hours into the game but the only characters I've seen that even kinda look Black were male servants. I haven't seen a Black female character at all. But lo and behold, White female characters are front and center. This is disappointingly typical. In trying to create a Black character ultimately, I ended up with an Asian dude with a really dark tan because the customization tools are focused on Asian people or White people.
Graphic glitches. BD:O has serious draw distance problems. Personally, I'm playing on a system that has 36 GBs of RAM, 32 system/4 VRAM with a Core i7 and a Nvidia 980 and also tested the game on a Ryzen 5 1600 X with a GTX 1080 yet the draw distance problems are so bad in Black Desert Online, its reminds me of a N64 game. Tweaking settings didn't help much. I saw a ship in one city parked in the middle of town half in, half out of the ground, animation glitches, vanishing assets...it makes the game very hard to record.
Story...What story? All I know at this point is there's this black power that wiped my memory and talks to me for some reason, ruins that people are exploring for some reason, soldiers that are terrified of imps for some reason (really, since they were dumb and weak when I fought them) and people are traveling just fine even though there are monsters out. Again, why am I needed here?
Even with the negatives, the positives won me over. This isn't the MMO for everyone but I'm enjoying it because there's just so much to do and I can do it without a lot of hand holding and without the need for a party.

When I found this game on Steam I cried with joy a lil' bit on the inside. WARNING: THIS REVIEW MAY BE A BIT NOSTALGAIC!!
Let me start by saying in my opinion, this is the greatest Star Wars game I have ever played. I first started playing this game on the Ps2 way back when, and I can remember the day it came out.
Star Wars: Battlefront 2 is a great classic TPS/FPS style of game. In modern days and tech, the graphics are easily outdated and noticeably so. Now don't get me wrong this game still looks good, but in a "Pre-2004" type of way. SW:BF2 has many, many maps to try out, some being Clone Wars only (Republic vs. Droids [I can't remember the name of them for the life of me]) or Rebellion only (Rebel Army vs. Galactic Empire) and some being playable by all factions. With every map comes multiple (some more than others) gamemodes that are all very fun.
SW:BF2 also introduced it's greatest asset: Space Battles. My favourite part of the game, Space Battles can also be played with all factions, as well as grant access to each faction specific ship the main objective of space battles is to get 180 points during the battle. This can be attained by doing a multitude of things. You can get these points by killing roughly 130-ish ships, depending on which ones you kill, playing as the "Marine" class and flying over to the enemy's main ship and blowing up they're main parts, or buy using whatever ship you've chosen to blow up the outer parts of the enemy's main ship. It is great fun and where I've spent most of my time playing this game.
Back on the ground, you have the choise to either play in a TPS (Third Person Shooter) or an FPS (First Person Shooter) mode of playing. With 6 different classes for each faction, (2 of which must be unlocked during gameplay by achieving points, with the additional 7th "Hero" being unlocked the same way.[usually a jedi]) allows for experimentation on each class to explore the diverse ways to play them. For instance a Sniper is better on larger maps as it is better to hide and shoot from a long distance, and Pilots are better on maps that are meant to be played using a lot of Siege Vehicles. All the faction's respective ground vehicles are all well balanced, and not too difficult to take down.
All in all I have loved this game for a long time, and I hope you like it too.

Many of the core prinicples and mechanices still are present here. Cover, flanking, suppression, etc. are all still important concepts to master. However you not only fight the enemy but the weather as well. You constantly have to ensure your soldiers have a fire nearby or cover to protect them from the cold. Its this new dynamic that sets COH2 apart but also can lead to some of its biggest frustrations. Leave your soldiers exposed for too long and they will die from the elements. This concept makes sense from a realistic standpoint. However in practice it can make a game that already requires a significant amount of micromanagement to be awkward.
In the end Company of Heroes award winning blend of real time combat and territory control return with new features that make the harsh soviet winters just as deadly as the german war machine that you face.
**DLC**
The DLC for COH2 thus far has been ...alright. While I appreciate being able to play as the american forces and the OKW; I find it odd that these factions were released as standalone multiplayer addons when they usually would have been included in a standalone expansion with a story campaign. Perhaps even more baffling is that after OKW and US forces were launched as standalone multiplayer factions? They then did release an American campaign.
Ardennes Assault is pretty solid and offers a unique campaign that plays a bit like an actual war where your missions/battles gain you territory on a tactical map. Now the British forces are again getting their own standalone multiplayer DLC. I have a feeling that when I buy these 'campaigns' I am being charged for something I have already bought in the multiplayer DLC.

Best ARPG ever created.
+Graphics and sound design.
+Great itemization with many factors to consider, and not just straight % stat boosts.  You can even create entire builds around gear-based abilities outside of your chosen classes!
+Character customization is broad without being shallow (looking at you POE passive tree).  Choose two classes to mix, round them out with devotion system that gives you buffs and more abilities.
+Get as complex or simple as you want with abilities, some builds work with just 2-3, others can have 7-8 by the end.
+Gameplay is smooth as silk, fast movement speed, and possibly the greatest invention I've ever seen in ARPGs with the "continuous attack" function that automatically moves on to the next enemy as you hold down the mouse button, no more clicking on each enemy at a time!
-Story is a bit throwaway at the moment, but could be very interesting with a little fleshing out.
-Enemies aren't as diverse as the other big games in the genre, but content is still coming so we should see this get better.
-Some classes combinations feel like they aren't powerful/sturdy enough, many builds that are viable into Ultimate difficulty require certain classes and abilities (soldier passives, demoltionist blast shield).
I've been waiting for the next big Diablo 2, and this is finally it.

Before anything else, let me say that I wanted to like this game. I'm an artist myself and have studied both illustration and animation. I was honestly expecting to connect with this concept. Sadly, my artistic senses were offended more than anything. I feel bad for saying this about any other artist's work, but this is also one of the few Steam purchases I deeply regret.
Like the title says, it's unfinished. Not even in any artsy way. The only lament I experienced from this game was that of my wasted money.
Maybe the idea was good at some point, but the mechanics feel broken, and navigating the world is terrible, which really just killed the experience (hence my very short playtime on record). I went into this hoping for a short, thoughtful, story driven experience, but instead I was apalled by bad coding and environment design. Simplicity can be great; I knew what the game looked like from screenshots, and I was still expecting to like it. Instead, it felt uninviting and badly planned out. This is an example of an indie game where simplicity and idea doesn't win me over.
The 2D animation and the video of the artist drawing are easily the best parts of this game, but I found myself mostly looking at the equivalent of Google SketchUp blocks without textures, meshing badly with the hand drawn art. Those who are finding deep artistic meaning in this probably have far more going on in their head than what's going on in this game.
Bottom line is, I feel like the creator of this game had ideas that they couldn't properly convey in this format.

You're an unfinished sketch and must try to reach the pencil of your creator to finally know who you were meant to be: to do this you'll gather a few powers (such as helicopter cap, running or jumping shoes etc) and use them to traverse the few levels that make up the game.
While a surely interesting concept Unfinished sadly offers a very bland and short gameplay experience, one that not even its few memorable moments can save.
-simple but effective art style
-one level (pictured in the screenshot) is truly gorgeout to look at, original in its design and serves as the game's most enjoyable point
-story is a bit of a mixed bag as a few genuinely interesting ideas are brought down by an equal amount of dull exposition
-platforming sections are generally dull, some can get quite frustrating aswell
-movement and camera controls feel awkward
-most levels feel a bit too barren as they lack any kind of detail
-at times it can be hard to understand where you're supposed to go
-standard movement speed is fairly slow
-just as its Store pages say it's quite short (I'd say 45 minutes)
I took a few days off before finally reviewing this game as I had conflicting feelings about it...I see it's been created as a work of love and the theme is plainly dear to the dev, some of the art is also truly nice. Sadly as an actual game Unfinished really falls flat as the bland levels and barebones gameplay take their toll on the player: I just didn't have much fun using the awkward controls to switch powers at the right time or to try and aim my jumps correctly to move through a few platforms.
The gameplay simply isn't refined enough to be engaging and there's not enough to do to make up for its problems: most levels look and feel the same and the new powers you'll unlock don't do much to mix things up, you'll just be moving forward, jump and/or float a bit until you reach a new zone, rinse and repeat.
It's a real shame as the game can be quite enjoyable when it drops the dull platforming and leaves you to explore a bit while giving some narration, the fact it does so while introducing some vibrant colours into a mostly black and white world also helps tremendously in making these moments shine. Sadly this happens basically only once and it simply isn't enough to make up for the rest of the game.

Best ARPG ever created.
+Graphics and sound design.
+Great itemization with many factors to consider, and not just straight % stat boosts.  You can even create entire builds around gear-based abilities outside of your chosen classes!
+Character customization is broad without being shallow (looking at you POE passive tree).  Choose two classes to mix, round them out with devotion system that gives you buffs and more abilities.
+Get as complex or simple as you want with abilities, some builds work with just 2-3, others can have 7-8 by the end.
+Gameplay is smooth as silk, fast movement speed, and possibly the greatest invention I've ever seen in ARPGs with the "continuous attack" function that automatically moves on to the next enemy as you hold down the mouse button, no more clicking on each enemy at a time!
-Story is a bit throwaway at the moment, but could be very interesting with a little fleshing out.
-Enemies aren't as diverse as the other big games in the genre, but content is still coming so we should see this get better.
-Some classes combinations feel like they aren't powerful/sturdy enough, many builds that are viable into Ultimate difficulty require certain classes and abilities (soldier passives, demoltionist blast shield).
I've been waiting for the next big Diablo 2, and this is finally it.

This game was recommended to me by a friend at release and I support the recommendation. I enjoyed the learning curve which was not bad in terms of units but took me some time adjusting to the economy and pace.
Pros
+Pace is neither long winded nor over before you know it. The game regulates this with simple unit cap and depleting resources. Tech progress is more about choosing a strategy than waiting to get up to it.
+Graphics are appropriately pretty without bogging me down.
+ Factions are distinct and balanced well enough from my non-competitive viewpoint.
+Controls are intuitive and the game is generally not super micromanage heavy.
+ Premade maps are diverse and well made for their purposes.
+Building a counter force is doable
Cons
-Build order. You must have the basics taking up extremely limited space at all times because replacing them with upgraded versions will prevent all construction. I just want to ditch my little factory for a big one when the map won't let me put down a hub since there are mountains in the way. But if I do that I need to find someplace to stick a little factory otherwise I am not allowed to build anything at all.
-Economy is feast or famine. Early game is just waiting for the first gatherer to finish then wait for the little drones to bring it back. It's a very boring two minutes that can only go two ways. More early variety would be nice. Then if you have enough resources it doesn't really matter since the cap prevents using them. Only one resource is also a bit boring imo.
-Upgrades are available to choose from pretty early on. You only need to pick the one that corresponds to the unit or two you are using. That's it. Nothing really to work up to, If you want to play with tanks then you build a tank attachemnt and select tank upgrade. End of story no progresssion arc.
-Epic units are not diverse. Each faction gets one and it's not that powerful.
-AI could use some tweaks, they tend to not use the map to its advantage.
All in all I think it's a good game that is catered towards shorter matches whereas I want a war not a skirmish.

My girlfriend and I just finished Child of Light, and it was quite well done! Here are my thoughts.
The visual presentation is stunning. We were both consistently blown away by how beautiful landscapes and characters were. Same goes for the soundtrack - as a pianist with a love of piano music, it resonated with me. Powerful yet serene, sorrowful and joyous.
Gameplay was a nice mix between exploration / environment absorption and challenging combat. We played on Casual and felt it was suitable.
The characters were each well-developed enough, memorable and provided enough variety combat-wise to make me care! This is often difficult.
I absolutely loved the Oculi system - it provided both meaningful upgrades and creativity in crafting. Loads of room to experiment, too! I spent a lot of time wondering about gem combinations, which tier was the highest, can you combine diamond + onyx (yes = spinel!), etc.
The co-op play was outstanding, too! GF does not like complicated systems and Igniculus let her help in both exploration and combat. Really reminds me of Wind Waker's Tingle Tuner asymmetric co-op gameplay. I'd love to see more of this approach to co-op.
In short, Child of Light was an outstandingly strong game - cohesive, enticing and thoroughly enjoyable. 10/10, would recommend to everyone!

Fun, tactical, strategy squad/base building game where the fate of nations, indeed all of humanity, hangs in the balance with every mission choice. What it lacks in soldier customisation from the original UFO series, XCOM makes up for with beautiful graphics and fluid gameplay.
I have lost untold hours on this game, striving to keep my soldiers alive long enought to gain the skills they need to survive, and to research the technology required to combat the ever increasing intensity of the alien invasion.
I have cackled gleefully and mouthed "Boom! Headshot!" as an elite sniper takes down an alien halfway across the map in glorious cinematic action. Gritted my teeth in exasperation and watched helplessly as nations critical to the funding of my XCOM forces were absorbed by the ever encroaching Alien forces. Cried out in dismay as veteran soldiers got cut down in battle and then desperately filled out my depleted forces with inexperienced rookies, praying they make it through the next mission.
This is a game that sucks hours out of your life until finally you either emerge bloody and victorious, or it crushes you in ignomious defeat. Overall game replayability is limited but there is some variation in the way you approach each mission tactically and the strategic campaign overall. Plus you can make big stompy cyborg troops and gentically enhanced super soldiers! This game is like a neverending supply of your favourite food of choice and you will find yourself gorging on it constantly, until you are sick of it, and take a long break from eating it again before returning to gorge on it once more. Or you won't.

I have given this game my self-created describing marks of:
[Intense] and [Tactical]
The "Intense" mark is given to single-player games who can* give you 'intense' adrenaline rushes.
I.E games where great punishment is the terms of defeat.
Other games with this mark: Day Z, Minecraft
*Intensity is a subjective experience, and it's up to each individual how much emotion they put into the game, this mark just says that it has the potential to become very intense.
The "Tactical" mark is given to games who promotes or demands "Think before you act" mindsets.
I.E games whose pace is relatively slow, combat unfolding as the game progresses.
Other games with this mark: Dota, Total War

What if your dreams, ideas, and creations all had a life of their own? One of man's most greatest abilities is to create, rather that be life, tools, or art. Sometimes though, creation isn't easy, sometimes things are left undone, inspiration is a valuable commodity that doesn't come easy. You will explore these concepts and more in this interesting and entertaining puzzle game. You play an unfinished doodle, who seeks identity in a world of art and chaos. The story is shared between Artist and Doodle as they both go through a journey of discovering themselves and purpose. While Unfinished - An Artist's Lament is a rather short game, what it does have to offer is extremely enjoyable aesthetically and gameplay follows suit. Finding unfinished drawings, you add abilities to your own drawing, such as spring boots, helicopter hat and other whimsical powers. The puzzles in Unfinsihed are rather simple, the game never draws focus away from what matters, the story. This leads the game to feeling like its full of good ideas but ends rather suddenly. While this was obviously intended, a part of me couldn't help but wonder what else could've been had the ideas and powers/levels been expanded upon. Nevertheless Unfinished - An Artist's Lament is a journey of self actualization that is fun, pleasant, and makes you ponder your own creations and goals that you never quite completed. This game is a fine example of Gamer Art and should be treated and enjoyed as such.

A well made classic. Very good writing, but gameplay has some minor bumps
The good
-Fantastic dialogue and characters.
The important characters (with the exception of Freeman himself) are all very well written and voice acted. You can
easily gague their personality from only a few lines
-No cutscenes
The important stuff usually happens in front of you or you'll hear about it over a loudspeaker. Granted you may as well be in a box on the moon for all the influence you have over what happens. Some of the scenes also tend to drag on and leave you with nothing to do.
The meh
-The Source engine itself.
I know this was a big deal when it came out, and its' still pretty cool how much you can do in the levels. After you've solved one sea-saw puzzle or arranged some boxes up in a pile to climb out a window, you've seen it all. Some of the levels get too excited about making you "solve" Source engine puzzles and they become more annoying as the game drags its' feet.
-Level design.
Most of the levels drag on for too long. The environments are bland as well. I got really sick of the post-industiral suburbs and warehouses. Some of the alien stuff looks kinda cool, but I think it can lean too heavilly toward the surreal aspect of alien design. I sometimed look at the alien stuff and think, "that just doesn't look like it could function at all in any world" Of course the the game would come flying in saying, "THAT'S JUST BECAUSE YOUR HUMAN BRAIN DOESN'T UNDERSTAND ALIEN DESIGN."
The bad
-Gunplay.
So the gunplay isn't that bad, but it keeps bothering me the more times I have to spend with it. You have too many weapons on your person at all times and you can getbogged down quickly while trying to scroll through them all. Most of the guns you get early on will become useless once you pickup their big brother down the road. I often found myself wishing, "why can't I drop this old gun I don't use anymore so I can hold more ammo for the new gun I do use?"
Most of the weapons have an embarrassing range and disgraceful accuracy. There are only two weapons that reasonably hit an ememy more than a stone's throw away, and neither of them have a decient ammo pool. The granades also slip and slide like bars of soap. They are only usefull in highly contextual settings. Like an ememy sitting in a box at the end of a narrow hallway.
-Freeman himself
This may be part of the joke, but it reflects badly on these well-written characters when they lend all thier trust, faith, and best weapons on a man who has never spoken to any of them. Everything special and useful about Freeman was given to him. From his suit to his crowbar. It could be that the whole point is not Freeman himself, but rather what he stand for. Like a flag. Even still we have no imput from Freeman at any point. He could have died in his H.E.V suit in the first gun fight and we're just playing as the suit from then on and the story would still make as much sense. Maybe even more.

This is a difficult game for me to review.
Unfinished is an interesting short game. You play as an unfinished drawing who wants to be complete.
The game serves as an effective metaphor for the creative process in general: everyone who has tried to create something, be it art, writing, a game, or whatever, can recognise the story this game tries to tell.
The art style is great. All hand-drawn, and it stays this throughout. The art is accompanied by soothing music.
The narrative is told through voice over -- sadly no subtitles -- that is clear, if at a little low volume compared to the music.
Gameplay wise, you walk through white, empty environments to find body parts (different legs, different bodies, different heads), all of which give you enhanced abilities. As you progress the levels become more... drawn.
Unfortunately Unfinished is hard to get in to. I was stuck at the first real puzzle for far too long, since the game didn't make it clear at all that I could swap abilities in mid-air, and I only found this by chance.
It is also short. Too short perhaps for Steam refunds. If I hadn't gotten stuck at the  beginning I could've finished it within 30 minutes.
While a bit rough the game is mechanically sound and the story resonates with me, as a fellow (want to be?) creator.
As for the price point, €5 is perhaps steep for such a short game, and (disclaimer) I didn't buy it for that price: I had a 50% off coupon. At that price level (€2,50 or less) I can recommend it to everyone.

Unfinished: An Artist's Lament is a heavily story driven game. You play as a sketched out sort of stick figure who's chasing down the pencil that drew him, in an attempt to become "complete". It must be understood that this is not an action packed game and if you try to play it as such, you will not enjoy yourself. You're tasked with solving puzzles to make your way through each level while chasing down the aforementioned pencil by using tools that you find along you way. Each tool is applied to your stick figure's head, torso, or feet with some puzzles requiring you to use a combination of your different pieces of attire. The puzzle solving, while simple, is unique and entertaining, but not enough to keep someone captivated. However, the game makes up for its simplicity with its story. The narrator, and evidently the man who drew the stick figure in the first place, can be heard dictating different key moments in his life as an artist. The artist, struggling to look for work, faces the same struggles his stick figure creation does in the sense that neither of them are complete. As someone with experience in the field of art, the story struck a very emotional chord with me and was that much more meaningful. If you are looking for solid gameplay and replayability, this is not the game for you. But if you're looking for some quick and cheap fun, with what I think is a rather amazing story, then I would definitely suggest Unfinished for you. To enjoy this, you have to be able to appreciate the game for what it is: the story of the struggles of an artist, plagued by how he could never finish his work, only to feel lost and never truly complete himself. Unfinished is a unique and fun experince, perfect for the average puzzle solver, and relates to everyone in one way or another. The good:
Long engrossing story
Nice graphics
Sound that compliments the game and adds atmosphere
Well thought out quests
-----------------------------------
The bad:
Very lazy randomised loot system even from "bosses". More often than not you'll get warrior armour with mage stats, mage armour with strength on it etc. I played through the entire game without finding a single item for various slots on my main characters with a worthwhile stat on it.
Afterthought crafting. There is no workbench or anything like that to make items on, you just drag and drop stuff around to see if it combines. Which is fine, but the "recipes" you find are pretty much useless, giving vague hints at combinations. As a result you'll end up just googling "Divinity Original Sin crafting".
The crafting requires that you gimp one of your main characters as items you produce are level based. There are henchman you can level up to be solely crafters, but unless you level them to max they will only be able to produce items of their level. This becomes an issue when you realise there is a finite amount of XP in the game (there are no random encounters to grind out XP).
The freeform way you can do quests sometimes results in a quest you can't complete as finishing one quest may result in a "hand in" NPC being killed/leaving. Sometimes the outcome of a quest isn't obvious till it's too late and then you need to decide between loading an earlier save and losing sometimes hours of gameplay, or having an unfinishable quest left in your quest log forever.
--------------
In summary I do recommend this game as I've certainly got my moneys worth out of it. It does have some issues but they can be overlooked for the most part. As a completionist I abandoned the game at one point because of a couple of broken quests (see above), but I liked it enough to replay it at a later date to complete it.

A Yu-gi-oh! game that can potentially cost as much as a half month's worth of groceries...sign me up.
I'm at a really weird spece right now. I was a fan of the show and the card game since Nightmare Troubadour for the Nintendo DS but I am kinda getting tired of the series in general. It's a turn based card game that almost everyone should be familiar with by now. There is alot to absorb if there are any new players to the series but it has a very user-friendly interface with tutorials that should make the game easy enough to pick up an play. The price is actually very fair and the campaign is lengthy enough to more than justify the price. There are also little cutscenes for certain pinnacle monsters when they attack giving the player a bit of anime authenticity.
This may sound a bit strange but the inclusion of playing though the campaign with the protagonists deck with the additional option to play as the antagonists decks is a little addition that I happen to find most attractive. I imported a copy of Yu-gi-oh! Tag Force 6 for the psp because it had some voice acting in it. It's little things like this that really makes a game for me and reinvigorates my desire to purchase a game from a series that has slowly lost its appeal.
There are two major issues about this game that I just can't get over. Card acquisition is one of the worst aspects I have ever experienced rivaled only by millenium duels for xbox. I'm sitting on over six figures worth of duel points because I am  completely disinterested in: picking a charcter, selecting yes, viewing the contents, waiting almost two seconds for the special card....ugh. If there is a bulk option that I am unaware of PLEASE let me know because at this point mashing the enter button for hours is not my idea of fun. Secondly, and most importantly, THE DLC. Before you try to hammer it in that you are not required to purchase it; that doesn't make the temptation and consumption disappear. KNOW THIS, for those of you that didn't bother to read the game description, you will not get access to Arc-V upon purchase. You will get an introduction only with an option to buy cards from the series afterward and now the frustration begins. Let's say that you just want to purchase all of the Arc-V material so that you can have the feeling of an all-around complete game. Now your game has jumped from 20 dollars to 70. Once you have that under your belt its only a matter of time before you figure, "meh, mght as well buy the rest." and now you have a 105 dollar Yu-gi-oh! game. That is insane, ridiculous, and purposefully done by Konami.
If you can resist the urge to pay ridiculous dlc prices, this game at base price is more than worth your time and money based only on the single player aspect of the game.( Multiplayer is an added bonus) Don't be fanboyed into getting everything that this game has to offer or you may find yourself donating blood to pay your rent.

Although the vanilla version of the game didn't quite live up to standard, the game's expansion packs in Gods & Kings and Brave New World lifted the game to another level--with complex gameplay that delivered in addition to pretty good graphics.  I personally find that the ability to play as up to 43 civilizations absoutely depicts the endless possibilities to conquering this game.  Unique about Civ V is its ability to never fully bore you, as there are always new challenges, maps, civilizations, scenarios, victories, difficulties, and more to keep you going for one more turn.  Furthermore, Civ V has a vast multiplayer experience like no other, with the ability to customize settings nearly just as precise as you can with singleplayer.  The ability to all take turns at the same time and progress through time together is fantastic.  A nifty little scoreboard even shows how your civlization stacks up against your friends.  However, multiplayer or not Civ V has become a timeless classic for myself and many of my other friends.  I will admit that I haven't played Civ VI (yet), but honestly I really don't know how the developers can top what they've done with this game.  The game is nearly perfect, although I would appreciate if the AI was a bit more realistic.  I've often found myself betrayed by my greatest ally in a matter of just a few turns, and I've even seen wars occur among AI that last only a couple of turns.  Trading with the AI could also be a little challenging sometimes, but for the most part it isn't too big of a problem, because overall the AI does do a pretty good job balancing the game out.  In conclusion, I certainly recommned Civ V to anyone who hasn't purchased the game.  It's a well thought-out game with overwhelming positives and very little negatives about it.  A must play for sure.

In a world strongly inspired by Nordic Mythology, where Gods went silent and humans and horned giants called Varl face off against hordes of metal-clad beings called the Dredge. You play as Hakon, Varl warrior who becomes the leader of their amy in quest against the Dredge and as Rook, a hunter from human city who becomes the leader of the exodus of his people in face of the Dredge invasion.
The game is visually and vocally stunning, filled with deep lore and interesting characters and it merges itself well with the mechanics that have you make choices and then face often unexpected consequences. Very few games I've seen can go so much out of their way to ensure you face the result of your actions, sometimes in a very unexpected way. The game makes you also manage 3 resources - caravan's morale which affect how well you fight, resources that will determine how long it can go before people start starving, and fame which serves to both buy resources but also items for your characters and advancing them. In many cases, you will be forced to choose whenever you want to risk going with the food you have for who knows how long but the stronger team for battles or vice versa. Or if you can afford sacrificing resources for a day of rest to increase the morale. The battles themselves have you play a turn-based skirmish against a group of challenging enemies, that even on easy mode can satisfy more demanding players. All of this makes Banner Saga an excellent combination that will please people who were looking for an engaging story as well as fans of harsh, but forgiving, gameplay.

Finally I believe I have amassed enough hours, to review this game.
So what is Civilization? If you haven't already guessed, it's a turn-based, 4X (eXpand, eXplore, eXploit and eXterminate) game. It basically puts you in command of the civilization of your choosing, and you have to lead them to victory and "Stand the test of time" by beating your opponents in a Cultural, Diplomatic, Space, Time, and the most fun way, Domination victory. Starting from the ancient era with little technological knowledge and one city, fighting barbarians with swords and spears. Gradually progressing through the different technological and time/eras, fighting with gunpoweder weapons, researching flight... eventually reaching the point where using nuclear weapons in war against other civilizations is the daily norm.
Civilization V is more simple than Civilization IV (but you can fix it with mods from the workshop), but it has higher quality textures. So do not let that drive you away from this masterpiece.
Absolutely amazing....but really needs the 2 expansions, or else it gets dull rather quickly (ok not entirely true strictly speaking, it is quite a lot of fun, and the workshop can really spice things up, even lacking BNW (Brave New World) and GAK (Gods and Kings).
But if you get the complete edition, not only you are compatible with the majority of mods out there (which there's an abundance of astonishing mods), it offers more gameplay mechanics such as the faith & religion system (GAK), and more troops and more gameplay options, units & civs (e.g Great War units from the BMW expansion etc). Overall, it's a solid game (with the expansions that is), but with Civilization VI out, I don't know whether you want this as a cheap alternative to Civ 6, as the games have different mechanics (such as the tile system working differently) and an altered but otherwise nearly the same gameplay. 3) Right click actions in UI's are completely inconsistent. With experience I'm sure this will get more fluent, but for the time being I'm sometimes scared to right click in menus for fear of it doing not what I want it to.

I do enjoy the game but two aspects of BDO really take away from what I feel "could" be an excellent MMO in the North American market.
- The Marketplace is perhaps the worse tool I have seen for in-game commerce in my twenty years experience playing MMO's - Its the weakest thing I have seen in recent memory and feels like it was designed by a bunch of clueless kids!
- The lack of dungeons and poor development of the PvP scene (compared with the KR version) is dissapointing.

Grey Goo is EXACTLY what the RTS genre needs. It brings back the great components of the genre like LAN play, base building, a polished campaign, and heavy macro, while slyly adding amazing ideas like brush cover, MOBA QWER Hotkeys, FOV, and the all-new GOO faction. This game is not a joke - it's an incredibly polished and (most importantly) fun game that you must try.
What's incredibly fascinating about this game is that it has the power to appeal to both old RTS fans and younger gamers who have never played this genre. While most RTS games take an eternity to get started with, this game has simple rules. The complexity of Grey Goo truly lies in strategy and tactics, and not in its GUI or micro options. In the interest of comparison, this game took the asymmetry from StarCraft, solid macro gameplay from C&C, some extra components from Supreme Commander, and made it all better.
Honestly, comparing this game to the above RTSs isn't even fair. Give it a shot and you'll see for yourself.

I'm writing this review after 50+hrs of playtime and finishing the main game incl. all side-quests on hard (15-20 of those went to ♥♥♥♥ing around in multiplayer).
Pros:
+Amazing graphics

+Even more fun in co-op
+Skilltrees and leveling-system
+Tons of stuff you can get distracted by while questing ;)

Con:
-Melee combat feels pretty random. Until lategame even the average biter can kill you since "headshots" are more luck than skill.
-Coming from console this game is not a great shooter. Don't expect challenging firefights or great hitboxes.
-Clunky and sometimes annoying controls
-The UI needs some PC love and is very annoying to handle since it was obviously created to work with the capabilities of controllers.
-Very small default FOV to achieve the above mentioned performance. If your PC is able to handle it set it to +10
-Spawnpatterns of zombies are kinda weird sometimes if you want / have to loot a certain spot. Many times it took me 20mins to clear a small area around a car or crate because virals kept spawning in groups of 5 along with the normal biters.
PS: This game is fun in parties but it turns into a real horror setting once you play it alone. Especially the interior levels in the second district. For the full experience I recommend this game to played in both modes.

The weeb in me loves this game. The RPG lover in me is left wanting more. The actual gameplay amounts to, breaking the enemy's guard, and then use your strongest attack until the enemy is dead. If you are not on the same level as the thing you are fighting, you're dead. And you'll need to grind. There are plenty of enemies that give a lot of experience so once you find those enemies you can get a lot of experience quickly.
The actual gameplay of this game is not that fleshed out. You can move around and position your characters before you attack but the game does nothing to make you change where your characters are standing. An enemy MIGHT walk out of range from your party members and you MIGHT have to move them over an inch to attack them again. But there are no enemies that force you to move out of the way of a devastating attack. There are no enviromental hazards that force you to plan your movements during fights. Nothing like that. So being able to move your characters in fights is basically pointless.
There's no real nudity in the game but there is a lot of cleavage and mention of breast sizes so it does well to titlate and make you laugh. But it doesn't do enough to challenge you in fights outside of: Are you high enough level? Ok you win. In conclusion, the fanservice is good, the gameplay is not. That being said. I can't really NOT recommend this game. I didn't get exactly what I wanted out of it. But that's not to say that you won't.

I did enjoy this game a lot, I played through it about 3-4 times now, but I cannot recommend this game.
Positives:
- Good story line and music, great atmosphere and a fresh way of story telling to the player.
(I love how the music begins to become a "whole piece" after the passing the first wall.)
- Platforming puzzles add depth to the game, creating a feeling of wanting to become "finished".
- Great narrative prompts to player.
Negatives:
- The music is a BIG part of this game, but if you get stuck it becomes annoying VERY quickly.
(At the beginning and on the last level there is a high pitched sound, and the music is on loop)
Muting takes away a lot away from the game.
- JPEG instruction sheet is not enough, a beginning tutorial at the start to understand how the game works would be infinitely better.
- Controls are a bit clunky. (Cannot hit 1-3 while moving to select a different item, must ONLY be pressing 1-3 at that time)
- Game forces player to admire artwork or listen to storytelling at some points, which can be a positive, but given the context that this game is a platformer it was done in such a way that it became more annoying rather than adding value to the story.
Overall I think there are a lot of improvements that can be made to the game. The length of the game is perfect. It just needs some more polish. Thanks for making this Andrew I liked a lot of your ideas!

Playing FTL is both the best and worst thing at the same time.
While it's definitely fun, complex, well made and well thought out, the game is both the best "roguelike" space sim I've played in a long time, and the most horrible exercise in masochism I've met since I tried to play a MMORPG where there were no "noob" safeguards.
While offering enough options to make a strategy enthusiast drool, but enough action to satisfy fans of action, the name of the game, as always, is "Resource Management."
Or it would be if you were allowed to save your game. At all. You can quit, and pick up where you left off, but outside of that, don't expect to be able to re-load and undo a terrible mistake at a critical battle.
That said, it's horribly addictive. It has just the right amount of "I can do this" combined with the game's ability to blindside you with something you're totally unprepared for.
The only thing that really irritates me is it keeps some of it's own rules secret. For one thing, I'm still not clear on the power requirements for certain weapons, and they don't always tell you how long it takes to charge them in between shots. A super-missile weapon that takes 30 seconds to fire isn't even going to make it out of the tube because by then you'll be in ten different pieces, all of which are on fire. On the other hand, the first-level ion cannon fires a little over once a second, but by halfway through the game is as useful as sneezing at their shields and hoping they catch cold.
I'd be fine with all this if the very end of the game wasn't "Good job, well done surviving, now patch up that wreck and go take on the enemy flagship, will you?"
"Excuse me? Do you know what I went through just to get here? Why the HELL would I take on a suicide mission with three holes in my hull, two surviving crewmen, almost no fuel, no missiles, and some super-cannon that needs ten minutes powerup time before it can light a cigarette?!?"
To which I can only assume the game replies "Too bad, bend over."
This game pulls zero punches, and the only way I got through it was by being overly suspicious every time I started doing well. If you feel like you're winning, you've overlooked something.
Still, it was on sale, and I got a few hours entertainment out of it.

Disclosure: I was provided a review code for this game.
My Quick Look on Unfinished - An Artist's Lament
I beat this game in 30 minutes.  It's *very short*, overbearing in its delivery, initially obtuse, yet there are a few moments when this game shines.  Here is a gif of my favorite moment in the game:
There is this moment and a few others where everything the game is trying to do succeeds.  Other times, the purpose of explaining an Artist's anxieties can become overbearing.  And I'm honestly not sure if I'm supposed to be critiquing that as a fault of the game or if that is the purpose of the game's design.
I like the game.  I like that it was attempted.  There are parts that were inspiring and there were parts that were annoying.  The very beginning of the game is the definition of obtuse.  Is it obtuse on purpose?  Is that frustration I'm feeling *supposed* to happen?
If it was, well then job well done!  If it wasn't, well then, that part could have been done better.
Still, I like short games and Unfinished, with all of it's faults, still left a positive impression on me.

FTL is a game about strategy and managing your resources to your fullest. It's a game about doing that and inevitably getting killed despite doing such to the absolute best of your ability. Which is part of what makes it so great and so terrible. You can spend one run doing everything right and lose and you can spend a run doing practically everything wrong and still win. That's a problem with procedural generation and a boon for the game itself. Every run feels different in the level of power and the obstacles that you come across. I've spent 33 hours in this game as of time of writing and yet I can still boot it up and start a run and feel like it's completely different from any of my other runs. Which is awesome.
So, if you enjoy that kind of thing, even to the point of masochism, buy this game!

This game givens me a cleaner interface with the old classic rules.
With that over and done with we can begin.
The single player duel campaigns and challenges rum smooth with little difficulty, during the duelist of course you will be able to use one of your own decks (max 10 slots) or the deck of the duelist your playing as. There are packs assigned to certain duelists and it doesn't take long to grind currency. If you want to build the deck of a certain duelist you can see if they have a certain pack and also check the guide that was put up for where certain cards are. As you complete certain duels you'll receive template's for the duelists deck and the cards let's say for Kite can be optained by dueling him or opening his booster packs in the card shop. As for multiplayer then I suggest using a different platform such as Ygopro as this game is highly underpopulated. The real reason I use this more then YgoPro is the smooth and clear interface. If you are lacking cards the DLC is also a possibility to find them. All in all I give the dueling gameplay a 9/10, deck construction gameplay a 10/10 and the card detabase a 5/10.
The downloadable content is really good put given the price of the game itself is way too much I think the DLC  should be free and that would maybe help to justify the price but regardless that isn't the case and with Konami can we be suprised? To put it simply the DLC is only something you should really buy if you need it's respective cards. I give the DLC card content 9/10 and the campaign content 5/10.

Grim Dawn is an incredible Action-RPG in the vein of Diablo, Torchlight, or Titan Quest - its spiritual predecessor from many of the same developers.
First off, the game lacks some features which draw people to similar games. Multiplayer is minimal, with no well-established interplayer economy (you can trade, but there's not much community for it and items are worth whatever you think they are). There are no ladders or seasons - just play how you want, when you want. After beating the final boss on the highest difficulty, there's not much more content, although you can still spend plenty more time farming better loot and optimizing your character, and there are a few supremely challenging extra bosses to test yourself against.
All that said, this is my favorite game in the genre by far. I play by myself with whatever items I can find and my own build concepts, and Grim Dawn is perfect for that. Loot is exciting, classes and skills are mostly well-balanced, and combinations are endless. Rather than picking a single class, each character gets to choose 2 out of (currently) 6 available Masteries, and uses whatever combination of skills from both that you want.
The campaign is a good length, and though the main story is not amazing, the lore of the world itself (which you can learn more about from notes found around the game) is very cool. Post-apocalyptic settings are very common these days, but Grim Dawn manages a fairly unique feel, and drops tantalizing hints about what might be in store for future content. Each character can unlock 2 additional difficulties to replay the game, in pursuit of greater rewards and higher levels.
If you've enjoyed other ARPGs, you really owe it to yourself to try this game. It's fun, well-made, and has endless replayability. You won't be disappointed.

I've seen many call this game "Smash Brothers meets Pong" and that's roughly correct. Lethal League is similar to Smash titles in its ease of access (being pretty simple to understand and play) and its competitive depth. Its similar to Pong in being focused around the ball, the one lethal element of the game. You and your opponent(s) are striving to hit this ball, tagging it to yourself and making it lethal to your opponent until they successfully hit it back (or miss, get hit, and die). The ball will steadily speed up after every hit as long as players remain alive, ramping up the intensity. Continue this until all but one player have lost all their lives, and only the champion remains!
Local and online multiplayer are supported, with 2-4 players. You can play 1v1, FFA, teams, or strikers (similar to soccer) modes. There are a couple different ball types you can try as well to mix things up, along with general options (stock count, time limit, etc.) There is matchmaking, but it's not skill-based (the community isn't large enough to support skill-based matchmaking anyways).
The game is great if you want to just hit buttons and peg your friends with baseballs, and also great if you're looking for something with competitive depth. While the execution barrier is fairly low, you have a lot of freedom of movement/options, and the smarter and more experienced player is still favored to win. Regardless, the game does a great job of hypeing the player up, as hits take progressively longer to complete as the ballspeed increases (giving the feeling of them putting more and more force into the ball), and the screen starts to shake, the background changes, 'impact distortions' occur, all the colors go negative, characters get speed afterimages, and finally the stage goes completely white if you get the ballspeed up enough. Each notch of this progressively makes things more intense, especially the first time you see them!
The only drawbacks to me of this game is the playerbase size and occasional crashes. This game has seen occasional boons in playerbase (usually following sales), but on average there's about 60-100 people playing at a time. Games go fairly quick, and you usually won't be waiting more than a minute in quickmatch queue (at least during peak EU and NA hours), but you may run into the same people multiple times. What you don't have in quantity, though, you do have in quality. There's almost always a few people in the group chat willing to play, and many are experienced players who are welcoming and helpful. The competitive LL community is, overall, one of the best communities I've been in.
The other drawback is a recurring crash that can occur in multiplayer games of more than 2 people. This only occurs maybe once every 6-7 games, but it can get annoying fairly quick. Fortunately, the game loads almost instantly, so getting back in the action is fast. It's annoying but manageable.
I highly suggest you try this game out, especially if you have friends to play it with. $15 may be a bit expensive for some (it was well worth it for me, 450 hours of play and counting), but I would definitely recommend this to anyone at $10 or less.

Bite Size Review - Black Desert Online
The Good:
- Graphics look really good
- Character creation is really extensive
- The entire game world is open, no loading screens after the first one when you log in
- Combo based combat feels good and make the game more interesting
- Life skills remind me of Runescape (meaning there is a lot to do and master more than just combat)
The Bad:
- The game is very grindy, some people will love it, others will hate it
- The game is not very well optimized (out in the world it's ok, but as soon as you get into a city with other players, the frame rate drops like crazy)
- PvE AI and variety is pretty poor, most enemies just walk toward you like zombies
- You need to buy the game, but it does feel like a Free to Play game
- PVP is based heavy on gear, meaning only the players that put 1000s of hours in will be competitive
- RNG Loot Upgrade systems can be a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥br>- No dungeons or any interesting PvE content, Endgame is very much focused on PvP
- The real money shop in the game, does sell items that do give players and edge over each other
- Many of the systems in this game, REQUIRE you to leave your computer logged into the game to function (energy and workers)
The Verdict:
The graphics look amazing as you zoom in on your characters and notice the details in their faces. There are many different and interesting classes to pick and choose from. The life skills are fun to mess around with and level up as well, this part of the game reminds me a lot like Runescape with all of it's skills and I really enjoyed this part of the game. However the PvE and PvP part of the game is where other systems in the game clash with each other and make it extremely hard to feel competitive. The RNG loot upgrade system, having to remain logged in for your character to gain energy, having to remain logged in for your workers to work.
So here's how the worker system functions - you send your workers out to work on harvesting raw materials or making items in little workshops that you can use or sell to other players. Now logically you would think you could tell your workers to work, set them all up at the end of the day, and then log out for the night and come back in the morning and have a whole new bunch of stuff to play around with. Logical right? But in this game that is not the case - you have to be logged in to the game in order for your workers to work!
In a day and age when every single person on the planet is encouraged to conserve energy this makes no sense to me. And it's not like the people leaving their computers on are more dedicated to the game or anything, they are away from their keyboards too. Everyone needs to sleep, I just don't want to leave my computer on all night etc. Bottom line: It sucks and since I am not willing to leave my comp on 24/7 I feel like others who do make millions more per day than me, and it is hard to stay competitive with them since money in their game is everything. I am not a hippie type wanting to save the planet or anything but really though - why the ♥♥♥♥ do we need to keep our computers on for these systems to function? It does not make sense. EVE Online is another MMO that has similarly deep systems, but EVE lets you log out and have processes that you setup, and they continue when you turn your computer off for the night - and I wish this game functioned in the same way.
Overall I would say BDO is an OK game.  The PVP is apparently really fun to play and the graphics are stunning for an MMO. The life skills are also really good and fun to do for awhile. However as I have said there are a few parts to this game that really♥♥♥♥♥♥me off - and these parts make it seem hard for a new player to catch up to the top elite. But at the end of the day, I paid $7 for it so I feel like I got my money's worth just messing around in the game world.

TL:DR version:
Thank me later
I'll just list Pros and Cons.
Graphics
Co-op
Parkour System
Crafting
Weapon Variety
Weapon viability-there is no "best" weapon for a given encounter, melee works as well as ranged in most cases.
Progression
Dropkicks
Progress in one game is saved to the next
Story is a bit weak
Can only craft things 1 at a time.
Let me explain.
Honestly for 60$ this is a steal and techland should be applauded for not being moneygrubbing♥♥♥♥♥hats. This game plays smooth as butter and everything works intuitively.
I'll start with the cons.
When I said everything works intuitively, it's more like almost everything. No craft X amount seems small but after you've crafted 20 molotovs/medpacks/lockpicks in a row it can be a bit annoying. The story is also a bit, well dumb IMHO. Starts off strong but loses alot of steam, the villian is just bland and it's hard to care about the side characters. They're more tropes than characters sadly. The GRE lady was a better character than most of the characters you interact with. There are a few hidden gems and even a few moments where you go, DAMN why wasn't that character like that the rest of the game! Just alot of wasted potential in the story/characters IMO. I'm sure some people would disagree.
To the PROS!
The crafting is fun and makes sense, no using a jellied eyeball of a newt to craft a lockpick. All the parts going in make sense on the final product. Co-op runs great and has plenty of options for you to handpick co-op partners and or play with anybody. The parkour is silky smooth, it's like AC parkour but feels more responsive, maybe that's just because of first person view. The weapon variety and viability is amazing you can use a gun and it feels great, you can use a bow and it feels great, you can run up and crush a zombies skull with a sledge hammer and it feels great, you can slice heads off with a machete and IT FEELS GREAT! There are zero trash weapon types and nothing feels overly clunky. Well once you get a little more stamina, everything feels weak in the first couple hours of gameplay. I actually like that feature as well, there's a sense of accomplishment the first time you one shot a zed. Dropkicks is self explanatory. The saved progress is great as well going from normal Dying light to the following and keeping my levels and stash is a wonderful feature. Thank you devs.
All in all this bundle is a steal. AAA studios(Ubisoft/EA/Activision) would sacrifice their own children before releasing just one of these games for under 100$. Both games are extremely well fleshed out and full of content.
Bravo Techland. You made an oversaturated genre feel fun again.

I've just finished my first playthrough of this game, so it's time to write a review of it.
In XCOM: Enemy Unknown, you take command of Earth's last line of defense against an alien invasion.
Gameplay: There are two parts of this game, since it's a hybrid of strategy and turn-based shooter. When the game starts, you choose a continent to build your XCOM base on. The choices confer bonuses to your base. At the XCOM base, you will:
-View/edit/hire/customize soldiers (up to 99 units) in the barracks. The DLC offers extra customization. There are several classes: Assault, support, heavy, and sniper. Each soldier has a loadout that consists of a primary weapon, an item, armor and a sidearm. All items are upgradeable via the lab and foundry. Soldiers can also be renamed, if you want to make it personal. Each soldier also gains experience and progresses on a level track that allows you to select one of two abilities or traits at each tier up to the rank of colonel. Additional upgrades for the squad (such as increasing the squad size above the starting limit of 4 per deployment) are available in the XCOM base.
-Research technologies so you can manufacture better equipment in the engineering lab. There are a lot of technologies to research, and they unlock after performing autopsies, interrogating captured aliens, and at certain points in the story. Alien technology can also be researched once it is collected from missions. Research takes time, and adds another layer of strategy. The engineering lab functions in the same way.
-Purchase upgrades for existing equipment in the foundry (also takes resources and credits)
-Build and maintain interceptors to shoot down UFO's
You are also able to build additional rooms in the base such as resource generators (resources being power, scientists and engineers. This allows for a VERY cusomizable strategy. Managing the XCOM base could almost be a separate game.
The XCOM base also houses a situation room, which shows you the 'panic levels' of the countries involved in the XCOM project. Sending satellites to these countries makes them send you more resources, and it's a good idea to get satellite coverage for all countries early on in a playthrough, as there are bonuses conferred by having satellite coverage over an entire continent.
The base management portion of the game operates much like a board game. Time passes towards a monthly council report in which you are graded and given funding. If 8 countries leave the XCOM project, the game ends. You can choose to ignore UFO sightings and whatnot if you have a large scale plan, but ignored countries will panic and you have to balance out your decisions. If you enjoy some (actually not too stressful) management, you will like this portion of the game.
The other part of gameplay is turn-based. As UFO sightings occur and missions pop up, you send squads of XCOM soldiers to deal with threats on the ground. This is where the meat of the game is. Strategy is key. The soldiers drop in a random environment. Each soldier gets two actions a turn, and can move, shoot, or dash to use actions (dashing uses two actions). The environments are destructible and cover is exceedingly important. Soldiers also have a range of class-based abilities that they can use each turn or every few turns. The enemy AI is pretty good, and there are a lot of different enemy types to consider when on a mission. Gameplay can be very risk/reward-oriented. It plays really well and is quite hard to put down.
Pros:
+Unique experience in each playthrough
+Deep customization of the XCOM base and XCOM soldiers
+Crisis management on a global scale is challenging and interesting
+Research/upgrades add a sense of progression that is hard to top
+Nice visuals, and lots of small cutscenes for research projects
+Satisfying and addictive turn-based combat with a good bit of challenge and variety thrown in
+Good sound, but nothing to really write home about
+Passage of time makes every decision matter as the invasion ramps up
+Future playthroughs allow game modifiers for more challenge
Cons:
-Story is fairly generic, even though it works well enough that it won't ruin the game for you
-There is a small pool of mission objectives. While each deployment will play out differently, you'll either be killing all the aliens, disarming bombs or escorting citizens in all of them. The only exception comes with priority story missions.
Gameplay: 10/10
Visuals: 8/10
Story: 7/10
Sound: 8/10
Replay value: High
Overall: 9/10
It should be noted that there is an expansion called Enemy Within that improves upon the base game in almost every way by all accounts.

One glorious shmup. It has all the colours and then some more! It needs the mother of all photosensitive epilepsy warnings!
I have a feeling my eyeballs are going to hate me tomorrow, but they love me today. Oh, they love me today!
If you look at the trailer, you will have no idea what's going on. At least, I didn't.
What's happening is you're a little shooty thing that forever shoots upwards (autofire! nice and relaxing!), and all the hundreds of other things on the screen heading downwards are enemies, bullets and power-ups.
All you really need to pay attention to, in order to survive, is you need to not run into anything that's not a power-up. It's fairly simple; there are only two power-ups, and one of them are "souls" that auto-target you when you hit an enemy. Oh, and - you can move anywhere, you're not restricted to left and right. :)
As well as your autofiring gun, you can push the fire button to shoot a second gun. This gun kills (most) enemy bullets, and is powered by the souls I mentioned earlier.
Each level lasts as long as the music that's playing in it. The idea is to shoot as many enemies as you can in that time, keep up a chain, and not get killed too much.
So - fun, simple, classic arcade-style mechanics, a challenge that seems *just right* (well, it scales up as you go through the levels, but it seems eventually doable), plus crazy visuals (this is an understatement!), good music, tight gameplay that doesn't give you a split second to blink - all makes for a great, exhilarating time!
But I think this is a game to play in short bursts.
Just in case my eyes decide to go "you know what? this is too much! we quit!!". Haha!
UPDATE: Just so you know, the next day arrived and I turned out not to be blind after all!
