Classic PC RPGs have absorbed hundreds (even thousands) of hours of my life since I was a teenager, but after all these years, I can't say for certain that I love them. There are aspects about them that I absolutely adore, and there are aspects of them that make me grind my teeth.
Take Baldur's Gate, for example. It's classic. Iconic, even. For good reason, too. It's solidly-built, has a beautifully-designed world, interesting characters, a great story, and a fantastic open-world feel. It also has brutally-difficult try-try-again fights, a moderate lack of direction, and quite a few bugs/glitches. The first time I played BG, I had a game-breaking bug 30 hours in, and was dead in the water.
Divinity: Original Sin is certainly similar in that some-good-some-bad regard. During my playthrough, I found a lot to love, and a lot to hate. The story is well-crafted and interesting (although it does ramble), the characters each have their own motivations/backstories (and quests), it's open-world enough for you to miss important things if you aren't paying attention, the graphics are pretty good, and it's a meaty enough adventure to please anyone flying high off a recent dose of Baldur's Gate 2.
Now, before I list the cons I found, I have to re-state that I did enjoy the game. I definitely recommend it overall (especially since the enhanced "remastered" version is coming out for free soon), but there are bound to be people out there just as nitpicky as me, so I have to list what bugged me.
First of all, the difficulty in the first half of the game is RIDICULOUS. You will always be in an area, able to explore at your heart's content, surrounded on all sides but one by enemies that will curb-stomp you into oblivion. As a result, this "open-world" game is ostensibly linear, given there's only one area you can go to unless you want your face and limbs rearranged, redesigned, or removed. Then, once you hit somewhere just after the mid-point, battle difficulty falls off a cliff, and you'll be skating through gigantic brawls with ease. I can't really count that as a con, though, since it was a welcome relief for my poor molars.
Following right along with the difficulty, the balance in the game is really bad. For the first 50 hours, I built my main character as a ranger. She had high dexterity and speed, a fantastic legendary bow, and a full complement of gear boosting her bow skills. Battles were difficult, but doable. Then, 51 hours in, I found a unique dagger with high damage. I equipped it just to see what a dagger was like (changing literally nothing else I had equipped, even MY SKILLS), and became untouchable. Having spent 2/3 of the game outfitting myself as a ranger, and barely having any dagger skills at all didn't matter. One tiny equipment change, and I was zipping around the arena like a meth-head on fast forward, poking fatal holes in enemies left and right. I wasn't sneaking or backstabbing, just walking right up to mages and barbarians alike, and handily beating them toe-to-toe.
Granted, in RPGs, certain builds will always be more viable against certain enemies, but there were no scenarios that proved difficult for my little stabbing princess. It was funny and all, but when there is that big of a difference between build strengths, there is a problem. To be fair, there were a few pretty solid mages behind me providing support, but that half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥little dagger build was making even Madora (who is a BEAST of a warrior) look silly. I kid you not when I say I alone went head-to-head with the final boss while the rest of the team was cleaning up the trash he repeatedly spawned. It was so overpowered, it reminded me of the old JRPGs of my youth, when I would give all the best gear/upgrades to the main character, and trickle the hand-me-downs to the rest of the team (and it would be perfectly viable).
I wasn't trickling anything down to the rest of the team here, though, since each character had an almost completely unique set of equipment requirements. I had a ranger, a warrior, a spell-mage, and a wizard, all of which were focusing on different stats.
Before I switch down to talk about the smaller niggles and quirks, I have to talk about the combat system, the glitchy, buggy, nothing-short-of-poorly-designed combat system. The main problem I had with it is that enemies dance around a bit while they're idle, and there's no way to pause while giving orders, so targeting is a big fat ol' pain. Essentially, when you click on an enemy to attack, there's a chance the enemy's idle animation just leaned back and roared, making the game think you want to move to the spot of ground right where their head used to be. Even taking off my shoes won't help me count the number of times my character wasted an entire turn running across the arena to stand next to the enemy I just told her to shoot. Plus, there is no way to pause or cancel orders, so bye-bye turn, and good luck standing right next to that massive flaming demon, ranger. Literally the entire game, I was on edge about pixel-perfect mouse positioning and idle animations when I attacked.
Plus, getting the mouse cursor to recognize enemies is not the easiest thing to begin with. If a small enemy is standing behind a larger one (according to the camera), they can literally be impossible to target, even if the character you're controlling could reach out and slap them. I was BEGGING for free camera rotation (it only swivels maybe 30° currently) and a dedicated pause button.
My final issue (and the big one) about the combat system is that it straight-up lies. For example, Madora will be standing right next to an enemy, and to attack him, she requires 4 AP (action points). In reality, though, once you click to attack, Madora BACKS UP, giving the enemy an attack of opportunity (despite never leaving melee range), and costing an extra movement AP. Your turn plan is now screwed up, and you're injured. Sometimes those little details are signalled to you beforehand (it shows movement and attacks of opportunity), but sometimes they are not. Plus, it's not unheard of for skills that cost 6 AP, for example, to show you on the hot bar that they're only really going to cost 4 AP (they really do cost 6), so pay attention. Let's also not forget that the game often incorrectly calculates how many AP you will need to use. I noticed this a lot towards the end of the game. My dagger girl's attack cost 2 AP, but sometimes when I'd be standing right next to an enemy, it would say 3 AP required. When I attack, only 2 AP are used (as should be the case), but then it again says my next attack will cost 3 AP while it really costs 2. Repeat until you only have 2 AP, when the game will hold up its hands and stop you. Nevermind that you should only be using 2 AP and ARE using only 2 AP each time you've stood in that exact spot and attacked that exact enemy that exact turn, if the game thinks you need 3, you're done.
There are a bunch more problems with the combat system, but to sum up, it can't be trusted, and it is the undeniable weak point in the entire game. I would have very few complaints if they fixed it.
Other than those issues, the game is pretty great. It has 70+ hours of content, enough exploration/quests to keep you busy the whole time, full campaign co-op, multiple companions you can bring (Madora and Jafar were my 2), a whole slew of attributes/skills/perks to build your unique character with, and just about anything else you would expect from an isometric RPG. It's a fantastic example of how isometric cRPGs can be brought forward into the future.

Cons:

- Multiplayer could be improved a lot:
++ Players use too many overpowered cards (There are some restrictions, but funny enough raigeki is allowed)
++ Small player base
++ No punishment on forfeiting (and no win for the remainer either)
++ Your rank is based on the amount of wins only. Why not also record losses and introduce a rating system?
++ Add an option to fight without xyz, synchro and pendulum
++ Lobby system: Why not just add a queue that automatically finds you an opponent and sets up a duel for you? Saves waiting in a lobby with afk players.
- DLCs: Seem too expensive to buy them all

If you think of World of Warcraft when you hear the word "MMO," then prepare for a paradigm shift. Black Desert Online is an MMO where you can truly do and be anything. You can focus on combat if you like (the combat system, by the way, is fluid and extremely rewarding), or you can settle down and start a farm. Or build a boat and sail the seas. Or start a trade network and make millions. Or... well, you get the idea.
Despite its wide variety of playstyles, this game is not shallow; in fact, its width is only matched by its incredible depth. I'm not exaggerating when I say that I spent more of my first fifty hours reading the game's wiki than actually playing the game: you're offered so many choices that you'll need to do some serious reading just to get a basic idea of what you're doing.
It doesn't help that BDO offers little by the way of a tutorial (to be fair, a comprehensive tutorial would take days to get through) --after teaching you how to walk, look around, and equip items, the game tosses you into its vast world with a handful of silver and leaves you to fend for yourself. The learning curve is incredibly steep, and the game doesn't hold your hand. It's up to you to do your research and figure things out for yourself.
Altogether, BDO is a beautiful game with an incredible amount of depth and freedom. It's not for everyone, but for only $10, it's definitely worth a try. If you're bored with typical MMO's, I'd recommend this one in a heartbeat: it's a breath of fresh air.

When I found this game on Steam I cried with joy a lil' bit on the inside. WARNING: THIS REVIEW MAY BE A BIT NOSTALGAIC!!
Let me start by saying in my opinion, this is the greatest Star Wars game I have ever played. I first started playing this game on the Ps2 way back when, and I can remember the day it came out.
Star Wars: Battlefront 2 is a great classic TPS/FPS style of game. In modern days and tech, the graphics are easily outdated and noticeably so. Now don't get me wrong this game still looks good, but in a "Pre-2004" type of way. SW:BF2 has many, many maps to try out, some being Clone Wars only (Republic vs. Droids [I can't remember the name of them for the life of me]) or Rebellion only (Rebel Army vs. Galactic Empire) and some being playable by all factions. With every map comes multiple (some more than others) gamemodes that are all very fun.
SW:BF2 also introduced it's greatest asset: Space Battles. My favourite part of the game, Space Battles can also be played with all factions, as well as grant access to each faction specific ship the main objective of space battles is to get 180 points during the battle. This can be attained by doing a multitude of things. You can get these points by killing roughly 130-ish ships, depending on which ones you kill, playing as the "Marine" class and flying over to the enemy's main ship and blowing up they're main parts, or buy using whatever ship you've chosen to blow up the outer parts of the enemy's main ship. It is great fun and where I've spent most of my time playing this game.
Back on the ground, you have the choise to either play in a TPS (Third Person Shooter) or an FPS (First Person Shooter) mode of playing. With 6 different classes for each faction, (2 of which must be unlocked during gameplay by achieving points, with the additional 7th "Hero" being unlocked the same way.[usually a jedi]) allows for experimentation on each class to explore the diverse ways to play them. For instance a Sniper is better on larger maps as it is better to hide and shoot from a long distance, and Pilots are better on maps that are meant to be played using a lot of Siege Vehicles. All the faction's respective ground vehicles are all well balanced, and not too difficult to take down.

I'm writing this review after 50+hrs of playtime and finishing the main game incl. all side-quests on hard (15-20 of those went to ♥♥♥♥ing around in multiplayer).
Pros:
+Amazing graphics
+Great performance (especially for a console port)
+Open world
+Long and fun campaign
+Even more fun in co-op
+Skilltrees and leveling-system
+Tons of stuff you can get distracted by while questing ;)
+Dailies once you're done with the main story
+Many eastereggs and hidden areas / blueprints
Con:
-Melee combat feels pretty random. Until lategame even the average biter can kill you since "headshots" are more luck than skill.
-Coming from console this game is not a great shooter. Don't expect challenging firefights or great hitboxes.
-Clunky and sometimes annoying controls
-The UI needs some PC love and is very annoying to handle since it was obviously created to work with the capabilities of controllers.
-Very small default FOV to achieve the above mentioned performance. If your PC is able to handle it set it to +10
-Spawnpatterns of zombies are kinda weird sometimes if you want / have to loot a certain spot. Many times it took me 20mins to clear a small area around a car or crate because virals kept spawning in groups of 5 along with the normal biters.
PS: This game is fun in parties but it turns into a real horror setting once you play it alone. Especially the interior levels in the second district. For the full experience I recommend this game to played in both modes.
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Update
After another 60hrs of playing, finishing the Bozak Horde DLC and The Following incl. all side quests I still recommend the game although it leaves the bitter taste of a sloppy console port. The Cons I listed above still persist throughout add-on. Also there is no lategame, no real challenge. Once you're done with the game all you can do is reset the story line. Traveling between the add-on and the main game sectors is not possible.

I have  a hard time to give GoT the Telltale game a clear yes or no. But overall, the No impressions felt stronger to me than the positive one.
The game is clearly playing like 6 GoT TV episodes. Many of the protagonists die and the world of Westeros is a ♥♥♥♥ed up and grim place. So overall, if you enjoy the TV series, you may likely enjoy the story of the game. It is dense, good storytelling, and you actually experience Westeros for yourself. Kinda.
But here comes the deal. I played other similar games, like "Life is Strange", and the one thing that also hinders the game is the fact that it is based on a TV series. Especially because Telltale made IMVPO a grave mistake by involving major TV characters as vital characters in the game. If they were just cameo characters, it would not matter so much. But if you face Ramsay Bolton, it is like having an adversary playing in God Mode cheat. You know as someone who watched the TV series, you simply can't harm him. Those TV characters are like Gods, because for the same of the TV series they have to remain untouched and unharmed. You if you have anyone of them before you, you know you will pick the short end of the straw, no matter what. And it takes quite a bit of the uncertainty of a story-driven game, since you know what sort of character Ramsay or Cersei are.
Second, whereas in "Life is Strange" I had the feeling to have choice and impact, in GoT I had the feeling my decisions matters not at all. Whether I was friendly or hostile, helpful or aggressive - the outcome was always the same. I felt I could not influence or change the story at all, like I was on rails and the disaster was destined to happen no matter what. It does really feel bad, when you take lead of a character in a situation where your character is railroaded to die, no matter what you do, and what YOU think you would do, is not possible for the story-line. The deicisions I had in "Life is strange", made sense, because it was a modern setting and you acted reasonably within that setting. However, here, I often thought "I would have done something completely different". Only you can't. I felt artificially restricted into decisions and actions that were far from anything I would do.
GoT just makes for a very bad world to put a story-driven Telltale sort of game in.
Finally. The gore. I know GoT the TV series is gory at times. But I realized it is one thing to passively watch gore in TV, and being actively in a game where gore, torture and mutilation happens. I endure it in the TV series, but as part of a game, where I usually identify myself with the characters I lead, it is was just a few levels too much, and IMO unnecessary. In video games where you lead your characters, the feeling to be "inside" just put a psychological pressure on me, I found no longer "entertaining". They should not have showed everything in such detail in a video game.
Bottom line: as interesting as the story was, I felt too less playing a game, and way too much watching a film where my choices didn't really have any impact. And for a game, that is too less.

Heavily influenced in its design philosophy by Tetsuya Mizoguchi’s magnum opus
,
is a love letter to abstract japanese shmups such as Kenta Chao’s cult classic
or Taito’s contemporary classics like
or
.
And do you remember
? In this game from japanese studio Opus, the premise was to doing a postmodernist retelling of a classic JRPG structure by synthesising all its mechanics in 30 frenzy seconds.
does something similar with the shooting genre. Each one of its 10 main levels is played individually with separate leaderboards. And each level is designed based on the structure of a musical track, transforming incorporeal sounds in fascinating musical allegories that talks about the overuse of drugs and the mysticism found in
’s neon glow corridors.
With the duration of each track running in the 3 to 10 minutes range,
does a magnificent work condensing in such a limited time frame the refulgent 0rgasm sensation of doing an entire 50 minutes loop in your all-time favorite shmup. Each song has a very different taste and feeling based on the pulsing tempo of its BPM. Sometimes, playing
is an experience similar to enjoy the classic approach of a
derived shmup full of charisma and cheerful love like
. And in other occasions, it’s more close to play a Bullet Terror Hell Madness that occurs inside Michael Haneke’s perverted mind.
The key to express why
is an instant classic and one of the better shmups conceived in the last decade is the term Destruction. For years, the shooting games have been obsessed with the idea of putting more an more bullets on screen. In the mid-‘90s, this increase of the number of bullets on screen had a sense. It was a manner of breaking the technical limitations of its time period, pushing the hardware to make captivating and almost impossible dreams of the past come true. But with this race to increase the number of bullets on screen, comes a problem. In the last years a lot of shmups have focused its experience in the immaterial act of dodging bullets, rather than in the physical and sensitive pleasure of spreading the Chaos and Destruction causing a lot of things to explode.
is able to put put dozen of billion of bullets at the same time on screen. But it never lost its focus from the infinite pleasure of Destruction. And even its smart scoring system is centered around the idea of Total Destruction. Every single ship destroyed makes more an more powerful our main weapon. And we have an even more destructive secondary laser weapon that can trespass small bullets, clearing the screen of enemy fire. Because
is conscious that making a billion of things explode at the same time in an utopian chain while it burns our retinas with abrasive flashing lights, is much more fun that simply see some solitary bullets floating in the vastness and solitude of space.
After decades of playing every single shmup classic, I can say that none other game has been able to equal the frantic sense of intensity and absolute level of Destruction found in
. And the proverbial idea of making of each track a full playthrough, highlights this captivating-senses joyful destructive feeling, fusing Eros and Psyche in a dazzling and cosmological 0rgasm. Condensing in 5 minutes runs the sense of realization of be able to complete an entire shmup classic. Distilling only the most intense and significative parts. And showing in every second the reasons we play videoagmes. The reasons we love videogames.
And the random nature of each level and its adaptive level of difficulty, makes of each playthrough a completely new experience. Every time that you play
, you have this magic sensation of going to your favorite arcade in the 90s, seeing that a new shmup cabinet from Toaplan has arrived. This incomparable feeling of experimenting for the first time a completely new universe full of flashing lights and captivating electronic tracks. That comes packed with masterful bullet patterns and a perfect crafted scoring system.
is the most accomplished occidental shmup to date. That feels like one hundred of forgotten japanese classics in the same game.

The game is deep and will provide hours of gameplay.    The game and world can be a little overwhelming for entry players like me but I am giving it my best shot.
What I like:
The character creation is awesome.   You can use a preset class or customize something you want to play.
The world is huge with lots of interesting places to explore and I like the way you have to investigate and move items to find what you want or secrets.   It's not always going to be obvious what you have to do to find what you are looking for.
Crafting is interesting and open.   Like everything in the game the components are not just handed to you.
Anything in the world could mean something in the game.   You run by a little mound on the ground... you might want to take a second look.   NPC wondering around the market... say hi and check out the trade.
What I don't like:
The music and voice acting is sometimes cheesy and distracting.   It's hard to get into the role playing part of the game with music that sounds like the theme from Eddy Murphy's 48 hrs movie.
Voice acting is sometimes distracting at times,  example paraphase:  "remember when the captain stoled the queens carriage to go joy riding",  "joy riding".. really?
Sneaking is kind of silly.  You turn into a big bush or rock.   Again,  it's distracting to me and takes the role playing fun out of it.
Lots and Lots and Lots of reading.
Overall,  It's a fun game.

I would prefer not to rate this game but I have to, so I picked  'not recommend' because the game is overpriced and IMO overrated.  In short, the game has excellent visuals and great sound, however, its main elements – story and tactical combat – are mediocre.  Buy it if you really like the art and music and especially if you get it cheap.
The longer version. The story is entirely linear. This is not a problem: “railroad” approach presents an excellent opportunity to write a deep and engaging tale because the writer knows exactly how the events in the game proceed. Think of Banner Saga recast as the journey of the fellowship of the ring. OK that may be a too tall order. :) Anyway, the opportunity is wasted in Banner Saga: the background/lore is promising but the overall story is quite bland (with many clichés) and is depressing for no good reason. The story tries to be harsh/realistic and epic but often feels over the top. Writing in dialogues is good and “cut scenes” are excellent thanks to great art. Dialogue choices are also fine in general. However, too many of them are simply smoke and mirrors, that is you get basically the same response regardless of your “choice”. More annoyingly, you often are not given enough information to make a meaningful choice. The results of such “choices” feel arbitrary, occasionally also punishing like whims of a bad GM in PnP RPG.
The combat is pretty standard for tactical turn-based games but it has some unique elements. The elements do not make the combat great but different. They allow some novel tactics but also make combat gamey, which in turn undermines the story. Moreover, the combats are repetitive affairs because the battlefields are featureless, there is not sufficient diversity of enemies and you do not have enough information of the skirmish when selecting your party, which means that you tend to pick the same “safe” combination of heroes.
Finally, note that you cannot effectively plan ahead in this game. For instance, you have almost no idea how long next phase of a journey lasts and therefore you do not know how many supplies you need. As another example, you may invest a great deal of resources into a combat effectiveness of a character only to lose that character because of a story event. However, I did not feel that the game was too harsh on normal difficulty: my party never starved and I always had enough strong heroes. In other words, do not expect a survival game because Banner Saga is not one.

Please do not think of Ace of Spades, Minecraft, or Team Fortress coming in to this, treat it as it's own game, because it is. All gameplay elements are well balanced, and tie together incredibly well. In the context of pure gameplay, there is little you can say against it. It is the best game I've ever played, and that likely won't change for a long time, I'm certainly a candidate for being the #1 fan.
Currently the biggest problem is the playerbase. It is quite low, and slowly diminishing. I'm sure the developers will be looking at ways to pick this back up. If you'd use a USA, or UK server, you shall be okay, but otherwise I'd suggest not purchasing the game. Queues may take a little longer than other games due to the low playerbase. However, if you're in a long queue, please do not leave, it creates a perpetuating issue that is only solved by players being patient.
The game handles high ping as well as it can with client side hit detection, however it heavily affects other elements of the game. Anything above ~150 and you likely won't enjoy the game to it's full extent.
The community has a whole is a pretty positive one. There will of course be those who aren't, but they are a minority. Please try to encourage this trend if you play. You can also find many discussions on the forum to openly speak about the game with other players.
If you find yourself being beaten by experienced teams constantly, please do not give up the game. Instead, try and improve, or wait before queuing to try fight another team. It is a problem, but one that is not currently solved. Just try enjoy the game regardless.
The game is essentially free of any game ruining bugs. There is quite a lot of bugs, however you will experience almost none of them during regular gameplay and they have little to no effect. These bugs will be fixed eventually. Do not consider this an issue.
Cheaters/Hackers are not an issue. You'll see the occasional one, however they'll be banned, and the game is VAC enabled. Don't expect them to ruin your overall gameplay experience.
The development team historically was quite responsive to players, however this has lately diminished, but this shouldn't deter you from the game. They also do regular live streams on Twtich and Hitbox.
You should try out the demo that is available, it lasts forever, and gives you three characters to play. All characters are balanced, and the game is not pay to win in anyway. You can fully enjoy the demo, though I encourage you to purchase the game if you enjoy it.

The strong characters, the felling that when it may seem you have everything going in order it all turns against you and the moments two characters just get along or clash intensely make the game.
The only major thing I would say negatively, would be that some choices seem to just be place holders, they don't really change much if any at all. Overall I find it to be a great game and truly enjoyable, worth the money you throw at it.

==========
In the first thirty minutes of Saints Row IV, you’ll shoot your way through a military base before disarming a nuclear bomb in flight, which wins the hearts of the nation and the presidency of the United States. You’ll sign off on a cure for cancer or end world hunger, and fend off an alien attack with a turret gun on the White House lawn. It’s immediately clear that Saints Row has finally abandoned any of the pretense at gritty underworld realism that was so at odds with the slapstick of previous games in the series. This is the game that finally provides an appropriate thematic context for Saints Row’s mechanics, one that sees the Steelport Saints emerge from Grand Theft Auto’s shadow once and for all.
==========
In Saints Row IV, you once again take on the role of the leader of the Saints, a now globally recognised gang. The good times don’t last long though, as humanity’s worst fears are realised when an evil alien race known as the Zin invades Earth. You and the other members of the Saints are held hostage in a simulated version of Steelport. With the help of your hacker friends Kinzie and Matt, and combat backup from the rest of the crew - including Vice President Keith David - you must disrupt the system enough to break free and hopefully save the human race.
The game plays much the same as Saints Row: The Third. You control a customizable Boss of the Saints through a variety of missions and tasks in the simulation in an attempt to disrupt it and do some damage, enough to save your crew and escape. Ultimately culminating with a final showdown against the Emperor of the Zin Empire, you will meet some new faces along the way and even some from past games in the series (Sorry, not spoiling it for you)!
The main features of Saints Row IV are the superpowers. As you progress the story, you'll unlock several overpowered abilities that are designed to help you in your quest to dominate the simulation. Super Sprint allows you to travel faster than any car ever could, and combined with Super Jump you can clear multiple city blocks in a matter of seconds. You have a limited stamina bar, but it isn’t long before it becomes irrelevant. At that point you can leap around to your heart’s content. You also get access to telekinesis, elemental energy blasts, and even a Super Stomp which, when fully upgraded, hits with the power of a nuke, clearing an entire block! These powers are a fresh new addition that can be used for even more zany antics around the Steelport simulation.
Your menu is where you'll be spending your hard earned cash (cache) and clusters to upgrade your abilities and superpowers. Honestly, you will spend several hours just jumping around the simulation collecting these clusters. Since the platforming is so good, it almost becomes a compulsion to head straight towards a cluster when you see it.
The main story is where Saints Row IV shines. The writing is superb, although you will definitely want to have played at least some of Saints Row: The Third to appreciate a lot of the jokes. The game is filled with laugh out loud moments, not only from the dialogue, but even just from the missions you find yourself taking on. Each of your crew members has their own loyalty mission, which grants them superpowers of their own upon completion. These are the big side missions that are worth doing, while other quests in the game aren’t really necessary unless you’re going for all of the achievement. The main missions alone will take you a decent amount of time, perhaps around 10-15 hours, and to complete everything in the game will take up to around 20-25 hours, especially if you want to get Gold rating in all challenges.
The Matrix came out 16 years ago, and only semi-recently did I even get to see all of the films. It’s getting to the stage that movies get to when you hear your friends saying “What do you mean you’ve never seen The Matrix!?”, and then say to themselves “...oh I’m getting old”. However, as one of the most important films in its genre, you can forgive Saints Row IV for making quite so many references to it, which after finally watching the films myself stood out like a sore thumb.  Everything from “finding an exit”, down to diving into the very bodies of enemies and destroying them from within gets a mention. Heck, the whole simulation idea is straight out of the Matrix.
The combat still holds up well too. In addition to all the well-known weaponry from the previous game, you have access to all kinds of new flashy alien tech. The Dubstep Gun, The Singularity Gun and the Inflato-Ray are some of the most amusing, and most satisfying things to use in any recent video game. Mayhem missions return, where you cause as much damage as possible in the time allotted. Insurance Fraud has you literally playing in traffic to generate money. Instead of car racing, you will be racing using your super jump and super sprint. You can hack shops in a minigame which is a slightly altered and more infuriating version of Pipeline. These side activities provide a distraction from the main quest line, but none of them are particularly worth spending too much time on unless you are a completionist.
==========
Although it is a simulation, you will be familiar with Steelport if you played the previous game. The landscape is much the same, with most of the old locations in the same place. It is noticeably different though, with a liberal scattering of alien hardware, and a lack of sky and water.
I had mixed feelings on the way the game looks. I wasn’t a big fan of the dark and gloomy visuals of the simulation, but they eventually grew on me. The way every texture shimmers every now and then as the simulation occasionally slows up is actually pretty cool.
Overall the game looks very nice. Some of the billboards and signs scattered thoughout are surprisingly detailed, not to mention hilarious. The cars still look as great as ever, and you can still customize them any way you choose. Though with access to the superpowers, you will probably not being using any vehicles as your main mode of transportation.
==========
Boasting a massive soundtrack featuring over 100 different tracks, Saints Row IV has your musical needs covered as you drive your stolen vehicles around the Steelport simulation. You can find a full list online easily. There's something for everyone, as the soundtrack covers some very broad tastes in music, even classical.
==========
For me the game hovered around 40-50FPS even when it seemed like the entire screen was exploding, or when I was running at hundreds of miles per hour through city streets leaving a trail of destruction in my wake. The only time it occasionally hitched was during an autosave, but it was barely noticeable. I didn't have any other issues at all. The game has full controller support, and can be enjoyed using a controller or mouse/keyboard. It's easy to play using either one.
==========
Overall Saints Row IV is a marvellously enjoyable game, while still suffering from a few of the complaints that the series has always had. The main quests are great, and although the side missions are not painful to play, they don’t quite pack the same punch. If you played and enjoyed Saints Row The Third, then picking up this sequel is a must. Equally if you’re looking for a game that lets you run around as a badass with special powers.

Everlasting Summer is a brilliant game. Well and truly fantastic. The game is itself a Visual Novel, absolutley as Visual Novel as you can get it, with CGs and waifus and many choices to make, so don't expect riveting gameplay. Rather expect your enjoyment to come out of it's rather fascinating story. The game revolves around Semyon, a 25 year old man living in circa 21st centuar Russia, a man who is somewhat of a sociatal recluse. After boarding a bus to a school reunion and falling asleep on it, he awakens to the sight of a soviet era pioneer camp, filled with a wide array of colourful characters. It's here that the story picks up, and you're led through a week of choices and interactions with the cast as you try to live a relatively normal life as a now teenage Semyon whilst also trying to figure out what the hell has just happened and why it's just happened.
See, this is where Everlasting Summer strives in, this underlying feeling of almost dread from the mystery presented to you, something only even further unnerved as the fellow pioneers give you very vague answers as to exactly where you are, giving the camp an almost limbo esque vibe. It doesn't help that the pioneers around you all act so normal, making you and the entire situation an abnormality. Sadly, this games strongest point, the fridge horror based aspect of the story is also partially it's downfall. For whilst it is a thrilling mystery to solve, it's also one that you largely have to do yourself. There are 6 base endings you have to get in order to unlock what is considered the true ending, and despite how much of a true bore it can be persueing each route (par one which differs drastically from the rest), it is entirely nessecary to experience each one to get the big picture, as each route offers it's own little tidbit of information on the mystery at hand.
However, even after going through each ending, you're still left with a bit of a headscratcher. As I said, Everlasting Summer is not the kind of game to just pass on the answers to you, infact it won't even tell you the answers, more so it's like throwing clues at you and seeing you struggle to come to a conclusion that you don't even know is right. Despite this, Everlasting Summer is a fantastic game, and was fun to play. I found the charactes engaging, the route interesting to go thorugh and see the eventual conclusions, piecing together a solution to the mystery, particularly coming up with my own theories about the plot of the game and the mysterious Cat Girl that appears on the menus and is hinted at, but never becomes present. I found Semyon's own route to really give the most insight into the situation.
The sound is also fantastic, the music composed by one Sergey Eybog is a treat to listen to, with each piece really helping to set the general atmosphere of the scene, helping the player to further experience what Semyon's experiencing, to put you into his perspective and to empaphise with him. A game that can make you truly understand the fears and frustrations of the main character is one that deserves praise. The visuals are also rather nice, though the quality of the characters portraits and the CGs does fluctuate quite a bit. There are also lewd scenes that, whilst censored, can be patched out, though this adds nor takes anything from the story, they are just there if that's your kind of thing.
At the end of the day, Everlasting Summer is a true visual novel. Little to no gameplay, waifus galore, and eroge scenes to spare. Despite these though, despite it's initial presentation, Everlasting Summer is a truly fantastic game worth your time, even without putting the many hours into achieving the true ending, just one or two goes is worth your time, for despite the lack of gameplay and action, it makes up for it in spades with marvelous characters and a well written storyline.

It pains me to say this seeing as how I was one of the main people to put effort into making this game better (I wrote the Project Elpis expansion for this game), but it's dead. It's not the lack of updates for the bugs in the game (there are still a few, but nothing game breaking) that killed it. No. No one plays the game anymore because while it's fun to shoot things in space and such, the developer drove the last nail in the coffin for it by REMOVING LAN PLAY FROM THE GAME.
Yeah, it's a 4 year old game. Perhaps it shouldn't be supported anymore. But placing something critical for the game (LAN play is the best way to play this) and letting your licence expire for this part of the game after you took peoples money is just not something I can support anymore.
Yeah, various EA games turn off their servers after 4 years or so and that sucks as well. But Carmine is NOT EA. Well, perhaps he is now.
To be fair, Carmine says the 3rd party is the one to blame, but a solution exists. Release the version of the software that has a non-expiring licence like he provided me. So he is able to solve this dilemma.
So overall, this game is crippled and can only be played online now. I, for one, will not be tricked again by Mr. Guida again.
EDIT  (July 24, 2017):
So Mr. Guida states that there is no way to get the 3rd party server running and the CEO of the company Photon (which provides the LAN and Cloud services) is saying wouldn't renew his license due to the company no longer offering that option.
Why then are they still selling (and offering a free on-site server for 100 connections free) the service then?
I signed up and wanted to test it out to make sure that I could download it.
I can not get the server to activate with this because I lack the App ID within the licence and such. But Mr. Guida can download the free licence that is unlimited and provide that file in a new server program and give it out. The only way he may not be able to is if Photon decided that his game is no longer allowed on the service.
When Mr. Guida states that the company is no longer supporting the server program for stand-alone, he is simply being lied to by the people at the company or he is being disingenuous. I will leave it up to the players here to decide, but there is a solution for getting back LAN to this game at the time of me writing this.
I will keep editing this review if things change since Mr. Guida has decided to block me from not only the forums here, but also the facebook page and the reddit page. He is, of course, allowed to do this as it's his platform. However, I feel this information needs to be given to players who bought a LAN game and now are not able to play it in LAN form.

For fans of the critically acclaimed Company of Heroes, comes COH2. It's essentially a standalone expansion pack, not adding anything incredibly new to the IP. Some of the changes actually take away from gameplay and leave the game feeling lacking. The cover mechanic which made COH1 so great returns, but with less benefits in COH2. The blizzard mechanic is a cool... addition, but after seeing it once, you wish you could turn it off; it interferes with the pace of gameplay and punishes players that are already losing. The commander abilities seem watered down and do little to make you feel as if you are controlling a special regiment of an army. Day 1 DLC is also extremely shameful and makes the game feel like a cash grab, at 1.99 for a re-skin of either a light, medium OR heavy set of units (infantry not included) for a total of 6$ for the entire set..of paint. Well... where do I begin? I never had the privilege of discovering the old XCOM games during my childhood, in fact XCOM was the FIRST turn based strategy game I have ever played, so initially the format was a little weird for me, but the game was so intriguing, so well made. XCOM: ENEMY UNKNOWN is about an alien invasion of Earth, you play as the commander of a secret military organisation called XCOM. The first mission which doubles as a training mission shows you all you need to know to get started... it’s not draining and it’s not under informed.
In an actual mission you take control of 4 soldiers (which later can be 6) and each soldier has two action points per turn... you can run a small amount and then shoot, hunker down or even provide an overwatch so if an enemy moves, that soldier will automatically take pot shots at it. Or you can dash/sprint a longer distance which takes up two turns. Once all the soldiers have had a turn it’s the aliens turn to manoeuvre its troops. The goal of each mission is basically wipe out all the aliens but you have different scenarios... there are bomb disarm missions, alien abduction missions and missions where they slaughter humans and you got to save as many as you can...
But that’s not the beauty of the game... the fun part also lies at the end of each mission... you return to your base which looks kind of like an ant farm that’s been cut in half (as your base is underground) after you complete a mission, all the dead alien bodies, weapons and metals etc are taken to your base.... you can build satellite uplink facilities, foundries for weapon/tech upgrades, engineering facilities to build satellites, weapons, armour and jets, there are research facilities you can build to study the dead aliens and their tech in order to build yourself better weapons...
The game also has a funding system... whenever you build a satellite and place it above a country, you get a certain amount of funding for that country... the satellite detects UFOs in which you have to send your jets up and try and shoot it down... when you successfully shoot it down, you send a team to the UFO crash site where you engage in a mission to kill all the ETs and upon completion, whatever you haven’t destroyed in the alien craft will prove useful in your research and development... alien power sources, navigation systems, food stations, medical facilities etc etc
You can also develop weaponry for fighter jets and even create better ones later, and have them stored in certain areas so if a satellite detects a UFO in South America, you can only attack it if you have an interceptor jet in south america..
You also have a ‘grey market’ where if you are desperate for funding, you can sell alien tech on the black market... you can even sell damaged alien tech that you don’t actually need for a fraction of the price... Occasionally a country will request certain goods and if you have it, you can hand it over in exchange for extra cash, scientists or engineers... Now if you fail to protect a country and their panic level goes in the red... they will pull out of the XCOM project and you can lose funding or potential funding (if there’s no satellite operational over that particular country)
You can customise your soldiers, change their load out, upgrade their abilities and what not... the more kills they get, the more they get higher in rank and become better priceless soldiers. This game is PERMADEATH so you will occasionally need to recruit more soldiers and place some recruits into  missions with other experienced troops, so you can level them up and gain XP, as you wouldn’t wanna face the later missions with new recruits...
There are MANY different alien species, some extraordinarily weak, some ridiculously OP, you have got to plan your attack accordingly, don’t get too cocky and be prepared for ambushes...
This game is a simple game with a not so simple play style and is a great challenge... I recommend playing this on easy first... because after a few missions... it starts biting back really hard... Don’t underestimate the damn Chrysallids, mutons in large numbers and of course... the sectopod.
I could seriously go on and on but there is just too much to cover...
Graphics are fantastic, very sci-fi and pretty to look at and nice use of colours
Sound is exceptionally good... especially on loud stereo headphones
Gameplay is brilliant as it sticks to the table top format... just because you can see the enemy doesn’t mean you can hit it... it goes by 'chance in %' and 'critical damage chance in %'
Can be frustrating sometimes where your troops will miss ridiculously easy shots, but it all comes down to their will, whether or not they are panicked or supressed... but every now and then it’s just a bug!
SAVE OFTEN > I like to save at the beginning of missions just in case one or more of my favourite soldiers get smashed...
Seriously though.... this game is a 9.5 out of 10
Highly recommended for fans of UFOs, Aliens, Sci-Fi, Military tactics, Turn-based RTS and Strategy
Other similar games would be ‘The Banner Saga’ and maybe ‘Breach and Clear’
Word of advice... don’t rush through the storyline... take your time and research as much as you can, get those satellites up as they bring you extra funding per month... keep upgrading the soldiers with new gear and weaponry... Ideally... you should have ALL satellites (at the least 75%) up before you even take on the alien base that requires the key...

Ok, seeing that this visual novel has got something like 30.000 reviews only on Steam (they make up more than my town's population as per the 2015 census and that's quite amazing) I don't really think I can add something interesting or particular..
Here it's not just an acknowledgement of my complete mediocre, second-rate and useless abilities to write (in general), but just.. statistically speaking, in 30.000 reviews everything must have already been said about this awesome free to play visual novel.
There are like.. more than 200 guides. It's crazy.
And I really don't know what to say.
Graphics are great, in my opinion the characters have been rendered in an amazing way and in general all the artwork is greatly done.
The game features lots of different choices and lots of endings too, it took me literally hours to find all the possible endings with every girl - you sort of "open a chapter" for a particular girl thanks to your choices during the dialogues and you'll follow that road until the bad or the good ending, hopefully.
The visual novel takes you into the mind of a depressed boy who finds himself on a journey to the past, in a wide camp (with beaches and many other things XD) in which the game takes place and it's full of beautiful girls - as the title says, in the area you'll play your role in, it's always summer :)
As Semyon, your task will be that of waking up from the cold, snowy everyday life and explore every possibility that the game offers you, of course revolving around love themes but also horror and thoughtful ones.
I find myself a little bit puzzled about this game and the audience it has obtained - it's one of the most beautiful visual novels you can find on Steam, of course, but really.. it seems that everyone played it, literally! :)
Anyways, it's a good choice and not only for the free price but also, as I said, for its solidity and its high standard of quality that stays great through all the different routes, since it seems that everything has really been polished and studied; I found myself often surprised by the routes and the endings and there are virtually no errors and no things to adjust - maybe, if we had to find a little thing, they could have added more expressions and more graphics for what concerns the protagonists - the girls, I mean - but it's really ok as it is.
Every route has lots of depth and takes much time if you want to explore and get to know everything and well, it deserves to be read from the beginning to the end.
I'd not call this a masterpiece as I read, between the thousands of reviews I saw here and there some lavish enthusiasm but anyways.. it's an awesome visual novel, and a great game. Regardless of the grade in which you will get involved in the story, which can vary from person to person (I'm a little bit older than the main character unfortunately xD), Everlasting Summer definitely deserves to be played with a thorough and deep approach 'cos ok, it won't be a 10/10 game for everyone, but it has virtually everything that a visual novel can offer and if perfection isn't part of this world, this is still one of the best visual novels I've ever played.
Play it with these feelings and don't be iper-hyped, you'll not get disappointed anyways ^^

I really do get the feeling that Saints Row 4 is pretty much a Saints Row 3 DLC, I really do. The difference is that this is a continued story and somewhat new style of gameplay where the player has "cheats" (superpowers).
The superpowers, to me, are a huge step back as it completely throws out much of the core gameplay from the previous games. In this game, you have the ability to fly, use telekinesis, run super fast, etc. There is no use for any vehicles since they have become obsolete and inefficient; running and flying can get you to or away from the fight much quicker. The physics have gone berzerk (not intentionally) in the game as well with many enemies clipping or glitching all over the place into buildings and cars flying. Guns, for the most part, are the same and do not seem to be overpowering or underpowered. The story is fine but is confusing if you are not on top of the previous games' stories. There is no more "pad" where all your homies stay, it's just you and your friends in a spaceship with no real function.
Aside from that, there are some weird co-op bugs that are incredibly annoying.
The game has the comedy but not the best parts of the previous game.

This game is an odd mashup of things like Tekken, Super Smash Bros, Pong, and a bit of Dragonball Z mixed in for good measure.  If you get a couple of friends and all play together, this game is one of the best times you'll collectively have.  I haven't played in the open multiplayer so I can't vouch for the online community, but playing against friends is simply fantastic.  The online multiplayer will occasionally desyncronize when starting a match, but it only takes about 10 seconds to exit the game, restart it, host a new lobby, invite your friends into it, and restart.  The desync error also is not particularly common, certainly less than 10% of matches will have this issue.  Not a serious detraction from the overall game.
There are, however, two things missing: a replay system and a spectator mode.  There are many situations where it would be nice to have a replay so you can answer questions like "How did that shot hit me?" or "That was an awesome move, can I see that again?"  I hope the devs will eventually include some form of replay management.  The inclusion of a spectator mode would make this game viable for some tournaments and casting.  I doubt it'll rival things like LoL or DOTA for popularity, but at some events it would be great to have a Lethal League tournament going on as a side-attraction or something.

Compelling, engaging, and frustrating. After a long and tiring search for a new Tactical RPG to play, I finally settled on the Banner Saga pack during steam summer sale.
I absolutely did not expect what I got for my money. What I expected was a grid and some fighters to push around and maybe some thin story to give me a reason to do it.
What I ended up with was a deeply compelling campaign, thrusting me unprepared into the role of a leader, feeling all the weight of every decision I make. Watching my caravan move through bleak landscape after bleak landscape really pushes the feeling of a long journey grinding away at your fortitude and morale, meanwhile constantly worrying about whether my supplies will hold through the next stretch of our quest. Do I buy supplies and ensure my caravan makes it to their next destination? Do I take the gamble, hoping the next town will sell me supplies at a third of the price?
The combat system plunges much deeper than it would appear at first glance - Preset heroes with preset classes and no way to change them, with no modifications to their skillsets save for improving them based on renown gave me the impression this game was more of a text adventure with shallow battles to push it forward. With every battle, however, the depth of combat revealed itself. Which unit should begin where? In what order should the units move? Do I strike at my foe's armor, or take the opportunity to make a weak attack at their health, in the hopes that it will drain their strength enough to prevent the death of my own allies?
In combat, and out, every decision carries the weight of the immediate future with it. Ask the wrong question, make the wrong choice, trust the wrong group, and lose time, resources, and potentially much worse. No more than every twenty minutes I find myself shaking my head and sighing, trying to weigh my resources and potentially the lives of my allies, or even innocent strangers, against having a few more fighters, or supplies for another day.
TL;DR
10/10 Game with an engaging story forcing impossibly difficult leadership decisions with no right answer, backed up by deeply challenging strategic gameplay, a beautifully ambient soundtrack, wonderful art, and top-notch voice acting. A game to be enjoyed in its entirety, and neither strictly for its combat, or for its story.

I've tried giving this game a chance 2 times now. To me it's just a visualizer software that reacts to the music with merely particle effects. I would have wanted the enemy patterns be spawned in sync with the beat to make the game feel more reactive to your music (Tried different genres: metal, house, techno, ambient). Right now it just feels that the music and gameplay are in completely different layers and that doesn't work for me.
One could argue that there is some spawns reacting to the music but it doesn't feel that way. Often times you get bored and frustated when you start thinking all the things the game could have been. The spawns are too vague and unresponsive. I feel the main intent in design was to analyze the song length, create some sort of an enemy buildup into that timeframe and then spawn enemies with an intensifying interval towards the end. It's not a really elaborate system but a really generalized one.  It doesn't feel reactive to the music or feel particularly interesting.
Here are a few examples that I wanted to see:
*Having the enemy sprites pulse to the beat at times and giving you extra stuff if destroyed in a swollen state.
*Having different enemy types pulse to different beats in the music.
*Having certain archtypes of beat sequences built to the system. For example in house music the rythm, buildup and lead are quite predictable, those could be used as standardized information and made into gameplay events.
*Every hi-hat spawning a small single enemy from a corner starting from top left and ending in bottom right.
*Every bass hit it could spawn a round pattern of small popcorn enemies etc.
Maybe if the core gameplay were more engaging, I would not have cared about enemy beat sync, meaning the lack thereof, that much. Right now I don't feel like it really holds it's own though. It feels there are many enemy archtypes that could be used to make the gameplay more engaging and less predictable.
Also the enemy sprites look clumbsy and lack animation which gives me a somewhat unfinished feeling while playing. They stick out.
To me this game was not enjoyable due to lack of polish and expectations not being met.

Captained a ship with two friends. They took helm and tactical, while I split myself between captain, engineer, and science.

Zurna space. Zurna are heretics, so we kill some of them, and then try to raid one of their transports.
It's not going so well, we end up warping out. The Zurna follow us, until we reach Santoor space.
Some kind of anomaly in space, and Santoor patrolling. I, being the maniacal captain I am, order my helmsman to fly straight into the anomaly.
Nothing happens but the Santoor get angry, and start shooting us for tresspassing on their religious grounds or something. We start wiping them out.
A Zurna fleet warps in for backup, but shortly after, a Davul fleet warps in. They help us in the slaughter, and we survive the battle. Before it's over, Hive start coming, and causing chaos. We escape.
A few jumps later, we go to the Davul home world. Our helmsman seems concerned that we allied with space demons, when we see their spiky space station and lava covered planet-hell.
We ignore our concerns about our new allies and make our way into Santoor space. We kill alot of santoor and Zurna on the way, and fleets start following us. Lots of epic battles.

Scan the station. 99% health after 10 minutes firing at it alone.
Santoor backup arrives, but so does a Davul and Udu fleet. We wipe them out and proceed to attack the station again.
Scanning. 98% health.
We continue sitting in place and firing at the station.
I scan again.
97% health.
We decide there's no way we're destroying it alone. Just as we do, a Santoor and Zurna armada comes in.
10/10, would ally with space demons and start galactic war again.
Afterwards we mess around, fighting eachother in solos, until 6 AM.

I still have the battle music in my head, the soundtrack is really soothing and gorgeous. The visuals are also great. I can't praise the watercolour elements of the art enough.
The main gripes I have with the game is (as others have said) that it seems really rushed.
The last dungeon area goes by super quickly, and then suddenly you are fighting a big boss. Next, it literally takes you from the end cutscene of that fight to the last boss... and then the end cutscene. Which is a voice over talking about action things that WOULD have made an interesting third act to the game, but as it is, there really doesn't feel like there is a third act. Which leaves you feeling a little miffed.
The few 3D models that are in place can be glitchy. (once or twice I went in battle, and Aurora's hair didn't load, so she had this pink buzz cut) I was frustrated by Aurora's movement until she got wings. It was very slow and almost felt like my computer was lagging. Once she gets her wings (pretty early on), the movement improves. It seems to me like they based her movement on her flying, because it looks pretty good. Kind of an underwater fluid movement. That just doesn't work for her walking, running, jumping on land.
Like I said, there doesn't seem to be a third act. The second act starts when you are in the dark tower and defeat the first sister. Then somehow the moon makes you age up instantly?? This is never really explained. You have to draw your own conclusions.
Other things that are not explained: the confessions (notes) you find in the last part of the game are not written in rhyme, and talk of things like the internet, etc... which adds a level of mystery, a kind of alice in wonderland feel of a person being thrown into a fantasy world; but it is never explained further. At all. So it's just kind of jarring. You never find out who this person is. I was pretty positive that I explored every nook and cranny, yet still some confessions and chests eluded me. A little frustrating.
I didn't mind the rhyming too much... it's unique. I do wish it could have been better written. As others have said, a lot of times it comes across extremely clunky. The confessions especially were almost impossible to read. And I like poetry. They were just... a lot of fantasy jargon in rhyming form. There was nothing to them. There were some lines of dialogue though that made me grin. Mostly with Tristus, the sad jester, and Finn.
Overall though, the design (apart from those rock dudes, they were straight up geodudes from pokemon) of the monsters and characters was great. The design of the battle sequences was very inventive and enjoyable too. I liked how you didn't have to have party members involved in the battle for them to gain experience. That was a huge plus. Also, how if you wanted to switch out a party member, it didn't take up a turn, they got to act right away.
So there are definitely a lot of positives about this unique little game! It's all rather a mixed bag. If you have some spare cash, and like easy to play, calming games, then go for it. I'm glad I played it. I just wish the ending's pacing hadn't been so terrible.

Pros: pretty, centered around girls and women, music
Cons: white white white, awful writing, poor pacing
Gorgeous Watercolor Scenery
Child of Light by Ubisoft is the prettiest game I’ve ever played. Every frame of every environment looks like it could be hung in a gallery. Seriously, just look at this:
The environments and backgrounds were simply breathtaking. The artwork and the squid-like hair movement made the game for me.
Girls Girls Girls
Let’s talk about how many women and girls there are throughout the entire game! SO MANY WOMEN AND GIRLS. It starts and ends with girls, which is how it should be. Aurora, the main character. The Lady of the Forest, who is the Queen of Light. Rubella, the first addition to the party. The Capilli leader. Norah, the sister. Magna, the giant. Cordelia, another sister. Gen, an orphan.  Umbra, the queen.
The story’s premise and narrative also reveals a very matrilineal focus as the struggle for the throne involves primarily a feud between two queens, and their daughters are the ones who inherit that pain and burden. The narrator also reveals herself to be a mother and even a queen (perhaps Aurora herself), as the game wraps up with “Soon it will be your turn, princess, to leave on an adventure.”
I do not believe that they make up a majority of the named characters in the game (based on my quick tallying of all the characters I ran into), but I’m honestly just excited that there are this many at all. It’s so refreshing to see a game spotlight young girls for this coming of age story.
Not-Princess in a Tower
Child of Light puts a flip on the typical princess in a tower trope. This time, it’s the dad wasting away in his tower as the princess journeys to save him. He ends up getting “fridged,” or killed off just to move the plot along and provide the main character motivation to exact revenge, a role typically reserved for hot girlfriends or beautiful damsels. It’s refreshing to see this role reversal, if the trope must exist in some form.
Religious Imagery
I get so excited talking about this. Child of Light is just drenched in religious imagery, heavily reminiscent of Christian arts and biblical stories, and it’s beautiful. From the moment Aurora wakes up on the altar, there’s something not just magical but spiritual about the world.
The game opens with a cinematic of long, narrow stained glass windows as the narrator introduces us to the plight of the Austrian dukedom. Already, it’s like we’re walking around a brilliant, illuminated cathedral in the moonlight.
In the image above, the Queen of Light is depicted with her head surrounded by a large sunburst. It’s easily recognized as a parallel to the radiant halos in religious imagery used to indicate holiness. The Queen of Light proves to have power over life itself and various other miracles (granting Aurora flight, for instance). Her title and this halo serve as an early indication that she is more than mortal and holds not only kindness in her heart but also divinity.
All of the story’s major cut scenes, which narrate the plot of the game, similarly feature stained glass cinematics, styled in a way that clearly reflects the stylistic features of the popular storytelling medium found in Christian churches.
The story features resurrection, a flood, and a new beginning in a new world—all significant themes of major events in biblical narratives (the resurrection of Jesus and the Genesis flood).
Yet, unlike actual Christianity, the world and story of Child of Light is entirely centered around women and girls.
Aurora is the savior. She is resurrected—twice.
The wise woman, the Lady of the Forest, is a mother. It’s revealed later that she is actually the Queen of Light, living on after her mortal death. Even though the Queen only shows up in the game a couple of times, her presence is felt throughout it all, through the flute song that Aurora and many others recognize as the Queen’s melody as well as the repeated mention of her memory as a beloved figure and leader among the people.
On the other side, darkness is also represented by a woman and her daughters.
Child of Light brilliantly tells its story in a way that feels so familiar and sacred while at the same time refusing to put any spotlight on men, who traditionally dominate Christian and other religious spaces.
The Not-Magic Flute
I absolutely loved the role of the flute in the game and story.
It’s not magic. You can’t use it as an item in battle. Instead, Aurora uses it when there’s nothing else. It’s a coping skill. Nothing changes, but you feel better, and so do those around you. And that’s important, especially in circumstances of loss, grief, isolation, and chaos. A lot of video games champion a do-it-all strongman hero who just loves saving the world and wins rewards through direct actions against evil. But here, our characters have emotions, feel sad, feel lost, and need help. Yes, they slay dozens of evil creatures and save little villages, one at a time, but it’s hard, and sometimes they make mistakes, and sometimes they don’t know what to do. The flute and its song gives them peace, reminds them of home, and renews their hope.
The music in this whole game is beautiful all around, but the flute song is particularly special and really touching because of the way Aurora uses it to ground herself and practice self care. Coping skills are so crucial to every journey, and I’m so happy it was included in this game in such a significant way.
Okay, lets get into the dirt.
So, this game is far from perfect. Here are my complaints.
♥♥♥♥ You, Robert
Robert is a piece of♥♥♥♥♥♥ honestly, and he never gets put in his place. His story arc is 1000% the overdone trope of “If I just try hard enough, gain enough money and hero status, I’ll get the girl.” Why anyone thought this story belonged in this game that is otherwise about awesome and genuine love for family and community… I have no idea. Margaret, Robert’s love interest, is super awesome and totally tells him off with a sweet “Boy, you don’t know me!” in her first appearance, but, unfortunately, she is forced as a trophy into Robert’s life during the ending round of story arc wrap-ups.
Why do all the royal girls look the same?
I get that they’re sisters, but they’re not blood sisters, and why would you pass up the opportunity to draw and create several unique and individual female characters. It just felt so cookie cutter to me, like “We just have 1 model of a girl and we’re gonna copy paste that for all the girls in this game—maybe change their hair color."
I’m used to seeing this happening in gritty action games, where there are no playable female characters and women are used either as decoration to "set the scene” or as disposable but sexy bodies. So it is weird to see this practice repeated here in this game centered around female characters. And the rest of our party is so diverse in the way they look; I don’t know why they decided not to carry that over to the main character and villains.

You have to respect this game.
I start my review with that line because this game, in its entirety, is brilliant.
First and foremost, this game delivers; it says it's a tactics game, and it's a well and done tactics game. You work on the standard grid/tile based system and work with units that move and attack opponent units with (later on upgradable) weapons. Your soldiers are human, that is to say, they are capable of performing above the call of duty or failing and panicking at crucial moments; they are also mortal, and death for them means another name on the memorial of the fallen. All in all, it feels like you're actually working with people; you're commanding real men and women in combatting the alien threat - for all the good and frustration it brings.
Next is its atmosphere; the way the game is presented and delivered matches the high-tech feel of the scenario, and the crisp graphics and information overlays serve both artistic and actual function. I was enraptured by the game, and as a sci-fi fan, the whole universe and premise just fueled my drive to play the game. Everything only served to heighten your experience and draw you in even more - from the heightened feeling of smug success every time you perfectly accomplish an operation or perform some miraculous hat trick, to the soul crushing horror when things go to hell and everything comes crashing down.
This game is irrevocably difficult. Oh, any casual player would find themselves frustrated but challenged - not so easy to finish the game, but nothing impossible; that kind of mentality. Play it on Classic or higher difficulty, and you start questioning the numbers, and falling back to more surefire tactics to get things done - and there's that niggling feeling that charging in, as fun as it sounds, is a horrible idea. Play it on Ironman and all your mistakes punish you and hurt you more than you think it could, so much so that your pride is taking a blow that this game is spitting in your face.
It's challenging you. Telling you that you can't beat it. And for the life of me, I've sunk how many hours into this game (maybe even double because of unrecorded offline play), but I still keep coming back. I come back to step up to the challenge and immerse myself in such a wonderfully built environment that puts me in control of an uphill battle - a battle that I've lost so many times already, enough to be called a masochist by my peers.
But let me tell you this.
This game may have beaten me,
but I'm going to keep coming back.
And someday, I'm going to 100% this thing.
And win.

Comrades! In this glorious visual novel you can finally find your communist cupid, your soviet sweetheart, the leninist love of your life!
You step into the shoes of a young man who falls asleep in the 21st century only to wake up a  boy in an 80s communist pioneers camp. It's obvious that something's not quite right and you can either spend your time trying to solve the misteries of the summer camp or just relive the joyful days of youth and maybe even find true love.
There are several love interests to choose from, most of them with both a good and a bad ending. The outcome will depend on many decisions you can make during the game. There are always some overlapping events (thank Marx for the skipping-option) but every path you choose offers exclusive artwork and scenes.
Even if you try to keep the protagonist's virginity intact / try to make it back to the real world, the game offers several new scenes that are nothing like the main love-paths. The additional romance even supplies you with a whole new spin on the story.
What this huge paragraph was trying to say is: this game offers so much replay value, so much playtime, that I can't believe this is a fre VN.

I give this a strong recommendation for a free game. For a pay game it would be mixed as it is so unpolished. The story is good and surprisingly subtle as the narrator's own deficiencies drive events and he displays an interesting combination of self awareness and lack of understanding. It can be frustrating because he says things which create problems and the player has no opportunity to influence him, except in a few key decision points.
The artwork is quite charming but it is also a weakness. We see a screen of an empty parade ground and the caption says the parade ground was full of people. Also each character has a maximum of 2-3 different faces, some of which are inappropriate for the accompanying description.
After playing this I tried some other similar games and found them not as good. In particulary, I hadn't realised how good the artwork is for Everlasting Summer. The people are much more real and that really adds to the immersion of the game.
To get through the game requires an enormous amount of clicking to bring up text. One play through took me 6.6 hours and I am a fast reader (that may have included a bit of AFK). To get different endings you can set it to automatically fast forward everything you have already done. That makes it just about worth replaying. But it still takes about an hour to find each new ending which soonfeels like too much effort.
Overall it was good fun and I am glad I played despite the basic quality. It may have felt more personal to me as my partner happens to be a Russian called Lena :)

I really do get the feeling that Saints Row 4 is pretty much a Saints Row 3 DLC, I really do. The difference is that this is a continued story and somewhat new style of gameplay where the player has "cheats" (superpowers).
The superpowers, to me, are a huge step back as it completely throws out much of the core gameplay from the previous games. In this game, you have the ability to fly, use telekinesis, run super fast, etc. There is no use for any vehicles since they have become obsolete and inefficient; running and flying can get you to or away from the fight much quicker. The physics have gone berzerk (not intentionally) in the game as well with many enemies clipping or glitching all over the place into buildings and cars flying. Guns, for the most part, are the same and do not seem to be overpowering or underpowered. The story is fine but is confusing if you are not on top of the previous games' stories. There is no more "pad" where all your homies stay, it's just you and your friends in a spaceship with no real function.
Aside from that, there are some weird co-op bugs that are incredibly annoying.
The game has the comedy but not the best parts of the previous game.

Pros:
+ The background art is nice, I guess
Cons:
- Awful writing
- Shoddy translation
- Low-quality CGs
- Questionably chosen and used soundtrack
Long Review:
To be frank, this game is awful. I'm bewildered by the fact that it has an overwhelmingly positive user rating on Steam. I’ve never read anything so incompetently written. Questionable translation aside, the conversations are barely ever more than a few sentences back and forth before Semyon goes back to brooding, and when longer conversations do occur they have no structural flow, jumping from one topic to the next with zero logical consistency. I’m honestly inclined to believe the author simply can’t write dialogue, since he frequently has Semyon tune out when a longer conversation might occur. This means that many potential longer dialogue sections are skipped, and it also has the side effect of making Semyon seem like a self-absorbed jerk.
The writing isn’t the only issue with the game. While the character sprites are mostly passable, the CGs are atrocious, and look like they collectively were whipped up in an afternoon by a high schooler with one art class under their belt. Additionally, while the individual tracks on the OST are fine, there’s no stylistic coherency; generic VN music is mixed with high energy electric guitar tracks and cheap 90s porn music. The music is also rarely used, and when it is it’s often during scenes which don’t warrant the particular track choice. At least the background art is nice.
If you’re looking for a good visual novel… this isn’t it. Don’t waste your time. There are much better free VNs of this length.
Final score: 2/10
