The 3rd RTS to be released by Petroglyph, Grey Goo is honestly a weird title all matters considered. On one hand, this is the most traditional RTS Petroglyph has released to date. This definitely makes it seem like Grey Goo has fewer defining qualities than its predecessors: Empire at War and Universe at War. At their repsective glances, Empire at War had its Galactic Conquest structure, and Universe at War had a focus on Faction differentation arguably exceeding the likes of Starcraft (Whether it did so successfully is highly up to debate).
Grey Goo has neither of these defining traits- its structure is completely traditional in both its campaign and skirmish gameplay (It doesn't even have a light version of Galactic Conquest like Universe at War tried to), and its factions are nowhere near as differentiated as Universe at War's were.
Now this level of traditionalism is indeed a selling point for many, since outside of Grey Goo (and a few other isolated games like Starcraft 2, arguably Homeworld Remastered, and some indie titles here and there) there aren't really many RTSes coming out that do this structure anymore. So in theory some people will appreciate Grey Goo for that alone.
But in brutal honesty, considering just the purely traditional RTS stuffings within Grey Goo- there are plenty of older RTS titles that fare better. Its not that Grey Goo does anything horribly, its traditional elements are solid overall. But everything it does traditionally has been done better and made more interesting by other RTS titles. Whether it be better optimization, better balance, more interesting traditional faction AI, more varied units, or more interesting campaigns, you're definitely better off with older RTS titles in that regard.
But this isn't really fair to Grey Goo- because that's not considering the few truly unique things it does actually do underneath its traditional surface.
And its all because of how much focus Petroglyph clearly put into the Goo's skirmish AI. Being a completely mobile faction, the Goo are able to use elevation to hide their unit-producing mother goos. The Goo AI knows how to do this. and is NOT predictable when doing it, It won't just leave the Mother Goo on the hill for a random amount of time- it will ACTIVELY wait if you have it surrounded. Or the AI will figure out where the gap in your LOS is and try to use it. Or if you get too close to its hill trying to surround it, the AI might just come down and absorb those units. The Goo's AI feels like some of the most dynamic AI we've gotten in an RTS for quite some time. Its certainly not perfect as it will make questionable movement and attack decisions in plenty of situations- but it remains a joy to play against.
Its just a pity that most everything around the Goo AI is lackluster in comparison. Unlike the Goo's AI, the AI for the Beta and Human factions is a complete bore. They don't do anything you haven't seen done better by other traditional RTS AIs.
It might not be much of a definiing trait to clasp onto- but overall the Goo Skirmish AI alone is arguably worth the price of admission to what would have otherwise been a competent, but rather stale RTS.

This is one of my new favourite games. I've been following it since it was first announced,and finally took the plunge when I was able to get it for just under $25 AUD recently from another site. From what I've played so far (22 odd hours),It's worth that and more. The game is so brutally intense,and not many game's freak me out as much as this one does during the night cycle or standing on the edge of a massive bridge/building/crane with limited room to move. I'm loving the story,quirky characters and nicely incorporated but not over the top comedy. The combat is extremely satisfying,and the game as a whole is so much more polished than the Dead Island game's. Co-op is seamless whether joining or session being joined,and I haven't come across any jerks (yet). I've only come across a few bug's so far,which were hilarious and rare anyway (zombie stuck through the floor in between a double storey level,strange zombie ragdolling and movements). - Recommended only as supplement to watching the TV Show, not as a stand alone experience.
I like episodic gaming, I like Telltale and I love Game of Thrones, the TV Show. I have to say, that as a whole I really enjoyed this series, BUT I find it much harder to get into to the story after these long breaks. This has nothing to do with the episodic format, cause I can jump into other episodic games like "Life is strange", Resident Evil: Revelations 2", or "Tales from Borderlands" after months long breaks and be immersed immediately. I cannot do this with Game of Thrones, and I think this leads back to the characters, which, although likable, are not truly lovable. They are simply very bland, almost as the color-palette of this game.
So that is my major gripe, the characters, and that is something that the TV Show is mostly doing perfectly. By the end of the fifth episode I had not a problem to choose, because I was so invested into those two people, whose life depended on my decision, but rather because of my emotional detachment in regards to them.
I even found my self trying to "eF" things up, to actually cause some disasters, cause the game failed to invest me enough, so I would strive for a happy ending for those characters.
The last episode KINDA makes up for the earlier shortcomings and secured me as a customer for the second season, but I do not think I will get it on full price this time around.
As stands now, in my opinion, this game is a perfect addition for the weeks between the TV episodes, when, after yet another morbid cliffhanger, you feel the need for a GoT-fix... But  playing this outside of watching a season and having to wait months for new episodes, I would say, that this is rather unimpressive.
What else requires a mention, is that the TellTale graphics at this point really require an update. This style works for "Borderlands" and "Walking Dead's" cartoony style... but after so many episodes it does not hold well for a property as gritty as Game of Thrones. The music also is rather unimpressive.

As a fan of pretty much everything else Telltale Games has released, I'm very saddened to have to say how disappointing this game has been so far. While visually it feels like westeros, and it's all nice to have a bunch of the actual TV series actors reprising their roles here, ultimately the experience failed to capture what I find so important about the whole ASOIAF series: interesting, three dimensional characters. by the end of episode 3 I don't think I've encountered a single character unique to the game that has anything resembling depth, and of the characters from the tv series that appear, Ramsay Bolton was the only one I felt they did anything interesting with...and even that wasn't much. Lord Whitehill is basically a cartoon villain, and Asher is the only Forrester that comes off as remotely interesting.  Worse still, like the unfortunately lackluster season 2 of TWD, the entire thing feels like an endless parade of awful things with nothing positive to balance things out no matter what you do. While I thoroughly enjoy stories with a darker tone, there has to be something to break that up once in a while otherwise it becomes numbing, which it totally does here.
I'm certain that this kind of game could have worked in this particular setting, but the writing here just doesn't come close to measuring up with the source material, and thoroughly misses the tone in the long term.  I'll revisit it once the final episode is released, but at the halfway point, I just don't care about anyone in this game.  And that's not what you want in a GoT property.

*Sigh*. This game had so much potential, but Telltale in their laziness or rush to get the episodes completed has, in their usual fashion, failed to deliver a game in which your choices actually matter. Quite frankly it is a failure of all Telltale games that each and every story ends the same way, with the same characters surviving to the end, regardless of the fact that you might have tried your damnedest to keep X alive, or to prevent Y from happening. In a lot of ways, Game of Thrones is the worst offender of any of them. Earlier TT games didn't give you huge choices to make that would conceivably change the plot drastically. Game of Thrones does. But from my experience, having those decisions gives the player too much freedom for TellTale...apparently. Regardless of your choices, the game will reward you with some circumstance of which the upshot is "F**k your choices." Sometimes, no matter how hard you try, the game does not allow you to successfully complete endeavors you explicitly choose to do, just because the plot they have chosen requires that a certain outcome occur. This illusion of choice is cancerous. It is glaringly apparent, and taints the entire experience from start to what will ultimately be an unfullfilling end. Please stay away from this game if you want your choices to matter. In the end, it's rather insulting.
Choose your own adventure books don't deviate from chapter to chapter only to have the same things happpening regardless of your choices. What's the point of making a game centered around choices if they don't matter? Yes I understand its a lot of time, effort, and money to produce alternate routes and so forth, and to pay for Peter Dinklage and Lena Headley to voice their respective characters, but if you're not willing to do that, TellTale, then please spare us all the trouble of making the game.

This is a fairly good reboot, which has streamlined the gameplay so that one can concentrate on the tactical puzzle/battle and the strategic logistics of getting to it in the 1st place.
It has all the classic elements of research, tech, base building and global favor to maintain funding, ufo crash, terror sites and special missions but certain aspects may feel dubbed down compared to the originals. Eg; Ufo's cam only be detected by satellite there's no ability to maintain air patrols or follow the ufos until they land or arrive at their base etc, in fact the single base assault is now part of the story with plot linked prerequisites.
The unreal engine gives the best graphics to date and the map is rotatable via 90degree increments. Follow cams and bullet cams with slow motion cinematics help jazz up the experience and add a level of immersion missing form some of the previous/similar titles. The player also has the largest cosmetic customisation to date semi-independent of the equipment being worn by the team.
Although unofficial their are mods available eg
, along with cosmetic and mission adding dlc. 'Enemy Within' is a major DLC that deserves its own review being more of an expansion.
Replayability is further increased through 'second wave' setup options that tweak the core mechanics of the game and some of which only unlock after one has complete the campaign on various difficulty levels.
Multiplayer is available in pvp skirmish maps of fixed goal and points per team for unit selection purposes. The number of different maps available to the whole game is a little limited and some are easily memorised both in sp and mp.
The biggest downside of this game is the persistent bugs that were never fixed which can be broadly catagorised as;
load errors, ai infinite logic loop errors, camera problems and physics/ragdoll errors which are still persistent (albeit less often) 3 years after release.
Would recommend to anyone who likes nice graphics and casual turn based tactical puzzles.

Being a big fan of the old UFO/X-COM games I was anticipating this one to be "the" right successor. But something went wrong in the process, the words coming to my mind right now that I've beaten the game are "simplification" and "console game". Couple of examples - you are not allowed to build more than one base, you are not allowed to play with the inventory of your cannon fodder, the action/movement in the tactical part of the game doesn't resemble anything close to the original UFO games and yes, the camera and its controls were pain in the a**.
Anyway, I enjoyed the play until mid-game, after that it started to feel boring. Once you research the plasma weapons & badass armors and build the advanced fighters it became a bit too repetitive without a real challenge.
So, after all it was not so bad, but it's obvious that I (and many other players looking onto the heated discussions over internet) was expecting much more of it. Would give it 6.5/10 rating.
P.S.: I know there are hefty mods around that might change your experience a lot, search for "Long war" if you are a fan of the original series of those games. All of my opinions above are based on the vanilla game experience.

Teamwork.
Intense matches.
Cool characters, blocks and abilities.
Explosions.
Every match I learn something, no matter if it's a win or loss.
A simple new build strategy.
How to better support my team.
Tendencies of enemy players.
Defense is extremely rewarding.
It feels like every choice I make matters.
Here's a fun story from a single match.
-----------------------------------------------------
An enemy attacker jumps into the base triggering multiple traps that drain his health as I throw gas grenades from above to finish him off. :D
I jump down and re-trap the base a bit and then move back to my high ground position.
The same enemy finds the staircase I built early in the match to reach the top of the building.
He runs up it and is instantly killed by the mines I've hidden in blind spots. :D
I repair the damage done to the staircase and re-trap the blind spots.
The same enemy comes back.
Not wanting to use my stair case again, he scales the building from a different position by carving his own path.
But upon reaching the top is so intent on chasing and shooting at me he doesnt notice the mines I've embeded into the floor for protection.
He steps directly on them, bringing his health down low enough to where I kill him with one shot. :D
He's done some damage to me so I heal up at my hidden health block.
Then I repair the floor but don't have enough block points to re-trap the mine field. :|
So I move out of position to do a bit of resource farming and then come back, but I place only a few mines so I can conserve block points.
The same enemy comes back a bit smarter and builds a radar, just before reaching my position, that reveals the traps near me.
Feeling confident he charges in, hitting me with lots of bullets, avoiding the few traps I have in place.
I hit him with a couple shots, but I know I can't win a straight gun fight against him.
So I jump down a level and run to a stack of boxes for cover.
The enemy chases, spraying bullets.
Quickly I build 3 mines on the back side of the boxes, drop a couple gas grenades at my feet, and then back away, positioning myself next to another hidden healing block I placed sometime ealier in the game.
Because he chased me away from my defending position, we are no longer in range of his radar, so he can't see the trap I've just improvised.
The enemy comes around the boxes, guns blazing.
He wants to kill me bad!
The gas grenades go off dealing him minor continuous damage.
Then he trips the mines and they explode his face off. :D
5 seconds later the attackers on my team deal the final blow on the enemy base.
Victory! :D
During all of that I had to manage killing other enemies that were doing damage to our base, supporting team mates by building health and ammo blocks in changing key positions, repairing block structures, leveling ground, blocking and traping enemy tunnels, etc.
-------------------------------------------------------
A very cool game.
Smart play pays off.
Team work makes the dream work.

Try it!

Saints Row IV is a culmination of what happens when you combine stellar gameplay and design, with over-the-top antics and crazy missions. There are so many things developer Volition did right that make Saints Row IV such an enjoyable, replayable adventure, however outlandish or warped its turns take along the way.
In the first few hours of my playthrough of Saints Row IV, I became the President of the US, cured cancer, was captured by aliens called Zin,
, ate pancakes for breakfast and stubbed my toe. While all of this may sound so cliché, Saints Row IV then opens itself up to a plethora of player customization, ridiculous weapons and over-powered weapons. Saints Row IV was designed to be destroyed, but these basics are just a small amount of what it has to offer.
After leaving the '50s re-enactment of Steelport, you return to a simulation of the city that has been overrun by Zin. As soon as you enter Steelport, you are introduced to clusters. Clusters are the 'super-power currency' to Saints Row IV. Collect enough of these, and you can upgrade and beef up abilities such as Super Sprint, Blast, and Telekinesis. The latter all have elemental variants, from the fundamental 'Fire' and 'Freeze', to bigger and better things like 'Explosion' and 'Mind Control'. These new attack methods can be used at any time inside the simulation, and are what make Saints Row IV a new experience to fans of the Open World genre.
Steelport's map is dotted with collectibles and minigames. One of my personal favourite minigames was Professor Genki's Mind Over Murder game, which was hilariously silly and stupid, but so enjoyable. I especially loved the game-show-style commentary incorporated in it, with two hosts discussing how I played as I went along. There are also Audio Logs that contain fragments of peoples' past and Zinyak statues to destroy.
Although Saints Row IV is mainly about the constant alien bloodshed in the wake of the apocalypse, the Saints' story is one I will remember. Behind the impudent facade a lot of the characters portray is a level of caring, they want to help their friends and they all care for each other. No matter what obstacles they overcome, the Saints have the power to pull through. This isn't to say there won't be falling outs, but for the majority of the main missions, I never felt like I was uninterested.
Side quests, on the other hand, were Saints Row IV's downfall. I saw them as 'time fillers', to make the game appear longer, and to give you a little incentive for when you finish at the end. Sometimes, I was happy to take on Matt Miller's boring missions, only so I could receive the Mind Control reward at the end. I'm so glad the side quests were optional, because if the story was as bland and monotonous as these, I would have put down my controller and not picked it up again. Most of the side quests were what you would sort of expect. While you were asked to do things from different people, it was always the same 'Go here, blow stuff up, come back.' style of side quests you would expect. This isn't to say that blowing the stuff up wasn't fun, it's just the way they were instigated showed no sign of distinction between them.
Saints Row IV presents itself as an in-your-face, balls-to-the-wall style game that doesn't back down on anything it delivers. But that doesn't mean you can't spend quality time making countless changes to how you look. There are so many different customization options at the Image As Designed plastic surgery, I spent about three hours deciding between a wide-eyed Elder Scrolls Argonian-like man with a female voice, or a purple hulk with blue hair and a Cockney accent. I finally settled for something simpler and human-looking, with a thick British accent. I felt compelled to keep it, even though I knew I could make something better. Something about the original character you create stays with you, and sometimes I didn't even want to change my outfit in fear of 'losing' my character's personality.
Overall, Saints Row IV is an over-the-top, blasé third-person adventure, complete with aliens and an impeccable story. Saints Row IV is outrageous, but under its whole bad♥♥♥♥♥guise lies a wonderfully constructed joy to play. It is entertaining, stupid, and just plain fun. Volition sure knows how to give players a good time.

This game is amazingly good at avoiding the mistakes other Yu-Gi-Oh franchise games make, including the ones the card game makes. More puzzle oriented than Hearthstone or similar, but you can still build your deck like in an TCG. The game is not too fast-paced and you can redo tutorials if you have trouble remembering things. I would suggest watching reviews and tutorials to get an idea of whether you would enjoy this game or not.  There is so much going on that it offers something for (almost) everyone.  It may become disorienting to go blindly into the game without prior study of its mechanics.  The game does not hold your hand through everything like some MMO's.  This is not for casuals.  At the same time, if you are willing to put the effort into learning the game, it can be a relaxing and calming experience.  You don't have to grind endlessly (unless all you wish to do is reach end game ASAP).  You can go fishing, run trade routes, set up a network of automated workers, tame horses, set up farms, etc. etc.  There is much more than just killing mobs ad infinitum.  Yes, the grind is real, and it is pretty much required if you want to level at a reasonable pace.  But thankfully, combat is extremely fun in this game.
The combat is very similar to Tera in that you must position yourself and aim properly.  There is no selecting targets, which makes it very fluid and dynamic.  This style, for me, is very satisfying and exciting.  I am playing a wizard (the main spell caster class) and the spells make me feel very powerful.  From the chain lightning with huge range that I can zap entire groups in mere seconds to the earthquake spell that decimates anyone within a few meters.  There are many spells and players can focus on the ones they enjoy most.  Want to throw fireballs and make explosions and other fiery death?  You can do that.  Prefer electrocuting your enemies.  Try some lightning spells.  Or maybe you want everyone to just chill while you send ice shards, freezing fogs and blizzards their way.  There are some cool little surprises too, like how I can turn my single lightning bolt (sent down from above like real lightning) and use what is called black spirit's rage to turn it into an aimable lightning storm barrage that lasts for several seconds, enough to fry anything withing your range.  EXTREMELY FUN!!!  I also have a ninja (the stealthy and swift stabby class), and he is also very satisfying to play.  Fighting is extremely fluid and you can dance around groups of enemies while slicing them into ribbons.  Being a bit squishy, the class relies on this speed and mobility to stay alive while providing a swift death to his enemies.  They have done an excellent job at making the class play how one would imagine.  I haven't played any other classes yet, but I am sure they are similarly designed.
I am only in the mid levels with my characters, but I have had a lot of fun so far and don't feel the need to rush to end game.
There is no "just one more turn".

So it's an open world sandbox that has zombies in it. I guess that's interesting. Apparently this game is basically a better version of Dead Island, but I never played that so I don't have any reference there.
Standard-ish zombie plot: Zombie plague, lots of people die, survivors among the undead who are even worse, government assistance that's really shady and unhelpful, etc. The main character you play as is kind of interesting in the sense that he starts out as a hidden agent just doing a job and ends up getting much more invested in what happens thanks to plot events. Also I'm soo glad there wasn't a romance, because it sure looked like that's where things might be heading.
Gameplay? You kill zombies (and people) as well as do alot of first person platforming. Ok. My dislike of platforming (due to my lack of skill at it) is well-established in past reviews, but those were THIRD PERSON platformers. This is much worse. Some of the climbing parts of this game really annoyed me. The combat is a bit middling too in the sense that your weapons break constantly and your character seems to run out of stamina far too easily. It was only when I gained access to some decent weaponry and a competent amount of supplies that things started to tilt in my favor. I do like how guns have the trade-off of being good but also being a lure for zombies, even if it did mean that most cases where I used guns in the open world ended with me having to flee after generating a literal mountain of zombie corpses. XD
There's also this day/night cycle where you get more XP at night, but it is considerably more dangerous. I rather liked it, even if your only real options are to either run as fast/stealthily as you can or funnel the zombies into a buiding with only one entrance and use that as a killzone until dawn. The latter pretty much ate through all my ammo. XD
So how is the game? It's decent. Platforming can go to hell, the main villain who is doing a bad Joker impersonation should have died in a fire instead of how he ended up dying (Spoiler: the bad guy dies), and there never was enough alcohol for my Molotovs... but it was fun. Or rather it became fun once I had leveled enough that I could buy ammo from merchants and therefore use guns regularly despite them attracting zombies. Maybe I just like violence more than running around a city scavenging for string and other parts to craft things. I'd rather use those things!
As for all the online stuff, I have no clue. My internet is being a horrific pest lately and keeps dropping connection. It's really depressing. :(
I think i'll play it some more, but not to do all those damned side-quests. Rather... because roaming around a city filled with the dead has it's fun moments. Woohoo violence!

I will start by saying that I am not normally a huge fan of turn-based combat. As a result, I was a bit reluctant to purchase this game. I will say, however, that I am quite glad I did. This game is best described as the anti-Starcraft, and I mean that in the best possible way. Its been developed by veterans of the Command and Conquer franchise, and it shows. The game is polished, beautiful, cleverly designed, and, more importantly, FUN. Every aspect of the game, from the QWERTY based hotkeys, to the creative, fun and interesting factions,  to the economy focused on letting you play at the game of war, instead of babysitting harvesters, is designed for those players who have felt abandoned by recent RTS games, with their focus on laser tight micro and hotkey memorization. This game is about your strategy, how you can out-think your opponent. Micro, build-order, timings, they have their place, but they are not the crux of the game.
The factions are all cleverly designed. The Beta are the closest to a standard C&C faction there is. They have equal capabilities in offense or defense, with their units being fairly durable. In defense they focus primarily on units and their walls (Yes! This game has walls, and they're viable to use!), in offense, they have a very balanced arsenal to pull from.
The Humans focus primarily on defense, with a large variety of turrets to choose from, walls that they can walk/shoot through (the enemy cannot, however) and a powerful air-force. They suffer however, in that every building is tethered to a central core, meaning they often lack map control. Their units are typically more numerous that Beta units, but more flimsy. Personally, they're my favorite faction.
The Goo are the strangest, most creative faction I've ever controlled in an RTS. They have no buildings what-so-ever, instead spawning all of their units from amorphous "Mother Goos". The Mothers must be fed, either by consuming enemy units, or Catalyst, the games resource, so that they grow in size. Once they reach a certain size, they may split off portions of themselves to spawn units. They are very aggressive, with many units having the ability to climb cliffs, and they retain excellent map control and anti-air. They lack any sort of an air-force, however.
Regarding the campaign, I just want to mention that the campaign was somewhat weak in terms of gameplay, relying too much on artificial difficulty and forcing you to play your faction against its weaknesses more often than it allows you to embrace its strengths. This is especially prominent in the Goo section of the campaign. I LOVED the story however, particularly the universe it sets up. Finally a fresh universe that captures my imagination, its been far too long since a game has done that.
TL;DR: I cannot lay out every awesome thing this game does here, so, if you don't want to read my whole essay, than know this; this game was worth every penny of my $50. It is a stunning example of how creative design is just as important as perfect polish (which, unlike Petroglyphs last outing, Universe at War, this game does not lack), and deserves your time and your money.

My beef with it is the same as every Telltale "game" these days: it isn't an adventure game, and in fact it is not a game at all. There are no puzzles.  Gameplay consists of putting your cursor on top of hotspots, reading a description of a clay pot or some other random meaningless assortment of pixels, then either engaging in dialogue or walking to another setpiece and repeating the observation of the clay pots and the non-consequential dialogue and whatnot.
It is a (barely) interactive cartoon, where nothing you do makes a difference, aside from a few lines of dialogue getting swapped based on your response. There is no game to play.  You can press any of the four buttons on your gamepad randomly throughout the entire game and aside from a few dialogue swaps, it's the exact same experience each time.
For a "game" where the emphasis is on experiencing the story rather than playing a game (especially one with the HBO name on it), you'd think the art direction would be better.  The Wolf Among Us had such great art direction, I had almost changed my mind about Telltale, but this game turned me right off again.
I knew going in that this was going to be more cartoon than game, I guess I was curious what the story adds to the Game of Thrones universe.  On that point, it is a decent addition. I love the soundtrack, though I wish that it was a bit larger, there seem to be only a handful of (amazing) songs that play. At 40 dollars it's not a bargain, but I would say that this is worth it, especially if you can catch it on sale.

The controls take some getting used to, but the game is damn fun once you figure them out.
Unlike most shooters, players have an insane amount of mobility, and the ability to slow time at will. You can leap through the air, powerslide along the ground, and climb ledges. Naturally this degree of mobility will lead to some really awesome kills, which the game rewards you with a second or two of slow-motion. This basically encourages players to not stay in one spot, and kill enemies in very stylish ways.
Another mechanic the game has which takes some getting used to is random objectives. Primarily the game is a deathmatch, but once in a while the game will give players an objective, such as being the first to reach a specific point, or kill a certain player before the rest. Naturally you are rewarded points by being the first to do so, and can make the difference between winning and losing a match.
The game isn't perfect, though, and I do have some gripes about it. As I said before the controls are pretty strange, and take some time to figure out. The game teaches various gameplay mechanics and stunts via popup windows during gameplay, which can be distracting. Another problem I have is grenades, especially when paired with the "Nitrophiliac" ability. They're a little too easy to spam, and I was able to get far too many kills with ease by littering the battlefield with them, not to mention that grenades generally are an instant kill. My last complaint is respawning, where instead of spawning in a Team Fortress-style respawn room, you are instead dropped at a random point in the map. And you can bet that generally there will be enemy players nearby. So it forces you to quickly adjust to your new surroundings, and try to not get shot in the back. Fortunately this complaint is lessened by the fact respawning is instantaneous.
For all it's quirks, Double Action: Boogaloo is a unique spin on deathmatches, and is damn fun to play. And the best part is that, despite being a Free to play game, there is no "Pay to win" element that plagues other f2p's on Steam. There's a lot of players, and the developers are teasing at new content on the horizon. Basically, it's a game I find very easy to recommend.

I love Beat Hazard, and I'm not really a fan of twin stick shooters. I bought the game because it had an interesting premise, and I loved the game because it really succeeds in turning that premise into a great time. Beat Hazard has almost a Guitar Hero/Rock Band feel without the gimmicky side effect; it is a game that will have you playing for hours just because "oh, (song name) had a great beat for this! I want to try (song name)!" And this is as your spouse/friends/family is sitting beside you, watching you play while asking incessantly, "Can I try? Can I try?"
The playability is literally endless. Literally. Music will always exist and new music will continue to be made, and you can play this game to the beat of said music via the form of mp3s (among others) and streaming. Be prepared to download songs you never wanted to admit liking just to try them out in the game. Be surprised as you find that certain songs offer you more challenge than you thought they would.
When Beat Hazard claims the gameplay flows with the music, they're not just saying that. The beat picks up, the enemies fly faster, the colors get brighter, the bullets shoot faster. This offers a new level of strategy unheard of in other games, because if you know the song you are playing well, you'll know when it picks up and slows down and you can play accordingly.
A few last positives before I end the review. The game tracks your high scores for each song that you have (for downloads, at least, I haven't tried with streaming). The game is easy to learn and great fun even for those (like me) who don't tend to like twin stick shooters. Great to launch at parties/get togethers/game nights. Great game to jump in/out of if you only have a few minutes to spare gaming. Multiple modes and unlockables. "Just one more" type of gameplay. Can be humorous at times to watch the enemy ships react to the music. It's actually kind of cute to watch them all quickly file onto the screen in a song that picks up quickly after a slow start, as if they all were sleeping off the screen until the blaring beat shook them to consciousness.
Overall, great game. I'm giving it a 10/10. Buy it if you like music. ;)

This game has very few shortfalls and was very entertaining - lots of replayability, though i would recommend buying its expansion pack at the same time; "Enemy Within" as this allows far more customization of your individual soldiers as well as awards/medals and obviously, extra mission variation and content.
Pros:
- well thought out and simple interface, everything has a purpose here and its explained well enough even for turn-base tactical rookies like myself, stats system is totally self explanitory.
- looks good, weapons and explosions - buildings and destroyable cover.
- engaging gameplay with a good prospect for replayability.
- varied soldier types, nearly every perk is useful in some way and they can all support different playstyles, except snipers and squadsight ... that is the ONLY perk ive found you HAVE to pick.
- every action has a consequence, you cant just bull rush the objective and not take casulties and casulties can cost you time or your best trained soldiers life, its also a game where you cannot save everyone - you must carefully manage how you respond to alien abductions and terror attacks to mimimize worldwide panic and keep x-com nations in the game.
- encourages careful play with your assets, money, alloys, weapon parts and most importantly, troops - losing an experienced soldier can be disasterous, pro tip; always end your turn in cover!
- like almost all turn based games, there is no limit on your turn - you can spend as long as you like considering your next move.
- no autosave by default - its an option, but i believe the devs intended it to be a game that once youve made a choice its final but with the way gamers are these days, if there wasnt an autosave feature it would be considered herasy of the highest order.
- soldiers behave like real troops under heavy pressure and may panic and make snap descisions.
Cons:
- Movement system is a little junky when working with altitudes, mech walkers jetboot module cannot see higher altitudes when there are movable tiles directly under them.
- Grappling hooks on armor are buggy and may launch your troops across the map instead of say; climbing to the top of that building.
- soldier voice packages are a little limited, even though Enemy Within added much more - many nationalities still lacked a flare in their speech and many languages were not included.
- final boss fight easier than the battleship raid, infact, i believe the hardest mission i played was the one where you have to call down an airstrike and get out when youre surrounded by chrysalids.
- too many troops, not enough bad guys!
All in all, if you like this genre of strategy game ... then this is definately a good game for you, if you can stand the sometimes infuraitaing RNG like missing on a 99% hit chance.

The game focuses on the Easter Front of World War 2, you can play as the hard hitting and gritty Russians and their infamous penal battalions, or the strategic and cunning Germans with their dangerous Panzer tanks. Over all I give this game an 8 1/2 out of 10. Congratulations to Relic on producing another great game!

Lethal League is a fantastic fighting game that shines at its brightest with friends due to its accessibility, complexity, and consistency in providing incredible moments during matches. It plays like a fast-paced and dangerous game of ping pong and dodgeball where the ball will knock the stuffing out of you if you're hit.
The accessibility comes from the simple concept of hitting the ball is good while being hit by the ball is bad. The tutorial  (located in EXTRAS) will take you through the basics and teach you enough to start smacking the ball around in different directions in different ways. You'll be exposed to the basic attack which adds only one speed to the ball, a charge up attack which can add up to x2 the current speed of the ball, and the down smash which always doubles the speed of the ball. You'll also be introduced to bunting which pops the ball up into the air no matter how fast it's going, your special which is usually the attack button during hit lag/pause (that freezing moment before you release the ball), and the jump button. You can also taunt or taunt + direction to emote.
The complexity comes from all the subtleties found within the game. Each character has their own special moveset in regards to how they move, jump, and control their special. For example, Sonata has a double jump, Candyman have a floaty jump that reaches the top of the screen, while Latch can jump onto and then climb up and down walls. You can clash with other players resulting in one or both being stunned, bunt attacks, bunt bunts, control the direction of bunts, adjust your attacking angles, reduce the hitlag/pause by bunting before performing an air down smash or a charge attack so your opponent can't counter easily, and so on to the point that there are some helpful guides in the Community Hub that can improve your game once you're ready.
As for moments, there are so many. One of my favorites happen to be this one match where I exchanged a ball going at 1,000,000 speed several times with a worthy opponent. Keep in mind the ball starts off at a default speed of 8 unless you change the settings. Here's a video showing some three player gameplay with different settings:
Finally, I'll mention the settings because you can drastically change the approach of how to play depending on what you choose. The game has two modes that I know of, stocks (think SSB) and points. Stocks rewards the player who's able to stay alive. Points rewards the player that can attain the most kills/knockouts. Ball tagging on means you don't have to fear the ball you just hit while turning it off means it's a danger to everyone at all times. You can also change the ball if you're at a high enough level. So far I've only played with the Big Ball which seems to have a bigger hitbox and a longer hit lag. You can also set the time limit or turn it off if in case you want to play for the most kills in five minutes or first to twelve kills.
P.S. Play with friends or people. It's much, much less fun to play against the AI. You can use the in-game matchmaking or peeking in the Community Hub chat to find pick-up games if you don't have a group of friends for ball smashing.

This game gets a thumbs up from me because I fully support Konami releasing Yu-Gi-Oh games on Steam. However, there are a few issues that I would like to glance over.
Content. Content-wise, there aren't many differences between this iteration and the previous one, Millenium Duels. Pendulum decks are available but mostly via DLC. This is also the only way to access story related Arc V content. There are "draft play" games, where you open packs and make a deck from the cards that you pull. However, this mode does not contain much substance either.
Multiplayer. You can play others through ranked or quick play, which is fine. The problem surfaces when you are beating someone in an online game and they "disconnect". You are not awarded with a win, and annoyingly, they are not punished. Players can therefore quit to steam until they rack up a long string of wins. This problem has led to multiplayer servers being for the most part, empty.
If you are looking for a PC Yu-Gi-Oh sim, just download DevPro. However, if you like the idea of collecting cards and starting with a basic deck, then this game more than suffices.

A very solid RTS from a surprisingly competent studio, Grey Goo feels like a tribute to classic 90's RTS games, only updated and modernized.
The story was quite entertaining and, though predictable, it kept me coming back to play the campaign. One cannot choose the faction to start playing with, and everything is linear in terms of story progression, but that lends itself to a bit of narrative flair, such as the reveal of the Human faction (as technically "alien" invaders of Ecosystem 9). The cinematic CGI cutscenes are quite beautiful too, again in a way that reminds us of Blizzard's venerable work in Starcraft and Warcraft.
I enjoyed the graphics a lot, and it bears pointing out that recent updates seem to have made the game run better on my system, as compared to the original, unpatched version. A lot of work clearly went into the art direction here, and it shows; the factions and setting, rather than being "entirely" original, draw inspiration from multiple sources (again tributing classical RTS and science fiction) and come up with something that is quite lovely and memorable. The soundtrack is also quite beautiful, with C&C veteran Frank Klepacki giving us an appropriately inspiring, bombastic sci-fi music.
The gameplay takes a bit of getting used to. The interface feels clunky for some reason, and it will be a while before it feels natural. The UI commands in the main menu also seem to take a bit longer than expected to... "happen".
The AI in this game, at least for me, felt a bit too hard even on lower difficulties; when I first started playing for instance, the second campaign mission took me several tries to finish on Normal (and I don't count myself as a novice in strategy gaming), and to be frank I am still waiting for a way to get through the last stretch of the last mission. Then again, challenging campaign AI might not be a turn-off for everyone, or it might just be that I am bad at playing.
This game feels like the opening chapter of a saga, and it is quite transparent that the developers would like to make a sequel. Hell, the achievment for finishing the campaign is even called "The End of the Beginning". I'm excited to see in what direction they decide to take this idea, and hope they will be able to iron out the last few bugs that remain.

What does Grey Goo do wrong? Not much, to be frank but there are a few things that could've been made better. First off the differences between the two humanoid factions are mostly cosmetic even though there are subtle differences in how units work, unit stats and general playstyle. Particularly base building is vastly different. I just feel they could've been diversified a little bit more.
EDIT: Replay is now in the game (2016-02-15 edit)
The lack of a proper replay function hurts ranked play and stymies people who want to improve by watching their games from an outside perspective. This is one thing I believe should be prioritized.
The game runs like crap on a lot of people's hardware. There's been a lot of performance patches lately that have dealt with most of those cases. I personally still have a wildly fluctuating framerate in menues and videos, but gameplay is mostly buttery smooth.
While I liked the shorter campaign (16-ish missions) some people don't and the lack of multiplayer maps is also somewhat hurting the game, even though I personally find them to be enough. Learning a few maps and finding ways to use the maps to your advantage is a lot more fun than having yet another bloody map every time you play. But it's a con, so I'll list it. Also see map editor.
While this is hardly unique for Grey Goo, it's still a thing that drives people up the wall. At first glance, Goo's artillery can seem overpowered as hell with their HUGE range and potential healing. In addition Goo's splash-tank upgrade turns enemy armies into paste (no pun intended) against an unprepared opponent. Human's artillery also works as mines? OP! Etc etc. Grey Goo is fairly balanced, but it takes a lot of playing before you actually realize this. Early on it just seems broken.
I dunno why I'm listing this as I've beaten the campaign on hard on the first try. But I've seen billions of threads about this. Grey Goo is apparently hard.
The AI is, for the most part, good and will put up a decent fight against a middling level player. It has some issues though and can sometimes break down completely and just "sit there".
Grey Goo is overpriced in todays market. It's quite worth the price, but it's not going to sell well with such a high price tag.
The soundtrack is really, really good. Even I, who normally shun everything remotely dubstep-y, can appreciate the Goo soundtrack even though the Humans have the soundtrack that I personally like the most. It's also written and performed by legendary Frank Klepacki of the C&C games.
Grey Goo looks gorgeous, not just in gameplay but in the cutscenes and menues. Top notch quality all around.
I personally love the anti-micro pro-macro style of RTS that Grey Goo is. I detest micro-heavy RTSs with a passion and am so sick of Starcraft Clone #451 coming out. Grey Goo makes a return to the strategic part of RTS. Army composition, economy and positioning plays a big role here and you'll rarely be "caught out" by lacking twitch skills.
The maps are great to play on, the factions seem fairly balanced (although I'd argue that Goo can be somewhat underpowered) and the connectivity is rock solid. I've never had a single disconnect or even lag in a single match so far which is impressive seeing as I play almost exclusively with people "across the pond".
The faction as a whole. It's unique, yet recognizable. Anyone who has played Zerg or Tyranids will recognize the frantic "zerging" style of gameplay, but at the same time the lack of bases, or rather mobile bases make the Goo a very unique faction.
Some may call the story basic, but I personally enjoyed the story and how it was told very much. A lot of likable characters as well so this gets my thumbs up.
I list this in pros as well, because the times when the AI does play well, it plays really well. It's solid enough to give me a bit of a challenge on Hard, but it's of course nothing compared to a human player.
The developers have been releasing regular performance patches, and as of time for this review to be posted, they're also working on their first big balance patch. The ongoing support means this game has a lot of lifetime ahead of itself.
Hell yes, I do. Grey Goo is the best RTS to be released in recent years. That doesn't mean that Grey Goo is the next coming of Messiah in RTS gaming. No. It's a pretty iterative continuation of the C&C style of games. But it does it well and it's a solid enough game for me to recommend it. I still have tons of fun playing it and I expect you will too. If you are hesitant, wait for a sale. It's a pretty hefty price tag after all.

This eighth visual novel from Zeiva Inc feature a female protagonist Chi An who was born colour blind. After an encounter with the dragon Tian Zhao, Chi An was able to see all the colours around her again. Years later, Chi An would be betrothed to her childhood friend Ming Jie who is studying and working hard for her with the blessings of both sides's parents, while Tian Zhao would re-appear into Chi An's life again and cause Chi An to question her perceived lack of personal freedom and the responsibilities expected of her. Chi An would also meet a half-dragon boy Tian Xi and a dragon priest Xu Wei, both with their own background story and personal motivations where Chi An could have an ending with.
Although there are no Steam achievements to obtain in this game and the Steam take screenshot button feature doesn't work, the game has an in-game achievement page that will track and show all unlocked in-game achievements that are awarded upon fulfilling various different conditions over multiple playthroughs where bonus unlockable extra content in the form of a side story, CG, character backgrounds and developer comments will be awarded upon obtaining all in-game achievements. The game has beautiful artwork, great opening and ending movie, theme song and soundtracks. On a linked Tumblr page of Zeiva Inc's website(Orz Corporation), a soundtrack DLC and a guide for the game was announced to be in development(3 June 2017), while an announced (reverse) harem ending (1 April 2017)seem to be in the bonus unlockable side story. The guide is now available at Zeiva Inc's website. I had originally planned to recommend the game when at discount of less than $10 (as it takes less than 10 hours to obtain all achievements, read and unlock all bonus content) or if the announced soundtrack DLC comes in a free DLC and when an annoying bug where a red screen might occasionally appear and block out all view of the screen is fixed, I have decided to reconsider and recommend the game at the current discounted price of 20% off at the time of this review after reading through the developer comments that this game took up to 6 years to produce and involved a lot of hard work from the developer. Overall, recommended for fans of Zeiva Inc(me, me! xD), those who enjoy visual novels in an ancient Chinese setting with a bit of background information on traditional Chinese culture, beautiful artwork, great soundtracks and does not have any Steam achievements.

FTL: Faster Than Light Review
Indie star-ship management rouge-like.
:
FTL Faster Than Light has an endless amount of replayability, making it easily the best purcahse I have ever made from all of my library. Although it seems like such a simple game on the surface, the cominations are endless with you at times thriving with your 4 burst laser mark 2s, and other times scraping by with your dual laser and mini beam until you can repair your hull in a shop and hope you can even find a decent weapon.. IF you can make it...
Due to the massive amounts of weapons in FTL Faster Than Light, the replayability factor is huge. The game is extremely challenging for beginners as they try to reroute their power in every which system and even depower their weapons to put more power into their engines in hopes that they dodge a volley of missiles. The weapons are grouped into a few types: Beam, laser (projectiles), flak cannon, bomb, and missile weapons. Some weapons consume 1 missile when fired, requiring you to scrap missiles off of enemy ships or buy them in stores. With the completely free Captains Edition mod, 100s more weapons are added all basing themselves of variants.
The game at first is extremely hard even on Easy mode, I must admit. The game is so unrelentless to beginners due to the fact that you're forced to learn from your heart-breaking mistaks that you make time and time again, only to learn from that mistake and try to prevent it via managing which systems are upgraded and when you upgrade your weapons.. If you find any good ones in the shop or find any. After playing for about 40+ hours on Easy, I got really good with it, and I can make it to and usually beat the Flagship every run. Normal mode is essentially a middle-grounds once you're skilled with Easy, but Hard mode is total hell. Hardmode for once forces you to make some morally grey decisions such as stealing a package of supplies a rebel ship just dropped as you hide and wait... Oh wait, it turns out it was just vaccinations for the local plague.
The game is just awesome. For only 4 dollars as you can see I've gotten my fair time out of it, and I still play it. I will admit though, after about 60+ hours the game does get a little stale, but once you jump into hardmode it's a whole new story. Captains Edition is also a great mod to add on with this. The infinite combination of weapons and the entire Federation's life relying on your cunning and strategy is just great. You do get some morally greying choices that you may just have to make instead of being the good guy all of the time.
10/10 -- I would pay 30 dollars if I would have known how fun this would be; I underestimated how much I would play it!

Good gameplay, great music, bad campaign, inconsistent and pretty random story, mediocre performance, looks amazing.
But I have to think before recommending. It's easy to get lost in a "oh god no slow RTS of this kind Red Alert 3" mindset, but that immediatly sprawls doubt into my mind - while it's immediatly visible that this was made by people who worked on great games before, why did they have so much trouble with making unit control good? I mean... it's hard to explain.
For example, in C&C3 and RA3, I could send 16 bombers on 16 different targets in 20 seconds. Here, it's nigh impossible to micro like that. All units of one type are bunched up in the selection box, and even the control is pretty basic. Attack move, hold ground, guard, that's it. There are no abilities. The strategy is limited to "bunch up 200/200 units and A-move" or "get artillery and slowpush every single inch". Even economy was automated almost to the point of not existing, and micro is... almost discouraged.
Even the units don't do many different things. Just build 1 type from each category + some artillery and you're golden, maybe some AA but only after they've revealed they have aircraft. Anti-armour from light units, tank from heavy units, and a fighter from flying.
Epics are more interesting, but... they're tad too powerful. Place an Alpha in a chokepoint, nothing will ever get through. Two Hand of Ruks are capable of killing a stream of thousands of Goo. Etc. It's really hard to kill an epic unit once it's out. No amount of strategy available will save you if they have support. Hand of Ruk can easly decimate 200/200 of units. And in the campaign, oh god, when you face epic units of Humans and Beta, it's always on a map with many, many chokepoints and narrow fields. It's impossible to position against AoE
The build menu is good. It's basicly what was in C&C3, but with less hotkeys. The idea of the tech tree is pretty interesting. You get to pick 1 out of 3 upgrades, however some are just straight up better than others. That effectively limits the tech tree significantly, as usually most people will always pick the same upgrades.
I can't get my thoughts straight. So I'll tl;dr - it's the same type of a game as C&C3, but inferior in gameplay mechanics and campaign. Doesn't mean it's bad. It's a good. But not good enough. It's clusmy. It's basic. It performs badly.
Edit: upgraded my PC to the best I could. Second most powerful 980GTX and a new CPU. Game still runs like crap.

Brains...
So it's an open world sandbox that has zombies in it. I guess that's interesting. Apparently this game is basically a better version of Dead Island, but I never played that so I don't have any reference there.
Standard-ish zombie plot: Zombie plague, lots of people die, survivors among the undead who are even worse, government assistance that's really shady and unhelpful, etc. The main character you play as is kind of interesting in the sense that he starts out as a hidden agent just doing a job and ends up getting much more invested in what happens thanks to plot events. Also I'm soo glad there wasn't a romance, because it sure looked like that's where things might be heading.
Gameplay? You kill zombies (and people) as well as do alot of first person platforming. Ok. My dislike of platforming (due to my lack of skill at it) is well-established in past reviews, but those were THIRD PERSON platformers. This is much worse. Some of the climbing parts of this game really annoyed me. The combat is a bit middling too in the sense that your weapons break constantly and your character seems to run out of stamina far too easily. It was only when I gained access to some decent weaponry and a competent amount of supplies that things started to tilt in my favor. I do like how guns have the trade-off of being good but also being a lure for zombies, even if it did mean that most cases where I used guns in the open world ended with me having to flee after generating a literal mountain of zombie corpses. XD
There's also this day/night cycle where you get more XP at night, but it is considerably more dangerous. I rather liked it, even if your only real options are to either run as fast/stealthily as you can or funnel the zombies into a buiding with only one entrance and use that as a killzone until dawn. The latter pretty much ate through all my ammo. XD
So how is the game? It's decent. Platforming can go to hell, the main villain who is doing a bad Joker impersonation should have died in a fire instead of how he ended up dying (Spoiler: the bad guy dies), and there never was enough alcohol for my Molotovs... but it was fun. Or rather it became fun once I had leveled enough that I could buy ammo from merchants and therefore use guns regularly despite them attracting zombies. Maybe I just like violence more than running around a city scavenging for string and other parts to craft things. I'd rather use those things!
As for all the online stuff, I have no clue. My internet is being a horrific pest lately and keeps dropping connection. It's really depressing. :(
I think i'll play it some more, but not to do all those damned side-quests. Rather... because roaming around a city filled with the dead has it's fun moments. Woohoo violence!

Grey Goo is the latest RTS offering from Petroglyph and the first effort of new developer Gray Box studios. It comes with a full featured 15 mission campaign consisting of 5 missions for each of the three factions to tell a story in the style of StarCraft or WarCraft, eight multiplayer maps that can be played 2v2 or 1v1, and a strong skirmish AI for those players who either don't feel the need to play online, or cannot for whatever reason (more on that later). Taking place on a lush habitable world called Ecosystem-9, Grey Goo is an impressive achievement and a sign of great things to come from developer Grey Box. It also kind of sucks, and that is a real shame, because there is no reason for it.
First, the good. Grey Goo's three races are all extremely interesting and just bursting with flavor. The humans on Ecosystem 9 are members of an expeditionary fleet who have arrived to survey and colonize the planet. Their units are all drones (save their awesomely cool epic unit, the Alpha, a kilometer tall exoskeleton that fires a sweeping laser blast) to emphasize the lack of available human personell, their bases consist of linked nodes and rely on impressive turrets powered by artificial intelligence to defend themselves. The beta are a more traditional RTS race, relying on robotic fighting vehicles and infantry; they build their bases off of many smaller hubs that can be placed anywhere in your vision range. Perhaps most interesting are the titular Goo, a mobile race that builds no structures, but who employ many mobile masses of goo that serve as your resource collectors and factories. Taken together, the races feel very fleshed out and interesting, and I was impressed by the imagination that went in to them.
The developers also succeeded immensely at their goal of streamlining the game. Units themselves have no individual abilities, so the player can focus on production and positioning; every single structure and upgrade can be conveniently built directly in the UI with the Q, W, E, and R keys; along with a seldom-relevant population cap, there is only a single resource to manage. Grey Goo also looks gorgeous on low to medium settings and still runs well on my relatively old machine.
Finally, Grey Goo's campaign is also a really impressive technical feat. The developers wisely avoid giving you too much up front, and during the course of your 15 mission campaign they reveal a complete and interesting universe that, frankly, I am very excited about. Each mission is bookended by some impressive CGI, and while you get fewer action oriented cutscenes relative to other games, it still feels like you're playing a game made by professional people.
Of course, if you have the misfortune to be actually playing the campaign, that feeling will quickly erode. This is one of the worst, most poorly designed RTS campaigns I've ever seen. I don't want to give the impression that I am saying that lightly either. Grey Goo's missions are chockablock full of moments that will make you throw up your hands in genuine rage and exasperation, or cause you to bellow "WHAT?!"
In one mission you are tasked with building the Beta's epic unit and then crossing the map with it. Literally seconds in to the game you will face a complete attack wave, and the only way you can prevail is by exploiting the incompetent AI and maneuvring your single unit (you will not have had time to build even one at this point) and picking off their army one by one while they attack your buildings. In another mission, you are required to find an escape pod for one of your AI crew members, activate it, and then return it to your base. When I found him, the activation simply failed to trigger, and even after I had completely wiped out the enemy forces, I was unable to complete the mission. In general, the map design consists of narrow corridors that make necessary micromanagement of your units an incredible chore.
Even when the game is functioning as intended, it is outrageously difficult for no good reason that I can see. I was at one time a Master league StarCraft player, and breezed through the StarCraft 2 campaign on Hard. I found Grey Goo a test of my skill, and unfortunately a test of my patience. I was pushed to my utter limit while attempting the campaign on hard difficulty, and I eventually swapped to normal and still found that punitive, so I dropped it down to Easy to cruise through the final three missions. It was still a long slog each time on that difficulty (made more painful by the fact that the developers went trigger happy with spawning enemy epic units in the final stages of the game), and I averaged around 40 minutes per mission, most of which is comprised of a slow battle of attrition through carefully arranged enemy defensive structures that have far too much health. A patch has since toned down the Normal and Easy difficulties, but they are still a complete chore to play, and in no way enjoyable except as a crucible to test yourself.
The campaigns fail completely as a teaching tool as well. Early in the Goo campaign you are told that your mobile factory and harvester, the Mother Goo, can collect resource spigots by moving over them. They do not mention that these spigots regenerate even if your Mother Goo just sits on the resource point, and that in 100% of occasions your mother goo should sit stationary, collecting resources. In fact, almost none of the units get a proper introduction the way they would in other RTS games, and I am still confused as to why you would ever build the Beta's siege unit when it is so squishy and expensive, and fails to outrange towers.
Fortunately, the multiplayer components of the game are good, if in need of some balance fine tuning. Unfortunately, barely a month after launch, it is nearly impossible to find someone online to play with. It isn't clear if this is because the game has been largely abandoned, or because something went badly wrong on the developer end, and the multiplayer is apparently region locked for reasons no one can understand.
Grey Goo oozes promise. I have every expectation that when we get the enticing sequel that the campaign promises. it will be a home run. But this first effort falls far short of the mark, and you should only play it if you are absolutely dead set on doing so. I went in determined to like it, and Grey Goo's remarkably bad campaign and nonfunctional multiplayer beat the appreciation out of me in no time.

As a Bullet Hell Shooter, it's one of the smoothest I've played, and doing it to my music is really fun. However, the ultimate 'thumbs down', however tentative (consider this a 6/10), is because the game pisses me off so goddamn much.
Mainly it's the Shadow Missions; they're just way too unforgiving. As in, 'you will probably wake up covered in someone's blood' levels of unforgiving. Say, for example, a Shadow Mission saying "Beat 3 Songs on Insane Difficulty." Fine.
Songs only count if they're 3:30+ long. Fine.
If you die ONCE during this song (considering you have like 5 lives from the outset so if you're any good you should seldom fail a mission) it won't count towards your mission progress.
This is where you're gonna get angry. REALLY angry. You could get to the last 10 seconds of a song and die to a missile you couldn't see due to the game's patented Seizure-o-vision, and the game will flip you the bird and your time will have been wasted. If it was an instant game over when you died, it would be a bit more bearable, but as it is? You're gonna swear, you're gonna break stuff, you're gonna fantasize about meeting the people who designed these missions and kicking them repeatedly in the crotch.
Back to the topic of the flashing lights, I started getting a headache within SECONDS of hitting the goddamned MAIN MENU. The photosensitive seizure warning at the start doesn't do justice to just how much eyestrain you're gonna experience. On top of that, the obnoxious flashing lights make it near impossible to see the, say, red glowing seeker mines or the tiny missiles that'll kill you and give a solid 'F U' to your current Shadow Mission.
I'm perfectly fine with games being difficult, so long as they're FAIR. Super Meat Boy is fair. Dark Souls is fair. In both of those games, when you die, it's YOUR FAULT. Here, though, you could die to something you couldn't even SEE through the flashing lights, and the game will essentially kneecap you.
I'm sorry but, for whatever fun I was having, I'm more likely to remember my foaming rage than I am to remember any enjoyment.

Woodcutter Simulator 2013 is an exciting simulation game. I would firstly like mention that games such as this must captivate you with its simplest mechanics - and WCS13 does exactly this. Each tree felled offers a rollercoaster of emotions, it makes one feel things that they have not felt since they were a child, emotions such as pure innocent euphoria.
I have "cut" hours from games such as DotA 2 and MineCraft in order to play WCS13, and I am glad I did. WCS13 has not only boosted my confidence and ability as a lumberjack in real life, but has also improved my organisational skills and ability to meet dead-lines. You see, the in depth job-assignment-system (JAS) requires the player to continually think about the most efficient method to complete the given task. Boy, those dead-lines are indeed heart racing. But they are as exhilarating as they are rewarding. With each cash payment for your job you know you are closer to purchasing the next vehicle that will further your experience in WCS13.
Despite all this, the creators of the game were still able to produce such a charming yet casual sound-track. The catchy, upbeat songs will have you almost jumping out of your seat ready to dance!
I give this game five cleared Brazilian Rainforests out of five.

XCOM is a brilliant turn based strategy game that puts you in the shoes of a commander leading earth's forces against an alien invasion. The premise is that the organization XCOM is earth's sole defense against an unknown Alien force. You lead a squad of 4-6 soldiers and battle an opposing force in either an objective based or pure deathmatch. From the start, every decision matters. You must make decisions that will keep your soldiers alive, gain resources, and appease the multiple governments who are unable to reciprocate your kindness. As the game goes on, your soldiers will either die or advance in rank and become better equiped and suited soldiers.
What XCOM lacks is a compelling story as well as it's missions. The characters of the story are there to provide help and really don't add much to the story. The story is also fairly linear and can sometimes be bland. The missions can also sometimes suffer blandness as maps and scenarios become reused. However, this is improved towards the end though this means you might have to grind through the beginning.
If you enjoy sci-fi strategy games then I definitely advise you to pick up this title. I also advise to buy the DLC Enemy Within and play that since it's the exact same as Enemy Unknown except with some additional features. For the most realistic experience, don't load a save once a soldier dies; however, this is a personal choice.

Like many have already noted, the first map is lovingly crafted and polished and I enjoyed it quite a bit. But that was the first ~15 hours. After that the story suddenly becomes inane, instantly predictable cliche. To further rise the problem, the core gameplay is obsessive map sweeping. You HAVE TO inspect every pixel of the map, because plot items are either put in generic containers, identical to the other thousands, or in hidden mounds you have to detect.
It also has (or had when I last played it) a crippling problem with sequence breaking. I run too far ahead in the game on the later maps without finishing the plot on the first one, got an item identical to a plot item from the first map and used it in it's place... And got a cutscene with a voice but no character model, because I haven't met that character yet (which in itself is stupid) talking about stuff that hasn't happened, because I broke the sequence... I just played the game as normal, and did stuff that seemed logical until it turned out that the devs did not intend it and didn't plan for it. That's a crime in an open world game, because I haven't exploited bugs or anything.
Plus, it prides itself in "not holding your hand" yet still employs map markers at arbitrary and unnecessary moments. That makes it so much more irritating and confusing because for the first 10-15 hours the game makes an explicit point to explain directions rather that point them out. Then suddenly map markers. Again, it seems as if the devs just got tired of the effort and just wanted to puch you through. Unfortunately, it happens at the first fifth of the game.
I didn't finish the game. I got about 2/3 in, then just couldn't be bothered anymore. I did search for the ending, to see if there was something to regret missing... No, it was excatly, to the plot point, identical to what I had predicted for the game. And what I predicted was the most cliche, boring scenario possible.
Only buy for a price you feel is acceptible for 15 hours of gameplay and lack of closure.

After playing Artemis Spaceship Bridge Simulator a lot I finally wanted to try Quintet, which I did consider a clone before - yet the developer himself states he didn't know of Artemis when he started Quintet (
) - let's just believe that.
So the first impression of Quintet was: A LOT more polished interface - it actually looked like a game from after 1995. It still also has its flaws (why do I have to go to sub menus to decide whether I want to play single player, multi player over lan or multi player over the internet) - but still the interface is a lot more intuitive and usable. Never enter IP addresses manually anymore.
On second view, it also looked like a lot more playable over the internet. I could just hop onto a server directly and start playing, very easy! In comparison, Artemis is really difficult to organize a game on the internet...
Additionally, Quintet features clients for virtually ANY OS: Windows, Linux, MacOS, Android, iOS, Browser(!)... that makes gathering your friends a lot easier.
The quick and easy start and very usable interface also took place within the game: Compared to Artemis, it's a lot more fast-paced, action starts right away, no big strategic planning from what I saw. This has its pros and cons of course: It's very user-friendly and beginner-friendly, but it's not as deep a simulation as Artemis is.
I've only tested Quintet over the internet yet. I love Artemis for it's social game factor - a bunch of people sitting in one room shouting commands & information at each other. As I've not played Quintet this way, I can only assume the following: Due to the fast-paced nature and the different style (e.g. all stations in Quintet have the full 3D view, while the stations in Artemis only have their specific computer system) I assume the game to be less communicative than Artemis.
My personal conclusion is: Artemis is best for deep and long play with your friends at home, Quintet is great for a quick spontaneous game over the internet, alone or in a group.

Enjoyable game overall. The beautiful art and music stand out and the developers seem to have actually woven some meaningful Choices & Consequences into the story of the game having some major repercussions regarding heroes and events. The downside to that is that they've built a lot of the more general "Choices & Consequences" and hero survival options aside from said rare events based on rather meaningless seeming "dialogue choices" presented in Pop-up screens, which seem a bit stupid and arbitrary and can come off as an annoyance, since 95% of times you're essentially presented with a dialogue and choices you have to click that very similar to this:
"Choose Option A if you want a strong item, 10 Morale, 20 Renown, 30 Supplies."
"Choose Option B if you want nothing to happen."
"Choose Option C if you want to lose 40 Fighters, 10 Morale and 20 Supplies."
And for some of the hero-based conversations:
"Choose Option A if you want Hero X to die."
"Choose Option B if you want nothing to happen."
"Choose Option C if you want Hero X to join your group."
Once you've figured out that the text and story-based explanation for said choices don't really matter that much and there's always an obvious "good" and "bad" choice and 97% of these dialogues have no consequences aside from that no matter what you pick (they could've essentially replaced the choice lore with what actually happens as listed above, since other than that it's mostly flavor), you naturally want to start to Min/Max said events.
Another thing is that the difficulty curve is weird, you start off with the game Handholding you through the first Chapter or two, making you think that you can take your time, smell the roses and play however you want and at some point the game throws "WAR!" after "WAR!" at you (in-game combat events), you got to use every bit of Renown to level all your heroes to stand a chance and there's usually 2-3 of them walking away from battles "Injured" and in every battle you got to try to get the cripples away from danger to prevent said from happening since there are no healers in Banner Saga. Then near the end of the game, after the two caravan groups meet it gets easier again as you got multiple Lvl5’s and the Mender that can repair armor and kill stuff diagonally with lightning.
Liked the combat system, having to choose for various enemies if to go for Armor or Strength/HP directly with consequences e.g. potentially getting the armor down but them hitting and knocking down one of your characters with full STR or starting to hit STR/HP and having to run around the battlefield with 2 characters left with low STR themselves trying to snipe the stragglers in the enemy ranks that can barely hit through their Armor because their STR got so low, using low-HP enemies as shields to block the live ones from getting there (since the lower Strength they have, the weaker they hit and with only 1-3STR left the chance to hit gets really low and Deflects happen a lot) or starting on one part of the battlefield and mowing down everything there before the enemies from the other side get there, Special abilities were helpful but not particularly Overpowered either.
The ending was kind of a let-down with a “Deus Ex Machina” character with basically super powers appearing from nowhere when seemingly all was lost and your party has been running for months and some of the story-telling can feel a bit sluggish due to tendency for unending Visual Novel-like dialogues with non-moving no-voiceover sprites for exposition. But overall I liked it due to fantastic art style, music and interesting lore (spent lots of time just reading the map descriptions and trying to figure out where everything is in relation to one another) and it left me wanting to see how the story goes on and what happens next, so it managed to convince me to buy the second part of the Trilogy.
