FTL: Faster Than Light Review
Indie star-ship management rouge-like.
:
FTL Faster Than Light has an endless amount of replayability, making it easily the best purcahse I have ever made from all of my library. Although it seems like such a simple game on the surface, the cominations are endless with you at times thriving with your 4 burst laser mark 2s, and other times scraping by with your dual laser and mini beam until you can repair your hull in a shop and hope you can even find a decent weapon.. IF you can make it...
Due to the massive amounts of weapons in FTL Faster Than Light, the replayability factor is huge. The game is extremely challenging for beginners as they try to reroute their power in every which system and even depower their weapons to put more power into their engines in hopes that they dodge a volley of missiles. The weapons are grouped into a few types: Beam, laser (projectiles), flak cannon, bomb, and missile weapons. Some weapons consume 1 missile when fired, requiring you to scrap missiles off of enemy ships or buy them in stores. With the completely free Captains Edition mod, 100s more weapons are added all basing themselves of variants.
The game at first is extremely hard even on Easy mode, I must admit. The game is so unrelentless to beginners due to the fact that you're forced to learn from your heart-breaking mistaks that you make time and time again, only to learn from that mistake and try to prevent it via managing which systems are upgraded and when you upgrade your weapons.. If you find any good ones in the shop or find any. After playing for about 40+ hours on Easy, I got really good with it, and I can make it to and usually beat the Flagship every run. Normal mode is essentially a middle-grounds once you're skilled with Easy, but Hard mode is total hell. Hardmode for once forces you to make some morally grey decisions such as stealing a package of supplies a rebel ship just dropped as you hide and wait... Oh wait, it turns out it was just vaccinations for the local plague.
The game is just awesome. For only 4 dollars as you can see I've gotten my fair time out of it, and I still play it. I will admit though, after about 60+ hours the game does get a little stale, but once you jump into hardmode it's a whole new story. Captains Edition is also a great mod to add on with this. The infinite combination of weapons and the entire Federation's life relying on your cunning and strategy is just great. You do get some morally greying choices that you may just have to make instead of being the good guy all of the time.
10/10 -- I would pay 30 dollars if I would have known how fun this would be; I underestimated how much I would play it!

Everlasting Summer is a visual novel that was made by Russian (or "post-soviet", yep) people and came out in 2013. In 2014 in English. Apparently it started as community effort around 2008 or so on the imageboards. And 'imageboard' never fails me to bring cringy memories of the youth obsessed with anime, anonimity cult and about how they are oh-so-alone, heh. But no one cares about my bias, so. None the less, it started in open development as eroge about imageboards mascots. Then development closed into a team, there were some drama, leaks, such. Due to change in scenarists it went to more "dating sim but suddenly srs story". And then they changed the guy answering for the plot again and it got another "srs story".
Mind it, I personally wasn't following game development, I've got all this info from one-two Russian sites.
And well, since the person answering for the latest iteration of the storyline didn't want the various images to go to waste he ended up using images designed for previous plot, creating a bunch of weird and pointless scenes that go nowhere.
Thus this game is a bit of mess. Kinda dating sims, your choices impact what girl ending you would get. It sure has that harem feel to it somewhat.
There are actually adult scenes here and there but they are barely the focus, you have to download adult patch off the site. In Steam version they are replaced with black screen and text never descripes such scenes anyway. I was OK with that. No need for pr0n in mah USSR propaganda.
That, and writing is something else. To be honest, it's not so bad in Russian languange. A lot of your times will be wasted with pointless one-liners of hero thinking something obvious or such. However I tried English version and let me tell you, it was a pain. I would not recommend it to English audience, some of those sentences just don't translate, don't flow well.
And not only that, the hero is just awkward. Especially in the first half-hour or hour of a game when you only get to hear his pointless oh so painful monologues. That is the worst part of a game, all the monologues about how he is pointless human being. It goes past just "anti-social" when he comes out of bus and instead of immedietly noticing that he is in front of camp entrance and going "OMG just like in my dreams" he somehow manages to not even catch it in his view despite it being in front of him and goes out somewhere out there and then curls down and cries.
Oh, and girls are stereotypical. There is in-canon explanation but it's still unfun.
The core, the main 7 days actions that you spend in the novel just isn't worth it. The endings are somewhat cliche, nothing amazing. Big plot twist isn't much amazing either, not good enough to make up for what you have to read all time. Nope, not even Lena. Because I played Higurashi. And so did the writers, as seen with mild jumpscarish pic-reference at the beginning of the game when hero mishears "Rena".
I mean, the writer himself told people that all the plotholes are just plotholes. From what I have heard that is.
So yea, the only way I people loving this game is either because it's the first visual novel that they tried or because it fits a simple subjective taste. Like, if one was around the Soviet pioneer camps. Well, personally I am too young for these. That, and there is no Stalinism. And I don't want Hatsune Miku panties shot in muh USSR propaganda, so.
Well, okay, it actually isn't that bad. Negative review doesn't mean that it's the worst thing ever, just that I want to show that it's not 10/10 game in this world of Valve's binary rating review system. If anything the writer can actually deliver real good work outside of original project. More exactly, YouTube out Miku's route, that is actually some unrelated non-canon story that was planned to be DLC before shoved into game as Miku's route, it's awesome. And then try to YouTube or beat game without getting any girls and maybe YouTube out the catgirl's (Yulia) route before trying out (whether yourself or YouTube again) One Pioneer's Story, the official mod-DLC, just check in menus. It still fails to explains the game world fully but it's an awesome read that gives some great backstory. Better hero personalities in both Miku's route and One Pioneer Story too (latter is known as Zhenya's route).
I think that the team has talent and can write some excellent novels and content, it's just that the very core main part of Everlasting Summer is suffering from being what I believe was development hell.

A great zombie game for any fan of the genre or someone who is interested!
Dying Light mixes parkour with zombie survival in a great way. There is an extensive story mode and many optional side missions to do a long the way. The map is farily large which is split into two main areas, its very detailed and most buildings can be entered. Safehouses scatter the world which you must clear out and take hold of to try and survive the night. The night dynamic in the game is also a great addition. There have been many adreniline moments while playing this game like running on rooftops in the pitch black with nothing but a torch and a horde of zombies chasing you. This game is truly one of my favourite zombie games out there.
The only problem I can think of with this game is the online experiance. Players will usually leave you for dead as well as stealing all resources/weapons. If you want to play with others I highly recommend playing with friends. Also Be The Zombie mode is a bit naff with not many players online to play it so you struggle to find a match, thats just my opinion though.
The new DLC (The Following) is a nice eddition to the game and gives it a refreshing look taking you to a new map with new weapons and characters and the new introduction of vechicles. Its a great DLC and offers a kind of "second game" on top of the base game which extends the game's play time.

I gave it more than a fair shake.  It hurts me to write this review.  I love strategy turn-based RPGs, and am sad that we don't have more to choose from.  This game has some great artwork and the characters are amusing.  I like the depressed overall atmosphere, which is very appropriate for what's going down.  I don't even mind the prestige system.  Yeah, it bites when a promoted character dies from an event, but hey, bad things happen when the world goes to♥♥♥♥♥♥ and sometimes that means losing someone I'm not sure I can do without.
If a game is billed as a tactical RPG (rather than, say, a virtual novel), then it had better damn well bullseye the combat.  Instead, TBS fails to hit the target.  The AI adopts a KO strategy, which is pretty standard fare.  The problem is, the player cannot adopt this same strategy in return due to alternating turn order.  It benefits the enemy when pawns are killed off, because that killed pawn's giant ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ brother now gets more turns to kick the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of your team.  The best strategy is to leave pawns limping and bleeding all over the battlefield with 1 HP remaining.  What the hell sense does that make?  The player cannot respond in kind because getting team members KO'ed results in lasting consequences: losing food for the army, or not dealing with a full deck next battle.  It seems a lot of players consider this combat system to be intuitive.  It's bass-ackwards to me.
If this were a virtual novel and I could skip the combat, I'd have had a better experience.  Instead, and I say this with great regret, I have to pass on the rest of this series.

None of your choices actually matter in this game. They might change a line of dialogue or some such somewhere but in short order the story loops itself back into the same place no matter what you do.
That in and of itself is not surprising in gaming. However, what is very frustrating is that your choices SHOULD matter. You aren't some minor sideline character in this. You play central characters making major decisions. But no matter what decisions you make, the outcome is the same.
With that in mind, what we have here is essentially a movie where you get to make some choices that masquerade as big decisions. Since there is no real gameplay to speak of, about the only thing left to critique is the story. And honestly, it sucks.
The game weaves you too deep into the Game of Thrones universe. As House Forrester (House who?), you meet many, many major Game of Thrones characters. How did none of this ever make it into the show or books? It feels much more like a cash-in on the popularity of the characters than a well put together story. In the end, the story just isn't believable.
TL;DR: You make a lot of seemingly important choices that actually don't matter. This leaves you with only the story to enjoy, which itself is very subpar.

Brains...
So it's an open world sandbox that has zombies in it. I guess that's interesting. Apparently this game is basically a better version of Dead Island, but I never played that so I don't have any reference there.
Standard-ish zombie plot: Zombie plague, lots of people die, survivors among the undead who are even worse, government assistance that's really shady and unhelpful, etc. The main character you play as is kind of interesting in the sense that he starts out as a hidden agent just doing a job and ends up getting much more invested in what happens thanks to plot events. Also I'm soo glad there wasn't a romance, because it sure looked like that's where things might be heading.
Gameplay? You kill zombies (and people) as well as do alot of first person platforming. Ok. My dislike of platforming (due to my lack of skill at it) is well-established in past reviews, but those were THIRD PERSON platformers. This is much worse. Some of the climbing parts of this game really annoyed me. The combat is a bit middling too in the sense that your weapons break constantly and your character seems to run out of stamina far too easily. It was only when I gained access to some decent weaponry and a competent amount of supplies that things started to tilt in my favor. I do like how guns have the trade-off of being good but also being a lure for zombies, even if it did mean that most cases where I used guns in the open world ended with me having to flee after generating a literal mountain of zombie corpses. XD
There's also this day/night cycle where you get more XP at night, but it is considerably more dangerous. I rather liked it, even if your only real options are to either run as fast/stealthily as you can or funnel the zombies into a buiding with only one entrance and use that as a killzone until dawn. The latter pretty much ate through all my ammo. XD
So how is the game? It's decent. Platforming can go to hell, the main villain who is doing a bad Joker impersonation should have died in a fire instead of how he ended up dying (Spoiler: the bad guy dies), and there never was enough alcohol for my Molotovs... but it was fun. Or rather it became fun once I had leveled enough that I could buy ammo from merchants and therefore use guns regularly despite them attracting zombies. Maybe I just like violence more than running around a city scavenging for string and other parts to craft things. I'd rather use those things!
As for all the online stuff, I have no clue. My internet is being a horrific pest lately and keeps dropping connection. It's really depressing. :(
I think i'll play it some more, but not to do all those damned side-quests. Rather... because roaming around a city filled with the dead has it's fun moments. Woohoo violence!

XCOM is a brilliant turn based strategy game that puts you in the shoes of a commander leading earth's forces against an alien invasion. The premise is that the organization XCOM is earth's sole defense against an unknown Alien force. You lead a squad of 4-6 soldiers and battle an opposing force in either an objective based or pure deathmatch. From the start, every decision matters. You must make decisions that will keep your soldiers alive, gain resources, and appease the multiple governments who are unable to reciprocate your kindness. As the game goes on, your soldiers will either die or advance in rank and become better equiped and suited soldiers.
What XCOM lacks is a compelling story as well as it's missions. The characters of the story are there to provide help and really don't add much to the story. The story is also fairly linear and can sometimes be bland. The missions can also sometimes suffer blandness as maps and scenarios become reused. However, this is improved towards the end though this means you might have to grind through the beginning.
If you enjoy sci-fi strategy games then I definitely advise you to pick up this title. I also advise to buy the DLC Enemy Within and play that since it's the exact same as Enemy Unknown except with some additional features. For the most realistic experience, don't load a save once a soldier dies; however, this is a personal choice.

to start this all off, i love the hell out of this game. so it may be just slightly biased.
first off, gameplay.
the gameplay is a top down strategy point of view as you try to clear a map that can go from a small forrest to 3 building with the alleys. your soldgiers start out crapy but as you advance, you unlock lasers plasma wepons, armor, jetpacks, and much much more. you can use anything from a nade to a radar scan to help in battle (equipment sold seperatly). the game can be very hard in the start. your guys have the aim of a blind grampa and can take about as many hits as one. you can two tilres away and can miss by a mile, which adds some comedy to the game aswell. there are two kinds of battle. land and air. the air involvs your fighter hunting down a ufo and shooting it down (or getting shot down). the land battle follows shortly after. the graphics are amazing by the way. so all in all great gameplay  PS: i personaly enjoy making litle mental biographys of my troops.
now we takle the base
the base is where you set up, well everthing. you can build labs to reserch new wepons, armor, equpis, fighters, and fighter wepons. then you have the workshop/ foundry. the worckshop is where you build most of your stuff that you reserch. the foundry is a more mechanical lab. here you can buy upgrades and unlock little combate robots that replace your soldgiers in battle. now we go to the hanger. here you can send your fighte to any part of the world and modify them. now the baracks. this is whee you can check out your troops and buy new recruts. as a nice tuch you have a memorial to any fallen soldgiers. i have personanaly mourned over many a comrade there. mainly due to the privet storys i make about them. then theres the oficers academy. this is where most of the good stuffs can be bought. anything from better squad size to half the time in the clinic can be bought here. oh and the stuation room. this is where the good♥♥♥♥♥♥happens. this is where you can sell extra alien corpses ufo parts, etc. to get monny and send your sats across the world to scan for ufos and get a better monthly income.
now the ufos. these are your primary sourse for tech for the rest of the game. these are the things you need fighters for. when shot down, you have the option of raiding it for loot. when looted, the UFO is turned into a special resource called elerium. this is used for most later game stuffs. then theres alloy. alloy is need for just aboot everythig in the game that you make. it is needed for the entire game. then there is the components. these are need for most mid game and late game structures (like the elerium power generator) and techs.  for example the elerium power generator etc. so to roun it out, the ufos are the "gate keeper" to most tages of the game.
to cap off this review id just like to say that game is very fun, and has its moments of sadness (the memorial) and its tence moments. withought doubt recomend this game. or wait and get the sequal.

A great game, if you like turn based combat, great coop multiplayer and a slow paced game that gives you 40+ hours of content, go and get this game, but be warned, any updates to this game from the publisher (or modding community) are unlikely.
A quite complete list of features and scores is available here:
Stat System:  8/10
☑A classic stat system that allows you to spend points as you like in any combination
☐There are no races or racial traits that you chose, everything is available
☑Most stats are easy to understand and everything has tooltips
☑Respec is available but very rare, so you have to plan ahead
☐Spell progression is a bit slow, since you have to buy skills at a random selection at shops in town.
☐Some paths have a slow buildup, especially if you lack gold or get a bad selection in town
☑Late game you will have about 15-50 spells, depending on your style
☑Spells scale with stats and levels, but some will become obsolete
☑Certain traits have a huge impact on your playstile like glass cannon or lone wolf
Items and crafting: 8/10
☑Item progression is good and you always find something new quite fast
☑There are rare crafting meterials you can find but also buy in the shop
☑You can craft anything without knowing the recipie, but you will find some of them in the game
☐Late game crafting makes you literally immune to nearly all elemental damage really braking the game
☐Some crafted items were buggy in the release version, but that may be fixed
Combat System: 10/10
☑Combat is turn based, but not restricted by tiles or anything
☑Every ability has a target indicator showing it's area
☑Every spell changes the environment in some way or another. Fire, Water, Ice, Poison, Lightning interact in a specific way together and allow for great combos
☑If you lack specific spells there are always alternate ways of doing things e.g. barrels with poison or fire etc
☑Animations when trying to target your spells slow down your speed, but they prevent too much boredom while waiting
Quests: 6/10
☑There is no guideline or hand holding involved in the quests, you can solve them in a number off ways that actually make you think and find a solution, not just simple monster slaying
☑Riddles and semi minigames, some of which are interesting
☑The game has a huge amount of quests and little details that you have to pay attention to
☑A semi open world that is divided in large areas so you have to load the game only once and play for a long time without interruption

Lethal League is a fast-paced fighting game that combines all the 'beat-em-up' action from Super Smash Bros. with dodge-ball. The aim is to K.O. your enemies by hitting an anti-gravity baseball into them while not being hit by it yourself. There is also a multi-player mode where instead, the objective is to hit the other team's target to accumulate points. If you want a different kind of challenge then don't fret, there's a mode for that too. In this mode, you have to work your way through a series of battles against CPU. If you want to brush up your skills there's also training mode. The game is currently lacking in characters and stages, but the developers are definitely planning to add more in future updates. Overall, if you want a challenging, competitive and fast-paced indie game to play with your friends, then have a go at this.

So, I keep seeing a bunch of posts on here and the website forums with people complaining about things that thye want to see introduced and how the game sucks because it doesn't have X feature or Y perspective.
Everyone should keep in mind that although this is a *cough* fully functioning and working game, it could still be considered in Beta mode. There are regular updates coming out for it, and the devs are working on many many things, and constantly introducing new aspects to the game. With these updates come problems. Such as 14.0 being released and Linux users seeing their game go to hell because of it. Right now, I think Quintet is absolutely wonderful. I only have 2 games on my Steam favorites and Quintet it my top one. Do I think it could use work, yeah definitely. no game is perfect(Except Portal and Portal 2. May those never die), BUT, I love how the dev team is striving for excellence.
I've already donated the $5, but if I had more money, I'd donate $100+ to the game. I can't wait until this game reaches its full potential.
---
so lets get into the gameplay: This game is fully functional for every player regardless of if they donate or not. When you download the game, you register an account through Quintet. This takes Literally 2 seconds. Once inside, you get the ability to make a ship, or to join someone else's ship. Each ship has 1-5 stations(Called consoles in the game):
Captain - gives orders to his crew, highlights ships for each console to target, sets the alert status, and chooses where the ship can warp to.
Helm - Flies the ship and engages warp drive
Tactical - Fires the weapons, and has the ability to monitor the hull status as well as each shield the ship has. Depending on the ship race/size you may have different weapons/looks.
Engineering - The lifeblood of the ship. Assigns extra power to the ship, but is restricted to one bonus in each of three categories. Monitors Hull and the Ship's systems statuses(minus shields), repairs the ships systems, and has 3 abilities ranging from teleporting to throwing down turrets, etc.
Science - Scans enemy ships, has 3-4 abilities like engineering, monitors the ships shields, remodulates your shileds, pushes/pulls enemies, etc.
Now, not every ship has each of these stations. Ship sizes range from solo(1 crew member, aka just you) to quintet(5 crew members, aka you and 4 others). the bigger the ship, the more people you can have on your crew, the "more formidable" you are, sorta. It depends on your ability to fight, as well as your race.
Now, there are 6 races in Quintet. Humans who are neutral to all, Zurna vs. Santoor, and Davul vs. Udu. And then there's the Hive. Everyone hates the Hive, but otherwse the AI race members will only antagonize those races who they are fighitng, unless they're provoked. Each race's ship has its own strenghts/weaknesses.

I have a thing for music games, geometry wars, and asteroids.  Effectively, Beat Hazard is a ombination of all of those things.
Because the gameplay is generated by your music your mileage may vary by a lot.  This isn't like Audiorsurf, where each song is playable if boring: certain songs are not playable at all.  The reason behind this is that sometimes nothing can happen in the song you're playing, or worse, monsters might spawn just before you hit a slow point.  The biggest issue with this game is that the music not only dictates monster spawns but also has a direct influence on your basic attack: You will not be able to kill things during quieter parts of the song.  This is absolutely game breaking at times.
Still, if you know that you can avoid the problem, and honestly I really like the gameplay.  Beat Hazard has changed a lot over the years, to the point that I don't really recognize it from when I first played it.  There's an overall level up system and some perks, but they're not so important to the gameplay (at least that's my opinion).
Unlike audiosurf this is hardly a chillout game.  This isn't something that I'll boot up when I just want to listen to music and maybe have something to do in the background: the gameplay gets pretty intense at times.  It's not necessarily difficult, but it does remind me of how harrowing geometry wars can get.
I like this game but I don't play it very often, and gameplay isn't so different between songs that it feels unique.  For the most part each song plays out pretty similarly, which is good and bad.
At the end of the day I think you should have this in your library.

If we could get past all the raging fandom for the game, filled with "Nep/Nep, would Nep again", I'll just be here for a moment to actually talk about the game in general.
Sound good? Here we go.
Hyperdimension Neptunia Re;Birth 1 is one of a three-part gaming series named "Re;Birth", which is a re-imagining of the original Hyperdimension Neptunia games. It's been given a much more improved battle system, graphics, and overall improvements here and there. We're given a revamp of a couple of old features, and overall the game feels more polished/finished than what it used to be. I'll admit that I could even play the original Hyperdimension Neptunia on the Playstation because it was so abysmally bad, in both framerate and just gameplay in general.
The concept of these games is a comedic approach to the console wars, in a world named 'Gamindustri" being the setting for most of the games. We have four nations that are comedic representations of the three major gaming consoles, as well as a fourth one based on a canceled real-life console: The Sega Neptune.
They are as follows:
-Leanbox (Xbox)
-Lastation (Playstation)
-Lowee (Nintendo)
-Planeptune (Sega Neptune)
In the world of Gamindustri, these four continets all have a Goddess that fight eachother over "Shares" which is the amount of faith the people of Gamindustri have in their respective Goddess. Things have primarily been at a stalemate, until one decisive battle leaves the Goddess of Planeptune in an amnesiac-like state, which is where our adventure starts.
Hyperdimension Neptunia has a bit of a rocky start with it's story-telling method to it's game. The initial start of the game is pretty much entirely directed by Neptune's whims/fancy. Neptune breaks the fourth wall often,  and references meta-puns that will leave you laughing, or at least smirking in the very least.
After Histoire provides direction, the story begins to pick up a little, with Neptune traveling from continent to continet to collect items that are important for her quest, occasionally meeting resistance here and there.
While cut and dry in it's execution, I don't exactly think the story is this games selling point. What -is- this games selling point however, is what i'm about to get to next.
Hyperdimension Neptunia's characters, as well as it's setting are the premise for possibly one of the greatest satire's on the console war's in gaming history, if not the best so far. Each character of the series is memorable in their own way, and as the saying goes: "Different Strokes for Different Folks" you will inevitably find someone in this menagerie of a cast that you really enjoy to watch and listen to.
Some of the locations in the game are obvious nods to various games that have came out (Such as "Hyrarule Snowfield" which is obviously a play on "Hyrule", from Legend of Zelda) so they also add a funny level of enjoyment to it.
Character interactions in this game are probably the main selling point for this franchise. There's plenty of comedic relief to be found with Neptune's shenanigans with other characters of the cast that leave you reeling in laughter.
Combat in Hyperdimension Neptunia Re;Birth is a turn-based system in which upon a characters turn, the current unit will be able to move wherever they wish within a "Movement Circle" and will be able to target enemies and allies with their targeting recticle, and up to as many allies/enemies as they can fit into that recticle.
You have the standard actions allowed in combat, such as Attacking, Defending, Using and Item, Using Skills, Running away, and swapping. However, the two functions of this game that make for interesting play is the "Transform" button, which is available to all  Goddesses, and the "EXE Drive" which allows your character to do massively damaging attacks in exchange for using bars in the Drive Gauge.
Combat is pretty easy to learn, and generally each enemy can be approached in the same way, which leads to a bit of redundancy/repetitiveness in the combat system. Some bosses and enemies in the game are legitimately challenging, so it's not just a cheese-through game, thankfully.
Level design is vibrant and colorful, though repetitive. You'll notice that some area's are literally just re-hashes of other areas, which makes for a small bit of dissapointment, as there's nothing particularly special about them.
If you're looking for a "Fun-Filled RPG Game with Humor and Enjoyment" then I can recommend this game easily. It's definitely a game that will keep you entertained and occupied. There's plenty to do, (and I really mean plenty) despite how easy the game might seem initially. There's a lot of items to collect, and stuff to unlock. So completionists will enjoy the subtle challenge of making sure they're grabbing everything.
Final Score?
Honestly? Probably get's a 7.5/10
It's enjoyable enough to warrant a playthrough or two.

The best Yu-Gi-Oh game to date, with the most cards available of any out right now.
Here's some tips to help you start playing:
1. You get DP just by surrendering, but you get triple the amount by winning. Grind the way you want.
2. When you win against an NPC you get 3 random cards (that you don't own) from their decklist.
3. The game saves after a battle or when you exit deck edit. This means you can buy boosters in bulk and exit the game if you don't get the card you want; log back in and your DP will be reset.
4. Beat the ARC-V Campaign first - it's a single tutorial level - and unlock 3 boosters with the most recent cards in the game. These boosters have powerful archetypes like Burning Abyss, The Phantom Knights, and Odd-Eyes/Performapal/Magician
5. We have fantastic fan support: thecardhub and the Yu-Gi-Oh wikia have lists for every booster and decklist. Use these to find the archetype you want to play, and grind away.
The biggest con is the DLC. Some powerful archetypes and important generic support cards are locked away in DLC, and I don't think they'll go on sale anytime soon.

Rough around the edges and barebones but for the price you are paying, it is better than anything that is officially available to the west.
Pros:
- Huge Card pool
- Earn points and purchase cards (unlike World Duel Carnival where all cards are available from the start)
- Abridged versions of Duel Monster, GX, 5DS, Zexal where important duels in the anime are played out with the option to play actual deck used by the duelists at that moment or your own custom deck. Finishing the duel once unlocks reverse duels and challenge mode duelist
- Challenge mode lets you play against Story characters but with a strong and competitive themed deck (e.g Mako Tsunami running Gishkis, etc.). Completing all stories unlocks around 90+ duelists
- Online mode where you can duel other players.
- DLC isn't a consumable currency like how most games are nowadays that would nickle and dime you.
Cons:
- Oozes low budget in every corner since presentation are barebones but understandable for the asking price
- Too expensive DLCs, I reckon $2.99 would be a decent asking price. Though DLC is not mandatory, some very specific cards and archetypes are locked behind the paywall.
- Quality of life settings like option to turn off/speed up animations, buy multiple card packs and open at the same time, manual saving,etc. are absent.
- Unable to set matches without banlist even when you are playing in a non-ranked match
- Lack the ability to give an AI a deck to use and duel against. This feature has been a staple in Tag Force/World Championship games on the DS and it sucks that it is not present here.
All in all the game is worth the asking price though it is a bit rough around the edges. Grab only the DLCs that you really want but it isn't mandatory. Take a friend or a few to play with in order to fully enjoy the game. Having someone as a duelling buddy that is also passionate about yugioh can really make the game so much fun. Let me first say that I *cautiously* recommend this game. What I mean by that is that I *don't* recommend this game to a wide number of people, but I believe there is a subset of players that will enjoy what Grey Goo offers.
Grey Goo is somewhat a return-to-form for some of the former Westwood team (Command and Conquer series), and that's very apparent here. The build, repair, sell systems bring back fond memories for me of eveything from Tiberian sun to RA3. The factions follow a lot of industry standards. Firstly, there's three of them. Second, one is very technologically advanced (ironically the Humans in this case), another is more rough-and-tumble (Beta), and the last is a force of pure destruction seemingly without conscience (Goo). See also: Protoss, Human, Zerg - or the equivalent in most other RTS games. That said, there are distinctions which make all three interesting - and the Goo provide a new sort of challenge because of their mobility. Possibly a challenge which still hasn't been properly balanced, depending on whom you ask.
Performance-wise, Grey Goo (at present) is merely acceptable. A lingering issue since launch relates to stutters and the inevitable slowdown that usually occurs 10 minutes into a match. I'm talking the difference between 90fps at the start and 20fps by the end of a match. This seems to be more an issue in multiplayer/skirmish than it is in the campaign. The devs have promised this will be addressed in the next major patch within a week or two. For reference, I played the game on a GTX 760 with an i5 4690k, but users on both sides of the spectrum from my hardware have confirmed the same issue.
As for the singleplayer, WETA's influence with character design is one of the stronger points. The storyline is certainly serviceable but likely won't surprise too much. Difficulty was recently more-evenly balanced than launch. Previously the game proved quite challenging even on the easiest settings.
The long-short: If you're looking for a new RTS and don't mind the above-listed flaws, Grey Goo is a game from a talented team that may be worth your time. There's a lot of love here, to be certain; it's just too bad it wasn't more fully-realized at launch. If, on the other hand, you're looking for the next competitive RTS, this likely won't fit the bill. The community is small at present - though most are very nice. It's hard to say what (if anything) the devs will do to promote the game going forward, but I'd be very surprised to see it suddenly become an eSports sensation. Still, I enjoyed my 51 hours with Grey Goo.

First off the story is great. The characters are good the branching paths decent albeit rather minor in a lot of cases and the background world interesting. That is where the good aspects of the game end. The combat.... god damn i have never seen a system so broken and poorly thought out and the strategic aspect is minimalistic and repettetice albeit not anywhere near as bad as the combat system. If you have patience then sure you can just ignore the negative aspects of the combat and speed through the game for the story and characters and walk away satisfied. But if you are in anyway interested in this game for the combat it's not worth it at all. Basically that is the main review imo if you want to read further its just a rant of how terrible the combat system actually is.
So the combat system.
1.) In my opinion the most immersion and balance breaking mechanic for this game is that regardless of the numbers of enemies/allies in a fight one ally unit goes, then one enemy, then one ally repeat etc. and the only exception is when there is only one remaining on either side. This doesnt sound to bad until you realize that with 2 enemies and 6 allies (default party size) the enemies can move 3 times for every once an ally moves. This means that it can walk up to your tank armor break, armor break one shot and you cant move that tank or defend. This also means your archers are all dead unless you set up traps or have the last enemies be crippled because the maps are tiny in comparison to movement speed. This works for you too so by all means bring 2 berserkers and slaughter half the map attacking 3-5 times for every hit the enemies get in if thats your style. It works in most cases but lacks versatility in some situations so i bring 3 which makes most fights a breeze.
2.) Humans SUCK in this game. Compounded by the first point humans (as apposed to varls (giants)) do not have the health and armor to reliably keep from dying when you leave 2-3 enemies alive as most humans even heavily armored ones die in 2 hits or are so crippled they are useless and a drain, Theoretically humans can be useful that is assuming the first mechanic isnt in the game. With humans providing support for the tanky varls up front or as skirmishers to take out enemy archers but given the mechanic the more versatility the less damage output and the greater threat of  unavoidable death in 6vs2s vs 3vs2s. Dont bother with them Varl have about double their hp and 1.5x their armor and even when you are down to the last 2 enemies or you mess up before that point and take a lot of damage they can still deal a lot and take a lot while if they were human theyd be dead 3 turns ago.
3.) Health is damage. This can work but not with rule 1 (theres a theme here i know) because with 1 and 3 in effect the most logical thing you can do is leave about a dozen enemies alive all on 1 hp. It goes random enemy random ally so the enemy will be forced to waste its turn using enemies which cant hurt you and are resigned to knock off 1 armor off of your like 19 (if you are using varl). Given that a lot of varls special attacks are AOE they can mop them up no problem making humans even less viable with few useful AOE attacks.
4,) The AI is suicidally annoying. So most AI in games like these are at least somewhat immersively programmed. They dont suicide for the benifit of their leader all the time and tend to stick to cover and formations like in Xcom as a random example off the top of my head, Not so in banner saga. You have a low hp archer across a flaming puddle of oil behind enemy lines around a corner and you will be trapped in an utter death trap if you enter. Of course you enter random hired mercenary because.... idk you want your team to win at all costs because you are a poorly programmed ai. Also with point number 1 they will go up the your guy who just moved and hit them over and over again as your other troops desperately single move after them. This isnt aaas much of a downside but it drags attention to the gamebreaking faults even moreso as well as making low hp humans EVEN less viable.
5.) Regardless of the strategical context your starting location is random and you cant see enemy turn order until you set up in the tiny alloted starting area you do have. For instance the context was that i was leading a battle we ended up winning with ZERO CASUALTIES between about 800 of us to 600 of them this was early game btw i didnt have the OP super leveled Varl late game and even brought humans (so naive). I specifically advanced in formation to ensure an organised push and the map designing RNG put me in the middle surrounded on all sides. -_- so what i thought i put the varl closest to the big enemies and my humans to the smaller weaker enemies. Turns out the smaller weaker enemies went first while i had my varl selected to go first so i literally had to watch as because i made a bad call bringing humans let alone human archers into a battle the enemies walked up and one shotted 2 of my guys before they could even retaliate. Like i said aside from those 2 injuries there were no deaths in a battle of hundreds and we slaughtered them. Also a theme here but maps making you spawn in random locations with random enemy turn order makes humans EVEN. LESS. VIABLE.
In conclusion. It makes sense in this game tactically to never bring the majority race into a battle EVER, to enter battles outnumbered very heavily, to leave as many enemies alive on low hp as possible and to think the AI will suicide whenever there is a chance to screw you over. I generally like gameplay which is balanced, allows for multiple strategies and isnt so incredibly backwards in terms of what is intuitive. It catastrophically breaks immersion and takes away from an overal interesting story. If you can ignore all the gameplay flaws you'll like it. I tried i really really tried to like this game but god damn i cant overlook its combat when it is such a large aspect of the game it is not worth it. Imo dont buy unless you have a high tolerance to bad unintuitive gameplay.

The best way to play this game is just defend your base until you have a huge amount of units and then kill everything that's in your way. Boring.
Aside from that it misses a certain "something". AgeOfEmpires, Starcraft, Command&Conquer - all of these games have a different style, interesting units, interesting races. GreyGoo however has 3 boring factions, a handful of boring units and (that's the worst part) a low player base.
Buy this game when it is on sale for ~10€. But don't waste 40€ like I did.

-Combat system sucks.  I like D&D style, a mix of tactics, character skill, level, and chance.  Also, it would be nice if there was initiative.  The Biggest gripe I have about combat is the turn order.  If you outnumber the enemy, their strongest remaining guys get multiple turns while you have to wait and cycle through your entire line-up to get the heavy hitter you need to finish the job, assuming he isn't hit 3 times and rendered ineffective.  Because there is no initiative system, you have to strategically deploy your guys and manuever your men, and the enemy, in a manner that renders the AI's ability to turn spam their heavies ineffective.  An initiative system would eliminate the need for this tactical trickery.  Though, combat is still fun, just not ideal.  This con wasn't enough to swing my recommendation to a no.

Grey Goo is a very unique RTS game that I think an RTS fan will enjoy. It is well polished, and has challanging singleplayer missions that will last you about 20 hours on normal difficulty. The factions are all different and some are, as far as I am aware, unique to the genre.
As of writing, the game is awating several developer updates to fix issues related to matchmaking, multiplayer maps, and assorted lag. These problems may turn one off from buying Grey Goo, and rightly so. However rest assured that the devs are addressing these problems currently. While there are limited multiplayer/skirmish maps ATM, the map editor/Steam workshop has allowed fans to create maps of their own. Combined with forthcoming offical maps and there should be alot of content to have.
Comparisons to C&C and Starcraft are natural and common, but IMO they are unfair. Grey Goo is just too different in gameplay from either to compare so lightly. Don't be fooled though. While you do a lot of face melting in this game it still brings a lot of challenge. With that many monsters to kill, if you are not melting face you are likely in real trouble, so bring your A game.

I have a thing for music games, geometry wars, and asteroids.  Effectively, Beat Hazard is a ombination of all of those things.
Because the gameplay is generated by your music your mileage may vary by a lot.  This isn't like Audiorsurf, where each song is playable if boring: certain songs are not playable at all.  The reason behind this is that sometimes nothing can happen in the song you're playing, or worse, monsters might spawn just before you hit a slow point.  The biggest issue with this game is that the music not only dictates monster spawns but also has a direct influence on your basic attack: You will not be able to kill things during quieter parts of the song.  This is absolutely game breaking at times.
Still, if you know that you can avoid the problem, and honestly I really like the gameplay.  Beat Hazard has changed a lot over the years, to the point that I don't really recognize it from when I first played it.  There's an overall level up system and some perks, but they're not so important to the gameplay (at least that's my opinion).
Unlike audiosurf this is hardly a chillout game.  This isn't something that I'll boot up when I just want to listen to music and maybe have something to do in the background: the gameplay gets pretty intense at times.  It's not necessarily difficult, but it does remind me of how harrowing geometry wars can get.
I like this game but I don't play it very often, and gameplay isn't so different between songs that it feels unique.  For the most part each song plays out pretty similarly, which is good and bad.
At the end of the day I think you should have this in your library.

Block N' Load is, in it's most basic form, a mix of Minecraft and Team Fortress 2 - a valiant idea, but executed poorly.
The issue with Block N' Load is that it's incredibly fast paced with 5v5 matches between selectable characters, one of those characters I'll talk about here; O.P. Juan Shinobi is, as his name implies, incredibly overpowered with a teleporting ability and a Katana that does ridiculous amounts of damage while at the same time, receiving little damage himself. Despite other people playing characters like 'Astie', who should, by logic and common sense, be more mobile, he is able to stay on top of them and in many cases, extend what the range of his katana should be, hitting people far away from him with his katana.
It wouldn't be so bad, if it wasn't for the fact that multiple players can choose the same character. I gave Block N' Load a good amount of time, and some of it is fun and entertaining, but the vast majority of it is just unplayable and unenjoyable from a player's standpoint, the breaking point for me, was a game where I faced 5 'Juan Shinobi' characters at once. It was an awful experience to play against, and every game with more than 1 Juan on the enemy team has been incredibly unenjoyable.
A few other gripes;
The game is so fast paced that it's difficult to actually figure out what the hell is going on. The tutorial is very poor and doesn't educate you on what you should actually be doing. You have a very small amount of time to choose your character, what blocks they'll take and then figure out what their abilities are, and then you jump right in.
I'm going to try and give this game another try, up to at least 6 hours of played time, but for now, I'm going with a 'No'.

Nothing would make me more upset that sitting through this game another few hours for someone to say, "dude...its only like 8 more hours of this before it gets good."

Near 5he end of this game, i was starting to get bored.

It took me 109 hours to finish the game. For what was essentially supposed to be an attempt at rushing through the story and largely ignoring the side quests, this was way too long for my taste.
I lost interest halfway through, when I realized that nothing I do in the game has any impact on the world or its characters at all. I help the citizens of Cyseal fend of the undead plague, I kill all the orcs who are threatening to overrun the city, I sneak into the mayor's house, kill his daughter, and steal all of his gold cups, gold plates and pictures from his walls (because why the heck not?), yet nobody acknowledges any of that. All the NPCs will ever talk about - all I'm ever able to talk about with them - is how they are  afraid of the undead and the orcs. Nothing ever changes or matters. How am I supposed to feel immersed in a world, where I can "break" into a vendor's house, take all of his personal belongings, and consequently sell them back to him? And by "break into" I mean I go into his (unlocked) bed chamber and close the door behind me, so he can no longer see me. Or I just abuse the invisibility spell and take anything I want from right under his nose.
Speaking of abusing mechanics : You can get teleportation spells and devices rather early on, which continuously  enabled me to do what essentially felt like sequence breaking by skipping locked doors, entering and going through dungeons from the wrong side, or just moving over ground the developers didn't even intend the player to move on (your characters are basicly locked in place, but you can repeatedly teleport to move forward).
Generally I oftentimes found the solutions of quests and puzzles, before I had even found the quest itself.
Now, on the bright side :
- The battles are a lot fun, and challenging for the most part. There are many different enviromental effects, buffs, debuffs and status ailments to play around with. And speaking of status ailments, D:OS is one of the rare instances, where any enemy - including bosses - is actually susceptible to status effects. A zombie is obviously going to be immune to poison, or a fire demon is going to be healed, when it's set ablaze, but generally not even the final boss was immune to disables, which basicly let me repeatedly cast a combination of spells, which completely stun locked him for the entirety of the fight, so he never even got a second turn.
The enemy AI is a little bit stupid, though. Many of the foes had more than enough damage and movement points to instantly kill my glass cannon mage during any of the fights, but they barely even tried to attack her, which is even more fortunate, when you realize that a dead character doesn't get any EXP. This is important, because there are no random encounters or any respawning enemies in the game. If you have a character, who missed the EXP for a slain enemy, they are gone for good.
- The game features a very complex cafting system, albeit maybe a little bit too complex. Unfortunately the crafting is locked behind so many walls of inconvenience, that you'll probably never even bother to craft anything. It starts with the recipies. If you want to know how to craft something, you need the recipe, which you may or may not find as loot anywhere in the world. Because the loot in this game is almost entirely randomized, it all comes down to luck if you ever find a useful recipe. Next you'll need to level up either one of the "crafting" or "blacksmithing" skills, which obviously takes away from your combat skills. And finally you have find AND create a vast number of different ingredients and tools to create something that you may never even use (like potions....or food.....or useless weapons).
To sum it up, the game felt like a slog past the very first area. It's unnecessarily long, and I really just wanted it to end. The NPCs and the game world don't care about the player's actions at all. There are too many broken or inconsequential gameplay mechanics.
I do not recommend it.

Company of Heroes 2 is just as great as CoH1, even better, I can't find that much negative to say about the game, only positive stuff. Great game, Great moments, Great community. Has one of the best campaigns I've played, minus two of the missions which aren't my type of mission. Stealth and Strategy doesnt go hand in hand. It does put both sides (axis and allies) in a bad light, but it's war, both sides did terrible stuff. TOW (Theater of War) is also a great new thing for the game, and really adds to the CO-OP side of the game. some missions even allow 3vsAI which is cool. TOW also lets you play on both sides (DLC doesnt, Case Blue is german side while Victory at Stalingrad is Soviet) So you can say there is a german campaign aswell, and it can be played in coop mode.
MP (Multiplayer) is also quite fun, I havent played much multiplayer myself, but playing with friends against the AI is so much fun, and that is what have kept me playing.
the DLC is great, despite some of it being overpriced its worth it. And thank you Relic for sometimes giving the community some free DLC.
TWFA (The Western Front Armies)
Is also great, even though I've only spend about 10 hours I can already say that the expansion is worth the money. The Oberkommando West is not like the other factions and really shows germany's economy problems at the end of 1944 with high priced vehicles, and resources being more valuable, but also gives us some of the heavy armor we've all been waiting for in a game, who would of have thought that we would see a Halftrack with infrared lights?
The U.S Forces are great too! really gives us some new toys, That we didn't see in the first game, and the ability to de-crew vehicles on command, that really leads to some interesting tactics, the downside is playing with the AI and seeing it steal your decrewed vehicle... Maybe you shouldnt let the AI get too close with their own vehicle crews?
AA (Ardennes Assault)
Dont' buy this campaign if you're not a SP player or intend to only play it once.
The campaign itself is broing, not much of a challenge. There is no strategy to the metamap. All you have to do is walk around the map with any company and win the mission. It doesnt matter whether your company is cut off or anything, you can do as you please. The enemy does also not get any penalties once you cut them from a supply line. The missions themselves are also not that great, most of them are regular Victory Point games, so just go play skirmish as USF? They try to make these missions more interesting by adding in special handicaps, so you can be so unlocky you have to wait for 5 minutes for resources, again boring. The descriptions of the missions are also very misleading, they make the mission look way harder than they are. They do also make it look like some of the missions are timed, eventhough they aren't. You can play the campaign three times, if you have all 4 companies, before you'll start to find it very boring.
The downside of the game is the war spoils (something like that), it works like the Team Fortress 2 drop system, only worse, I guess its bugged. But other than that its a great game, great graphics and great performance, mostly, sometimes delays appear when giving a unit an order.

Another Swing and a Miss for Blaze Epic
While this game fixes some problems of the previous game, it adds new ones, basically leading to no overall improvement. So thankfully, there are some changes. You have a health bar, instead of 1 hit kills. You also can double jump, and you can dash, which leads to better maneuverability and reliance on reflexes and not repetition. Another nice addition is you can wallrun up the entire wall, instead of 3 steps, which makes that nicer as well. There also seems to be a bit of a story, and graphics may be improved a tiny bit.
Then there's the problems. Like the previous game, as people have pointed out, this one still has branching paths, where one is the final way to go and the others are fulfulling portions of unlocking that way. This means not knowing and blindly running down the wrong path, and if its not the right one, all the backtracking. Same with even if you go the right way, you still have to backtrack, which is repetitive. But then, in the potentially dumbest design move I've ever seen, something no other platformers do, for good reason, every screen you have to clear every single person before moving forward. Theres no doors or energy fields blocking you, you just stop at the corner of the screen. So yes this means in parts backtracking, you cant quickly run back, you need to go around the screen killing each guy that takes 5-7 hits to die, and theres usually like 4-5 guys each screen. What if you accidentally run to the next area and back to the previous one? Oh you need to kill EVERYONE again. Or if you accidentally go forward and back in a door? You need to kill EVERYONE again. What about in those branching paths where you wanna go the top right path? You need to go to the exit to each path on the screen and kill everybody just to go the one way you want. It makes this game unbearable, and I can't imagine how he thought that was a good idea, unless he just wanted to inflate game length. Either way, the poor level design, mixed with this new terrible mechanic, ruins it. Here's hoping his other games aren't as bad as these!

This game is probably the most charming i've ever played. After reading through the negative reviews It's easy to notice that 90% of them complain about Uplay, which I personally had no problem with. Now lets get into the details.
From the trailers and images of the game, you can immediately tell how pretty it looks. This game is nothing short of legendary. The is very unforgiving, especially during the later sectors. You will be brutally thrown into combat with no hope of survival. Your oxygen will run low, your systems will get destroyed, your ship will be ignited a thousand times over.
This game is very much a complicated one. You need to micromanage a ship as it goes through randomly generated areas, each with its own random event. You can play this a million times and still be finding something new on each go. You will never be able to win the same way twice.
There will be times where you can't get through Sector 1, even when you find a good weapon and with a good ship, because an Ion Storm + Missile wiped out your systems. There will be times where you get to Sector 7 without finding a decent weapon. There will be many, many times where you lose in a harsh way that screams of failure.
Your first win in this game will be many hours into it. 4 hours? 8 hours? Each playthrough lasts between 5 minutes and 2 hours, depending on circumstances. Your first win will not be an easy one. Your first win will come as a surprise to you, at the last bit of health...
If not for anything else, get this game for that moment. Get this game for the moment where you win, look at the names scrolling through the screen, and find yourself proud for the crew who fought so hard for you.
This game has some flaws, though. The upgrade system is too linear in my opinion. Your crew doesn't get better little by little, but instead in massive spread-out leaps. All the ships pretty much end up the same way with the same systems by Sector 8, with maybe a few differences (especially with the gimicky ones). The game could have been improved by making the upgrades different, adding more events (every single 'you see an automated drone' or 'pirate chasing civillian' mission is pretty much the exact same), adding more enemies...
You will not regret this purchase.

My absolute favorite genre of all time, is RTS. It's been a while since we've got one, when I heard about Grey Goo. I was interested, the fact that it was an RTS peaked my interest... Then, even better news, I saw that old Westwood developers, Petroglyph was making it, Along with Frank Klepacki composing the soundtrack? I HAD to get this game. I was not disappointed when I got this game. It's a fantastic RTS, One of the best in a while. Grey Goo is extremely fun, and it's pure strategy. If I had to describe it in a summary? Think of it as Sumpreme commander and Command and conquer put together, a well made old school RTS, that gives me nostalgia. The Three factions are Goo, Human, and Beta.
Positive aspects of Grey Goo:
-The 3 factions are unique, and play very well. The Goo faction is unlike any faction I've played, the mechanics of it are extremely unique. For example, The Goo faction doesn't have a base, but instead giant blobs of Goo, which are basically nanocytes, that will split and morph into units. While Human bases have conduits that connnect them, and their structures can teleport along the conduits, restructuring your base.
-The Soundtrack... Is just epic. Frank Klepacki did an excellent job here, as slow paced themes will play when you are building up, and some of the most upbeat themes in the background when you fight make for some epic moments. The music most assuredly cannot be more perfect.
-Every unit has a purpose, none of them are useless. This is VERY unique considering most RTS's I've played have units that are just useless, and you can never use them.
-The user interface, and hotkeys are bound exceptionally well, you can do pratically anything with the Q,W,E,R,T keys.
-With the workshop included, and editor given out freely to the community, this game cannot run out of maps. I agree with this idea strongly, as this gives the game a very long lifespan.
-The way that the game is designed, makes it easy to learn, but hard to master.
-The AI, for skirmishes, is done very well. They play how you'd expect them to. As a bonus, they adapt to your tactics. For instance, if you were to go for air mostly, the AI would pick this up, and make Anti-air units to counter it.
-Most importantly... The game is very well balanced, there is no OP faction that dominates others.
-Unit designs are just excellent, I love the designs on all of them. My favorite designs are how the Epic units look.
Negative aspects of Grey Goo:
-Only four colors, for each faction. This is just a nitpicky thing for me, but I'd like an option to customize the colors, to give more than the standard colors.
-Very little starting maps, but this can be taken off due to the inclusion of the workshop.
-Some unfitting sounds. For example, the Beta Commando should have a strong sounding gun, I mean, it's a giant cannon. But it sounds like a pea shooter. But this is very minor, as all other sounds are great, and fit.
-You HAVE to have a good graphics card, and a strong computer. Otherwise, this game will not run well on it. The options might help, but if you don't have a strong computer, expect framerates to tank heavily.
-It doesn't really innovate, or take any changes. This is a very minor for me, but if you are expecting something new on the table of RTS, there isn't.
To sum it up, this is a very good RTS, Easily one of my favorites. If you loved the old westwood command and conquers, or enjoyed Supreme commander, this game is a MUST BUY... It's an excellent throwback, and one that gives satisfaction, and nostalgia.

First off I have to say that I enjoyed playing the Banner Saga (TBS) even though I found it “stressful” at times. Believe it or not, the story was actually affecting me – the pressure to find my clan a new home or even safe haven was unrelenting – and I realized later that the fact that I found it stressful meant that the game had succeeded, in a way. The story is told from two ends, from two perspectives. It’s a little confusing at first, but you get the hang of it as things pick up.
+ (pluses): The game is beautifully rendered, even though it’s entirely in 2D. This goes to show that good games don’t require high frame rates, obscenely expensive graphic cards or computers that cost as much as a downpayment for a home.
+ The score and authentic (I’m assuming) Norse vocals are mesmerizing and totally bring the game to a new level in terms of immersiveness.
+ Turn-based combat, with a perk system for different classes of fighters. There is also a pre-combat setup phase, for deeper strategy, and special items that can be equipped to boost stats.
+ Compelling (and unrelenting) storyline. You feel the clan’s desperation, and pressure to find shelter as you flee from place to place. Some players complained that there is too much emphasis on logistics and feeding your party; at first I tended to agree but after I completed the game, I realized that this was necessary to hammer home the desperation of the quest.
+ Believable characters and permadeath add to the RPG mix (games are only saved at fixed points). You lose a character and it’s like a kick in the gut. Should you have done something differently? Do you wait for stragglers or push on? Your decisions matter.
= (neutrals): I realize that the feeding of the party is crucial; however, I feel that the gameplay could have been better balanced in this area. Using fame to buy food? Seriously? Maybe the party can be auto-replenished at locations instead? Otherwise the player simply skews the entire gameplay towards accumulating food, which makes this kind of meaningless, because TBS is much more than that.
- (minuses): While the map is beautiful, it’s not interactive and rather pointless. I realize this is not a traditional RPG where you can backtrack and revisit locations, but the information on the map is difficult to correlate to what’s happening to you in real-time and where it’s happening. So why even bother having one?
Overall, TBS is a good game and I enjoyed playing it. There is some replayability, even though the story is linear. Would a character have died if I did something differently? I’m looking forward to playing the sequel and to seeing where the story takes us this time.

In this time of complete absence of traditional, well-polished RTS titles on the market, Grey Goo feels like a breath of fresh air. Following the classic C&C formula, it offers a welcome distraction from the more fast-paced, micromanagement-oriented games like COH and StarCraft. The campaign is actually pretty good, the story has a feel of a literary sci-fi novel to it. I like the interesting twist in faction design, with the humans being more high-tech and alien than the aliens themselves. The third faction, the Goo, is unlike any faction I've seen in any other RTS, and plays very differently compared to the other two. And of course, it wouldn't be a worthy successor to the C&C franchise if the soundtrack wasn't composed by Frank Klepacki. I definitely recommend this game to any C&C fan out there!

Such a dissapointment. I wanted to like this game, i really did. The story elements and quick time events really appealed to me. But there were too many cons to outweigh the pros. None of your choices actually matter. The story was lacking as well. Yes, we get it, bad things happen in westeros. We got that things are bad for the Forresters and well, they just only get worse. It's the TV show only the badass moments are fewer and far between and everything is really dreary and dull. The equation for Telltale storytelling became unfortunately simple. Bad things happen 90% of the time, chance for good things to happen, hope is crushed and more bad things happen in a completely predictable "twist". At this point i just expect the worst every time. Other than that all it's really just....unpleasant. Idk about everyone but I play games to escape for a while, to meet challenges then over come, or at least feel the thrill of possible outcomes but this game is great at crushing hope even before it starts, killing any real effect of drama and leaves you with a dreary documentary showcasing the worst of human traits.
A few notes on character development: Your rivals the Whitehills are pathetic characters. Lord whitehill acts like a fat whining bumbling child who doesn't get his way. Literally every other thing he says is an insult or a death threat. You can really tell the writers wanted you to hate the character but I just ended up hating the writing and unbelievability of the character. And just when you think you can't take any more, his son is even worse! The entire time I am thinking to myself there's no way these clumsy bumbling ♥♥♥♥s could rule anything. And finally, putting Ramsay, an invincible character in there was idiotic. He's literally there just to give you♥♥♥♥♥♥ Whenever I saw him I thought great "more b-tching through exposition." Or Whitehill, Gryff, or Cersei or....come to think of it this game is just people b-tching at you.
In any case you're better off spending your money on TFTB. It's absolutely brilliant and I can't wait for more, and pass on this drearfest. If all of you potential buyers think you can deal with the unfortunate parts (which is many) of this game where you literally just put up with unrealistic crap from whiney man-children with a god complex, by all means buy this game. The fighting scenes are rather fun but too few for my taste. I genuinely hope people enjoy this game who actually buy it. Okay listen... I just had to stop playing this game to write a review.  I am absolutely blown away with the quality of this product.  I have played every diablo clone under the sun, and this one is the only one to do it better.  This is the first time in probably 10 or more years that I played a game that had a story with dialog that kept my interest.  Every single game regardless of the genre has stale dialog, with barely any cohearance.  Each quest is meaningful, keeps my attention, and is just plain fun.  Most games these days are all about asthetics and forget that the "fun factor" is the most important element.  GD developers definately focused on fun factor.
The cons are few and far between... such as the sub par graphics, and the fact I can't get 60fps even on the lowest settings, even though in most games I run full trottle.  I have faith these types of developers care about their games, and will keep updating to make it run smoother.
The music is awesome! It's dark as hell and fits with the gritty graphics...  I feel a lot of 90's nostalgia when I play this game... but the 90's never came close to a product like Grim Dawn.  The soundtrack gets me so focused on the game I forget I'm playing a game at all sometimes.  And that my friends, is the key ingredient most hardcore gamers are chasing in our ravenous quest for the perfect game.
But the most important point I think I should make, is that when you smash bad guys:  ....it feels really GOOD!  I'm getting a much more pronounced dopamine release than from diablo, every time I crush a skull, then go through my prized loot, and decide which peices go with my set; a feeling not unlike ripping through christmas presents as a child, and deciding which toy to play with first.
Just like diablo, there is some mysterious trigger in my brain every time I smash something.  It feels the same as shooting off a gun in real life.  It's a mix of screen shaking, exploding flesh, and crushing sounds that make up this intoxicating feeling.
There are so many points I want to make....so many "little things" that no game ever gets right - but GD did.... So let me just sum it up:  If you were looking for a diablo clone and don't mind a little sub par graphics (and being a pig on hardware resources) this is the best experience you will have.  The price is ridiculously cheap for the scale and quality of product.

The game follows Semyon, a seemingly depressed twenty-five year old in modern day Russia that tries his best to isolate himself from the rest of the world. One day while riding a local bus route, Semyon is mysteriously transported to a Soviet Pioneer Camp. Confused and disoriented, he tries to answer questions such as how and why he has arrived at this place. Most importantly, Semyon tries to determine if what he is experiencing is real. At one point, Semyon looks up at the stars and asks himself,
“The stars in the sky could have died millions of years ago, but I can still see their light. Does that make them any more or less real as I stare at them?”
This is not an exact quote, but the best that I can remember. It was a line that stuck with me throughout my entire playthrough as Semyon questions reality, perception of reality, and the creation of one’s own reality.
