UPDATED REVIEW AS OF OCTOBER 27, 2017: Went from "Would not recommend" -> "Would recommend".... what holds true:
THE BAD / Ehhhhhhh:
While the game is $10 or less, you'll either get the base game and eventually sink some cash into pets, or research that the explorer's pack is the most worthwhile. Pets prevent you from pulling your hair out while farming mobs because if you kill 20 things in one hit, you spend 5 seconds looting all the bodies. Repeat that for more than 5 minutes, you're basically playing looting simulator 2017.
"Subscription" based services are sold at ~$15/month (30 days) and it gives a massive increase towards ingame currency via you paying less taxes because of the subscription.  However, you can bypass if you play smart and with the 1 day free option per 14 days if you save up your daily loyalty points. Use this 1 day per 14 days or whenever to sell all your important/expensive items before time's up to maximize money. Loyaltys give great rewards like increased weight and inventory slots though... so it's up to you too.
Combat is great, but like the issue with pets and high taxes in regards to selling loot in the marketplace (unless you have the subscription). You're also going to have low weight and thus won't be able to grind for long sessions unless you trash most of the loot that you pick up (which is also kind of counter-intuitive of having pets). This can be semi bypassed with putting loot on your mount/horse but if it dies then I think your loot's gone too and most monsters aggro on your mount/horse - even the really low level stuff. It's really just the stackable loot and up to 3 ish different stacks that you can store on your mount/horse too.
PvP IS based on your combat LEVEL and GEAR. More money = better gear. You can pay IRL $$$ for items to sell for ingame currency for this gear, but I really doubt it's that much of an issue to most people. It's just, PvP is not really skillbased unless you have the same gear as your enemy. HOWEVER, in terms of 1v1 and even 3v3, I think that PvP is more skill based lately as long as you have average gear (non-boss armors are viable if you understand you class's playstyle enough).
Don't think anyone has a full set of maxed gear because the rates at which you can upgrade armor and weapons from +18 to +19 alone takes HUNDREDS of MILLIONS of silver (ingame currency). Put this into perspective: you can grind maybe 10M/hr at best with RNG drops. You can sell $40 costumes in the game to other players for like 20M silver (they're about 40M, but you pay a 45% tax so let's just say you get 20M). And +19 isn't even the max, +20 is and the rate at which you can upgrade that exponentially increases in difficulty (people easily spend 400M+ to get the maximum success chance of ~10% from +19 to +20). Not only that, all gear past +16 will decrease in their enhancement number if you fail the enhancement AKA failing +17 will make it fall to +16. Also remember, you will have to do this for 4 armor pieces, 3 weapon pieces (so 7 total) in regards to this upgrading cycle. I'm not even going to go into the accessories upgrading cycle because that's 10x more expensive EACH and has 6 total pieces (2 rings, 2 earrings, 1 belt, 1 necklace). But hey, when you preservere and achieve your goals in terms of gear enhancement, it feels so amazingly great. Just know that it will eventually work, but it will also potentially take weeks per piece. Will you commit to that?
Overall, you CAN get by with just +17 and +18 based gear and it isn't THAT hard in my opinion to achieve, +19 and +20 is for diehard players, just note that it will take a while before you can do it (months). Pets are mandatory (so expect to sink ~$30 minimum if you just get the base game), it's not that P2W but the game is very grindy because of the harsh failure mechanics, and "endgame" is kinda like AFK minecraft Runescape simulator 2017 + gear&level based PvP. If you can handle that, get this game. If the game looks interesting, $10 or less isn't much to at least test out. Hell you could even try the trial version on their main website I think for free. One thing to note though... this game isn't very well optimized. If your computer isn't great in terms of GPU, expect less than 10 FPS on the lowest settings. It drops to 2 FPS when more than 3 people are around you and a pouplar town easily has more than 20 people at once.
=======================================
The Good:
You will get addicted to this game one way or another if you love to play an actual open world MMO. It is partly RPG, but whatever class (s) you play, you're not really roleplaying with them.
Because gear can be incredibly rare to obtain/enhance, whether it be from the Marketplace or actual grinding, once you get it you'll be hit with the biggest ♥♥♥♥♥♥ic reaction ever. Real talk. Legit. It shouldn't really be looked down upon as to how rare things can be, but take it like an actual challenge and goal to set for yourself.
The graphics to this game really are amazing, the game is in constant development and there's so many things to do on a daily basis. You will feel like you are in the game without a doubt. Even on the lowest graphics settings, if you really want to play the game, you will find a way to modify the game settings so that it will run for you.
Logging on will reward you with a number of goodies on a daily basis, even if you can't play often, you can just check up everyday and play for 20 minutes on the weekend. Even if you are competitive, people won't advance as fast in this game as you think they will. You will catch up, just work on yourself when you get time and you'll be near/at the top.
It doesn't take too long to get be in the top 10% of players. It takes ages to be in the top 1%.
I want to flip my entire dining room table and walk 10 miles away from this spot.

A fantastic way to start/learn how to play (and/or practice) YuGiOh.
GOOD:
-Has a fantastic tutorial, diving into every aspect of YuGiOh; really in-depth.
-Has a commendable campaign; five story arcs (YuGiOh, YuGiOh GX, YuGiOh 5D's, YuGiOh ZEXAL, and YuGiOh Arc-V.) that allow you to play as each duelist in each battle taken in said story arcs.
-When you defeat a duelist in the campaign, you are given the option to play the duel in reverse. This means, instead of playing as Yugi against Pegasus, you'll play as Pegasus against Yugi.
-Outside of the campaign, there are powerful "Duelist Challenge"s that allow you to go up against a CPU that's using an extremely powerful deck.
-When you defeat the duelists in the campaign and/or the Duelist Challenges, you get the recipe for the deck they used, allowing you to use it yourself.
-When playing as a certain duelist in the campaign, you get to use the same deck they used in the story arc/show. However, you are also allowed to use your own custom deck for the battle instead.
-When building a custom deck, there are many helpful tools that help you search for specific cards. This system can thin down the 7000+ cards in the game down to a single archetype.
BAD:
-This game doesn't seem to be getting updated very much. This can be a problem when new rules/ban-lists/cards are released in the future. (Let's hope it gets updated very soon.)
-The DLC (as of currently typing this) all together for this game stand at a whopping 85 dollars. There are some exclusive cards you cannot unlock in-game inside that DLC, too.
-There's a very small limit to how many decks you can have saved at a time (only 32). This can be pretty frustrating when you create a lot of decks that you like but have to delete some in order make room for others. Alternatively, you can just write down what cards you had in a deck if you ever want to recreate it again, but the luxury of just having it avaiable without having to delete would have been fatastic.
-You have to pay an in-game currency (called "Duel Points") on card packs in the "Card Shop" to get more cards. Now, you get pleny of duel points from just simply playing the game, so that's not the problem. The problem is, you only get 8 cards from purchasing a single card pack. There are around 775 cards in each pack. The game randomly gives you the cards, meaning that once you acumulate a high amount of cards from the card pack, you'll start to get duplicates... A LOT of duplicates. While this is true to buying real life card packs, it's just a very tedious system when you want/need a specific card (or, if you're like me, and you want all of them), you can't get it because you keep getting dupes, therefor wasting duel points.
-The multiplayer, while great, tends to get very slow/laggy at times. You can really see the difference when you play the campaign for a few hours or so, and then play multiplayer just once. It's not a super bad lag/slow, but it can be really off putting when you haven't gotten used to it.
-Certain monster cards have an attack animation. Sounds pretty cool, right? Well, it plays every single time said monster attacks another monster, thus slowing down gameplay for no real reason other than to show off that single monster. Some monster attack animations can last up to eight entire seconds or more. They would be fine if there was an option to turn them off/disable them, but there isn't.
-The game has an annoying effect prompt system. Certain cards will trigger the effect prompt every time you or your opponent does something, simply by just being in your hand. There are three options for effect prompts: "Default", which has the prompt to show up the most out of the three, "Simple", which allows you to hold down a specific button to skip most prompts, and "Pro", which does not show prompts whatsoever unless you hold down a specific button. "Pro" would be the best option to get rid of the prompts, but unfortunetly, if you do not hold down the specific button to show the prompts, the chance to activate an effect WILL be missed and therefor won't activate at all. "Simple" is what I myself use, but even then, the prompt shows up when there's no immediate reason to activate an effect; sure, the requirements are there, but I shouldn't have to hold down a button to force prompts off. TL;DR, the prompt system is pretty annoying and there needed to be a middle-ground between "Simple" and "Pro".
-On a slightly less bad note, the card artwork in the game is obscured with the logo of this game. It's not a big deal, but it is highly unnecessary and ruins the great work the artists put into making the art. (It obscures a pretty big chunk of the artwork. For example, in one card, there's a man praying to a statue. The logo obscures the man, practically making him invisible. I only found out about him being there by seeing the card's artwork on Google without the stupid logo.)
FINAL VERDICT:
Legacy of the Duelist was definetly the best starting place for me to get into YuGiOh. As a kid growing up loving the first gen anime on television, it was a JOY finding out I can relive all the battles that took place in it. (I was SO excited to fight Pegasus.) As I type this, I've put over 100 hours into this game, and have only just recently 100%'d the first gen YuGiOh arc, and have only beat just five of the Duelist Challenges from that arc alone (out of 19). So I'd say this game can be worth 20 bucks, definetly; especially if you were like me, and grew up loving the first gen on TV but never properly played the actual card game itself before. This is the best place to start.

Very solid game.  Extremely tight controls and a fair difficulty (whenever I died, I felt it was because I messed up, not because the game was poorly designed).
The main character is just plain FUN to move around.  She can double-jump, climb up and down walls, dash, air-dash and more.  Attacks (so far) include a basic quick attack and a heavy attack that launches enemies either horizontally or vertically (depending on where you attack from).  You can juggle enemies in the air, and even step on them (some of them?) for use as temporary platforms.
The environmental hazards are as deadly to enemies as they are to you.  Combine that with your launcher attack, and you have a 2d game that provides the same sort of 'kick the enemies into the spikes/off the cliff' fun as Bulletstorm.  Satisfying and often hilarious.
While there's an interconnected world that you occasionally have to backtrack in, each screen is its own little puzzle.  You have to defeat all enemies AND make it to the exit area in order to continue.  There are no lives.  If you die, you restart at the start of the current *screen*, which removes a lot of the frustration from the game.
I mentioned backtracking.  I've only had to do it once, so far.  (You come across a locked door in the middle of a screen.  The key is found a few screens later.  You must then go back to open the door.)  Unlike many other games, this didn't feel like a chore.  The puzzle-y nature of the screens meant that going backward felt like a completely different challenge than going forward the first time.
Art design is good, with two exceptions: ledges and pipes that you can climb on can occasionally melt into the non-interactive background.
At time of writing, the full price for this game was $2.19 CDN, or about $1.99 USD.  At that price, this game is an absolute steal.  It's easily worth five times that.  Highly recommended.

If you've played a Blaze Epic game, then you're likely familiar with the common elements of their brand DNA. You're going to run, jump, and take on hordes of enemies in a screen-at-a-time retro platformer world straight out of a third-gen-console's heyday. You're going to encounter some interesting freerunning, wall-rebounding and midair mechanics, as there are notes of flight to be found in every game. Some people just don't get along with gravity, and I sense with every new Blaze Epic title that Blaze himself -- coder/musician Larry Stover -- dreams of momentum as an expression of will and spirit, and of horizontal surfaces as just a little boring, frankly.

Some people just want to run, gravity be damned, and if you're one of them, I think you're going to like Ninjahtic Mind Tricks.

Its predecessor Ninjahtic featured some splendid conservation-of-motion wall jumps, and introduced to the Blaze Epic game stable simple but significant stealth elements -- enemies spot the protagonist, wait for a clear shot, and take it, when in range. Careful planning of timing, sneaking up behind enemies, yielded easier kills with less risk, and careful timing of jumps even allowed our hero to springboard off of "stomped" enemies and gain extra air time.

Ninjahtic Mind Tricks sees our hero return with expanded parkour chops, now able to run up vertical surfaces, double-jump, dash, and execute two types of attacks -- both offering slightly different strategic advantages, and best explored carefully during the introductory test battle. The action's springier, wilder, and twitchtastic -- the game regularly moves at speeds that require one to commit sequences to muscle memory, and those "unlimited lives" will come in handy -- as will the opportunity to sit at screen's entrance on many levels, study the enemies, and plan one's attack carefully. Once you commit to act, once you leave the safety of being unseen and leap out to strike, to travel, to act, you will need to execute exactly what you committed to muscle memory. The game is magnificently unforgiving of indecision from its player, of pausing to think, mid-leap. Think first. When you act, act with a polished inner mirror, its surface free of dust.

It's really rather uncanny, how quickly this game pulls you into that headspace, forces you to think and react like the ninja you're playing. While Ninjahtic Mind Tricks has superficial resemblence to other Blaze Epic titles, this isn't the sublime swordsmanship and crowd-brawl tactics of Shin Samurai Jazz, nor is it the weighty, meaty, Prince of Persia-esque freerun-and-fight of Way of the Pixelated Fist. It's even quite different from the first Ninjahtic, faster, twitchier, wilder, even more anchored in plan-then-execute clarity. Going back to Ninjahtic after playing it, I feel heavy, and a little slow.

The game's static level-screens don't scroll, and you'll be glad for that -- you can see all the action at once, track all the obstacles, enemies, and environmental variables at once. You'll also be glad for that life bar; it makes mistakes a touch more forgiving, but you'll likely soon aim for no-damage runs through each stage. (That ranges from plausible to hair-tearingly hard, in places.)

Of the stable of Blaze Epic games, this one's the fastest-moving, requires the most planning per stage, and once you enter its zone and commit its moveset to twitch-memory, conveys the sense of impossible, breakneck flowing motion and GO GO GO GO GO like none of its siblings. This game is, I think, Blaze Epic's current masterpiece, even if my personal favorite remains Shin Samurai Jazz. I love Jazz for its atmosphere, particularly evocative soundtrack, and curious juxtaposition of noir and late Tokugawa/early Meiji ronin stories. It was a thematic masterpiece and a solid game besides, but Ninjahtic Mind Tricks features a solid narrative and a downright masterfully tuned game that, I believe, commands even greater attention. It's a joy to play, and the feeling of guiding our protagonist at speed, translating plans to finger-twitches, and executing them in a moment of hyperattention followed by a gasp of "I'm...still alive, wow!" -- well, it really captures a bit of that breakneck ninja experience.

How many games can we say that about, really? Many game immerse us, yes, and present challenge, but how often does a game successfully translate the experience of being its protagonist to the player? This is no first-person shooter; this is a tiny retro platformer with chunky graphics. That it manages to convey something meaningful about the world it depicts, that it's immersive at all, to any degree, is quite an achievement.

This is quite possibly the best expression of the ninja platformer I've ever played, and I'm really blown away by how much nuance is crammed into such a tiny game with such a straightforward, finite move set. This isn't a genre I realized was lacking anything, mind you, until Blaze Epic came along and started writing new games. I didn't think there was anything left unsaid by the many historical titles past. Ninjahtic Mind Tricks isn't just a great ninja platformer, it's a reason to revisit the entire genre of ninja platformer games, because there's more to say about 'em, and Blaze Epic just said it.

This is absolutely worth the two bucks, and a one-man game shop who's this devoted to bespoke, mastercraft little platformers like this is worth watching very closely.

Child of Light narrate the story of a future princess that wish to save his father from his deadly loneliness through a long journey to a new world where she was sent away from her father.
The story, music, voices and graphics make that game become a tantalizing work of art which will please teenagers and adults.
Fighting are subtle as you may have a lot of mechanisms to work with beginning with your first partner a firefly. Your new partner will help you to slow down one enemy or heal the wound of one of your partner at time using its own power. You will need the mouse? or the right controller stick to move him.
You'll then have a lot of friends to help you in your journey. All of them including you have their own skills, and a 3-branch skill tree to master. You can only use 2 character at time but can switch to another one when one of your ally is about to be ready.
Also during your quest you'll find some occuli shards, which after being crafted are stronger than before. Every occuli have its own power depending of the color and the size of it. An Occuli can be equipped to one of the three slots of each character. Finally Occulis have a different powers depending on which slot they are assigned.
The game difficulty can be set to normal or hard mode whenever you want. The hard mode makes mostly bosses becoming real bosses as you'll need to be smarter than them. Some boss may be frustrating but preparing a strategy will help a lot to slay them all.
The game doesn't stop there. Indeed the game features some puzzles about a dozen where you need to use the help of your firefly friend or use some objects to interact with.
There is also a whole new world to discover revealing some 'confessions' which are the game's collectibles, star dust (item that can instantly increase one stat of any ally), treasure chests (that may have occuli shards or potions), quests givers (several), lots of foes and many healing plants.
I can only strongly recommend you that game if you love RPG games !
Perhaps one of the most frustrating mechanism of the game is the interuption feature. If your character is hit by a foe while casting a spell or only using a potion, he is interupted and pushed backward. But you can hope that the other ally will be hit or defend yourself waiting for the right time. You can also always rely on your firefly friend. So there is almost always a way to avoid that.

The Banner Saga was one of those games that came out of nowhere and really suprised me. A great mix of choose your own story adventure and tactical combat. Odd at times, but as a whole a great game.
The Banner Saga's art style is what initially drew me to the game. I loved the beautiful hand drawn backrounds and 80's cartoon style cutscenes. However few and far between they were.  The characters in The Banner Saga are also all hand drawn and look fantastic, With slight movements to give each of  them some life and characteristics. The only frustration I have with the art style would be that I wanted more. More animation; More cartoon style cut scenes.
Then comes the soundtrack. There is not is not much to say about The Banner Saga's music exept that it is very good. A great soundtrack that fits the nordic  feel of the game.
Next is The Banner Saga's story; which is one of doom and glome. You will play as aViking leader in charge of a caravan. Trying to outrun or defeat the drege menace (an army of inteligent and feirce golem peoples) who have begun to poor across the world (again). It will be your decisions that decide the fate of the 100's of people in you company. Including main story characters who can die perminatly and will not show up in future Banner Saga games.
From the first moments of the game you will notice that Banner Saga's overall story is pretty weak, The overall narative it is trying to tell is fuzzy at best. Leaving to many unanswered questions and plot points that pop up out of nowhere.  That said, the game regains most of its glory in its character interactions. Making you care at least a little bit about each of the people your are in charge of. Watching one of the main characters charge head long into certain death. Axe at the ready. Was one of the best feelings I had in the game. It's  the decision making and tense moments between life and death of a character that will keep the story intresting.
Which leads into the games difficulty settings, which can make The Banner Saga a brezze. Or an absolute chore. On easy difficulty the game is basicly story mode. Allowing players to march through the various battles and challanges without having many wounded characters. Which is a very big deal, as the gameplay focus greatly on attrition and how you can work around non-ideal conditions. On Hard mode however the games difficulty ramps up so much so that the game can feel unfair at times. In my playthrough for example. I had so many playable characters, that I couldn't level them all effectivly. Leaving four or five of them far to weak to help in combat. This is a small gripe considering that you can simply prioritize a few characters, but it would have been nice to see some of the other bad♥♥♥♥♥vikings swinging thier axes in battle.
That brings us to the combat . On offer here is a Tactical Turn Based system. In which the player,  alternates moving or attacking with one of thier characters, then the enemy takes a turn. Moving and fighting this way until the battle is over.  The Banner Saga shines because of it's unique combat mechanincs.
For starters. Units on ythe battlefield have two basic stats. Armour and health. Not to go too deep into I will say that Health is a character attack / damage and there overal hit points. Meaning that the less health they have the less damage they will do and when Health reach zero a character is knocked out of a fight.. Armour on the other hand is a shield that blocks incomming damage. Other than that each character has a special ability. Anything from a besereker attack that slashes an enemy to pieces or a shield wall attack that helps with defence.
Combat feels unique enough to stand on its own. A hard thing to say in the realm of turn based strategy games. With the only fualt being that some battles feel more like puzzles than tactical situations, but those are so far and few between that its only a small gripe.
I  very much enjoyed my time with The Banner Saga. It's characters were odd, unique and badass all at the same time. Its world was bright, beautiful and engaging. And although the game can be frustrating at times,  I think the reason I like The Banner Saga the  most is becuase it's  somthing diffrent. And for  only 20$ The Banner Saga is a must own .

Overall this is an excellent game.  Shockingly it  brings both excitement and tension to ATB style turn based combat, a feat few games can manage.
Starting with the bad to get it out of the way:
-The characters and story seemed to have been designed with the hopes of being whimsical and wonderful, but to me they fell flat.  It doesn't help that all speech is in rhyme (with the exception of one character), a feature I found more annoying than endearing.
-The ending is very abrupt, and leaves one with the sense that the developers were encouraged to cut the game short in favor of other projects.  My play through was less than 15 hours, even with a hearty helping of side-quests and general exploration.
Now on to the good:
-Tricks, traps, and puzzles are scattered throughout the levels as well as a plethora of useful treasures. This makes exploration both interesting and satisfying.
-The mouse is fully integrated into the game in the form of a helpful light spirit who can gather certain treasures and stun enemies.  I was surprised just how engrossing this small addition can be, as it draws even more of your attention into the game as you consider both what to do with your character and her spirit companion simultaneously.
-All party members have unique specialties and are readily swappable during combat, opening a wide strategic field from which to choose your methods for defeating the enemy.  Played on Expert mode, you will need them all!
-Played on Expert mode, combat is tense and thrilling.  Each character, both ally and enemy, appears on the shared ATB bar, moving at different speeds according to their speed.  When they select an action on their turn, they then move into the "Casting" section of the bar.  If struck during the casting phase, they will be interrupted and set back significantly on the bar!  Being that your spirit companion can be used to slow monsters (yay for mouse integration!), you must now carefully consider how to manipulate the bar to ensure that the enemies are the ones to be stunned rather than your party, and mistakes can turn even a normal battle into a desperate struggle!  This extra dimension is, quite frankly, genius.  I have never been so engaged in ATB style combat.
Overall, though Child of Light is a short game, I would still absolutely recommend it for the current $15 price tag.  Don't miss out on this one!

On this review, I will be writing the pros and cons instead of just telling you how good the game is. I just wanted to say that this is an awesome RPG with beautiful graphics and with a great mix of platforming.
Now let us talk about the bad parts of the game(Don't let this convince you into not getting the game if you were thinking about it).

As everyone is saying a great throwback to the old C&C style RTS games.
The UI is very well thought out and then done very well too. Almost everything of importance you need is under a few QWERT clicks if you need to build anything, might get a bit getting used to but once you got the hang of it, it's very fluid and feels very natural.
I find it fun t see the Humans be the most advanced race for a change. You don't see that often in sci-fi and was fun to see something out of the norm on that. Most of their units are AI drones.
The Beta are an alien race less advanced, and you start the campaign with them. Both them and the Humans play rather similar even if the Beta are less exposed to AOE attacks, which the various epic units, especially the Goo's and Beta's are good at.
the Goo really do play differently, they are like nanomachines. Sort of like the zerg from Starcraft but then self replicating nano machines. They are grey and form large blobs from which they build their units. Hence the name of the game. They are the Grey Goo.
The Single player campaign is engaging and has a good story. And the vids that tell the story are extremely well done, with great voice acting too.
However. It is a rather short campaign. All told, about 15 hours long. Took me a bit less.
The AI can put up a fight, depending on how you like to play yourself. Myself being more a defensively minded person, it can be a bit tricky at times as the general rule of thumb seems to be to take the offensive early on and get as many resource hubs as you can as quick as you can.
I like how you have to make certain choices in what tech skills you're gonna go with. But... Having said that... Some of the tech skills just seem to be alot better then the other potentials in the group. Basically. All 3 races have 5 grups of tech skills and every group has 3 choices in them. But you can only ever choose one in each group.
But some of the choices jjust seem so much better then others. For instance. All 3 races have an anti-air land unit. But all races have a skill to make it so that that unit can also attack ground forces, making that unit immediately much more viable and important. Especially as it's usually a rather strong unit too.
But this is more a balancing issue they should be able to patch out in the future. It is not a big thing and doesnot detract from the game.
Where the game does lack is in the Skirmish and Multiplayer mode. Note that as I write this, I have not yet had time to try out multiplayer. But seeing problems that I do feel should be mentioned for people that want to do multiplayer. For now too few maps, but that will get better in time, so not a long term issue. But needs to be mentioned that they could've added a few more with a bit more variety in them nonetheless.
The AI oppononent can make it tough on you. But depends on how you yourself play. My advice against the comp is to be agressive. Just keep pumping out units and take as many resource nodes as you can. Especially with the humans this is no problem, as the harvester building is safe in your camp and the extractor is free of charge with that so you can rebuild it whenever you loose a node.
In multiplayer... The humans have a huge weakness that will be exploited. All their buildings need to be connected to powerlines. Which can be destroyed too easily. Don't get me wrong. You'll loose quite a few troops to this, and you can make make tech upgrades to mitigate this. But when the Epic units start hitting the field. This will be a huge problem to Human players.
The betas are much less vulnerable to this as their bases are much more spread out. Having said that. the Humans defensive structures probably still are the strongest in the game. For the rest these two play very tradionally.
The goo don't have buildings and are far more mobile. And their goos from which they build their units can all traverse mountains that other normal Beta and Human forces can't cross. As I said above the best analogy I can think up of as I type this is that they are like the Zerg. Even if zerging might not be the best tactic from the start. All of their units I think are less powerfull then the others units. So you need numbers with them to win. Still... Harassing attacks will do wonders with them.
As I said. The Umans might have a large weakness. I'm not sure how it plays out in Multiplayer. But I hope it won't be too bad and if it is... Then I hope that the devs can do something to balance that issue better.

Okay listen... I just had to stop playing this game to write a review.  I am absolutely blown away with the quality of this product.  I have played every diablo clone under the sun, and this one is the only one to do it better.  This is the first time in probably 10 or more years that I played a game that had a story with dialog that kept my interest.  Every single game regardless of the genre has stale dialog, with barely any cohearance.  Each quest is meaningful, keeps my attention, and is just plain fun.  Most games these days are all about asthetics and forget that the "fun factor" is the most important element.  GD developers definately focused on fun factor.
The cons are few and far between... such as the sub par graphics, and the fact I can't get 60fps even on the lowest settings, even though in most games I run full trottle.  I have faith these types of developers care about their games, and will keep updating to make it run smoother.
The music is awesome! It's dark as hell and fits with the gritty graphics...  I feel a lot of 90's nostalgia when I play this game... but the 90's never came close to a product like Grim Dawn.  The soundtrack gets me so focused on the game I forget I'm playing a game at all sometimes.  And that my friends, is the key ingredient most hardcore gamers are chasing in our ravenous quest for the perfect game.
But the most important point I think I should make, is that when you smash bad guys:  ....it feels really GOOD!  I'm getting a much more pronounced dopamine release than from diablo, every time I crush a skull, then go through my prized loot, and decide which peices go with my set; a feeling not unlike ripping through christmas presents as a child, and deciding which toy to play with first.
Just like diablo, there is some mysterious trigger in my brain every time I smash something.  It feels the same as shooting off a gun in real life.  It's a mix of screen shaking, exploding flesh, and crushing sounds that make up this intoxicating feeling.
There are so many points I want to make....so many "little things" that no game ever gets right - but GD did.... So let me just sum it up:  If you were looking for a diablo clone and don't mind a little sub par graphics (and being a pig on hardware resources) this is the best experience you will have.  The price is ridiculously cheap for the scale and quality of product.

If you are a fan of Action RPG's then you will enjoy the time sink that Grim Dawn requires. The game is slow in the beginning though still being fun. In the late game Elite-Ultimate difficulties this is where you can test out how your build is preforming. Grim Dawn has a unique system: Attribute points Physique,cunning,spirit otherwise known to some as Strength,Dexterity and Intellect.
They have 6 different classes to pick from Shaman,Arcanist,Nightblade,Occultist,Demolitionist and Solider.
Each character you create has the option to choose 2 different classes to combine into there ultimate character.
There is also a Devotion skill point system, you must unlock shrines across the map to get a point you have a maximum of 50 points. It runs on a joint the dot basis, one point into a devotion object you unlock certain character traits you gain benefits from completing a devotion tree  you gain bonus points.
To a new player of Action RPGs you are looking at around 100-200 hours of solid gameplay. To a veteran of the genre you are looking at around 50-100 hours before you decide to create a second character.

So far Black Desert Online has been a good experience: its very sandboxy and you can spend days doing many different activities. Want to become a trader? Get a cart and plan some trade routes. Want to be a horse breeder? Go tame some wild horses, level them up, and breed them together to get some great mounts. You can create an NPC ran production empire where you just feed your workers some beer to keep going.
Many aspects of the game feel like it's a single player game with some oddly-scripted npcs running around and gathering around the storage areas or fishing, but the multiplayer aspect of the game (PVP) is alive and well.
My main con for this game is the marketplace, where you trade items. To be brief, it's laggy as hell and getting the items you want can be near-impossible. Since the game has came out, i've probably bid on 130+ pearl shop items on the marketplace with no luck so far. I understand that a lot of people are bidding on them, but come on.
If this game goes on sale again for $5, I plan on gifting a copy to all of my main gaming buddies.

It's Asteroids, the Epilepsy Edition.
Beat Hazard is a very fun arcade shooter where you pilot a ship, power it up, and destroy anything in your way, all to your own music. The control is great (allows for keyboard or controller) and the effects are pretty amazing, very bright and colorful. Also, there are many additional ships by designers in the Workshop, so experimenting around with other people's ships (and making your own) adds to the fun. The intensity of the enemy waves increases based on difficulty level and the intensity of your music. Obviously, some genres of music will be more preferable than others.
If you're going to get this game, I highly recommend getting all the DLC. iTunes support will obviously let you play your iTunes files, Shadow Ops gives you objectives to complete in the game to raise your rank (allowing you to pick certain ships in the Workshop), and Ultra will add a wider variety of enemies (and probably other stuff, I don't know).
Overall, Beat Hazard is a fun game that I keep coming back to periodically as a stress-reliever. Sometimes you just wanna blow sh*t up and listen to your favorite music, and this game does a great job of combining them both.

Lethal League is what its game description says: a 2D fighter where players hit an anti-gravity ball and yadda yadda, but that's not important.
What is important, is just how plain effin fun this game is. Just the joy of smacking a ball with a skateboard while playing as a super advanced robot wearing a sleaze hat and KOing someone just gets me off. The mechanics are easy to learn, but hard to master. Be prepared to get your♥♥♥♥♥♥kicked by the AI when trying to learn the game.
This game has different modes including a standard 4 player arena, training, challenge mode (♥♥♥♥ this mode), and solo practice. You can play FFA with 4 people or 1 v 1s (which IMO are less hectic and more fun). You can also play as 2 v 2 teams in the arena which makes up for interesting matchups.
Where this game shines is in its soundtrack. My god how well it plays with the game. Its upbeat, techno style music just pumps adrenaline in me, especially when the ball goes at fast speeds. Did I mention that already? Everytime someone hits the ball, it picks up in speed. It starts off in small increments and gets larger by the second. Eventually the ball is going SO fast its just a blur and a step foward on the screen can get you killed. I cannot express how much fun trying to pin down the ball is when literally no one know wtf to do.
Lethal League is an easy game to run, almost no problems (there's always that one dude who disconnects in the middle of a game, thus laggin' it up for everyone) and has guaranteed hours of fun in it. But be warned fellow Leaguers, this little "Candyman" ♥♥♥♥♥ character is the craziest thing (OP IMO) I've ever seen. His special ability can teleport the ball anywhere, and is super annoying. I'm learning how to counter it now (must stay calm), but in the end it feels so rewarding when you beat someone using him. Don't get me wrong.  Saints Row IV is fun.  I really enjoy jumping around, the puzzles, and the awesome and humorous dialogues from previous games.  It's a great time.
However, you don't kill a single human being in the entire game.  Yep, you heard that right.  My gleeful sociopath didn't kill one human.  The whole game takes place in a simulation where nothing is real.  I mean, it's not real anyway, but at least it's not usually fake *in the game*.  What's the point of being a god-like gangster if I can't accidentally kill a few civilians?
Also, the complete reuse of Steelport actually makes the game feel kind of unfinished.  It's almost more like an expansion or a very big DLC than a standalone game.  Most of my time is spent in the same area as in Saints Row: The Third, which is still the best of the series.  Sure, superpowers let me see it from a new perspective, but it's kind of strange to play in exactly the same areas as in the last game.
SRIV has the same port problems as SR3.  It's slow, even on a very good computer, and recommends the highest settings when it lags on anything short of low.  Many people complain about this, and I can play much better games on my computer without a hitch.  It's too bad, because the game looks pretty good most of the time.
Adding loyalty missions to go with the open-world missions actually brings a nice structure to it.  Plus, adding bronze-silver-gold gives new options to shoot for without compromising success in the loyalty missions.  It's the one advantage it has over SR3.
So, basically, a very good game.  I loved it, played every mission, and then never touched it again.  It's worth the price.

This is the first negative review I have ever written on Steam, please bare with me.
I consider myself a Telltale fan; I've played through The Walking Dead, The Wolf Among Us, and Tales from the Borderlands. I enjoyed each of them immensely. I've loved every book in George R. R. Martin's A Song of Ice and Fire. I've avidly watched every season of HBO's Game of Thrones. This purchase was a no-brainer for me and I was really looking forward to it.
After completion, I spent hours contemplating if there was anything I enjoyed about this game. The game is depressing. It makes you feel miserable and powerless. It becomes a struggle not to detach because of frequent, inescapable brutality.
The choices force players to pick between humiliations. Will you grovel pitifully or accept a beating? The outcome is the same regardless of your choice. So which is more enjoyable: watching your face get bashed in or demeaning yourself? This doesn't just happen once; it happens every single episode.
There is no silver lining. The most enjoyable choice a player could make is not to play.

In this game, you have to fell trees. Lots of them. Initially with a chainsaw. For each tree, you need to watch a minute (60 seconds) of unskippable animation that is the same every time, accompanied by cheesy "best of telephone hotline" synth music. This game is making me lose my will to live.
You'll be bored to tears before you earn enough money to buy the more interesting equipment, and there's no guarantee the boredom will stop even then. I haven't gotten that far yet.
Other "features" include
* plenty of invisible walls
* water that doesn't actually do anything (who needs bridges)
* shoddy modeling (saw one house sunk into the ground up to the windowsills)
* shoddy forests, looks more like trees stuck on a meadow than natural growth
* does not actually simulate woodcutting, merely animates it
* walking is faster than driving
* the game gives you hours to complete tasks done in minutes
* glitches galore (autojumps high when running over small obstructions, saw sound continues when going to the pause menu, sun still makes shadows when set and below the horizon, you can fell yellow-banded trees anywhere, not just where your mission says you should - just keep felling in the forest you're in, game puts you in the car no matter where it is - leave cars at different points on the map to travel quickly, van drives 70 km/h over any type of terrain).
* more boring than any truck simulator in existence
Woodcutter Simulator doesn't actually simulate woodcutting. The "tree radar" is ridiculous, the chainsaw felling technique is downright dangerous (always cut with the side of the saw, never the tip; do remove the wedge after cutting it; the wedge cut should only cut 1/3 to 1/4 of the diameter into the tree; the back cut needs to be at least 1 inch higher than the bottom of the wedge), and the direction the tree falls in bears no relation to the direction of my cut (I've had some trees fall towards me, even). Falling trees can't get stuck on other trees, and there would be no way to free them if they did because you can't fell trees the game doesn't let you (another indication that this is not a simulator).
I recommend this game to people who enjoy the feeling of having wasted their money, or who like to show off to others what truly boring games they own. Everyone else, don't buy at any price.
Going outside and watching the gras grow will be a better use of your time than seeing badly modeled trees fall in badly done "simulation".

You like ARPG's?  I would be highly surprised if you somehow didn't like Grim Dawn after playing.  Is it perfect?  No, but then is anything perfect?  Grim Dawn comes close to being a perfect game in my opinion.
The pros far outweigh the cons.  My bigest complaint is the small amount of storage space given considering the plethora of items you will be finding and wanting to keep for making other characters.  You can download GD Stash to help with the limited inventory issue for all the epics you will want to hold on to.
Speaking of characters, lots of different ways to build something fun and unique.  Yes, there are specific builds that wreck more than other builds, but every character I have made has been fun even if it wasn't the optimal way to do things.  You have the ability to retool your character to an extent which makes it easier to experiment with your chosen classes, but you can't completely start your character over once making class choices and putting points into stats which is another small complaint, but somewhat understandable as there wouldn't really be a point in going through the game again if you could just change your character at will.  That said, there is already a great character editor for Grim Dawn (GD Defiler) if you want to go that route.
Choice is a big pro and also a slight con in this game.  You will spend far too much time trying to figure out exactly what you want to do, especially when you get an item that would work amazingly with a skill you don't yet have.  Alt-itis is strong and you will constantly be tempted to start new characters to try out an amazing weapon or armor set you just found.
The story is kind of weak, but it is a bit interesting.  Who really plays a game like this for the story though?  Wrecking fools and vacuuming loot is the point of ARPG's and Grim Dawn is no exception.
I've played most ARPG's, but Grim Dawn (and Titan Quest, GD's older brother) are the ones I keep coming back to.  One somewhat irritating flaw with Grim Dawn is the age of the engine.  A super powerful computer isn't going to do you much good with how well the game runs.  CPU speed is king here.  The game doesn't really care about how many cores you have or what your video card is and will run well on just about anything in the past 5 years, but you will probably notice slowdown in massive battles due to the game engine being optimized for single core processors.  The biggest drawback to using the same engine Titan Quest used, but certainly not anything that will keep you from enjoying the game fully.  Just don't be surprised if you don't pump out massive FPS at all times.
Grim Dawn is an amazing value at full price, but on sale an absolute steal!

I haven't played this game much, but it is already getting on my nerves. There are a few really questionable design choices that really ruin what might have otherwise been a good game.
1) Its an RPG, but you don't get to make your own choices. If your character just did what they wanted and the game followed a pre determined story I wouldn't mind, but it doesn't to that. You will be given two choices, you will make one, then your party member will force you into a completely RNG based mini game that will sometimes end with your character making the opposite decision of what you wanted. When these will sprout up is completely unpredictable.
In another RPG a lawful NPC follower might force you to follow the law, but here they seem to just disagree with you randomly with out reason . I looked online, and there are ways of improving your odds, but that brings me to the second issue.
2) The information provided in game is no were near enough to play effectively, a stat will say something like "improves some spells" when you mouse over it. It wont say how, or how much it improves what spells. So leveling is basically just fumbling through stats and abilities hoping you get something that is some what effective, or going to the internet and looking up exactly what every option does every time you level up.
3) Walls of text. If you think this review is a bit long winded, don't even think about getting the game. Nearly all of the interactions you have with NPCs consist of them spouting out three paragraph monolog after three paragraph monolog. By video game standards what they are saying is pretty well written, but after you have read through 20 or so pages of text that would be at home in a god awful fantasy novel you will find your self zoneing out, or skipping through half of NPC interactions. Oh and the few spoken lines that NPCs do have are repeated over and over on a loop, you will walk through a market and hear the same line 5 times (think "then i took an arrow to the knee" only 50 times worse).
People say the combat is good, but right now I am about 4 hours in and I have only had 4 fights, none of which lasted more then a minute. So far the game is pretty much just poorly written pages of text and moral decisions that the lord RNGesus makes for me. Save yourself the tooth grinding and the $30, don't get this game.

After trying Duel Links and being very annoyed with the 3 monster/spell&trap zones, I decided to search steam for a game that would hopefully be a more accurate representation of the source game. This game did not dissapoint.
Pros:
+ As previously mentioned, it's an accurate represention of the original card game. If Duel Links bugs you as much as it does me, then give this a shot.
+ Lengthy story mode that lets you play through some major duels in the first four to five (see below for separate DLC pros and cons) Anime series. You always play as the character who's supposed to win, so there are no "you have to lose" situations.
+ Given the option to play with story decks based on the cards udes in the anime, but you can also play against anyone with decks you've made yourself.
+ You start with enough cards for a few structure decks, and unlocks packs with story progression. More fun to open packs than have every card from the beginning, after all.
+ Playing a single duel in any mode (with the possible exception of the online matches that I've yet to try), you always earn enough Duel Points to buy at least a pack or two, even if you lose. Winning usually nets you enough for three or four packs. (My biggest gripe with the 5Ds game on the Nintendo DS was that you had to win around five duels to buy a sing pack.)
+ Reverse duels unlock after beating each story mode level, where you play with the deck who is supposed to lose, but try to win anyways. Screw canon! (Can be played with story or your own decks, of course.)
+ Challenge Decks unlock after you defeat each instance of a single character in Story Mode (regular and reverse), where you play a more powerful deck based on that character's usual theme. Can only be played usuning cards you own.
+ Very large library of cards avaliable. I have over 3000 and still haven't unlocked any 5Ds or Zexal packs, nor bought many Arc-V packs. Includes Syncro, Xyz, and Pendulum cards, as well as the original monster, spell, trap, fusion, and ritual cards.
+ Defeating any deck in story or challenge mode unlocks a schematic for the deck. You can start a new deck with a schematic and then edit it to your liking, or play any level with a schematic you own all the cards for by selecting user deck.
+ Losing any story/challenge duel gives you one card from the opposing deck. Winning gives you three, and if the deck has a signature card, the first time you win you will always get it.
+ One tutorial in each story series. Original series gives basics on how the game works, GX shows off fusion monsters, 5Ds shows Syncro monsters, Zexal shows Xyz monsters, and Arc-V shows off pendulum cards.
+ Tutorials are skippable, just press 3/middle click to play them as non-tutorial duels.
+ Lets you build decks with banned cards. Probably not in ranked multiplayer though. (My second biggest gripe with the 5Ds game I mentioned earlier was that everybody used banned cards, but you couldn't use any at all.)
Ehhs:

You like anime, visual novels, RPG's, and kawaii all over with a cherry on top? Well this might be just the game for you!
I have played this game for about a week now, so I guess it's time to let you know my thoughts on it. This honestly is much more fun that it first appears to be. At first, you may question the gameplay and how the overworld functions - I did a first for a little bit - but once you dig into the gameplay and story, that doesn't seem to be a big problem at all.
For those that don't play that many RPG's, or that have only been familiar with RPG's such as the infamous Final Fantasy franchise, this may seem like a dissapointment, but I can assure you, you will not be dissapointed! I myself, hadn't played a JRPG before, only FFVII, FFVIII and a little of FFXIII, so the battle system and overworld were a little alien to me, but it's not that complicated - it's very easy to get used to after practice. If you are any big fan of anime and as a plus, visual novels too, this pretty much combines both with an RPG. I also like to mention that the character often 'break the forth wall' by poking jokes at some particular RPG mechanics. E.g. A fight narrator (Neptune attacks.....It had no effect....).
Only thing I'll have to say as a negative is that this game does require some grinding in places in order to have a fair fight in places that advance the story. Though after a while, I found some charm in this as there are some monster that you can count as "bosses" that can help you level pretty good, while at the same time providing a challenge as well as giving you experience in fighting tougher opponents.
Overall, I said it before and I'll say it again; if you love anime, visual novels, kawaii and characters often 'breaking the forth wall', then this game is for you. I highly recommend it!

First In-Game Adventure: You start out as a random guy with a chainsaw standing in front of a house and you see that you are next to three recycle bins. You wonder who you are and how you got there, and why you are standing next to three recycle bins. You see a tree and you decide you want to cut it down. You run up to it in super lag at 1fps and try to stick the chainsaw which you don’t know how you got into the tree. You try to start the chainsaw but it says you are holding the chainsaw in the wrong position. So you give up and decide to explore. But then, all of the sudden, you feel the need that you need to cut down some trees. You have no way of getting this information, you just know in your mind that you must cut down three trees. So you decide to cut down these trees and you realize that you can run faster sideways than you can forwards. You don’t know why, you just do. In your head you visualize a map. You have no way of getting this map, you just picture it (in the top-right corner of your screen). You run to this place where you feel the trees are and you magically stop. You have reached the end of the world. Small world right? Then you turn around and you see a hideous, very scary sight. You see…a mountain that is literally covered in trees!!! Then you see a crane and decide to jump in it so that you don’t have to look at that hideous mountain anymore. You don’t know how you got in it or what you pressed, but you’re magically in the crane. You can’t get out. You’re stuck. The game is over.
Second In-Game Adventure: You start out as a random guy with a chainsaw standing in front of a house and you see that you are next to four recycling bins. You once again wonder who you are and how you got there, and why there are now four recycling bins. Maybe the garbage man came and dropped off another one? These questions remain in your head leaving you in confusion. You see a tree once again and you decide you want to cut it down. You think that maybe this time the chainsaw will actually start…You thought wrong. Once again the chainsaw doesn’t move. You decide that maybe this tree just has problems and doesn’t like you so you decide to run away from this tree that doesn’t seem to like you and you run up a hill. You then remember that you can run faster sideways than you can forwards. You don’t know why, you just do. So you awkwardly run sideways until you come to another tree. You think that this one looks more friendly and will want to be your friend so you can cut it down…You thought wrong. As soon as you get up to the tree and raise your chainsaw, the tree pulls you into it. You don’t know how, since you were standing about 5 ft. away from the tree. How can this be? You are stuck with these puzzling questions waiting to be answered. Anyway, the tree pulls you into it and you go into the tree. You don’t know how, all you know is that you are now inside the tree. But then, things get much more scary. You then fall out of the tree and start falling into a world of whiteness. You look up and you can see that you have fallen out of the world. You can see the bottom of the world fading as you fall farther and farther into the world of whiteness. You look down into the whiteness. It looks very…white. But then, as you start to think that things can’t get any worse…You thought wrong. Black and white lines cover up your screen. Everything fades. The game crashes. You are back at your desktop. Worst simulator game ever…

I'll be honest, initially I bought this game as a joke. I mean, how can a game simulating woodcutting be good? Amirite?
But when I loaded up this "♥♥♥♥♥♥" little woodcutting game I immediately felt like Judas was to Jesus. How could I hate and laugh at something so beautiful? The main menu is sublime, the quaint melody and the beautiful scenery made me feel like a child again. I shed a tear, called my family into the room and offered them the greatest pleasure of viewing this masterpiece alongside me. Of course, while initially sceptical they accepted.
Upon choosing the single player option you can choose to play either a tutorial or go straight into the main campaign. As I didn't want to keep my audience waiting I chose to jump right into the fray. It was nothing like I expected, there was no waking up, grabbing a cup of tea and calling the wife before setting out to chop wood. Your one and only goal was to chop wood meaning in a dark souls-esque style you wouldn't be able to prepare for the oncoming mission beforehand due to it's open world nature. I was beginning to feel foolish in front of my family for not choosing the tutorial but to my surprise it was all explained in game anyway! After being issued a mission "Kill 4 trees" a picture of a tree on the minimap directed me to my goal and I ventured to it on foot.
*30 minutes later*
After reaching the tree marker I was instantly admist a sea of trees larger than those seen during my adventure to the goal. This was the place, the place of do or die. Walking to my first cuttable tree (you can only cut trees with bands around, showing the care for enviornmental safety this game has - a vital feature to stop people imitating the game on any random tree) I pulled out my chainsaw and felt a thrill. This was my first kill. Watching the gruesome yet wonderful animation (lasting approximately 7 minutes) the tree had fell and disappeared but regardless of reasons my objective of killing four trees was marked "1/4". A wry smile and a strange bloodlust filled me as I continued towards the other trees. "2/4", "3/4", "4/4" and I was done.
I felt like a god returning to base. I held the fate of those marked trees and I could sense the fear within them. I killed a few more to make an example to those who would dare rebel, keeping my people (trees) safe from those anarchists. At that point I decided to turn off the simulator, for if I strike the wood too often my people would live in fear.
The true addiction to this God Simulator lies in the multiplayer. Will the kind, foolish god win the support of the people or will the more assured, logical god win the rise to power? Of course I already know the answer.
I don't want to rate this game as I no longer consider it a game. But to all who purchase it be warned for I am God in this world. Fear me. Loathe me. Envy me.

Beat Hazard is quite the interesting game. It offers some rapid-fire shmup action combined with multicolored flashing lights and the ability to integrate your own music library. Altogether, it offers a fast paced, ever changing audiovisual experience.
Yes, the game has its flaws. Gameplay is rather straightforward, and there is not much offered by music integration, aside from some frustration when calm sections result in an extremely weak ship. For many people, the visual effects are too distracting, and in some cases, can cause aching eyes or seizures.
Beat Hazard is not for everyone, particularly those uninterested in shmups and those with epilepsy or similar physical handicaps related to flashing lights. And if your music library is entirely composed of ballads and lullabies? You should definitely avoid this game, or at least think twice about purchasing it before you tire of the games included music selections. However, if you enjoy rapid space stick shooters, have a fancy for light shows, and/or own a decently sized collection of upbeat or high-energy music, then this is the game for you.

I'll be direct to the point on my review for this game.
I have given up on playing MMORPGs around 4-5 years ago as it is time consuming. I tried BnS, Revelation Online, Tree of Saviour, Ragnarok Online 2, Guild Wars 2 and many more but I quit after 2-3 weeks due to boredom. I notice how cliche MMOs are nowadays and the start is always so generic, but after trying out Black Desert Online, my love for MMORPGs started to turn around. I can't believe I actually like the game.
Black Desert Online is an MMORPG like nothing I've ever played before. Players are given the freedom to do as they like, be it life skills or combat training. The game starts off with a tutorial til level 10 ish or when you reach your first town Velia then from there on you're basically on your own to explore the world and learn things by yourself (which to me is totally amazing because I would find MMOs that spoon feed every bit of information entirely boring).
Yes, this game is almost 80% solo gaming until you reach about level 50 where open world PK is unlocked and grinding parties are highly recommended but for me, the solo game doesn't bother me as much when I have plenty of other activities that I can do such as arrange and organize my worker empire, do life skills, roam around the world explore more knowledge etc. It would be very pleasing if Pearl Abyss decides to add team dungeons or more guild related activities to promote more party related quests.
I would say this game isn't for everyone. Yes, you need to give it a chance and play for a little while whether you'd like it or not. People who quit the game earlier on are most likely people who wouldn't want to give more effort in a realistic MMO but people who stay are those who feel immersed in the world itself.
The only thing that irks me is the gender locked classes. :/
Also, most people giving negative reviews are the ones who barely played the game for more than 3hrs or so. I'd like to point out as well at how ironic people are giving out negative reviews but still play the game.
The game is great, it's just not for everyone. Not everyone could be pleased.

An excellent story, worthy of the HBO series and George R. R. Martin's original!
Telltale has perfectly captured the spirit and intrigue of Martin's creation, forcing you--the player--to make critical decisions based upon both logic and emotion. You will be immersed into the politics and relationships effortlessly, seeming as if you had been a part of the world long before you clicked "Play." Navigating through the situations and inter-personal connections is made more difficult when you discover that there are no "right" answers; each decision deviates you down a path that presents you with more and more difficult decisions, but you're always second guessing the decisions that you've made. Will you choose to protect your friends, even if it's at the expense of your family? Will "incorrect" decisions still offer you the opportunity to complete your ultimate objectives?
While the "Build-your-own-adventure" component of the game is exemplary, there are a few problems with the game. The graphical interactivity (WASD) is limited and (unless I'm missing something along the way) seems gratuitous and unneccessary at times. Often I have found myself pressing "W" to move to the next part of the scene, trying (unsuccessfully) to find clickable items along the way, only to find that "W" was the seemingly sole purpose. Additonally, fight scenes sometime require three hands to complete easily on my Mac; the mouse movement for dodges and ducks is imprecise, so I had to drop the mouse for the arrow keys along the way, only to have to switch back to the mouse to click (attack) an enemy. Despite this, the fight scenes do allow retries; only a couple of fight failures have continued the story without allowing a second attempt.
Technical issues for the Mac: If you're using OS X, the game runs smoothly, but entering full screen and exiting the game require keystrokes, as the top-bar menu is not available once the game is launched. To enter full screen, choose Shift-Enter; to exit the game (after a Save, first!), use Command-Option-Esc.
All in all, I cannot put this game down! I also can't wait to try a second save file and see exactly how far each branch spreads from the base of the tree.

As usual, the gameplay is what you'd expect from Telltale- average, there's only so much you can get from quicktime events and set dialogues but I don't care about that because I play Telltale for the storyline and character developement.
I'll start with some praise, the lore is excellent, voice acting good and the character design is good, I personally like the art style and think the over all look of the game (bar sketchy fire animations) is nice. However, all of this doesn't mean a thing when you feel that throughout the entire game, no matter what 'choices' you make there will always be one outcome: you lose. Over and over again. But it's not like when reading a game of thrones book where you slowly build up hope as that story gains momentum only to have your hopes wrenched away from you in agonising detail, done so brilliantly that you can't be angry because Telltale have tried to do what G.R.R Martin took a lifetime to accomplish in a year and have failed miserably. The feeling that you get in other Telltale games is a rush of excitement as you take decisions which may alter the course of your story for better or worse.
In Game of thrones it feels like you are being dragged face-first through a muddy puddle whilst at every 'choice' you get stamped on by a steelclad bootheel.
This game has not been particularly enjoyable because it feels as though no matter what decision you make, anything you do is doomed to fail. The story is a narrow corridor which has no bend in it. Choice A is♥♥♥♥♥♥♥choice, Choice B is also a♥♥♥♥♥♥choice, Choice C is also bad or you can be silent. No matter what you do though, the same thing will happen, you'll lose.
At episode 5 there is only two characters who I actually like left standing. I'll probably play the 6th episode but in all honesty I wish I had not paid the £20 that I did for this.
tldr: Buy it in a sale or don't buy it at all. 4/10 (from a Telltale fanboy.)

In games, as in any medium, genuine innovation is rare.  This is not, in itself, something that should surprise anyone. As well following from a kind of  general law of reality (I'm thinking of Spinoza's eloquently expressed truism that "all things excellent are as difficult as they are rare."), commerical art -- and what art, today, isn't commercial? -- is subject to all sorts of exigencies that ultimately add up to incentives to follow the apparently tried and true and to avoid the road not taken like a hospital that only doles out flesh-eating viruses and bankrputcies. After all, if you're investing the kind of time and money that goes into a AAA game or a Hollywood film, why wouldn't you try to take as few risks as possible in the hope that you can thereby ensure a return on your (often vast) investment?
One reason, of course, is that consumers are capricious and paradoxical in ways that (thankfully!) can be counted on to continually confound people who think they've found the magic forumla for the next mega-hit. Thus, on the one hand, people clearly like (and are wont to buy) things that are like other things that they like. The studio exec. nows this. At the same time, however, when we remember what made us first fall in love with a certain genre (or with a place, a pasttime, a person)  often what we remember most fondly is not that 'this met with our pre-existing desires', but that this encounter, *educated our desires*, made us into a certain kind of desiring-being.  It's the difference, ultimately, between finding an itch that we never knew we had (a sudden awakening of inhoate desire) as opposed to coming back for our umpteenth compulsive stcratch. To the corproate exec. types this is infuriating: consumers want (and will demand) that their tastes should be catered for and indulged to an inch of their lives...right up to the point that we feel that we're being pandered to at which point, we start to feel that we're being treated like drug addicts, that the dealers are cutitng our stuff with random crap that we never wanted and that actually, thank you very much, we prefer the desperate thrill of having stumbled across an undiscovered country rather than being served up the same crap day after day like a child...
It's with all this in mind, that I should say  that The Banner Saga is not only an excellent game, but it's the best thing to have happened to rpg and strategy games for about a decade. What exactly is so good about it? Well, if you've seen the screenshots and the trailer, I'm hoping that I won't need to sell you on the art-style and thus it's extraordinarily beautiful, hand-crafted retro-charm. I could also add that the game makes many allusions to what looks like a unique and intricate lore that is, at the time of the game's release, still only minimally fleshed out. In addition, the story is compelling, the characters (though tending towards they archetypal) are generally intriguing and the turn-based combat has considerable depth. All of this, however, could be said about any number of games. So what makes TBS so different?
If I had to try and put isolate what makes the game so brilliant and so surprising, I would start by saying that as well as the sense of something new (an original IP, a distinct lore, a distinctive art-style) in a market whose governing principle is: "you want more of the same, don't you?", what really makes the game stand out is  the way that its rpg and resource management mechanics (as well as the games fundmaental *difficulty*) are integrated with and contribute to the tone of the game's narrative and its wider world.
To explain, TBS is, at its core, a narrative of desperation. It is a story of flight, of exile, of trying to survive and to keep the people you love alive under circumstances so dire as to be almost hopeless.  In TBS, it's an axiom that people (a lot of people) are going to die, even and espeically if you are motivated by nothing more than trying to save as many people as you posisbly can. What is so satisfying about the way that the game manages to connect this  narrative-thematic dimension with the core gameplay. Granted, a skilled strategists might find they get through the game with fewer losses than people who are less adroit, sneaky, determined or just prone to look up strategy-guides. For me, however, the real beauty of TBS is attested by how few times I found myself reloading my save game. This may seem odd (and it's not entirely true -- I did reload a few times to try and avoid certain consequences of my actions). Nonetheless, the game constantly reinforces the way that because your choices  do have ramifications (a desideratum on many gaming wishlists, especially among rpg fans), you cannot both ask that htese  consequences exist and that they should be in your control. Put differently: the game makes it seem not only difficult, but out of the spirit of things to try and 'optimise a set of outcomes' or 'to get the good ending'. As a result of this, every decision you make in the game seems weighty, just as every fight seems like (and irrespective of how much you've levelled up your characters) like it might just be your last. Disaster awaits around every corner. Acting on principle will sometimes lead to disastrous consequences, but so might a cynical pragmatism. The effect is that your partaking in something real, that you're not so much living out a fantasy where everything turns out wonderfully as much as you are a lead character in a tragedy: like you're roleplaying the entire cast of one of Shakespeare's history plays.
Overall, what I really loved about this game was the way that it used (relatively simple) mechanics, decision trees, resource management and fairly difficult turn-based combat, to enforce the sense that my characters were fighting for their lives. I felt bruised and battered playing this game. I winced everytime a character got hit. I felt something akin to the shock and grief that my characters must have felt when a loyal companion who'd gone through hell with the party, suddenly disappeared forever not in the midst of a heroic sacrifice but out of a random occurrence or worse through one of the numerous unintended consequences of one of my carefully thought out decisions.  In fact, even the way that I ultimately kind of *sucked* at the game (e.g. being less than masterful at resource management), contributed (a rare thing) to my enjoyment of it, in the sense that it exacerbated the sense that I, like the protagonists, was heavily burdened with responsibilities that I did not know whether I could handle: that I was letting down the people I was trying to help, that I was  vacillating between letting people starve and letting them getting picked off by monsters, that I could and (continually *did*) fail by both virtue and vice, idelaism and pragmatism, trust and distrust, boldness and caution. I'm scribbling too much, but for now, I'll just say everyone (especially fans of crpgs, turn-based strategy or resource management should get this), as should anyone (designers, anyone?) thinking about the Holy Grail of the integration of narrative and ludic elements. A minor masterpiece, I can easily imagine this one playing a prominent role in classes on game design, especially where "ludic-narrative integration" (pretentious as the phrase may be) gets discussed.
TL;DR: Gut-wrenching. Extraordinary integration of gameplay elemetns to contribute to the overall brooding, tragic, 'unforseen consequences' atmoshpere.

========
The Good
========

"In the end, "Grey Goo" is indeed a welcome throwback to the classics I've grown up with and is worth plenty of repeat visits.  It does everything it can to make your life easier (what with the QWERT keybind controls and auto-harvesters for the Humans and Beta) but falls short on the skirmish/multiplayer side of things.  It really would have been awesome to have the ability to set up and see a "4 vs 4" or "2 vs 3" or something along those lines.  I also found the AI to be a bit too aggressive and difficult, even on "easy".  I lost many matches against the "easy" AI and I consider myself to be a moderately experienced RTS player (though I admittedly love to turtle, which this game seems to discourage).  This ruthlessness will most certainly frustrate newcomers to no end and at times, I honestly wished that I could tell the AI to tone it down a bit and expand more slowly.  With the above issues in mind, those short on money may want to wait for a price drop (like I would have done had I not received a press key)."

Divinity: Original Sin is a classic example of how old-school RPG is made anew. It is the product of old-school gameplay coupled with its own niche and original features.
- Slow-paced tactical turn based combat
- Widespread treasures in the form of clickable debris and vessels (barrels and the like)
- Multiple non-linear quests completion
- Multiple character builds and party compositions
- Free roam and exploration
- Massive lore and dialogue
- Use of elements and Terrain where they cooperate and collide as a gameplay mechanic (water channels electricity and such): Imagine Magicka meets tactics
- Conflicting opinions of Main Characters determine the outcome of a quest (only applicable if you play co-op).
- Bad interface
- Starts strong with many things presented as well as a variety of quests, but severely diminishes against the end, content feels rushed.
- Story drags out.
- Little or non-existant voice acting for games with pre-made characters (story-wise).
- Certain decisions/negotiations with NPC revolves on the result of rock-paper-scissors match with the NPC, this absolutely destroys immersion where whether the decision of walking away unscathed or ended up massacring them rests on luck.
Overall, I had a blast playing this game with a partner and there are many memorable moments throughout the game. However, I do feel that this game is highly overrated and it is nowhere at the top of my list. It is still a game that I would recommend to RPG fans out there simply because there are not many well-thought out and engaging RPG games that you can play with your friends out there in the market.
