I had never heard of Beat Hazard before until it randomly popped up in the Steam Summer Sale, so since I really love the music-enhacing gameplay mechanic in most games, I thought it would definitely be worth just under £3 for the Beat Hazard bundle package. This is, without a doubt, the best £3 I have ever spent on Steam.
I have become hopelessly addicted to this game. I've found myself waking up earlier than I usually would just to play this for a little while just to get my day started along with a hot mug of coffee, this is definitely a good game to wake you up if it is nothing else!
The best thing about Beat Hazard is that both the gameplay and playability are as large as your music library. The more music you have, the more there is to do, plus there are lots of ulockables, collectable, perks, acheivements, game modes and even more ships to chose from so there are plenty of play styles to try out on all of your music, and even radio stations.
Alongside the fact that Beat Hazard is a brilliant, fun and highly addictive game within itself, it is also a great way to rediscover your own music and to discover new music with it's online play and internet radio links. There is very little to fault about this game and rather than spending money on strobe lights for a party, you'd be better off playing this on a big screen.
The only thing that I would say to watch out for when buying this, like so many other people have mentioned, is that it features extreme flashing lights/colours throughout the entire game, so it is a hazard itself to people with photosensitive epilepsy; If you are epileptic, I highly advise you avoid this game as even on the lowest visual intesnsity, it is extremely bright, colourful and flashy.
This game comes with an epilepsy warning on it's sale page and before the game even loads, it is there for a reason, trust me! You have to stop playing after a certain period of time as it begins to kill your eyes!
Above all, as an avid music and game lover, this is a perfect casual game that I am very glad I took the time to buy. I would reccomend it to every music fan out there (especially the Electronic/Industrial music fans, Funker Vogt is the perfect band for this game), just not to people with photosensitive epilepsy.
On a side note: I dont' understand why people are constantly comparing this game to Audiosurf. Both are extremely different in terms of actual gameplay even though they are both rythm-based games and are both good in their own way. Rather than saying "Get Beat Hazard instead" or "Get Audiosurf instead", I say get both, especially when they're on sale.

As a fan of the simulator genre, and someone who spent five years felling trees, I had realistic expectations for this game.  It failed to deliver in nearly every way possible.  This is a horrendous failure for the genre.  They essentially remove the player from every aspect of actually cutting wood, and engage the player in every other way possible, all the ways they didn't advertise.
Clunky Controls
I hope you don't want to drive in anything other than straight lines, and I hope you are used to walking around taking 3-foot steps at a painfully slow pace.  The mechanics of the game require you to be in a particular spot to initiate action, and while your slowest walking speed is painfully slow, they seem to want you standing on a dime, because you just can't take a small enough step to be in the right place the first time.  Oh, and did you want to look around with the mouse?  Get some tape for your RMB.  Did you want a chase cam for your vehicle?  I hope not, because once you set the cardinal direction you are looking with the mouse, you're locked on.
"Wanna go for a walk?"
A more accurate title may have been, "Walk around with a chainsaw simulator" you will spend more time wandering around the map getting to the objectives than actually performing them.  Your walking speed is painfully slow, your sprinting speed is rediculously fast.  Really, why would I buy a van to deliver myself and supplies to the jobsite when I can run there faster and my legs never need repairs?
Safety last!
The game makes an utter mockery of safety.  You are felling trees, what would you wear?  At least stick with the stereotype and give me a flannel shirt!  I get the impression you are out felling trees in a t-shirt and shorts, hell, you might even be wearing flip-flops (you can't see your feet, which is probably for the best) As you cut the tree, the cutter keeps the bar only half-engaged in the wood, just asking for a nasty kick-back, and hey, what are wedges? who need one of those? If you are going to simplify gameplay to the point of being no-fun at all, at least be safe and accurate!
Booooring!
You know what the most exciting part of felling trees is?  It's the art and science of cutting the tree, getting it to fall with the lay of the rest of your cut logs, gaging the wind, slope, and making precise cuts to guide the tree onto your targeted bit of ground.  They took all this skillful operation of an exciting bit of equipment, and pared it down to a cutscene.  Not a particularly good cutscene.  If I didn't have practical experience, I'd be led to believe that Stihl makes giant red markers, because that's obviously not a kerf you're leaving on the tree! In the height of opposite-land, while it takes you a painfully long 30 seconds to make your face cut and back cut, limbing the tree (the longest and most boring part in real life) and makes it the part you look forward to, because it means you again have control, and can walk up to a tree and push a button... wait, you won't look forward to that.
Graphics, does anyone have any graphics?
The max resolution is well below my standard screen resolution, and with all the graphics cranked to max, well, it's lackluster.  You'd think a chainsaw would call for some visible particle effects, but I guess they wanted to reinforce the idea that you're just drawing red lines on the tree.
Heavy Equipment
Yeah! heavy equipment, maybe they skimped on the chain saw parts to emphasize equipment operation, right?  WRONG! the heavy equipment is as irritatingly over-simplified as the rest of the process, and as boring to use.
I've owned this game for half an hour, and I already have buyer's remorse... did I mention I got it on sale? If this game was free to play, it would be over-priced.  You should be paid to play it.  Save your $5, if you want to waste time, there are many actual games that can waste it more enjoyably.

I've played this game for about an hour now, and so far I'm really liking it. At first I didn't get why there was no music on the first game, and then I got VOL's and nearly shattered my eardrums, it's a first time thing, but I think there could at least be a first-time warning. I also began to realize that my music was being drowned out by explosions and gunfire, which can be turned off, but I think they're a bit much to begin with. There are some cool options, my entire library works perfectly (with replay gain, that's definitely a big plus), and this game is definitely worthy of the seizure warning on the front, if you haven't already gathered that. I think this game would be pretty good for passing the time, especially after you get a new album or something. Thing is, I got the entire bundle on slae for $5, and while this is a great game, I would pay the $10, but I really think that should inculde the shadow ops stuff and the ultra stuff as well. The ship creator that comes with shadow ops is very intuitive from what I've seen (I haven't made anything yet), but it looks like you can upload any image and tweak the stats to your liking. Issue being, again, I think that should be built into the game rather than DLC. Visually the game is fantastic, but I think the whole theme could be wrapped together a little nicer, as it's a little all-over-the-place. In game it looks very nice, and I LOVE how the clouds and stars pulse to the music: that aspect is perfect. What isn't perfect is that the enemies don't sync into the music as good as they could, and it seems like, in comparison, Symphony does a bit of a better job, but I've only seen videos, so I can't confirm that. The perks system is cool, but I think there could be more, as your selection is kind of limited, and I also flew through a ton of ranks really quickly (and I'm not super good), so maybe those should be harder to get. Also, it will randomly go through the included music in the menu, which I think isn't.. exactly... adequate.... Overall I think it's a neat casual-to-hardcore game with some great replayability and a price that could come down just a bit.

While I understand I'm going to be in the minority here, I found Banner Saga very frustrating to play through, and I essentially had to drag myself to the end of the game. There's a lot of cases of 'false choice' in which it seems like you're able to change the paths of the game but one choice just ends up losing you people or supplies. There are choices that you make and then will have negative consequences later (such as killing your fighters) and you don't have much of a way to envision what is coming along. It wasn't a matter of "Oh I didn't treat my fighter properly so he left", but "This guy randomly killed my other fighters". By the end of the game, any decision I had to make I was dreading because I knew that there was a right and a wrong way to proceed, and one would just end up with everything progressing that little bit worse.
Overall, I simply didn't find the game that much fun. It was a study in dwindling resource management while trying to guess what decision the developers wanted you to take. After dragging myself to the conclusion of the story, I was left not feeling as though anything had properly wrapped up, but as though I had just seen some long-winded introduction to a 'great saga' that I have absolutely no interest in forcing on myself.
If you think this has a happy ending, you haven't been paying attention.

Wow... Child of Light is a really great game. It's not good, it's great. It has all the mechanics that make a game interesting.
Gameplay-wise, Child of Light utilizes a hybrid real time and turn-based combat system. Instead of a fixed initiative system, you will have little markers that will race towards the action zone. Whoever's marker reaches the action zone first gets to act. However, there are ways to mess with the marker race to slow down your opponent's markers in real time. E.g. Using Igniculus to blind your enemies so that they slow down. You can only use 2 companions at any time against up to 3 enemies.
Conclusion, you must try this beautiful game. The accompanying piano music plus the beautiful watercolour visuals are a confirmed treat.
1. Storyline
It's amazing. It starts off with in 1895 Austria with the story of princess Aurora. Her mother is a duchess who died while Aurora was young. Aurora's father, the king, brings up Aurora on his own. Later on, he marries a dark woman as he is lonely. Coincidentally, her new stepmother allows the window to be left open and Aurora catches a cold which causes her to get sick (I think it's pneumonia) and she dies.
If you read on, the story delves deeper into the land of Lumeria and a find a deeper battle between Umbra and the Light.
2. Combination of Mechanics
You have Igniculus, the ball of light which you can control with mouse or a 2-player controller. You use him to activate mechanisms, slow down enemies in combat and blind enemies.
3. Combat System
Initiative based system which is amazing. You even get to use Igniculus to slow enemies down.
4. Flying
That won the game for me. Instead of the double jump cliche, flying took the game to a whole new level. It expanded the possibilities of the game so much more.
5. Light Puzzles
Pretty cool.
6. Background and Foreground
Amazing. When I saw the giant moving in the background, it really made my day.
7. Attention to Detail
Aurora's hair falls about when you jump and fall off ledges. It's beautiful. It's the little things like this that make the game amazing.
8. Igniculus, the Elemental
The glowing orb is so useful, let me list the ways.
a. Hints on your quests
b. Collecting energy and health in combat
c. Blinding enemies while travelling
d. Slowing enemies while in combat
e. Activating mechanisms which require light
f. Picking up Confessions
g. Story buddy
h. Healing
i. Illumination
9. The Bells in the Capilli Village
I love it. If you fly into the bells, the bells jingle.
10. Music
The piano accompaniement is so soothing and beautiful. Kudos to the composer.
11. Characters
Rubella - Jester Healer
Golem - Ancient Golem
Finn - Capelli Mage
Norah - Swift Fighter (Betrays you)
Aurora - Leader Unit
Robert - Mouse Archer
Gem - Sorceress
Oengus - Fighter
Tristin - Better copy of Rubella
1. Contact Points between the Floors
Before you get Flying, sometimes just getting up onto a second level is extremely difficult.
2. DLC
A lot of the game is DLC-based. But I'll let it slide because the game is amazing.
3. 2 Character Combat
2 is too few. It would be better with 3.
4. Repeated Monsters
Although there are many uniques monsters, you will find repeats where monsters just change colour from green to red to blue to black. There is also a case of changing monsters from a live version to a zombie version, but I like this one.
Total number of uniques are
a. Boar man
b. Ogre
c. Spike dog
d. Needle nose flyer
e. Ghost Horse
f. Alligator guard (Has a Zombie version)
g. Bird guard
h. Spirit of Death
i. Leaf insect
j. Centaur Archer
1. Ailment List
Could you provide a hot tip to show what the ailments mean? I had to guess that paralyze meant you couldn't move on the action bar.
2. Igniculus
a. Distracting large and dangerous enemies
b. Uncovering hidden symbols which can't be seem unless illuminated
c. Getting eaten by a large beast.
3. Multiplayer
I'm actually wondering if you could split the heroes and Igniculus on an online battle.
4. More Monster Slots + Hero Slots
I would like to see a 3 v 7 battle, like the 3 heroes being surrounded. Just like Final Fantasy.
If you're a fan of Strong Bad, Max, Tycho, or Heavy, just go buy this. You will be a fan of all the others within an hour.

Wow, I think the metacritic reviews of this title were unduly harsh. This game deserves much higher than a 77. High 80s is more reasonable.
Things to note:
+The game is gorgeous. That's pretty damn rare in the RTS market.
+Grey Goo implemented a race that turns traditional base-building strategy on its head and didn't break game balance.
+It plays and feels like an old RTS, but updated and streamlined for the modern era of competitive gaming.
+The multiplayer is freaking fun. Like seriously fun.
+Grey Goo has added the ability to control every aspect of building/unit production via the Q,W,E,R keys. Making a Refinery is as easy as QQ and click where you want it. This frees you up for even more micro.
-The campaign isn't very good. Petroglyph relied too heavily on artificial difficulty (poof! The enemy player suddenly has two epic units just because you broke down a certain section of wall!). They delighted in taking the glaring weakness of whatever race you are playing and make you do that thing over and over again. The turtle race doesn't get a level where they get to turtle. The "I have no turrets" race has to defend against endless tiny raids. Etc. And it's short with like 5-6 missions per faction.
-Either this attracted some really skilled people, or all of the players have no life outside of Grey Goo. Seriously, I haven't won a matchmaking game yet.

A go to game when you want to just sit back and relax. I love turned based games as the pacing is slow, no need to rush and with a good strategy everything comes together in the end.
XCOM is basically a special unit that has been set up to counter an alien invasion. The soldiers that are recruited/involved are of both genders and of a vast international variety. You take the role of the 'commander' a faceless entity who issues orders on the battlefield to your 5 man unit while also juggling research/engineering/training back at home base.
Starting off you have limited options but the game does well in introducing new features, the interface is user friendly and everything is well explained.
As you get further in the game you have lots of options; Do you build a satelitte nexus? - So you can have full coverage over Asia/Africa?, Do you invest all your monthly earnings in Research&Development?
You have to be careful as some countries might leave the XCOM program if the panic lvl stays in the red, diplomatic missions and satellitte coverage can help reduce this.

Goo buy it! Grey Goo is an awesome RTS!!!
There is something about great RTS battles that you take with you for life, and GreyGoo is a new proving ground for those experiences to flourish. It offers both a rich cinematic-laden experience for the single player campaign, as well as a challenging and competitive multi-player experience (check out the GreyGoo Twitch streams).
Ever since I first played the original Warcraft I have been an RTS fan. I'll never forget being at my friend's house for a sleepover where we linked two computers with a serial cable and played a Humans vs. Orks deathmatch. We'd let our peons and peasants hack at trees all night and wake up to spend all our vast resources of gold and lumber for an epic battle. Fast forward to now and we have GreyGoo, a fresh RTS experience that brings back to the forefront all the things I remember loving about RTS games in the past, while also distinguishing itself in a modern way amidst the other giants in the genre.
In short, GreyGoo has a great story, AWESOME cinematics/graphics, unique races, and gameplay. It's definitely worth it for any RTS fan, and the money you pay is saving you the torture of the Free-To-Play ad ridden, pay-to-win, pay-to-not-loose-years-of-your-life model of games!
So whether you are a long time fan of the genre, or are new to it, goo get this for your RTS collection!

Many of the reviews I've seen from people who purchased this game seemed to have only played 2 hours past the tutorial and gone off to say that the game is too complex. Yes, the game will require you to watch an hour or two of youtube videos for background research as to how to earn in game currency and if you don't have the patience to do so, you will most likely struggle down the road.
The combat is very smooth and combos are satisfying to perform. It utilizes players to play defense instead of prioritizing on hack and slash gameplay (in higher levels). Grinding from 1-53 is a breeze but a few levels after, the game really begins to start becoming a real challenge to keep up with gearing as well as the open world PvP after level 50. This process from 1-53~ is the tutorial to set you up for the real combat system at level 56, and it seems that most people who are giving this game poor reviews, have yet to even reach that point of the game.
Earning money in the game can be done in many ways, but again many of the negative reviewers seem to believe that the quickest way to obtain currency is to p2w. A few things to acknowledge is that the marketplace/auction house only allows players to place 5 real money items a week, they sell for 25 mill and cost around ~$30. If anything, this game is pay2lose if you're willing to play $100 a week to earn 125 mill of ingame currency that can be obtained in a week by grinding or setting up a node empire.
The game follows non-linear progression and allows all players to play whichever way they please. Do you have a life outside of BDO and can't find the time to play the game? Well, set up workers to obtain materials to craft and sell to the market for currency. This system allows players to earn currency actively and AFK, it is complex initially but once you play for more than 100 hours, and start researching as to how to min/max your workers' progression, the effort you put in becomes very rewarding.
Overall 8/10

At first I didn't get why there was no music on the first game, and then I got VOL's and nearly shattered my eardrums, it's a first time thing, but I think there could at least be a first-time warning. I also began to realize that my music was being drowned out by explosions and gunfire, which can be turned off, but I think they're a bit much to begin with. There are some cool options, my entire library works perfectly (with replay gain, that's definitely a big plus), and this game is definitely worthy of the seizure warning on the front, if you haven't already gathered that. I think this game would be pretty good for passing the time, especially after you get a new album or something. Thing is, I got the entire bundle on slae for $5, and while this is a great game, I would pay the $10, but I really think that should inculde the shadow ops stuff and the ultra stuff as well. The ship creator that comes with shadow ops is very intuitive from what I've seen (I haven't made anything yet), but it looks like you can upload any image and tweak the stats to your liking. Issue being, again, I think that should be built into the game rather than DLC. Visually the game is fantastic, but I think the whole theme could be wrapped together a little nicer, as it's a little all-over-the-place. In game it looks very nice, and I LOVE how the clouds and stars pulse to the music: that aspect is perfect. What isn't perfect is that the enemies don't sync into the music as good as they could, and it seems like, in comparison, Symphony does a bit of a better job, but I've only seen videos, so I can't confirm that. The perks system is cool, but I think there could be more, as your selection is kind of limited, and I also flew through a ton of ranks really quickly (and I'm not super good), so maybe those should be harder to get. Also, it will randomly go through the included music in the menu, which I think isn't.. exactly... adequate.... Overall I think it's a neat casual-to-hardcore game with some great replayability and a price that could come down just a bit.

WARNING: If you're looking for an easy out-of-box type of experience, then stay away from this Sim.
Do I recommend this game?... 50% Yes, and 50% No. If Steam used a Star Rating, I would give it 2.5 of 5 Stars. It's a love / hate relationship. I love the idea of this Sim, the creativity it involves, the scenery, the sounds of nature, and the sounds of machinery. It has free play value, or you can create your own strategy of how to complete a task.
But, I do hate the technical difficulties the Sim dishes out and you have to waste time fixing them. It's sad you have to do such things on something you paid for. On the other hand, recovering from an object collision detection error has a challenging element of it's own. Some errors you can fix within seconds, others may take minutes.
After ironing out the graphical errors and finding the right settings that work best, it's a pretty fun Sim. However, I'm a "chill out" type of Sim person to begin with and I have patience with editing game files. I'm a hobby programmer, so I have an unfair advantage other gamers don't have.
I would also like to point out I've discovered there are 2 different sub-versions of Woodcutter Sim 2013 that both say they are version 1.0.0.6. One version does not include the Flatbed Truck, but the Steam version does. For some people that might not be saying a whole lot, considering it was a last minute add-on that wasn't planned out very well. For one thing, the engine tune sound does not change while driving the Flatbed. Another thing, the trailer has Drive Wheels instead of Free Wheels, which tend to push the tractor over in both slow and fast turns. However, this does amount to combined horse power so you can climb hills faster while transporting the Feller. On the other hand, it's hard to drive the Flatbed around tight corners in reverse because the 2 Drive Chains work against each other. So, there's advantages and disadvantages to work with there. You have to compromise with strategy and learn the terrain.
The PhysX for the Sim was not coded for entire realism, but you do get the "jest" of things while operating the machinery. You will not find proper weight and mass PhysX in Woodcutter, nor any of the previous Sims released by UIEG. The collison detection still needs lots of work, because you should not be able to fold a tractor parallel to the trailer, that's just absurd. You also should not be able to drive a Utility Van into a Feller at ground level and cause the Feller to fall over, but I guess I'm just nick-picking now... lol.
Speaking of those Collision Detection errors... If you play Woodcutter using the default settings, then there's a high probability you will experience gradual degrading functionality. Especially with the logs, trees, and vehicle tires. Sure, everything starts out great, but eventually the game engine is going to "burp" and you'll find yourself fighting with the Self-Loader Truck while attempting to pick up "ghost" trees or logs. The crane clamps will begin to pass completely through the objects for no apparent reason. Sometimes shutting down the Sim and restarting it fixes the glitch, but it's not always going to work like that. The same is true for vehicle tires when they find an invisible hole in the pavement to fall through or get stuck in (restarting the game might work, might not). Paying for vehicle assistance sometimes proves to be a failure as well and you'll still find yourself restarting the game to fix it. You might find yourself dropping trees straight through the ground, or see a tree bobbing around in the grass like a fishing cork. You might even discover an invisible object in a place where it wouldn't usually be as you slam into it while moving around in the forest and it causes you to dump your load. Sawmill logs might magically vibrate themselves straight out the end of the trailer and you'll have to gather them back up. If you put trees in the yellow log truck, they might slip backwards as if they are sitting on grease (what happened to tie downs?). You can press the "1" key to jump out of the Self-Loader Truck and your shoulder can tap the tractor and cause it to flip over on it's side, then you have to work the crane again and push the tractor back over. Luckily the trailer is more durable and allows the tractor tires to pass straight through the front-end... LOL... but don't count on it, you can still lose your load in the process. I could go on and on over the crazy things I've seen in this Sim, but the point is to be careful and be aware these things can happen. Save your game often and name them so you'll know where to start over at, if you have to.
There is something you can do to help avoid the glitches more often. Search the WoodCutter discussion threads on Steam for the file "device.icom" (notice the period) and you'll find instructions. Basically you have to turn down the graphics and increase the refresh rate.
You can also use cheat codes to help you get out of a jam, so also search for "cheating.login" (notice the period) and you'll find instructions for that too.
What is this Sim worth? As it stands now, probably $2.49 and lot's of patience. At least you get material to work with, but you have to figure out how to make it run better.

Overall I enjoy the game quite a bit but it's been quite awhile since I last played a jrpg and I'm still only in the second chapter.
I'm finding the jrpg a breathe of fresh air since the last time I've played it one was when I was very young (so keep in mind I have very little experience so have nothing to compare it to.) Overall in the 2nd chapter there hasn't been too much grinding as long as you space things out from story missions to random dungeon for fun, and maybe random item hunt to get a plan you want. All the characters gain exp regardless if they participated in the fight. (Probably a standard feature now but I remember hating leveling individual characters in my old jrpgs.)
Controls for the keyboard took a little to get used to but now I don't even care anymore as I've gotten the hang of everything. I did rebind the secondary hotkey for the A button to numpad zero so it'd make it easier running around spamming space (aka Y for finding items) then num0 (aka A) to surprise attack monsters.
So far I really enjoy the humor but I watch a lot of anime and so I'm used to that sort of humor. I do enjoy all the references and such as well. Basically the story is meant to be lighthearted fun (so far) and isn't meant to be taken too seriously. Basically at it's core it's just a group of people exploring, helping people, and having fun/interacting with each other. (If you dislike the characters then you will probably dislike the story, if you're like me and used to these kinds of characters and enjoy the "Gamindustri" setting then you'll probably find it a bit of fun.)
TLDR: I'd say get it on sale and anything more then that I can't say for sure as idk the standards for jrpgs. Since for me everything is a breath of fresh air, because I haven't been playing them that much recently.

I was browsing the steam catalog for games and somehow I stumbled across this game. I don't know what or why I even bought this game, I've never even heard of NepNep before but I just bought it (it's on a 66%(?) discount, maybe that somehow encouraged me to buy it)
and it was worth it.
Story:
The story isn't actually that great, you won't find a thrilling story like Steins;Gate(although you'll find references) or a computer smashing, keyboard throwing, tear flooding story like Clannad(no, no references, fortunately) but what makes the game shine is the characters. If NepNep wasn't NepNep, or Noire wasn't a tsundere, I'd probablly just skip the whole text. The character dialogues really cracks me up most of the time and I really love how they make references and breaking the fourth wall jokes.
Gameplay:
I'd say it's pretty good, no annoying sudden battles like the one with the annoying blonde dude who's a pro at underwater soccer (I know, my last console is the ps2 and I just got into PC gaming). It took me about 35 hours to actually finish the story (plus grinds). Battle's doesn't fell repetitive and boring most of the time and one wrong action could spell doom if you're not careful. This however, doesn't apply if you overlevelled. In the last bossfight, I got too cautious and grinded hard just to find me getting 200-700 dmg (except for that one magic, can't remember name, insta killed Green Heart). So, if you're trying to find a challenge, don't go overboard with the grinds and you'll be ok.
Music:
I don't really give much attention to the BGM in every game I play but when it's good, I'll notice it. With that said, the only one I particularly like is Noire's theme and that's it. Everything else was fine and it fits the situation but any serious themes will just be broken by NepNep. The effects aren't bad, but it wasn't particularly good either, it's above average
Characters:
NepNep never fails to bring a smile to my face everytime she's on the screen. I played the whole game on Japanese, I won't lie, I dislike english(dubs, not the whole language) but the difference of NepNep's impression I got by going dub is like me eating an orange that tastes like chicken. It's that weird. That doesn't mean it's bad, but I won't recommend it. IF and Compa although kinda irrelevant to the story, wasn't really left out and I'm grateful for that, because I love IF's VA, which also voices my favorite character in my favorite Visual Novel, F/SN. Most of the character's personalities are really likeable, especially Noire(Unless you hate Tsunderes, like most fa@#ts, sorry). I was pretty sad that the supporting mascot characters are just there to help move the plot, I was hoping I get to know more of them, especially MAGES..(extra period intentional)
Verdict:
So, do I like it? Yes. Should you buy it? Yes. Even though you're broke? Yes. What if I have a life and kids to spend time with? Don't lie to yourself, you know your wife/husband could take care of them, so just buy it already.
8.5/10 will Nep my NepNep

I picked this up today in the sale and so have barely even started, but I feel compelled to write a review anyway. If you haven't played it, I STRONGLY recommend that you do so. I'm only about an hour into it (up to just beyond the first boss) and I'm already spellbound. It's like a fairytale/Disney movie. The video sequences are all told via beautiful stained-glass scenes (remember the intro to Beauty And The Beast, or Sleeping Beauty? That.) The dialogue is often in rhyming couplets, which lends to the fairytale charm of the game. And don't get me started on the hand-drawn backgrounds or the music. Oh my God, the music. Outside of the Final Fantasy series, this is fast becoming my favourite soundtrack. Speaking of Final Fantasy, the combat is very similar in the sense that it is turn-based, dependant on speed - which I adore. I love the idea of the plot (the sun, moon and stars have been stolen and it's up to you to recover them - fantasy plots are my favourites.) Outside of combat, the game is played via side-scrolling environments. Everything just looks FANTASTIC. It lends further belief to the "games are art" ideology.

A beautifully engaging and enjoyable surprise. Bought on a whim during a sale, I would love to see a sequel/new offering in the same style more than any big name blockbuster in the last ten years.
The important word here is "Child", but in the best way imaginable. Whether it's the fairytale styling, sidescrolling platforming adventure (reminiscent of hours whittled away at a NES/SNES with Mario), or the innovative yet Final Fantasy style combat dynamics, everything about this game is warmingly charming and harks back to elements of different stages of your childhood.
Beautifully animated, impeccable soundtrack, satisfying but simple XP skills tree and gems (bonus skills buff) crafting, I couldn't put this game down for the admittedly short (<10hrs) storyline, but immediately upon finishing I just started again! Only slight negative comment is the speech/narration is all done in rhyming verse, which occasionally gets a bit forced/hackneyed, but not enough to break this game's wonderous spell.
I, personally, would have been happy to pay the £12 rrp in retrospect, but some might not, given the short story arc. But if you spot this on sale, I cannot recommend it enough, everyone should snap it up immediately!!

It was hard for me to make this the first game I ever gave a negative review to (and shocking) because I simply love telltale games as much as I love Game of Thrones. But this game just isnt what I was looking for.
*SPOILERS*
To start, youre playing as 4 different charecters in rotation. Now, this is a cool concept to an extent because it makes it like an episode of Game of Thrones; youre a Man of the Knight's Watch, a Northerner Lord who was pledged to the Starks (this game starts as the Red Wedding occurs) as a result, your family is pretty much a complete ♥♥♥♥♥ to the Boltons and a lame other fictional House, the Ironhills.
You cant do much to control your fate whatsoever; it's a rollercoaster, not a sports car. Now this rollercoaster can honestly be really damn fun at times, and for 10$ on a steam sale I do recommend this game. but 30$? Nah. Happy I paid 15. Now that im done talking about money, onto the other two charecters you play as.
Mira Forrester is the firstborn daughter of your House Forrester, and she is a very unloyal handmadien (because the rollercoaster makes you be) to Lady Margeary. Her charecter gets the attention of Tyrion Lanister, and this is a part of the rollercoaster I like. And having Cerseai judge and treat you like garbage is pretty funny. Beyond that, as this charecter, despite trying your hardest, which I did, you REALLLLLY CANT fufill why youre allegidely even apart of the plot, which is to use your influence to stop the Whitehills in Kings Landing, and to somehow, even though your family was always loyal to the Starks, strike a deal with the Lanisters to ensure your safety. Yeaaano.
Out of the four charecters, my favorite to play as, simply because it was a fun part of the nonessential to the plot but awesome adenture through Essos in search of meeting the Great Khaleesi as a Forrester who was banished from Ironrath (that's their kingdom, they say Iron alot in this  game). You go on a pretty cool storyline with Asher Forrester, and the best part of it all is that I just killed him off instead of killing off the first charecter mentioned, Rodrick Forrester. A badly fixed scenario which is blatently intended to decide who you would rather have as lord of the house. This entire game could have been focused just on the North. But no, the rollercoaster wanting you to ride around Wersteros and Essos like the damn trine thing in the introduction of every episode. The developers said, "We need someone in the North, someone at/north the Wall, someone in King's Landing, and someone working with Khaleesi, because these are all the important plot lines we see on the show that you can now intereact with!" Decent idea, but it didnt work. The game spreads you thin like too little butter on a piece of bread by making you go around the world and do mainly pointless things beyond what you do in the North. One thing I liked is that alot of the actors gave their voices for the game; it is fun to talk to Jon Snow, the Lanisters, Margeary, and Khaleesi (tho she has a random attitude in this game that doesnt match her charecter in the show.) Overall, giving the game a 6.5/10. If youre a fan of the show like I am, this game's worth 10$ like I said. But telltale games, along with whatever collaberation came from GoT completely laid a goose egg on what coulda been alot better of a game. Though I did enjoy the rollercoaster, i didnt pay for a rollercoaster. I wanted the damn sports car; the chance to be king of the seven kingdoms or something epic along the lines of that. and if youre going to force me to be these 4 charecters, fine, but give me more choices than 2 important choices; one you make in episode 1 as the 5th charecter i didnt even mention is in this game (he gets killed beyond your control because, rollercoaster), and the choice to close episode 5 I just made of keeping Rodrick alive instead of Asher. There was never a promise made to me that this game would be great, but I assumed with the history of great Telltale games I've played that this game would be. Instead, I am dissapointed.
I didn't mention the graphics and movement flaws; lets just put it this way. If they were better Ida rated this game probably 2 points higher.

This is a tricky game to review because, personally, I came to Grey Goo with high hopes but willing to forgive a lot just to have a new fun entry in my favourite genre that isn't Starcraft. I love RTS games and want to see more of them, so take that into account while reading this review.
First, some technical problems. I'm running on a PC that was mid-ranged in 2012, and while the game itself mostly performs fine, the menu system has horrifically bad performance, stuttering at almost every opportunity. The in-game HUD is pretty large, and it's not always easy to tell what's going on at a glance since there's a lot of swapping similar panels out for one another. Unit pathfinding can get pretty bad, units push each other around (including into enemy fire!) and sometimes units seem downright unresponsive.
The three different factions are quite interesting. I like the mobile, sneaky approach to the Goo's design, which goes against the swarms-of-units that you expect given the marketing; actual unit production with the Goo (you produce  sneaky, weak units that turn into more specialized units) is really innovative, but it's also tedious and difficult to manage, and easy to lose track of a Protean here or there. Playing against the Goo can become painful, though, because it's so hard to track down their ever-moving Mother Goos. The other two factions are fairly standard in RTS terms, though the Humans have a more lone-fortress approach to base building while the Beta are more about sprawling and forward expansions.
In terms of moment-to-moment gameplay, I'd say that it's overall good solid fun, with a nice feel of ebb-and-flow once things really get going. A few caveats: units die extremely quickly and are completely disposable; area-of-effect attacks are, given how fragile units are, ludicrously effective; and the "epic" units are too slow and, yes, fragile to feel truly epic (though they do have massive AOE attacks that can wipe out dozens of units at a time, especially the insane Hand of Ruk). On the other hand, the brush cover mechanic that lets you hide units in forests is brilliant, and the developers aren't stingy with that cover either. Combine that with the Goo's mobility and the way that terrain height affects visibility, and you get an RTS where terrain actually matters significantly in combat, which is great.
As for the campaign, I've just played through the entire thing, and it's a mixed bag. The developers saw fit to make the AI in the campaign extremely aggressive, even on "normal"; by the third mission in, the AI was rushing my base with a dozen or more units 90 seconds into the game (a point at which it's almost impossible to have built more than a handful of units). In many cases it pays to avoid and skirt around mission objectives until you can amass a large force, since progresssing through objectives usually triggers even more aggressive AI behavior. There are other missions, though, where it's fairly easy to smash some key bases and wait around to build epics that will destroy everything else. Overall, the difficulty varies wildly, though at least the challenge gives you a sense of accomplishment.
In terms of the story components, the cutscenes are gorgeous (best CGI faces I think I've ever seen in a video game), and the narrative itself is original and interesting, with some pertinent themes about science, exploration, and responsibility towards life. Unfortunately, the game itself doesn't let the story shine through; there are story elements mentioned in marketing materials or on official websites (or even on the Steam trading cards!) that never actually get dealt with in-game, which seems silly. Much of the narrative feels rushed, like they had more they wanted to say and do than they actually had the money/time to implement. The narrative has a solid core, but it needs some fleshing out to be truly great.
Overall, I would say that Grey Goo is a promising, if flawed, RTS; a pretty good game, but not a great one. It's good enough that I hope they get to make a sequel, and that they get the opportunity to iron out the kinks from this initial offering. With a
more attention to user-friendliness across the board, and a more fleshed-out and confident approach to the narrative, this game could really be something special.

I'm not exactly well-versed in the current state of the RTS industry, but I played and loved Age of Empires and Starcraft 1. Grey Goo is exactly what an RTS should be, cutting out the fiddling with worker units and managing multiple resources, having mappable and easily-memorized hotkeys, a very simple unit setup (12+1 units per faction), and factions that take some getting used to. No faction ties you into a specific playstyle; all can, to some degree, play aggressively, defensively, economically, and so on, but the factions definitely have radically different paradigms. Don't listen to the people who say that Beta and Humans are the same, the two play completely differently, especially in terms of static defenses and unit production. Some are saying that Goo needs a nerf, I don't agree. I've beaten and been beaten by Goo about an equal number of times, and while it has some very strong attributes to be sure (Goo artillery is really awful to go up against, and proteans are... ugh), a properly massed army or a properly defended base should have no real issues. You WILL settle into a preferred faction, and you WILL enjoy playing match after match, noticing your own improvement time after time. To tell the truth, I didn't buy this game. I was gifted it. It's a great game, but the $50 price tag is hefty. For $30, I'd say to pick it up without a doubt. $50 is steep, but I think it's worth it.
The map editor is there, but it's buried in the game files and is sort of a pain to use. At the time of this writing, there are very few actual player-created maps on the workshop, mostly there are "test maps".
The community could help with this, given a more accessible map editor, and since the devs are supporting the game with updates often, more maps are likely to be forthcoming. However, at this time, there are around ten maps, and only, I believe, three 4-player maps, only two of which are suitable for free-for-all.
At present, there are three victory condition options and three teams options, plus an epic units/no epic units option. This game would benefit from support for three-player games, and see below.
Grey Goo currently supports 2-player matches and 4-player matches. As mentioned above, 3-player would be a good addition, but also, if the game can support large enough maps, up to eight players would make for some awesome matches.
This is a bit silly, but I would love to see more than four color options present. The four available do make the menu seem simple, but adding another row of color choices wouldn't detract from that, and might be interesting. Bottom line is that sometimes, an enemy unit from the same faction as me will show up, and I'll think they're my unit until I look at the mini-map, or my units start shooting. This might be caused by my unfamiliarity with the game (I have only 20 hours logged at present), but some of the current color schemes are rather similar, at least for Human and Beta factions.

I understand that the compaign isn't terribly important for an RTS like this, mainly focused on Skirmish and Multiplayer, but it is at least intended to be a tutorial. Sure, tutorials can be accessed via the menus, but it's generally fun to play through the campaign first.

"Beat Hazard Ultra" - Review
Gameplay:  6/10
A fun game. Modern effects meets old skool arcade gameplay. If Galaga was invented today this game would be it. If you're a fan of the acrade syle or want a bit of nostalgia with a modern twist, then this game is for you. The basic idea on which the gameplay is based doesn't change, but the in-game options, level ups, currency and extras add a little variety to mix it all up nicely enough to entertain. Initially the gameplay feels tricky if not strange and unintuitive, however over time it becomes a bit more like second nature rather than stressful frustration.
Game ambiance: n/a
Reliability/Stability: 10/10
No crash or instability issues to report.
Story/Plot: n/a
Concept: 7/10
Arcade style games like this have been available since the 70's. To think that a new one can be created today, so successfully, is almost astonishing.  The classic arcade space-themed gameplay is offset with the  original idea of not only incorporating your own music playlist, but having the game react and respond to the music. This certainly brings a fun new perspective to this genre.
Concept execution: 7/10
With many features such as multilayer online co-op gameplay with friends, perks, power-up's and a variety of single player modes, this game will keep you busy for a while. Or at least, as lite fun goes, it'll entertain you enough until you decide which major title you want to play next.
Textures: 5/10
Generally speaking the textures in Beat Hazard are average for a game, but not underdeveloped. You could say they are just enough and nothing more. This can be forgiven however as the focus of this game is more about beat triggered special effects and skill rather than mind blowing textures.
Modelling: 5/10
Again, the modelling isn't necessarily the main aspect of this game, and again like the textures, it is just enough. They are enough to allow the game experience to be enjoyable and that's the whole point.
Graphics: 8/10
The special effects in this game are dizzying, strobing and seizure inducing. Glorious if you like it, hideous if you don't. Either way you can't deny it's extremely colorful and eye -twitchingly pretty. Turn the room lights off, the screen brightness up and strap yourself into your favorite spaceship!
Sound: 6/10
The sound isn't too bad, given the premise of this game revolves around music. It's what you'd expect from an arcade game but with a more modern production quality. Love it or hate it the volumetric and situational dynamics are there, perhaps a little overdone and exaggerated, but then it does have to stand side-by-side with the huge visuals. If you enjoy shooting spaceships with big audible bangs and explosions then you'll defiantly have fun here.
Music: 10/10
I have to give this 10/10 for music because it's comprised  from my personally playlist. You will too unless you couldn't care less about music, in which case this game might not be to your taste.
Adjustable shadow mapping: No
Bonus/Extras: none

How much you like this will probably depend on how much you like your own music and the idea of fighting a huge boss at a particularly climactic part of your favourite song. Gameplay-wise, Beat Hazard really doesn't offer anything new, but it's an incredibly addictive, over-the-top flashy lights-wielding (check the epilepsy warning on the loading screen!) timesink with some rather nice touches.
The game seems to suit trance/electronica and (technical death) metal best from what I've tried so far - anything with high-intensity parts is a good fit as this both powers up your ship's weapons and increases the number and scariness of enemies. Nothing quite like mowing down a seemingly never-ending stream of ships with rainbow beams of PURE POWER! Conversely, if you hit a quiet bit in the middle of your massacre everything suddenly becomes terrifyingly hard to kill with your tiny guns.
My favourite part about Beat Hazard, however, has got to be the addition of the Volume powerup - you can start at max volume if you're boring, but you really just appreciate your music more when you have to work to make it loud and epic. You will also never forgive yourself if you get yourself killed whilst trying to turn up the volume, but such is life.
This gets a big thumbs up for music lovers - others not so much, but it's still a fun little over-the-top dual-stick shooter and worth picking up cheap, at least.

I personally found this game... underwhelming.
The issue stems from what the game promises, or seemingly hopes, to deliver to the user. A radically fun experience powered by your own music. The description of the game made me hope to have a racing and heart-pounding experience much like audiosurf, but it felt more like drinking a Red Bull compared to doing cocaine.
To put it bluntly, Beat Hazard is a space shooter. Your lazers, the enemies spawn points, and their flight patterns, are all dictated by your music. You only have about 2 powerups that just change the potency of your weapons, and the volume of your music. You collect money, which is used to buy and upgrade perks, that only increase your score and nothing else. You 'rank up', a leveling system, based on your scores from the songs you've played, but don't get much out of it.
All in all, Beat Hazard is a seizure-enducing, messy, and underwhelming experience. Only electronic music could really fit the game's theme, and the game by itself is entirely obsolete without the DLC. And even THAT is obsolete thanks to Beat Hazard Ultra. The game encourages you to create it's steam badges to get new ships that are only minor changes, and a majority of the fun features isn't available without Shadow Operations Unit DLC.
The game is fun for a length of maybe 15 minutes, while the player holds the mouse button and waits for the level to be beat. The enemies may as well be made of clay, the lights and particles blinding the entire screen, and the explosions even less exciting. Beat Hazard is like taking ecstacy only to be immune to it after it wears off forever.
Going back to Audiosurf.

This game is pretty disappointing. You can play the card game just fine, but the presentation is about as bland as it gets. The backgrounds are really badly modeled, the music is just background noise, and there's no voice acting. A few of the popular monsters have a little model and animation when they attack, but they aren't modeled or animated very well either, and it's kind of annoying for the same animation to play each time you attack.
None of that pizazz should really matter too much for a card game, but the multiplayer is too dead to find much enjoyment in, and there isn't even anything to the single player content besides the story duels, which are entirely luck based if you use the "story deck" and entirely too easy if you use your own deck, and the duelist challenges, which are harder than the story but all based around a very specific deck archetype. You can't just like, set up a random duel with the AI and change some options or something. Also, as others have said, I appreciate that you don't start with every card, but I don't like that they give you no indication whatsoever as to what is in which booster pack. This game isn't much good as anything but a simulator, so having to grope in the dark over where to get the cards you need to build a fancy new deck isn't very accomodating of that.
I guess I'm just let down since Duel Links for free on your phone actually has really good presentation and healthy PvP, and I thought this could fill the single player void, but there's not a lot here besides a working digital version of the full card game. If all you want is a digital simulation of the many Yu-Gi-Oh cards, this will do fine. But if you're looking for a versatile single player video game, or even just random online PvP, I can't recommend it.
8/10 for Yu-Gi-Oh, 4/10 for being a bad video game.

I swear I only managed to get to the end twice only to smash full speed into the brick wall that is the rebel flagship. Since the encounters are random you can be put into a bloody minefield of pirates and rebels, or you could be completely fine to coast through the sectors to only gun down a few poor sods for scrap. Be careful though this game will punish you if you waste resource,  which is great because I fell it promotes exploration which will never grow old. So to some it up it's a fun but challenging game with great customisation and encounters that will keep you addicted for hours, and hey if you ever get bored there's tonnes of Mods out there that will spice up your F.T.L experience! Well its yu-gi-oh.
As a simulation of the card game, its pretty much flawless of course.
The good:
The campaign of classic matches from the anime is great. Whats even cooler is the ability to play these matches from the reverse perspective, so you can play the iconic Yugi/Kaiba duel both with and against Exodia.
Huge card database. Looks like every card pretty much ever.
Online play. Not much to say, it works pretty well, but it would be nice to be able to configure custom matches (such as using an older banlist). This way you could go online and find someone who actually wasn't running pendulum decks...
The bad:
Its so damn slow. Why is there no option to speed up the animations? Seriously half of my playtime is loading animations
Control issues. I have issues sometimes of in-duel my keyboard suddenly not registering, and have to use a mouse.
Cards are not arranged as they were in real-life boosters, so you have to forget everything you know about card sets, only recognise that archtypes are grouped, so there is that benefit i guess.
You do not know which cards a person has until you pull them from the boosters. WIth each person having over 250 cards it can take you FOREVER to complete 1 set. I've opened over 250 Kaiba sets now, and still don't have 1 of each card, let alone a playset of each. It took me 249 boosters to get 3 Trade-Ins. And that was after working out who had them.
It WILL take you FOREVER to build the deck you want, because there is no trading in the game, no method of purchasing singles, and no way of even checking which set has the card you need. This is where this game really falls down completely compared to actually playing yugioh. There is no aftermarket, no way of getting what you actually want except dumb luck against pointlessly high odds. I'm 2/5 complete on the campaign now, yet I've completed 0/20+ card sets (and I've only bought from 2 of the sets to get my Gimmick Puppets)
Overall:
Well if you are familiar with devpro/yugiohpro, its basically that with a little more polish and slow as hell animations. Its pretty good, I would definitely recommend this.

In many ways Grey Goo feels like the game Westwood wanted to make when they were making the original C&C's. While it differs in many respects - and it is by no means a simple clone of the original franchise with a new setting, GG definatly falls into the C&C style RTS as opposed to the much faster paced Starcraft style RTS.  The game awards strategic thinking with new mechanics such as brush that hide your units and elevation that could also potentially hide your units. The big new feature in terms of strategy which I don't see often in RTS is the inclusion of artillery which requires the user to tactfully make use of spotter unit or planes to get the most out of their long range bombardment.
Aside from new startegic elements the game also shines in the uniqueness of each faction present. While units within the factions can get a bit same-y the factions themselves feel different. I never once felt like I was just playing a re-skinned verison of the Beta when playing the Humans, and the Goo is completely different from the other two factions.
The campaign lends itself to some of the best CGI I've ever seen for the cutscenes and it harks back to the old Red Alert style of between mission cutscenes and in-mission dialouge which creates a surprisingly detailed story that is slowly revealed in Medias Res style throughout the campaign. The campaign missions themselves are nicely varied but do get a little unfair when you're unaware of how the other factions work. For example the final Beta mission is needlessly hard if you don't - like I didn't, understand how the Mother Goos work before tackling the mission. But regardless with each mission sitting at an average length of in and around 35 minutes and there being 15 missions the campaign alone would be enough to get your money's worth in many respects even if you never touched multiplayer or skirimish.
Stepping away from the mechanics and narrative for a moment: graphically and aesthetically the game is beautiful. While the maps at present offer little variation each faction has its own style and sticks rigidly to it. The beta for example are more steampunk-esque with their hard metal creations while the Humans have more sleek and futuristic robots at their disposal. The game's art direction also has nice little touches such as friendly units in brush being highlighted in green or the fact that each faction gets its own unique UI.
All in all GG is a return to the RTS style of the C&C era with fantastic art style and mechanics to boot. While the maps could use some extra variety and while the story is hardly the most ingrossing of tales GG has a degree of charm that reminds me greatly of the old Red Alert games. It's a game I heartily recommend to fans of RTS, regardless of which style of RTS they prefer.
Download it, you wont regret it.

"Do you hate the Boltons? Well now you can hate them even more! Buy Game of Thrones: Hate the Boltons Game Series by Telltale Games!"
As an avid fan of George R.R Martin's "A Song of Ice and Fire" and the T.V show based on his books, I was impressed with the amount of loyalty to the series Telltale Games has incorporated into this game. For the record this is my first "Telltale game" and as such the experience was new to me. Every moment of this feels like a real episode of Game of Thrones, the politics, the♥♥♥♥♥kissing, the planning and of course the killing. It does a good job of establishing the new characters and making the player feel their emotion as they overcome their situations in the world of Westeros.
(TV Show spoilers ahead)
The events of this game take place just after the Red Wedding. The secessionist Northern Army has collapsed and the North is in ruins. The game revolves around House Forrester, an ancient northern House whose lord was killed at the Red Wedding. With the merciless House Bolton now Warden of the North seeking to establish its dominancy House Forrester's very future is at stake. You take control of a variety of original characters not in the main series, all of whom are related to House Forrester, and deal with their issues. The story contains the essentials of Game of Thrones, the aspects we all know and love: the politics, family, bloodshed and swearing. All of these are well incorporated into the six episodes in Telltale's game.
The game's six episodes are spread out across both Westeros and Essos, from the Wall to King's Landing to even Meereen and Yunkai. Along the way you come into contact and get to interact with the characters from the TV show we all know and love. Cersei, Margaery and Jon Snow just to name a few. All of whom are voice acted by their respective actors. As expected, the quality of their deliverance is top notch and worthy of Game of Thrones. They're portrayed as if they were delivering lines in the actual TV show and this is something that adds immersion to this game. Their writing and behaviour remain loyal to their TV counterparts.
Even some of the new characters are interesting and are portrayed memorably.
As this is a Telltale game, it gives you a small amount of freedom to choose what you want to say and do. Because you are playing as a weakened House your real only option is to play it smart, but then again, isn't that what the TV show has taught us [so far?] I guess it depends on the player on whether the amount of freedom the game offers you is enough or not. For me personally I thought it delivered a nice range of options without going too far overboard. Just keep in mind that your choices affect what happens. Don't be cocky by thinking the game is predictable. The choices you make might seem like the right ones but they can blow up in your face instantly. Going back to the story the game offers you different ways of helping your family. Each one is unique and offers many different paths to the final goal. It might mean breaking promises and oaths you've made, it might mean leaving behind or abandoning people and it might lead to the end of the relationships you've built with the NPCs, and even the end of House Forrester. You may choose to put family before everything else or to pursue a different agenda.
As I said earlier, each episode of this game runs almost like a real episode on TV. It's mostly about talking and interaction. There are some combat scenes in which you use QT events to pass them, such as tapping Q and pressing WASD to dodge attacks etc. If you are looking for action, you've come to the wrong place.
Graphics and performance-wise, the game runs smoothly on my GTX 560 Ti. The graphics have an interesting watercolour look to them, something that all Telltale games share. However to be honest I would appreciate it if Telltale got to work on improving their game engine as some textures etc look very bland and dated. I know story is more important than graphics, but graphics should still be taken into consideration.
I am glad Telltale have chosen to make a game about Game of Thrones. Next up we need a Skyrim-like RPG.
I am impressed with Game of Thrones by Telltale. I feel like they remained loyal to the show. The events portrayed in the six episodes are exciting and contain the suspense, drama, swearing and bloodshed that makes up Game of Thrones. I recommend it for die-hard Game of Thrones fans. If you are new to Game of Thrones, I recommend that you have watched Season 3 to be familiar with the events of this game (or have read and finished A Storm of Swords.)

Do you enjoy bullet hell shooters?
Do you enjoy staring at colourful flashing bright lights?
Do you like playing your own music while playing a game?
Do you want a game whose levels are tailor made to your music tracks?
If yes is your answer to all of the above (or 2 or more of them), then get Beat Hazard, now.
Beat Hazard is unlike any of your old school bullet hell shooters, creating a unique sense of gameplay to each of anyone's music track. The game would undoubtedly make your eyeballs pop with its insanely ridiculous usage of colourful lights, and if you love to make your eye pop as so, then do yourself a favour.
Gameplay is simple and is easy to pickup, making it playable for casuals or those who arent used to bullet hell shooters. But of course, there is a place for those who are hardcores in the genre.
However, there are flaws in generating a unique sense in each level of a track. Based on my experience, the game solely depends on your track's tempo. I.E. when your track has a quick tempo it becomes more intense and vice versa. This is a problem for some songs which switch from high to low tempos and vice versa, making the level extremely hard. So there are a couple of hiccups within the game.
Overall, Beat Hazard is fun and extremely so if you enjoy fast and intense music. The 'custom' feel to each game for each track is definitely not perfect, but Beat Hazard by itself is already a great bullet hell shooter.

Before even considering buying this game, I will give you a warning: If you got really interested in how the tactical battles were designed, you WILL be let down by the end of this game.
While I can't blame the developers for the cliffhanger on the huge TEASE that was Banner's Saga 1, since they announced from the beginning that this game would be a trilogy. I can still complain about the way they handled tactical battles because that's one of my main grips about this game. Up until the end of the first game, almost every battle introduced a new mechanic, or some new tactic to use in battle. When I reached what I later found out to be the ending, I thought the tutorial was finally over, and the real interesting battles would begin, and that's what happened... for about 3 fights... then it ended... Come on.
And ending like that felt like a huge♥♥♥♥♥♥block, and it ended looking like the entirety of Banner's Saga 1 was just a big tutorial for a new, better game. With that kind of approach, you have 2 options for a sequel, you can either:
a) Begin a whole new tutorial for Banner's Saga 2, because maybe you added new features, maybe you have to take into account new players or people who waited several months to play the sequel and need to learn again. Alright, now we get another huge tutorial, that will probably end just as the game ends again, just like the first game, making people like me feel unsatisfied, or
b) Start the game assuming people played the first game and know everyting about the tactics and gameplay. Alright, now your first game is just a huge unnanounced tutorial, diminishing all the value of the progress made in the first game. "It was just a tutorial, stupid."
Both are not good ways to make the player feel satisfied with your gameplay. And that's sincerely what happened to me. I was completely let down by that in the first game, and can't bring myself to play the sequel, since they are probably using solution (a) or (b), and that's just bad. You have t make the gameplay of your game self-contained between games, while also giving the player a chance to really apply them, not give 2 tutorials, or make the entirety of the first game a huge tutorial.
They may have had the best of intentions while developing the first game, but it still feels really crappy to do that, and I am amazed no one ever mentioned how the final battles felt really lackluster during the game's development.
Oh, and if my play time didn't clue you in yet, this game is too shot for a tactical game. And since this is an episodical release, you have almost no reason to being a new game, unless you want to override your previous choices.

Serious Review:  I bought this in the Ultimate Franchise Pack because it was about $14 and it came with everything Saint's Row related on Steam.  Great deal.  So I came into this game with dirt poor expectations after having played Saint's Row The Third.  But, this series has gone from a GTA clone, to it's own entity...and that is not necessarily bad.  I thought the Saint's Row Series was a large steaming pile of♥♥♥♥♥♥because I played SR3 first.  Boy...was I wrong.  I bought SR2 (The best in the series) and I knew I was greatly mistaken.  SR2 told an amazing story and was the first in the series to introduce character customization as in-depth as it is here.  It told a beautiful story that let you choose how to go through it, which gangs to fight first, and had a large array of varried activities from fight clubs to races and even some good online large multiplayer game modes.  All of this but the Customization was taken away when SR3 hit the scene.  In this, the 3rd Street Saint's are now celebrities.  It takes away everything serious and makes awful jokes, not awful as in morbid like 9/11 ones, but things like Fart in a Jar, a giant purple♥♥♥♥♥♥♥bat, and a sex appeal slider for how big your♥♥♥♥♥♥♥or boobs are.  The game was incredibly short and linear and by the end, you were essentially immune to everything, making it not fun.  In SR4, however, they imbrace the craziness, comedy, and humor that SR3 merely foreplayed with.  You start out with a Call of Duty cameo, afterwards, you become the President of the United States.  It then moves into a cameo of Fable 3, not in medieval times, but having you make choices that ultimately don't do♥♥♥♥♥♥  On your way to give a speech, you then get attacked by aliens...yes, ♥♥♥♥ing aliens.  That is what mostly turned me off.  However, as I played, it got more and more legitimately funny.  You are then taken through a linear corridor of generic aliens called the Zin, and then to a turret section and it makes fun of that as well.  Afterwards you are dropped into a parody of The Truman Show, then you enter the main game, which is a giant Matrix parody. A masterful work of art from start to finish, and a delight to play.
Here we have the story of Aurora, a young girl from Austria who is suddenly transported to an ancient and mysterious land, suddenly having to fend for herself against the strange creatures and dark forces that inhabit it. Along the course of her journey, she'll meet different types of creatures, some human or human-like, and others of a more animal nature, (often I was reminded of Zelda games) and several will join her team. As expected for an RPG, they each have different strengths and weaknesses, and you can hone their skills to build your dream team. And together, the team will travel the land, fight monsters, solve a few puzzles, and try to help Aurora get back home to her father.
I'm not huge into RPGs, so it takes a really good one to capture my attention for very long. This game as an RPG is not only incredibly fun to play, but it's also very innovative in a lot of ways. Turn-based combat gets a bit of a twist here, with a sort of timeline that determines when you and your enemies will strike. The speed varies based on your stats, what attack you're using, how fast your enemies are, and if any status effects are applied. If an enemy strikes you while you're preparing to attack, your attack may be interupted. But if you're clever, you can also use this against an enemy and interupt their attack. I don't know if this approach is completely original, but it's the first I've seen of it, and to me it made turn-based combat a whole lot more interesting. Every move you make can be timed and strategized to defeat opponents with different types or strengths. There's also a Pokemon-like element system where elemental attacks can be used against enemies that are weak to that type. And you can instantly swap out a member of your party for another one if you need to change up your strategy.
Another nice addition is that you have a blue fairy, Igniculus, who you can contol independently of Aurora. He can help you solve puzzles, gather items out of Aurora's reach, do basic healing and even slow down enemies during combat. His energy is a renewable resource that's an essential part of the gameplay. You'll get used to controlling two characters onscreen at the same time, and using both of them to complete tasks or strategize for combat. Igniculus can even be controlled by a second player if you have another controller.
I can't say enough nice things about the look of the game. Everything is rendered in a beautiful watercolor style, and some areas are simply incredible to explore. The screenshots just don't do it justice - you have to see for yourself how good this game looks. The soundtrack is also beautiful and very appropriate, and the combat music was done well as to not be annoyingly repetitive considering how much you'll hear it.
The leveling system is very generous, some might say too generous, but it helps the game to not feel like too much of a grind. I enjoyed the combat so much that I battled with every enemy I encountered - it just never got boring to me. Leveling up gives you skill points which you can use to improve your stats, attacks, defense, and other abilities. There are also items in the world that can permanently increase your stats, as well as Oculi which are crystals that can be crafted. I ignored this for a while, but once I understood how it worked, I became obsessed with Oculi. They are fun to craft and help you plan the strategy of your team by adding bonus effects to their attacks and defense.
The world is pretty big, but you have fast travel which unlocks automatically as you discover new areas. There are a handful of side quests that you can take on if you'd like. Some of them get a bit backtracky but I didn't mind it - generally the longer the quest, the better the reward. For the main quest, exploration is very important. It may take you a while to figure out where you need to go next as there's very little handholding here. You just get a slight hint about what you're supposed to be doing, and that's it. I found this very refreshing.
The story is pretty simple, but it holds together well and I found myself invested in the world-building as I went along. I loved the dialogue - most characters speak in rhymes and riddles - and this helped to build the characters a bit and show how they relate to one another. I particularly enjoyed when Igniculus asked Aurora questions about her world or what it's like to be human. Her answers were often simple, yet profound and moving coming from a young girl.
Overall a very enjoyable game. If you liked Ori and the Blind Forest, Dust: An Elysian Tail, or other games like those, you may enjoy this one even more. I still have yet to finish Ori because the difficulty started to ruin my enjoyment of the game. If something simpler and lighter than that is your wish, Child of Light will grant it. Took me about 15 hours to finish, but I took my time exploring and engaging in every battle and side quest. You could likely finish the main story in half that time if you wanted to.
10/10 for me, very well done.

It's a free game, so you may ask - is it worth it ? The short answer is: YES ! The quality of the game surpasses vast majority of the paid titles. You shouldn't judge it by the F2P banner.
Even though the setting at first looks all too familiar for this type of game (a camp full of teenage schoolgirls), it comes with a twist, taking you to late 80s Soviet Union (with a bits of modern times Russia as well), adding a Pioneers movement (which I knew little to none about) to the mix. Am I supposed to romance girls in communist youth camp ?
I will admit honestly, that from a perspective of a guy from a former Eastern Block country, it didn't look like an attractive premise at all. Regardless, after I got past the entrance gate (mildly disturbed by the Lenin image welcoming newcomers), I was quickly immersed in the story and the world, as if I were the main character.
The writing took me by surprise - it is genuinely fantastic, avoiding many cliches of the genre (often by openly acknowledging them). It blends fantasy, mystery, romance, travels in time and space and more. It questions your morals or sanity at times. It can go from sheer childlike sillyness, through heart-warming romance to serious drama and (in one route) even C-movie slasher parody. Whatever tone it invokes, it is always entertaining.
As a bonus, you can even learn some small bits about culture of everyday life in Russia. The amount of content is impressive - each route has a lot of unique scenes and dialogues, instead of usual re-cycling you experience in many other games. English translation is also very good.
Semyon, the main protagonist is your archetypical, anti-social and depressed young male, but he's actaully likeable as a person. I could relate to him as his reactions were logical enough and realistic most of the time.
As for the girls, you can't expect the originality here, but there are some plot twists that keep things interesting. And it gets more interesting with each next route. The girls' personalities are better explained in the last 2 routes (Miku and Yulya), when all the pieces of the puzzle fall into place. I would say only it's an intelligent way to cope with the limitations of VN's format itself.
Maybe the greatest aspect of "Everlasting Summer": when most of the VN's reveal their cards quickly, and by 2-3 playthroughs you feel you know all the in's and out's of the game, Soviet Games (what a name!) manages to keep your interest, surprise you with the turn of events or change of tone of the story when you least expect it, right to the grand finale.
There are 6 routes to choose from: Slavya, Alisa, Lena, Ulyana, Miku (Masha), no romance option, and Yulya. I suggest to keep that sequence to make the best of the game and leave the surprises for the final route. Developers cleverly enabled Miku and Yulya routes only after you complete the others, as they provide explanations for the many questions in the main story.
Is just lovely. Great amount of details in the backgrounds and decent character design, except maybe for the few male characters, which come across bland (but really, who cares about them?). You could feel how much love went into creation of the game.
You can find how to apply the hentai patch in the guides and I would suggest to use it just not to miss a few CG's. Admittably, they are not the strongest assets of the game (compared to the high bar set by the rest of the game), but I would still recommend it for the game 'completeness' sake. There is no real eroge to speak of.
If you like VN's, romance, light-hearted humor, a bit of fantasy and well-written stories, you will enjoy "Everlasting Summer". I know I will pay attention to the other games by this developer. Congrats Soviet Games, and thank you for the great time :)
