This game is everything I love about video games. It's extremely engaging and a game that is enjoyed best with friends. You will start strategizing, planning out, and manuvering about how to make the best of a situation. You have complete freedom to do whatever it is you want, and your actions actually matter.
The writing is as strong as the gameplay. Since the actions you take have real impactful outcomes, you will pay attention to what people are saying, which makes you really focused on the awesome quests there are. This game doesn't dumb anything down. It expects a lot of you. It's challenging, but never impossible. Being able to make the environment a strategic part of a fight feels natural and fun, and you will miss the combat system once you play other RPGs.
You will want more, you will want to know what happens to the NPCs, you will want to defeat that boss, you will want to play this game all the time. Enjoy it while it's fresh. Take your time.
Personally, it's my GoTY. There's no shame in recreating your characther after a while. I've restarted countless times, and I experience the game differently each time.
It's the best game I've played. I wouldn't think twice about reccommending it to anyone who loves strategy and classic-style RPGs. Or anyone.

This is the game i've been waiting for, a RTS that's slow and about macro, not about micro.. The story is brilliant and the gameplay is really fun. The beta is a more standard faction, they can expand very easily and are focused on mechs. The humans are very futuristic. They are very compact and are all robots. They can mine from all over the map but they cannot expand their base that far. The goo can go anywhere. The mother goos are the baracks, headquaters and the miners. They are very mobile but the units are less durable than the other factions. I am really enjoying this game so far and i reccomend it to anyone who play the old command & conquer game.
Now they've added a 4th faction, the 'silent ones' as they're called in the campaign. They are similar to the humans in that they can build anywhere on the map.. They use resources in a different way.. They dont use x resources every secound for 30 sec but you pay the up front price for the buildings and units, meaning you cannot queue units.. I've been enjoying the game but i was hoping for a campaign explaining the 'silent one's' story.. Still cannot complain as it's a free DLC!

I haven't put much time into the game miself just yet, I'm only about to reach a hundred hours invested at the time I'm writing this review.
But I think these almost 100 hours are enough to make up my humble opinion of this game.
I miself am not a huge fan of MMOs because I kind of got tired of all of them being the same as World of Warcraft but since this one was on sale at the cheapest package haveing a 6€ price tag I decided to buy it.
When I purchased black desert online I was expecting something else from what I eventually ended up with. I expected a generic mmo with some grind, dungeons, instances and all that old and for me boring mmo stuff. Instead I got an open world game with an interesting world and amazing activities. And by "open  world" I mean that from lvl 55(which you can reach very fast) you can go whichever direction you want and do quests everywhere that are still relevant to your characters progression. Whether you choose to explore the desert or sail the seas I guarantee that you will get immersed in this truly open world game (if you are into such things ofc.). I think this game is a good game in its own way, but not as an MMO.
This game feels more like a single player game with some multiplayer elements. Why I feel this way is because even though there are mutiplayer activities such as PvP stuff and world bosses and whatnot the game just doesn't feel to be built for that. What I mean by that is that whenever I'm out in the world adventuring and having fun (which this game offers a lot of) it feels like a single player game, and whenever I enter a town or any place where there are a lot of other players, my FPS drops drastically and I start to have some pretty nasty stuttering. I'm afraid to try PvP because I feel that my mid range PC would not be able to handle it very well. Same with the rest of the few mutiplayer activities this game offers. The game is terribly optimised for massively multiplayer online playing but since the cheapest package is 10€ even when it isn't on sale I can't not recommend it because overall this game isn't bad. Playing it doesn't feel bad, it just isn't godd as an MMO, or at least not a "WoWlike" MMO.
Overall if you like huge open world RPG games, then this could be a good deal for you, but if you want to play it competitively, as a hardcore MMO, this game won't meet your expectations. This game is a game that is made to immerse the player into it's world and give him/her the chance to play as someone else in an other world... as this is what RPG stands for. I won't go into details about why hardcore playing isn't the best thing to try to do in this game because I feel like it isn't the main focus/purpose of the game and it shouldn't be threated/expected as such. This is a game you don't have to play as a second job to feel relevant in, because whatever you do is relaxing, fun and immersive if you don't take it too seriously. Just like the MMO shown in the anime series Sword Art Online, those who've seen the series know what I'm talking about. This game tries to be more like that. Or at least from my point of view it seem to try doing so.
And for those complaining about Xingcode... don't listen to them, Xingcode isn't a spyware, nor does it upload all of the stuff that is on your HDD (as some people say here, among the reviews...). Xingcode is just an anticheat for the game. It doesn't harm your privacy in any way, so if you were downloading 50 tons of cocain from cocainbay with your PC, even then you wouldn't have to be afraid of Xingcode selling your precious data to the CIA as the developers have no rights to share the small amount of information they get acces to throught Xingcode.
EDIT: Oh, and steam achievements are broken so it would be nice from the devs if they fixed them and maybe added some new ones too if that's no asking for too much.

Well, i don't really do reviews usually, but this one got me the pleasure to make one.
Quick Question that people will often ask:
Q: What is Black Desert Online?
A: Black Desert Online (BDO as i am going to refer to.) is a MMORPG Sandbox type which means you can exploit the world as much as you want but you will probably be stuck in the story for the 60 levels of your life (Note: I am only level 43 on my main character so yeah.)
Goods:
- No P2W.
Pay to win or as often talked about microtransaction (there is microtransaction but it's only cosmetics and pets but i will bring the subjects of pets later don't worry.) are pretty empty, you can grind for gear more and get more money to i don't know, become rich by selling rare loot?
- The game is replayable.
Even after awakening quests and the reach of level 60, you will be able to start multiple careers that will eventually lead you to be more powerful in PvE and economy terms (like you can start an enterprise of weapons or jewlery and etc...) but yeah, there will also be PvP in this game that you can access to,
NOTE: I haven't tried PvP so i am only referring to professionals in the game. They will say it depends on one person to another on their MMO PvP style, but usually alot of people enjoys it.
- Attendances rewards
Let's talk about it, what are they? People often says that some stuff are paid but this system gives away some of the stuff that we are talking about. There is the system of attendences reward of loyalties
You can even find 7D or perma costumes if you login enough! So as long as you login every even if it's for 2 seconds to collect it, you will still get it.
- The Combat System
It is by far the absolute BEST! Ive never seen an actual combo ability meta to do but it still is insane. For example you do unveiled dagger on the dark knight and directly after you do left click and it will trigger a skill you learned (the technique im talking about is Hidden strike on the Dark Knight).

Cons
- Nodes are really complicated.
I still don't know how nodes in general work, but they seem to connect to a city by an item called Ancient coin/penny or whatever it is. It's still really complicated and the fact that it requires to be in a guild to claim nodes is not my cup of tea. I do want to make a guild with friends is fun, but we'll talk about a thing with guilds in the next node.
- Guild Contracts.
This game seems to focus the guilds as "contracts." If you ever leave a guild, the game will consider it and restrain you from joining another guild until it has been a full day depending on which guild it comes from.
-The level system is strange.
When we talk about levels, it is really strange what we are looking at, some quests won't give you EXP unless there a diamond with [EXP+] as an item. Otherwise you need to kill monster to level up.

It's been a long, long time since I wrote my joke, hype fueled review of Lethal League.
I figured I go back and actually update this review with something serious now that I've poured my heart and soul into the game.
Lethal League at its core is one of the funniest fighting games I've ever played, and to this day I have no found any other fighting game that could top it. Doesn't matter if its Street Fighter, Tekken, Marvel, or hell even Capcom Vs SNK. No game I've played since has gotten anywhere near the same feeling I get playing Lethal League.
Starting out, Lethal League was a bumpy ride of glitches, crashes, and other little oddities that slowly matured into a stable game, even as the player population continued to drop. A very high skill cieling game where every character is viable and the only limit to what you could do with any one character was your skill level.
It's an excellent party game, especially when playing locally with friends. And it's music and visual style really bring the characters and action to life as you're smashing super sonic balls back and forth on aesthetically pleasing stages, all while getting caught up in the excitement.
With Lethal League Blaze coming in 2018, I feel like anyone who hasn't gotten a chance to play Lethal League should definitely pick it up on PC or Xbox 1(If console is also your thing) and give this wonderful game some love!

Non-serious Review:  I had sex with all of my crew members as Cloud Strife in a gimp suit.  10/10 would totally tap that again.
Serious Review:  I bought this in the Ultimate Franchise Pack because it was about $14 and it came with everything Saint's Row related on Steam.  Great deal.  So I came into this game with dirt poor expectations after having played Saint's Row The Third.  But, this series has gone from a GTA clone, to it's own entity...and that is not necessarily bad.  I thought the Saint's Row Series was a large steaming pile of♥♥♥♥♥♥because I played SR3 first.  Boy...was I wrong.  I bought SR2 (The best in the series) and I knew I was greatly mistaken.  SR2 told an amazing story and was the first in the series to introduce character customization as in-depth as it is here.  It told a beautiful story that let you choose how to go through it, which gangs to fight first, and had a large array of varried activities from fight clubs to races and even some good online large multiplayer game modes.  All of this but the Customization was taken away when SR3 hit the scene.  In this, the 3rd Street Saint's are now celebrities.  It takes away everything serious and makes awful jokes, not awful as in morbid like 9/11 ones, but things like Fart in a Jar, a giant purple♥♥♥♥♥♥♥bat, and a sex appeal slider for how big your♥♥♥♥♥♥♥or boobs are.  The game was incredibly short and linear and by the end, you were essentially immune to everything, making it not fun.  In SR4, however, they imbrace the craziness, comedy, and humor that SR3 merely foreplayed with.  You start out with a Call of Duty cameo, afterwards, you become the President of the United States.  It then moves into a cameo of Fable 3, not in medieval times, but having you make choices that ultimately don't do♥♥♥♥♥♥  On your way to give a speech, you then get attacked by aliens...yes, ♥♥♥♥ing aliens.  That is what mostly turned me off.  However, as I played, it got more and more legitimately funny.  You are then taken through a linear corridor of generic aliens called the Zin, and then to a turret section and it makes fun of that as well.  Afterwards you are dropped into a parody of The Truman Show, then you enter the main game, which is a giant Matrix parody.  There are nods to Deep Silver's other games such as Dead Island and stuff, there is a entire sequence that parodies Metal Gear Solid, your out of simulation zone acts as a parody of Mass Effect by making it as easy as the press of a button to sleep with your crew mates Captain Kirk style.  You do loyalty missions for your homies and unlock super costumes for your homies which parody other games and movies.  Such as one of them dressed as Morpheus from The Matrix, Sonya Blade and Raiden from Mortal Kombat, and some that I didn't recognize.  It even has a Dubstep Gun (stolen from the youtube video of course), a tentacle bat, a anal rocket launcher that you shove in to people's asses and launch them like rocket launchers, and super powers.  Also, the♥♥♥♥♥♥♥bat returns but you have to find it.  You can customize your weapons and they change from different colors to even different styles like a pump action turning into a Steampunk gun thingy.  The character customization is quite in-depth, the story is short but amazing, make sure to play all the other SR games to avoid as many spoilers from those as possible (and also understand a lot of the references and snide remarks.)  Throughout the game, you get all of these references and stuff from all of the previous games and they are a nostalgia rush for those who have played them.  The majority of the game has the game world set at night but when you beat the game in about 2-4 hours, you can adjust the system's settings by the kind of templates and lightings and fog colors and misc stuff.  The perfectionist will have a bit of trouble with this game but not too much because challenges now have a medal system and the challenges are usually rather difficult, at least for me.  Now speaking of difficulty, I played through the normal difficulty and only died once, and that was because I got trapped by a homie in a corner in a section where they took away my powers.  The multiplayer is pretty empty.  Empty as in, there is no one online to play with.  Either people are too busy being on their own in their own game or don't activate co-op in their settings from friends only to open to all.  And you must have ALL of the same dlc that the other person has, otherwise you can't join.  seamless co-op transition my♥♥♥♥♥  Cheat Codes are meh at best here, but they combined the cheats from SR2 and SR3 with a few new ones into this.  $14, a good buy for all of this, plus the DLC, but that's it.  Buy it when you can if you want.  I recommend this greatly.

I bought this game because of all the positive reviews and stupid (in a good way) looking setting.

The story doesn't win an Oscar but is keeping me engaged. Most of the fun comes from the cute dialogues and references to anything game related anyway. The charakters break the fouth wall quite often and the overall atmosphere is very light-hearted. The game just wants to be fun and make you smile and succeeds.
There are tons of items to find, buy and craft. Add a good variety of abilities, spells, combos, some kind synergies between characters (if they like each other, you get bonuses) and you get great possibilities to customize your party. If you like experimenting, the game might be for you. Getting all the Plans, trying things out can be pretty addictive.
The combat is turn-based on a 2D-Battlefield. Positioning is key, since all attacks have an area of effect. Standing at a wrong place can seriously ruin your day. Attack animations are also pretty good, so cambat is challenging and fun to watch. I strongly recommend a gamepad for the best experience. Playing with keyboard and mouse is possible but doesn't feel great.
I won't comment much on the graphics. Look at Screenshots and videos and decide for yourself. It's a bit outdated but not ugly. Works for me.
However, this game is not without flaws.
The combat can get repetetive after a while, since the game tends to be quite grindy. You often have to get a few levels because of a difficulty spike and the MMO'ish quests (Kill X of these, bring me Y of that) increase this.
The fact that dungeons and enemies are frequently recolored and reused does't make it better either.
Oh, and you have to save often. There is no autosave and when you're dead, it's game over.
To sum it all up: 7/10, fun game with some flaws. Would buy again

Recommended, but with a warning: this is a story rather than a game, and it's not often lighthearted.
The main character, Semyon, finds himself transported in time and space and becomes a teenager in a Soviet Pioneer camp from the 1980s. Unfortunately, I found Semyon nearly impossible to play, because he has a strong personality that is very different from mine, so he undermined my choices and I effectively undermined his. While I preferred to accept that whatever force had brought Semyon to the camp would reveal its secrets in its own time, Semyon was obsessed with finding out the truth and getting home. When I chose for Semyon to talk to a girl, he would have no interest. When I chose for Semyon to get to know a girl, he would pick a fight with her. The girl who seemed like she might know something that could help Semyon
, he didn't want to talk to at all. The girl who was clearly attracted to Semyon
, he didn't like.
The one annoying girl that I tried to avoid
, Semyon kept hanging out with, probably because she's as much of a jerk as he is.
So while at first I tried to make the choices I would make, Semyon ruined all of those, and I then just started making the choices that would keep him from annoying the other campers. By the end of my game (which took five hours or so), it was all a letdown:
I have read that there are 13 different endings, and that some of them actually involve Semyon managing to not screw things up with one of the girls, so there may be some replay value here. But it might be a while before I revisit the camp, because Semyon has such a hard time letting go and just enjoying the experience.
Despite my issues with the game, I do recommend it, as it tells a good story. It's free to play as of this writing, but would be worth paying for as long as you accept it for what it is and don't lament what Semyon won't let it be.

Everlasting Summer is a very impressive, content-heavy visual novel that could just as well sold for 15-20 dollars, but as a free game is really an amazing catch and definitely worth checking out. It's not without faults (the protagonist is rather unlikeable, some of the art isn't as good as one would like), but delivers an interesting and very well-written story with multiple branching paths and memorable endings.
While some negative reviews here criticize the self-pity and introspections of the protagonist, I think they fit his character very well and for people like me, that have some experience with similar neurosis and anxieties, it's quite relatable. Character interaction are done in a rather believable and tactful way, including the romance arcs - at least the ones I was interested in enough to either play them myself or watch on YouTube. Most of the art assets and music complements the story content very well.
In summary, I still find the fact this game is free amazing. For someone who's into VN it should be absolutely worth exploring for a 15-20 hours, in order to experience various endings and story paths. Some of the routes routes might have bizzare moments and not every question about the game's setting is answered in any of them, but the whole experience is still very much fun and memorable. It isn't any worse than most of the Visual Novels that you have to pay 10+ dollars for here on Steam.

Grey Goo is an interesting game.
The design is centered around keeping things simple: there are few units and they have no abilities and not much in the way of upgrades.  The interface is one of the best I've ever seen for an RTS.  And while after playing about 50 online PvP matches I still am not 100% decided on how much meat there is on the bone.  I don't think this is a game of endless strategic discovery.  That might no be a bad thing, it depends on your preference in this regard.
As of now I am still having fun, after all the game looks fantastic and it plays smoothly and is responsive.
My biggest concern is the design of the factions.  You have to play each faction differently and because of that there are built-in advantages given to each faction and to be successful you must explore those, and in the end it can feel a bit like "I was forced to play this way" - because, to be honest playing another way just won't work.
Take the Humans for example, you simply have no option to expand.  You have to turtle up in your base.
The Beta have to expand, but are much weaker in unit power and composition
the Goo has to be constantly on the move and making short term, quick decisions since they spawn units right on the battlefield.  You must have a pretty healthy apm to play them well.
If you don't mind that sort of paint by number approach to your options then you may end up enjoying this game greatly.
After about 30 hours of play time in I do recommend this game for people who are looking for a responsive, fun, old-school RTS game but don't necessarily need a ton of new discovery to be baked in to their game play.

Divinity: Original Sin is an isometric view turn based  RPG. The game features two main characters that are customizable in regards to appearance, stat distribution, and abilities. Though I played the game solo, it can be played co-op with a friend with each person controlling one of the main characters (I believe).
The game forces you to use the two main characters, and you can have up to two more companions at anyone time. There is voice acted banter between the two leads and you can even set their personalities at character creation so that the A.I. determines their choices during some of these times. But, I would say there isn’t enough scripted interaction between the two. And generally the choices are black and white: a yes or moral option and  no immoral option. If the two of you disagree a fight ensues...rock paper scissors style (literally). This method is used to solve all conversational arguments. At first it was some what funny, but eventually gets annoying as sometimes you win no problem, other times you lose horribly even though you were suppose to have an advantage. It’s just dang difficult to “read” a computer opponent. The other companions you find (you have to find them the game doesn’t force them into your path) have a quest and at times they will comment on actions that you have done, but overall they remain silent. If you don’t like those companions, eventually the game allows you to hire henchmen who start at a predetermined level and with predetermined stats. After you hire them, they level with you and you can make leveling choices. The game though is perfectly beatable with just your two main characters though (Lone Wolf perk helps this).
Combat is this game’s strength. While some people may sneer at it having a true turn based system, everything about the combat synergizes with itself. Oh, it’s raining, well my fire spells will do less damage, and my electric ones will do more. There’s poison on the ground, my fire spell just blew it up! There are buffs and debuffs that can be managed, positioning and healing can be important, but the true beauty is environmental control. Water on the ground freezing, setting the ground ablaze, creating an electrifying mist. Each one of these can be created by various combinations and they can affect both enemies and your team. There are various different weapons and armor, but it really boils down to int based, strength based, and agility based gear. While the combat is great, initially setting your character up for combat (specing) was not fun. “How do I distribute my points, there is so much...?” The game does not help you in this respect. You are on your own on how to create your character...but the beauty of this...if you started a caster, you can change him into a meaty warrior or a dexterous archer pretty easy. Any combination can yield good results, but it might not seem that way at first.
The world is huge (and hardly any loading screens...looking at you PoE), and filled with lots to do...almost too much to do. The game overall is long. I have over 90 hours logged on my first playthrough (though I would say at least 10-15 from me leaving it running in the background...yes I know I’m terrible). There are plenty of quests, monsters to kill, secrets to find. There are riddles and puzzles to solve, choices to kill or help creatures, intrigue. There are a few different environments to explore and tons of loot to find. Enemies have enough variety especially bosses to make encounters unique and intriguing. But with all this greatness, the game give you very little direction. Who do I need to talk to, where do I go next what do I need to do. Crafting is almost completely hidden. Sometimes there are hints and you stumble in the right direction eventually in your exploring but other time I had to backtrack talking to everyone in a town trying to figure out how to trigger the next leg of a quest.
The story is very generic. Your heros (source hunters...a little background is given) are headed to solve a murder which is believed to have been caused by dark powers During your investigation you and your partner open one heck of a can of worms (end of the world, the doom of all you know standard fantasy stuff). While not everything is predictable, you do get a sense of “Sorry, Mario. The princess is in another castle” feeling. I wish more emphasis had been put on fleshing out some of the main characters.
Overall the game was enjoyable easily recommendable but with the warning that the game takes a lot of time to finnish.

Telltale Games does a really good job here of evoking what I love about Game of Thrones- painting the characters into corners and forcing them to make agonising decisions. And as a video game, you get to experience that agony much more directly. And just like the show, everything KEEPS GETTING MORE TERRIBLE ALL THE TIME. Apparently I'm a masochist, because I love it.
As an adaptation of the TV show, it also works very well- everything looks just like in the show (with the exception of Margerey, who veers into the uncanny valley occasionally) and the voice acting is terrific, even from the new characters.
One small gripe I have is that the achievements are a bit pointless. You get an achievement for completing each chapter and nothing else. I don't need an achievement for that- give me achievements for persuading such-and-such, or deciding so-and-so. Rather than "you completed unit 5 of game", I'd prefer "You chose honour over power" or "You got Lady Prewett to agree to a truce", for example. Then the achievements would be tied, like the game's narrative, to my own actions, rather than simply having completed a certain amount of multiple choice questions.

TL:DR I enjoyed this game enough to play it for 156 hours so that should tell you all you need.
While there are some negatives they didn't spoil my enjoyment of the game.
LONGER VERSION:
Some of this may seem overly critical or negative but I get more out of reviews that tell the issues one person had, so I can decide if I can handle them or if they are deal breakers.
POSITIVES
A good story that starts with a simply investigation but turns into a reality endangering quest.
The areas are quite large and full of encounters. Monters don't level with you, they are set so you can die if you travel too far.
The way magical elements interact was a bit weird (poison explodes with fire) but once you understand the mixes you can decimate a powerful group. My main character was a geomancer/pyromancer. The geo side brought up poison clouds and puddles, which the fire ignited for massive damage. Just be careful not to include your own party in the blast radius. Companions will leave the party if you attack them too much, even by accident.
Turn based combat with action points is used quite well. When levelling get speed and perception increases after your primary stat (str for fighters, dex for archers/rogues, int for mages) as it gives more action points.
SOME ISSUES
Finding skill books to gain more powerful spells etc was enjoyable, but after you reach level 12 there really isn't much. There are a couple skills at level 16 or 18 per class but they aren't overly impressive. I found that for most of the game I'd find or make equipment and wouldn't find anything better for about 5 levels.
The crafting system was a bit annoying and mainly trial and error. Recipies can be found but they are cryptic clues rather than an actual ingredient list. I simply tried combining stuff and saw what it made. Maybe that was the point but there was no in game assistance.
Some combat clicks were quite frustrating. Large creatures tend to sway while waiting for their turn. This can move them out of your cursor's click area makeing you move instead of attack. This can be critical and made me have to reload several times as a couple small tactical mistakes can end in defeat.
There is no morality system so you can do whatever you want. You can kill quest givers and thus complete their quest (although not optimally).
Towards the end of the game I went back to the first two locations and killed everyone and looted their corpses. The game allowed it and didn't comment on it. As long as you have compelted the quests from these people there are no issues plot wise in ending their lives. I discovered that if my archer attacked with standard bow attacks (ie not special ammunition or magic) the townsfolk ignored the attack. Their attitude decreased but they never attacked back.
Minor spoiler alert ***This made it really easy to destroy a particular village before they turned on you. I had them down to three people before they attacked instead of over 20.***
By the mid point I had soooo much money I couldn't spend it all. By level 16 all character knew every skill in their chosen fields except for the single level 18 ones. Stealing items is easy by simply talking to an NPC, switch to another character then grab what you want. Kill someone behind a closed door and no one will notice. I even killed NPCs by selling them tenebrium (basically poisoned rock) as they slowly rotted to death.
The game is very large, and I often felt overwhelmed with the size of going to a new area. This is a double edged sword. You want enough content and areas to give it scope, but you can go overboard. I think Divinity hopped over this line and back again several times. Balance is hard to achieve and I think the devs did a good job overall but failed in certain areas.
Stealth skills were next to useless. I didn't need to pick pocket anyone. It is based on skill versus weight or value. I found I couldn't get anything worthwhile by pickpocketing, but by stealing their stuff from their office and selling it back to them I could get the items I could pickpocket anyway. Sneaking was required exactly twice, the second time I had the invisibility spell so didn't need to sneak. Picking locks wasn't necessary either. I simply cast a fireball at the chest or door and it destroyed it without damaging my weapons. The only issue is when you come across a level 20 chest or door as you can't damage it unless you are the same level. In these cases a magical unlock spell is available (minor spoiler ***crafting level 3, pixie dust + blank paper =blank witchcraft scroll. Magic quill and ink + blank witchcraft scroll = 10% chance of unlock spell.***)
RECOMMENDATIONS
For your primary two characters ensure they are different. I started with a full mage and an archer that worked well, but I needed a melee fighter (which you pick up as a companion in the first town) to take the agro off the ranged characters. I struggled in the first few levels but it enhanced my need for tactics.
In the first town there are a lot of undead which are immune to poison and orcs which are resistant to poison. My primary poison skills were thus almost useless. The only thing I could use them for was to ignite with my fire spells. After the town, they come in quite handy but I remained here for about 7 levels (ended at level 23).
If you have the extra content that provides Bairdotr I highly recommend her use. She is an archer with hydro mage skills (healing and ice). I added witchcraft to Madora (primary melee charcter) which worked perfectly as she could get in close witha charge, reduce resistences and stats for all close to her, then melee the crap out of them. Everyone else stuck to range with elemental effects that destroyed the enemy with their lower resistances. You don't need to follow my exact example but my point is that you build a four man team with skills that compliment each other and you can massacre the enemies.
Get at least one character with repair of 1 and loremaster of 1. It will save you having to go back to town to repair damaged weapons or identify magic. With magic items my loremaster character increased to level 6 but only spent one skill point in it. Level 5 is all you need to identify any item in the game.
Read all dialogues and quest item books/scrolls. They give clues.

What put me off this game was that I have had countless hours with other games of the MMO genre and as a result, things that I would consider to be standards of that genre when it comes to interface, questing presentation, and the enticement to play with others are not here.
Black Desert Online would be a wonderful game on its own, if the MMO aspects and multiplayer were removed. The design and presentation of what makes the game an MMO experience is simply not polished enough in its current form and is unsettling to a veteran of the genre. Many other games of the same genre simply do the fundamentals of "multiplayer online" better.
For those that seek an interesting story experience and don't mind the MMO aspects being significantly weaker, this game can be a great experience. But those who are seeking something better than the MMOs they were playing previously will be put off by the weaker fundamentals of the genre.
Overall, I do not recommend this game for the demographic that every MMO seeks - those who want to play something better than what they already do.

So, where to even begin. I guess the most important thing here is that this is certainly not the MMO for everybody. This MMO manages to pack in something for every kind of player out there, but that actually doesn't mean it will appeal to everyone.
First of all, I'll cover the topic of the pricepoint, since in the very most lenient sense here, it's "variable".
It's $10 to get into the game. No monthly fees, nothing. That's pretty handy. The price point is at least low enough that for most people, even if they don't like the game, they won't have lost out on much. Now, chances are, the price point is that low because THERE ARE MICROTRANSACTIONS, IF YOU WANT THEM. I'm putting this at the beginning of the review because I know that this will either immediately deter people, or encourage them to hear me out on this. The best way I saw these described was as "conveniences". You can get items that rival the cash shop items, but it will take time, and it will take effort. But, there is nothing to stop someone from simply getting a headstart on the game by dropping a little extra money on the game. Is that bad? Well, at a $10 initial price point, I don't think so, because almost all of the cash shop items are convenience items, i.e. streamlining workers, getting a nicer boat without investing time into it, getting gear to speed up fishing initially, etc. The game counteracts this by allowing a lot of things to be completed AFK, such as fishing, or even autolooping a running path to level up your stamina (seriously, you can just have your character run infinitely between two points and get levels out of it, I can't make this up). Need to level your mount? Check the "auto feed" option, stock up on carrots, set an autoloop, and go sleep or do productive things while your character travels between points A and B and your horse learns new skills. So honestly, the cash shop items are certainly a thing which most people would look down on, but I haven't even seen the need for them. That said, I could have higher tolerance for grinding (see my Maplestory hours, let's not talk about it).
Now, on the topic of grinding, this IS a korean MMO, and it's gonna involve a lot of grinding. The AFK system is honestly a god-send, I'm telling you. However, the combat is very dynamic and frankly the best I've ever seen in an MMO (it does seem very similar to TERA, but definitely more rewarding and satisfying). For skills grinding, a fair amount of it can be done while tabbed out, so the grindy feeling there is alleviated to a fair extent.
As far as skills versus combat, this game does a very good job of letting you choose your own playstyle. Want to make it to the second town and then level all the way to 55+ and make millions by fishing? Sure, go ahead. Want to immediately start a farm and create a monopoly on food goods in the player marketplace? That works too. Set up trade routes between nodes and make all your money and experience through buying low and selling high, it doesn't matter, you get rewarded with level exp for so many things in this game, you can choose how you want to play the game. You can even treat it almost as a single-player game with the Black Spirit quest line, so play how you want to. And hey, if you're still into the kill-quest style MMO, that's all here for you too, and you won't even have to touch the other skills. It's relieving to play an MMO that lets you decide how you want to play it.
Something I have not been a part of yet is the guild system, which entails warring over territories or capturing areas to claim tax to pay guild members and such. I don't know too much about this, but from what I've viewed, it seems incredible to wage all-out-war with other guilds for essentially control over money. The PvP seems to be a big part of this game, and I'm hoping to make it to that end-game experience soon. And yes, before you ask, these wars DO entail forts, cannons, armies, etc, which just seems super awesome. Other guilds though seem to take the game casually, and only want a community to play with, so that's diversified as well.
Now for the more technical stuff. The graphics are gorgeous, the combat is fluid and feels OH SO GOOD, and the AFK feature is even enhanced by an option to minimize the game to the tray. The chat is very spammy with system notifications when you first join the game, but the settings menus help with all that and it should take you just a couple trial-and-errors to figure out what you do want to see broadcast and what you don't want to see. The quest handling is nice and will even autopath you to destinations, and despite minor environmental hookups (I got stuck on a staircase once) it's a very reliable system and can streamline the early game.
Now, so after all of this, why can't I recommend it to everyone? I mean, I'm giving it a thumbs up, am I not? Well, it's because there is very little explained to you in this game, and that's probably because if they did, you wouldn't ever end the tutorial. The game has so much complexity to it that you're going to want to have YouTube open, whatever databases or guides you can find, a friend on skype, really anything to help you understand a new part of the game you've decided to dabble in. For some, that's incredibly daunting and I can't say everyone would enjoy the game based on this aspect. And this isn't me saying "GO BACK TO YOUR BABY MMOS YA BABIES" I mean seriously, this game is a lot to take in and I'm surprised even I can handle it. While I believe you can take the game in any way you like, you still might get curious one day and find a whole new aspect to the game that doesn't suit your fancy, or it's just so horrifically complicated at first that you aren't going to understand it until your 15th fail stack. Now personally, I don't mind having to research an aspect of a game, and I even personally have a journal where I jot down notes for all sorts of games I play (I'm a huge nerd, I know this). But some people want to hop in and just play to end-game, which is okay. Having to find and research your way to the end-game isn't always fun, and I understand that.
So with all of that said, my final verdict is this: if any of this sounded appealing to you, give it a shot. Given that it casts it's net very wide, you can probably find something you'd enjoy in this game. But, be prepared to do some research, as some of the time you're just going to be confused, no matter how much experience you have with MMOs or in-game economies. If the mention of a cash shop that DOES benefit players deterred you entirely, then, ah well, that's fair, and I'd even encourage you to look elsewhere. Despite it being solely convenience items, I can't dispute the fact that they do exactly that. And finally, if all of this sounded appealing to you, I almost plead with you to play this, as I ended up finding the MMO I was looking for, and I hope you do to.

The Banner  Saga is a beautiful tale of survival in nordic-like fantasy world. It plays itself out in two halves: as a interactive novel with slightly animated art attached (in which you pick your choices and read the text of each character), and as a turn-based tactical combat game.
Pros:
-Beautiful art.
-Ok plot, well narrated though.
-Combats are fun, and challenging in Hard difficulty.
-Your march in the caravan is fun and requires resource management, plus some RPG elements involving the characters.
-Apparently your decisions do alter your experience.
Cons:
-No voice acting, dialogs have to be read.
-Open ending (there is a second part already).
-Combats are ok, but several improvements can be done: clearer effects of special abilities, more variety in enemies, maps and options
(IMPORTANT: I played all of the game -except the final battle- in Hard difficulty, and I noticed that playing it hard offers a more variety of enemies -more evolved, harder- than Normal difficulty).
-It♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥me off that you would have to spend points in characters to upgrade their level just to found them killed in the storyline. Upgrading should be points free.
-The caravan march is fun, but the suppossed effects are not well planned: having your people starving or simply walking will either reduce your population or lower the morale, which eventually only affects the difficulty of your combats.
-I'm not sure the reach of effect that your decisions have: seems like it affects more the "how" the story plays out than the "wha" (events).
I clearly see several points that I'd liked the developers to improve for the second part, but this first game is a worthy experience: yes, combat could be better; and yes, your decisions could have much more weight in the story; however, this saga, franchise, has an amazing potential in all areas; and this first part is a good proof of it.

Child of Light is a beautiful game. Its overworld is like a giant, living painting.
Exploring plays a bit like a platformer (though you are given a lot of freedom in how you move around), and battles are triggered by touching enemies. There are countless secrets littered all over the map.
The battles are turn-based and use an interruption mechanic. Being attacked while casting your attack/item/spell delays your turn. You can utilize this to disadvantage enemies, sometimes forcing them to take numerous hits in a row. Very satisfying.
The biggest flaws are the low difficulty, and writing. Expert mode feels like Normal mode in other games. You'll solve the few puzzles in seconds. Challenging enough to be fun, but a higher difficulty mode would have been great.

Grey Goo is a new offering from Petroglyph, a company with an impressive RTS pedigree (its members were involved with classics such as Dune II, Command & Conquer, Universe at War and others). Its premise is a return to the traditional RTS design philosophy, discarding new trends (many of them result of the search for e-sport status) such as weak defenses, ultra-fast pace, death-balls, and micro-intensiveness, trends that reward fast twitch reflexes and perfect build orders instead of strategic acumen.
I believe they have succeeded: if you are tired of these trends (and you can bet I am - Starcraft II was a huge disappointment for me) and fondly recall old RTS games with epic, long yet relaxed matches over LAN, you'll probably find something to love in Grey Goo. As it somehow always happens to me with Westwood Games, it took me a bit of time to get used to the game flow and interface (boy I sucked at the beginning), but once I did I had a blast.
Furthermore, Grey Goo offers an appealing setting, supported by rock-solid audiovisual design (Weta Workshop had part in conceptual design, for starters). For me, this is one of its greatest strengths. The game offers a more proper "science fiction" background than your typical PC-game fare (more given to the "science fantasy" genre), with a nice touch of wackiness. I enjoyed it for its interesting concepts (microscopic wormhole travel via nanotech, Von Neumann probes gone awry, an original but not quite apocalyptic "grey goo" scenario, humans that are more technologically advanced, aloof and "alien" than the aliens proper, etc.), for its general "vibe" (an grounded yet optimistic outlook reminiscent of 70s space fantasy, instead of the typical cynical and nihilistic take of most games), and for its honest story (featuring relatable characters that don't randomly act like psychopaths for artificial dramatic effect).
The other key strength of the game is the "Goo" faction itself. While Humans and Beta (the other playable factions) have different mechanics as typical in modern RTS, this creepy faction offers a truly unique experience. For starters, they have no buildings - as Goo, you have mother masses of formless goo moving around the map eating resources, and growing to perform mitosis. The formless goo masses that result can be used as units in their own right, or morph into specific forms that fulfill a more specialized role. It sounds very strange, but once experienced it becomes second nature and a nice respite from the usual RTS gameflow.
Those were the highlights for me - but for an important general outlook of the game, I'll use a pros vs. cons list:
Pros:
- Three different and interesting factions, including the titular, creepy and original Grey Goo.
- Rock-solid gameplay with traditional design of the Westwood school.
- Excellent graphics and visual design.
- Excellent sound design (background sounds, voice acting, unit sounds and ambiance are all very well done).
- Superb soundtrack courtesy of Frank Klepacki himself (author of dozens of classic game soundtracks - maybe you know him from Red Alert, Emperor: Battle for Dune, Universe at War or others - if not, you should!).
- An interesting science fiction setting that makes you like the factions.
- A solid campaign with good difficulty, an interesting story, and a lot of well directed, top-notch cutscenes (from now on I'll keep track of their maker, Axis Animation).
- A terrain editor ships with the game.
Cons:
- The campaign, while satisfying, is a bit short and its mission design could have been more varied (for me Warcraft III: The Frozen Throne, an otherwise forgettable game, is the gold-standard in this regard).
- The Skirmish and Multiplayer modes are fun but bare bones - it would be nice to have more options, game types and maps to play around.
- Some users report lower FPS than expected. I cannot verify nor comment since my 8 year old, technically unsupported PC logically struggles with the game but still manages to have a pretty  playable experience (which I'm pretty happy about).
To close, I loved the game as it hit a lot of right stylistic and game design notes for me, so I admit I'm an enthusiastic and biased (who isn't) reviewer. Nevertheless, I would sincerely recommend it for any RTS fans that enjoy the aforementioned design philosophy or had their interest piqued by the setting.

Not too sure what to write here so heres a recipe for Pancakes instead
Ingredients:
1 1/2 cups all-purpose flour
3 tablespoons sugar
1 tablespoon baking powder
1/4 teaspoon salt
1/8 teaspoon freshly ground nutmeg
2 large eggs, at room temperature
1 1/4 cups milk, at room temperature
1/2 teaspoon pure vanilla extract
3 tablespoons unsalted butter, plus more as needed
Now to make it
1. In a large bowl, whisk together the flour, sugar, baking powder, salt, and nutmeg.
2. In another bowl, beat the eggs and then whisk in the milk and vanilla.
3. Melt the butter in a large cast iron skillet or griddle over medium heat.
4. Whisk the butter into the milk mixture. Add the wet ingredients to the flour mixture, and whisk until a thick batter is just formed
5. Keeping the skillet at medium heat, ladle about 1/4 cup of the batter onto the skillet, to make a pancake. Make 1 or 2 more pancakes, taking care to keep them evenly spaced apart. Cook, until bubbles break the surface of the pancakes, and the undersides are golden brown, about 2 minutes. Flip with a spatula and cook about 1 minute more on the second side. Serve immediately or transfer to a platter and cover loosely with foil to keep warm. Repeat with the remaining batter, adding more butter to the skillet as needed.
6. Procedure for adding fruit to pancakes: Once the bubbles break the surface of the pancakes, scatter the surface with sliced or diced fruit, or chocolate chips, nuts, etc. Flip with a spatula and cook for 1 minute more, being careful not to burn toppings.

Being a Yu-Gi-Oh veteran (started in 2002), I wanted so badly for there to be a PC yugioh game that wasn't power of chaos or whatever those ancient games were, it felt right to me. I loved Dueling Network before NAS took it down, solely because of the fact that it was what everybody would have wanted, a dueling simulator that lets people who still play the game play together regardless of location. However, and I really hate to say this, this game is a major disappointment. I wouldn't recommend it to anyone, here is what I think about the game. Please note that the pros and cons could be exactly the same but there's good reason behind it.
Pros:
+Online dueling!
+No microtransactions! You earn the currency to buy cards.
+Replay value, you can do reverse duels in the campaigns to earn cards, or to see what it's like to see the bad guys winning
+You can use either story decks or your own decks in the campaign.
Cons:
-A lackluster campaign, it cuts out the relatively important duels.
-DLC, and a lot of it. They're opting to just release DLCs instead of updating the game to give us more updated sets. Want the complete experience? That'll be $105 total. You also pay around $50 to be able to play any of Arc-V's campaign, they only have the tutorial.
-Long tutorials in the guise of the pilot duels from each series.
-Online dueling is nice, but they took down Dueling Network and YGOPro to release this, when both of those systems are better than this game in its current state.
-Clearly a port, and a lazy one at that. They added keyboard prompts which is nice, but the code itself is messed up. Attack with more than 10,000 attack directly, the game crashes, or specific cards don't activate as intended, and there's clearly no hope for a patch, it's been about 2 months since the game's release, and only one patch came out that didn't really resolve any of the issues that's been talked about in the forums.
-No changes whatsoever to the game, not even graphical changes, the monsters look really lazy in the animation department.
-The game won't even run for some people who have DirectX 11 or 12 capable graphics cards and it gives you an error saying that you need direct3d level 10 or higher to play it, you have to hack the game just to be able to play it on some modern PCs
If you release a game with an online component you need to have some communication with your community. This is clearly abandonware and it bugs me that they took down programs and sites that actually had an amazing community (minus the toxicity that every community has) and the fact that they didn't fix any issues that the game clearly has is also bugging me and a lot of people in the online community. And a lack of anti-cheat system is a really bad idea in the long run.
Rating: 5/10

This 2-d overhead starship-crew simulator is deceptively indepth.  Each time you start up a new game, you will get a fresh ship and crew, which you must help survive through all the sectors until a final boss confrontation at the end.
Whether you complete your mission or are destroyed, nothing carries over to your next playthrough, but you are able to unlock  several new ship types and alternate starting loadouts for the ships.  There is some slight customization, you can rename your ship and each starting crewmember, and adjust crewmen colors.
When presented with options, you'll have to weigh the safety of your crew with the chance to acquire extra scrap.  Remember, noone is safe in a galaxy of terror, so try not to get attached to your crew.  You'll have the chance to recruit new members through hiring at space stations or rescuing them from slavers, and it is an enjoyable experience trying to preserve their lives while at the same time trying to protect your ship from enemy attacks.
You'll often have to make decisions that will have serious consequences.  Do you hang around in one sector longer in order to aquire extra resources, at the risk of the rebel fleet catching up to you and forcing a fight with an elite enemy in order to jump to the next sector?  Do you choose to travel into a nebula where your sensors are useless and your engine's power is halved, but giving you more time to improve your ship while the rebel fleet moves more slowly through the nebula as well?
The simple graphics are charming in their own way, the sound effects adequate.  The tension from fights are relieved by the ability to pause at any time to queue up actions, but you'll still find yourself tensing up whenever the enemy ship fires rockets, to see if they harmlessly fly by or hit a key system.
As for combat, their are multiple ways you can set your ship up.  You can focus on rapid fire enery weapons that knock down shields fast and allow you to use heavy beams to sweep across several rooms of the enemy ship.  You can focus on building up drone units, that launch and circle the enemy ship doing constant damage, or defensive drones that knock down missles before they can hit, or drones that travel throughout your ship, repairing the hull and fighting intruders.  You can install a teleportation chamber and send your hardiest crew members directly over to fight the enemy crew.
The total package makes for an engaging experience that first party companies try to achieve with huge budgets and complex systems.  It is a game you can play as a small diversion when you have 20 minutes, coming back to your save when you can, or you can spend hours at a time cruising the galaxy.  If you can appreciate the gameplay despite the dated presentation of the graphics, I would definitely recommend FTL.

Let's nominate this for the “I'm Not Crying, There's Something In My Eye” Award!
---
So you're not looking for just a game? You want an experience, you want to be sucked right into the world you're playing in?
Well, that's what this game did to me.
The saying "the whole is more than the sum of it's parts" was never more applicable than with this game. And it's exactly that, what makes this game such an awesome experience. The beautiful unique graphic style, the interesting rhyming theme and above all the stunning music by Coeur de Pirate, made it all come together in this rough but shiny gem of a game.
Let me be honest... It's not perfect.
The gameplay mechanics are solid, but not revolutionary. The battlesystem is comparable to the Active Time Battle system from Final Fantasy, with a few interesting tweaks to it.
The story is also decent: it has it's interesting moments, but can also be quite predictable at times.
But it's where all the elements are combined, what sets this game apart from it's kind.
All the characters have their unique stories and personalities to them, which made me feel for and with them. Most of the time I was just too involved with what was going on to even notice the little flaws in the story.
I never found myself craving for a more complex or interactive battlesystem, as the battletheme and graphics made every battle into an something epic. Besides, using each character's strenghts and weaknesses to their best can make the battles a lot more interesting, if you're willing to familiarise yourself with them.
At times, I found myself not wanting to progress to new areas, because I didn't want to stop listening to the music and instead just explore every interesting corner of the beautiful landscapes.
No, it's not the perfect game. But all the elements just seem to come together so naturally, that for me it left nothing more to be desired from.
I often still listen to the OST when lying in bed, reliving the experience and falling to sleep peacefully and satisfied.
Simply put: this game makes me happy...

Its visuals are too slowly animated.  The text is often full of typos.  There are a lot of weirdly used sound effects.  You have very little interaction with the story, not many choices to make, and many choices don't seem to change the overall story at all... and never result in a game over.  I would probably enjoy this story more as a motion comic.
That said, the characters are cute and lovable in their own ways.  There are a lot of girls, cute girls, which feel forced upon the male lead.  It's kind of silly, really.  I rarely saw male characters interact with the main character, who is male.  It's like the guys simply aren't allowed to say hi, or there simply aren't many of them.  There was one guy who introduced himself as some kind of celebrity named  Electronik, but his appearance as a camp guide was shortlived.
The main character is a little unrelatable for most of the internal dialogue moments, because while he questions everything internally, he rarely makes any effort to uncover the mystery of his whereabouts and constantly excuses himself for not doing so.  This effortless behavior makes it hard to suspend disbelief and ruins the story entirely.
Overall, it has a very slow pace, so I couldn't sit through it for more than a hour.  It's free-to-play, so you may as well try it, but I'd advise you to try some premium visual novels if you decide you like the genre.  There is potential for this 'game' to be a lot better with more animation, some voice-overs and a variety of choice-driven character arcs, but I didn't see much of any of that.

Besides graphics and cinematics and sounds, which i leave behind unrated, cause these are no important variables for gameplay to me, I can confirm the designers did a great job creating those three races and their mechanics. As one of them completely differs from the other two in mechanic, there is an interesting balance of gameplay design, still an unbalance in multiplayer gameplay to me. I will let the singleplayer- experience unrated due to lack of playtime in singleplayer.
So the multiplayer is what i was after, despitely I was dissapointed fast. The game can simply not compete with genre-siblings like Starcraft, and here are the reasons why I do think so:
Ladder: it's just to simple, no different leagues, enormous waiting times (in my experience), high loading time and just 'why'- disconnects from a server are no exception.
Sluggishness in control and movespeed: In general, to me, units are just too slow to react with them quickly on an enemies action, or get quickly an advantage in terrain. There is a high imbalance in movementspeed which is completly senseless, cause once engaged, there is no way of rescue any of your units. That genre-important mechanic takes it's killing blow in a, kind of, delayed unit's action. They are too sluggish in turning and firing and moving that you will have no chance to influence combat with micro skills, which is the next point->
->Micro-Skill: As a result of the point mentioned above, micro-skill just doesn't exist in a considerable way, that it would alter the result of a combat and thus takes no effect on game. For a RTS the possibility of benefits from microskill is obligatory to me. Thus the gameplay leak options in combat, that doesn't allow to just not watch your army die in a face to face battle. Due to a leak of 'active' or, well, at least 'inactive' skills of your units you get in sum around zero options to affect micro-gameplay. There are no 'active abilities' or 'skills' and that is not the point. That isn't the bad thing about it. It just doesn't support micro-acting, you understand.
->Makro-Skill: The overview of buildings, units and techs is very simple and get's you into the materia quick- which is a pro. Developers made a good job here. But... the diversity of options in builds and strategies and chances of reactions on enemies acting absolutely suffers from it. Having no options or alternatives left rather than just waiting for units to finally finish (they are structured for hours...) or believing in hope that everything will be fine when both armies engage like monkeys throwing♥♥♥♥♥♥at each other.
So: very restricted variety of options in general. Commonly, and thats even worse, your are forced to 'push-through' a build without reacting on the enemies acting, cause you just haven't the chance to. Due to lack of fast scouting-methods and thus no awareness of what's your enemy is planning you will have no else chance. At the point you can find out your enemies strategy it's far too late to react appropriate on it.
All in all it's just a count of army-size controlling early-, mid- and lategame.
Economy: no way to get an influence here beyond making the decission when to come up with more refineries/mothers. It's just auto-collecting. KKND2 had a 'more complex' economy mechanic.
Maps/Terrain: The maps are well designed, that is out of question, but they do not provide many possibilities of tactical maneuvers, except for Goo, which can climp hills and ledges without penalties, making the map itself a factor for unbalance. Another interessting mechanic are treepatches (or however i shall call them), which I personally think it's a great idea- in theory! In practise the idea isn't well reflected as I noticed fast. Units in there are invisible to enemies outside, making it impossible for you to get close to it, if you don't want your army seeing crushed without chance of counteracting. In add it's very difficult to get these postions spotted. Definition of imbalance.
All in all, the worst thing about Grey Goo after the first look is the leak of options you have in multiplayer, making it a 'low-click' experience which will get boring quickly. There is potential in the game, but who knows if rerolling mechanics will bring desired results. Therefore i don't recommend Grey Goo in connection with it's insane price of 46€ for far too less content.
Edit: There are several must-have mechanics missing in multiplayer:
-3vs3/4vs4
-observermode
-replays (very important imo)
-gamepause
-rejoin function

An impeccably produced RTS that harks back to simpler days, there is a lot to like here for fans of RTS - but there is also a lot not to like.
There are a number of issues with this game that whilst on their own wouldn't amount to much, taken together they really spoil what could otherwise have been a great game.
Problems include -
Sloppy click registration. At times the game will blissfully ignore a click or two at a critical juncture - whether this is because its cycling through a unit animation and can you please just wait a minute for me to finish, or whether at other times its just a fug of having to click something twice, overall the control can at times feel a little sloppy and sluggish. For an RTS that wants to turn the clock back this is something of a killer problem - good control feedback is a must for this kind of game.
Frustrating / Unimaginative campaign play. Endless hordes of hordes. Again. And Again. And Again. Whilst the campaign cut scenes are absolutely top notch and the story is interesting, the actual level design is abysmal with the same idea spammed out endlessly. Not to mention a difficulty level that staggers wildly from tricky to insane, and some questionable tactical choices can make some levels a real turn off.
Dodgy unit capabilities. The Flying hand of Ruk. Which has to navigate through doors. Because it can't fly over a wall. Or cliff. Or anything. On its own this is a trivial point. But when added to the sloppy control and poor level design just ends up making you want to repeatedly smash your head into a wall.
And don't get me started on the tactical genius of the forest cover which hides units within. This is a great idea in theory. In practice against a spamming level design its a chore fest of sniffing units out, wiping them out, only 5 seconds later to have your scouts wiped out and the enemy grief sniping you all over again. Wise tactical decision ? Yes. Enjoyable gameplay ? Hell no.
All of these problems pretty much sum up the game - love and effort has obviously gone into crafting this, but along the way they have made mistakes, cut a few clunky corners or made some just plain bad decisions which turns the final result into something of a flawed experience.
If you can see past the flaws then this is a solid old school RTS game.
If you can't then this game is a frustrating piece of meh - albeit with lovely production values.

Titan Quest set in a grim steampunk world. While it may be rough around the edges, I highly recommend it to every ARPG fan!
+ Multiclassing (up to two)
+ Build variety and replayability
+ Sweet loot
+ Myriad of side quests
+ Factions
+ Devotion skill tree
+ Interesting setting and lore
+ Ambience
+ Soundtrack
- No Rogue class equivalent
- Rather cheap and spongy bosses
- Minor stability and optimisation issues
Grim Dawn is an ARPG developed by Crate Entertainment, a studio founded by Iron Lore veterans. It is built on the Titan Quest engine so if you have played TQ before, you will immediately notice some striking similarities between the two titles.
A few words about the setting: the world is on the brink of apocalypse – demons roam the land, resources are scarce*, and humanity is divided as ever. To make matters worse, cultists (mad as the proverbial hatter) are fighting for power. The game begins with the protagonist being possesed by an aetherial spirit. The survivors hang him/her but the spirit leaves the body just in time and the survivors decide to set the hero free. Should one be more interested in digging deeper into the story, there are many well-written documents to be found on the journey.
The gameplay revolves around eviscerating thousands of monsters, collecting loot, and completing quests. The usual. The tools of destruction include swords, axes, maces, rifles, pistols, and crossbows (similar to Torchlight). However, there are a few elements which make the game stand out from the crowd. First of all, after reaching level 10, the player gets to choose a second mastery. There are six masteries: Arcanist, Demolitionist, Nightblade, Occultist, Shaman, and Soldier. What is interesting is that they are well thought-out and every class is viable, even if they lack synergy at the first glance. Moreover, every mastery supports a variety of playstyles and can be effective with both ranged and melee weapons. Secondly, there is a devotion skill tree which provide yet another layer of customisation. In order to get devotion points, one has to restore the shrines scattered around the world. My only complaint about classes is that there is no Rogue equivalent. Overall, the class system is very fluid and one can spent a lot of time tweaking their very own build.
Another unique element is the introduction of friendly and enemy factions. Gaining reputation with friends give the player access to faction-exclusive gear and bounties (side quests that can be farmed indefinitely) while becoming more hated by the enemies results in tougher spawns and, eventually, a possibility to fight a Nemesis monster (in other words, a BAMF). While most factions are inherently either friendly or enemy, the player will get to choose their allies.
While the graphics may not be the game's strongest suit, the surroundings seem to be well done. Grim Dawn also features a glorious Diablo-esque soundtrack which enhances the ambience. The voice acting is mediocre at best but, to be fair, this is not a deal breaker in a game like this. Speaking of shortcomings, the game has some minor performance and stability issues. Gameplay-wise, I find the design of some boss enemies cheap and annoying, rather than challenging but fair. They are kind of like high school jocks – tough in groups (and they always stick together), not much of a threat otherwise. Nevertheless, any enemy can be defeated with a proper application of skill, a decent equipment, and build.
In conclusion, Grim Dawn is a marvellous title that can provide dozens of hours of great entertainment. While it is rough around the edges, the game lives up to the hype in my opinion. I highly recommend it to anyone that is not allergic to the ARPG genre.
*The currency in Grim Dawn are iron bits. That's how scarce the resources are!

This is a beautiful TV miniseries. The voice acting is good. The animation is beautiful. The story is okay.
My problem with it is that the game is sold on the idea that you can take part in the politics of Game of Thrones when, in truth, you can't.
Obviously your choices couldn't have a larger impact on GRRM's story, and I never thought they would. But I was sold on the idea that I would be responsible for the rise or fall of a minor house. And the initial episode was reasonably good set up for that aside from one really important choice ultimately having no impact.  But the episodes following the first have become more and more like a plot railroad in a tabletop game.
Your choices don't matter. And in a game whose main enticement is the idea that you can play politics, not having your decisions matter defeats the point of making a game rather than writing a book. It's simply false advertising.
And for all those people whose response is "It's a Telltale game" (ie all choice is always an illusion), I say that yes, I have played and watched Telltale games before, and that in a line up with Walking Dead and Wolf Among Us, Game of Thrones is the worst game for not having your choices matter. Count up all your previous irritations and multiply them by 10. Despite the limited choices, I still love Wolf Among Us as a noir mystery. A mystery only has one solution, after all, so ultimately being linear doesn't bother me a bit. And while Walking Dead always has the same ending, you do have some choice in the matter of the lives and deaths of your companion characters. It feels like a real struggle for survival with real consequences for who you have at your side at the end.
Game of Thrones, on the other hand, feels like even when you plan well and make good choices, it's ultimately pointless because the game will arbitrarily decide that your choices don't change the path of the story or the arc of the characters one iota. I will finish playing this game, but if I could go back in time and stop myself from buying this game, I would. I've got better things to do with $30. Heck, I've got better things to do with $10. So unless this goes on sale for $5, the price of a matinee movie, skip it.

Very reminiscent of Dueling Network, both in its board and its deck constructor. Excellent card variety, though still missing quite a lot of cards (though I have yet to do anything with the DLCs, so I can't say exactly how many cards it's missing in entirety. Nor do I have all the cards in the game. Shoot me.) The game itself is... well... yugioh. If you're familiar with it, then there's not much to say. It's yugioh. A few minor complaints on my end, but if you can deal with them, then you've got a relatively decent (officially licensed!) yugioh game, which is more than I can say for 90% of the ones out there.
-Certain monsters have battle animations that can't be skipped. You'll see this most likely in your first or second story match when blue-eyes or dark magician decimates something. They get a little annoying but I haven't found too many cards that I personally use that have them. Blue-eyes, red-eyes and dark magician have been the only ones I've seen. If they're the only ones then I can deal with that since I don't like the decks that use any of those three and the decks I play counter them pretty hard anyways.
-Deck constructor's search function. It's not very easily visible, but while it's more in-depth than Dueling Network's was, it's incredibly frustrating to use no matter whether you use controller or keyboard and mouse. This is one of the areas where the game is most evident in being a crappy console port.
-Card packs and their card randomization. I've gotten card packs that have had more than the usable 3 copies of a specific card in them. I've seen packs that gave me absolutely nothing new, not only no new cards, but excess copies of cards. The game only counts up to 3 of each card in your deck constructor. I understand it's trying to keep booster pack realism but I don't like that I don't get at least one new card each pack, or don't get refunded on cards that are in excess.
-Trap card/quickplay spell notifications. This can be disabled and/or minimized, but by changing the notification type on activations from 'simple' or 'default' to 'pro,' which removes them altogether, it makes you hold a button/key in order to activate a card at a time when it would be viable. It's a little tedious and I don't understand it too well honestly. However, holding whatever's your cancel input (right click/B button default) allows you to skip the prompts completely, so there you go. Just keep an eye out so you don't forget to activate a card when you actually need it.
-Phase changing. The phase changing menu is pretty simple, but I've had a few mishaps where I've tried to attack with a monster when it wasn't the battle phase and had my monster switch to defense, which has cost me duels already. You really have to pay attention to what you're selecting in menus. It can be quite annoying if you don't. There are also some card effects that're taken entirely too literally in the game. For example, with Spellbinding Circle - if the monster it's affecting gets tributed, the circle remains on the field doing nothing. Similar issue with Mystical Space Typhoon and destroying activated spells without negating the effect. The card itself doesn't actually state that it negates effects, but so far as I'm aware, it has always been treated as negating them since it's used standard in nearly every single deck in existence. But if you try to use it on a Dark Hole when it's activated, you'll be wasting the thing. It gets pretty annoying actually.

First of all this game begins hard.  You will die a few times.  You will NEED spells, so build a magic user or hire one ASAP.  You need to save a lot, pay attention, use all your items like scrolls and potions and food.  After about 10hrs you can relax a little because it gets easier as you get more powerful and well rounded.
Everyone compares this to Baldur's gate RPG's.  It's similar view and style are obvious, it's well done.  The combat is turn-based, though.  Whereas in BG you pause, assign tasks and it all happens at once this game takes a one at a time approach similar to tactical games.  The one that comes to mind is XCOM, there's probably a closer match than that but you get the point.
The game relies a lot on elemental effects, fire damages but also lights things on fire.  Cast rain on that fire and it goes out and you get puddles of water.  Cast lightning on a puddle and you get electrocuted if standing in that puddle, etc.  It's great fun when you poison piles of enemies and catastrophically awful when you burn your party to ashes.  There is a lot if interaction with the environment outside of spells as well, barrels containing oil or water, puzzles, hidden objects, switches and traps.  A huge variety of special arrows, lots of status effects making characters weaker, faster, smarter, invisible, etc.
Recommended if you like a challenge at your own pace, if you like computer RPG's or just games that don't hold your hand like a 5yr old .  This has been my favorite in a long while.

I don't want to go into detail about the gameplay here, because others have done this often enough. To make it short: despite some major and minor flaws, the old-school-gameplay as well as the turn-based combat is the reason why people love D:OS. I understand that, because I like this part too.

What you get instead is a pure freakshow, where you aid the lovesickness of animals, solve dissensions with 'rock, paper, scissors', sneak around disguised as a huge rock or tree, speak with people that are talking nothing but stupid♥♥♥♥♥♥ fight against walking snowmen and fire-spitting mechanical chicken and so on and so forth. After 40+ hours I just couldn't stand this ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t anymore.
To sum it up: you won't find something serious to happen here. If old-school-gameplay is all for you, you may like this game. But if you are looking for some substance in terms of world, lore, story, characters and dialogues, stay far away from D:OS!
