I really, really, really love tactical RPGs. Really. I put in hundreds of hours on Final Fantasy Tactics, Breath of Fire, X-com: UFO Defense, Terror from the Deep, Enemy Unknown, and so on. It really takes the button mashing and power-leveling aspects out of your run-of-the-mill RPGs. Definitely a good thing.
Banner Saga is an excellent addition to the genre... but it definitely has a few things that do not recommend it. The variety of enemies (AND allies) is quite mediocre. Battles, as a result, can become pretty tedious. The battlefields themselves lack a lot of variety - there aren't the standard elements of the genre re: environmental barriers and challenges, height/depth, and so on. Not super impressed there - this isn't an old game that can be forgiven for missing some of the key elements. This could have added so much to combat - a very big missed opportunity.
I do love the story itself though. Viking lore is always neat, and when combined with bleak, dying world - it's a vibrant, wonderful story. Depressing as all get-out, but wonderful all the same.
I had a lot of difficulty with the final Big Bad fight - which is due to a lot of the game mechanics around the Reknown system. When the same resource is used to purchase EVERYTHING, including character levels, caravan supplies, and character accessories (pretty weak approach to customizing characters, by the way), either your caravan is going to have starving clansmen, or you're going to have under-leveled characters. Interestingly... I ended up with both. Which made me wonder - why am I even worrying about my clansmen? The game is constantly robbing me of supplies. My attempts to keep the caravan stocked feel utterly futile; I'm just going to level my characters next time.
Also: had I known that two of my characters were REQUIRED for the final fight, I might have actually developed them a bit. No idea that that was coming - pretty cheap, that. When the game works, it works well.  However, a lot of the time you will find your units shooting a stray wall post instead of attacking the enemy pelting them two feet behind them.  For a game who's goal was to not be the "twitch APM" style of game that StarCraft is, your army often requires a LOT of babysitting to be effective.
While it is true you don't have to micromanage your base much, I feel like there are a few inherently broken things.  When attacking, especially if there are walls, your units like to clump up to shoot the wall post they could just walk past and become perfect artillery bait...  And even a single artillery unit can annihalate your light troops.  It doesn't help that the AI -always- has artillery pre-placed in perfect "gotcha" positions.  Brush also seems to be a problem.  The AI seems to have issues when being shot at by something.  In most RTS games, if a unit gets shot at from something outside its range it will still attempt to engage so it doesn't just die in vain.  In Grey Goo they just... stand there.  Same for things attacking them from inside brush.  The game notifies you they're under attack.  But they just stand there dumbfounded as lasers rip them apart from inside the woods because they can't see the unit inside unless they move into the brush as well, or have a detector with them.
I have found that playing through the campaign requires several restarts until you find the "perfect" build order.  Mistakes are punished hard as the AI with all of their already completed and entrenched positions vs you starting with literally nothing means you have no breathing room what so ever.  The maps, however, are small for the most part so restarting usually isn't that bad unless you fail right at the end.  Also many of them are snaked with frustrating impassible terrain that can make fighting the grey goo a frustrating lesson in chase the mothers around the map since they can freely cross terrain that is impassible to the other races and are constantly spawning more mothers.
Those issues aside though, I still mostly have fun with it.  I'm not even sure why.  I'm definitly not a pro RTS player and I've even had to just stop playing several times after having to restart the same mission three or four times in a row because I'm not playing the game at the pace the AI wants me to play so I wind up with auto-loss when it assaults required mission objectives before I'm anywhere near ready to defend them.  Maybe it's just because I don't want to lose and keep coming back just to beat it...  I think maybe if I can break out of the Supreme Commander mindset and learn that the campaign triggers aren't going to wait for me like Supreme Commander's do and I'll do better.  Or maybe I'm just easily amused by the pretty particle effects and animations, but despite all of the game's weaknesses I don't hate it.

With incredible depth, a wonderfully implemented territory control system, clever mechanics representing the hardships of winter and some awesome explosions, this game is one of the best I've ever played. It's hard to overstate how amazing it really is.
Some games really show their true colors only from the inside, and Company of Heroes 2 is one of them. Sure, its pedigree is impressive: the original Company of Heroes is one of the highest-rated RTS games of all time, and is still played by a large and dedicated fan base even seven years after its release. Relic, the developer, is beloved for titles like Homeworld 2, the Dawn of War games, and Impossible Creatures. As the fans of many genres can attest, however, sequels don’t necessarily mean improvement. Companies can easily lose track of what their fans loved about a beloved original. Rest assured, Company of Heroes 2 does its predecessor and the RTS genre quite a service: from the outside, it’s a polished and visually impressive RTS. From the inside, it can quite often be breathtaking.
Graphically, this is one of the most visually impressive RTS games out there. From cannon fire knocking chunks out of civilian structures to the satisfying weight with which vehicles move to how wounded soldiers writhe on the ground in virtual agony, Company of Heroes 2 handles physics, lighting effects and tank and weapon designs with great care and attention to detail. Even on low graphics settings the game looks darn good and behaves nicely. Sometimes, graphics can get a little muddy with a ton of greys and browns, but that comes, I think, as much from the subject matter as anywhere. This is not a game befitting of bright, primary colors.
Its depth will take some getting used to for the novice, and the veteran of Company of Heroes might have some adjusting to do and might question whether some omissions or upgrades are truly steps in the right direction, but I honestly feel that despite its somewhat lackluster campaign story, Company of Heroes 2 has a broader appeal than its predecessor and brings interesting decision-making to the mix with its weather mechanics and the ability to requisition abandoned enemy material. You will not regret picking this one up, I can assure you.

A fantastic open world Survival Crafting Parkour Melee-Combat with Zombies Extraordinaire, Dying Light is a great game that will certainly give you a lot of bang for your buck. Made by the same guys that created Dead Island, you will see bits and pieces of that somewhat disappointing experience interspersed with some new brilliant ideas.
The melee combat is fast and it is brutal, especially at first. Zombies don’t fall apart like they’re made out of paper (like in Dead Rising) and they feel like real, physical objects in the world. They’ll grab and shove at you while you’re trying to get away from them, and it takes many, many bashes with the numerous melee weapons to take them down. You really get the feeling that sure, I’m an able bodied Parkour badass and I can take on one or two zombies reliably, but if three or more are attacking you, there’s a real chance that you can die. It really convinces the player to move quickly through giant crowds, versus standing there and fighting them one after another, because you will most likely die. I recommend playing on Hard difficulty if you want to give yourself that extra challenge. I can’t remember another main stream zombie game (except for maybe ZombieU) where the zombie enemies are such big threats, it makes every encounter feel dangerous and exciting. Much more of the game isn’t focused on fighting them, but avoiding them with platforming and free-running. Every weapon will break eventually, despite having multiple repairs. This gives me bad OCD, as I'm almost unwilling to use my best weapons since I'm "saving it" for tougher enemies. However, I think this is a feeling that the developers wanted to instill in its players, that nothing in this world is permanent and everything will eventually fall apart. By the end, weapons last long enough to be less of an issue, and this prompts you to try out many different melee weapons since you'll be breaking them all the time.
The Parkour in this game is the best I’ve ever seen in a FPS, for sure. Mirror’s Edge had great mechanics as well, but in that game I always felt like I was doing things I didn’t mean to, while in Dying Light I feel like everything my character performs in game was what I was trying to do. If an object LOOKS like you can hold on to it, 99/100 times you will automatically grab on. There isn’t any fancy wall running or anything, but the movement is so fluid and smooth that it isn’t required. Shoving my way through a field of zombies, only to leap on one’s shoulder’s onto a telephone pole, and shimmying up to jump onto an apartment balcony is a great experience. Within a couple hours you’ll already feel great mastery of the free-running, it feels a lot like a first person Assassin’s Creed, albeit smoother and faster. This is probably the most unique and well done portion of the game, without it will feel like a Dead Island-like melee slog, but the danger from crowds of zombies plus the simple intuitiveness of the free-running means you’ll love parkouring everywhere. Just getting from objective to objective is a ton of fun.
As much of an untouchable badass you feel like during the day, the game’s title “Dying Light” will always be on the back of your mind. As soon as the sun sets, the world is bathed in an impenetrable night, illuminated only by your puny flashlight. It’s one of the more realistic night times in video games I’ve seen, you really can’t see jack♥♥♥♥♥♥in the dark. The dangerous Volatile type zombies are big, buff, fast runners that will chase you down and end you very quick, so you’re always on your toes, trying to stealth your way around them. If they find you, it’s a panicked, terrifying sprint to a safe house, where you feel like a hunted animal (somewhat Outlast-like). This dichotomy of day time and night time play go together very well, and players are encouraged to do objectives/ missions during the night because of doubled XP bonuses. It’s also great that time progresses throughout your gameplay, so you can all of a sudden be caught out in the open AT NIGHT because you were too busy killing zombies for fun or in the middle of a mission, forcing you to frantically find shelter while groping blindly in the darkness. Great stuff.
The graphics of this game are beautiful, palm trees wave in the wind, ramshackle buildings are rife with details, and the setting sun casts a beautiful glow over everything, despite its warning of impending doom. This is one of the better looking games out right now, and it seems to perform very well on systems. Facial animations may look kinda weird, but the NPC designs are full of character and the game is well voice acted. Unfortunately, the base story is pretty predictable and full of zombie genre tropes, but the gameplay more than makes up for it. Near the end of the game you’ll be pretty overpowered with weapons and firearms. One thing that was a common complaint of Dead Island was that the firearms felt very weak, but in Dying Light they actually feel like guns, deadly and powerful. Ammo is pretty scarce so I would almost never use it, but when I decided to bust out my pistol that’s when things got real. There are also human enemies that you can fight with melee, and they are pretty tough to fight, but it’s always comical when they pull out a machete and I shoot them immediately, much like Indiana Jones in Raiders of the Lost Ark. Thankfully the lack of ammo means that I can’t use these guns ALL the time, and it’s better to save the bullets for the human enemies that do have guns.
All in all, one of the better open world games to come out recently. Great fun in single player, but even more fun in co op (up to 4 players). It’s great to parkour and kill zombies together, and there are tons of little competitions that you can dynamically choose to compete with your partner with, whether it’s parkour racing or looting stuff. Dying Light recently had a huge expansion released called The Following that has been amazing during the little I’ve played. Techland has joined CD Project Red as another great Polish Developer, and I can’t wait to see what they come up with next.

Basic game facts
Grey Goo is an old-school RTS of the most direct descendant of Westwood Studios, the creators of Command and Conquer. That heritage shows clearly in the game. Since the last years only brought us MOBAs and Starcraft-type clicking frenzy games, Grey Goo returns to the roots: No unit skills, no tedious micro-tasks and a focus on strategy.
Playable Factions
The Humans
With technology evolved to an almost magic-like level, the Neo-Humans have created a society without war or woe by delegating most tasks to AI entities. After abandoning their quest to find other intelligent life, they are called to Ecosystem 09 by a mysterious signal to find themselves confronted with the need to wage war against two unexpected opponents.
Playing the Humans gives the player one central powersource, to which each building has to be connected and the ability to build strong defenses and harvest resources from every point of the battlefield.
The Beta
After barely escaping extinction by a force they call "the silent ones", the remaining members of the Morra (called Beta by the Neo-Humans) find refuge on the Planet of Ecosystem 09. Within a generation they colonize the planet and harness it´s rich resources to prepare thier way back to the stars. Using kinetic and explosive weaponry, they find themselves attacked by unknown hostiles, which are diffrent from those they fled from.
Playing the Beta one builds hubs anywhere on the map to power buildings and share technology among them. So, the Beta can build outposts everywhere and fortify every chosen position to harvest it´s resources.
The Goo
Originally created by the Humans to cartograph the galaxy using the so-called "keyholes", the Von-Neumann-Probes were abandoned by their creators, when they canceled their efforts to find intelligent life. Made to adapt to changing circumstances, these nanomachines evolved into the Goo, an all-devouring army traveling via the keyholes from world to world, devouring everything on the way back to earth.
Truly innovative for the genre, the Goo has no base but formless nano-blobs that move over terrain and produce new units by consuming resources, growing and splitting off smaller parts, which are turned into combat units. The formless Goo can traverse mountains and most impassible terrain and consumes enemy ground units and structures it comes in contact with.
Gameplay
Singleplayer
The singleplayer campaign is compelling and offers the player a well-made narrative told in high quality cutscenes and missions with changing types of objectives. From the classical "annihilate the enemy" to "escort the civilians to safety" the classics are covered. There are six missions for each faction. Every mission has bonus objectives of varying type of difficulty. The character design is nuanced and interesting, since the Beta have much more in common with the ancient humans (us) than the Neo-Humans do.
Multiplayer
The Multiplayer-part is one strong side of the game. It has dedicated servers and is comparably well balanced, especially considering the existence of the Goo as playable faction. I found the macro-focused gameplay of GreyGoo the very anti-thesis to the current and announced Starcraft II. APM is not as important as having a good strategy and reacting well to your opponents decisions.
Graphics
Nice, polished models and effects and design by WETA. Really pretty for an RTS. The big explosion effects are missing, except for the game-ending epic units, which are, following their nametag really really epic.
Performance
Works fine with my machine. Heard of people with older rigs having slight problems.
Notable special features
Language
Petroglyph Games hired the very person that created the language of the Na´vi from the movie Avatar to create a language for the Morra (Beta)! It is used and subtitled in the campaign cutscenes and maybe there will be the possibility to actually learn to speak it.
Music
Made by Frank Klepacki, the lead composer of the great Soundtracks of Command and Conquer, Dune and many more has created three soundtracks: Clean synthesizer music for the Humans, heavy Industrial for the Beta and classical music mixed with dubstep for the Goo!
Motion Capture
The facial animations of the characters in the cutscenes have an unusual high quality as seen in barely any game before.
Editor
They included the very Editor they used for the campaign design into the game! It´s industry-level, has lots of features and is getting patched and expanded.
Advanced AI
The AI of the game does not cheat. It scouts you, adapts to your strategies and has no economic advantage. AI personalities and AI difficulty can be randomized.
Problems
Small playerbase
The playerbase is relatively small because the marketing left to be desired. One can basically always find someone to play against, since there is a steamgroup for Grey Goo, but the long lists of custom games one would wish for are not reality.
2-4 players
The game only supports up to 4 players in multiplayer at the moment.
Only 9 maps
The map pool is tiny in comparison. Map contests and upgrades will likely follow.
Balance issues
There are some imbalances, that need work. If and how the devs will react to those, is yet to be seen, since the game has just been released recently.
No destructible environment
It´s not important but I´d like to see the Goo eat trees it moves through! It´s kinda strange to see military structures crumble and get consumed while the fauna gets spared. There is also wildlife missing and structure and unit models do not show sustained damage properly.
No observer or replay function
These are not ingame. The developer announced to be working on them since some time and promised to add them soon.
AI issues
Nonresponsive units just standing around somewhere or abusable pathing flaws plague the AI. Additionally, RTS-experienced players will have no problem defeating it.
Summary
This is the very game, Command and Conquer fans have been waiting for over the last years! I am confident that they will work on the small flaws of this well polished product and that more is to come!

Telltale's Game of Thrones is a wonderful game, but it falls short in some respects.
If you're looking into this game, you're probably invested in the show, like myself, and perhaps the books as well. If you are, I'm not sure how you'll react to this game. This game is Telltale at its best. Your choices really feel like they have weight, and the overall goal of helping your House, the Forresters, really solicits your investment as you get to see it from a whole generation's eyes. The family dynamic is really well done, and some of the twists and turns will have you reflecting for hours afterward. Each character is very well written and voice acted, and each one has their enticing features. It's a fantastic game in its own right, and it's well deserving of my reccomendation. However, I don't feel the Game of Thrones license is properly used here.
The ASoIaF series uses death as a major plot device, being infamous for its use. The show takes after its source material in that manner. The game, on the other hand, keeps the death on the down-low. Each death tends to be shocking, yes, but the amount of it is very much toned down. I would blame this on two things. The ESRB and the significantly downsized cast. I think the ESRB can be blamed for a lot of the toning down of violence and disturbance, even though those are some of the reasons the show and books are such interesting studies of human nature.
That's not my biggest issue with this game. While Telltale is know and renowned for their unique, immersive storytelling, they didn't alter their formula for this game. In the show and books, each characters has feats that are good and bad. There's no heroic, chosen one, protagonist. In this game, the Forresters are portrayed as the wholly good force, there's no bad to the good characters, and there are no bad characters. The antagonists are portrayed as these malevolent, vicious people who hate the Forresters for seemingly no reason.
Besides this somewhat cliched nature, the game is thoroughly enjoyable and a well-told story. I reccomend it, but don't expect the level of drama and suspense you get from from the TV show and books.

A gripping tale of vikings, men and other ethnicities in a far away land. An enemy from the past emerges, bound on destruction. You follow 2 groups trying to fulfill an order or just plain fleeing from the advancing armies.
Landscapes of beauty and despair pass by you while you try to keep your loved ones close, bolster morale, manage food and fend off attackers. You engage in turn-based battles, level up your fighters, decide on the fate of many, uncover mysteries and secrets that raise more questions, especialy about the nature and motivation of the enemy.
The gameplay loop consists of travel/caravan management and turn-based battles.
Decisions range far and wide:  who to keep in your caravan, who to help (or not), how to approach new found allies or foes. Some decisions may come back to haunt you.
The emphasis lies unfortunately on rather boring turn-based battles and there are numerous ones.
Easy mode lowers the strength/armor of enemies and fallen allies don't receive wounds.
Normal+Hard add injuries that have to be removed by sleeping in your camp (making the trip longer and consumes supplies.
The game tries to change things up, some battles are forced, some avoidable, some decisions must be made even if you have no way of making an informed decision. While that sounds good on paper many encounters/decisions I made felt ultimately in vain since the game has certain "chokepoints" in the story where you don't feel any agency at all.
A limitation by the small team and budget I hope.
My biggest gripe is still the unimaginative gameplay, you can choose the turnorder of your fighters before the fight and their positioning. This is where the game gets gamey for its own sake. Instead of giving you freedom they restrict your positioning before the battle forcing a certain "challenge" on you each fight. Sometimes you can't even choose who your allies are making some fights extremely drawn-out because the developer chose for you. You can't really plan ahead since you don't know the turn order of your enemies beforehand. Many classes sound nice on paper but ultimately have no effect on battles, I found myself coming back again and again to the same formations because they almost one-shot each enemy.
I still recommed this game for its atmosphere, soundtrack, art and story alone.

This series is the JRPG equivalent of that one kid at school who half-asses everything and gets solid C's for their grades. That's Hyperdimension Neptunia, it tries to do something unique and then just gives up halfway through. It's thoroughly flawed, necessary grind heavy, and once you've played one game you've literally played them all; I can confidently say that as a fan who’s played them all. Yet despite these flaws the meta humor CAN actually be pretty enjoyable sometimes, and even a little cute. BUUUUUUUUUUUUUUUUUUUT unless you are into fanservice and silly game humor I really can't suggest it. Still, there are things here to salvage that I personally think are worth playing it for it:
Great voice acting: the actresses really make the humor; honestly, some of them really stick out too! Specifically Compa's actress stands out as especially good at her job.
Writing: the writing is good, it's why people ended up making the 2010 game a cult classic (among...other reasons) if anything you should be able to find enjoyment out of the dialogue as well as the characters. They're all typical anime character tropes but they are played with to some degree.
Story: the story is why I bought the 2010 game and all of its subsequent releases in the first place. It's literally about the console wars vs. piracy. Honestly, it’s simple but effective tale, far from deep but enjoyable anyways. Luckily for you, this game IS the first game only not....as....terrible.
If you're looking for some deep or complex JRPG then turn around and continue looking because this game is NOT going to give you that. Like I said, Hyperdimension Neptunia is a very lazy series that slowly makes improvements with each new game. For each positive there is a negative, making this game largely unimpressive. But in this weird way there is this charm that can draw you in.

If you're used to turn-based combat games, be warned Banner Saga's approach is unique and will take some practice at first. You set the battle order of your pieces, move/attack with your first piece, the opponent does the same, then you move/attack with your 2nd piece, and so on. This forces you to plan a few turns ahead in combat and carefully spread your attackts to lower the enemies' strengths faster than they lower yours. It's challenging at first, but you'll often have access to training grounds to practice with nothing at stake.
Enjoy!

With incredible depth, a wonderfully implemented territory control system, clever mechanics representing the hardships of winter and some awesome explosions, this game is one of the best I've ever played. It's hard to overstate how amazing it really is.
Some games really show their true colors only from the inside, and Company of Heroes 2 is one of them. Sure, its pedigree is impressive: the original Company of Heroes is one of the highest-rated RTS games of all time, and is still played by a large and dedicated fan base even seven years after its release. Relic, the developer, is beloved for titles like Homeworld 2, the Dawn of War games, and Impossible Creatures. As the fans of many genres can attest, however, sequels don’t necessarily mean improvement. Companies can easily lose track of what their fans loved about a beloved original. Rest assured, Company of Heroes 2 does its predecessor and the RTS genre quite a service: from the outside, it’s a polished and visually impressive RTS. From the inside, it can quite often be breathtaking.
Graphically, this is one of the most visually impressive RTS games out there. From cannon fire knocking chunks out of civilian structures to the satisfying weight with which vehicles move to how wounded soldiers writhe on the ground in virtual agony, Company of Heroes 2 handles physics, lighting effects and tank and weapon designs with great care and attention to detail. Even on low graphics settings the game looks darn good and behaves nicely. Sometimes, graphics can get a little muddy with a ton of greys and browns, but that comes, I think, as much from the subject matter as anywhere. This is not a game befitting of bright, primary colors.
Its depth will take some getting used to for the novice, and the veteran of Company of Heroes might have some adjusting to do and might question whether some omissions or upgrades are truly steps in the right direction, but I honestly feel that despite its somewhat lackluster campaign story, Company of Heroes 2 has a broader appeal than its predecessor and brings interesting decision-making to the mix with its weather mechanics and the ability to requisition abandoned enemy material. You will not regret picking this one up, I can assure you.

I REALLY wanted to like this game.  I love tactical turn-based rpgs, the art and music are beautiful, and the Viking theme is a breath of fresh air.  However, this game bored me to death.  The combat gets old after a couple hours because the strategy is the same in every battle (chipping away at the enemy armor while hiding your weaker units behind dudes with shields).  It doesn't help that the story and characters are both bland.  It's almost as if a bunch of artists got together with this great theme but forgot they had to (or didn't know how to) make a fun game in order to tie everything together.
What's disappointing is that there are so many similar games (that did it right) they could have used as inspiration: Fire Emblem, XCOM, Final Fantasy Tactics, Advance Wars, etc.  These games focus on gameplay first; story and theme complement gameplay but are ultimately secondary.  The Banner Saga does the opposite and comes up short because of it.

This game is truly a wonderful experience from start to finish.
There are a lot of hard choices to make, though some may argue that the impact isn't big enough throughout the game. The biggest change could be that you loose a certain character, but most of the time it affects some of the ressources you own. In the end, two playthroughs won't be that much different story wise, but who ends up surviving in the end may change. The combat is tactical without being too complicated to grasp. There are only a few rules to learn, but they offer some very interesting situations, especially the constant lack of Renown, the in-game ressource that allows you to buy items, supply and level up your characters. You will constantly juggle between these options, wondering if you can make it to the next city with the few days of supplies left, hoping that nothing bad will hit you on the way, and investing your Renown into upgrading you characters. Or maybe you should acquire that sweet sweet level 5 item that you may end up never using since it is so hard to level up your troops... You won't be able to acquire everything, and that may annoy some people in the end.
The game isn't too long, about 10 hours for a full playthrough, and ends up a bit abruptly. However, the ending makes you look forward to the sequel, which I haven't played yet. The story is great and keeps you wondering what will happen next, how will you caravan survive this unforgiving pilgrimage.
Now, the game truly shines with its art style and animation which give life to this world you are exploring. And the world is HUGE too! If you really enjoy looking at world maps and learning information about each and every corner of the world, the game allows you to do that. However, keep in mind that the game is linear and that you won't chose where you want to go.
Overall, it is a great experience that I highly recommend. It is a sad world to explore, but a very satisfying game to experience.

If you're looking for that overhead head-scratching adventure to play with one friend, you've finally hit the jackpot.
Fire up the VoIP, grab your RPG buddy, customize a class, and keep your finger on the quickload button!
With an old-school take on "open world", Original Sin adds most of the options that should have been standard RPG elements for years. This includes, but is not limited to, liberal object manipulation: If it's not nailed down, go ahead and move it to your liking. That is, if you think you're strong enough.
Another should-be industry standard they've adopted is crafting: While their crafting system is not entirely black-and-white intuitive, a few quick references to a wiki page will leave you well on your way to a nicely enhanced arsenal.
You will find yourself battling foes several times your better in nicely rendered scenery, using every element at your disposal to defeat your foes. Mostly the literal elements. Whether you're luring a horde of goblins through a wall of fire, or adding a few extra volts to that pool of water those pesky humans are standing in, you're sure to begin to see each battle as a puzzle its' self.
All in all, the lack of cosmetic customization is far outweighed by the satisfaction of using the many tools that you will accumulate, with which you may reduce anyone who stands in your way (or beside your way, or for that matter, within visual distance) to little ashen piles.

If you're a fan of action RPGs, like me, this game is one of the best to play at the moment. It has all the elements that made the original Titan Quest series great, but now it looks a lot better, with richer animations, better combat than most ARPGs out there (only worse than Diablo 3's and pretty on par with Torchlight 2's, both pretty good ARPGs too, with their ups and downs, of course).
This game looks grim, indeed, the world is not a fairy tale full with heroes with amazing powers, everything looks depraved and decayed, our own character is a no one, strange circumstances have put us, the player, on a very difficult situation and we must prove ourselves that we can be of some worth in this world Grim Dawn has to offer, while we keep uncovering the mysteries around what has been done to us, as we saw in the introductory cinematic.
What makes this game interesting, compared to other similar titles, is that everything seems to be well crafted, with a lot of love put into every aspect of the game from the developers, it feels like a true RPG, combat can be a bit simple (similar to Path of Exile's combat here, maybe), and each character "class" or spec seems to have several variants to play around with, so if you like to experiment with different builds, this game is nice on that aspect.
The game also has mod support, I've seen some interesting mods out there already, and I'll try them in the future since, much like with Torchlight 2, I think this game will become even more awesome with a couple big mods installed, and it seems to be the case right now already.
On the negative side, I'd say the game engine could have been a bit more optimized in the sense that the game will only use one of our CPU cores at max, then not much of the rest, so it's hard to get like 144 FPS constantly and you can expect some FPS drops on intense combat situations too, because of this. With an i5 4690K and a GTX 1070 I can play at 110+ FPS reaching 144 at times (on a 144 Hz, VSYNC enabled and everything maxxed, 1080p), but I can see some frame rate drops to the 70s sometimes in heave combat scenarios, because of the CPU limitation within the engine itself, so keep this in mind; I also tested the game on a GTX 770 like 6 months ago and I could easily sustain 70+ FPS everything maxxed, so don't worry about GPU performance, because it’s the CPU the one that limits your average frame rate here.
Overall, I see this game will be still getting free upgrades and DLCs, and that’s awesome too, and I can see myself playing this game as much as I've played other ARPGs like Torchlight 2 or PoE if they keep adding content. I assume it must be even better with friends, but I haven't tried the multiplayer yet.
For the price, this game's a must for ARPG fans that like their games gritty and dark, with a good amount of exploration, freedom and even secret places and quests to find, so give it a go if you're looking for an action RPG.

Surely enough, I moved as normal. However, when it came to looking around, moving the mouse only moved an on-screen cursor, not changing the direction I was looking at all. Again, I used my instincts and held the right mouse button and moved the mouse again, this time the camera moved. I cried some more as I moved about, being forced to strain my finger by having to hold right click for the whole period of play, similar to 'Roblox'. After almost playing this game for 2 weeks I can finally put in my review for this game. I've been looking for a MMORPG to play for a while now and I haven't found the one to play.
Pros
- Amazing graphics
- Great combat system
- Not p2w
- No bots
- All classes have their own unique fight style
- In depth trade / farming system
- Players get rewarded for their time
- Doesn’t matter how much real money you spend in the game, you can’t buy contribution points to help you maintain cash flow in the game.
- Every class has their own unique play style it’s not too hard to master them.
Cons
- Heavy grinding
- Community is toxic and weird but if you’re a lone wolf or can find the right group, you’ll stay
- Inventory slots / weight though it can be expanded and trained on
- Achievement is still bugged
- There aren’t much guilds that will help due to their high requirements
- Gear is pricey but with time you can get the greatest gear
- The enchanting system is REALLY difficult due to how hard it is to get them to higher levels it’ll cost a lot of money
- There isn’t a level cap but it is hard to grind starting at 50+
- PvP is something you’ll run by a lot when you reach level 50, if you do not have the gear, be prepared to be camped on by higher geared people
- Game requires high end PC parts to enjoy the full game quality
Overall after play this game, I can say that this game is REALLY fun and there are some pros and cons to it. This MMO is not for everyone, it's very different from any MMOs like WoW, GW2, and TESO. This game has a good combat system like Vindictus, though vindictus is a dungeon style game, it's great to see a MMO have the same combat style. I can also say this game reminds me a bit of Silkroad Online with the trading and it's really fun. The system in game is a bit complex, crafting, gathering and enchanting but a couple of guides online and guilds can really help you. Their guild system is also a bit different, you get paid to be in a guild and a lot of the guilds have really high requirements. A lot of people say this game is paid to win but it's not, they really thought out the system so it's great. There are cosmetics in the game but they can also be bought with in-game money. Also, there are no gold bots in this game which really makes it fun and equal for everyone. I will say now that the game will require A LOT of time to get really good gear, but if you're really dedicated you can enjoy the game just like I do. I can say the market system is great but really difficult for some people to snipe some items, but it makes it fair for everyone and also eliminates gold bots.

This game is truly a wonderful experience from start to finish.
There are a lot of hard choices to make, though some may argue that the impact isn't big enough throughout the game. The biggest change could be that you loose a certain character, but most of the time it affects some of the ressources you own. In the end, two playthroughs won't be that much different story wise, but who ends up surviving in the end may change. The combat is tactical without being too complicated to grasp. There are only a few rules to learn, but they offer some very interesting situations, especially the constant lack of Renown, the in-game ressource that allows you to buy items, supply and level up your characters. You will constantly juggle between these options, wondering if you can make it to the next city with the few days of supplies left, hoping that nothing bad will hit you on the way, and investing your Renown into upgrading you characters. Or maybe you should acquire that sweet sweet level 5 item that you may end up never using since it is so hard to level up your troops... You won't be able to acquire everything, and that may annoy some people in the end.
The game isn't too long, about 10 hours for a full playthrough, and ends up a bit abruptly. However, the ending makes you look forward to the sequel, which I haven't played yet. The story is great and keeps you wondering what will happen next, how will you caravan survive this unforgiving pilgrimage.
Now, the game truly shines with its art style and animation which give life to this world you are exploring. And the world is HUGE too! If you really enjoy looking at world maps and learning information about each and every corner of the world, the game allows you to do that. However, keep in mind that the game is linear and that you won't chose where you want to go.
Overall, it is a great experience that I highly recommend. It is a sad world to explore, but a very satisfying game to experience.

I bought the game on sale, if you don't have people coming over regularly to play against you on multiple steam controllers, you might want to grab it on sale? But if you have friends with it's definitely worth the $10. Really a super fun game.

Child of Light is a turn-based RPG. It's fun. It's engrossing. It's gorgeous. And the music is just amazing throughout. I will focus the bulk of this review on the turn-based element as it is essential to playing the game and completing all tasks ahead of you.
Yes, you have a main quest, but along the way, you find that your friends have problems of their own and you will need to venture off and solve their problems, too. Do not worry, the story does not usually stray from stronger monsters, so you are usually well-matched.
You control two characters at a time, which is a little few considering most people enjoy the four-player turn-based times of old. Do not be discouraged, as you can swap on the fly both characters, as long as it is their turn. So if you are low on health or lack the protection from the element your current enemy dishes out, you are able to switch to another character and start anew on that turn.
NOTE: If you are in the 'wait-window' (where you are about to act out your play decision for that character), your new swap-in will go back to the beginning of that wait line (not the beginning of the turn) and depending on their overall speed, perhaps a little further back from the line. You won't necessarily lose a lot of time for that turn, but you will not come in mid-stroke and deliver a promising blow. If an enemy is between the wait line and where your previous character sat, it will go before your new arrival takes action.
Your characters do not equip armor or anything, this is supplemented by Oculi, small gems. These can be combined three at a time to make a stronger version of itself. You equip one on your weapon, your clothing or your timeline. On your weapon you can gain elemental damage, the higher version the gem, the more percentage the damage and sometimes a combat action effect like paralysis. Same for your clothing, however, it is for elemental protection and defense effects like +EXP bonus or a +ALL Element protection or physical/magical defense across the board. The timeline connection brings to fruition +Evasion while casting, +Interruption of enemy in Wait status, +Stats, +Casting Speed and a good one, dtarting on the timeline further out than normal.
These oculi are few in the first six chapters, so you will bounce between three or four main characters at first, until you can get more in the end-game for flexing your strategy. Do not let this discourage you though, between every battle you can switch the oculi to whomever you want and the process is a speedy one. And uPlay even lets you buy more through their reward process if you want to spend some uPlay credits (although I did not take this route, and probably will not).
If you try to stick to the same two characters, you will find it far more difficult to proceed after Chapter 6. Up until then you will be okay and will be able to mix and match and learn each characters strengths and weaknesses. Each character is diverse. You will not find any two alike but in a way or three. Take Aurora for instance, she can heal, but she cannot revive like Rubella. Aurora has Starlight, effective against Dark, but only Finn has elemental damage against the other elements. Unless of course you use oculi on another characters weapon, but even then the damage will be far less than Finn's magical prowess.
It's good stuff. This game shines in the dark. I thoroughly enjoyed it on both Wii U and here on PC.
Now all that aside, you will still find fun collecting the stardust (permanent stat increase), potions, oculi and confessions (notes to bring light to some lore) scattered across the land. But be prepared to fight. To get everything this game has to offer, you will need to master the combat mechanic and lay waste to many an enemy. It is a good thing all characters level-up together so you will not have to gather clean-up experience later because you will be able to switch your characters and oculi throughout and build a strategy worthy of your name.

I've played this initially with some reservations. Mainly, since I am inept with Russian, the Russian parts and some of the poor spelling and grammar did not do the story justice with the way it alienates me. Overall, looking into the story as a series in itself when you play different routes overshadows its flaws. It's an interesting concept: the storyline isn't exactly the same, but you have a whole basic element of combining different things and making stories out of it. In fact, this leads to some stories having different endings, and split between good and bad.
I started reading the guides on how to complete it properly, because boy - you will be lost without some clue on how to finish the way you want! Fortunately, starting with the good endings eventually leads to opening up the bad ones, as well as 2 extra unlocks of girls you have very little interaction in comparison to the other main characters. It's a nice little bonus. As for that, let me give you the background:
The main protagonist is Semyon, a young adult who at some point gets transported to a younger self back in time, but it's a place he's never been, let alone heard of. The story is more stranger as you progress, that since Semyon is used to the post-Soviet era, this throwback and the isolation of the Pioneer camp he resides shuts him out of knowing where he really is - and if it's even real. Any attempts in trying to find an escape or answers is thwarted, so the only way out is to go through with it, in all 7 days of the camp. The place is as much strange to him, as he would be a strange visitor purportedly from the future. Fortunately, the residents never question his presence, as if he is meant to be there.
Now, the main goal to complete the achievements you end up doing, of course, is to reach a route to form relationships with each girl. Yes, it does lead to romantic heights (I patched this up to get the H scenes), although this isn't the only part of the story, as you will discover the possible truth of the world that Semyon is living in, leading to scenes of 4th wall proportions that push the question of the camp being a reality. It's the journey, my friend, that you need to experience to see for yourselves what you'd like to accept.
As I played along, I notced 3 characters in this tale that you do not reach routes for, despite the other 2 minor characters. Indeed, just 2 adults appear to reside in the camp, and all but 1 female you meet are the only ones you have scenes for. This was my downside of playing this VN, leading me to feel disappointed there weren't some racy scenes with the adults (because, hey, it can't be real, so does morality apply?), despite the steamy events between the youth. This lead me to feel this game was incomplete in this department, but I am impressed with the work it did to detail with the girls.
Among the jokes and references throughout the game, I noticed an uncanny resemblance of a few of the characters not unlike those in Katawa Shoujo, of which the dating game also plays there. Slavya, I identify with Lilly Satou. Lena's purple hair is reminiscent of Hanako. The short stature of Ulyana is almost a direct reference to the sporty Emi. I shall not forget the intelligent, glasses-wearing maturity of Zhenya (she is the only girl with no route) as the hard, yet soft Shizune Hakamichi. KS's nameless Nurse himself has a heterochromic female counterpart in Viola as the camp nurse. Even the motherly character of Olga could be a direct comparison to Yuuko Shirakawa. Although each of these characters have their differences, some of their personalities, appearances and quirks share certain common denominators. In a way, it could have been an easter egg of sorts, but that's just how I see it.
I have yet to utilize the ability of using mods and playing other created stories, but I look forward to exploring them in the future. For now, my main goal was to complete the story and my report of the gameplay. It was an entertaining set of tales weaved out a plot. Some ranging from romantic, adventurous, and even some in the horror genre. The foreign (to me) nature it bases in Russian culture (as opposed to KS's Japanese fare), is a nice change of pace to see other ideas and environments playing a role in the stories in a VN format. The drawings, writing, and music set the stage of a great performance to rate a positive review. I do encourage others to try it.

Urgh, I nearlly clicked "recommend", but only because, like me, it might be worth adding another 4p local multiplayer game to your library if you're collecting them.  But only for something a little different, not because it's particularly good.
In the end I decided it's wierd to have a "recommend" and then actually rip it apart in the description. So I changed it to a "don't recommend" to catch the eye of the devs in hopes they might take on the feedback.
It's main problem is it's just not obvious how to play.  You all kind of randomly kill each other over and over and over again, in a chaotic mess ove over-sized bullets that bounce off the wall and are moving too fast to react to.  Half of your deaths are by shooting yourself.  Yes you can eventually get better at it but the fact that everyone's initial game is just random deaths where you can barely make out what's happening amongst the chaos, is a testimant to how unintuitive the whole thing feels.
By comparison, I use TowerFall in game tournaments at the college I teach at, and people who've never played before quickly become used to it  and really get into it, even people who don't normally play games. It's quite obvious what you're doing - you can jump on heads, aim and shoot, and re-collect your limited arrows.  You can clearly see the cause and effect - everything is a good size, and a good SPEED, and not cluttered at all (in spite of having 4 players on one screen) and everything important (aiming, kills, etc.) is broadcast very very clearly.
AND YET it is still very competative, and you can get very skilled at it, and it can be classified as "twitched based gameplay" (just as Charge Shot does).  I have seen some♥♥♥♥♥♥from Towerfall, man.  You can get so good at it.
With Charge Shot, we played it for a good 10 minutes and I still don't feel like I "get" it.  I get that you kinda don't want to be horizontal with anyone, and if you do pass in front, press the shield button and you'll more than likely bounce the shot they fire at you and kill them.  But everything still feels 50-50.  Wins don't really feel like wins, just "oh that turned out in my favour randomly, cool, I guess."
It does come down to the controls a lot;
The jet pack thing feels fairly frustrating, the delay before it sends you upward doesn't seem like you can use it to get out of the way quickly, and when it does pick up speed, it's so fast you can't really use it effectively and mostly go all the way to the top.  So you kind of just float around, kinda trying not to pass in front of anyone.
The bullets are very big, very fast, and bounce off the wall, so once someone fires in your direction, you're not going to dodge it - in fact you're likely to kill yourself from your own shot due to the bounce.  That's really unintuitive, to fire a weapon which has such a high chance of killing its owner.
On top of that, each shot has a huge amount of kickback, which added to everything else, is the icing on the cake in really taking control away from you and feel like you're trying to remote control a toy car on a bed of marbles by pushing it around with a stick.  That's an analogy I just came up with to express the lack of control we felt we had over the characters.
Look, I'm sure the developers really love this game and are "good" at it and have fun with it, otherwise they wouldn't have put so much polish on it.  I just don't feel like it was tested on other people very much.  I don't think it's a good idea to make a game that only you can play, it needs to be acessable as well as being competative and skill based.

A fantastic open world Survival Crafting Parkour Melee-Combat with Zombies Extraordinaire, Dying Light is a great game that will certainly give you a lot of bang for your buck. Made by the same guys that created Dead Island, you will see bits and pieces of that somewhat disappointing experience interspersed with some new brilliant ideas.
The melee combat is fast and it is brutal, especially at first. Zombies don’t fall apart like they’re made out of paper (like in Dead Rising) and they feel like real, physical objects in the world. They’ll grab and shove at you while you’re trying to get away from them, and it takes many, many bashes with the numerous melee weapons to take them down. You really get the feeling that sure, I’m an able bodied Parkour badass and I can take on one or two zombies reliably, but if three or more are attacking you, there’s a real chance that you can die. It really convinces the player to move quickly through giant crowds, versus standing there and fighting them one after another, because you will most likely die. I recommend playing on Hard difficulty if you want to give yourself that extra challenge. I can’t remember another main stream zombie game (except for maybe ZombieU) where the zombie enemies are such big threats, it makes every encounter feel dangerous and exciting. Much more of the game isn’t focused on fighting them, but avoiding them with platforming and free-running. Every weapon will break eventually, despite having multiple repairs. This gives me bad OCD, as I'm almost unwilling to use my best weapons since I'm "saving it" for tougher enemies. However, I think this is a feeling that the developers wanted to instill in its players, that nothing in this world is permanent and everything will eventually fall apart. By the end, weapons last long enough to be less of an issue, and this prompts you to try out many different melee weapons since you'll be breaking them all the time.
The Parkour in this game is the best I’ve ever seen in a FPS, for sure. Mirror’s Edge had great mechanics as well, but in that game I always felt like I was doing things I didn’t mean to, while in Dying Light I feel like everything my character performs in game was what I was trying to do. If an object LOOKS like you can hold on to it, 99/100 times you will automatically grab on. There isn’t any fancy wall running or anything, but the movement is so fluid and smooth that it isn’t required. Shoving my way through a field of zombies, only to leap on one’s shoulder’s onto a telephone pole, and shimmying up to jump onto an apartment balcony is a great experience. Within a couple hours you’ll already feel great mastery of the free-running, it feels a lot like a first person Assassin’s Creed, albeit smoother and faster. This is probably the most unique and well done portion of the game, without it will feel like a Dead Island-like melee slog, but the danger from crowds of zombies plus the simple intuitiveness of the free-running means you’ll love parkouring everywhere. Just getting from objective to objective is a ton of fun.
As much of an untouchable badass you feel like during the day, the game’s title “Dying Light” will always be on the back of your mind. As soon as the sun sets, the world is bathed in an impenetrable night, illuminated only by your puny flashlight. It’s one of the more realistic night times in video games I’ve seen, you really can’t see jack♥♥♥♥♥♥in the dark. The dangerous Volatile type zombies are big, buff, fast runners that will chase you down and end you very quick, so you’re always on your toes, trying to stealth your way around them. If they find you, it’s a panicked, terrifying sprint to a safe house, where you feel like a hunted animal (somewhat Outlast-like). This dichotomy of day time and night time play go together very well, and players are encouraged to do objectives/ missions during the night because of doubled XP bonuses. It’s also great that time progresses throughout your gameplay, so you can all of a sudden be caught out in the open AT NIGHT because you were too busy killing zombies for fun or in the middle of a mission, forcing you to frantically find shelter while groping blindly in the darkness. Great stuff.
The graphics of this game are beautiful, palm trees wave in the wind, ramshackle buildings are rife with details, and the setting sun casts a beautiful glow over everything, despite its warning of impending doom. This is one of the better looking games out right now, and it seems to perform very well on systems. Facial animations may look kinda weird, but the NPC designs are full of character and the game is well voice acted. Unfortunately, the base story is pretty predictable and full of zombie genre tropes, but the gameplay more than makes up for it. Near the end of the game you’ll be pretty overpowered with weapons and firearms. One thing that was a common complaint of Dead Island was that the firearms felt very weak, but in Dying Light they actually feel like guns, deadly and powerful. Ammo is pretty scarce so I would almost never use it, but when I decided to bust out my pistol that’s when things got real. There are also human enemies that you can fight with melee, and they are pretty tough to fight, but it’s always comical when they pull out a machete and I shoot them immediately, much like Indiana Jones in Raiders of the Lost Ark. Thankfully the lack of ammo means that I can’t use these guns ALL the time, and it’s better to save the bullets for the human enemies that do have guns.
All in all, one of the better open world games to come out recently. Great fun in single player, but even more fun in co op (up to 4 players). It’s great to parkour and kill zombies together, and there are tons of little competitions that you can dynamically choose to compete with your partner with, whether it’s parkour racing or looting stuff. Dying Light recently had a huge expansion released called The Following that has been amazing during the little I’ve played. Techland has joined CD Project Red as another great Polish Developer, and I can’t wait to see what they come up with next.

Clocked about 32 hours in this so far, nothing but the base package. The base package is incredibly expansive, unlike some older Yu-Gi-Oh! titles, example Power of Chaos - Yugi The Destiny, which had somewhere around 190 total cards if memory serves me right. This title has thousands, just how many I don't know. They can all be acquired ingame by either beating duels (earning signature cards directly, depending on who you face) or by spending points in the shop to buy card packs. You get a nice chunk of points per duel, usually 800-1000 if you lose and 1500-2000 if you win. Packs are either 200 or 400 points a piece, with 8 cards in each. Very easy to earn yourself new cards, and there are no microtransactions. The only other purchase you may consider besides the base game would be one of the DLCs, but more on that below.
The campaigns are interesting and let you play through duels from the shows, Yu-Gi-Oh, GX, 5DS, ZEXAL and ARC-V. Not all of them, but enough to follow the story if you haven't seen them. Note that I have only seen the original show, so I can only speak for that one, but the others have enough text between duels to get the point across.
All in all; for 19,99 this is absolutely fantastic. Actually, it's fantastic without the cheap price but it helps make it even better. It's good enough that I'm considering buying DLC at this very moment, which includes specialized decks and cards as well as some new campaign duels, presumably to fill in the blanks.

An anime-styled turn-based RPG that shamelessly panders to, and subsequently parodies, the gaming industry and its community. What could go wrong? Little, it seems. From the brisk, upbeat background tracks to the eye-catching graphics, cartoonish in nature, yet remarkably detailed, this is a game that could have gone down the gutter, and yet is an endlessly pleasant surprise to those who play it.
The action is tight-knit and dynamic, with a simple, yet effective hitbox system and skills galore to ensure that no battle is the same, unlike the vast majority of other Japanese turn-based RPGs, where everything is the same old hit-and-grind.
The story is heartwarming, and though in its determination to bring up every cliche one could possibly conceive, the storyline might seem a little cringeworthy at times, the cutesy voice-acting and reactive changes in music and character visuals make the game seem like one part RPG, one part visual novel, which is always a bonus. (Note: If you have voice-acting turned on, use the Japanese voices. The English dubs are, as usual for most anime / games, dismal.)
The controls take some getting used to - since the game is a port from the Playstation console system, the ABXY and L/R buttons are mapped to various keys around the keyboard, and getting them into your memory takes a little while. But it is worth the time, because this game is a treat for anime lovers, and a nice break for those who just want to enjoy a good, low-stress Japanese RPG. Overall rating: 8.5/10

After a discrete experience as a videogamer I learned to classify games into macro-categories, more or less like steam tags. But there are some games, some little pearls, that lie outside every class. If you open the store page of The Banner Saga, it'll tell you that the game is a turn based RPG. Don't believe it. The tag is a lie. That is such a reductive definition that is like to say that the Hamlet is just a tragedy.
The Banner Saga redefines itself presenting a game experience that does perfectly what a game should do: it carries you into another world, makes you feel what the characters feel, to the point I wasn't able not to finish it in one day.
In the short, but at the same time long days of marching followed by your caravan, you feel the weight of leadership, the eyes of every person weighting your decisions, the fear of hunger for every day you pass in the open, with the supplies running short, the relief of entering a village and rest.
Regarding the combat system, it may not be very innovative, but it wasn't meant for casual players, that's sure. On normal difficulty, enemies will smash you and leave you wounded for days, even after victory, if you don't put strategy and caution in your decisions. To cut it short, just because you are giant wielding a battle axe that doesn't mean that rush into enemies swinging it is a good idea.
I suggest everyone to play this game. If you want more than entertainment from a game, if you want to feel something, if you want to fear, joy and cry (I admit it, just a little in the end), give it a try.

Few MMO's have ever got me hooked, and the last one being Guild Wars 2. Gw2 was great, but I can say this game surpasses it in every aspect.
Again the best I have ever seen in an MMO. I generally like the look of most things despite running this on medium/high settings.  However, the optimization definitely needs work. I can get 60+fps on max easily in the wild but in the cities or other heavily populated areas I dip down to 20's to 40's .
The combat is absolutely amazing. It isn't complex, but some classes require you to learn a lot of combos which can confuse some people. The combat ruins fluid and is absolutely enjoyable.
I haven't gotten to pvp too much, but Duels need some work. There are times where the opponet and I can not hit eachother but then it works a few seconds later.
The quests aren't very entertaining but I found myself enjoying the main story line. I also enjoy how late game quests really help with the whole grinding aspect. Many of the quests fortunately have seperate ones that are very similar so you can do 5-6 at the same time, which is convenient and nice.
Life skills such as trading, fishing, gathering and others are a nice aspect to the game and provide an alternative to combat for making money and such. Some people actually enjoy this part of the game more than the combat itself, which is unsurprising as it is very intuitive and rewarding. I don't find myself wanting to spend much time with this but I possibly will later when money becomes more of a necessity for me.
Trading/Nodes/Map/Workers etc. : They are confusing to learn at first, but once you get the hang of it you'll see that the game offers something brand new to the MMO genre and it is filled with depth.  I definitely see this having a large impact on the game for players and I believe it overs a lot more longevity to the game.
Overall, the gameplay is extremely fun and I find myself playing for up to 8 hours at a time - that never happens for me!

Everlasting Summer:
A wonderful game, possibly the best visual novel on Steam, certainly the best I have played!
The theme is interesting, the twists and turns confusing, yet it draws you on. The music is wonderful, and the price...well, it's free! (but it would be worth it even if it was priced at 10£).
Without revealing too much, there are so many layers to this game, from philosophical musings about what reality really is, to meta-commentary (at least i read it like that) about losing emotional connection through gaining "victories" too easily. And therein lies my one regret...I kinda wish i had just played through this on my "preferred route", because it really is a very sweet game if you do so (unless you get the bad ending of some characters, especially one, then it is more bitter-sweet). But then I would have missed out on the huge mystery Everlasting summer really is.
Pro's:
+Free!
+The music.
+The feel of the game.
+The setting (how can you feel nostalgia for something you never experienced?)
+The writing (really quite good).
+A main character which should be fairly relatable to many players.
Con's:
-The main character can be a bit of a♥♥♥♥♥♥at times.
-Can be a bit dark, does contain monsters and suicides.
-Does not use the excellent style of semi-moving animations beyond the opening.
Either-or's:
+/-Does not provide you with a clear-cut answer to what was really happening.
+/-The art is done by different artists, meaning that characters can look a bit different in different CG's (though not in conversation screens).
+/-Yes, there is a "hentai" patch. No, you absolutely do not need it, as it doesn't really add that much to the game. I would say this game is more about the feel's than the "feel's", if you get what I mean :p
+/-Yes. Yes, there is a cat girl. Why is there a cat girl? Beats me, but it seems a lot of these games needs to have one. Anyway, she is kinda cute, and very infuriating. Kudos to the devs for a clever explanation of why she is there, even if it doesn't explain why she is...a cat.
Verdict: 8/10 -Clearly worth it, even if they start charging for it!
P.S. -There is a short follow-up fan game called "Frosty Kiss", made by another developer. I have not (yet) played that game, but it might be worth looking into. I believe it is also free on Steam.

Everlasting Summer is your classic visual novel harem, where your choices will affect the outcome. The story revolves around a 25 year old hikikomori named Seymon. He finds himself reverted to an 18 y/o and in a Pioneer’s Camp, after mistakenly falling asleep on a bus ride one winter. Though there never really was a conclusion as to how this had happened but it does not appear to be a main focus. The goal of the game, as in any harem, is to develop a strong relationship (or more) with the other noted characters. There is a bad/good ending for each of the characters whom you choose to conclude the story with: Slavya, Lena, Ulyana, Alisa or even your own route. Miku and Yulya’s routes are unlockable. My personal favourite was Slavya’s good ending
.
Because the store page for Everlasting Summer has a "Content in this product may not be appropriate for all ages […]" forewarning, there will definitely be some vulgar images and/or language. In this case the numerous panty shots, implications and other sorts of fan-service. But all of this overlooked, I did find the art and animations done well. The textures are soft, and there are varying shades and gradients on much of the background and our characters. At times, the BG itself is designed with much depth that it looks real: such as the scene at the Porch where you meet Alisa lock-picking at night. The characters we see on the other hand, are more outlined and do stand out from the BG. My only complaint here is that the character uniforms could have been more fashioned to suit the camp. There weren’t much special effects or animations in the gameplay either, when compared to what is shown in the trailer. Regardless, this did not hinder what image the game presents to the players.
The music was just as amazing. No voice actors were used, but the background music helped to establish the mood of the atmosphere, based on the scene or dialogue you are at - the gentle piano and harp piece that plays when are with Marsha at the beach – or the rock music triggered in the final scene of Lena’s route, in the bad ending, presenting a vicious tone in her dialogue when she is yelling at Semyon.
To wrap it up, this game did give me a fulfilling interactive experience, as well as a satisfactory conclusion, regardless, of which ending attained. The story isn’t top notch imo, but is a great start for players who are starting into playing VN or wants to play a classic!

I usually don't write reviews, but with so many people having an issue with uPlay I thought I would post what worked for me.
I read the reviews and comments before purchasing Child of Light on sale and I figured if I couldn't get it to work that it wouldn't be a total loss.
So here's what worked for me:
1. I did install the game, but DID NOT do the first time setup right away.
2. Before first time set up, I went online to Uplay and downloaded it from their site. Then made an account.
3. I then went to steam to get the game code. Copied it.
4. Went back to Uplay and went to "activate product"
5. Pasted code and it was added to my library.
6. THEN I finally hit play in Steam and did the first time set up. It asked me to link steam with Uplay. I did but I don't think you have to.
And the game has run smoothly ever since :)

It took my friend and I over a year, intermittently, to complete this game on co-op, primarily due to our differing time-zones and schedules. It was a year well spent. This game is expansive, the story was involving and the ability to roleplay your characters as different personalities  was refreshing. If you're planning on buying this game, there are some things I would like to point out first, so hear me out.
(Scroll to the bottom if you don't want to read)
PROS
-Gameplay is great: The parkour is fun, the zombies level with you, and the day & night cycle keeps the gameplay interesting when you're out exploring the city. The crafting system is well done, and the weapons eventually wear out, so there is a resource system associated with combat (to an extent).
-Atmosphere: The voice acting is pretty good, the game changes dramatically at night, and the side quests are actually pretty fun if you enjoy competing tasks and listening to NPCs with personality. The zombies also get more interesting as you progress through the story. And last, but not least, if you have a decent PC (it doesn't have to be too good), the high quality visuals are pretty tasty.
-Free DLC: The creators gave everyone the enhanced edition, free of charge! There's even a free game mode where you can even play as a spiderman-like zombie.
-Co-op: The game is a single player rpg, however you can invite friends over into your lobby. It doesn't matter if they're ahead/behind you in the story as the game bases the story's progression off of your playthrough. In my opinion, the creators of Dying Light did this pretty well. There's even a fast travel system between players for mission scenes where one person dies/gets left behind.
CONS
-Story: Now, I really wanted to like the story. I really did, but let me tell you this now. If you haven't bought this game yet, DO NOT BUY IT FOR THE STORY! I played this game for 25 hours, switching between side quests and the main story, and when I got to the halfway point in the story, I thought it was the coolest thing ever! Then I got to the latter half of the story. That was when the writing got really bad. The main story became extremely cliche and linear, which I was okay with, however when I got to the ending, I was sorely disappointed. The ending was bad. Period. I won't spoil it, but it was not a conclusive ending at all. It felt extremely shallow and hollow and boring when compared with all the other amazing things I had done throughout the entire rest of the game.
-Finding a lobby: When playing as a NightHunter, I found it near impossible to find a game at night where a player was willing to drop everything he was doing just to have a match with me. Long story short, since the game has been out for a year, there's not that many players in the middle ground who are willing to play against me. New players are always too busy playing the game during the day, and the experienced players are nowhere to be found (probably on The Following DLC).
-Pacing Issues: The game has pacing issues. I spent 25 hours in the Slums Map before I decided to stop doing side quests and transition with the story. Unfortunately by then, I was already 2/3rds of the way through my skill trees and I already had a bunch of crafting items in my inventory. By the time I got to the second map in the game, which was the Old Town Map, or the city, I was too lazy to explore the map in its entirety since looting didn't really appeal at that point in the game. In the end, this was a personal problem for me, so I was content with it. The real problem with the game's pacing is with the story progression. IN ORDER TO BETTER ENJOY THE GAME, I RECOMMEND THAT YOU TRANSITION BETWEEN DOING SIDE QUESTS AND THE MAIN STORY. If you just play the game, rushing through the main story and not doing anything in between, the game will feel really short. You could even finish the game in two days if you played enough.
Last Mission - This deserves its own con, not because the "story/ending" is "bad", but simply because the last mission is not only narrow and uninspired, but in addition to that, you can't play it on co-op because of reasons I can't spoil.
Tl;dr
Story - 4/10
Gameplay - 10/10**
Co-op - 9/10
Worth the Price? (YES)
*Game is more fun when doing side quests in between story missions.

I have always been a PC RPG fan since the days of Baldur's Gate. In short, this game is worth playing ONCE for any fan of the genre, but a lot of things bothered me about this game, and I don't think I'll experience much more a second time around, so I doubt I will replay it anytime soon.
Pros:
* Combat System
* Story and Narrative
* Graphics
* Soundtrack
* Flexible Adventuring
* Choices and decisions affect character development
* Pretty deep mechanics that will take a while to learn. Some may dislike this and others may like it.
* Modding community seems to be pretty strong
Cons:
* The loot system is very boring.
* Very little voice acting except for the main characters, and even their voice acting is sparse. This is really a shame as a lot of time was obviously spent on producing a rich story and narrative.
* Multiple characters cannot act simultaneously even outside of combat. You cannot pause, give all four of your characters orders, then unpause to see them all act. You have to give one order at a time in real time.
* Replay value is pretty low. Every single character has access to the exact same pool of abilities, they just focus on different things. You can experience all the skills and combinations in the game your first play through. They should have provided at least some 'class abilities', something to truly differentiate each character from the other.
* Merchants rarely ever have anything decent to sell until the end game. You end up having tons of gold and little to spend it on making collecting loot near pointless.
* There are very few interesting items in the game that will actually change your gameplay or tactics.
* Crafting is tedious, difficult to learn, yet compulsory to pursue due to the terrible loot system. Even after learning everything the crafting system is extremely limited and again, boring except for a few special items.
* Main characters only have 'traits' to set them apart from their companions and henchmen. Even thought they are supposedly 'divine' and basically save the universe, all they have over the hencmen are a few pathetic points.
* Many 'abilities' are essentially useless for your main four party characters
* Getting into the right backstabbing position is really really annoying
* Many puzzles and riddles are tedious

When Battlefield, CoD and other FPS came out, replacing Unreal, Doom and other, older style FPS, Lucasart soon came up with their version of the genre. For the first time, assaulting an Imperial StarDestroyer felt just like that, flying your shuttle into the enemy landing bay and assaulting the core systems while others, or yourself, were outside, blasting away at enemies, all expecting to be able to play as iconic characters ranging from Darth Vader, Luke Skywalker to Han Solo and Ig-88.
