ChargeShot is another game trying to fit in to the flood of local-multiplayer games. Unfortunately despite a fun soundtrack and visual style it lacks the depth and replayability of other local multiplayer games. All the characters play the same and can do three things: move, shoot and deflect bullets. This would be fine as most of the stars of the local-multiplayer arena games excel due to their simple, easy to grasp controls. However games like Nidhogg, Towerfall, Samurai Gunn and the like have a much greater depth in their gameplay. This game feels particularly like a watered-down version of Samurai Gunn. The game moves too slow for what it is and most of the sessions my group had devolved into a game of pong with the shields. You can only shoot horizontally, making things entirely too predictable and there are no options for an up close game.
The stages are the only thing that provide any real variety with deathtraps, changes to the way your bullets fly and other alterations. While this can be fun , it rarely matters on a majority of the stages due to the excessively simple gameplay. You never feel the need to put yourself in danger or interact with the stages quirks due to the fact that it generally provides you no advantage to do so.
Ultimately, while it is a fine base this game really lacks the extra something to set it apart from the rest of the crowd.
Some things I think would make the game more fun:
-Speed it up
-Character Unique abilities, gun types or even different speeds and weights.
-A Momentum buildup with defelcted bullets (like Lethal League)
-Be able to shoot in more directions with more wallbounces
-More layouts for each stage type (Like Towerfall or Samurai Gunn)
I'm not saying add all of these things but as it is I feel the game lacks any 'holy crap did you see that!' moments which are a big part of making it interesting. After Playing each level about twice my entire group asked if we could go back to one of the other games mentioned above. I think the fact we were bored when usually we spend our time screaming and cheering and holding our breath during close games never happened with this game is a sign something is wrong.

You start the game as a nameless man with a chainsaw. You wonder who you are and why you are in front of a house. Right about when you get your bearing you are informed that if you cut down 8 trees in a forest on the other side of town you will be paid $12,000. They don’t phone you or contact you in any way to relay this information but you just know... maybe this is all in your head? All you know is that you accepted this commitment and have only 2 hours and 30 minutes to deliver. You look around, you have no mode of transpiration and no real indication of how you got there. The only option is to walk, or in this case sprint. As you are running through town you notice that there are other houses, other cars parked but no people. You run through the entire town and haven’t seen a single person or any signs of life at all. You arrive at the forest where you will begin your job. You find a flagged tree, carefully position yourself in front of it and get to work. After what feels like forever you finish your last tree. You are informed you have finished your job and money appears in your account. Except you don’t have a bank account, it just appears as if somehow you just know you have more money now. You are informed of another job, this one for 3 trees to be cut down next to a farm on the other side of town. You decide that you will spend your money on a van to drive there, everything goes black. You wake up in the middle of town in a van with no indication on how you got there. Who did you buy the van from? Where are they now? These questions will have to wait as your job ahead at the farm has you feeling anxious. You start to drive to the farm when you notice the van says you are traveling at 80 yet you are going slower than you can run. You do not see anyone anywhere in the town, everything feels wrong. The way the van drives, the way it just kind of rotates on its axis instead of steering. You pass the farm and stop dead in your tracks. There is a cow! You jump out of your van and run over to see the only other living thing in this entire world. The cow does not move it just stands there staring at you. You position yourself in front of the cow and look into its eyes and all you see is blackness. The game is over.

It didn't take me long before deciding that this is one of my favorite games of all time.
First, the beauty of the world and the visuals. Every chapter is worth taking lots of screenshots. The setting is simply wonderful: it's vivid, original yet with a familiar, classic vibe to it that kept me curious to know more about it all the time.
The characters are great: relatable, likable and well depicted considering the short span the game covers in play time.
And I loved the plot, too. What makes the story great is that it's very personal: there is a large, epic scale, but every character you lead has a personal reason to be there, which in turn makes you invested in the plot at large. It's not the trite old "save the world" quest, and I appreciate a bittersweet ending.
The concept of leading a caravan and people, protecting them, managing food, and trying to keep morale up while wandering through a war-torn country is something I enjoyed very much. Whenever food runs scarce or morale is down, I felt very anxious for the next opportunity to find supplies. The combat does tend to become rather repetitive despite the quantity of classes (it's just that only having one, max two special powers is a bit too barebone a mechanic to grant much variety), but I felt it had just enough depth to keep me invested.
A truly great game, which I couldn't recommend more.

How this game ever received such positive reviews is utterly beyond me. I really really wanted to like this game but was doomed to disappointment. After 12 hours of gameplay I decided this game deserved no more of my time.
PROs:
- The artwork is wonderful.
- Music matches the atmophere.
- It's nice that they tried something new (a viking saga intead of traditional orcs & elves).
- The combat can be somewhat addictive if you're a person who gets addicted easily.
And thats about it. We can next move to how this game tries to destroy everything that makes a game enjoyable:
CONs:
- The actual storyline is pretty generic.
- The game is as linear as a railroad.
- Characters have no depth or personality whatsoever. Dialogue with them is limited to few sentences. You really have no reason to care about who lives and who dies.
- You're constantly lacking renown (a resource used for basically everything in the game) which makes you unable to level your characters even though they have enough kills to do so.
- You're constantly lacking renown to buy any items (which you really can't get by looting either because you only receive items rarely or after extra-prolonged battles)
- You're constantly lacking renown to buy supplies to your caravan which leads to them starving to death.
- But your caravan starving has absolutely no importance whatsoever.
- You can't make any significant decisions. The only somewhat meaningful results your decisions have is some of your characters dying but since they have no personality to begin with it doesn't really matter either way.
- Every character has basically one active and one passive skill that get a little bit stronger with leveling up. No skill tree or any actual character developement.
- 4 or 5 different types of enemies and repetitive combat.
I'd give this game 5/10. If you've got way too much time in your hands feel free to use it on Banner Saga. If you're like me and don't have the luxury of hours and hours of free time each day play something worthwhile instead.

If you're a fan of action RPGs, like me, this game is one of the best to play at the moment. It has all the elements that made the original Titan Quest series great, but now it looks a lot better, with richer animations, better combat than most ARPGs out there (only worse than Diablo 3's and pretty on par with Torchlight 2's, both pretty good ARPGs too, with their ups and downs, of course).
This game looks grim, indeed, the world is not a fairy tale full with heroes with amazing powers, everything looks depraved and decayed, our own character is a no one, strange circumstances have put us, the player, on a very difficult situation and we must prove ourselves that we can be of some worth in this world Grim Dawn has to offer, while we keep uncovering the mysteries around what has been done to us, as we saw in the introductory cinematic.
What makes this game interesting, compared to other similar titles, is that everything seems to be well crafted, with a lot of love put into every aspect of the game from the developers, it feels like a true RPG, combat can be a bit simple (similar to Path of Exile's combat here, maybe), and each character "class" or spec seems to have several variants to play around with, so if you like to experiment with different builds, this game is nice on that aspect.
The game also has mod support, I've seen some interesting mods out there already, and I'll try them in the future since, much like with Torchlight 2, I think this game will become even more awesome with a couple big mods installed, and it seems to be the case right now already.
On the negative side, I'd say the game engine could have been a bit more optimized in the sense that the game will only use one of our CPU cores at max, then not much of the rest, so it's hard to get like 144 FPS constantly and you can expect some FPS drops on intense combat situations too, because of this. With an i5 4690K and a GTX 1070 I can play at 110+ FPS reaching 144 at times (on a 144 Hz, VSYNC enabled and everything maxxed, 1080p), but I can see some frame rate drops to the 70s sometimes in heave combat scenarios, because of the CPU limitation within the engine itself, so keep this in mind; I also tested the game on a GTX 770 like 6 months ago and I could easily sustain 70+ FPS everything maxxed, so don't worry about GPU performance, because it’s the CPU the one that limits your average frame rate here.
Overall, I see this game will be still getting free upgrades and DLCs, and that’s awesome too, and I can see myself playing this game as much as I've played other ARPGs like Torchlight 2 or PoE if they keep adding content. I assume it must be even better with friends, but I haven't tried the multiplayer yet.
For the price, this game's a must for ARPG fans that like their games gritty and dark, with a good amount of exploration, freedom and even secret places and quests to find, so give it a go if you're looking for an action RPG.

With
like these, does anything else really matter? Every screen of the game, be it the VN-style dialogues, the travelling, or the fights, look absolutely gorgeous. The Banner Saga is worth buying for them alone.
On the other hand, one thing I didn't care for at all were the cheesy and over-the-top
, especially Rook's. Thankfully though, they are scarce.
The
is simple but effective, with a million different classes that beg to be explored and combined. Moreover, the fights mostly follow the story, so they don't become grindy; the moment you get used to your party, it splits, or the story focus shifts, or something else happens to add new conditions and spice up the formula. For these reasons, fighting never becomed boring.
The fights also have little to no RNG, which is nicely balanced by the
of the game being RNG-heavy. Your caravan travels across the map, encountering different events and conflicts that you are invited to resolve, but you're not expected to know which choice will lead to the most positive outcome. It boils down to guesswork—which is, like I said, compensated with the fights themselves being non-RNG-reliant.
The
is nothing to write home about. It's rather generic low fantasy, which would be fine and dandy, if not for the fact that so much of the game is just a VN retelling said story. On the upside, it's unusual in that you're playing not a brave hero, but the leader of a fleeing group of people. On the downside, the "there is a Darkness spreading" plot premise is as lame as you can find in games. Another thing to note is that while the story is self-contained, it's not even remotely satisfying, since this is only part one, so in the end you beat a boss, but learn nothing of the events unfolding.
Oddly enough, despite all the shortcomings of the story, the game is very fun to play. It's very well-paced, switching between its various types of gameplay as it goes, always throwing something different at you. The combat is challenging enough to be fun. The main character is actually charismatic for the whole low-key thing. And the visuals are incredible.

A landmark title to be sure. It still holds up in a number of ways but some aspects of it haven't aged so well.
Graphics:
Actually not that bad for a more than 12 year old game, none of it looks painfully dated to me, but of course it fades in comparison with more recent titles.
Audio design:
Voice acting is competent, I wouldn't go further than that. With the exception of G-Man who sounds like a caricature of himself in this game. The sounds of guns make them feel kinda lame (along with the fact that most of them indeed ARE lame), which is a shame (no rhyme intended). The soundtrack doesn't feel very fitting to me in a number of places but it's used quite sparingly so it's not too bad.
Story:
While it is connected to HL1 via some references and familiar characters, I wouldn't really call it a SEQUEL in terms of story, it's more like a new story in the same universe. I never saw any implication of the dystopian reality of HL2 being a result of the Black Mesa incident. The buildup to the climax is actually fairly well done, the path from being an unarmed guy running for his life to starting a rebellion and taking down the corrupt dictator is nicely executed I'd say. There are also some twists which I won't go into detail about so as to minimise spoilers.
Gameplay:
• Arguably THE biggest contribution this game brought to the genre is its physics engine, which allows for a number of puzzles (which are, however, often still hardcoded to an extent) as well as ways of using the environment to your advantage, especially after you've got the Gravity Gun. The downside to this is that in a number of places the game really, really wants to shout "LOOK WE HAVE PHYSICS" in your ear and it can get annoying when you see a door behind a pile of props for the XYZth time and think "Yeah I get it, I have to punt these with the gravity gun until I can pass, could we just skip this part?", but still, it's a nice addition and one of the things that still set this game apart from the vast majority of other FPS titles.
• Most of the weapons feel really weak because most things are bulletspongy, and I hate bulletsponges. It's probably to incentivise creative use of the gravity gun, but you don't always get suitable props to use with it. Oh and you can't carry nearly enough ammo for the weapons that ARE worth using. I mean you can't even take down one gunship with full rocket launcher ammo so you need to rely on conveniently placed infinite ammo boxes. Why not just make the rocket launcher a mounted weapon if you can only really use it where the game wants you to?
• Level design can be somewhat confusing occasionally but I always managed to find my way to the destination so it's not frustratingly convoluted. In fact it's fairly linear, it's just not always obvious where you're meant to go (and I'm not saying that's a bad thing, I hate when games hold your hand too firmly all the way through). There are also a number of "secrets" (which is a term I use loosely for things that you're likely to miss if you're only interested in getting through the level), some of which require a bit of puzzle-solving to get to. I like games that reward exploration.
• Friendly NPCs (and antlions) can be extremely annoying because they are solid objects and love to get in the way.
• The first driving portion can be frustrating as you're relentlessly getting attacked by a helicopter you can't destroy yet. This disincentivises exploration which is one of my favourite things in the game.
So yeah, while not as perfect as some people would have you believe, this game is definitely worth playing.

I unreservedly recommend this game to RTS fans everywhere. Grey Goo is a completely new RTS universe with a distinctly Command and Conquer vibe.
I consider myself a long time fan of Petroglyph games. I put possibly upwards of 100 hours into Universe at War, and was perhaps one of the only people who signed up for Games for Windows Live solely to play ranked multiplayer in the game. I was in the beta for aborted games Mytheon and End of Nations and was in fact one of the most outspoken proponents of this latter game. But the bitter taste left in my mouth by End of Nations’ demise left me jaded at best when it comes to supporting games and, sadly, especially those by Petroglyph.
GRAPHICS
I always like to start with the low hanging fruit: typically, the graphics. The game is pretty good looking for what it is, though certainly not in the way that Company of Heroes is. Units and structures in Grey Goo are detailed, but look almost intentionally modeled after plastic or pewter game pieces – Human units in particular evoke the minimalism of white plastic chessmen. In contrast, the scenery is verdant and wild, with industrialized set pieces in particular looking pretty darn nifty.
The game’s color palette, especially that of the terrain, tends to be a little muddy, with most guides out there recommending that Gamma be set to 125% to get better visualization, particularly on twilight maps where the sunsets oranges and purples serve to further muddy things up visually. Visually, my only real complaint is the look of large outcroppings of rock or catalyst veins. The jungle scenery and mechanized terrain doodads are quite well done, but large aggregations of rock or ‘hardened Goo’ textures just don’t do it for me in this game. Easily my favorite visuals in Grey Goo are the Goo factions “formless” units – that is, Mother Goos and Proteans, and the Human Core.
The Core pulses, throws out holograms, and has awesome little shimmery lines all throughout. To me, it’s one of the most visually striking command centers in a game, and feels very much like the beating heart of the Human faction. Proteans contain some neat fluid dynamics and despite their near featurelessness are pretty iconic in their own right. I do wish, however, that there was some additional distinction between Small, Large and Mother proteans. Mama Goos have a little glowing cluster crowning their blob to set themselves apart, but Large Proteans in particular seem to lack a defining characteristic.
CAMPAIGN
This article is already tediously long, but single player is very important to many RTS gamers so I feel I cannot again leave this out. I can unreservedly recommend Grey Goo to RTS gamers who are looking for a decent story. Grey Goo’s story is not a hackneyed yarn about contesting some magical resource – catalyst is just a thing. It’s important, but not Spice Melange or Tiberium important. It’s not a space opera, comic bookish yarn about prophecies or magical space crystals – it’s much more Asimov than Lucas in its presentation. It’s a story of confusion and loss, of protecting populaces and understanding foes. It’s incredibly well presented in terms of production and actually fairly challenging – I had to change the game difficulty after the 4th campaign mission. Like the rest of the game, Grey Goo’s campaign isn’t pretentious or over the top, just well crafted and remarkably solid. I say bravo here...
C&C
Grey Goo is assuredly a game in the lineage of Command and Conquer. Many of the design choices have taken nods from the classic Westwood experience – the semi-automated nature of resource harvesting, the renewable (and single) resource, the necessity of player to watch their expenditures so as to not stall out their production, the soul of this game is the soul of Command and Conquer games in many ways.
But its heart is its own. Those who are nostalgic about Command and Conquer are more likely to enjoy it than others, but the combat model is not what they’d expect from C&C games. StarCraft gamers may find the game shallow or slow, though perhaps they might find the pace refreshing and the combat interesting, as I do. Those interested in single player are likely to be satisfied with the well composed story and interesting faction variation. There’s a lot here to love, if what was left out of the game (relative to whatever you’re comparing it with) isn’t a deal-breaker for you.

This game is a ♥♥♥♥ing mess. It's a fiddly obtuse slog. It has all the worst traits of early (yes; EARLY) 90s RPGs, point-and-click adventure games, and aggressively bad high fantasy novels.  I've played through the entire game, and I still can't figure out what the ♥♥♥♥ the designers were thinking. I honestly don't even know where to start with the multitude of problems this game has while still maintaining any flow to this review, so I'm just going to jump right in.
The plot, despite blatantly copying good (if wildly problematic) material from mythologies many players may assign great significance to, is not only filled with plotholes, but in fact threaded through them multiple times. Given the length of this piece of absolute ♥♥♥♥ing trash one could be forgiven for thinking it's some sort of literary ouroboros.

The design is incoherent. I could write a goddamn encyclopedia documenting all the ♥♥♥♥ups and things wrong with it. I'll just touch on some of the broad strokes: finicky ♥♥♥♥♥♥ crafting, combat and non-combat skills coming from the same pool (essentially *requiring* that either the game be unbalanced, or you maintain throwaway characters for crafting, selling crap, and stealing). the mechanics are often unclear, many abilities are entirely useless in a given situation, or almost absurdly game breaking. as an example; there's an ability that lets you heal when standing on blood. the first five or six levels are spent fighting almost exclusively undead, and it's useless. then you fight blood cultists and it turns into effective invulnerability. the game punishes you for fighting higher level enemies like an MMO, but it so very badly wants to be a sandbox and lets you go wherever you want, with little or no guidance where you might find appropriately leveled enemies. this means the first few hours of the game are spent in impossible frustrating combats because they simply forgot to include enemies of your level and pointers to them. The amount of padding is staggering. They had so very little game, and just strung it out over the whole convoluted nonsense plot (which is more padded than the anime adaptation of a popular young adult manga). the plot and the adventuregamesque (THERE IS ONLY ONE WAY!) solutions are so ♥♥♥♥ing arbitrary that you often can't tell when you've made a sequence break, bugged the game out, and (at the very least) missed experience points.

So here I am, sitting and wondering whether this game is any good. RPGMaker is a useful tool which you can use to create interesting games, but the Steam store is flooded with cookie-cutter save-the-world RPGs. I've enjoyed many RPGMaker games, though pretty much all of them were horror games that had little do with actual fighting.
My initial misgivings, understandable as they were, were quickly dashed with clever, witty writing. This is no Shakespeare, don't get me wrong, but any game that gets me to laugh for a minute straight as a result of a well-delivered joke is fine in my book.
This isn't to say the experience is all about going from one joke to another. It's more like a mission to stop evil interspersed with enjoyable banter and serious moments, bolstered by an interesting selection of metal music.
I liked the fact that exploring the world was a reward in itself, not just a way to accrue experience points. I have to admit I've never played a game where the heroes remarked on the stuff they were finding. All too often you find strange objects in other games and no one even bats an eye. This game has spoiled me in this regard.
The battles were ok. They weren't frustrating or anything, and there was a large variety of mooks to defeat, but at the same time it all flew by really fast. Maybe I'm just too used to this. I did, however, like the in-battle dialogues, they spiced things up during the big encounters.
All in all, this game was a pleasant surprise and I've enjoyed every minute of it. I'll be keeping tabs on what the dev cooks up in the future. Perhaps a sequel? The game's lore offers a lot of options.

Warning: Indepth review
Visuals
-Gorgeous watercolor artstyle
-Charming/cute fairytale-like character designs
-Extremely beautiful and detailed environments and scenery aided by the artstyle
-High attention to detail for character/skill animations. E.g, main character fumbles around a lot while wielding/using her sword because it is practically the same size as her
Audio
-Eargasmic fully orchestrated soundtracks
-Music styles range from lighthearted disneylike bgm to intense, adrenaline pumping musical scores to sombre, lonely, melancholic pieces
-Soundtracks that play during normal monster battles are so epic that they feel more like final boss battles instead
-Much effort and detail put into sound effects for every little thing. E.g., sound of barefeet stepping on wet rock as your character moves around a dark forest, or the metal tinkering sound of the crown when it hits the floor
Story
-Straight out of a fairytale, but with a slightly dark and gloomy atmosphere replacing the usual happy, uplifting mood found in these type of stories
-Some nice plot twists and turn of events that match well with the sorrowful mood of the story, but otherwise, fairly straight forward like most fairytales
-despite the generally sombre feeling of the story, still heartwarming at times
-At its core, a coming-of-age story. People looking for something with an intricate and deep plot will be disappointed
Characters
-With the plot being reminiscent of a disney movie, likewise the characters also follow suit (talking animals/ mythological creatures)
-Charming/cute characters that compliment each other well due to their distinctive personalities and character traits
-Main character (Aurora)  is an incredibly cute and sweet, but brave little girl. (Very likeable protagonist)
Dialogue
-Everything is spoken in rhymes; adds to the cuteness/fairytaleness of the story, but may become annoying for some people as the game progresses
Gameplay
-Old school turn based combat with several added twists
-Order of turns in combat dictated by a timeline mechanic, which is further influenced by an interruption mechanic when characters are attacked during the 'casting' part of the timeline
-Timeline/interruption/cursor mechanic help add to the tension/unpredictability of fights and fosters strategic elements unique to these mechanics (e.g, knowing when it is worth using weak, but fast speed attacks to interrupt enemies VS straight brute force killing the monsters with strong but long cast time spells)
-However, at its heart, it is still turn based battle, so it will not appeal to all people despite the previously mentioned mechanics that speed up the flow of battle
Recommend to everyone but the most diehard haters of turn-based battle.

Divinity: Original Sin simply is rich. It offers a tight packed action story for those who prefer to rush head on. It offers a lot of mysteries for those who like to explore their options. And it offers a lot of things to find out in a well-designed world. Don't worry if you make a mistake in the dialog option, which are very well made, it actually adds to the story. There isn't one correct path, you make your own.
The combat is just beautiful. It's been a while (in all honest can't think of any other example) since I've seen such a large variety of combat combination options. Every skill, special weapon or companion has the potential of limitless destruction or it can spell your undoing. The terrain can be used as your allay or can be turned against you in the blink of an eye.
And did I mention the humour? The conversations you can have with NPC contain real gems in them. You can also shape the personalities of your characters; making them behave either as villains or heroes, or anything in between for that matter. Which is even more effective if you play the game in Multiplayer.
And you enter the world of Divinity: Original Sin expecting the same old thing that has been coming out in the past few years, well, be prepared for a huge dose of disappointment. The game truly deserves the title Original Sin! It will make you beg for more and anything you play after it will fell lacking of something vital. :)

of the game being RNG-heavy. Your caravan travels across the map, encountering different events and conflicts that you are invited to resolve, but you're not expected to know which choice will lead to the most positive outcome. The

Combat, while turn-based, is some of the most harrowing and nerve-inducing I've ever experienced. Cons:

I did more reading the first time through and at times sure it seemed like a lot, but I was glad I did. If I had paid a little more attention I may have done a little better my first playthrough.
I really liked the open world feel that rolls pretty smoothly into turn based combat. All the different ways to win fights is incredible. If you master the elements, use choke points, crowd control, summon elementals, and use shields effectively you can win almost any battle. Early on I found myself picking off an enemy, retreating,, and then rinse and repeat. It's a nice option if you aren't that great. Battles are winnable without retreating but sometimes you really have to be crafty to pull them out without retreating.
The ranger is an incredibly fun class. Mage was good too. Melee was about as good as melee can get. The cool part about this game is you can make hybrid characters. If you are diligent in getting as much xp as possible you can have your main skill and a secondary one at a medium to high level. I highly recommend a second playthough to try out classes you didn't get to. There was a ton of stuff I never tried in my first run.
If you don't have any patience this game isn't for you. If you have OCD this game IS for you, but you must be OCD with patience :D
My second play through I was able to grab my brother in law to co op with me. Since I knew the story and basically where to go and how to progress I'm able to keep it moving along for him. We are playing through on hard. It's actually easier to me than normal. You have to really work together and care about your buddies character as much as yourself. In our run I got even better at using the elements and my brother picked up at a decent pace so we work pretty good together. Progress is slow because he gets tired easy on the slower moving games. but he keeps coming back for more!
For the achievement guys, this game is pretty cool too. Use a guide(seriously no shame in it) because steam only lists like 10 of the 80ish achievements. In short go through it as a good guy the 1st run. Then you can be more nefarious and evil the 2nd time through. I'm just about to 100 percent on this game. It's been a good ride.
Crafting is fairly extensive, that's great! Blacksmithing makes you good money but a little lacking in depth, useful but not super interesting. Also recommend a crafting guide. The way you combine stuff isn't my favorite but it gets the job done.
Overall a full, rich, and in my opinion bug free. I only had 1 bug my whole play through and that was my character having no limbs or head after being resurrected. Just a floating torso LOL! That was pretty funny though. Hope this helps you if you are on the edge about it.

What can I say, within the first 10 seconds you know two things:
It is an RTS
It is petroglyph (westwood blood)
The RTS games from westwood where togehter with games like tribes (and tribes 2) the games I grew up with. I love these classic simple RTS games that don't try to be more than what they are and just realize how good the core mechanics of an RTS are without all the stuff added on top. Also unlike Starcraft which I would call more RTT than RTS this game doesn't ask you to monitor each unit with near perfecion to be effective. It hence truly is an RTS that is an RTS and nothing more when you look at the mechanics at the core of the game.
But there are these subtile things, the Goo ofcourse being stand out playing unlike anything else and yet they don't deviate to much from the core meaning that they are fun to play, a bit different and bringing in an other dynamic to the game. Looking at the Humans their need for a clever base design and keeping it compact while needing static defence for the base as their mobile units need to defect extractors or be on the asault most of the time. The beta are perhaps the most classic of all the ability to just clunk down a base anywhere gives them great flexibility, but at the same time makes them vuranble to multi front attacks as their static defense relies on units of which you can only have so many.
The single player campaing is nice and plays well, though some missions need some tweaking specially one of the later beta missions presses you with attacks right away without you getting a chance to even build some basic force. Sure they can be overcome, but could have been done a bit better I say. The cutscenes and stuff are world class without question the animation and art is just stunning and the humans really edge on uncanny vally almost. Such work really adds vallue to the signle player campain.
Overal I would really recomend this game to anyone who likes RTS and specially the ones of yesterday and who think like me that many RTS games from recent times are either to Large and complex or to micro and should be named RTT instead.

I enjoy strategy games that take the topdown, grid-based combat system this game uses, like Fire Emblem and Advance Wars. This game has a much stronger narrative than those two games as well, but TBS's emphasis on its storyline honestly takes away from the gameplay.
I'm not scared of permadeath for characters, but the way this game uses it ruins a lot of the gameplay. If your characters fall in battle, they just get injured. Afterwards though, you get story decisions that can instantly kill characters or remove them from your party. Making choices that have lasting repercussions, such as taking risks that endanger your soldiers is fine and dandy, but multiple times now have the units that I enjoyed using in combat been taken away from me for story purposes. The investments I put into them are suddenly worth jack because the storyline decided that they should die and I'm not allowed to use the units that I rely on so heavily.
Oh yes, it's because of my choices but TBS has you follow the story of multiple characters that have their own personalities and backgrounds that would make them choose in certain ways. And, hint hint, unless you look up a guide to every choice, your party is going to randomly die because you selected the wrong choice. Not an enjoyable experience.
Gameplay 7/10, the strategy involved is rather nuisanced and enjoyable.
Storyline 6/10, I could enjoy it if it wasn't so at odds with how the game progresses.
Overall 3/10, the two just don't pair well and I feel it shows.

If you're planning on buying this game, there are some things I would like to point out first, so hear me out.
(Scroll to the bottom if you don't want to read)
PROS
-Gameplay is great: The parkour is fun, the zombies level with you, and the day & night cycle keeps the gameplay interesting when you're out exploring the city. The crafting system is well done, and the weapons eventually wear out, so there is a resource system associated with combat (to an extent).
-Atmosphere: The voice acting is pretty good, the game changes dramatically at night, and the side quests are actually pretty fun if you enjoy competing tasks and listening to NPCs with personality. The zombies also get more interesting as you progress through the story. And last, but not least, if you have a decent PC (it doesn't have to be too good), the high quality visuals are pretty tasty.
-Free DLC: The creators gave everyone the enhanced edition, free of charge! There's even a free game mode where you can even play as a spiderman-like zombie.
-Co-op: The game is a single player rpg, however you can invite friends over into your lobby. It doesn't matter if they're ahead/behind you in the story as the game bases the story's progression off of your playthrough. In my opinion, the creators of Dying Light did this pretty well. There's even a fast travel system between players for mission scenes where one person dies/gets left behind.
CONS
-Story: Now, I really wanted to like the story. I really did, but let me tell you this now. If you haven't bought this game yet, DO NOT BUY IT FOR THE STORY! I played this game for 25 hours, switching between side quests and the main story, and when I got to the halfway point in the story, I thought it was the coolest thing ever! Then I got to the latter half of the story. That was when the writing got really bad. The main story became extremely cliche and linear, which I was okay with, however when I got to the ending, I was sorely disappointed. The ending was bad. Period. I won't spoil it, but it was not a conclusive ending at all. It felt extremely shallow and hollow and boring when compared with all the other amazing things I had done throughout the entire rest of the game.
-Finding a lobby: When playing as a NightHunter, I found it near impossible to find a game at night where a player was willing to drop everything he was doing just to have a match with me. Long story short, since the game has been out for a year, there's not that many players in the middle ground who are willing to play against me. New players are always too busy playing the game during the day, and the experienced players are nowhere to be found (probably on The Following DLC).
-Pacing Issues: The game has pacing issues. I spent 25 hours in the Slums Map before I decided to stop doing side quests and transition with the story. Unfortunately by then, I was already 2/3rds of the way through my skill trees and I already had a bunch of crafting items in my inventory. By the time I got to the second map in the game, which was the Old Town Map, or the city, I was too lazy to explore the map in its entirety since looting didn't really appeal at that point in the game. In the end, this was a personal problem for me, so I was content with it. The real problem with the game's pacing is with the story progression. IN ORDER TO BETTER ENJOY THE GAME, I RECOMMEND THAT YOU TRANSITION BETWEEN DOING SIDE QUESTS AND THE MAIN STORY. If you just play the game, rushing through the main story and not doing anything in between, the game will feel really short. You could even finish the game in two days if you played enough.
Last Mission - This deserves its own con, not because the "story/ending" is "bad", but simply because the last mission is not only narrow and uninspired, but in addition to that, you can't play it on co-op because of reasons I can't spoil.
Tl;dr
Story - 4/10
Gameplay - 10/10**
Co-op - 9/10
Worth the Price? (YES)
*Game is more fun when doing side quests in between story missions.

This feature is actually unique to BDO that makes it interesting to all kind of gamers. But the fact, how easy it is to make tons of gold than someone who actually plays the game, ruins the fun for new learners.
All in all the devs are really working hard to keep up with small updates and patches almost every week. But the frustration comes from the game itself, lack of raid/endgame, the tedious grind and insta Pay to win possibility(check the section i talk about gold above) makes it more of a chore than something you really enjoy playing for a long time.
Still dont listen to me try it out, you will have a blast for a while. Remember patience is key in this game, everything in this game takes time. Dont open your wallet too soon, think before you spend real life money!

6/10 in my opinion. A whole lot of fun can be had in this game but there are some majorly deficient things in this game.
Pros:
-Game looks gorgeous even on medium.
-Combat is pretty smooth and all classes feel great.
-Plenty of ways to make money in the game.
-Most of the jobs, particularly hunting and horse taming can be quite fun and rewarding.
-Game tends to have plenty of people on (sometimes too many)
Neutral:
-Gender locks classes, although unlike most asian MMOs, this one has male exclusive classes along with female instead of just lolli girls. *cough* Tera *cough*
-Gear progression is slightly confusing in that there is no level reqs for gear meaning you can find the defacto best equipment and put it on by level 1, so it becomes kind of a chore to figure out what gear is best for you and it becomes kind of boring when you already have the best gear by level 20. I guess that means there's less fluff for that sort of grind though.
-There is no universal banking system, instead each town has it's own stash you can put stuff in, You technically have a lot more banking space then you would in other MMOs but you will have to travel to get stuff you need which forces you to manage your♥♥♥♥♥♥quite often.
Cons:
-In addition to inventory slots there is also a weight limit to how much you can carry. While I do get that in terms of having weight on armor and potions and stuff like that, this also applies to your money. Like I said before, bank space isn't universal meaning you might have money spread out all over the place because you don't want to carry it.
-The grind is VERY real in this game, from what I heard nobody has gotten to the level cap yet as it would take literal months of killings mobs. The only way you level up is by killing mobs by the thousands which isn't a new concept for MMOs but the fact that quests don't give any combat exp at all is infuriating.
-The community is by far one of the most toxic I have ever seen in a video game, Looking at the game chat all you will see is racial slurs and homophobic statements. I'm going to assume these are mostly just trolls but it still makes me want to dig out my eyes. HIGHLY suggest turning off at least the roleplay chat as the people on that channel tend to be the worst about it.
-Voice acting and story line are horrendously done. This isn't a big surprise coming from an Asian MMO though so it's kind of meh to me.

Every so often, there's an itch that only a retro-style turn-based RPG can scratch, and Metal as ♥♥♥♥ scratches better than one of those hands-on-a-stick things that all our grandmothers have in their house.
Reminiscent of games such as Dragon Quest, Legend of Zelda, and Final Fantasy, Metal as ♥♥♥♥ puts you front and centre as Chael, the last paladin of the Metal Order, on an epic quest to stop three evil bards from summoning A'marthius into the world.
Meet up with some badass compadres to rip evil a dozen new holes, and most importantly, be METAL AS ♥♥♥♥!
------------------------------------------------------------------------
Metal as ♥♥♥♥ offers a solid 6 hours of playthrough provided you aren't smashing the skip dialogue key, and upon completing the game, you aren't left feeling cheated because frankly it's extremely wallet-friendly.  Its world is full of small details, such as funny notes and Easter eggs.  Each character you encounter has their own dialogue, much of it being absolutely hilarious.
My one criticism of the game is in that some of the dialogue feels a little forced when attempting to be dramatic, similar to an epic B movie from the 80's.  While this is a criticism, it's not actually a detracting factor and actually seems to enhance the experience.  While playing Metal as ♥♥♥♥, you might experience a feeling similar to, say, watching the original Evil Dead; there is comedy, there is drama, there is an element of horror, but most of all there is a feeling of "god dammit, this kicks♥♥♥♥♥quot;.
If you are looking for a difficult game, this isn't it (nor is it intended to be).  Metal as ♥♥♥♥ is intended, as the creator notes, to make you laugh.
On a technical note, due to the engine used to develop the game, you cannot change resolution so when you first launch the game it will come up in a small window.  To fix this, hit ALT+Enter, and you're off living the Fullscreen-Fantasy^TM.  You may also want to adjust your volume prior to starting the game, as the music is as loud as it is rockin'.
Overall, this game is a must have.  Buy it now, and thank me when you are sitting back enjoying this bad♥♥♥♥♥adventure.  Personally, I'm looking forward to seeing more from this developer in the future.

Rather than retiring to the suburbs and just doing crime once in a while, the Saints and the Boss sort of retreat into a videogame (involuntarily, admittedly) so that they never have to grow up.
You have superpowers, you're unstoppable, you've already won, and lost, completely, at the same time. Saints Row IV is a joyless, pretty, nihilistic commentary on one perspective of the state of the media-obsessed world.
Play the badass ending of Saints Row the Third and stop right there. Then go do something better with your life.

HL2 is more open than HL1. The sky and water are nice to see. But its pacing isnt as consistent as HL1.
Its very atmospheric traveling alone in the world in a lengthy driving section of the game. It sucks that you cant see Freeman's body. It feels like you're just a ghost driving a car, it ruins the immersion.
There is also a horror section at a place called Ravenholm which may be the most memorable level in HL2. There you meet a very eccentric shotgun-wielding priest.
Combat is fine but not great just like HL1. Guns dont feel great except for the shotgun and magnum. But enemies are atleast less bullet sponges.
You cant shoot while using the zoom function.
The rocket launcher only holds 3 rockets. Its main purpose is for taking down gunships, choppers and giant three-legged robotic creatures called striders. Unfortunately they tend to take more than 3 hits to put them down. But atleast the rockets can be guided with a laser. Just hope that it doesnt get shot down before hitting its target. Its an extra pain when there are multiple gunships.
For some reason the flashlight, oxygen and sprint share the same power source from your HEV suit. A terrible gameplay decision.
Notable weapon:
-the Gravity gun, allows you to pull and throw objects as dangerous projectiles.
-Bugbait, allows you control an army of Antlion (a new giant bug enemy able to dig and fly)
The game also introduced an enemy even more annoying than the headcrab: the Poison Headcrab. One hit and your HP goes down to 1 (the HEV Suit will gradually restore some of the HP lost)
The game ends on a cliffhanger, as do its 2 episodic dlcs.

VIDEO ISSUES RESOLVED: I had some trouble with huge framerate issues at first. However, after researching on the GreyGoo support page I found some things I could do to fix the problem, such as disabling SLI, etc. I tweaked my Nvidia video card 3D settings to allow the program to control the settings and tweak a couple other settings and now it's working great!! I'm running on a GeForce GTX 860m Asus Laptop and now playing on HIGH graphics/full resolution 1920 settings with no framerate or lag issues.
If you are having these problems and you have a NVIDIA card.. go to your Geforce Control Panel and manage 3D settings. Change your preferred graphics processor to High-Performance NVIDIA processor, and go to the Adjust image settings with preview... and select Let the 3D application decide. I left the Set Physx Configuration to Auto-Select. After making these changes the game worked perfect Good luck and kick some RTS butt!

My feelings about this game are a little mixed, but mostly positive.
I like the Nordic background, the cartoon-like artstyle and the storylines. The concept of two groups of heroes starting at opposite sides of the map, uniting and mixing before endgame works very well. The system of character development and equipment is simple, but immersive enough. I also appreciate the additional gameplay layer of troop management (numbers of combattants/civilians, provision, motivation - finally reaching a village where you can buy food is a meaningful event after losing soldiers to starvation on a long march!) Morally ambiguous decisions in dire situations do appeal to me.
One thing that prevents this one from being a really great game is the combat system. I appreciate the relative strategic complexity of separating armour and strength, while some other turn-based games only show a health bar, with unchanging damage and protection values. But still, I have my issues with it. Is it realistic that I can attack the body of an opponent without damaging his armour? I cannot imagine that. The distribution of heroes and enemies on the arena follows a few patterns that are repeated too often for my taste. I do not like that there is no chance involved when determining the damage your attacks do - even a weak fighter should have a lucky strike now and then (predictability kills tension). Also, I have a problem with the alternating order of action between the two fighting groups (instead of a more realistic principle of one action per character per round): For example, if one group has six fighters and the other one two, the two will act three times as often as each of their opponents. In the end, you keep weak enemies alive as long as you can just to prevent the heavy hitters from punishing your wounded soldiers. This is very unintuitive.
Such things make the combat system feel a little artificial to me, and I do not see what some critics found so brilliant about it.
More importantly, the decisions you make only have minor effects on the final outcome, the storyline has only one ending essentially, so you pay 20 EUR for a single playthrough unless you want to see the minor variations in the story that result from your choices. Do you really care wether the final boss is killed by hero 1 or hero 2? I did not.
The gameplay serves its purpose, but it falls short compared with other roleplaying games. The substance of this game is the immersive atmosphere of the storylines. My verdict: 6/10.

what i like the most is how suprisingly tactical, and competitive it cam be.  you can really "pro-out" on the game if you want, and it's a blast.
developers are highly sensitive to balance and player feedback, and have been very reactive in implementing correct changes/additions.
as of writing this review, the only "negative" to this game i can write is that it has a somewhat low population playing, so can make matchmaking a bit wonky... you often can get some mismatched skill levels playing in your match, which leads to mutual frustrations... but is something i hope turns around if it gets more popular.
game plays a lot like an old arena game, but with base-building, so is a ton of fun in many ways.  you can play the "fragger" if you want, or the more thoughtful base-builder, cunning trapper, or mad skybridge-buiding scientist.
artstyle has a lot of enduring charm too, and the characters are all well crafted, voiced, and animated.  can't wait to see what other characters they come out with in the future.
game has a free demo that allows you to play the full game, but with a limitation on character choices, so you owe it to yourself to give it a try at least.

Banner Saga is a mix of interactive story telling, a bit of micro management and turn based strategic combat.
A large portion of the game you will be following your caravan around as it tries to escape from the faceless evil named Dredge. These enemies are really unsettling in a way, but to tell you more would be a spoiler for the game. While trying to survive you're going from town to town and will experience events on a regular basis. These sometimes change depending on your previous decisions, but for the most part they are isolated and scripted cases, meaning you will pretty much always encounter the same events in every playthrough, but the decisions you make can and will change the story. You will have to watch for supplies and morale while on the road as well as your actual people. Supplies can be bought for renown, which is earned in events and battles. When your supplies run out, morale is dropping and your people are starving. Morale itself determines how strong your heroes are in battle (stat boost willpower). And if your people keep dying, well I never found out, but maybe there IS a game over? In any case, losing too many fighters to starvation will mean you will lose even more in the big battles in which your "army" has to fight. To be honest though at least on easy and normal difficulty this doesn't really matter all that much. I wish there was a greater emphasis on managing morale and your army.
The other half of the game is spent in tactical, turn based battles, in which you control up to 6 heroes. You can choose who to take into battle and who to leave behind. If one of your heroes falls, he gets injured, which may knock him out for the coming battle, but none of your guys or girls can actually "die" in combat, only through events, which is a good thing, since you can't save in Banner Saga. What happens is there to stay.
Your units have 2 main combat stats: armor and strength. If armor is a lot higher than strength, strength attacks can be deflected. Strength on the other hand represents the direct damage your units can do, so you need to strike a balance between armor and strength attacks. Usually it is best to start with a str. attack to stop the enemy from damaging you too greatly, but depending on the enemy you may need to then wittle down his armor. However, your heroes can only destroy a maximum of 3 armor (if you've skilled it) per turn. If you did not invest in armor break you're screwed in the later stages of the game. You can use another stat, will power, to increase any damage (or movement) you made. What is annoying is that you can only move your hero ONCE, even if he has movement points remaining. Especially with special attacks (each hero has a unique special and passive ability) you don't always know the exact range.
Generally speaking I would say that combat is perhaps a bit unbalanced or I'm just not very good at it. You have your basic human melee fighters who just get destroyed by big Dredge enemies, your human archers who need to get almost in melee range to shoot the enemy, opening them up to counter attacks in the next rounds, which can easily spell their doom, and the big Varl, bearded giants, who take 4 squares of space and can get in each other's way easily, but pack a real punch. The only human I found REALLY helpful on the battlefield was my main guy, Rook. Everyone else was obnoxious to use, but you just can't take 5 Varl with you, even if you have enough to fill your ranks. That just makes no sense. So you are stuck with fragile humans who can die in 1 or 2 hits to the stronger enemies. Since it's also a bit hard to tell which enemy moves when (you have to click the portrait to find out, because most look the same), this can lead to a battle quickly going south.
After winning a battle you get renown and depending on WHO killed your enemies you can level up that hero. Herein lie THREE more problems:
1. Only the heroes who actually finish an opponent off get the kill credit, so you always have to check who you want to level up and how many kills they need to do so. This can lead to you actively gimping your battles, because your stronger heroes do way more damage. They have better stats and can wear better items due to their higher level (max 5). In the worst case your weaker heroes who would need the level up wouldn't get them and since all your heroes start at level 1 this can become a problem, especially for a newer player.
2. Renown is the shared resource to buy supplies, new items AND level ups, which get progressively more expensive. This means you can severely hurt yourself by levelling up a hero only to realize 10 days later that you didn't get enough supplies, because of negative events or because the journy is far longer than anticipated. Since only 2 of my heroes reached level 5 in the end on easy I think there might be not enough renown around. I only bought a few items at the start and even had to suffer starvation in between and it was still not enough.
3. There can be points in the game in which you simply lose a hero. If that hero was high level, well ♥♥♥♥ you. Tough luck. Have fun with replacing him or her with a significantly weaker one. It is a bit irritating if you have no control over such events. Yes, of course, this is something that can happen in real life. In reality though you don't have a bunch of inexperienced losers that are only in the reserve, but only battle hardened veterans, since they are constantly fighting. This is especially annoying when the game FORCES you to use a hero, even if you told said hero you didn't want him involved! So in the last mission I was stuck with using a useless level 1 archer, who didn't survive 2 rounds and did virtually no damage...
Those are my main gripes with the game out of the way. The story is beautiful and brutal, the graphics are pleasing to look at and the sound is haunting and epic. Now that BS 2 is out the end of BS 1 is also more forgivable ;)
You should not skip this game!

Konami has come under widespread scrutiny from the gaming community in recent memory after pulling a kamikaze on Kojima's studio, laying off staff at random studios, announcing franchise-ending games, and then later shifting most of its investments and attention to pachinko slot machines. How is Yugi holding up in the lava pit of a triple A company falling from grace?
Positive Impressions
-Relive some of the incredible duels and moments from the hit animated show. Thank you for finally bringing Yugioh to Steam.
-Play through key duels of the five individual 'seasons' (classic, GX, 5D, ZEXAL and ARC-V) in a whistle-stop tour.
-Each duel can be fought from two perspectives. Firstly on the winning side, which then unlocks the option of returning in the shoes of the opponent for a second perspective.
-6,000+ cards in the base game alone, with an additional few hundred more tucked away in DLC content.
-You can choose to duel using the story deck or user created decks.
-Freedom to create, rename and delete up to 32 decks. Decks can be used in single player (no restrictions on deck composition) and multiplayer (some restricted cards such as Monster Reborn and Harpie's Feather Duster).
-Challenge mode for those wanting an increased difficulty against campaign characters.
-Plenty of battle rewards for each campaign encounter.
-You can progress through the campaign using a pure classic deck (as I did) without adopting bothersome ritual, ARC-V or other more recent cards. You may need to alter you deck to block or counter the swathes of effect cards from campaign 3 onwards, but it works.
-Steam associated achievements, badges, wallpapers and emotes for the die-hard Yugioh collectors out there.
Mixed Impressions
-Some encounters ARE missing from the campaign - such as Joey's duel with Bonz - but I later spotted some missing content hidden away in DLC packs. Konami has to pay for the maintenance of those pachinko machines one way or another, right?
-Why was the PC version delayed by more than a year after the release of its Xbox One and PS4 counterparts? Plus, they slapped 17 DLC packs (each priced at £3.99) on Steam for a total price tag of £68.
Negative Impressions
-While I experienced no issues with the multiplayer component during duels, setting up a private lobby with friends can be a fiddle.
-Multiplayer needs some sort of filter so players can choose to battle against their preferred deck compositions.
-The game feels like years old unwashed window curtains. The menu, interface and models are ugly and out-dated. Where is the glossy presentation? Why do monster models look like incomplete prototypes? Why are battle animations half-properly done and only apply to some monsters? Why is Yugioh a decade behind the likes of Pokemon, Digimon, Final Fantasy or other well established franchises?
-The story is pieced together with still images and text. You will not find memorable animated scenes from the show or voice work to narrate the dialogue.
-Battle pack feature and ranked multiplayer are both a waste of time. Neither mode is populated enough to support either mode.
-The musical score is not directly from the show and the selection is vastly limited to a handful of tracks (<10). Major duels in the Shadow Realm should sound more meaningful than the battles leading up to that one pinnacle duel.
There are infuriating aspects to Konami's PC release and the game as a whole, but I had (and will continue to have) a great time with Legacy of the Duelist. Highly recommended for all fans of the show.

Ok, I played through this game 3 times and invested over 400 hours into it so I think I can give an honest review. I really can't say I don't recommend it but I have a love hate relationship with it instead. First off, you can't beat this game without a walk-through. I don't care what other reviewers say, there are puzzles that are so counter-intuitive that you literally would have to spend an eternity trying out every possible permutation to eventually come across the correct combination so you can progress.  In addition there are so many game breaking mistakes you can make from poor character builds to killing the wrong person that the chances of doing everything right borders on impossible.  The story is boring and convoluted leaving you little reason to even care about your character.
So why did I play it 3 times? Gameplay. This game has some of the most fun game mechanics I've ever experienced. Battles are truly fun requiring some serious strategy and if you do a correct built, you can do epic damage even to the most daunting boss. I really hope someone uses this engine to create the story this game deserves. With a good writing team this easily could have rivaled Baulders Gate or Fallout.

-Story mode decks which are not immersive. For 5D's, Speed World would've been nice. YGOPro has it, so this could've probably also. Card games on motorcycles for the win.
-Booster packs giving useless extra copies. Before I started opening Yusei's booster packs, I was aiming to get Malefic Truth Dragon. Yusei's pack has about 800 unique cards in it: Truth Dragon was literally the very last unique card I got from that pack. Until that happened, it had given me over 10 Shooting Quasar Dragons, which are supposed to be "rare". RNG can screw you really hard.
Overall I'll have to give this a solid 8/10. Although the above issues annoy me greatly sometimes, the fun to be had still outweighs them so many times more. If you're a casual Yugioh player and/or you like the anime shows, this is a must buy.

Been waiting for a good MMO and this is it.
Combat is fun and grinding is rewarding. Quests are alright. Their rewards are worthwhile though. Graphics are amazing and the map is huge. Life skills are varied and addicting to level, There's lots of stuff to do. You can do things like start farms and hire workers to automatically take care of them and earn you gold, but I have not done this yet. You can sail and visit islands, which I am looking forward to figuring out. You can bread horses. Getting money really isn't that hard, and that is awesome.
If you don't like the game at first try a different class. Classes like the witch do not get good until later in the game. Awakening weapon, a second weapon you can switch off, makes combat and grinding a lot smoother.
Game encourages you to have it open all the time, so you can run it in the background or even in the system tray. I like this, I don't feel bad about having it open for various reasons like training my horse or monitoring the marketplace in the background.
The negatives: It could use a more interesting story. Costumes aren't that great. Pets collect items for you when you fight, but you need at least 2 of them or you will still have to pick things up manually. Chat is annoying but what MMO chat isn't. Enemies are varied with art and stats, but they all have the same elements and feel very similar, like each group of baddies went to college and learned the correct way to build an evil base.
Biggest negative is the anti cheat, which is black box rootkit/spyware. I did not know this before I started playing, so I guess the damage is done. The game is too much fun for me to uninstall, so they got me D:

Oh what a gift this was! This was my first Simulator game, and my oh my what a terrible experience it was.
This game is riddled with bugs, which makes me question whether it even went through any quality control what so ever. The first bug I experienced was a lack of control of where the hell my guy was moving, at first I thought my 360 controller fell off my tower again and the analogue stick was wedged forward, but sadly it was not the case. Other bugs which players may encounter are:
- Loading a save game and falling through the world.
- Just falling through the world in general randomly.
- Trees falling through the world after being cut down.
- Trees falling on vehicles and knocking them over.
- Sprinting into a vehicle can launch the player into the sky (Actually the best part of the game when I got it to work).
- Driving through trees!
- Random invisible walls when trying to skip across the terrain when the objective is just behind the hill you're trying to get over.
- Trees not falling over after cutting them, which means you need to shunt it with a vehicle for it to fall. Otherwise you can't cut down another tree...
- Random game crashes
Other than the horde of bugs, sorry I mean features, which this game has to offer it lacks a tutorial which informs you how you actually play this game e.g. how and what trees you are allowed to cut down. This was not so obvious at first, this teaches me for not playing the 2012 version eh? Anyway, there are video 'tutorials', but the videos are just soundless with text displayed at the bottom giving you of very little detail, maybe the developers couldn't record them selves talking without laughing hysterically at what they've thrown together. I'm not one for Fighting games. I never could get those complicated button combos down.
I liked Super Smash Bros. in the first two iterations, but from Brawl on it just felt like... something was missing.
And while I like the simplicity of games like Dive Kick, the limitations on the controls limit my interaction with the game itself and thus my investment.
This game is like all three rolled up into one perfect
ball.
The mind games and opponent prediction of a fighting game is all there, and
gratifying.
The controls are simple move, jump, hit, and bunt, which are
.
Each fighter has their own special move and strike ranges, some of which are easier to pick up than others, but everyone has a ridiculous skill ceiling to reach. (Don't believe me? Play a few online matches and you'll see what I mean)
And the chaos.
the chaos. Imagine Smash, but you're fighting 100 people at once, all of which with reflectable projectiles that one hit KO. There are hilarious times, frustrating times, intense times, but most of all
times.
This game is essentially Pong, where your paddle has to swing, and can move around the entire map, losing a point only when it's struck.
It doesn't sound like much, but *everything* in this game is executed perfectly.
I have roughly 5 games that I will recommend whole heartedly, because I believe they are perfect experiences.
This game has been in my library for about half a month, and it has been newly added to that list.
The sound design, just force-feeds you adrenaline. Once the ball starts reaching hundreds of miles per hour you can
the strength behind each swing with the crashing sound effects alone.
Each stage has a unique song that just gets your heart pumping. Even in the oddball case of Candyman's "Ordinary Days", you focus a lot more simply because of the music and quite simply play better.
The graphics look like something from the early 2000s.
But don't let that take away from the visual design. No it's not using 4k 2440p "oh my god I can see his nose mole" realistic graphics. It doesn't need them, and it is better for it. Each map is based around a character and provides a little more insight into their background WITH the background. And god forbid you reach ball speeds above the thousands... Let's just say, that's a trip.
(As of my writing this) There isn't much (if any) story presented to you through the multiplayer or the Challenge mode (though there
a final boss), but this game really doesn't need one.
You're playing this game to smack around your friends and strangers with thousand mile per hour dodge balls.
Really, does it matter if there is no cosmic threat you have to defeat, or evil artifact you have to obtain? Hell no. Even if there was, you'd still smash their face in with the dodge ball all the same.

Follow-up from 11-15-17:
I still love so much about this game, but there are still major flaws in the Steam release and otherwise that continue unaddressed and may never be corrected.  The achievements have been long-term broken.  When asked, their support gave a "we'll fix it when we fix it" answer.  There are guest passes sold with the packages that allow for an exclusive title and pet in the non-Steam release but are completely unavailable for Steam users.  These features are so easy to address, but continue to be ignored.  On the bright side, some of the gripes I listed previously have been addressed and I'm very thankful for that.  But at the end of the day, no matter how badly I want to recommend this game, I can't sign off on a release with broken features that are being ignored by the developer.  The instant these things are corrected, I'll flip my review to positive.
As an aside, the dye system in the game is more of the lootbox lotto ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t you see popping up everywhere, unpredictable, unbelievably expensive, and a pathetically cheap cash grab.  This is something that has been broken for so long that they can't fix it now because it will cause the players who sunk irresponsible amounts of money in to it (because they have a behavioral health issue) to band together and form a riot.  Can't be fixed, won't be fixed, so it doesn't influence my review per se, but it's worth mentioning.
Original Review:
I know I'm going to get no end of hate for this, but I'll start by saying I really like this game.  I've been a fan for a long time.  It has some deal breakers that I can't overlook.  I fully intend to change this review to positive if I see these issues addressed, but until then, the experience is a little too rough around the edges.  So know that if you♥♥♥♥♥♥on me, you're ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ on someone who likes this game and is interested in encouraging other people to play.
There are PVP arenas scattered throughout the world that are in no way labelled and provide no warning upon entry.  You run in to one of these early on and if you don't know what it is or why it's there, a swarm of creeps will follow you in and murder you.  That's all good and well IF you knew where you were and what the intended purpose was, but short of that, this is♥♥♥♥♥♥poor planning for a game that is otherwise pretty well thought out.
My other major gripe is that every server is packed with players the majority of whom are AFK clustered around a body of water auto fishing or clustered around a storage area processing materials.  This causes server load problems and also looks like♥♥♥♥♥♥  It looks like the goddamn woodstock of fishing/crafting, which sounds like an interesting concept for a game on it's own, but that's not the intended purpose of this game or at least the publisher has not intentionally billed it as such.
Lastly, this is a personal interest and so not really as significant as the two aforementioned issues, but the thing I've never enjoyed about MMOs is the first M.  I don't like people enough to want many of them around.  I've got friends who I play games with, but I'm not interested in strangers and making friends with them.  It would be nice if there was a cluster of casual player servers restricted to people who play less than 60~72 hours per week.  This would be a nice feature for people who appreciate a game like this for the experience but find servers crowded with grind-centric players to be off putting and immersion breaking.
As an aside, if The Goddamn Woodstock of Fishing is ever created, will buy no questions asked.

This game felt like a true RPG. Not running around an open world doing whatever you want RPG, but one that has a fascinating story and arc while retaining player choice. It looks great, like an older animated movie. People look good, the landscape looks better. The story is wonderful (although I do find it uses one of the greatest tropes in fantasy storytelling), and after one playthrough I feel as if there were several great plotlines I never explored because of choices I made. The lore is interesting, although many seem to have enjoyed it more than I did. Choices are rarely easy, and range from reasonably mundane to game changing in terms of importance. You quickly form a bond with many characters, and soon start really playing from the perspective of a protagonist. The bleak atmosphere is very well done, and you end up with something that feels almost like Game of Thrones: the goal of survival in a cruel world. Some things you can affect, others will happen whatever you do. People will die because of mistakes you make. Combat is interesting, and doesn't drag the gameplay down, but it won't be what you walk away remembering.
You're going to try not to cry at the end. You're going to watch the final scene all the way to it's end, and then, if you're anything like me, you're going to want to buy the next game in the series.

This game is an absolute must-buy for Yu-Gi-Oh! fans. I stopped watching after the GX series because the series felt like it was getting way out of hand (dueling on motorcycles?, over-the-top character designs), but damn the new gameplay mechanics are absolutely wonderful (synchro/XYZ/pendulum summons). This game does a wonderful job of presenting all the old and new features of the Yu-Gi-Oh! trading card game. If you were one of those people who loved playing Yu-Gi-Oh! back in the day, then this game is a no-brainer: BUY IT.
Single-player mode is a bit of a drag, but fun nonetheless. Campaign-mode is fairly simple to beat if you use your own customized deck, rather than the default deck provided for the mission. In addition, the campaigns as a whole were poorly told. I get that the game was only highlighting certain duels in each series' history (Yugioh, GX, 5D's, Zexal, Arc-V), but the story-telling could have been much better. Plus, it felt as if some series' conclusions were unfinished (particularly GX, 5Ds, and Zexal). Challenge mode is much more difficult, as the CPUs actually use advanced decks and strategies to duel you. That being said, I found it extremely rewarding to play through both single-player modes.
On to purchasing card packs. Win or lose, you are provided with battle points at the end of each duel that are used to purchase card packs. Accumulating points and obtaining rare cards in packs are both much easier than previous Yu-Gi-Oh! games (looking at you, Duel Generations for Android).
Now for my favorite aspect of the game: deck-building. Like I said before, obtaining cards is much easier than other Yu-Gi-Oh! games. I loved being able to look through my card collection, read each individual card's info, and build my own decks. The game makes it easy to organize and search for certain cards through its features (i.e. filtering, sorting).

Let's dispense with the constant flak Telltale games are frequently mired in;
Does the game possess more story branches than a tropical rainforest? No.
Does the game adapt to choices you make whilst playing? To a certain extent, yes - but the game is rather vague as to what the extent of that adaption really is.
Does it matter? Absolutely NOT.
If you are a fan of, or have enjoyed Telltale's games in the past, you know exactly what to expect here - and if you are a fan of Game of Thrones then you have absolutely no reason to not buy it. The game on it's own merits is fantastic;
Pros;
- Game of ♥♥♥♥in' Thrones
- Appearances from major characters and their actors as voice talent. (Tyrion Lannister, Margery Tyrell, Jon Snow to name but a few).
- Well written plot, spannign several characters in several locations around the world and even beyond The Wall.
- Suitably dark, decidedly malicious in some parts.
- Telltale really have managed to capture and replicate the epic feeling within the story and the world -- weaving an entirely original narrative runnig alongside the books and TV series (in terms of continuity, the game begins at the Red Wedding).
Cons;
- A (rarely) poor line of distinction between the 2 styles of graphics, backgrounds are clearly painted, however the textures on the models are also painted, on occasion the style of animation makes this *really* obvious and can sometimes be a little jarring. However, it's easily ignored.
- Some of the QTE's appeared to be unfairly twitch-centric prompting occasional retries.
- Major choices are binary in nature, yet can be automatically resolved if you are too indecisive.
- Episodic release (at the time of posting, episode 5 just released).
- Holding shift and moving your character seems to make them shuffle about 10% quicker than without hilding it, I'm not sure what the point of that is beyond just a cruel joke at people trying to run around.
This is not a "choose your own adventure" e-novel, this is interactive story telling at its finest. It does have its quirks, but honestly, what game doesn't? To it's benefit however, none of the above cons affect the games overall enjoyability.
