I've never been into role playing games too much, mostly because I preferred the medium of books to get my filling on epic stories. But I've always loved strategy games. So this latest installment by Larian (whose last published game fell into the 'never try' category for me) took me by real surprise when it added an engrossing tactical element into the usual questing, fetching and grinding.
Divinity : OS goes back to the old-school days of cRPG's and delivers everything in a well polished, graphically brilliant and  strategically satisfying package. The gameplay is the main focal point and the thing that will keep making you come back time and time again. The story is a bit on the generic side, but the humor is quite enjoyable (subjective). I say this, but there are certain moments in the game which are genuinely heart-warming or saddening. The depth of certain characters is also expressed in segments, but the overarching story is your text-book fantasy fare.
Though this can be a detrimental point for some games, the combat mechanics and sheer amount of stuff to do in this game more than makes up for the story elements. Though people are divided on turn-based games, the implementation of TBG (turn based gameplay) into the combat of D:OS makes every encounter thrilling, especially in the opening few hours. Enemies will be your level or outlevel you (until the late mid-game) or come in swarms. If you find loads of enemies who are more than a couple of levels above you, running would be your best option.
This element of discovery is missing in most modern games and therefore can be dissuading for the people who are used to missions and people of interest being clearly marked. I've used online guides plenty of time to get out a real stalemate in the game where I just didn't know if I had missed some item or some dialog. This can lead to lots frustration for certain people (especially those who don't like using guides). This is not a fault of the game or the gamer, it's just a indication of the types of games most people play.
But if you can get through the tedium and the underperforming main story, then you'll find yourself quite enjoying the mechanics of gameplay and the scenery. I would recommend this game to those who enjoy strategy games (turn based or not) and are looking to try something different. The quest system and constant searching about for solutions and items can be disorienting to many, but the solutions are mostly simple if one applies some thought.
There is co-op for the entire main campaign, but I haven't tried it out so can't comment on the pros and cons of it all. But the single-player experience is more than enough justification for the price tag.
And with the new extended edition that was announced (being free of charge for people who already own D:OS) this game should definitely be on your watch-list.

Tl;dr - A beautifully illustrated and designed story with an alternatively tedious/challenging game of squad tactics built into its core. Or -- a solid squad tactics game wrapped in a wonderous package. (6 of one, 1/2 dozen of the other)
Remiscent at times of King of Dragon Pass, Oregon Trail, Dragon's Lair and a touch of X-Com, built on what appears to be a vault of lore, about the only thing I don't like about this game is that there isn't enough of it.
Not that it's too short (it is fairly short, but it tells a good story and games need to end sometime) or that I wish there were a sequel (there is, actually, there might be another yet) but just that for as much as I love the look, the music, the universe, the tone, I wish I could get more fully immersed. Maybe that would be the game taking its time more, or needlessly complicating the battle mechanics with more tactics and gear and customization options, or if the trail part of the game treated the numbers differently than just numbers -- morale ticks away, supplies tick away, the populations tick away in rough correlation to encounters and choices, but sometimes it doesn't feel like it really /means/ anything.
That's my main quibble, and it may not even be relevant -- the game as it exists is a fine example of the game it intends to be and a welcome addition to the fledging genre. Story, art, music, mechanics -- Play this game.

I'll start by saying the mechanics are very good. The digging and building both work very well, and the shooting is fun. I don't think the shooting is anything revolutionary, but it's not bad by any means. The classes feel relatively balanced.
Adding minecraft mechanics to a shooter doesn't actually add too much. It's an interesting concept, but there really isn't much it adds in terms of strategy (and it adds very little to shooting). There needs to be so much more done to really be tactical and deep.
This game does all those things needed. While the game may only look like a shooter with minecraft mechanics, it uses those mechanics and many others to create a game all about tactics, resource management, and most of all deception.
That's a very nice summary, but explaining why the game is about those things can't be done in a paragraph. The objective in this game is to defend your team's cube while destroying the enemy cube. There are so many strategies that both sides can use.
Maybe you'll charge in and try to hit their cube with your shovel, maybe they'll have mines waiting for you. Maybe they'll dig under your base and try to disarm your traps, maybe you'll see them on your radar (which you have to set up, and can be destroyed) and dig down to them and throw some grenades in their tunnel. Maybe you'll try and sneak behind their enemy lines and set up a spawner so you can attack from a better angle, maybe they'll use radar to find and destroy it. Maybe they'll put down radars on your base to try and find your radars, and destroy yours, or you'll see them and stop them. Maybe you'll have a teammate set up some mortars and try to get close to call in a mortar strike on their defenses, maybe they'll send in a teammate to find and destroy the mortars. Maybe you'll build a bridge in the sky above their defenses, put a bomb down, and then destroy the block under it so it falls, maybe they'll dig out whatever's supporting your skybridge before that happens (blocks can't just float like in minecraft, they'll basically ragdoll if they're not attached to the ground at least through some other blocks touching it). Maybe they'll dig under your base and place bombs to completely devastate your defenses, maybe you'll disarm them, or maybe you'll turn the huge pits around your cubes into an even more effective defensive structure.
There are so many ways to attack and defend in this game, and they give you so many tools to be creative.

Firstly let me say, if you have not read or watched game of thrones but have played a telltale game like the walking dead before, go watch GoT, you will benefit for two reasons. One, you get to play this incredible game and actually understand it rather than wade in the dark not understanding anything about the world, and secondly you get to watch one of the greats in terms of TV shows nowadays. It kinda seems like i am reviewing the show almost aswell as the game here, as parts, especially past episode 3 interact with the actual story, and it is very nice to see how this story is going on in the sidelines, to see characters like daenarys, cersei, tyrion etc and how this story fits the timeline of events in the show. Furthermore something i have found is that your loyaklty is very much tested to certain characters, from the show and from the game, which can very much make you think at least 5 times beofre you make a certain action in my experience. in the first episode you visit places such as Ironrath, which is the home of house forrester, whom you will be following. You also visit King's landing and castle black. each area is beautifully recreated, feeling as if you were watching GoT. The chacters are very much GoT esque, if that makes any sense at all, you can almost instantly attibute many members of house forrester to house stark, which is something i find very interesting as house stark is a favourite of mine.
Secondly the choices in-game are as would would expect fro ma telltale game, they question your morals and integrity, making you actually fearful of consequences on the way the story will pan out, for example ( and is has been really hard trying to think of a non spolier choice) you have to pick a sentinal for house forrester, one the one hand you have a war like leader, and the other you have a much more peace seeking diplomat, each has thier pro's and each has thier con's for the situation, now let me tell you that it took me 15 minutes just to choose which one to pick! and that ladies and gentlemen is why telltale are so good at what they do, i spent 15 minutes deciding on a minor decision in hindsight but characters have throughout the episodes referenced back to my desicion in relation to the story which is something i like alot. one minor nitpick would be that the timer on conversation choices does seem a little fast, i have had to reload scenes in order to actually pick the answer to a question i wanted, instead of the one i was rushed to pick, but then again, that can be a neat little trick, making you think fast, weighing up options before you can think of a full argument to complemet your choice,and in some places it is very much appreiciated. Whilst some people have had issues with the fact that your choices do not effect the story in the way they would like, i have had no such problem your choices as i have said before are used agianst you and used for your benefit in some sections, your choices do impact on who lives, who dies and how characters view various members of house forrester. i have only played a little of the walking dead, and watched the rest, but it seems to me like telltale have done there what they have done here, in not changing the outcome of the story (i cannot speak of the whole story as it has not been released yet, only up to the end of episode 4) but some choices i have encountered seem to have a possiblity to them that they may impact on the way it ends, so to clarify, it doesnt seem to me that they will change the outcome as a whole, but the way the end happens, if it is anything like TWD, then that will be what happens.
One thing that has bugged me, is the art style, i keep trying to like it, but i cant, what im talking about is not the character designs, they are wonderful, but the backgrounds and scenery. They are done in a rough pastel kind of way, so the edges look as if they have been coloured in with a pastel crayon. To me it just looks messy and i dont know whether this is just my encounter with the game, i tried tweaking all my graphics settings and it just stayed the same, but im still unsure.
So to sum up
PRO'S
A brilliant story, interweaving with key moments from the end of season 3 to the beginning of season 4
Characters are likeable, hateable and sometimes you really do feel as if you are a forrester, wanting to do anything to survive.
choices do tear you apart with indecision at parts
Very nice character models and the voice actors are very much appriciated, and i must confess, i did let out a little girly scream, even though i am a man when i saw my personal favourite characters,margaery tyrell, tyrion and deanarys.
Con's
It is my opinon that i find the art style to bug me, constantly seeing torches for instance, that look like the have been drawn by a 5 year old. but this for many people will not be an issue and it does not take away from the game in the slightest.
So to sum up in a couple of words:
If you havent seen GoT, watch it and come back and pick up this game, you wont be disapointed at all, if you have watched it up to the end of season 4 just to be safe of spoilers, what are you doing, BUY IT!

Going in, everyone should understand that this is a challenging game. It can get frustrating when you lose over and over. However, it is definitely possible to win. The closer I got, the more addicting it became until eventually I broke through and got my first victory. I have since managed to beat it with nearly every ship, mostly on easy, though just one on normal. So, for those who say otherwise, it is absolutely possible.
The game blends decision making/administrative skills with luck. Much like anything that has a more or less procedurally generated progression (I'm thinking of the stage design of Spelunky perhaps), the game requires players to be patient and know that the odds can definitely be stacked against them. But, these moments are always learning experiences that can be used in future playthroughs (which, I should mention, for a game-winning run takes anywhere between 3.5 to 4 hours).
The added content (kind of DLC-ish but comes with the game directly) brings another layer to the gameplay adding other hurdles to figure out. This content can be turned on and off through the UI, so even if a player doesn't like the added difficulties, they don't have to deal with them, nor do they have to pay extra to get them.
All in all, the 120 or so hours I put in was well worth it to explore the galaxy and the mechanics. Players certainly don't have to put that much in to enjoy it however.

Follow-up from 11-15-17:
I still love so much about this game, but there are still major flaws in the Steam release and otherwise that continue unaddressed and may never be corrected.  The achievements have been long-term broken.  When asked, their support gave a "we'll fix it when we fix it" answer.  There are guest passes sold with the packages that allow for an exclusive title and pet in the non-Steam release but are completely unavailable for Steam users.  These features are so easy to address, but continue to be ignored.  On the bright side, some of the gripes I listed previously have been addressed and I'm very thankful for that.  But at the end of the day, no matter how badly I want to recommend this game, I can't sign off on a release with broken features that are being ignored by the developer.  The instant these things are corrected, I'll flip my review to positive.
As an aside, the dye system in the game is more of the lootbox lotto ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t you see popping up everywhere, unpredictable, unbelievably expensive, and a pathetically cheap cash grab.  This is something that has been broken for so long that they can't fix it now because it will cause the players who sunk irresponsible amounts of money in to it (because they have a behavioral health issue) to band together and form a riot.  Can't be fixed, won't be fixed, so it doesn't influence my review per se, but it's worth mentioning.
Original Review:
I know I'm going to get no end of hate for this, but I'll start by saying I really like this game.  I've been a fan for a long time.  It has some deal breakers that I can't overlook.  I fully intend to change this review to positive if I see these issues addressed, but until then, the experience is a little too rough around the edges.  So know that if you♥♥♥♥♥♥on me, you're ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ on someone who likes this game and is interested in encouraging other people to play.
There are PVP arenas scattered throughout the world that are in no way labelled and provide no warning upon entry.  You run in to one of these early on and if you don't know what it is or why it's there, a swarm of creeps will follow you in and murder you.  That's all good and well IF you knew where you were and what the intended purpose was, but short of that, this is♥♥♥♥♥♥poor planning for a game that is otherwise pretty well thought out.
My other major gripe is that every server is packed with players the majority of whom are AFK clustered around a body of water auto fishing or clustered around a storage area processing materials.  This causes server load problems and also looks like♥♥♥♥♥♥  It looks like the goddamn woodstock of fishing/crafting, which sounds like an interesting concept for a game on it's own, but that's not the intended purpose of this game or at least the publisher has not intentionally billed it as such.
Lastly, this is a personal interest and so not really as significant as the two aforementioned issues, but the thing I've never enjoyed about MMOs is the first M.  I don't like people enough to want many of them around.  I've got friends who I play games with, but I'm not interested in strangers and making friends with them.  It would be nice if there was a cluster of casual player servers restricted to people who play less than 60~72 hours per week.  This would be a nice feature for people who appreciate a game like this for the experience but find servers crowded with grind-centric players to be off putting and immersion breaking.
As an aside, if The Goddamn Woodstock of Fishing is ever created, will buy no questions asked.

Double Action: Boogaloo is a spiritual successor to one of the greatest Half-Life mods, The Specialists. As being based on the mod, it has the same type of John Woo inspired action gameplay and the awesome "slow-mo" effect. While it plays just as great as the original, Double Action has some different mechanics such as killing streaks that give you advantages with "Style" points. It's like a revamp of the former power up/frag point system. Just like the original, it comes with several beautiful and big maps that, despite their size, don't slow down the action. A downside I would have to say is I feel like there should be more characters to choose from along with more arsenal (I believe this is going to change with updates). I also hate the "Boogaloo" part of the name but hey, personal preference. Overall, Double Action: Boogaloo is a solid modification and I would highly recommend playing it.

Double Action: Boogaloo is a lighthearted shooter sure to bring about some laughs with your mates. Choose 1 of several perks, choose your weapons, then fly through the air in combat.
Attack: Left click is shoot, Middle Wheel click is melee, f is grenade if you have it equipped
Stunts: Right click makes you tackle-dive, ctrl then right click makes you slide-tackle. In most cases it is good to always be using your stunts
Shift: more accurate aim, very useful with the Vindicator rifle on the rooftop map
C: activate slow motion if you have time built up
B: Switch your weapons or ablility at any time
My Strategy: Brawler with Vindicator + H.E. Grenade or Brawler with Vindicator + Undertaker
Vindicator is a powerful rifle decent for short/mid range, but great at long distance. Use Shift to snipe a few players before propelling your body head first to the lower rooftop, guns blazing.
Grenade is good for multikills, and areas where players mosh together, not much else to say about that.
Undertaker is a fast sub machine gun for close quarters. It works will with the Vindicator in that once you empty the vindicator's clip, you can quickly switch to the Undertaker to get a quick life-saving kill before reloading your primary.
MELEE MELEE MELEE MELEE MELEE MELEE MELEE MELEE MELEE MELEE MELEE MELEE MELEE MELEE MELEE MELEE
Did I mention that you should melee as a brawler? Your melee strength is higher as a brawler, and kills, especially melee kills, build up a brawler bar. Once it is in the 80s or higher range, you can switch to your fists by pressing 1 and then left click. Your fists should be glowing. Now run around spamming left and right click, you will rack up tons of multikills on close-quarter parts of maps, like on Rooftop.

Definitely my pick for the most fun to be had in a game in several years! Lethal League is a projectile fighting game which starts off easy to learn, then quickly scales into either a chaotic mess of fun to be had with your friends or a very interesting competitive experience. With a gameplay system that's much deeper than it would seem at a glance, Lethal League provides fun to whoever is willing to give it a shot, and I'd highly recommend you fork out a few bucks for the game that keeps on giving.
It being a multiplayer game, it does suffer from the usual lack of opponents issue when you want to play against someone in less than ideal circumstances. The art of the game certainly isn't particularly striking or unique in any way, just enough so to serve its purpose. Lethal League also suffers from a lack of diverse content, but that's forgivable as what content there is has been polished to a mirror shine.
Every shortcoming listed is easily ignored in favor of a Higher Fun, and you should definitely get in on the chaos everyone's talking about!

First let me say I'm a bit bias.  Any game that takes on the Metal genre is already a great game.  But now can that great game become something I really love.  I could name a few examples where I expected this to happen but didn't.  I could also name a few that barely where even a bit better than my expectations simply cause it's claims to be a metal type game.  So in this case I'll grade this game in two ways.  One, how it compares to other games in general and two, how it compares in the Metal genre of games.
I did not go into this game with very high expectations.  As stated previously it can't be all that bad after all it's got Metal as a backdrop.  So comparing it against other games in general I'd say it met or overcame my expectations.  The only negative in general thing I have to say about the game overal is the lack of graphical settings but I soon found myself forgetting about that and enjoying the story/gameplay/music/fights/explorations just to name a few things that helped me forget.  I'll mention the others below when comparing it against Metal games.  Seriously, great, funny story telling even if you don't get the Metal references that are a plenty.  The turn based combat is simple to pick up and easy to plan your attacks.  The art work isn't perfect but it sure as hell isn't any where close to the worse I've seen.  Overal I'd leave you with this.  I have a major gaming ADD problem and using a first time out in a game I'm lucky to play an hour.  Next thing I new I was at 2 1/2 hours in this game and it was past my bedtime.
Now to compare it against other Metal games this is one of my top 2 or 3 games.  Hands down the most fun, less stressful, great metal riffs (although I wish it had a bit more to begin with), and helped me totally escape reality.  OH and I laughed so hard at this game.  Any metal head will love the metal references.  They are in your face.
Thanks Crankage Games for a fun game.  I think sometimes developers forget the fun part in gaming but you sure didn't.  I look forward to your next project and hope you keep puting out the fun.

I love Divinity: Original Sin. It isn't without flaws, but I don't rate games on their technical excellence, or their lack of bugs. To me, a five star game must absorb more time than is normally required to complete the game, it must immerse me in a world that is somehow unique and interesting, and it must provide game mechanics that are not only addictive, but intelligently implemented and interesting. Divinity: Original Sin hits on all of these notes, and when it misses, it barely misses at all.
Some might laud the game for its difficulty curve, and I won't disagree with them. The game starts out fairly difficult if you don't build the right party. It doesn't hold your hand, and it doesn't explain jack. It has a tutorial, but it only explains how the basic combat mechanics work, not how the quests are structured or how relentless and unforgiving the enemy AI can be. In a normal RPG, you expect your foes to have gimmicks and tricks to beating them. That is one of the biggest downfalls of RPGs, and even great games like Persona 4 can faulter in this area. D:OS on the other hand doesn't give a♥♥♥♥♥♥about convention. The enemies will have anything and everything you could have at your disposal at the ready. Fighting an archer? Well prepare to be hit with a variety of specialized arrows that you can receive via loot or crafting. Fighting a mage? Expect to see spells that you should have bought, but you didn't get enough gold. It always feels like you are out-classed at least a little bit, especially early on. The game even expects you to be level 3 or 4 before leaving the first town! Me and my co-op partner kept trying to leave the town to adventure, and the enemies just out-leveled us and beat us to a pulp repeatedly until we gave up and started over. Once we grasped the full mechanics of the combat, however, we suddenly were able to hold our own, even against higher level enemies.
The game has strong environmental presence in the combat. It's action point based, so you can only move a certain amount and attack until you use up your action points. The environment can help or hinder you, depending on if there are things in the way, or if there are certain simple things, such as a puddle, in the middle of the combat area. Puddles can be electrified to stun enemies (or friends) that are touching them. Poison is extremely flammable, and poison clouds and puddles can be ignited to either explode (dealing massive damage to anything nearby) or burn to set enemies aflame. Steam can be electrified to provide a storm cloud of blinding and stunning pain. Burning ground can be turned into steam via a rain storm or water arrows, or you can fire a poison cloud arrow into it to create a nasty explosion. If it's raining, you are more likely to freeze enemies or stun them, and be frozen or stunned. The interactivity between elements keeps going and going. It truly makes you consider all of your options, and for once every status effect at your disposal is useful. You can reduce enemy action points, poison them, blind them, burn them, and more. All of these effects are not optional, sometimes they are down right necessary to give you the opening you need.
Besides combat, the game is rich with story and characters. Every character has something to say, and sometimes you don't agree with them. Sometimes you need something and they don't want to give it up. You can try to persuade them, charm them, kill them, or reason with them. Trying to talk your way into (or out of) a situation often results in a disagreement that can only be resolved via a rock-paper-scissors mini-game. This feels RNG based, but it is still a fun way to resolve arguments and sometimes can get you out of a difficult fight or straight into one. You never know what to expect from anyone, and that is the beauty of the game world. The story is written in a witty way, and the dialogue is often cute and funny. It all works to where this world you are fighting to defend comes to life. It's well done, and rarely tiresome.
Overall, a modern classic. For $40, you get 70 hours of game play at least. The game is huge, and truly open world. You can try to go anywhere and the game won't stop you. You can steal quest items, you can kill important people to the plot, and you can murder an entire town, if you so choose. Larian Studios have produced the Divinity game they've always wanted to make, but couldn't due to publisher pressure, and it shows. A masterpiece of the genre, a revitalization of the ideas, and an overall must-play for any RPG fans out there. A solid five-out-of-five.

First of all I bought this game at the summer sale for 1,39€. I don't think I would buy it if I had to pay over 5€, but let's get into it.
The download took about two minutes, and I could enjoy the game right away. I picked up my Xbox 360 controller and sat down after I had a quick coffee.
I was met with the most flashing and colourful startup screen ever, and even the menus were pretty intence. This game is not for people with epilepsy, so don't even try it if you think you have it. Now the menus and settings was pretty easy to navigate, as you would expect from an arcade shooter.
The game came with a lot of music, but it clarely wasn't my taste, so you probably have to download some yourself. It can be hard if you don't have much technical knowledge though, as you have to browse your folders and find your music manually.
Anyways, I bought the Mega Bundle, so I could play m4a files from my iTunes folders. But you can actually just convert your iTunes music to the mp3 format to play them, so the DLC s pretty useless. I did miss a Soundcloud implementation though, it was pretty good in Audiosurf 2.
So I selected 'Wake Me Up' by Avicii, and gave it a go. The start was very similar to the good old Atari game, Astroids. Big astroids came flying by and became smaller pieces upon destruction, as you would expect. But after some time, the game became something pretty different.
Lots of spaceships attacked my ship and performed the old art of kamikaze. Most ships doesn't shoot projectiles, but they try to destroy my ship in many different ways. Some ships gather around me and try to squash me, some try to pull me like a vacuum cleaner and there is even a ship that will try to choak me like a king cobra. So there is obviously a big variety of enemies.
The best part was probably how the game adopted to different songs. I could play almost any song I wanted and the gameplay would still be awesome.
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Fun and addictive gameplay
Great variety of perks and powerups
Cool colours and graphic effects
Many levels, unlocks and achievements

Local and online cross-platform co op
No bugs/glitches (after my experience)
No Soundcloud implementation
Too fast to level up at the start
A little too pricey for an arcade shooter
Useless iTunes & m4a file support DLC
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Once you know your controls, all you have to do is let loose. If you ever wanted to be in a ridiculous John Woo movie, this game is for you. The controls are responsive, hit reg is solid even during lag spikes, and every weapon (including your own fists!) feel strong like they should. You can even change between third and first person
On occasion you will encounter bugs, but they aren't anything game breaking. At the very worst, someone can just kill you or you can commit suicide to get out of them. The spawn times are very short anyway.
Level design is great. Plenty of things to vault over, take cover, slide under, and flip off of on every map.
Slow-motion is a very awesome feature. Everyone gets slowed but the person who triggers it isn't slowed as much. There is the reflex perk that increases this too.
The perks are nice additions to support different play styles.
Scoring is only dependent on points, and you get these points by completing the random objectives or dealing damage/scoring kills in very stylish ways, so it's a breath of fresh air from the bog standard K/D/A.
Again, highly recommended if you're a John Woo movie fan or like games like Max Payne.

Let's ignore the rootkit issue for now. I decided that I could live with it and tried to play this.
My downvote is for this: NOT FOR PEOPLE WITHOUT SUPERCOMPUTERS, INSTANT INTERNET SPEEDS, AND MORE LUCK THAN A FIELD OF MUTANT CLOVERS!
Now, I don't have super-fast internet speeds, but I'm fast enough that I have no issues with other MMO's.
This took forever to download, but that's okay. The size I can live with for the quality.
So, I download the game, launch it, and... Error 2. What's this? I click the "more info" button, and.... their page says nothing about it. Turns out to be something about timeout between steam and them. That's annoying. Start the game, Error 2. Repeat for a couple hours, restarting steam and validating files, and trying other games. Finally get to a screen asking about if I have an account. Click the button to create.... Error 2.
I'm determined by this point to get into the game. Hopefully once I've registered and in the game, there will be no issues between steam and them, right?  I fill in my details and create the account, and I now have to enter an emailed verification code. Still getting Error 2 every time I want to advance, but I keep clicking it forever and hope something happens. Suddenly, I get something new: Error 112. Something about validation... so, maybe something went wrong. Re-sent my validation email, and... they give me the same code? what gives?. A quick google says that this error is just an issue on their end. great. Now I get constant issues between steam and them, and with them on their own. This has taken hours, and I haven't even hit the main screen yet.
Eventually, I get the game launched. I fiddle with settings, lowering and optimizing. everything seems fine. Connect to a server.... times out within a second. try again, same thing. They don't even seem to want to give it a bit of time.
The next day rolls in, and I try again. Servers seem rather empty now. I connect, have a character made, and try to log in. lost connection to server. Oh, and guess what? instead of just going back to character select, or to server select, or to the main menu... it quits your game. Really?
I do this a few times, and decide instead of clicking the connect on the bottom of my screen, I'll click the connect button on the character. Bit odd having 2, but not unusual. This time, it gives me options for things like detail, screen vibration, pathing, etc... why is this different from the connect on the bottom? Oh well. Manage to actually get into the game this time! and.... connection lost. quits the game.
I can play games of higher quality than this. online. I've played games with servers across the pond. I have never had such issue trying to connect, even a few years back when I had dial-up speeds.
This has all been a frustrating waste of time.

I play Yugioh since 2004, be it with real cards or digital games. I have played every digital Yugioh game on PC, PSP, Nintendo DS, GBA and some of the games on big consoles.
Pros:
The only good thing about this game is the story mode- especially if you know the storyline beforehand and are familiar with all the characters, you will really enjoy the story mode.
Reverse duels are also very fun, in my opinion.
During deck creation, the "related cards" section really helps out, especially for people who don't know many cards by heart.
Cons:
Game is a very, very lazy port to PC. Controls arent very good especially on deck building.
It is not overpriced, but there shouldn't be any DLC' s.
Unlocking cards should have been better, we should get some kind of compensation when we receive a card we already have 3 copies of. In other series like Tag Force, we could exchange our extra copies (3+) for some other random card.
The online gaming is terrible- extremely laggy, and a lot of leaving here and there.
Attack animation of some popular monsters get really boring after seeing the same pixellous animation over and over- we can't skip them.
Overall, the game is fun if you just play for the story, i enjoyed the gx and original series storylines, but i quit the game afterwards.
For online gaming, definitely go for YGOPRO or something like that.

1st off this game is ♥♥♥♥ing metal. I wasn't expecting much when I picked this up. I fully expected this to be just another generic rpg maker game, with just some shameless metal pandering tossed around here, and there. I was pleasently wrong about this game.
This is a rpgmaker game, and there are some stock assest used here and there, but surpisingly this game has a decent amount of orginal assests. The soundtrack deserves  a special mention as it is really great, and the dev should consider having it up as a DLC option.
Metal as ♥♥♥♥♥ has great atmosphere and many moments that will make you think "damn that was ♥♥♥♥ing metal.'
This game  isn't your standard recruit the character, do their little quest and then forget they even exist, until some plot makes them relevant again  later in the game.Each of the characters have distinct personalities, will give their take on things, and will be very talkative throughout the journey. The banter between chracters reminds me very much of the old Lunar jrpgs. Also just like Lunar most  objects are interactive  rewarding maybe finding items. some character comenting on it or even a  small amount of xp for clicking the random thing. People with OCD beware as you will be clicking up a storm trying find everything.
Plenty of metal references are littered thoughout the game, some are mainstream freindly, with others being a bit obscure that will make you smile if you recognize them.
There are a couple of  negatives though. The battle system is for the most part cookie cutter rpgmaker fare with the standard attack, magic, item etc...options. The game is fairly challenging, but the afortmentioned bare basic battle system doesn't light the world on fire in the excitement category. Metal as ♥♥♥♥ is also on the short side. If you count my idling  you can beat this game in under 5 hours.  In a way that can  be a +  as it is a very entertaining 5 hours, and  Metal as ♥♥♥♥ does not wear out its welcome like a lot of other comedy focused rpgs end up doing. Not many A-RPGs are being made these days and out of the few available, not many are worth mentioning.
I have played most big titles these past years (Diablo III, Path of Exile, Titan Quest, Torchlight I&II, Grim Dawn...) but have been able to stick to only two of them over the years: Path of Exile and Grim Dawn.
What I like about Grim Dawn:
- It's playable without an internet connection which means no lag and no disconnects.
- The campaign is pretty long
- The classes are interesting enough to provide plenty of replayability
- The gameplay mechanics are pretty solid (not as complicated as Path of Exile but still allowing plenty of customization).
- Crucible expansion that finally offers an alternative to playing the campaign over and over again.
What I dislike about Grim Dawn:
- No real incentive to play multiplayer
- The campaign is too long and the game can get boring when playing higher difficulties.
- The crucible expansion could have been so much more exciting and is getting boring quickly.
- Graphics could be a lot better given the technology we have these days and that the game is mainly offline.
In a nutshell, Grim Dawn is a dark themed game with a long campaign. The game mechanics and controls are good and the game was mostly designed for offline solo gameplay, although multiplayer is available via LAN / internet. The skills / attribute system is decent but the devotion system is what made the game more interesting. PVP is, like in all ARPGs, pretty pointless. I love traditional C-RPGs so it's hard for me to love a game that doesn't really have a rich storyline and well-developed characters but the gameplay is interesting enough to keep you addicted for a while. I've played GD for about 700-800 hours over the years and the only regret I have is that the Devs could have made the crucible DLC a lot better and the animations / spells could use some eye-candy given that the game is played mostly offline.
If you like laid back solo gameplay and don't want to get a headache, Grim dawn is probably what you're looking for. If you like number crunching, optimization and endless possibilities, then I recommend Path of Exile.

One of the greatest tech demos ever made 10/10
But seriously, this game was revolutionary on its release and I still feel like nothing else has come close to it over a decade later. For those that missed this when it first came out, Half-Life 2 is basically why we have realistic physics, facial expressions, environmental lighting, and 3D sound. They pioneered so many different technological breakthroughs and set the bar for what all video games, let alone FPS's, could be.
Not only is it the technological marvel of its time but it is also unrivaled in terms of gameplay. There is so much variety that seamlessly integrates with what you are doing in the story. It's hard to even know where to begin when talking about how great the gameplay is. One minute you're committing ant-lion genocide and the next you are commanding them to slay anything that isn't you. You could be solving a slow meticulous puzzle one second and then suddenly have to deal with a wave of man-hacks. All this variety, cohesion, and suspense make for a truly gripping experience that is impossible to put down.
If I had to have a complaint it would be that a lot of the story is a mystery until you dig deeper into the lore of Half-Life. "What are these combine things I'm killing and why do they look like humans if they are aliens???" are questions I had so I know other people have had them as well. There are logical explanations for everything but most of it is merely hinted at in the game. Some very important details about the game such as the 'Seven Hour War' are footnotes in the game that could easily be missed by an unexplorative player. Even someone like me that's played the game countless times had to look up videos explaining very basic things about the games story. This is more of a nitpick than a deal breaker but it's the one flaw I feel the game has.
Some highlights of the game are the way it feels extremely vast. Escaping from City 17 and driving miles away only to return later felt right. It felt like I took the long road and I had to work to get where I went. It felt like I had left the City and moved a long way away to the outskirts of town and when I came back to City 17 via detour it still felt just as believable. This is one of the games greatest strengths. Its sheer size is massive and yet the scale is so believable because you feel so immersed in the game. I feel like my life is in danger when I'm several hundred feet up in the air on a wobbly bridge because if I fall off I fall a very long way before going splat. I feel like I just drove many miles out of the way because I did. I wasn't magically teleported anywhere (*cough*...you know what I mean). If I ended up some place, it's because I fought tooth and nail to get where I was. This makes the game feel extremely real in ways that most games don't. Add that to the fact that there are no cutscenes that break this immersion and you have yourself a hell of an intense experience.
This game has truly stood the test of time. It still feels fresh and fun so many years later and doesn't seem nearly as dated as its (amazing) predecessor. There are few games that I can just sit down and play nonstop without loosing interest. It's very rare that a game will glue me to the edge of my chair the way HL2 does. This is why I consider it to be one of the greatest video games of all time...even if you have no clue what just happened after you beat it.

On day one release I went into multiplayer and to my surprise, no one was playing multiplayer, at all.  I went to the forums to find out the game is Region Locked and the only region that has a real population is the California, Chicago, New York City, and London.  So I could choose to trade my speedy download speed on Steam to temporarily be able to play multiplayer.  It's one of those bone head launches.  Why would anyone think launching a region locked multiplayer game was a great idea?
So after changing my region to the US I found that if I waited for 25-30 minutes I could find a game.  Not optimal, but it's there.  Unfortunately it seems that the population has basically abandoned the game already and finding a game and you'll spend more time finding a game than you will playing the game since everyone uses some form of range cheese to win.  All the units of the game are hard counters to some other unit so if you guess wrong as to what unit to build, you lose.  The scouting unit of the game is air tech meaning if you unlock the ability to scout, you will lose to an artillery rush.
So if you're buying the game, it will just be for the campaign.  Some people will say the campaign takes 15 hours.  That's hobblegosh.  If you are STRUGGLING on the campaign it will take 15 hours.  But a solid hard difficulty plathrough of the game will take no more than 9 hours total.  It is a 15-mission campaign.
There are three factions.  The Alpha are sort of like the Protoss (except the alpha are humans).  The Beta are kind of like the Terrans (except they're aliens).  And then you have the Goo which are a unique faction that will multiply in a rather unusual manner.  Add in a bit of C&C charm and you have a solid RTS game.
The game has a lot of really minor problems that are easy enough to fix, but shouldn't have been there are launch.  Pathfinding is really weird.  If you click a flying unit to a location it won't go the fastest path.  Instead it'll just to loop around the map to that location.  No unit chooses the shortest path.  It's all very weird.  AA and artillery units will always run ahead of your army.  This can be compared to something like Starcraft 2 where speed primarily decides what is in front.  But the "move at lowest speed setting" always does a weird shuffle on the units.
Also get used to hearing about your buildings be under attack... over and over and over and over.  Every single time anything hits one of your buildings instead of pinging the damage on the map (like every other RTS) it will tell you in a clear voice what's being attacked.  So if you are being attacked at five sites on different targets then you'll get overlapping voice messages that will drive you insane.  Certain campaign missions are especially terrible for this as it is a constant stream of Goo forces attacking you.
But it's a solid RTS game with no population.  The campaign is a short experience in which the story telling elements are exceptionally short.  On top of that some of the maps are poorly optimized.  Maps featuring high numbers of units will feature gameplay lag that will not be fixed from lowering your settings.
It's rather unfortunate that this game had such a poor launch otherwise it could have become the next Company of Heroes or Men of War.  But, like most scifi RTS games, the population fizzled out very quickly.

Star Wars Battlefront II is the direct sequel to its predecessor Star Wars Battlefront (and yes not the one made by EA, you know the good one) The game has a couple of significant imporvements to its predecessor and things that fans wanted over time in the orginal like: Sprinting, Playible heroes and villians, more modes other than conquest, and Space Battles, The game however did not include Bespin: Platforms a fan favorite map that was widely played on the orginal version. Star Wars Battlefont II changed the history of 3rd person and 1st person shooters with addictive gameplay and overall fan hype. People to this day still will boot up old orginal Xbox and Playstation 2's to get that nostalgic feeling of whooping the Republic on Coruscant as Darth Maul only dying one time but getting 114 kills in the process of doing so. However the PC version will always be the superior, adding mods to the game really make it come to life as you can bring back the classic orginal battlefront maps like Bespin: Platforms, Bespin: Cloud City, Kashyyyk: Docks, Kashyyyk: Islands, Geonosis: Spire, and don't forget about both of the Rhen Var Maps, Naboo: Plains and Tatooine: Dune Sea Maps. You can even get new fresh maps like Haroon Kal, The Endar Spire, Concord Dawn, and even Alderaan. There are even mods that add new eras of war like my personal favorite that adds the Knights of the Old Republic factions in the Republic and Sith Empire as well as fully textured character models and heroes and villians. one downside to the game is Multiplayer servers that were backed by Gamespy have ultimately shut down and have been down for a couple of years now, however there are other 3rd party multiplayer services that host servers such as Gameranger for example. Other than the Mutiplayer aspect of the game the rest of it is beautiful and was made to really please fans. I strongly recommend this to anyone as its an essential buy for anyone and a great game to have apart of your steam collection whoever you may be. P.S. Be sure to buy the game on May 4th - May 8th as the regular Star Wars Day deals are going on and you could most likely get the game for around $3 at almost 70 or 60% off its orginal price.

Ok this is not full review but don't bother write anymore. This is just how sad stage social interaction is in BDO.
Ok first little bit about myself. I started sandbox mmorpg gaming at young age when I got first PC (over 20 years ago) and played game named BATMUD. Ever since I have loved idea of freedom in games. Ever since I have played many other sandbox games and lastest what I have played long time is EVE online, about 6 years now. And also played Entropia Universe quite long with friends.
“Black Desert Online is a sandbox, living-world MMORPG. Experience fast-paced, action-packed combat, hunt monsters and huge bosses...” and so on straight from Steam page.
First of all what sandbox brings in mind is:
-Freedom to do whatever you want.
-You can affect other people with your decisions (For ex. You decide to be armorsmith so you craft gears to others for money and help them to advance in combat).
-Huge amount social interactions and group play.
And then MMORPG what brings in mind:
-Well mmorpg stands for massive multiplayer online role playing game…
-Even more social interactions than sandbox.
-Fantasy for that you work as group against enemies.
I could continue both lists for long time but I try to focus this time just for social aspects of both themes.
And what other sandbox mmorpg’s has:
-Marketplace / Auction House
-Chat
-Group play (in leveling and specific item farming)
-Dungeons
-Raids / World bosses
-Guilds (Working together working for node war, gvg, making ship/or anything, guild inside trading, supporting new players in guild. And whatever, you name it)
-Player to Player Trading
-Hauling / Trading
-PVP
-Crafting
… (This list could continue even longer but you get the point already)
Ok and what social interactions BDO has:
-Marketplace (where you can’t even decide prices).(?)
-And General/World/Server chat. (Don’t say RP chat… ffs this game needs moderators).
-Field bosses (?)
-Guilds (Working together working for node war, gvg, making ship).
-PVP (To some extend)
-Dueling
-½ Crafting (?)
-Hitchhiking to Pirate islands
Ok I explain ? marked first:
You can’t set prices in Marketplace.
Why that is bad for social interactions? For first of all it ruins crafting in this game (for ex. there is no point to put Boat to marketplace at all, what then ruins some social interactions from this game because you have to “craft” it by yourself and most likely never meet anyone while you’re doing that).
You can’t have marketplace “war” at all. Undercutting other players and etc.
While I understand this design and reasons behind it I still don’t like it at all. You can stop inflation and deflation but there should be better way to do that than this.
Field Bosses:
Well what I have watched streams and everything there is almost 0 interactions in this, only social element what this got is Discord IHA channel about boss spawns. After that you run to that place, attack boss and hope for loot. If no loot, go do other things before next spawns. If loot, go do other things before next spawns. As you can see in-game there is most likely 0 social interactions in this “event”. There won’t even come any importance feeling for player to kill field bosses at current stage. (Dunno have they changed but if loot is dependent of your damage done if not then next is relevant). Taking out “Holy Trinity” from MMO games are generally bad move, at least for social gaming (I don’t even get why the hell companies have decided to drop Holy Trinity). There is no importance for anyone. Everyone is as useless / useful as anyone else, everyone just thinks himself. For ex. Valkyrie sees someone is at low hp, but she won’t most likely use heal for half dead unknown player because she isn't rewarded for that (This applies also outside of field bosses. More about this in Party section).
PVP:
Well... Karma is a *****. I don’t quite get why single faction games make things like this. It punishes you for PVP and keeps everyone on leash. Not nice, also as social interactions. Again limiting something what sandboxes would never do this way. Check EVE online bounty system That alone would create new social interactions outside of PVP just changing PVP. And that would give world PVP whole new meaning (and more Ninjas).
And this is not exactly but this game needs tagging system for mobs. Karma griefing is too common.
And ½Crafting:
Why half crafting? Well most crafting is useless. And not rewarding. Only crafting “professions” what are useful are Alchemy, Cooking,Refining, Wagon / Horse accessories (If I’m missing something tell). Too many “crafting professions” are useless at current stage. Enemies drop better gear than you can craft what is totally against idea of sandbox. I would agree if bosses drop material what is required to endgame gear but not this, straight best loot from boss. -BANG “social interaction is dead”. And for RP players that is quite big hit, I don’t RP that much but I straight away decided to drop even idea to start in this game.

Group play (Leveling / Farming items):

This game has minigame named Trading, what comes first in mind is similar to EVE online trading. You haul stuff from one marketplace to another and sell higher. But no there is none social interactions in this. When I first time saw Wagons I thought “AH finally game where hauling is useful like in EVE” But then started to play and was quite disappointed.

Going in, everyone should understand that this is a challenging game. It can get frustrating when you lose over and over. However, it is definitely possible to win. The closer I got, the more addicting it became until eventually I broke through and got my first victory. I have since managed to beat it with nearly every ship, mostly on easy, though just one on normal. So, for those who say otherwise, it is absolutely possible.
The game blends decision making/administrative skills with luck. Much like anything that has a more or less procedurally generated progression (I'm thinking of the stage design of Spelunky perhaps), the game requires players to be patient and know that the odds can definitely be stacked against them. But, these moments are always learning experiences that can be used in future playthroughs (which, I should mention, for a game-winning run takes anywhere between 3.5 to 4 hours).
The added content (kind of DLC-ish but comes with the game directly) brings another layer to the gameplay adding other hurdles to figure out. This content can be turned on and off through the UI, so even if a player doesn't like the added difficulties, they don't have to deal with them, nor do they have to pay extra to get them.
All in all, the 120 or so hours I put in was well worth it to explore the galaxy and the mechanics. Players certainly don't have to put that much in to enjoy it however.

After playing a few games I discovered I really liked it so dished out the cash and bought it.  At the start of a game each team is closed off to prepare their defence of the cubes.  This involves building/destroying walls, setting traps and adding defences.  Once the "curtain" drops the game starts in earnest and you will have to defend the cube against the other team as well attack their cube.  You can do this by running in gung-ho, sneaking around the defences or tunnelling in from below. There is a variety of pre-set characters who are cartoonlike (in fact very Borderlands) but very well drawn with amusing one liners (which do start to get annoying and can give away your position). Yugioh! Legacy of the Duelist is a very fun game.
As someone who played and watched Yugioh  throughout childhood to early-mid teenage years, I can say this game was immensely nostalgic and more.
The game is an online format of the same famous card game that the whole world has heard of, but facilitates the abilities of the cards itself, removing any hassle a player may have encountered in real life or other online versions of the game. It also includes EVERY card in the TCG, whearas previous games on other devices only had a select amount.
The game includes a very lengthy campaign of historical duels that goes through the plot and iconic matches held in the TV show of ALL series and seasons (Save a few like when Jaden dueled a dude to be Alexis's fiance when he didn't even know what the word Fiance meant xd)! You have the option to either use the deck the character you are playing as had in the show, or bring your own. Once you win each iconic duel you then have the chance to try and be the OTHER person and experience the bad guy side of the match which I think was incredibly toughtful of the developers. Once campaign is beaten you can then face each character once again who is equipped with a high tier meta deck for you to try and obtain rare cards.
Other than campaign the game has an online casual and ranked match system which fufills all multiplayer desires one could have in terms of Yugioh. There is also an arena mode similar to other popular card games such as Shadowverse or Hearthstone, where you draft a deck from a series of draws to either play against a real person or computer opponent.
One major difference between this game and services such as Ygopro is that you have to play the campaign to unlock the ability to use in game currency to open packs, simulating if you went to the store and bought the individual packs for your decks in real life. You do not start out with every card in the game to instantly make a high tier meta deck for competitive yugioh. It is fairly easy to obtain points for packs though, as each victory against a computer opponent in campaign or casual reaps enough currency to open 3-4 packs of your choice, which there is a mighty collection of in order for the player to target what type of cards he wants. i.e. the Jaden Yuki pack gives lots of Elemental Heroes and fusion support while the Akiza Izinski offers a wide array of staple Plant monsters and support. Many of the rarest and powerful cards however are unable to be obtained within these packs. You must use what you have to beat the characters who are equipped with the powerful meta deck in order to obtain the cards. Each victory against any computer opponent will drop a few cards from thier deck for you.
In terms of actual game difficulty, I would say this is a rather difficult game to get started on. That is coming from someone who has been playing and watching Yugioh from the original series up past 5D's. The game would be incredibly ruthless should someone who does not have prior experience try to pick up this title. The game does a decent amount of explanation as to how new mechanics work (Synchros, XYZ, Pendulum), but does not give an indepth tutorial of the game itself. The campaign originally starts off fairly easy but quickly ramps up in difficulty. If you are trying to do every level using the historical deck, it does put you at a disavantage because in the show the characters generally won through putting faith in thier decks, which is unfortunately not very reliable for us XD. As the campaign progresses, the yugioh timeline progresses, and enemies get much stronger decks because the show demanded the enemies get stronger for Yugi and the other protagonists. This leaves the player facing the very same challenges they did. Basically you will get absolutly steamrolled. Even if you are a veteran. The campaign eventually reaches a point that you will even get rolled using a custom deck that the game built for you. Early on you could use a Synchro, XYZ, or Pendulum deck to absolutly destroy Season 1 Kaiba with because those mechanics did not exist at the time, but that changes fast. AI eventually do get high tier meta decks that instantly WRECK anything you could have possibly put together at that point, and the only way to rally counter them is with your own meta deck. Which you need to beat in order to craft so it is quite the dilemma...
In terms of multiplayer difficulty, it is not wise to play online against randoms, as many have high tier meta decks that you would be originally unable to create for a long time. TLDR; if u buy this game to say ♥♥♥♥ singleplayer and jump into multiplayer, you are gonna have a bad time.
Concerning the fact that you have to actually work to build up your deck, some may not enjoy that but I for one enjoy that aspect of the game very much. I loved reliving opening packs to try and get rare cards that I could put to use. It is extremly satisfying having worked for the cards that make up a deck that you win with.
If you have played Yugioh in the past and enjoyed it, (I don't mean only collect the cards and not play at all) this game is definetly worth the money. I loved reliving the battles fought by one of my favorite TV shows as a tyke and enjoyed heightening my previous skill within the game.

A worthy alternative to other ARPGs like Diablo 3.
A better way to explain why Grim Dawn is better than Diablo 3 would be to give an example.
I play a true pet build, where your pets do all of the attacking while you stand behind them and buff or debuff enemies.
In Diablo 3, they would never allow such a build because it would be a botter's dream to farm items.
However in Grim Dawn, they do not need to preserve "loot integrity", and so they allow all sorts of builds, including the aforementioned pet build.
There is multi-player, however the devs did not balance PvP because they want to focus on single-player experience more. Multi-player works but isn't a smooth experience.
Overall, Grim Dawn is strongly recommended for ARPG lovers.

okay, im going to break this review in a few parts just because i feel it would make it much easier to read, if you want a condensed version, scroll to the bottom and read the overall section.
1: setting:
the setting doesnt make much sense, granted ive not done every ending (yes, it has multiple endings and it seems like each one explains a little more about the setting, or at least the ones i did) but from what i can understand its time travel into the 80s to a russian pioneer camp (those stopped around the early 90s)
2:artwork:
the characters are beautifully drawn, the backgrounds are very resilient of something like Monet (bastically the artwork is beautiful and vibrant) however in some of the important scenes where the sprite and background are merged into one (theyre also called CG) the art seems lacking.
3: STORY:
the story seems to throw too many plots at the player, not answering any of them. the worst part is when something happens to a pioneer, but the story never explains why the events happened or why they dont recall. ultimately it doesnt even matter. it was still probably my favourite part of the game with its dark imagery and horror feel. the game can take a full 180 and go from upbeat to making you want to cry and feel nothing for a while (yeah, i got a little attached to a certain shy, purple haired character and had an unfortunate ending). each route will take you through the story of each character depending on who'se route you pursue (i strongly advise going at it blindly, just making decisions for yourself the first time)
4: overall:
there are a few odd things with the story and artwork, but those minor details dont really matter, because reading and playing this, you will more than likely end up attached to a certain character and it truly is an experience in itself. an added bonus, its free.  even if you dont much like dating sims, play one good route, then do the miku ending. preferably in a dark room, at night, with the windows open so you can hear all the insects.
announcing the elephant in the room:
yes, there is a nude mod, yes you can get it, yes, i have it, no it really didnt affect the story at all and by the time you get to the nude scenes, youre too emotionally involved to give a damn about some cartoon♥♥♥♥♥♥ i would not reccomend the nude patch, it was a waste.

I'd like to play the sequel soon because I have to know if the world is ending & why or why not & what the heroes can do about it & what happens to them & how. It's too bad I'm only just now finishing the first one now when Obsidian's new isometric CRPG Tyranny is coming out in like 8 days! I'm pretty picky, so I usually don't know of this many games I'm so excited about at once! "
& I don't give such high praise very often.  This has got to be one of my top 10 favorite games of all time.

Get ready! To get♥♥♥♥♥♥on! This is forced-choice (ie choose A B C D or None) railroad ride that also taps into the split-second do-or-die elements of Dragon's Lair and it's like. One of the big selling points for me was that choices you make effect the outcome of the game. I'm up to Episode 3 and I've learned that ~1 in 12 of the choices you make actually have any effect on the game, and even those are hardly noticable. Without spoiling much of anything: choosing to maim vs, kill an enemy still results in the same consequences several times. Choosing X or Y still results in the same dire consequences for your character several times. Choosing ally A or B still results in the... you get the idea.  Your choices do affect some of the dialogue, in that people will reference a choice you made, but really the game is on a rail: You're still going to be exposed to the same game experience despite many of your choices.
In the true spirit of Song of Ice and Fire(or Game of Thrones), your characters are constantly getting♥♥♥♥♥♥on. Like all the time. Terrible things happen to them again and again and again. Characters you learn to love or hate die and survive respectively.
ALL THAT being said, the game is still a lot of fun to play. I'm loving the story and much like the show or books I'm eating up the episodes and always wanting more. I love feeling immersed in the world in a way that other media can't deliver. I love the retro-style feel of hitting left or right to jump out of the way of sword-cuts and whatnot while still having decent graphics to look at. I love all the choices for dialogue that really shape your character's personality and wondering which answers will be best. That's the thing that really immerses you: you have to think like a plotting, scheming, kiniving ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ straight out of Kings Landing for many of the choices. What information should you withhold? what information should you ask for? what should you reveal? It's a real hoot. Granted all your choices pretty much mean jack♥♥♥♥♥♥ it's still a lot of fun.
Will your character get♥♥♥♥♥♥on? Yes. Will your painstaking choices mean nothing? Yes. Will there be gritty and unhappy endings? Yes. Would I recommend this game? YES. It's worth the time and money IMHO, even if you're not quite getting what TTG is claiming.

The reason i'm comparing this one to the Cyanide game is, if your budget is tight you may want to pick the one that appeals to your favorite style of gameplay.  But you clicked to here about this game and, after playing it a bit i find i am liking it more and more as the story progresses.  The movements and fighting are primitive, i play on PC so most of your play is like this, A key, D key, S key, E key for action, mouse to zero something, thats about it.  I love "Thrones" so I'm getting into the story end of things, I am very pleased they got most of the real actors to voice their characters!  But if constant action is what you want you may be disappointed.  The gaps between talk and action are not terribly long, you will have constant choices to make,but, all the action is programmed- you just have to initiate it at precisely the right time or you die. To move left, you hit A, right, hit D, If you need to push or pull something, you keep hitting "E" key repeatedly, and so on.  The artwork, and story are better then adequate, there's a lot of foreshadowing and unpredictability to it.   If you can g et used to the  "Dragon's Lair" flair to the action, you might find that you actually like this game "rather a lot".    I recommend  this game, but perhaps only for "Thrones" rfans who want good art and a good story...if you're unfamiliar with the storyline and/or not a fan of the TV show or books, there may not be a huge fun factor to offer to you.

Do you like Star Wars? Do you like giant battles? do you like utter annihilation? If you thought to yourself reading those questions with a YES! then this is a game for you! Star Wars Battlefront II is the direct sequel to its predecessor Star Wars Battlefront (and yes not the one made by EA, you know the good one) The game has a couple of significant imporvements to its predecessor and things that fans wanted over time in the orginal like: Sprinting, Playible heroes and villians, more modes other than conquest, and Space Battles, The game however did not include Bespin: Platforms a fan favorite map that was widely played on the orginal version. Star Wars Battlefont II changed the history of 3rd person and 1st person shooters with addictive gameplay and overall fan hype. People to this day still will boot up old orginal Xbox and Playstation 2's to get that nostalgic feeling of whooping the Republic on Coruscant as Darth Maul only dying one time but getting 114 kills in the process of doing so. However the PC version will always be the superior, adding mods to the game really make it come to life as you can bring back the classic orginal battlefront maps like Bespin: Platforms, Bespin: Cloud City, Kashyyyk: Docks, Kashyyyk: Islands, Geonosis: Spire, and don't forget about both of the Rhen Var Maps, Naboo: Plains and Tatooine: Dune Sea Maps. You can even get new fresh maps like Haroon Kal, The Endar Spire, Concord Dawn, and even Alderaan. There are even mods that add new eras of war like my personal favorite that adds the Knights of the Old Republic factions in the Republic and Sith Empire as well as fully textured character models and heroes and villians. one downside to the game is Multiplayer servers that were backed by Gamespy have ultimately shut down and have been down for a couple of years now, however there are other 3rd party multiplayer services that host servers such as Gameranger for example. Other than the Mutiplayer aspect of the game the rest of it is beautiful and was made to really please fans. I strongly recommend this to anyone as its an essential buy for anyone and a great game to have apart of your steam collection whoever you may be. P.S. Be sure to buy the game on May 4th - May 8th as the regular Star Wars Day deals are going on and you could most likely get the game for around $3 at almost 70 or 60% off its orginal price.

I've seen someone move around and talk just fine, after showing a moment at their first joining they're invisible to me. I see zombies dying around me, and apparently they see me and follow me. But I can't see my friend unless it's occasionaly somewhere standing in place where they're not suppose to be.

Woodcutter Simulator 2013's environment is very pastoral and eerily serene. Set in a presumably German valley, the player can hear a constant and unyielding cacophony of chirping of birds in the distance.
With regard to the presentation of violence against trees, you're limited to accepting a contract with specifically designated markers. In order to fulfill this, the player walks towards the tree, checks the radar on the bottom right, and begins to rip into that deciduous flesh. Upon felling the great beasts with the chainsaw you'll hear their moaning creaks and be treated to a third person perspective of the tree collapsing.
Unfortunately the engine does not model physics too well and you're not free to hack away at trees. The act of cutting down a tree is simply a matter of pressing a button and watching an animation. So with all of this in mind I'd say that only simulation devotees and people like myself who enjoy investigating the curios of Steam should pick up this title.

A minecraft and TF2 knockoff, but probably one of the best knockoffs I've played in a long time.
The game blends building and destruction from Minecraft with the modern weapons, graphical style, and gunplay of TF2.  Add on some strategy for the icing on the cake, and you've got Block n' Load.
The game stays true to the "No game's the same" line, as every time the teams are different, and thusly the strategies change from map to map and team to team.  One time, I played against a five-player team made entirely of Cogwheels.  Other times, the teams can be perfectly balanced and equally matched to the point of one destroying the other's cube as they watch their own cube blowing up.  We BOTH lost!
The controls and climbing can and probably will feel clunky to dedicated FPS players, as they're a bit odd.  Optimization COULD use some work, but it was made with Unity, which is not brilliant for optimization.
All in all, I would recommend for anyone who wants something a little different in the FPS department.

Funshine Bear was hurtling towards my screen with sniper precision. My 7-year old daughter is a stuffed toy-throwing expert. She *really* fell in love with the lead heroine, Aurora, and each dramatic encounter would leave her aghast as the story unfolded. In this case a plushie bear attack was warranted as Child of Light got real right there. Funshine Bear might have lost a bit of stuffing too. The game was my choice for our daddy-daughter gaming nights and we enjoyed it so much, it warranted two playthroughs.
Upon first firing up the game, what immediately hits you will be the gorgeous artwork and orchestral music.  It grabs you by the arm and just fills your senses with a massive serotonin hit. Backgrounds are exquisitely crafted with several motifs ranging from grey-blue ghostly forests to lava-filled mountain passageways in the belly of a giant colossus.  Scene by scene, level by level, you will experience lush hand-drawn imagery and meticulously crafted character art design. Each level has it's own art tone, much like a watercolor painting that conveys emotion and depth.  Also, the characters you encounter have an amazing originality and natural warmth in their faces.  You'll easily be able to recall them even months after you complete the game.  Honestly, Child of Light has some of the most beautiful art direction I have ever seen.  At no point in the game does this attention to detail falter. It is consistently gorgeous with an air of childhood fantasy accentuated by it's unforgettable theme song.
Then there is the story and dialogue, done entirely in iambic pentameter.  Which to some may be annoying, but I personally found it to be an amazing surprise.  My 7-year old followed it a bit more easily than some other games and the rhyming conveyed that fairytale vibe you'd expect.  I will say that after awhile, you do encounter some odd dialogue that either barely makes sense or doesn't seem to rhyme as well as other passages.  While it's not a major issue, sometimes I didn't quite follow what was being explained.  Doing an entire game in iambic pentameter is no easy task, so having a few odd bits here and there didn't really affect my enjoyment.
The story follows a little princess from a kingdom in Austria that either died or mysteriously ended up in a mystical land called Lemuria.  I couldn't really follow how in the world she got to Lemuria, but almost all the story takes place there except for a few cut scenes of her father.  You explore and fight, gaining skills and friends who join your party along the way.  Each character is from a chapter in the story such as wizard villagers, giant mice with superb financial skills, an acrobat circus girl and her whiney missing brother, a giant soldier dude who seriously needs a manicure, and a young fish girl who probably has the coolest attack of all by knocking her opponents backwards to gain an attack advantage.  Boss battles tend to be tentacled monstrosities or evil villains turned into aquatic-looking baddies with minions.  You attack the tentacles or minions, but it's best to get the head as much as possible and don't bother to use any potions or life saves until the last few bosses because you will seriously need them then and only then.
Gameplay consists of a really interesting blend of crafting gems for skill points, a time limited RPG attack system, and a very nice method of switching party members to change up the strategy.  It works quite well.  The fighting occurs along a time line, giving you some unique methods of attack and defending.  The gems can be used to help against evil monsters by bolstering your character powers with skill against certain elements such as fire, earth, water, or lightning.  However, if you are familiar with turn based combat, I'd suggest playing on the hardest level.  Eventually, you'll fall in a groove of picking the right set of persons to attack and the right partner to heal them regularly.  I'm not particularly good at turn based combat, but I didn't die until the last few boss battles.  Even my 7 year old girl was able to handle the majority of fights after she saw the way I beat them, and pretty much only asked for help with the bosses when she played by herself on the second playthrough.  It's a little too easy on the normal setting.  You'll have to play with the character selection a bit to figure out which one has the best attack, but other than that it's fairly straightforward.
It's quite hard for me to critique this game, it has so many positives going for it.  Could it be a little less fairytale-ish? Um, yeah.  It could, but in doing so it loses some of that charm it's shooting for.  Was the combat boring? Not at all, occasionally tedious at worst.  With all the options given to you there is a lot to play around with in attacks and strategy.  Knock an enemy back in the timeline, defend until the right moment, switch out a character at the last moment, use the little firefly to slow down the enemy attack.  I could go on and on.  Do I really want to play a game about a little girl?  At first, not really.  Then as I played on I began to enjoy it quite a bit.  Child of Light has some of the best style, art, story, music, characters, and combat for such a small title.  I think the only weak link were some of the puzzles which were all on the easy side.  There were a few side quests to do, but I only did half of them.  It was preferable to enjoy the game story and combat rather look around for quests to complete.  This game shines brightly and is well worth the time to finish to the end. I highly recommend it
