I won't be covering much what's good about the game, since it's pretty much simple. It's a finely working Yu-Gi-Oh videogame. (OH AND YEAH the AI is not that bad after all ! Prob the only thing make it stand out from YGOPRO, and having to grind each lil cards can have its charm.)
However  i find it more relevant to speak about the lil cons i've noticed in the game, nothing crazy don't ya worry .
Main con ! The ♥♥♥♥ing animations that you can't turn off,  for certain notorious card and effects such as fusion XYZ/Pendulum etc , which just leech 7 seconds of your time, it kinda disturbs the rhythm/smoothness of the duel, but that's pretty easy to correct with a patch , which they'll hopefully release. I mean c'mon just havin the option to disable that crap, isn't too much of a request.
Then you have a cringeworthy problem, that i can't even understand. Like wtf Konami, this feature was included in the Nintendo DS Games.... Basically, you have to deal with 10 seconds of garb animations, everytime you buy an 8 card booster, and that can't be SKIPPED. So now put yourself at my place, i have 70k units of the game's currency to buy boosters that are worth 400* each ;), one has to be patient ehehehehe . I just wish they could implement a system like in the previous games where you can just select an amount of card boosters you wanna get and then add to it a direct option that opens them all simultaneously. Whatevah, i think that it's good to point that♥♥♥♥♥♥out, cuz it's kind of a turn off to me, to spend literally 2 hours unboxing cards ingame...
Also the game could use some "interface smoothness" improvements overall,♥♥♥♥♥♥gotta go faster and the clicks have to be more responsive. Oh and yeah i dunno who makes their game engines whatsoever, but srsly , would be sick to have the FREAKING POSSIBILITY to browse and search cards in your collection with a proper SEARCH BAR where you can TYPE whatev, like seriously they released like idk how many games and they still never managed to implement that functionnality ... Nevertheless that's nothing to worry about, you're still gonna get dem Yugi feels playin this game.
Ultimate issue, which left me a bit skeptical is the online matchup, or the multiplayer situation in general. I just can't seem to find an opponent 90% of the time... True story, maybe it only happens to me, but yeah, i doubt the game will develop a bigger player base anytime soon, so i'm not certain whether this problem outta be solved in the future. But yeah you can already play with your friends which is already sick enough, or just get in touch with other ppl on the game's forum and eventually set some games with em. Haven't tried yet, but i'm sure that it's doable.
Despite the long rantin i shared with you, i'm having a lot of fun with the game, it's stable, and it's a pretty good time filler, i always have it open in windowed mode with some music in the background and my usual Firefox setup open. Game's pretty neat, and i can only recommend to buy it.

I very much like this game for several reasons. 1. The replayability. With all the DLCs and maps there's incredible replayability. I find the gameplay amazing as it can be a nice blend of war stategy, many scenarios are based around this, and cultural blossoming. I've tried playing other games like Hearts of Iron IV but it always feels lke I'm just slowly watching some commander conquer the world. Finally, if you like history it could be a game for you. Playing as crusaders to retake the holy land, stopping a Japanese invasion or leading a Japanese are all packed into scenarios. The only scenario that's not that great is the American civil war which is to easy, maybe that's where a beginner like you could start off. Anyway despite being over six years old this game is still a gem to be reckoned with.
P.S. Only buy the complete edition. The game is trash without all the DLCs.

One of the greatest tech demos ever made 10/10
But seriously, this game was revolutionary on its release and I still feel like nothing else has come close to it over a decade later. For those that missed this when it first came out, Half-Life 2 is basically why we have realistic physics, facial expressions, environmental lighting, and 3D sound. They pioneered so many different technological breakthroughs and set the bar for what all video games, let alone FPS's, could be.
Not only is it the technological marvel of its time but it is also unrivaled in terms of gameplay. There is so much variety that seamlessly integrates with what you are doing in the story. It's hard to even know where to begin when talking about how great the gameplay is. One minute you're committing ant-lion genocide and the next you are commanding them to slay anything that isn't you. You could be solving a slow meticulous puzzle one second and then suddenly have to deal with a wave of man-hacks. All this variety, cohesion, and suspense make for a truly gripping experience that is impossible to put down.
If I had to have a complaint it would be that a lot of the story is a mystery until you dig deeper into the lore of Half-Life. "What are these combine things I'm killing and why do they look like humans if they are aliens???" are questions I had so I know other people have had them as well. There are logical explanations for everything but most of it is merely hinted at in the game. Some very important details about the game such as the 'Seven Hour War' are footnotes in the game that could easily be missed by an unexplorative player. Even someone like me that's played the game countless times had to look up videos explaining very basic things about the games story. This is more of a nitpick than a deal breaker but it's the one flaw I feel the game has.
Some highlights of the game are the way it feels extremely vast. Escaping from City 17 and driving miles away only to return later felt right. It felt like I took the long road and I had to work to get where I went. It felt like I had left the City and moved a long way away to the outskirts of town and when I came back to City 17 via detour it still felt just as believable. This is one of the games greatest strengths. Its sheer size is massive and yet the scale is so believable because you feel so immersed in the game. I feel like my life is in danger when I'm several hundred feet up in the air on a wobbly bridge because if I fall off I fall a very long way before going splat. I feel like I just drove many miles out of the way because I did. I wasn't magically teleported anywhere (*cough*...you know what I mean). If I ended up some place, it's because I fought tooth and nail to get where I was. This makes the game feel extremely real in ways that most games don't. Add that to the fact that there are no cutscenes that break this immersion and you have yourself a hell of an intense experience.
This game has truly stood the test of time. It still feels fresh and fun so many years later and doesn't seem nearly as dated as its (amazing) predecessor. There are few games that I can just sit down and play nonstop without loosing interest. It's very rare that a game will glue me to the edge of my chair the way HL2 does. This is why I consider it to be one of the greatest video games of all time...even if you have no clue what just happened after you beat it.

First off this game is AMAZINGLY polished. You won't get any of this unfinished/beta/alpha crap. The graphics are very good. Gameplay is smooth for me even in high unit battles.
This game is a throwback to the Command & Conquer days with its own twist. People who don't enjoy the fast paced nature of Starcraft 1/2 and like to spend more time strategically planing instead clicking all over the place then this game may be up your ally.
This game is by no means easy just because it is a more laid back RTS. Several missions I struggled with on even Normal difficulty, and I like playing Starcraft 2 campaigns on Hard and above.
You don't need to fill up your refineries with worker units. They auto produce resource haulers as necessary. This makes defending what you own much more critical.
Unit production buildings can have more than one unit set on repeat so it cycles building to what you define making setting up army compositions very simple.
The Tech perks you select really define how you choose to play each game. For example. A Lancer(Humans) fires a channeling beam that does more damage the longer it fires without stoping. Sound Familiar? Well you can select an upgrade that transforms its weapon into a railgun that travels a set distance and pierces targets damaging every unit in its path. So you need to decide if you want a building killing mega beam, or a light unit shreading Rail-of-a-Good time.
The exception to many of the things I have listed is the Goo faction. They have a much diferent playstyle that involves no permanant buildings. instead you have a Mother Goo(Mobile home base of sorts) that grows in size as it absorbs resources and units. You then split the Goo up into smaller sizes and morph them smaller ones into units and such.
All in all each race feels likes its own. Some of the early units feel generic, but that changes when upgrades and more advanced units come into play.
There are a few things I would like to see implimented. When you fail a mission they should prompt you to restart without making you load back through 2 other screens and have to reskip the cutscenes(which are awsome btw). There are a few other things I had on my brain but I lost them. Nothing that really detracts from the games enjoyment for me.
I'm hoping to see expanded campaign content in the future.

Hyper Dimension Neptunia Re;birth1 is a turn-based jrpg that quickly immerses you into a Fantasy world ruled by goddesses that are fighting each other for control of Gamingindustri. The story is very funny and the characters break the fourth wall quite often mentioning the player(you) and the video game itself; while even giving references to other franchises like Pokemon.
If you do not care for side quests/objectives and only the story, then the game can be cleared in less than 10hours but if you want the true ending it will take atleast two playthroughs plus nearly all side dungeons. The regular trash mobs should never give you a problem but the bosses can kick you around a decent amount.
At some points you may have to go back and grind some to be able to take some bosses on, if you cannot afford healing items or taking too much damage. The attack animiations are pretty flushed and the cinematics for supers are well done. Most of the time the enemy AI seem to just attack whoever is closest to them and does not use their own abilities frequently enough. And constantly clearing dungeons can get repetitive as there are no puzzles to solve, objects to interact with, etc.
The game offers plenty of playable characters but you may only have 3 on the field and three on the bench at any given time. All characters can be customized by crafting/buying outfits from the stores or getting clothes in chests through dungeons.
In summary, this game can be a breath of fresh air if you've been looking for an rpg with a little twist to it. And you can have lots of fun following the story and watching the cinematic attacks. I'd recommend this game if you are also into tactical-turn based rpg games. In my opinion it is not quite worth 30 dollars though so catch it on sale.

Claiming Uplay ruins this game is like saying your significant other farted and that’s why you got a divorce (unless your issue is Uplay won't let you even start the game because if your spouse is dead, go get remarried, at your own pace of course).
Child of Light is comparable to classic RPG from the Playstation/2 era. It's a bit different in that the main character isn't a brooding or hyperactive teen who grows into a god but a child just looking for her father’s love who may actually be the weakest character in the game - although, depending on playstyles and upgrade paths, this can be argued. The Lady Aurora is a child of unknown age, but clearly very young, who falls into a coma-like/dies status at the start of the game. While in that coma dream/afterlife she travels to the World of Lemuria where she does typical video game stuff: meet people, gain battle ready comrades, have some allies become enemies and enemies become allies, defeat monsters, do stuff with the sun and the mood, grow both emotionally and physically, save a world or two. Ya know, same old, same old. While she's in Lemuria, though, her father, The Duke falls into severe depression leaving him unable to anything about the impending destruction by flood of his (land-locked) Austria. Side note, Duke is a made-up title as Austria stopped calling its rulers Dukes in either 1365 or 1804 if you consider Archduke to be different from a normal Duke. The more you know!
The combat of Child of Light is classic turn-based with a timeline allowing for speed to be an important factor in how fast you go and cast spells/skills. With speed, and a quick attack cast, you have the ability to interrupt an opponent (or get interrupted) out of an attack and send them back to the beginning-ish of the timeline. Each character has their own strengths and weakness and their own purpose in combat. Wither that be to cast a certain elemental type or just to soak of damage. Characters can be switched on the fly with only the cost of timeline resetting.
The timeline is also how the game becomes "multi-player". The second player controls a ball of light (Firefly) named Ignatius who has the ability to slow enemies. He can also heal allies and restore MP using flower pollen (which may have an official name I don't recall). Out of combat, Ignatius can light up the dark and that's all he can do. Good luck having fun, Player 2. If it's just single player, you control both characters.
New Skills are learned at level up and are used to customize each character. Do you want a character to be physical or magical? Learn a stronger single target spell or one that hits everyone? Learn a Buff or a debuff? Etc.
Combat may be turn-based but exploration is platform-esq. Unlike all other platform games, CoL has a flight mechanic that is active full time, whenever you call on it. There are no limits on when or where (besides things being in your way) so it allows for hidden and hard to reach passageways and secrets. Most of the things you're looking for are other characters (I almost missed Rubella - the first combat eligible ally) and confessions - which are diary and poems that either give backstory on the land of Lemuria or connect Lemuria to the real world somehow. There's just as much upward♥♥♥♥♥there is side-to-side.
The art style is stunning. Not just the visually but audibly as well. Visually, Child of Light is something out of a prodigy’s watercolor dream. I say prodigy because watercoloring is something most people consider childish which works because of Aurora’s age. There's a lot of duality, of sorts, in Child of Light, not sure how much is intentionally but it's there. When it comes to dialogue, it's a poet’s heaven. Everyone speaks in A-B-C-B rhyme (meaning the second and fourth sentences rhyme). It can be a bit painful at times as characters struggle to fit the scheme but this is, somewhat rare, and overall, I thought it was marvelous. I'd love to see more games use different styles of speaking rather than boring spoken prose.

Saints Row IV.  If you want a cheesey over-the-top game that involves super-powers and unrealistic guns and gameplay then this is for you.  Below I'll give my input on whether this game is worth it, or not.
The Pros:
You can literally become a superhero, you can jump up buildings, run faster than any car, set things on fire or turn them to ice, telekenetically throw tanks and helicopters around and simply cause absolute chaos in the city.
With a nice arsenal of guns you can open black holes, inflate people, disintegrate every car and person you see, lift people in the air with the abduction gun or simply run around with a rocket launcher blowing everything up for no reason.
The Cons:
It takes time to level up your superpowers and with the amount of collectibles available it can get a little frustrating trying to find 'that last one' that keeps evading you.  Along with that the marauding 'wardens' can frustrate you even more.
Although the arsenal is nice there could have been a bit more of imagination in the way of what the guns do, in my opinion they concentrated more on how the guns look (Through aesthetic customization) and not on how many guns there are or what they can cause.
Overall Rating:
A good game to hop into for an hour or so just to blow things up, but not a long-term game.
I'd give it a 6/10, a decent purchase but don't expect much out of it and in my opinion not worth it without the expansive DLC.

I LOVE walking sims, played my fair share and have loved every one of them until now.. I'll start by saying that the graphics and art style of this game are dead set brilliant. This game is a visual feast especially in the forest and farm sections.
Also it's quite well optimized, I played through on the highest graphics settings at 4k resolution on my 1060 gtx and it ran a constant 50 - 60 fps in doors and about 40 - 60 out doors so hats off to the developer for that.
The negatives however, it took me just shy of 45 minutes to play through this from start to finish on my first play and that was reading everything, exploring all surroundings and stoping to take in the scenery because by god it looks fantastic.
Now some may argue game length isn't a good indicator of how good a game is and that is true 100% agree, however in this case the story telling throughout was just not good and honestly it felt like massive chunks of the overall story were missing entirely.
For this game to hit it out of the park the following is what I would have loved to see (not these are my oppinions everyone is going to be different):
1) I believe if they invested in voice acting it would have raised the immersion of the story and world considerably (and I mean pay for AAA voice actors).
2) Utilized more cut scenes to dig further in to the overall story.
3) Added more puzzles similar to the one on the farm with the doll that also assist with narating the story.
Basically this game feels like a demo where you're playing a cut down version of the first level of a full game. Really unfortunate. Perhaps we'll see a more filled out game from these developers and with a much deeper story.

I'm an old-school XCOM fan from the 1990's original.  While this game is STILL not as AWESOME as UFO Defense,  it still has a lot of offer and is well worth the investment.
Additionally, if you have not played the original XCOM: UFO Defense, pick up a copy off steam.  Its cheap and if you can accept decades old graphics, it is the best turn-based strategy game and the progenitor of an entire genre.
Please keep in mind that I am comparing this game to the 1993 original and while that might not be fair, tough.
PROS:
Better graphics, obviously since Enemy Unknown is 20+ years newer. (still, there is a certain charm to dos based graphics...)  The cinematic cuts in the action are spectacular and really make you feel for your men when they get mowed down by hot plasma fire.
Maintains themes from original game.  There are differences to the game, I won't kid you, but alot of the main aspects of the game reflect the original.  You have a customizble base and unit loadout, scientists and engineers for research and manufacuring, and most importantly, the starting weapons are so inferior that if you don't research and upgrade quickly you are toast.
CONS:
Less control on the battlescape.  In the original, movement and actions were controlled via time units and you could move step by step and turn whenever you wanted to provided you had enough time units. As soldiers were promoted and gained combat experience their respective number of time units increased making them more veristile on the battle field.  In Enemy Unknown, each soldier can take two actions each turn.  JUST TWO.  And those actions are conditional.  For example, for most troops if you shoot as your first action, you are not allowed to move for the rest of that turn wth your other action. Also you have to plan your movement with a soldier all at once. You cannot move step-by-step.  This means that if you order your soldier to advance to cover and in the middle of that move they reveal an alien, they are still going to move to where you ordered them even if that location is not tactically sound any longer. This is silly and unrealistic.  I'm pretty sure that if I was running for cover and discovered an alien threat while on the move, I would not just blindly dash to the spot I had previously chosen and put my back to that threat.
It was the best of times, it was the blurst of times?!?

First let me give you TL;DR version of what I going to write below: Hyperdimension Neptunia Re;Birth 1 is one of the best JRPG I have ever played, I do not had that much fun in any game for a very long time. If you are not affraid of "little" grind and you like comedy and 4th wall breaking - what are you doing? Buy it already!
Ok now to the point: At the start you need to know very important thing: this is >J< RPG with all cons and pros of the genre. You need to ask yourself if you like anime, loli-character, boobs bigger than your head, tons of grind and weird enemies (say hello to walking Mario Pipe or Visual Novel screenshot). If you decide to take that challange - you just won.
Do not expect God-Know-How-Epic or twisted storyline. It is solid at best, but it`s real strenght, that makes it so enjoyable and remindable, lies behind 4th wall. Amount of gags, references and breaks of your screen is so high that you just ignoring lack of twists or deep plot. It is all about dialogues, and they are simple yet perfect. I can guarantee - you will laugh a LOT. Not many games these days are made like that...
You will meet a lot of remindable personalities, which is surprising for me, because I do not expect anything special from side-characters. All of them has something unique and I actually do not find a single one that was boring. In addition they all voice-acted. Voice acting... this is the biggest problem with this game... sadly. Game itself has dual-audio option that allows you to change language even in the middle of battle or cutscene, which is nice. Unfortunately only JP version looks fully-voiced, ENG has only most important story-releated scenes voiced. If this is a very bad thing - you need to answer for yourself, for me it definitly is. This is one of the few japanese-styled games when I actually prefer dub over original version, because it is done very well.
But how`s gameplay itself? As I said at the beginning: it is Grindy JRPG, so expect... well - grind. But do not run away, it is not that boring as grind in many f2p korean MMORPG! Why is that you may ask - it is because there is TONS of crafting materials to grind and you will make a TONS of different things from them. That makes grind less forced and you may actually want to do it by yourself just to get that materials to craft cute bikini for your loli-character... you perv.
Battles are turn-based, somehow they reminds me of Final Fantasy (old ones), they are just more enjoyable. You can customize your own attacks, which are really nice-looking, especially on PC (original version is from consoles) where everything runs smoothly. High variety of characters allows you to make you own dream-team and (what is surprising!) there is no useless ones. Overall gameplay may be repetitive, but there is many customisable options that negates that problem (not entirely, but it is better than do not have alternatives at all). That is important, because that game is really long (I finished 1st playthrough in ~30 hours, with a quite high amount of grind).
Well, at the end I can only tell something pure technical. Game runs smoothly even on old notebooks, but even if you have problems with freemate you need to remember that this is mostly turn-based game, so that shouldn`t affect your overall fun. Audio is solid. Music is perfect, I cannot say anything else. OST is amazing, even tho (or maybe because of?) most tracks are "taken" from original Neptunia 1/mk2/Victory.
What is my overall verdict? It is not a prefect game, duh it is far from perfect... but it changes nothing. What makes a good game a good game is gameplay and ability to keep you in front of monitor for a long time despite of its weaknesses. Hyperdimension Neptunia doing it in perfect way: by making fun of itself. For it`s very low price it is one of the best, if not even the best game of JRPG genre avaiable on Steam and PC overall.

This might be the best value for any game I've ever purchased. I got it on sale for 15$, but after putting 200+ hours into it, I can say it is easily worth double or triple that. The only ARPG's I've played that can compare to Grim Dawn are D2, D3 and PoE. I'm not trying to debate which is better, but those 3 are universally recognized as 3 of the top ARPG's in the last 10 years. The only knock against grim dawn is that the multiplayer is a bit weak. This is a game meant to be played in single player, but has some multiplayer capabilities. It's not horrible multiplayer, but I wouldn't describe it as a MP game.
There is what they call a dual class system. You have a skill tree for your main class and then at level 10 you can invest into a second class or put everything into 1 tree, whichever you prefer. There are multiple viable builds and tons of loot. Another negative could be that there is too much garbage loot, but still this is knit picking. For those ARPG veterans the game can feel easy until you have beat it once at which point it gets a bit harder. The objective is to beat it 3 times all the way thru, the 3rd time is pretty damn tough.
It doesn't feel boring going thru it 3 times because various things carry over each time, you will also spot new areas you missed or couldn't unlock the first time thru. The DLC out is also really fun. It's basically a never ending mode of constant waves. Every 10 waves you can either leave and take your reward or keep going and risk it for a higher reward.
If you even remotely like Action-RPGs then this is a must have title. If this game came from a well known company it would easily be selling for 2-3 times more. I know it might not look that great in the photos and all. That's what held me back for a while, but this is definitely one of the better games I've ever played.

Block N Load offers a nice variety of classes with more being constantly added, this allows for pretty much non-stop fun. Once you've learnt a class you begin to feel like a master with them, knowing how and when to use your guns/abilities. Each class has their own blocks and special block to use, these give them an edge in battle whether it be defensive, offensive or supportive.
Each class (some more than others) takes time to master, I really enjoy this side of gameplay due to it's rewarding nature of bonuses at level ups and new skins (as well as being able to destroy your opponents).
There is a happy pool of maps to play on and you are given a choice between 2 when you join a lobby. Each map is unique and takes time to learn. As said for the classes, new maps are also being added.
A slight negative is the regional servers; with the EU server I have been experiencing lag and not even being able to get into games, because of this I've had to play on NA servers despite the high ping.
Overall it is very smooth, the movement is simple and enjoyable because of the rate at which you scale the maps, when learning this can be annoying at times (sprinting and jumping at someone and then flying over the edge of the map) but you'll soon pick it up. The gun play is great, each unique with different ranges and block damage.
This leads me onto the building/destroying side of things; the fact I would enjoy this game if the maps weren't interactable has to say something (a good something) about the gameplay, but being able to do this adds an unimaginable amount of creativity.
To conclude; Block N Load has been a breath of fresh air for me in the FPS genre, it's large range of potential for future competitive play and continous updates makes me really want to stick around and see how everything turns out.
My final opinion on whether you should buy this game is: Yes, and if you used to play Minecraft and TF2: Hell yeah.

A solid shooter, not exactly dependent on music. Music intensity affects the spawn of enemies and your firing rate, slowing to a crawl in silent parts. It's nice to play with your music, but this isn't Audiosurf-style interaction. I know the meme is to play with high visual intensity and abuse yourself, but just turn the visuals down to 50%. I wish there was a lower setting than that, as the visuals just cloud everything. No one cares what setting you use.
New weapons make tracks more interesting, but the progression system makes the game hardest at the start. I wish there was a difficulty option between Hardcore and Insane, as there is a fair amount of time where you don't have the ship upgrades to reasonably beat long Insane songs, but Hardcore becomes too simple. The Shadow DLC is compelling, adding new ship options and support for auto-fire ships to further increase the variety. However, the DLC does not change the musical interaction, so the gameplay is identical.
It's easy to pick up and play, and pretty enjoyable. There's good replayability in theory, but I don't think the shooting is varied enough to come back to it regularly after finishing off all the challenges. Audiosurf has more gameplay options to keep things fresh, but this is still an enjoyable shooter with all the DLC. I'd say $10 USD for the full package would be a great deal, so 30% off everything is pretty fair when that happens.

Back in 2004 Valve released the sequel to their critically acclaimed Half-Life series. It attracted universal praise and paved the way for future FPS titles. Now over 10 years after its release, does it still stand the test of time?
With regards to gameplay, HL2 has an intuitive control system that is easy to master and feels right at home with any modern day shooters. The level design has excellent variation and creativity, whether you are speeding through canals on an airboat or overrunning Nova Prospekt with a swarm of Antlions, each chapter has its own unique feel. The pacing is also well balanced, with high intensity action scenes often followed by slower paced puzzle areas. This helps to prevent repetition and keeps gameplay feeling fresh.
There is a decent enemy selection, ranging from Combine military units to zombie hordes; however the AI does feel a little dated by today’s standards. At best the enemy behaviour is quite predictable, and at worst often exploitable. Squad AI also deserves a dishonourable mention as it is incredibly annoying when friendly squad members continuously block tight corridors or refuse to jump down from higher levels.
The weapon arsenal is a fairly standard layout comparable to what you would find in most shooters, however the ground breaking exception to this is the gravity gun. HL2 was revolutionary in its use of physics and even years later the design concept of this weapon still manages to feel innovative to me. Although you can largely go through the game without making much use of it, there are a couple of fun achievements that force you to rely on using gravity gun based attacks and techniques.
The puzzle sections are relatively easy, usually focusing on showing off the physics engine by manipulating environmental objects, but they are passable and serve as a nice diversion to the obligatory action scenes.
Graphically, Valve’s pioneering Source Engine has of course started to show its age but it still manages to do a competent job. The fact that it was designed as a modular engine means that Valve has been able to apply upgrades relatively easily, providing vast improvements in graphical quality as the series progressed. The character models still look decent enough, and the facial expressions / lip sync movements of the main characters (Alyx in particular) are fairly impressive for their time.
The environments and lighting are also still solid. The transitional sunset sequence in the Water Hazard chapter stands out in my mind. Occasionally some of the background images look very flat, but this can be forgiven considering they are never the primary focus of attention. Visceral sound effects and small details like dropped shell casings and blood splatters help to elevate the experience. The soundtrack itself is a mixture of short electronic tracks and ambient sounds which I personally feel is a bit lacking and out of place at times.
Like its predecessor, Half-life 2 uses fluid, in game story telling that does not remove the player from game play. The story itself is fairly light and the game relies more on environmental narration and atmosphere. This subtle style does work quite well, but it can result in some sections of the game feeling like you are simply travelling from point A to point B and it is fairly inconsequential why you are doing so. What the game does do incredibly well is creating the atmosphere and tone of the environment that the game is set in. Within the first hour of gameplay I can feel invested in the oppressive, dystopian society of City 17. The main characters are also memorable which is helped by some decent voice acting.
Overall, even when assessed by today’s standards, HL2 still manages to provide a fluid and satisfying experience. There are some highly innovative gameplay elements which have been integrated into a classic FPS framework. It is an incredibly well polished presentation with very few glitches or significant criticisms. It should be an essential part of anyone’s Steam Library and it genuinely does stand the test of time. So, if you have not played HL2 in a while (or ever), then what are you waiting for? Wake up, Mr Freeman. Wake up and smell the ashes.

It begins really nicely with an extremely well-done and impressive intro cinematic, and in fact "cinematic" really describes the single-player campaign as a whole. A huge effort has been made here to create a compelling story, with every mission ending with a cut-scene and some of them beginning with one as well. Voice acting during said cutscenes is excellent, and unit voice acting is also pretty decent - you don't hear the same lines every two seconds when giving orders, so that's nice -. On the topic of voices, they actually hired someone to invent a new language for the Beta aliens, and they use it! I can appreciate a company going the extra mile for this kind of thing, even if said aliens switch to English when you're playing them. I'd honestly have liked it more if their whole campaign was subtitled instead, but that's my personal opinion. Soundtrack is also pretty nice and varied.
Now, I have two main issues with the single-player campaign. The first one is that it's pretty short : 3*5 missions isn't much, even if some are challenging enough even on Normal difficulty. The first two missions of a faction are usually some kind of tutorial, so really you get three full-length missions per faction. But when you see the amount of extra work they did for every one of said missions, it' can almost be acceptable. However, they're also quite badly designed as far as actual gameplay is concerned, and that's more problematic. Almost every single mission follows the exact same pattern of : start with very few units and buildings while enemy is already fully developped, rush some early units for defense to repel the constant assaults, then start building a huge army and crush your enemy without encountering much resistance. Objectives aren't particularly varied, they're of the "Destroy every enemy" variety almost all the time with generally one different mission per faction (i.e. the Beta campaign has the only actual siege defense mission). The designers also seem to
like the concept of magically spawning enemy units, which I've always found terrible in RTS games and a proof of designers being unable to create actual difficulty. It's frustrating to face, but it also limits player creativity because you cannot try a bold assault to try and destroy some of the enemy facilities to relieve your main base from the constant assaults for instance. Even worse, sometimes the "magical unit" is an
, which is extremely powerful and is supposed to take 5 whole minutes and a lot of ressources to build. Sometimes the epic enemy unit will spawn even if you've already beaten the player it supposedly belongs to, which is completely stupid.
This is sad, because obviously the developer put a lot of work into this campaign... so I have to wonder why they didn't spend a little more resource on the actual design of the missions. It's all in the "exterior" of the campaign, but the meat of it is actually pretty bland and not that interesting once you get to it.
More on the gameplay : the factions have a very distinct look&feel especially as bases are concerned (or lack of base, for the Goo) so that's very good. However, a LOT of units are extremely similar in every faction, especially ground units (the Goo does not have aerial units, so there's more diversity there). Light tanks are very similar, artillery that fires from long range, etc. Obviously there's going to be some staples, but since units do NOT have any special ability whatsoever (except passive ones, like "attack applies a debuff") armies tend to follow a similar composition all the time. Compare to a game like Earth 2160 (which I'm going to use as example because it's similar on several points, including the aliens with a very distinct playstyle.) where the LC clearly has more manoeuverable units and some very unique weapons (like the electric cannon), but paper-thin units.
As far as multiplayer is concerned, the first thing you'll notice is that it's dead, with players sometimes waiting up to 20 minutes for a game that has a high chance of being over after your opponent used a cheese strategy. Most people have already abandoned the game at this point due to a combination of imbalance, lags and disconnects (including people abusing disconnects to avoid a loss, and somehow this still isn't patched as of 7th March) as well as performance issues for many people. Also there's neither replay nor observer mode, shocking for a game that pretends to cater to the e-sport crowd. The new balance patch is also terrible with devs using a sledgehammer to destroy half the units instead of trying to carefully balance the game, nerfs everywhere that will make some units and buildings close to unusable (i.e. teleporter). The rarely-used Humans somehow took most of the nerfs for some weird reason.
Skirmishes are terrible and their main "redeeming" quality is that unlike in many other games, the AI does not cheat by getting free resources or building its units twice as fast. That's good because it means less frustration/unfairness, but on the other hand it also means that skirmishes are ridiculously easy even on Hard, especially in a 1v1 setting. We're very far from C&C 3's Brutal AI for instance, that took me many tries to beat. The only other correct point is that "Free for all" is actually implemented correctly, so AIs will not implicitly team up against the player.
All of this is just negated by the fact that the skirmish AI sucks terribly and does not pose any challenge whatsoever, no matter the "personality" that you choose for it. In fact, that's why the AI gets tons of free units in the campaigns : because the AI is way too bad to be a threat if it doesn't start with a full base and 10 extractors. This means that there's really no point in playing the skirmish, not as a "preparation" for the multiplayer (which will probably be completely dead soon anyway) and not as a fun game itself. Compare to Stronghold Crusader that also had AIs with different "personalities", but they were actually a challenge. And this game was released more than ten years ago, and was also arguably more complex. There's no reason for such a simple RTS (compared to most of its concurrents) to have such a terrible AI.
In fact, the skirmish mode is so boring and uninteresting that the achievement page lists
of people as having the "Win 100 skirmishes" achievement. No.One. I'm pretty sure back in the days I won way more than 100 skirmishes in C&C Generals for instance, but this game also had better AI, more unit diversity and also much more map diversity.
Overall it's still a somewhat enjoyable game but waaaaaaay overpriced for what it is. If you really like RTSes like I do and are starved for a new game it can be sort of worth buying, but it's still not worth its price and even at 50% the content is light compared to many other games. However it's admittedly a relatively well-polished title : I haven't found a
bug and the game runs fluidly on max settings. (I do have a brand new computer though, and quite a lot of people have had performance issues)
This game is not worth its price, the single-player content is weaker than in a lot of games (which are usually much cheaper), lack of replays, observer modes and bad balance means that multiplayer is also going down the drain so if that's your main reason to buy a RTS, you're out of luck with this title.

Incredibly fun game, combining base management, turn-based strategy, and just a little RPG into a very fulfilling experience.   Would definitely recommend to any fan of turn based strategy or sci-fi, I've put over 20 hours in just a few days and plan to put in many more.
That being said, there are a few places where the game falls short.  NOTE: Many of these are confirmed to be addressed in the upcoming XCOM 2, but remain an issue in Enemy Unknown.  Though the customization is there and available, after a while I discovered it was lacking.  You can change the hair and face of the soldier, for example, but there aren't that many options, and the nationality of the soldier is not customizable.  The outfits are all uniform (no pun intended), and the only change you'll see to them is when the soldier is injured in the field and blood splatter appears on their chest/back.  No alternate customizable pieces, no color tweaks, nothing (beyond upgrading the armor itself).  Same with weapons, which have no alternates beyond maybe plasma rifle vs light plasma rifle.  No helmets either, which in a game where you have high powered advanced armor, seems like a bit of an oversight.  While this isn't a gameplay flaw, it nevertheless is something that could have had so much more potential.
This may be just me, but some of the RNG felt random.  My sniper may have a 95% chance to hit through a building and behind cover, but my assault shot gunner only has a 60% chance a few tiles away, without armor, behind light cover.  Similarly, Heavies almost never have accuracy over 50% it feels, like the game wants to force you to use them for suppressing fire or overwatch.  Again, this might just be me, so it's not a real con, but I felt the need to add it nonetheless.
Finally, smaller things, such as voice acting and base management, as well as the punishing country system not being immediately clear were apparent to me.  These are all arguably overshadowed by the numerous pros of the game, the largest of which I'll list, and the rest of which I'll let you find out for yourself.
The perma-death system FORCES you to be careful with your soldiers.  unlike other turn-based games where you can just keep trying and reloading saves, the perma-death system threatens your playthrough with a loss of a veteran if you play sloppily.  Some may say this forces the player to play passive and defensive, but I feel it makes the game feel fluid, a true campaign rather than just a series of levels.  It also makes those few times where you go for the risky play so much more rewarding when you pull it off.  However, you may find yourself reloading a previous save if you find your main squad getting rekt and can only replace it with rookies.  Don't worry, there's no shame in a rewind button every once in a while.
The level design is FANTASTIC.  Very rarely is a level recycled, and there are so many different environments and cover types, maybe one mission you'll be on a highway, using cars as cover and getting your sniper on top of a truck for better positioning, and in the next, maybe you're approaching an enemy downed UFO, moving through a river before peaking over a hill at the crash site, moving from tree to rock to tree.  Even the 1 or 2 maps I've played through twice had different enemy and enemy spawns, so even if the environment was the same, the experience was still unique.
The combat in general feels very rewarding, outflanking enemies and baiting them into traps, it all feels amazing.  When the screen pops up telling you you beat the level, killed however many aliens, and lost no operatives, you get a great feeling that makes you want to do it again.  Just a satisfying combat system.
I reiterate, lacking customization, weird RNG (maybe personal) and smaller things such as voice acting and punishing country system overshadowed by a unique and coherent perma-death system, phenomenal level design, and a very satisfying combat system.  Solid 8/10, and I can't help but look forward to the upcoming XCOM 2, which looks to improve upon the first in every way.

You will cuss at this game, because it will kill you. A lot. But for some reason, you'll keep coming back to it. FTL is amazing like that.
Take a completely randomly generated series of star systems. Add in several stereotypical alien archetypes that get mad at you for their own peculiar reasons. Sprinkle in a generous selection of randomized scenarios from Sci-Fi shows that always get the flunkies in the crew killed. (Boarding parties, crazy hermit on barren planet, giant spiders, rogue AI, pirates, etc.) Put in plenty of one-on-one fights between ships with lasers, missles, and drones, and you have a standard game of FTL.
I still haven't gotten to the "ending". I don't expect to any day soon. Every time you think you have an edge, something unexpected will invariably happen.
You have a simple interface for controlling what systems get power, what crew goes where, what weapons to fire, and even door control, which comes in handy more often than you might think. Your play style will be different depending on the ship you use and the situations you come across. Sometimes a store will have the exact weapons you need when you have the funds, other times it's best to max out your shields instead.
The advanced edition adds a lot of fun elements the original didn't have, but I still like the original best for the challenge it presents.

I have experience with Titan Quest, Immortal Throne, Dungeon Siege 1/2, Diablo 1/2/3, Path of Exile, Sacred 1/2, Torchlight 1/2 and other similar games. I am an original kickstarter backer for this game that waited until recently to play it for the first time (getting through a backlog).
I just completed a full playthrough as a two handed ranged Soldier on Normal + Veteran Mode. This game does offer enough to make it decent, but also has enough flaws for me to lose interest after beating the story (for now).
Gameplay
A lot of quality of life improvements over Titan Quest: Faster action, single potion types, quick portals, auto gold pickups, faster animations, generally smoother and faster all round. My main gripe with Titan Quest that kept me going back to it was how slow it was, so this is great. The balance had some crazy damage spikes here and there, the final boss got pushed over without a single potion use, whilst some general Hero monsters and sniper types almost one shot me. The inventory get's flooded with a lot of junk, it would have been better to have an unlimited separate inventory for crafting items.
Story
Very rich and deep with a lot of lore to read but I felt that it was cut short/unfinished.
Visuals
Absolutely stunning world art and decent all round.
Design
The bosses don't really have the wow factor that Titan Quests ones had, they feel like a normal enemy encounter with slightly different abilties and a different name. Some maps feature these placed rocks and barriers that block your path, in an attempt to improve randomisation, they shuffle them around when the area resets, this feels artificial and cheap. I feel there should have been elemental variations to most skills that use elements, so you can choose what element to focus on.
Conclusion
This game is definately worth the price, I recommend playing with a friend and blasting through it. There are a lot of options for character development and equipment.

Should you play XCOM? Yes, absolutely - and do it with the expansion. XCOM manages to mix squad-based tactics and a building sim in a way that doesn't just work, but feels fantastic (and it'd actually be a solid format for a Pacific Rim game). The scope and complexity are huge without ever feeling overwhelming, and you'll be faced with lots of tough but intriguing options and dilemmas. You'll get attached to your base and your soldiers, but don't be tempted to constantly load saves and shoot for a perfect run - dealing with big risks and challenges and setbacks are a huge part of what makes the game interesting. And it's also highly replayable with randomized missions and events, and a huge pool of maps.

Genre: Real-time Strategy
Developer: Petroglyph Games
Publisher: Grey Box
Grey Goo is a new Real-time Strategy (RTS) game by Westwood Studios veterans Petroglyph Games. Those familiar with Westwood would be aware of their impressive track record.  As you may have already read, Grey Goo feels like an early RTS, however it introduces many new ideas differentiating itself from its predecessors. There are three distinct factions to play as (the standard number for RTS titles today), the versatile Beta, the defensive Humans and the aggressive Goo. I'll take you through my rundown of the game assuming you're an RTS fan; I'll be making a few comparisons throughout.
What's that? You're not familiar with RTS games? Don't worry, Grey Goo more than explains itself with many tutorial videos before jumping into one of the game's two main modes, Campaign and Skirmish. Campaign is the single player narrative featuring multiple customised scenarios whilst Skirmish allows you to play against either human or AI opponents in free-for-all or team battles. Replay and Observer modes were added several months after the game's launch, a staple for the competitive multiplayer types. It's good to see the developers were not too preoccupied with competitive multiplayer, offering a lot of single player content. Plot-wise, Grey Goo does not follow standard sci-fi stereotypes creating an identity of its own (for example: the Humans are the most technologically advanced faction). The campaign is set on a tropical planet known as Ecosystem 9 and its compelling, 15 missions long and legitimately challenging (not merely an elaborate tutorial). Be prepared to click the restart mission button a few times. Whilst the campaign is challenging, not too many missions overstay their welcome, they'll hold your interest. The campaign takes you through each faction, the Beta (the most conventional one for RTS veterans), Humans (defensive) and Goo (aggressive). There have been suggestions that the Beta and Humans are too alike. They are somewhat similar, but have enough differences to distinguish themselves. For instance, the Beta have more offensive options and are far more mobile than the Humans whom must use power conduits to power their structures and stationary defenses as well as expand. The Goo is the stand out faction solely for its originality. Instead of constructing a base; resource gathering and unit construction are left to the Mother, a large Goo that essentially acts as a mobile all-in-one base that consumes everything in its path (including enemy structures). Each unit has a purpose and remains useful throughout the whole game, even early game ones. The factions each have their own equivalent of the scout, tank and artillery. Other more exotic units include the Goo's Bastion (a moving wall) and Dweller (a subterranean unit that explodes when enemies are nearby).
There are no super weapons such as Nukes or Ion Cannons here, instead replaced with "Epic Units" similar to those in Command and Conquer 3 encouraging the construction of large armies to back them up. The horizontal user interface is well designed, taking cues from more recent RTS/MOBA titles including hotkey layout. Another idea borrowed from MOBAs is the ability for units to hide in brush. Units may also be auto-queued in order to keep battles big and interesting. Resource collection, construction and unit creation have been beautifully streamlined. Resource collection in particular has gone from babysitting harvesters with iffy path finding to a "set and forget" sort of thing. The developers also opted to go with Supreme Commander's income system which translates well into this title. There are numerous technological upgrades each faction may choose from, they are divided into different categories, however you may only select one in each which gives more weight and responsibility for your choices allowing for some army tweaking depending on which strategy you wish to employ. Grey Goo may not be as fast-paced as Starcraft 2 but is still fast enough to keep players on their toes. Combat isn't too deep, more so emphasising unit composition over micromanaging a handful of units like in more recent RTS games. Another trend in recent RTS titles was their encouragement of aggressive tactics and punished anyone who did not expand quickly enough. Defensive strategies are, at the very least, viable in Grey Goo.
The visuals are impressive, you may max the game out even on a modest PC. There are notifications and detailed tooltip text boxes for everything keeping you in the loop throughout the battle. Each faction is well designed, from the Beta's mechanical, animalistic walkers to the Humans hovering, highly advanced drone arsenal. The campaign cinematics look great too, so great that Petroglyph may have even outdone Blizzard in that regard.
Everything either has a sound cue or announcement. There are no issues with the announcer or units trying to talk over each other (the announcer usually takes precedence) although you may hear them repeat themselves over and over ("Wall under attack..."). Units become irritated when constantly selected (a throwback to Starcraft) and let you know when they're in combat or have defeated an enemy. It's small details like these that demonstrate how much the developers cared for their product. The game's score was composed by Frank Klepacki (Command and Conquer/Dune). It's great. Longtime RTS fans may hear echoes of his past work in this game, in particular Command and Conquer: Tiberian Sun and Universe at War: Earth Assault. Each faction has a unique, dynamic soundtrack that changes depending on what's happening on screen.
Before describing the existing issues Grey Goo has, I should note that Petroglyph have since addressed a couple of problems it had upon it's release. Multiplayer disconnections are now, at the very least, less frequent and additional graphics options have been added. The game has also been properly optimised meaning the title screen no longer stutters and the game simply runs smoother in general, even on a PC that does not quite meet the recommended system specifications. True to their word, Petroglyph also added more units, multiplayer maps and another faction in subsequent updates. On to the issues...
Currently, there is no option to play an eight player skirmish match. Multiplayer is region locked, meaning you may only play with others within your part of the world. In order to play with other countries, you must change your download region in Steam, however this may result in a lot of lag depending on where you live. Unit pathfinding is wonky (particularly epic units), each one requires a bit of micromanagement to do what you actually want it to. Satisfying audio feedback from past RTS games, such as Command and Conquer, are not present here (no big chunky explosions when laying waste to an enemy army or base). Unit selection quotes are forgettable, nor do said units gain any visual indicators of particular upgrades unlike other games in the genre. I was also hoping to play with some campaign specific units only to be left wanting (there is one campaign specific unit in the Emergence Campaign downloadable content).
Usually, I would have waited for a sale before picking this up (this is Steam after all). But I've been waiting for a real RTS on PC for a long time. I couldn't wait, I wanted in from the ground up and wasn't disappointed. In my opinion, Grey Goo delivered. It's a creative, polished and genuine RTS title that fans of the genre will enjoy. Another reviewer noted most of Grey Goo's negative reviews were linked to it's weak launch. Petroglyph have since proven their dedication to their product by giving it the support it needed. Now it just needs more players...

Child of Light was a game I purchased early 2015 and just sat in my Steam library until a few days ago.  I am proud to say that I've finally come around to playing and finishing the game, and it was worth the time spent.
--Pros--
Art style: Simply beautiful! Watercolors and hard shading mixed perfectly. If you like playing really eye pleasing games, this is up your alley. It's art style will keep it a relevant game in the future, like other stylized games.
Music: Not a lot of music in the game but what is there is good.  All fighting music got me pumped for the next encounter.
Gameplay: A RPG with an action timeline you can influence by slowing enemies from attacking or interrupt altogether.
Made me think of other RPGs like Super Mario RPG and South Park Stick of Truth.
--Cons--

Story Script: This game is meant to be presented like a fairy tale.  As such, the story is presented in ryhme.  At times, it can get very annoying... The story itself is very easy to get into. Just the rhyming gets old.
Side Quests: All RPGs have side quests.  I didn't complete every side quest in game but didn't feel like the reward was compelling enough to.
---
Overall, I'm glad I finally took the time to play Child of Light.  I don't feel compelled to play it again now that I've finished it but it was a fun one-time play through.
Onto the next game!

When this first came out, I'd have told you to not buy this and use YGOPro instead, if you wanted to duel on your computer. YGOPro is free, after all. But this game certainly has some features that made me like it quite a bit once I purchased it.
The singleplayer campaign is really nice. It lets you play singleplayer while running through the plot of the shows, making it feel like a real game, rather than just a duelling simulator. The "story decks" the game reccommends you use provide an interesting new puzzle each campaign duel, quite effectively teaching you how to play certain archtypes. Some of the story decks can be annoyingly underpowered, but most of them provide a fun variety.
It also has progression in building your own decks, by earing points and spending them on booster packs. Building a specific deck can mean opening a lot of packs, but earning cards is still a lot of fun.
I also like the sealed play options, but I've only done a few sealed duels, so I can't critique that feature too much.
And yes, this is a port of a console came. But I was surprised and glad to find that it has full integration with PC niceities, such as mouse control. I'm not used to seeing a console port actually spend time on adding these features, and it really helps the game.
A note about the DLC: Don't buy it. It's overpriced, unless you're a diehard fan of a certan deck and want one of the few cards behind a paywall. Without the DLC, a vast majority of the cards can be obtained without paying a single cent.
Overall, it provides features YGOPro cannot, so if you're nostalgic for some Yu-Gi-Oh, I'd definitely recommend this game. It teaches you how to play, if you're rusty at the game (like me), and it goes on to give you all the joys playing this card game could provide. If you only care about ranked multiplayer, stick with YGOPro. Otherwise, this game is perfect for the casual Yu-Gi-Oh enthusaist.

To be honest I was really skeptical about this official YGO game being released. Having played since 2002 (both physically and digitally) and having also invested money in the old YGO Online, it makes you wonder why they stopped including the old grindy style of card obtaining and features people actually liked, something I've not seen since the NDS games.
Legacy of the Duelist not only brings back the much loved style of card obtaining, but it essentially makes it F2P, with very few cards that require DLCs, being this ones also additional campaign duels that justify the cost. Pretty much whatever you want to build, even meta decks, can be built without paying extra money.
The campaign is so awesome, especially DM/GX, that some of my friends that haven't played since Synchros came out have enjoyed the nostalgia-driven story. We all agree that allowing Story decks to be chosen is the best idea that Konami has had, since this has brought back the "old guard" of Yu-Gi-Oh back to playing the game. Battle pack duels also make playing with friends quite enjoyable, considering it's pretty much straightforward and doesn't require the players reading each and every one of the effects.
As an old player that quit the physical game 4 years ago I haven't tried online ladder yet, since I don't care about the competitive meta and all I want is to be able to have fun and build cool decks to test. The amount of offline and friendly play available allows casual and old players alike to enjoy the game without having to play against tryhard-ish people, something that cannot be said about other PC alternatives. The banlist not affecting offline play also allows to try old-school decks that could only be played in platforms like NDS after enabling the No-Banlist cheat.
Of course the game has huge room for improvement. Some of the suggestions would be:
- Duel Puzzles (official and fanmade) that a lot of people seemed to enjoy
- Deck recipe duels
- Tag duels
- Offline tournament mode
- Frequent patches (Bugfixes, new format, new cards)
+ Essentially F2P
+ Cool campaigns for both old and new players
+ Various modes for unlimited fun
+ Traditional 5 zone mode (I hate those 3 monster zone YGO games I've seen lately)
+ Very intuitive tutorials and interface
- Too many DLCs, some too pricey for what they offer
- A few times the game has crashed without any reason
-
, also pack opening slow (why would you not copypaste this from NDS games?)
- Adding cards to/removing from the deck could be easier (like right-click on mouse)
Final mark: 8.5/10
The game can be improved, but it's on the right path and is definitely on par or better than the PC competition. Konami has finally placed its bet on PC and boy is this a good way to start.

Leaving Lyndow is a walking simulator with some very light point-and-click adventure elements and mini-game distractions from indie developers, Eastshade Studios.
In Leaving Lyndow you play Clara, a young woman leaving her home town to join the Guild of Maritime Exploration. The game begins with you packing your bag to leave, and then lets you experience Clara's last few hours in Lyndow.
Lyndow itself is a port town that has recently suffered from a devastating landslide that wiped out all of the important buildings, though this doesn't feature heavily in the game. It does make me wonder, though, whether the developer may have more games planned for this game world.
The graphics in Leaving Lyndow are beautiful.
The game is played from first-person perspective, and it's obvious that a lot of effort has been put into the graphics. There are only half-a-dozen or so scenes, but each one has been very well crafted from a graphical point of view.
Lighting is superb -- though static -- and textures are very nice indeed. The nature scenes have an array of plant types to rival many AAA games and they're extremely well positioned, making these scenes look particularly nice.
Characters are well modelled, but weird. Faces are half covered, with clothing that reaches up to cover the mouth, making me think of Milena (from Mortal Kombat). I really hope that wasn't the artist's intent! Animations are a little restrictive and 'wooden', but not bad, just not quite up to the same standard as everything else.
There are a handful of graphics options. I found the default field of view to be too high, making everything seem a bit fish-eyed. I found a value of 70 to be much more comfortable, but still couldn't completely remove the effect when turning.
The music in Leaving Lyndow is soft and mellow, fitting the gameplay like a glove. Each scene has a different track, I think, but all of them are calm and soothing instrumental pieces. There's a lot of piano & violin, and some wind instruments (or simulated versions thereof). It really is very pleasant.
Sound effects are few and far between, and don't really play much of a role in the game.
There are no real voices, though the people you speak to make noises that sound a lot like a few syllables of 'Simish'. Background noises in the teahouse include a general sort of 'babble', too, though it sounds like more people than are actually present.
Leaving Lyndow is a first-person walking simulator. You wander about with WASD and control your view with the mouse, interacting with the world through the mouse buttons. It's very slow going, but not frustratingly so; the game is all about experiencing Clara's last day at home, so there's no need to rush.
The basic gameplay involves walking about, collecting a few items, interacting with objects in the game world that elicit comments or spark of Clara's memories of her childhood, learning about the story, and saying goodbye to Clara's friends and relatives. There are a few simple mini-games -- finding objects, playing tunes, rolling balls in a bowl, and playing a rudimentary sort of basketball -- but these are distractions from the story.
The game is VERY short. I completed my first play through in 47 minutes, and that included a couple of short alt-tabs to check achievements and write down a few notes for this review. I only received three out of seven achievements in that game, though, and three of the remaining achievements are hidden. Given that there are guides available that explain how to unlock the remainder of the achievements very easily, you're basically looking at about an hour to complete the game with everything unlocked.
My one complaint with the story is the abrupt ending. A nice cut scene or at least closing comments would have been welcome, rather than just dumping me back at the main menu.
Pros:
+ Absolutely lovely graphics
+ Peaceful music
+ Steam Achievements and Trading Cards
Cons:
- VERY short
- I couldn't quite remove the 'fisheye' effect
- Abrupt ending
Leaving Lyndow is a very short game, but it's also very reasonably priced. It doesn't quite fit my dollar/hour rule for 'good value', but I find it very hard to dislike, regardless.
The game world is interesting enough that I hope to see it fleshed out in more detail in subsequent games from the developers; the graphics are absolutely top notch; and it's clear that the game, short though it is, is a labour of love. If you're in the mood for a casual stroll through half-a-dozen or so interesting locations and reading a simple short story while you look at pretty graphics, then Leaving Lyndow may be the game for you.

Story - fairly standard for HOG's, nothing special here.  You can probably guess the plot just from the title of the game.
Graphics - nothing amazing, but very crisp and clear.  There are also special animated touches (like a cat statue whose eyes periodically open and watch you), that really add to the atmosphere.
Sound - the music was strangely addictive in this game.  There are some voice animations, but not much, as you don't interact with very many people.
HOP's - a really nice variety here.  You have your standard list based ones (with some interaction of objects to find what you are looking for), and some where you take the objects you removed from one HOP and put them into a different HOP.  There are also some that involved making something.  For example, you need a book whose pages have all been torn out.  After you find all the pages, you need to use a string from your inventory to bind them together, then as you close the book, you discover all the gold letters on the cover have fallen off, so you have to find those.  In the end, you really feel like you reconstructed this book.  All HOP items were properly named, and not too difficult to find.  I never had to use a hint to locate something.
Puzzles/minigames - this is where the game really shines!  It is absolutely packed with puzzles and minigames, of a tremendous variety and originality.  A great many of these puzzles/games I have not seen in HOG's before.  Most of them take a lot of thought to puzzle through, but I never got frustrated, and I never had to use a hint or strategy guide, making them just the right level of difficulty.
Features - The game does have a hint system and a built in strategy guide, but I never used either, so I can't comment on these.  There is no map (and thus no indication of areas with stuff left to do, or instant travel), but I found I didn't really miss the map all that much.  There is a decent sized bonus chapter at the end, with all new content.  There are 3 different difficulty levels.
Game length - Playing at the advanced difficulty level, the main game took around 6 hours, and the bonus chapter took around 2 hours.  This makes the game almost twice as long as your average HOG.  If you use hints and/or a strategy guide, it will, of course, be considerably shorter.
Overall - one of the best HOG's I have played, since I love puzzles and minigames, as well as interesting interactive HOP's.

Incredibly fun game, combining base management, turn-based strategy, and just a little RPG into a very fulfilling experience.   Would definitely recommend to any fan of turn based strategy or sci-fi, I've put over 20 hours in just a few days and plan to put in many more.
That being said, there are a few places where the game falls short.  NOTE: Many of these are confirmed to be addressed in the upcoming XCOM 2, but remain an issue in Enemy Unknown.  Though the customization is there and available, after a while I discovered it was lacking.  You can change the hair and face of the soldier, for example, but there aren't that many options, and the nationality of the soldier is not customizable.  The outfits are all uniform (no pun intended), and the only change you'll see to them is when the soldier is injured in the field and blood splatter appears on their chest/back.  No alternate customizable pieces, no color tweaks, nothing (beyond upgrading the armor itself).  Same with weapons, which have no alternates beyond maybe plasma rifle vs light plasma rifle.  No helmets either, which in a game where you have high powered advanced armor, seems like a bit of an oversight.  While this isn't a gameplay flaw, it nevertheless is something that could have had so much more potential.
This may be just me, but some of the RNG felt random.  My sniper may have a 95% chance to hit through a building and behind cover, but my assault shot gunner only has a 60% chance a few tiles away, without armor, behind light cover.  Similarly, Heavies almost never have accuracy over 50% it feels, like the game wants to force you to use them for suppressing fire or overwatch.  Again, this might just be me, so it's not a real con, but I felt the need to add it nonetheless.
Finally, smaller things, such as voice acting and base management, as well as the punishing country system not being immediately clear were apparent to me.  These are all arguably overshadowed by the numerous pros of the game, the largest of which I'll list, and the rest of which I'll let you find out for yourself.
The perma-death system FORCES you to be careful with your soldiers.  unlike other turn-based games where you can just keep trying and reloading saves, the perma-death system threatens your playthrough with a loss of a veteran if you play sloppily.  Some may say this forces the player to play passive and defensive, but I feel it makes the game feel fluid, a true campaign rather than just a series of levels.  It also makes those few times where you go for the risky play so much more rewarding when you pull it off.  However, you may find yourself reloading a previous save if you find your main squad getting rekt and can only replace it with rookies.  Don't worry, there's no shame in a rewind button every once in a while.
The level design is FANTASTIC.  Very rarely is a level recycled, and there are so many different environments and cover types, maybe one mission you'll be on a highway, using cars as cover and getting your sniper on top of a truck for better positioning, and in the next, maybe you're approaching an enemy downed UFO, moving through a river before peaking over a hill at the crash site, moving from tree to rock to tree.  Even the 1 or 2 maps I've played through twice had different enemy and enemy spawns, so even if the environment was the same, the experience was still unique.
The combat in general feels very rewarding, outflanking enemies and baiting them into traps, it all feels amazing.  When the screen pops up telling you you beat the level, killed however many aliens, and lost no operatives, you get a great feeling that makes you want to do it again.  Just a satisfying combat system.
I reiterate, lacking customization, weird RNG (maybe personal) and smaller things such as voice acting and punishing country system overshadowed by a unique and coherent perma-death system, phenomenal level design, and a very satisfying combat system.  Solid 8/10, and I can't help but look forward to the upcoming XCOM 2, which looks to improve upon the first in every way.

Should you play XCOM? Yes, absolutely - and do it with the expansion. XCOM manages to mix squad-based tactics and a building sim in a way that doesn't just work, but feels fantastic (and it'd actually be a solid format for a Pacific Rim game). The scope and complexity are huge without ever feeling overwhelming, and you'll be faced with lots of tough but intriguing options and dilemmas. You'll get attached to your base and your soldiers, but don't be tempted to constantly load saves and shoot for a perfect run - dealing with big risks and challenges and setbacks are a huge part of what makes the game interesting. And it's also highly replayable with randomized missions and events, and a huge pool of maps.

Grim Dawn is an ARPG just like Torchlight, Path of Exile, Titan Quest and Diablo series. However this one is worthy of it's own merits and definitely worth noticing.
What Grim Dawn does better than Diablo 3:
---
+ More atmospheric and moody.
+ Better lighting system.
+ Better music (possibly better than Diablo 2).
+ More stats than you can shake a stick at.
+ Better performance.
What Grim Dawn lacks compared to Diablo 3:
---
- A captivating story.
- That slight bit of polish.
- Character creation screen.
Grim Dawn is a better sequel to Diablo 2 than Diablo 3 is purely from a visual/gameplay point of view. It has a ton of depth, longevity and tons of character experimentation. It's more captivating than recent ARPGS of the same vein and is high recommended to ARPG lovers.
If you though Path of Exile was good. Then you're bound to find this amazing.

I'm not much of a gamer, typically, but I've got over 30 hours into FTL.  That should say something in and of itself.
First, let me say that FTL is hard.  Very hard.  Luck is a big part of the game, but so is making the right decision.  If you like the idea of overcoming nearly impossible odds to win, this game is for you.
FTL's sectors are randomly generated, so each playthrough is totally different.  There's a bunch of different ships to try, all with different strengths and weaknesses.  There's different weapons, typics of crew members, ship upgrades, and augmentations.  While this may sound overwhelming, it all goes together rather naturally, once you've played through a couple times.
Most importantly, it's fun.  While there are setbacks and situations in which you just can't win, never does it feel like I'm being robbed of a victory.  It does, however, sometimes feel like I've planned poorly, and that's the awesome thing.
One thing I do suggest -- play it on easy first, even if you don't usually do that.  Believe me, you'll need it.

The game is a grind, and I've always considered myself a hardcore player, at least when it comes to putting in effort to achieve a greater reward. But somehow, despite some of the best MMO graphics and combat on the market, they managed to make grinding to be able to do things such as PvP so bland, so repetitive, so tedious and unchallenging that I've come to the conclusion that it ultimately isn't worth it. This honestly really sucks for me. Don't underestimate the grind in this game. Look at my hours. I'm nowhere close to end-game, I'm nowhere close to even being competitive in PvP. Ask yourself: Are you willing to triple the amount of hours I have just to be DECENT at the PvP this game has to offer? There is no actual PVE content. The quests are bland and forgettable, and the only true way to level in this game at a realistic rate is to grind the same 2 spots, Sausans and Pirates, over, and over again, 8+ hours a day. That's the real PVE. It's true you can do other things, such as life skills, but most of those are just clicking a few buttons and going afk, and no matter how much money you get from them, you'll still need to get XP to level, which is only done through grinding. I tried, I failed. If you have the hardcore mentality and shrug off throwing countless hours doing repetitive tasks for a meagre reward, then TBH I'd recommend you apply that mentality to a real life job, as it will honestly feel like work. Forget every other complaint. If you care at all about PVE and questing, don't get the game. If you care about PVP and aren't willing to do the same repetitive task for hundreds and hundreds of hours just do be decent, don't get the game. But hey, if you like clicking a few buttons and going AFK and don't care about the other stuff, well...
