This is probably the best fighting game I've ever played before. This is the game I've always wanted to have but could never find something similiar to it. In short, here is the reason I think you should buy Lethal League, it's easy to learn the mechanics, it's fast paced and is VERY intense while still being a incredible amount of fun even when losing. Mostly because I personally like to see how others can outplay me rather than just getting beaten by a combo I didn't know.
Good things about the game
-GREAT NETCODING, with everything being done how lag just outright makes some games unplayable, Lethal League does a very good job at making a netcode that works so that if you/anyone else lags, it's stops momentarily for all people. Granted this could be a bad thing to look at as well, but I prefer not to get shot in the face by a person from across that took 5 seconds to load in and then teleport the ball to my face. Even when playing this with friends that had 200+ ping, it still played very well and none of us ever got lag when playing together.
-FAST PACED TO THE NEXT LEVEL, If you were to take Dragonball Z and just give everyone a baseball and a bat, this would summarize this game up very well. By how fast I'd imagine you pick up the objective in this game, which is just to hit people in the face with a metallic baseball. You'll notce it gets INSANE at higher speeds the ball goes, this drives the point home in when I say that the player with higher reflexes will win over the guy who knows how to hit X+B+RB+UP+DOWN+BVe$#=Insane Combos off the back of his hand.
-SIMPLE MECHANICS, In most video games that I personally play, I keep this rule of thumb. If the game isn't fun, I leave it. I dawn the title of CASUAL GAMER with pride because I don't want to read a book about how it takes to do these insane combos in video games because that isn't fun to me, I know it is for a lot people; but I am not one of those people. Which is why I am in love with Lethal League's easy to understand mechanics, there are 3 buttons and the movement. The Jump, the Hit, and the Punt. The two most difficult mechanics to understand how to do are the Charge shot parries and the Charge shot meter (Sorry if I butchered whatever they're actually called). Which if you really wanted learn you could take 2 minutes to look up in the Steam guides of how to be more effective. I currently have 12 Hours logged into this game at the time I'm writing this review, it took me mere hours to grasp the basics and only the day after to see how much deeper the game goes beyond that. It's a game I like going into because even if I stop playing it for a while, I know for a fact I can just come back and pick it up again without having to refresh myself on anything or even if they release more content I'd easily look it up or just try doing it myself to get the handle of it.
Bad things about this game
-CONNECTION ISSUES, This is a minor tidbit, but I noticed that sometimes the game will freeze and crash when starting a  match with 3+ people. This happens VERY rarely and a restart will usually just fix it, but it's just something I thought I'd mention.
-VERY FEW CHARACTER CHOICES, While being a relatively new game I don't want to bash on it since the current amount of characters it has at the moment is perfectly fine for me. But I know it can be frustrating to have a mirror match when you've found a character you really like to play because you probably know what's going to happen. Anyway, minor complaint again, but something to consider if you don't like that sorta stuff.
Conclusion: I would say this game deserves the high score it has, as I've said, it's easy to understand, it's simple and it's just SO DAMN SATISFYING TO MASH SOMEONE IN THE FACE WITH A BALL GOING AT LIGHTSPEED! And for $14 it's a STEAL compared to some games. If you want to find a Saturday night game with your friends or if your looking for a competitve game without the hassle of learning long and confusing mechanics of a new game. Try Lethal League, it's fun as hell and is hopefully going to be a supported game that will be around for a while with more content!
See you out there, and remember keep your eye on the ball!

I had once thought this series would remain forever exclusive to Sony's consoles so imagine my surprise when a Rebirth series finds its way to the PC. Rebirth 1 sets the tone with high quality presentation, allowing both battle sequences and conversations to come to life. The humour of the story is probably the biggest thing that kept me glued to the game, with Neptune in-particular being the life of the party, overly aware of everything being a game and drawing people in with her silliness.
Fortunately the game also has a very solid set of mechanics to back it up. Things do start off pretty slowly with a few hours minimum needed to get the most out of things, but once it starts rolling the battle system offers a multitude of options with specials, items and form changes. The ability to move around the field before launching an attack, taking advantage of the different attack areas of moves, is an interesting change from other turn based RPGs. The plans system is also great, letting you craft new things for the experience like adding new enemies to areas or adjusting the strength of monsters.
There are some drawbacks though. Difficulty is prone to spiking without warning and in general seems to expect you to be at a higher level than you actually will be if you're not excessively grinding. The game also reuses some of its level maps several times, simply with a change in enemies and sometimes changing the entrance point. The port can also be a bit buggy, although for me the only issue I encountered personally was a black screen during victory animations and this worked properly after I upgraded to Win10.

dying light was a fantastic game from start to finish. while i feel the story itself wasn't that long in either the main game or the following dlc, there was plenty of side missions and activities to keep me interested/distracted. 81 hours in and even though i've beaten the story, most of the side missions, and the following dlc (i don't have the bozak horde or ultimate survival bundle) i still find myself coming back to dying light for a number of reasons. the parkour system is the best i've ever seen. while the grappling hook detracts from the realsim of running around a city or across a countryside, it's quite an enjoyable addition and invaluable when it comes to quickly crossing the city of harran or getting back to your car to chase down the latest medical drop (SO happy they brought that back for the dlc) or rush off to help some random survivor from zombies or Rais's thugs. scattered around the city and countryside are plenty of challenges or races to keep you coming back. i wish there was a way to go from the city to the countryside without quitting to the main menu and starting up the dlc, but it's not much of an issue. i cannot stress enough how much fun it is to hop in your buggy and plow through a field of zombies and pop out the other side of the field to see yet another field of zombies to plow through. they really stepped up the carnage in the following dlc. i love it. and they don't make the car overpowered, either. if you smash into too much stuff and break different parts, the performance of the buggy noticably starts to suffer. ruined tires make you spin out, a busted accelerator means you're not gonna reach top speed fast enough. run out of gas and you're screwed until you find more. by the end of the main game, i wasn't that scared of volatiles or the night time anymore-the following changed all that. volatiles not only feel more dangerous, they're more numerous. and fast. so freaking fast. oh yeah! and the bolter liver repeatable side quest. hunting down bolters in your buggy to run them over and snatch their livers. all in all, if you like zombie games or parkour games or open world games, dying light is not a game you would wanna pass up

Well, I've never written a full-blown Steam review for any game, ever. Even if it's really good or really bad, I don't normally have the motivation to do so. That changed when I started playing Block N Load.
It's a spiritual successor to Ace of Spades, which was bought and remade by Jagex. Unfortunately, that alone would turn quite a few people away, because Ace of Spades didn't fare very well. However, almost all of the problems people had with Ace of Spades have been fixed up here.
The game is relatively simple: You get to pick between six classes (more will be coming in the future), including an insane scientist, an evil robot, and a Mexican ninja. Games are two teams of 5 versus 5, where you have about six minutes to build defenses and traps to protect these large machines called cubes and your team's base, then when time's up, the game starts and you can raid your opponents.
There are tons of different blocks that do different things. For example, my personal favorite is the fake block: It looks exactly like a connecting block, but when the opponent steps on it, it breaks away and he or she falls hopelessly into your trap, which could be bear traps, caltrops, sentry guns, poisoned dart-shooting tiki heads, or you could even make them fall off the map entirely. Another block is the Force Gate: You and your teammates can walk through it like there was nothing there, but your opponents cannot; they'll have to go around or destroy it. The variety of different blocks allow you to attempt to set up an impenetrable defense (although NOTHING is truly impenetrable!)
The strategies required in this game are far deeper than you might expect. Just throwing bear traps everywhere won't cut it. You need to think about where your attackers might approach or where to place radars and respawn pads. Since nearly everything in this game can be destroyed (including all the blocks and items you can place), you have to hide them away where the enemy can't find them. In addition, occasionally a powerful weapon called the Blockbuster will be sent in, giving you shielding and increased cube/base damage for two minutes... unless your enemy gets it first! Because the Blockbuster is only given to the team that can get it first, it becomes a frantic race to the center of the arena to grab this powerful item.
So, what are you waiting for, Blockhead? Come on and give it a go!
By the way, a tip for new players: Although it seems like a good idea, do NOT cover the cubes/bases with blocks. Trust me on this. You'll just end up giving any attackers free cover.

I recommend to anyone who love interactive and exploration first person or grab product on sale if you feel uncomfortable with its content. Plus, you get eight relaxing soundtracks for free.

Divinity Original Sin is a a throwback to old school isometric RPGs like Wasteland or Diablo, and has elemental similarities to many games.
Old school is in, so it's no surprise that many are lauding this game.  There are many great features to this game, but I'll start with the basics.
You control two characters to start, and can add up to four others.  Choosing your characters classes and abilities can be very important if you want to survive through your first playthrough.  The game does not hold your hand, and if you're expecting to just bludgeon your way through every fight without thinking, you will die.  It's strategy, but also action, and once you understand the system created, it's a lot of fun to fling fireballs, or drop boulder on enemies, or stab them.  Stabbing is fun too.
The two afore-mentioned characters are unique in that you control their lines of text individually, which means you can make them argue with each other, which is a great idea.  Unfortunately, if you were playing single-player only then you would be arguing with yourself.  Much like perfectly symmetrical violence, this does not solve anything, no matter who wins you're still losing the argument (though I suppose you are also still winning it) but this is decided by a game of rock paper scissors; an interesting mechanic, unfortunately outshown by the RNG element.  Because it is random, you're often leaving your outcomes in conversations to chance.  Sure, there may be some small amount of skill, but really it's just random.
Which brings me to my next thought;  save scumming.  This was a term I was unfamiliar with, but the concept was not lost upon me.  I "discovered" this "feature" at about level 5 or so, and it was a constant thereafter.   Being used to games like Dragon Age or even Farcry, I didn't expect D:OS to allow me to save whenever I felt the need to.  Much to my surprise it allowed me to save while I was fighting, while I was in conversations, while I was doing anything really.    What this allows for is god-like precognition.  Don't know how an NPC will react to you digging up the grave of their lost loved one?  Save first and find out!  Don't know if your next attack might actually heal your enemy?  Save and then smack them!  And most importantly, is that chest not quite what you wanted?  Were you really hoping for something a little more legendary?  Well just reload to before you opened it.  Still not it?  Try again? Again.  Again.  Again.  Again.  I must have done this a total of 100 times or maybe more.  I got to the point where I was so picky that I was basically min-maxing my characters until they were quite poweful.
Which brings me to my next point.  The game does something that few other games do.  It does a great job of correctly parallelling the process of growing stronger through leveling, with the plotline of the game itself.  I think this is a great concept and we see it at times, but I feel like the creators are almost encouraging save scumming specifically.  I won't spoil anything, but the game doesn't really keep what I'm talking about under wraps.  That's what I believe at any rate.
Divinity has some minor flaws.  Some puzzles don't make too much sense, and some are only difficult due to game limitations, but who cares?  The game has great voice acting, though sadly not as much of it as I would like.  It has well-written and interesting characters, a good plot and many choices to be made along the way.
Overall, I think it is well worth the price and I highly recommend it if you're willing to try some turn-based combat over shooting things in CoD or whatever.

After about 500 hours I decided to write a review for Grim Dawn, as I think the game is worth picking up for any fan of Dungeon Crawlers, Action Adventures, RPGs and ARPGs alike. The game plays just like most ARPGs, which I don't think is a bad thing. The ARPG formula is pretty well hammered out and there isn't much reason to re-invent the wheel.
The differences come in the way Crate chose to order the skill system. Firstly, we once again have a true "if you messed up, start over" ARPG. PoE was like that for a while but full respec has been added to the game. I understand that it's very tedious to do so, but it still exists. In Grim Dawn, if you mess up attribute points, or put too many points into a skill mastery, you cannot undo either of them, and must start over. You can respec points in your actual skills and devotions still, which means that the casual player can still always make do, even if they made a slight mistake, but the hardcore player can still be punished with unnecessary points in the right place.
I think thats the most important part of grim dawn. It's one of the things that Blizzard did correctly with D3: RoS, giving full playability to both the casual and the hardcore gamer. the difficulties beyond normal are also pretty hard. the game punishes you hard for going fully offensive and forces you into balancing out your character.
The skill system also pulls out a happy medium for both the casual and the experienced gamer. One of PoE's biggest shortfalls is just how daunting its skill system is for a lot of players. I understand that it is exactly that which makes it popular with a lot of people, but it also turns away a lot of potential players. Grim Dawn has a good balance between the mastery skills, and the devotion attributes. its not too simple and basic, but its also not overbearingly confusing. Also, just about any build is viable to a point.
Pros:
Good class balance
caters to both styles of gamers
Good skill balance

doesn't try to reinvent the wheel

Cons:

Hanako: Honor and Blade. Wow where to start here. The graphics are akin to a graphic novel in motion.  That's the closest description I can give for the artwork. the background of feudal japan is a beautiful backdrop in which to do battle against other samurai!
The game mechanics are smooth and there is a learning curve for each of the three classes you can play.  I would heavily suggest running through the training sims to get a good grasp of what your chosen class is capable of doing.
The traditional music which plays in the background can help to immerse you in the game as well as the sounds of the sword being drawn, the Naginata delivering a blow, and the sound of the ninja's Kusarigama flying through the air.
I am especially impressed with the way the Kenshi fights as the swordsmanship is fairly accurate. Slashes, thrusts, overhead blows, and even the way the sword is drawn is amazing for a video game. Even the footwork and stance have been addressed. The Naganatashi also has impressive moves! As far as the ninja goes, you really need to stay mobile with him because he has very light armor. However, played correctly, he is definitely a force to be reckoned with!
Replayability is also there. Team v team scenarios with different objectives keep a person engaged and on their toes!
Although this is an early access game, I believe the potential here to make it an outstanding indie!
I just hope that more players gravitate to the game as I have.  real players will make this game awesome! the bots tend to get stuck but that too can be improved I am sure.  Only small bugs I found so far. Bots being stuck on rocks and not being able to attack if you are positioned in a certain place.
My overall Rating for this one is an 8/10 - Great work so far on this early access indie! can't wait to see the future improvements!

I really thought I would like this game.  I love RPGs of all colors and the anime style was really appealing.  I was also expecting great humor from this game.  However:
- It took 15 minutes of cutscenes before I got to push the "A" button for the first time.
- Gameplay is described in a series of text-heavy slides, where battle overlays may have been more interactive and effective.
- Targeting schemes are difficult, even with a control stick
- Although I don't mind gratuitous female outfits, this game clearly caters toward the male audience.
- This isn't necessarily a con, but it adheres to several archaic RPG standards, including sparsely placed save points (why not a temporary save elsewhere on the map?  Cutscenes can be looooong) and recolored/reused enemies.  If the rest of the game was more engaging, I would overlook these, but as-is I would go elsewhere for a humorous game or fun JRPG experience.
Overall, I feel there were a lot of missed opportunities in game design (why not let us play in the first epic battle?) and, despite the gorgeous art style and cute characters, the game quickly alienates everyone but their target niche audience.

If you've looked at the videos/screenshots above, then you're already familiar with the game's strongest selling point - it's graphics, and the atmosphere it crafts. Some other thoughts on the game:
+/- Challenging, but not difficult.
+ Engaging battles - it is turn based, but at the same time you have to make lots of decisions in real time. In essence, you need to be quite active while "waiting" for your turn: the game implements an interrupt mechanism, as well as control on how to pace the battle, and trade offs on whether or not to impose this control. Very fun.
+ Nice versatility when it comes to customizing your character build on level up.
+ The game is relatively quick and has a nice pacing to it. At no point does it feel bogged down in grinding, or pointless side quests.
- The game advertises that you can hook up a second controller, but the range of things that a buddy can do is  very limited and very heavy on support. I doubt this is much fun.
- "Puzzles" are solvable by grade schoolers. When will they make a game that doesn't take for granted the intelligence of their audience??
+/- The mythology is deliberately and poetically vague. Some people find this frustrating, but I find it refreshing to not have everything spelled out.
+/- Finally, this is about the most melancholic coming-of-age RPG there is. At one point you meet a jester named Tristus with tears streaming down its face, for goodness sake.
9/10, and absolutely worth the price anytime you can get this game during a Steam sale.

To clear up a few things Black Desert Online is in no way a "Pay to win" experience. It is so much so, that the mention of BDO being pay to win has become a sort of meme within the game.
Secondly the pricing, let's compare this to World of Warcraft, also one of the most popular MMOs to date.
BDO(Black Desert Online) Is a pay once play forever mmo, with WoW(World of Warcraft) being a subscription based mmo.
Yearly cost for just being able to play the game: for WoW if you had brought the six month pass(which is the best price), that would total up to $155.88 every year. While BDO on the other hand, you only pay once without additional fees - Price ranges between packs.
Cash shop Items: WoW being largely cosmetic, while BDO is a mix of convenience and cosmetic items. In BDO You can also buy everything in the cash shop through the player marketplace(Cash shop items have fixed amounts of silver they can sell for, to negate p2w) and a lot of the complaining you see here, is largely due to ignorance over the games mechanics. You get inventory space as you progress along the main quest line. As well as being able to buy separate storage in each of the capital cities within the game. The game even offers you the "booster" as one of it's daily reward(s)(quite a few times I might add)
This is a post to also address the stigma around buying cash shop items. It's a cheap mmo, the prices are what they are for them to make profit and continue to host all of their servers. If you play the game for a year and have only spent your initial entry cost, you aren't getting ripped off in the slightest if you want to buy a cash shop item.
And as a side note; AFK fishing builds up quite a lot of time on steam. My actual play time would be around 15-20 hours(on steam), as of writing this review.

Yu-Gi-Oh! is the best Trading Card Game ever created, in my opinion.  It's easy to learn, but it requires a lot more strategy than most TCGs.  For years, I had no one to play the game with, and I even tried a few other card games to try to find a replacement... but I was never satisfied with any of them.
That's why I'm thrilled that Yu-Gi-Oh! Legacy of the Duelist is on Steam.  As soon as I saw it in the store, I knew I had to have it!  I didn't even watch the promotional video, so I wasn't aware of all the game's features when I began playing.  I was surprised and impressed by the special Kill Cam animations that certain cards have.
Thankfully, there are no micro-transactions in the game (I'd go broke LOL).  You win new cards and points for an in-game card shop by playing the campaigns.  The base game includes 5 single-player campaigns that follow the main storylines of the first season for each of the Yu-Gi-Oh! animated shows.  You get to play against all the classic heroes and villians, and can play with the same decks used in the show, or use your own custom deck.  If you play the Story Deck, certain cards are weighted to come up first so you can play the same strategy from that match on the show, if you want.  After winning a duel in the campaign, you can reverse the characters and play the other character (with the Story Deck or a custom one), and win more by replaying the duels.
The nostalgia factor is extremely high with this game, and the
make it a true joy to play.  If you've never played Yu-Gi-Oh! before and/or never saw the animated shows, I'm sure you would love this game if you're into Trading Card Games at all.  Plus the cute anime style will probably make you smile.
Duels are typically fast-paced and are won with strategy, rather than luck.  There is no "mana system," and players can only have 5 monsters on the board at one time.  A lot of other games have no limits and can result in massive, drawn-out battles with dozens of cards in play.  That's boring, and I don't think Yu-Gi-Oh! ever gets boring.

I've played this game 2x now, and believe it's a great game. It helps if you liked the predecessors (like Divine Divinity) and/or enjoy turn-based RPGs, both of which I do.
The combat system just might be the best I've seen in an RPG. Just fantastic. If Larian continues w/ this system in its future RPGs, we'll be quite fortunate.
The writing was a good mix of seriousness and zany, punny humor. A breath of fresh air, really. The voice-acting was great, the 4 companions (I went through them all in the 2 playthroughs) fun, and a lot of overheard dialog was funny as hell. The music was quite good too.
It's a game that rewards patience and exploration, which is my kind of game. The crafting scheme was a little murky, but thanks to these boards and a linked pdf, I got the gist of it well enough. I understand an upcoming patch will perhaps address this and certain balance issues.
Even the Steam achievements were enjoyable (the best: the one about Mangoth) and clever/funny. Not sure whether Larian wrote those; guess that would make sense...
The game has a lot of flexibility built into it. It seems like it was built around a melee PC; a mage; a thief; and an archer. Those were my parties both times, but w/ different builds and companion choices. I would recommend this for a 1st playthrough (at least), though I know people have tried 4 mages etc.
Complaints would be very minor and infrequent: voiced dialog loops of NPCs can be grating if you don't leave their vicinity. I had only 1 crash in a little over 200 hours of playing. I would have left pure "junk" out of the game (can't pick up, can't sell), as clutter gets to be overwhelming sometimes. That's about it.
Great game.

If storybook style games are not your thing, you would be doing yourself a disservice by not giving Child of Light a closer look. This game is far more than the simple point and click that many games in this genre offer. If storybook style games ARE something you happen to enjoy... prepare to be blown away. Although the story itself is a bit linear, you will find it holds a surprise or two. The combat is well executed. There is a bit of crafting, collecting and side quests. The ability to construct and enhance a party with interesting, well developed characters lends an air of complexity. And best of all perhaps, the games artwork and music are simply breathtaking. At times it felt as if I was playing within a master crafted water coloring.
Your journey into Child of Light begins when you take on the persona of Aurora, the precocious daughter of the Duke of Austria, in the year of 1895. Aurora falls into a death-like slumber one night to awaken on the mysterious and magical continent of Lemuria. She discovers the land to be under the despotic grip of Umbra, Queen of Darkness. While back in Austria, a bereft Duke mourns his comatose daughter, Aurora finds herself thrust into a daunting mission to bring back the sun and stars which Umbra now holds under her control. At stake is her father, the people of Austria, the varied inhabitants of Lemuria, and Aurora's own destiny.
As you set out to explore Lemuria in hopes of finding a dream path home, you will encounter the Lady of the Forest who will help to arm you with your four greatest assets. A magical sword of unknown properties. A seemingly useless flute. A firefly named Igniculus, who is much more than he may seem at first light. And best of all, the power of flight. Oh, did I forget to mention Aurora can fly? How awesome is that, eh? This one asset alone opens the map to means of exploration not usually encountered in games of any type, and you will most certainly have need to explore.
During the course of your explorations you will encounter many side quests, each of which can enhance your abilities in surprising ways. You will collect "confessions" which help to unfold the story and offer valuable insight. You will collect jewel like occuli which can be crafted and combined to enhance weapons and abilities. Best of all, you will encounter the denizens of Lemuria, many of whom will seek to join you in your quest, and help to overcome the minions of the Dark Queen, sent to impede your progress. Each of these fellow explorers will bring unique personality and abilities of their own to the party. You will find yourself in the company of a Jester that can't seem to rhyme or riddle. A capitalistic, love struck mouse. An untrained gnome-ish spellcaster. A frightening but depressed warrior cat, and perhaps even a lost sibling or two, but that's all I'll say on that. No spoilers for you, my friend.
Game Play:
Child of Light is a standard 2D side scrolling exploration game, with the added dimension of flight. I can not begin to describe what flight, to include the ability to hover in place adds to this game. It is not simply that it removes the "bleh" that sometimes occurs with side scrolling. It serves to open every square inch of the screen to exploration and discovery, which greatly adds to the games total playable area. As for the 2D graphics, the layered artwork in the game is not only beautiful, it adds a sense of depth one would normally expect to encounter in 3D graphics. It is very easy to forget what style of game you are playing as the land of Lemuria draws you in. In addition to exploration and discovery, there are elements of collecting, crafting, character advancement, puzzles and a pretty good combat system. It is designed as a solo game, but can become a two player game with one player controlling Aurora, while the other plays Aurora's companion, igniculus.
Building a party is a major aspect of the game. Every character, including Aurora, will come with an advancement tree specific to that character. As you gain advancement points through accomplishments and combat, those points can be used to expand and or improve upon character abilities. Points can be distributed as you see fit. In addition to advancement points your characters also gain in level. All characters gain level from combat, even if that character did not take part in the combat at hand. You have complete freedom in which characters you advance, as well as which branch of their advancement tree you wish to focus on.
Child of Light can be played at various levels of difficulty. It is suggested that you play through at the lowest difficulty level the first run through for the sake of experiencing the story, and increasing the level for a more challenging replay. Even at it's lowest setting you will find it challenging at points, especially near the end game, but not so difficult that younger players will find it near impossible to complete. Despite the linear aspect of the game that does not allow for alternate endings, I find the game to have a moderate degree of replay value. On minimal difficulty, you should be able to play through the entire game in 10 to 15 hours; Longer if you explore every corner and accumulate every collectible.
Crafting and Collecting:
Crafting in Child of Light is deceptively simple. The only item that is crafted are gem-like items called occuli. You can use occuli as they are, join them to obtain more powerful occuli, or combine them to create new occuli. Occuli are used for the sole purpose of enhancing gear and weapons.
The primary collection items are confessions. To avoid being a spoiler, I will leave it to you to discover the merits of collections for yourself, but be sure to keep an eye out for confession pages. See that piece of paper fluttering in the breeze? Yeah... you might want that...
Combat:
When entering combat, the action shifts to a combat zone. Up to two allies and three foes can engage at any given time. It is smooth and somewhat fast paced. Fortunately for you, party members can be switched out on the fly, allowing you full use of your entire party. You can even save a fallen character by switching them for a fresh party member.
The combat itself is a classic turn based RPG style that incorporates an action time bar. Each character has a specific set of abilities and the ability to switch them out allows for a variety of cooperative combo attacks. Bosses have various attributes as well so combo attacks can be used to exploit weaknesses or counter strengths. The time bar is the most important element of the combat sequence, and many abilities and attacks can manipulate it by hastening the time bar itself, or disrupting an enemy before he can attack.
Unlike many games I have played with this style of combat, selecting the defend option can often be a sound tactical choice that can save you from being interrupted. The defend option is especially useful when one of your combative characters possess buffing, supportive, healing and hastening spells.
Each party member has their own unique skill tree which can be developed along multiple paths to gain new abilities or improve upon existing ones. It should be noted that each character specializes to some degree. Some characters have powerful physical attacks. Others possess elemental attacks and counters. Some are fast attackers, useful in keeping foes disrupted, while yet others excel in a support role. The majority of skill points are best spent on passives to raise HP and defense while using the remaining points to gain and upgrade specific skills. All party members gain experience whether used in combat or not, which allows the entire party to advance as a whole.

On the down side, it is short (I was done in 41 minutes), and there is essentially no story.  This is no The Vanishing of Ethan Carter or Dear Esther.  The character models and animations were also poor and jarring, especially in relation to the static models.
This is not a bad game for a short distraction.  It is obviously a labor of love.  I would have dearly liked to have had more story, and more interesting things to learn.

I very much believe that Divinity: Original Sin is only for a certain kind of player.
Namely, one that doesn't get frustrated easily. It's a classic Fallout/Shadowrun turned based Tactics game, and I've quit playing it out of frustration (alt tab/close window) more times than any other game in recent memory. It's littered with so many minor problems (many of which other games have found solutions for) that eventually you'll throw your arms up and promise yourself that THIS TIME, you're going to quit playing it for good. But then 15 minutes later, grim and determined, you're back.
You see? I'm just trying to save you from this whole spiral of self-loathing and despair.
It's going to be spending 15 minutes organizing your inventory every time you find a bit of junk, or dying 10 times to a boss that's just one level ahead of you until you have to go back to an earlier save, or vainly trying to figure out what the actual next step of the questline is, or trying to glean the practical application out of the cryptic crafting books you find, or just the sheer amount you have to save to avoid redoing a lot of the crap that you've already done, yeah, one of these things will finally get to you.
Not that it's a bad game entirely, that's the problem. It's complex and diverse, the character classes are interesting and there's an intricate world to explore.
At times it reminds me of Dragon Age 2 - I've wandered through the opening town of Cyseal so many times I'm reciting the lines of the merchants/civilians/legionnaires before they even come on screen (the cheese merchant is my favorite, apparently in a time before celebrity movie stars he who had cheese was most popular).
There's just so many things that take so much longer than they should. You have to micro-manage everything and you end up with so much junk that you just start throwing it away, all those tantalizing craftables that I've used only a handful of times in the game so far. Someone else with a negative review did a brilliant job explaining the crafting system (using the example of creating a scroll) so I won't go into that.
Just thinking too much about this game is getting me tired. So I'll end with the most critical piece of advice I could give a new player: don't fight anything that's even just one level above you. Yes, if you save before the fights and get lucky enough on your 131st try you may end up winning, but trust me, the chance for a random bit of useful loot is just not worth it. Good luck finding enemies your level though. (When you get to Cyseal, find the city gate on the west side of town (that's not barred), and fight westwards to the lighthouse before trying the rest of the map. Otherwise, like me, you'll know all the cheese merchant's lines by heart.)
Oh yeah, forgot to mention this earlier but don't expect to level up more than once a YEAR.
LATER EDIT: Once you get out of the early Cyseal areas, the game actually isn't as bad in terms of mismatching you against enemies. Plus, you learn that enemies stronger than you are the game designer's way of saying 'do not come this way yet'. That being said, I imagine many new players still find Cyseal difficult enough that it becomes a serious impediment to continuing with the game.
However, all is not praise - I absolutely hate the♥♥♥♥♥♥♥rock, scissors, paper games. You make a decision, but your other accomplice protests, and you have to play this stupid game against them. Even when the decisions are SO♥♥♥♥♥♥♥OBVIOUS. Enemies are worse - I missed a whole mini-quest to recover a missing head because of one rock scissor paper defeat. Now where I am in the game, I have to beat an enemy TWICE and can only mess up once per duel (their Charm is at 6! While mine's only 3 - I can't tell what determines the score too). Whoever came up with this system should be beaten with a rock, cut multiple times with a piece of paper and finally put out of their misery with a pair of scissors.
OH YEAH - one last thing - always hold ALT after a fight to see the drops... I'm certain I missed a TON of stuff by not doing this earlier in the game. ALT will reveal anything you can pick up, including drops.

If I were to play this game of thrones in real life, I would be dead already.
The exposition- and politics-heavy narratives in 'Game of Thrones' are a good fit for Telltale Games' choose your own adventure style of games. What make this game stand apart from the studio's other works are its balanced multi-perspective gameplay and the ambiguity of your decisions on the overarching narrative. The latter, especially during those damned-if-you-do-damned-if-you-don't moments, brings much suspense and tension to the game, just like on the television show.
However, it seems like no matter what choices you make in 'Game of Thrones', someone you like or close to you will die anyway, which is pretty true to the books' and the show's spirit. From gaming perspective, this is particularly discouraging since I play games hoping to effect some form of change in the outcome. Yet, given that this game's story has to embed itself into the narrative established by George R.R. Martin's books and the television show, it feels like your decisons and actions are ultimately meaningless in the big scheme of things.
To make things worse, this game -- possible spoiler alert -- ends on a depressing note to fit into the still ongoing story in the television show and for the game's second season. The fact that this game ends with a huge cliffhanger is a mixture of excitement and great anticipation for me as a gamer, but also disappointment from narrative perspective. In the end, even after six episodes, 'Game of Thrones' feels incomplete and unsatisfying overall. Looks like we'll have to wait a year or two before we get to know what will happen next.
I will only recommend this game to players who are fans of 'Game of Thrones' and want supplementary material to the television series. For others, you may want to play this game after this game series is complete so you can experience the entire narrative in one go.

Faster than light was genuinely a really fun game.
It's a rouge style game except in this case the dungeon is interstellar space filled with hostile pirates and rebels. Each playthrough is heavily based on luck, which is not a bad thing. With the amount of scrap that you recieve for upgrades, it keeps you almost certain that no matter how strong your weapons or shields are, there is always some chance that a massive ♥♥♥♥♥torm is lying in wait for you at the next jump beacon that you are not prepared for. Decisons made are memorable, as you can lose your crew with all of the xp they've gained in their prospective fields, fairly regularly. The thing that FTL totally takes away from you as the player, is any sense of control of the world around you. You're just the lone federation ship, that is supposed to have some hope of taking on the rebel capital ship in a single fight, and if you play on even normal difficulty, it's unlikely you'll even make it that far before some ♥♥♥♥ing pirate ship with three defence drones and max shield upgrades ♥♥♥♥s you up on the third stage. The difficulty the game provides you in that uncertainty, is really fun to expierence.
However, after a few playthroughs of the game, this will start to die down as you come into the same random events, knowing which options are the right and wrong ones to take. And seeing how you will likely be dying often and will see the same events very often, it's pretty upsetting that the sense of total spontaneity is gone. If you decide to continue to play it after this point, it won't be about expierencing the game as the unique thing it was for the first 5 or so hours of play, it'll be more of a speed race to see how fast you can beat the game or seeing how badass of a ship you can customize if you linger around zones for as long as possible to get the maximum amount of scrap from it.
Overall, I'd reccomend getting this game if you want to find something truly different from most other games, at least for a few hours. If it's on sale or if you have the 10 bucks lying around, go ahead and get it. You probably won't regret it.

Black Desert has amazing PvP, but you have to jump through quite a few hoops if you want to get to it.
The problem is that the entire game is pretty much based around grinding. Want to level up? Grind mobs. Want to get silver? Grind mobs. Want to enchant your gear? Grind mobs. Want to have fun? Go do some PvP. But, of course, you'll be crushed in PvP if you haven't already grinded mobs for hours in order to get the money and enhancement stones to buy and upgrade gear.
Also, the in-game community is pretty awful. Server chat is incredibly immature, even when compared to other MMO world chats.
That's not to say that I didn't have any fun. In fact, if you can find a friend to grind with and duel with when you're getting bored, I'd say go ahead and get BDO. I'm just not the kind of person who enjoys grinding for hours to get stones that give you a miniscule chance at getting decent gear. More hardcore players than me would probably enjoy the game, but as someone who isn't willing to spend any more money than the base price, and who doesn't want to go through weeks of boredom to get to the fun part, BDO was way too tedious.
tl;dr:
If you're not a very hardcore gamer, and you don't plan on playing with friends, don't get BDO.
It is a fun game if you have friends to play with, but don't expect to have a chance in player vs. player unless you're willing to spend lots of time (or money) getting the necessary gear.

Sid Meier's Civilization V is the turn-based strategy game you want. Let me give a quick tl;dr first:
Amazing strategy, super fun with friends, deep, but easy to learn, pretty polished, but there are flaws.
First off the flaws of the game. This game is good, but it has it's fare share of problems. The first one that'd come to my mind first is the terrible AI of the game. Singleplayer games suffer greatly from this: the AI of the AI is linear. That means, that they don't play according to the spawn they get, or the situation they are in. Another flaw in my opinion is the  game engine. I think a game like this should run on a microwave. It might, at first, but you are going to have major overheating problems (possible pun not intended). My pc is not a beast, the game runs great, but it is heavy on the computer, and in menus the pc cries like a baby. Literally. My temperatures are upwards of 80 Celsius, but in general the problems are small compared to other games. There are other flaws, often to tryhard strategy-fans and civ veterans, but for a new player should be good.
Another point worthy of a word is that
. They greatly enhance the game experience and add tons of content and balances. I wouldn't enjoy the game without dlc. I know, it is annoying, but I didn't enjoy the vanilla game. So firstly, this is the first time I ever bought a game after trying it for free on the weekend. It's so addictive, I just couldn't stop. I've also never bothered with any Minecraft-esque games before, but the blocks make this game perfect for building and destructing.
The game currently has six heroes with varied playstyles and lots of fun to be had. You unlock different perks with them by playing as them and increasing their level, though it certainly is not overpowered to new players. Having a varied team works the best, but I never found myself restricted by bad teammates. It is possible to perform well on your own, but working as a team -as in TF2- just makes it more effective.
The atmosphere is very fun. You have an announcer to motivate you, and your hero has several voice lines to lighten the mood.
The world is at your disposal to do as you wish. The round starts with each team getting 5 minutes to set up their base. Destroy buildings for more blocks, build a huge wall, build traps! Anything is possible and you soon find the timer goes down fast.

If storybook style games are not your thing, you would be doing yourself a disservice by not giving Child of Light a closer look. This game is far more than the simple point and click that many games in this genre offer. If storybook style games ARE something you happen to enjoy... prepare to be blown away. Although the story itself is a bit linear, you will find it holds a surprise or two. The combat is well executed. There is a bit of crafting, collecting and side quests. The ability to construct and enhance a party with interesting, well developed characters lends an air of complexity. And best of all perhaps, the games artwork and music are simply breathtaking. At times it felt as if I was playing within a master crafted water coloring.
Your journey into Child of Light begins when you take on the persona of Aurora, the precocious daughter of the Duke of Austria, in the year of 1895. Aurora falls into a death-like slumber one night to awaken on the mysterious and magical continent of Lemuria. She discovers the land to be under the despotic grip of Umbra, Queen of Darkness. While back in Austria, a bereft Duke mourns his comatose daughter, Aurora finds herself thrust into a daunting mission to bring back the sun and stars which Umbra now holds under her control. At stake is her father, the people of Austria, the varied inhabitants of Lemuria, and Aurora's own destiny.
As you set out to explore Lemuria in hopes of finding a dream path home, you will encounter the Lady of the Forest who will help to arm you with your four greatest assets. A magical sword of unknown properties. A seemingly useless flute. A firefly named Igniculus, who is much more than he may seem at first light. And best of all, the power of flight. Oh, did I forget to mention Aurora can fly? How awesome is that, eh? This one asset alone opens the map to means of exploration not usually encountered in games of any type, and you will most certainly have need to explore.
During the course of your explorations you will encounter many side quests, each of which can enhance your abilities in surprising ways. You will collect "confessions" which help to unfold the story and offer valuable insight. You will collect jewel like occuli which can be crafted and combined to enhance weapons and abilities. Best of all, you will encounter the denizens of Lemuria, many of whom will seek to join you in your quest, and help to overcome the minions of the Dark Queen, sent to impede your progress. Each of these fellow explorers will bring unique personality and abilities of their own to the party. You will find yourself in the company of a Jester that can't seem to rhyme or riddle. A capitalistic, love struck mouse. An untrained gnome-ish spellcaster. A frightening but depressed warrior cat, and perhaps even a lost sibling or two, but that's all I'll say on that. No spoilers for you, my friend.
Game Play:
Child of Light is a standard 2D side scrolling exploration game, with the added dimension of flight. I can not begin to describe what flight, to include the ability to hover in place adds to this game. It is not simply that it removes the "bleh" that sometimes occurs with side scrolling. It serves to open every square inch of the screen to exploration and discovery, which greatly adds to the games total playable area. As for the 2D graphics, the layered artwork in the game is not only beautiful, it adds a sense of depth one would normally expect to encounter in 3D graphics. It is very easy to forget what style of game you are playing as the land of Lemuria draws you in. In addition to exploration and discovery, there are elements of collecting, crafting, character advancement, puzzles and a pretty good combat system. It is designed as a solo game, but can become a two player game with one player controlling Aurora, while the other plays Aurora's companion, igniculus.
Building a party is a major aspect of the game. Every character, including Aurora, will come with an advancement tree specific to that character. As you gain advancement points through accomplishments and combat, those points can be used to expand and or improve upon character abilities. Points can be distributed as you see fit. In addition to advancement points your characters also gain in level. All characters gain level from combat, even if that character did not take part in the combat at hand. You have complete freedom in which characters you advance, as well as which branch of their advancement tree you wish to focus on.
Child of Light can be played at various levels of difficulty. It is suggested that you play through at the lowest difficulty level the first run through for the sake of experiencing the story, and increasing the level for a more challenging replay. Even at it's lowest setting you will find it challenging at points, especially near the end game, but not so difficult that younger players will find it near impossible to complete. Despite the linear aspect of the game that does not allow for alternate endings, I find the game to have a moderate degree of replay value. On minimal difficulty, you should be able to play through the entire game in 10 to 15 hours; Longer if you explore every corner and accumulate every collectible.
Crafting and Collecting:
Crafting in Child of Light is deceptively simple. The only item that is crafted are gem-like items called occuli. You can use occuli as they are, join them to obtain more powerful occuli, or combine them to create new occuli. Occuli are used for the sole purpose of enhancing gear and weapons.
The primary collection items are confessions. To avoid being a spoiler, I will leave it to you to discover the merits of collections for yourself, but be sure to keep an eye out for confession pages. See that piece of paper fluttering in the breeze? Yeah... you might want that...
Combat:
When entering combat, the action shifts to a combat zone. Up to two allies and three foes can engage at any given time. It is smooth and somewhat fast paced. Fortunately for you, party members can be switched out on the fly, allowing you full use of your entire party. You can even save a fallen character by switching them for a fresh party member.
The combat itself is a classic turn based RPG style that incorporates an action time bar. Each character has a specific set of abilities and the ability to switch them out allows for a variety of cooperative combo attacks. Bosses have various attributes as well so combo attacks can be used to exploit weaknesses or counter strengths. The time bar is the most important element of the combat sequence, and many abilities and attacks can manipulate it by hastening the time bar itself, or disrupting an enemy before he can attack.
Unlike many games I have played with this style of combat, selecting the defend option can often be a sound tactical choice that can save you from being interrupted. The defend option is especially useful when one of your combative characters possess buffing, supportive, healing and hastening spells.
Each party member has their own unique skill tree which can be developed along multiple paths to gain new abilities or improve upon existing ones. It should be noted that each character specializes to some degree. Some characters have powerful physical attacks. Others possess elemental attacks and counters. Some are fast attackers, useful in keeping foes disrupted, while yet others excel in a support role. The majority of skill points are best spent on passives to raise HP and defense while using the remaining points to gain and upgrade specific skills. All party members gain experience whether used in combat or not, which allows the entire party to advance as a whole.

So, after playing this game for several days like an addicted maniac, I feel confident to post a review and share my thoughts about this game. First and foremost, English is not my native tongue, so I'm apologizing already for typos and grammatical mistakes. This review is, as any other review, portraying pure honesty.
Now that that's out of the way, let's begin!
The graphics are something that a MMO doesn't necessarily need to be perfect at. An example for that being Runescape or older World of Warcraft. Yet graphics do give it a nice breath of fresh air and show that they care for looks as much as gameplay.
It's easy to say that this game looks breathtaking. I don't understand people who say that it looks ugly. For me, with the settings on max, the game looks phenomenal.
The only aspect that shows how the graphics are getting older is with the textures. It's sad to see so much care put into things like skin, hair and lips, but only to be ruined by the clothing having an average texturing and meshing done.
I hope very much that the developers would update the looks on standard clothing and armor, seeing as the premium ones look good.
+ Beautiful scenery.
+ A lot of attention and care put into facial features.
+/- Generic MMORPG enemies (Orcs, Frogs, Undead, etc.)
+/- Clothing and Armour have average meshing and textures.
- Awesome, highly detailed weapons and clothing costs money.
9/10
Gameplay is something, that is the most essential thing for every game. MMORPGs are no exception to this.
Black Desert Online follows a more traditional Korean root. Grinding is expected, but loot is guaranteed to come as well. The combat system is fluent and very nice. It has quite a lot to do with moving, rather than just casting shields and hoping to survive. Here, you try to avoid all damage with dodging, trying to backstab the enemies.
What I haven't done yet, which is one of the most important aspects of this game after hitting 50, is PvP.
I am purposefully not completing a Level 49 Level up Quest after having read so much negative things about PvP. Knowing that players can just run up and kill you is something I do not want to experience at all. This may sound beyond stupid, but I want to play friendly and team up with people, rather than having to kill them and solo a boss. For my taste, this is something that would push me completely away and make me return to Blade & Soul. Though for all the 49 Levels I have been playing, I can say with most confidence that the PvE is good. It has some cons, but the pros outweigh them.
Another aspect of the game, is traveling. Unlike modern World of Warcraft, you either have a Horse, or you just run. Fast travelling is not a thing in the first 49 levels. And you will be running around a lot. Especially with how much loot you get from enemies, you need to put them at the market in the capital cities and just run back. If you don't have a horse, you're doomed with running constantly several minutes. I personally do not find this bad at all, seeing as it allows me to do some other things like check my mail or get something to drink.
+ Great and fluent Combat System
+ Nice amount of loot.
+/- No Fast Travelling
+/- AI can be dumb at times.
- PvP is forced after level 50
- Questing becomes boring after several hours of questing.
5/10
Very short subject, but to put it simple; Black Desert Online has the worst customization I've ever seen for an MMORPG.
Each clothing has a difference in Blade & Soul or World of Warcraft. Here, you can be lucky if your clothing changes color when you change armor. If you want to look special, you are forced to either grind a LOT of cash and hope you can score a lucky deal in the market, or you buy some awesome armor for real world money.
It just truly surprises me how bad the customization is. If you don't want to be caught in the micro-transactions of the game, you won't get anything. Sure, you have the daily rewards and can get on some days a piece of clothing that lasts 7 days, but that's it. If you don't buy or have amazing luck in the market, you're stuck with a vanilla-look. The only refresh is where you get a piece of clothing during a quest that looks only partially better than some other class-starter-clothing. And that piece of clothing is the only difference you are going to get.
+ Nice looking premium stuff.
+ Daily rewards for playing.
+/- Premium clothing don't give OP Buffs.
- You must pay or farm ridiculously crazy to get nicer-looking clothes.
- Daily reward clothing only lasts 7 days.
- Difference in armor is only statistics and color.
2/10
The skills are something what sets this game apart quite heavily. As with each MMO, you are capable of mining, gathering and fishing.
Where it starts to slightly differentiate is how you collect fluids from mobs, instead of skinning them for fur.
Where it really goes apart is how you can own a boat and go into the open ocean to fish. The further you go out, the bigger the chances of something happening, but also the bigger the chances of getting better loot. If anything, you go out with a guild with boats to hunt whales. Whales! How awesome is that? Another amazing feature is how you can tame wild horses. You can also breed horses, hoping to get a better horse.
These things are a very big and a definite change from the constant mob-farming you do.
You're also always in a relatively safe spot, so even if you hit Level 50, you can just stay in the city, crack open a cold one with the boys, lean back, and enjoy fishing and breeding horses.
+ Fishing is a pleasant change of constant combat.
+ Taming & breeding horses
+ Most of the time in a safe zone.
+/- Performing such skills requires energy.
- Mining, gathering and fluid collecting is very boring.
10/10

Where to start?  HDN is a blast!  I had a great time with it.  But I'll close on the good notes, let's get to some of the bad:
First, the story.  Don't get me wrong, it's funny, it's a clever idea and you'll be laughing at many points.  But, jeepers, you'll be reading lengthy bits of dialogue that cover absolutely nothing.  I don't know how much of the exposition revolves around pudding, but I'm ready to assume that pudding takes up more running time that the actual plot.  And that's what the story is: kill monsters, get pudding.
The game structure  is sooooooo redundant.  Go to the dungeon, get the widget, watch the cutscene, back to the map.  There is NOTHING to mix this up.
Then there is the fan-service.  Oh my gosh, the fan service...  I don't care about the costumes--they are far from the worst out there, but some of the cut-scenes are such repulsive, idiotic cheesecake that it's embarrassing to look at.  I just wanted to hose down Vert and IF by the end.  Seriously, I can barely stomach this kind of schlock.  To its credit, it never gets terribly explicit, but just the thematic elements are a real turn-off.
The characters aren't awful but they feel a little uninspired.  Like the creators just went off of a checklist of character archetypes and just scratched each of them off, and they did so to be funny, I guess.  Not terrible, but I wish they would have been a little more innovative instead of just saying "Hey!  These are generic anime characters!  Get it??  Because we're being humorous and clever!!".
OK, the GOOD!
COMBAT!!!!  The combat system is on of the  best RPG combat systems I've ever seen.  Usually with RPGs I play because I love the story, but HDN is different, the combat is awesome!  You can't just level up until you can hold down a button and win, you're always involved, and there's always a challenge to be had.  You have to think and calculate each move.  Position you party carefully else you might end up taking big damage from an enemy mass-attack.  On my additional playthroughs I skipped all the story stuff and just dove right into fighting more badies and collecting new stuff!
Next is the DLC.  These guys did DLC right!  It's not very expensive, but it adds lots of new features and play time!  The DLC allows you access to the Coliseum, and allows you to level up higher.  These two go hand in hand because you will need those levels to fight in the Coliseum.  Trust me, once you reach level 999 that still doesn't mean you stand a chance in these battles.  I beat them all but great fudge-nuggets, are these guys tough!
I mentioned the humor, and there is some good humor in this.  If you bother to follow the story, it will not inspire you, but you will laugh and enjoy the self-awareness of the whole thing.  I wish the overall writing was better because there is some real potential here, but if a laugh is all you hope for in a story HDN will bring it.
In short, it's fun.  The creators are not great story tellers, but they are great game designers and they did a great job in making an innovative JRPG with a lot of exploration and adventure.
8/10

Divinity is an old-fashion RPG that uses turn based combat sistem, isometric view, character creation with stats and skill and a huge load of dialogues (just think that the translation patch weight 1,4 gigabytes).
You take the role of not one but TWO heroes, the two Source Hunters sent to Cyseal to investigate on the death of Councellor Jack where it looks like the Scourge, a tainted magic, is involved.
Already this first choice is interesting, two heroes, you can play solo and decided their personality or even better you can play co-op with another user and you can take part to double dialogues options with another human!
The game mechanics are pretty simple, outside the combat sequences you have to explore, search and talk with the people, charisma challenges and sneaking will help you if you specialize in those. Talking will eventually reward you with "attitude traits" that will give your character a boost (even bad traits).
The combat is a turn-based combat system that uses the well know Action Points mode, you will have some AP based on your stats and moving or doing actions consume them, you can end your turn when you have depleted them or decided to save them for next turn. Then another character turn begins.
There is a level system and each level grants your character a stat, skill or talent.
The world is split in 3 maps (plus a minimap that serves as "base" for you but I won't spoiler), they are huge and full of quest but on the other side they are "only" three, this makes the game looks almost short even if it took me around 90 hours to complete it.
Item selection is huge as well with the classic rarity based system and the spell selection is not bad either.
All this is packed in a catching storyline with funny parts and a lot of references.
Divinity Original Sin is a must have!
Pro:
- Perfect for co-op but solo play is awesome as well
- Great story and huge load of quests
- Nice crafting system
- A good selection of difficulty levels makes it fit for every user
Cons:
- Class are not really balanced, enchanters are really strong at first but combat class are way better later
- Despite the big load of quest and gaming hours just 3 maps makes the game feel short
- The camera is quite annoying, especially when a single left click does all the actions, you may misclick
-----------------------------------
Sfortunatamente non ho partecipato alla raccolta fondi per questo progetto, l'avrei fatto volentieri.
Divinity è un gioco che strizza l'occhio a vecchi GDR con combattimento a turni, visuale isometrica, personaggi personalizzabili con stat e skill e un casino di dialoghi (la patch italiana pesa da sola 1,4 giga)
Non avrai il controllo di uno ma ben DUE eroi, i due Cacciatori della Sorgente che sono stati mandati a Cyseal per investigare sulla morte del consiglire Jack ucciso in maniera misteriosa, probabilmente tramite l'utilizzo della Sorgente stessa, una magia corrotta.
Già questa scelta è interessante, l'uso di due personaggi che potranno essere giocati in singolo scegliendo le loro personalità o, ancora meglio, affrontando i dialoghi "doppi" in cooperativa con un altro giocatore.
Le meccaniche di gioco sono abbastanza semplici, fuori dal combattimento dovrete esplorare, cercare oggetti e interagire con i personaggi, prove di carisma e di furtività vi saranno d'aiuto se siete specializzati. I dialoghi vi daranno eventualmente dei tratti di personalità che andranno a dare benefici ulteriori ai personaggi (anche quelli negativi).
Il combattimento è strutturato a turni con il noto sistema dei Punti Azione, avrete degli AP in base alle vostre statistiche e muoversi o fare azioni li consumerà, potrete decidere di usarli tutti e chiudere il vostro turno o finirlo in anticipo per salvare PA per il prossimo. Divinity: Original Sin is another masterful entry into the critically acclaimed Divinity Universe from the wonderful Larian Studios!
Divinity: Original Sin follows in the footsteps of it's predecessors, throwing the player into a magnificiently crafted world full of character intrigue, mystery, betrayal and hope. The story plot is free-flowing, allowing for "maximum" freedom in the choices one can make (and although it works quite well at the best of times), it often requires moments of linear gameplay in order to avoid stalls, glitches, etc. The written script is intelligent, often subtle in humour and philosophy. Character customization is similiar to previous titles, allowing for the greatest degree of freedom in hybrid builds and mashups of class types. Combat takes a different turn, heading towards turn based battles - although free movement exists outside of combat. Again, almost all items in the game world can be stolen, found, bartered or sold. Crafting requires a solid memory, as the instructions for craftables are found within lore books, often in rhyme and poetry. Divinity boasts memorable characters, easter eggs and references (in one instance a solid, yet humourful, recommendation to buy Dragon Commander)...
Original Sin's visuals are not spectacular, but unique and arresting to the eye. Colors are bright and vivid, spell effects are often satisfying, and character animations are smooth and fluent. The music of Original Sin is a fantastic element, as composer Kirill Pokrovsky comes aboard once more, delivering a beautiful, atmospheric soundtrack as befits the games style. The mechanics are well implemented and reactive, as you can create hazardous surfaces of fire, ice or slime with combinations of the elements. The content is satisfying (even the semi-pointless Golden Grail and Zandalors Trunks). The UI is simple to follow, the controls easy to master. Character voice overs are rare, but professional in tone and fluency of language. Multiplayer boasts an interesting concept of drop in/drop out gameplay, as the host of any game has complete control over the progression of all characters - only allowing for drop-in players to progress in the campaign, influencing little change over the character controlled.
Divinity: Original Sin is a magnificient title from a wonderful developer, and is absolutely well worth the money and time for those who enjoy tactical RPG experiences with freedom of choice!

I like this game. I really do. I don't recommend it. I already gave them my money and got invested in the story, but honestly, Telltale is going down a very bad path with this episodic game series. They advertise this game based around "choices" and "changing the story around yourself."  In this game, I don't care about my choices. At all. No matter which path I choose, someone will yell at me, someone will not, the game will progress at the same rate, with the same difficulty, and there may be a throwaway line about my "choice" later in the game. Overall, though, my choices affect nothing.  The same people will die, the same plot points will be hit, and I will continue to be paraded around a fancy setpiece by my hand.
Telltale: make more than one path to each objective, based on the choices you make. Make sections of the game objectively harder for players who take a certain path, and objectively easier for players who do not. Add different freaking endings to episodes. Yes, this takes more time. Yes, this takes more money. It's better.

I'll keep this short and sweet.
Pro's:
- Familiar "Telltale" artstyle leads to gorgeous storybook-like environments and settings.
- The story, characters, and dialogue are well-written. Each chapter of every episode has been engaging, and nothing has yet to pull me from the experience. I often find myself admiring (or loathing) characters just as I would their TV counter-parts.
- Your choices shape the way conversations flow.
Con's:
- Sometimes the chapters (and episodes) can feel too short.
- For the majority of the game, the choices you make really don't alter the outcome of the overall story; they're more used to reinforce the User's moral beliefs rather than actually shape the story.
Overall:
- Definitely a great Telltale game - and interactive RPG - that brings the same level of quality you'd expect from them. If you're not a fan of Telltale games, I doubt anything here would change your mind... but if you enjoy their games, jump on this right away - especially if it's on sale. Regardless, it's definitely worth the full-price.

This is a game meant for fans of the original series! With that being said there are several things that are completely different than the original. Here's a list of the what's good, what's been changed from original, and what could be improved.
Good:
- Easy-to-understand user interface for headquarters and battles
- Headquarters a lot easier to change and maintain
- Strategy is still definitely main focus of game
- Overall game easy to pick up and play
- Expansion content "Enemy Within" adds a lot more to base game rejuvenating XCOM
Changes from original:
- There is only one headquarters and skyranger/ship
- Limited to 4 to 6 troops instead of however many you had
- Management of troop equipment streamlined
- Management of headquarters and everything else streamlined
Improvements:
- Customization of troops could have been flushed out more
- Missions/maps were repeating
- Multiplayer was buggy (main problem due to connection errors)
But besides those little nitpicks, XCOM: Enemy Unknown and its expansion "Enemy Within" is definitely worth the buy!

Hanako: Honor & Blade features an unique fighting system that really defines the characteristic feeling of the overall gameplay. Each map is beautifully designed and distinguishes itself from the others, giving each match round a new visual impression. Digging deeper into the story of this game gives the maps an even stronger character, as the player spots the tiny details that are meant to symbolize difficult times or honor lost ones throughout the game.
Gameplay wise, it has a really solid core. You will encounter a few bugs and glitches while playing it, which is obviously due to the state of Early-Access. With the Ite (Bowman) coming out around next year, I expect to see more gameplay changes and improvements that makes Hanako: Honor & Blade a real competition to other fast-paced swordplay games.
You should take your time to roam and understand the different gamemodes as well as the combat system. Although the game is shipped with an combat tutorial, I would find it rather hard as a beginner to get the clear objective of each gamemode from beginning on.

It has Nep Nep.
But in seriousness, this game is a very light hearted game. Granted the characters are fanservices themselves, especially in CPU mode (looking at best transformed waifu Iris Heart <3), but their interactions and dialogues are pretty funny. They will always break the 4th wall, make joke about the game industry (see what I did there? In case you didn't know that, this game takes place in a world  called Gaminsdustri) etc. And Neps (or in Japanese, Nepu)!
Combat-wise is pretty simple; turn based and in each turn you get to hit them as many times as you like (or as Neptune says it "Nepu Nepu ni sheite yan yo!"). Hit them until they die and get rewards. Can't be much easier than that, can it? You also get to place which character go first, how are they position, and most importantly, what additional perks they get from their pairing (for example, some will give a XP boost, while some can shorten your turn time etc). If you are overlevelled, you will just steamroll your way past the mobs (unless you are doing the endgame coliseum, then you can't do that. Choosing the right partners and pairing and equipments are the key here).
Gear wise, it's not so grindy, unless you are planning for endgame DLC gears, where you can only get them from bosses that only can be beaten (and met) via DLC purchases. Granted the DLC ups the cap by 300 per DLC, but this is really needed to beat the bosses in maps and colliseums. Other than that, the only other thing that requires massive grinding is for crafting cosmetic items (processors, accessories and clothes). Granted, processors give you stats, but by the time you reach the endgame, the stats don't matter anymore (well, unless you are taking on the level 900+ coliseum battles).
Levelling wise, again it's not so grindy. Killing on Dangerous boss nets you tons of XP. 1 kill = at least 5 levels worth. Heck the most I saw was around 87 million, which is equivalent to around...... 60 levels? Though that was from an endgame coliseum battle. Even without that, at a certain level you can do coliseum battle with a XP reward while is around half of it. Still a massive levelling up, in my opinion.
Credits wise, it follows the rule for levelling, especially on Dangerous bosses or certain high level coliseum battles, where a victory over them  will net you tons of credits. I love turn based RPG's and Child of Light delivers a satisfying system encouraging strategy and diligence. It's simple, but as the plot progresses you need to employ new strategies and be smarter to keep up with new enemy variants. Child of Light is addicting and entices exploration. It's not far into the game that you gain a new power to roam around with which makes the game much more enjoyable and opens up the 2D map extensively to reveal a much larger world than you realized. Playing alone is fun in itself, but one of my favorite features in Child of Light is the cooperative mechanic that allows for another person to join in to help explore and fight through use of the mouse. Cooperative play adds a whole new element of teamwork as your partner can use the mouse to heal the party or slow enemies while you plan the next move.
The story and presentation of Child of Light is charmingly reminiscent of a classic Disney movie. The journey of Princess Aurora as she finds her way through a magical woods to find a way to save her father, while not breaking ground in storytelling, has that classic fairytale vibe that harkens the mind to more innocent and simple times. As you journey through the woods you'll come across several companions to join your party. While the cast of characters is diverse and their interactions amusing, you'll find yourself using only a couple through the length of the game--bringing an additional one or two out to deal with certain enemy types. This didn't really bother me, but it's to be expected when you have this many characters in your party in such a short game.
I suppose that's my only gripe with Child of Light--it felt short, but that may be because a friend and I beat it in the length of a day. I got it on sale and don't regret what I payed, but I can't help but feel thankful I didn't pay full price. Regardless, I had a blast exploring and fighting bosses with my friend. If you like RPG's with turn-based battle mechanics or a story that harkens back to the classic Disney Princess tales of yore, then you will enjoy Child of Light.
