I am not really into visual novel type of games (or at least, I think I'm not), this is the second game of this genre I've played so far (first being Va-11 Hall-A) and I am either really lucky with the quality of VN I choose to play or I might actually be a secret fan of this genre.
This looks like a classic anime-style visual novel. Pretty pathetic male main protagonist, put into a strange situation trying (or not trying) to impress/befriend a variety of staple anime-girl-archetypes. Doesn't sound very interesting if you put it that way. But there's more to this game than that.
It's set in an old soviet youth camp, with locations, activities and feel recreated and handcrafted with love. It's an incredibly immersive experience of wandering around, partaking in camp life (or trying to avoid partaking in it), all the while looking at gorgeous backgrounds, and listening to what I can only describe as one of the best soundtracks I've heard in a long while. The writing is not particularly impressive, but it's good enough, which is lucky, considering that most of what you do in this game is read (as per usual for the visual novels). The story was compelling enough for me to try and get multiple endings to just find out, what it's all about and experience more of the camp life. While for some this game might inspire sad feelings of wasted youth, misplaced nostalgy or love long lost, for me it was more about the fun atmosphere of childhood, ability to change and finding brightness even in the worst of circumstances.
The steam-version of this game does not include any hentai scenes. If you are really into that, you might want to find an official patch on this game's website, it adds around 10 scenes which otherwise will be 'censored' by a black screen. I don't really suggest doing that though, unless you really need that. I don't think it adds much to this game and actually can detract from the immersion and feel for some.
Some endings in this game are pretty hard to find/unlock. If you get stuck you might want to find a map of routes for this game on the web.
All in all. A solid experience, which I would recommend to pretty much anyone, unless you are really opposed to anime-style graphics.
Also the game is free, so really there is no downside to at least trying if you might like it =)
PS. I don't think I gave music enough justice, so I need to mention it once more: my personal top5 soundtracks of all time!

+ Balance seems to be solid, nice and asymetric with each race bringing a new perspective to the table at every stage of the game.

+ Polished design with no units or technology being truly useless (and all being flexible to some degree) whereas some older CnC games would often have units that never saw real use.
+ Fantastic map editor and custom map support.
+ AI is so smart it's probably self aware.
+ In game encyclopedia offers all the information you'd ever want and then some allowing for quick immersion into the game.
+ Simple and nostalgia ridden return to old RTS, this is a good thing.
+ Solid voices and cinematic work throughout.
+ Great OST with 1 hour and 45 minutes of music, Klepacki makes it.
+/- Campaign is 15 missions and devs opted for a more cinematic route of race-to-race mission flow rather than race by race selection and does a great job of getting you into the mindset of each race making transition into multiplayer smooth.
+/- Map pool is small for now (8 maps), but growing.
+/- Only 4 players supported for now, which may change.
- Not optimized for some machines, higher level graphics requirements, development is aware and attempting to address it. *
- Sometimes persistent alt tabs out of full screen can crash.
- Region locks, can be partially fixed with steam client adjustment but this can cause absurd lag for some people depending on geography. **
- No observer or replay function, though as of 1-27-2015 they are hard at work at implimenting it.
- PC release only
* - They are aware of the optimization issues and attempting to fix
** - They are aware of the region restrictions and matchmaking bugs and are attempting to remedy them as well
Final Rating: 8/10

The game is absolutely breathtaking. The art style is very weathered and homey. My favorite thing about the game was the windows. The entire experience took me an hour, and that's if you REALLY take your time. I think Leaving Lyndow is a very directed game. It knows what it wants to say, and it gets in and gets out quick, but leaves you time to linger.
Imagine if you took the feeling of leaving Pallet town for the first time, and stretched it out for an hour while adding an extra gallon of class and art. That's Leaving Lyndow. I think if Eastshade is able to improve upon Leaving Lyndow in even a small way, it will turn out to be a rather good game.
I think the art, music, detail, pacing, and design are all exceptionally well done, and very impressive. I think the character design is kinda creepy, but very homely. I think if the story aspect had half of the depth that the art and design had, it would be a very compelling title, even at its brief length.
I think where Eastshade could benefit most going forward is by having a dedicated writer as well as another programmer and some more play-testers. Leaving Lyndow is a very nice, small scale "Art" game. And that's good, but adding more "game" while keeping the same art will help the next game sell tremendously well.
So should you buy? I think Leaving Lyndow fits very nicely into the $4.99 price range. And its actually only $3.99 so, yeah. Its not much, but whats there is definitely worth it.

Probably one of the best tactical RPGs i played in a while. Very complex, took me 3 attempts to understand all of the mechanics (especially in the political world view part) - but definately worth while.
Pros:
- Intuitive battle system, with lots of tactical choices.
- Immersive and well balanced story.
- Decent graphics.
- Nice varieties of classes that feel quite different to play with.
Cons:
- Still has a few bug issues, that can be pretty annoying.
- It takes a while to get attached to your units. Unlike other tactical RPGs ive played they are completely randomised and can be fully customised. Some might like that, but it really annoyed me, that they were no defined characters you get a hang to such as in Fire Emblem or Shining Force.
- Battle get kind of repetitive as they are all kind of the same. They also appear to be random, the only thing chaning is the strength of enemy units as you progress.
PS: Make sure you buy the bundle, as its not much more expesive and gives you a lot of cool extra content: Modify your units to become cyborgs. Pretty damn cool.

While this genre is now often called the grandpappy of MOBAs and Tower Defense games in this day and age, I'm still an avid fan of RTSs and Grey Goo does not disappoint! It takes many of the best elements from the C&C series and incorporates some progressive new ideas of it's own!
- Single player is incredibly well polished, with great cutscenes, although the story itself leaves something to be desired.
- The QWERTY hotkey-bar setup takes a little while to get used to but is generally much more user friendly than other RTS hotkey configurations like SC and AoE.
- The foliage cover mechanic is a fun twist to traditional cloaking.
- So far balancing between the three factions looks solid, but I haven't played that many multiplayer games yet so we'll have to wait and see if it still feels right after that.
- I enjoy having the resource rate meter on the top right, like Supereme Commander and other games in that vein vs. just a straight up resource count.
- The multiplayer games I've played with my friends so far have been action packed from the get-go. Even with 2 factions having walls, turtling doesn't seem to work as a valid strategy for too long.
- The unit upgrades in the game are more strategic than, "This just makes my units beefier," like SC2 where you pretty much have to get some upgrades without thinking too hard about them.
- The Goo is probably the most unique faction I have EVER played in any RTS game. It will be a lot of fun to master!
My only major gripe with this game is that the multiplayer scene looks a little scant so far. More people who love RTSs (of which there may not be many) please buy this game so I can play with yo'll!!! :D

At first I thought it was an ok game, not as good as TQ but more refined with new fresh ideas. But at least for singleplayer it is right now just only frustrating and nothing else. It looked interesting, promising a rich story and decisions that actually matter. Well they do, not even nitpicking all the small flaws in that. The problem is not really all that is around it, the problem is the core gameplay. Monsters that get stuck in walls, vanishing from the map completely, resetting their "spawn" points there is this and that and small stuff like that. Many many little things. But most of all it´s the randomness that shuts down any serious attempt for interesting singleplayer builds. Not in Diablo, not in Path of Exile, not even in TQ and not in any other RPG have I ever encountered so much random deaths in which I have had no idea what killed me. Given I do try to make glasscannonbuilds work because I know I am by far above the average player in skill so glasscannon-builds in singleplayer was always not just the most fun for me to play but also a personal challenge. But I can not do that in this game, sure I can get through the main game, the final boss is a joke at best (not because a glasscannon can do it without dying, true glasscannon, not some 20k health "glasscannon" with full resistances at everything which is the recommended glasscannon because you took one item that is more damage than defense or lifesteal), but it is no fun. This game is no fun. There is no fun to play what you want. You either play multiplayer so you can play what you want because other players sacrifice themselves to build tanky to tank for you, but other than that no build is actually viable for singleplayer. This is a game that is created for hardcore players. But whenever I build something that is not completely stupid like: "I can only facetank for 20 minutes without moving from one spot and not a whole hour, this is too difficult" (and that is after retaliation builds were nerfed). Well whenever I build anything that is remotely interesting then it is not viable for anything endgame related. Note that endgame for me as a hardcore player is not the end of the story mode, but actually farming after the story is completed, which is what this game has a mainfocus on. There is so much content that is more difficult than the actual gameplay that I wonder if following the story is actually what this game ever intended to do. And to top it all of, neither kiting nor damage are encouraged to be used either. After mobs actually hit level 85+ themselves they are just super tanky so if you build glasscannon and get oneshot by them, it is not just that you can not do the same to it, you probably will need more than a full spellrotation to even finish them off. And that is normal mobs, heroes, bosses and nemesis monster are a whole other thing. I am sorry, whenever you propose some changes to the community this game has attracted with their catering to "hardcore" players, you instantly get shot down because YOU are the one destroying their fun in the game by making it too easy. I don´t even care about not being good at the game, I will gladly build characters that die a 1000 deaths but then I want to know what actually kills me, I want a fair chance at kiting, a fair chance to avoid skillshot. What I get instead are monsters that glitch out of their normal "reset" areas in narrow passages where they can shoot you through walls while you can´t do the same to them. You get descriptions that are absolutely lackluster in every sense possible. If you want to not ruin a character from the getgo by having an idea what could be a good build that is fun to play...well then you better get ready to search informations on the internet for hours and hours, because you won´t find them in the game itself at all. I get ranged mobs that shoot me from outside the screen. My abilites trigger mobs that are not on the screen, they can see me through walls anyways so not that it really matters. And bossabilites from salazar or the endboss or nemesis spawns that you can maybe block if you react very quick...but that is if you have a blockability, because there is no evading them that is possible. And they stun you with unavoidable abilities. Or they debuff you without the game showing it to you. Or you spawn friendly mobs that look exactly like enemy mobs so you have no idea what is even going on anymore. Once you triggered a boss that oneshots you it can be that you step into sight and he shots without an animation playing. ALL ranged mobs have the ability to shoot through their own bodies once you get in range (which is most of the times even bigger than your own range) and will hit you before they even turn around their own axis. There are by far too few points to ever use a second mastery in any useful way, especially when you go for arcanist or demolitionist. There are too many legendaries that are absolutely unuseable because they are just not balanced at all. Some setbonuses are so strong that using individual pieces is not ever recommended whatsoever so they take up the very limited inventory space. Devotions can trigger or not...you´ll find the information...somewhere, I´m sure of it...maybe not. But I mean you are a hardcore player if you bought this game so there is no problem at all, it´s not the games fault, it´s the fault of losers that are just not hardcore enough for it´s design...and after all, you can mod this game. Once you can mod a game that takes all responsibility of the devs, because after all, if you want to make the game better than just do it and don´t criticize...Or quit, which is what I´ll do for now. Maybe when I have no other game to play and like standing around mindlessly for a game and then click something every half a minute or so then I´ll come back. Man, this game has so much potential but it´s the little things. It was just too enthusastic with the challenge it took on, coming from kickstarter...there was just too much for too little of ressources I guess. In the end, I am still glad I tried it, but just sad that I´ll probably forget everything about it in a year, because there was absolutely nothing memorable to take away from it other than endless frustration.

I can't recommend this game anymore.
This game is just annoying. Since beta it's been nothing but a tease and I'm tired of it. There have even been changes to completely nullify the builds I've been interested in creating leaving fewer interesting options to choose from. I've supported this game for a long time and I'm just fed up within the convoluted nonsense.
I keep coming back to this game because it could be such a good ARPG but it's just not after you dissect it. The story is great, art is sweet, effects are awesome, but good god it's such a headache to actually play the way you want when it claims highly diverse customization. When you're trucking through the same content over and over and over you probably want to do it in a way that's fun every time. It's simple if you can decipher a build that you enjoy. There are tons of different ways to do it but most of them aren't fun if you like to do more than left-click. If you like gameplay that involves more than left clicking you'll be hard-pressed to find an effective build. You'll find yourself in a convoluted maze. I'm a person who wants to be more involved in the combat. I don't want to hold a button down. I want to react and respond to situations with my brain and with the tools I have.
I also want real flexibility in build customization and expecially when a game advertises it. I have spent SO MUCH TIME just trying to figure out if a build I want to play is actually possible only to find out 45 minutes and a headache after using the player-supported calculator and database that it's not. Nothing but cringe follows because this game advertises deep customization. There's a huge difference between deep within a gold mine and deep within a bucket of sand.
Thank god for the player-supported calculators that have potentially saved me much frustration. Seems like this is something that could be added into the game itself to help maintain immersion and allow players to plan their builds within the game instead of tabbing out, surfing the web, and wiping all immersion. The build calculators are really a godsend because I could've arrived at this point much much later. With all the work that's gone into this game, I don't understand why this hasn't been added.

Graphics are polished just enough that the game still appears current.
Game Balance - Fairly balanced as of this writing but there are a few heroes that could use a boost to their blocks or abilities to put them inline with others.
Singleplayer - A custom game or training mode allows you to get use to the maps, heroes, base-building mechanics along with the provided tutorials and videos. You can lock down a custom mode game with a friend(s) and train or strategize your gameplay for Casual or Ranked modes.
Multiplayer - Lots of fun with a decent group of people (or at least a group that's forgiving/helpful and not jumping down your throat). Games start pretty quickly in the Casual mode but the new Ranked mode takes up to 30 minutes to get a game together. Hopefully that is resolved with more people playing this game. Built-in voice chat that works fairly well too.
Maps - Quite a few maps to choose from and battle on. A good variation with all sorts of stategies for each and more maps being added fairly frequently.
Heroes - Fun to play and a playstyle for anyone. More heroes being added and they've been very well balanced. There's no set team and most times you can play what you want with hurting the team too much. Communication is key; type or speak call outs and strategy in-game.
Overall - I love this game. Great game, very addicting gameplay. So much fun to strategize building your defensive (and offensive) blocks then go after their cubes (bases). If you're looking for a comparison, as most posts claim, Minecraft combined with Team Fortress 2. I bought the skin pack purely to help the developers out and get more people playing this game. I suppose the skins are kinda cool too. =P
If you pick up the game, feel free to add me if you're looking for a buddy to group with. Always down for some BnL with good people.

Many call this game the unholy marriage of minecraft and TF2, which is true mechanically speaking, but the game has a lot of charm all it's own too.
Pros:
-Easy to pick up the game
-Runs on just about any pc
-Queue times are reasonable and often quick
-The mechanics of the game are fun and make every game experience unique because you have to think on your toes when defending or assaulting, following a "meta" would only serve to make you easy to predict and counter.
-It's NOT free to play, which given the nature of this game, is a good thing.  Plus no unreasonably long grinding for class leveling.
-The devs hold polls and take community input and seem to put a lot of effort into the gameplay and balance.
-
Cons:
-Only 5v5 but later on 10v10 will be included
-Variety in maps and characters and weapons are a bit lacking, but that's already planned to be improved later on
-It's easy to get griefed in this game, but luckily the game isn't free to play so you see far less of that in this game compared to others.
-The game needs a some what better anti cheat system.  You wont see hackers all the time, but they do rear their ugly heads.  Hacks I've seen so far are speed hacks and damage hacks, and no I they weren't using a block buster when I saw this happen.
-Team reliance, I love team games, but if you have really bad team mates, you're probably in for a loss, make use of that surrender button if that happens.
If I were to rate this game on a scale of 1-10, I'd give it an 8, it's a lot of fun for 20 dollars, I've been playing since the free weekend event for steam release and I already have 40 hours on the game writing this review.
The game could use some work and more content, but luckily Jagex seems to be getting on that as they recently opened a poll to vote for what features the community wants them to take priority on, things like 10v10, map editors, more weapons and classes and blocks, etc etc.

First off, I mostly paid little to no attention to this game upon release due to the zombie genre being so overdone lately... It seems like several new games come out every week sometimes and it just becomes easy to view as overplayed and people can start to lose interest. For that reason I haven't gotten into several recent zombie games that I may or may not end up liking as I also don't have enough hours in the day to get to other kinds of games that I'm also interested in. Not that I don't like the genre, I love the better zombie and other post-apocalytpic franchises out there, but sometimes enough is enough of something. But that said...
I'm not sure I remember the exact moment something finally sparked my interest in Dying Light, more than likely it was footage on Youtube, as well as hearing about active developer support and enhancements (always a big plus to me). I think after realizing it was also a parkour game and the story looked good, I finally settled on getting the base game when it came on a good sale somewhere. Right off the bat many things about it put it head and shoulders above much of the zombie and survival genres... First off and here's something you don't really see anywhere else: there's a huge variety in zombies, you have the standard walkers/biters, then the much faster runners (known as Virals and appear to be recently infected people who sometimes seem to revert to their former selves during combat and start to cry and cower but then immediately switch back to terrifying monsters that attack you with human strength and speed). Then there's an array of mutating abominations... 'Toads" that launch corrosive material at you from a good distance, exploders that run up to you and explode, 'Goons' and 'Demolishers' that are huge, deadly, and take a long time to take out, but the worst ones come out only at night: Volatiles and Night Hunters (the latter only played by other human players in online mode). Night time can be extrmeley difficult to be outside of safe zones because of the latter two.
The parkour element of the game IMO controls and plays much better than Mirror's Edge and the melee combat has been pretty fluid for me. The game mostly focuses on melee combat since loud noises attrack large numbers of Virals that are very difficult to take on at earlier levels and ammo isn't everywhere, but there are guns and some parts of the game where you'll more likely being engaging in gun fights with human opponents. The FPS mechanics aren't quite as good as standard FPS's but it pulls it off where needed. You also get access to archery eventually, which works well enough and gets funner with exploding arrows, electrified arrows, etc. Many melee weapons can also be modified and crafted to include fire, lightening, toxic, and other elemental bonuses as well as added damage and durability. You also eventually get access to fun tools like grappling hooks which lets you Spider-Man your way across the city of Harran with great ease and speed, and you also get to unlock many great fighting skills and survival perks.
The game is excruciatingly difficult at first and has learning curves that took me a few weeks to get past (when I had the time, others may figure some things out much sooner than I did). The online mode is fun and allows others to join your game and wreck havoc, though I opted to turn it off while I was learning all the aspects of how the game works as well as leveling my character up and gaining better weapons and skills. Online also doesn't make a lot of sense canonically because everybody is playing the same character, Crane, but it's still fun. You can also enable 'zombie invasions' in online mode, which I didn't understand at first because, didn't the zombie invasion already happen? Well what it turns out to be is allowing players that are playing the afore=mentioned Night Hunters to come in and try to invade your game at night time. I haven't actually gotten around to doing that yet but it looks like great fun.
So I'm 66 hours in as of this writing and only about a third of the way through the main story if I'm not mistaken. There is much to do and I haven't even gotten to the expansions yet. Technically-wise the game has run absolutely flawless on my system EXCEPT for occasional crashing issues on Linux but it's been happening much less frequently lately so it might be somewhat patched out? At any rate I've been able to play several long sessions in a row without it happening so that's good. Never experienced any frame drops in the thick of battle nor any other significant glitches and online mode has generally been flawless as far as I can remember.
And for those who care: NATIVE DUALSHOCK 4 SUPPORT. YES.
After getting over the initial learning curves and getting to where I could take on challenges, slice through enemies, and get through missions I've become quite sucked into this game and could easily classify this as one of the all-time greatest and that's no joke. If you've been watching footage and you think this looks up your alley then I would highly recommend it. 9.5/10.

Here's the thing, I like RTs and am a hardcore fan, but I don't like to go pro online, or anything like that as I never like online systems, and the same will be with this game, so I play skrimish, campaign and with friends, but STILL there are major problems I see.
Cons-
1. The Humans- The humans are more for turtling, but you can't build beyond your starting position most of the time because conduits can't go over any terrain basically. So supply lines get huge and you must divert your forces to protect the miners. The Beta and Goo don't have this problem, and THIS IS MAJOR!!!! because resources run out which pisses me off a little. Just make it either slow regeneration or less income once it reaches the bottom don't remove it all together.
2. Unit Cap- I don't want a game very similar to starcraft. I want a game like CnC with as many units as the computer can take, massive.... MASSIVE battles(also like many huge RTS games) having a unit cap takes away from that. It makes the game more limited.
3. Player Count- 4.....really? Only 4? From what I've seen 4 players is it which at that point I'm like, "LAME!"
4. Campaign gameplay- Well if you've played it, most people will probably be like c'mon wanna play the Goo campaign. Well 15 missions essentially and 90% of them are kill the enemy. there are at most 3 that aren't "kill the enemy". It's fine if it's like that but maybe have cool assaults or epic maps, nah. There are never more than 3 more commanders on the field. You only get an ally for one mission(haven't 100% the goo yet as I need a brake from "KILL THE ENEMY!") and that mission is kill the enemy. Not hold off and distract long enough to detonate the bomb(sorry spoilers) just kill the enemy.
There are probably other problems but before I stop.
5. Player Content- ok love it how they support the community....steam workshop? Um can you mod this for more unit cap or stuff like that?(You can but the config is a .MEG file...REALLY?!) They do support it but they shouldn't rely on people to make cooler maps to add to their collections. There is only like 7 maps...only 7 and most of them are very similar. I REALLY HOPE that the community through mods if they can and maps make this game much better. If they can make unlimited unit cap and balance the races more to cope with that. Make it so that the player count is 8 or above for better play(if they can) etc...
Pros...Sorry fror bashing on a game but people need to understand from a casual gamer what it is like playing a game and what you should get, but here are the pros.
Camapign Cutscenes- Beautiful and stay with the story. They can immerse you in the universe fairly quickly but sadly what it seems like you're doing from the cutscenes doesn't happen in the gameplay half the time.
Factions- Now I know I bashed on the humans but the factions are unique, especially the Goo. If they kill something they use the matter to grow and reporudce more quickly. The regular goo can quickly consume enemies that are alone or in small groups and can flee up terrain once done. owever to limit their OPness on the ground they get no air. Sadly the Goo and Humans are very similar to Earth's 2160 counterparts.
Epics- Now the epics are essentially the Titans of Warhammer. They are ultimate units and deserve to be for taking up 70 unit cap. However each is unique to the faction. The humans sport a collosal humanoid robot with a large beam that seeps and kills most units in it's path. The purger for the Goo is the ultimate evolution and can attack from range while also getting close and absorbing the enemies through a potent (I guess melee attack). The Beta get a mobile fortress which can produce units and house them for close range defense.
Learning Curve- Factions are easy to learn but definitely hard to master.
Now I know it looks like I dislike this game, I don't it's just I expect better now. I mean to put a unit cap and then express how the game would run smoothlymakes me say "really? maybe the game runs smoothly not because of the servers but the unit cap?" Also the factions still need work even though polish was done some very clear things should be fixed. like Humans and Beta should be able to build more command centrs(Goo can.....and humans need it to continue to expand). This game is worth the money but not more worth it and that makes me sad. Until player content streams in this game is not that great to me. Any RTS fans wanting something new though go ahead and try it, you'll get your money's worth.

(Mind you, I'm in no way photosensitive like some others who have left a negative review on this game have been, and I can handle rapid flashing just fine, but if it becomes gameplay-inhibiting, then the design is absolutely flawed.)
Problems with the game:
* Often screen-filling visual effects that prevent you from seeing what is going on. You can't dodge bullets if you can't see them...
* Overboard on the "flashy sparkly fireworks" effects. I mean, way overboard, and then some. It's not "cool", it's not "attractive", and it gives you a headache if you're not careful.
* The music plays very soft. I have properly balanced music files and they simply don't play at a decent volume in the game - for a music-focused game you'd expect the audio component to be at least adequate and give priority to proper playback without having to amplify it into clipping ranges.
* Scoring is meaningless: levels are random, so what rewards you get and points you score for a song is not dependent on the music at all. Score is determined by chance and not by skill, as a result.
* Music-based firepower will favor even, loud songs. You get a dynamic song with breaks and softer parts and you're pretty much at the mercy of whatever random fleets of ships are thrown your way with no way to fight them off. And woe if you hit a quiet spot when a boss is thrown at you. Good luck with that, get ready for a grind.
* Screen-filling visual effects that.. Ohwait, I already said that. :P Yes, it's a problem. Worthy of mentioning twice. It kills the ability to properly play a "bullet hell" game. Period.

Leaving Lyndow is a game about saying goodbye. Exploring the village where you have grown up, you're saying a last goodbye to your childhood and everyone in it before going on a trip to discover what the world has to offer.
The game looks breathtaking and has an amazing scenery with a world that feels a bit odd but real at the same time. Although everything looks amazing and has great detail from up close, once you start to look a bit further (to the parts of the map you can't reach), they look a bit empty and rushed. However, some great music helps immersing yourself in the world, and the sound effects are great in general. While playing Leaving Lyndow, you interact with different objects, talk to people and find out more about Clara, the character you're playing and her relationship with everybody. However, these conversations can be a bit boring and feel unfinished.
Now, Leaving Lyndow is a rather short game and can be completed in about 20-40 minutes. This makes it a bit expansive but still worth it if you like walking simulators and exploring. One of the reasons Leaving Lyndow is a bit expansive and on the short side, is because this game is getting used to fund and introduce the player to the game Eastshade. Eastshade will be a larger exploration game set in the same world. where you fill the shoes of a traveling painter.
I do recommend Leaving Lyndow, especially if you're looking forward to Eastshade and like walking simulators. Keep in mind, the game is short and a bit expansive, so waiting for a sale might be a good option as well. Overall a great game, with some fantastic looking locations and great details.

A short, but memorable journey we take by controlling Clara, a girl who is about to set sail and leave her homeland for a couple of years in order to follow her dream to become an explorer.
Now, this is a walking sim (a.k.a. first person exploration game) which means the road to the endgame is short. The game can be completed in 20 minutes or so. Still, the ride is enjoyable and if you are a screenshot aficionado like myself you'll take some shots once you reach the docks or find the throng of bloomsac's on the farm of Clara's uncle. During the game you interact with objects, talk to people and collect some items needed to be able to continue to the next area.
Beside the quicklauncher nothing tells you that this is a typical Unity-based game as it runs smoothly; you never get the feeling of seeing reused assets. And while you stop to look at the great vistas the game has to offer it is all accompanied by some of the greatest soundtrack I have recently heard in videogames.
Thumbs up, Eastshade! Looking forward to your future (hopefully much longer) projects!

This game is a gem. A successor of Titan Quest (TQ) and a welcome variant to ARPG from those of us who enjoyed but are a little tired of (the excellent) Diablo 3 (D3). Like TQ and unlike D3 here you make characters by combining 2 classes. Each class has many different branches. You also select stats when leveling. The result is a lot of depth and variety in customizing your character.  You can create a "pure" mage, brawler, ranged character. But even those "pure" archetypes have different variants. Or you can combine them to create a battle mage, a pet class, a gunslinger and many others. Speaking of guns, one of the classes is the demolitionist, which can use in bombs, mines, mortars. The game throws you less mobs than D3 so it is a bit slower, which again is a nice change, but not too much slower; you still be killing scores of mobs just not scores*scores of mobs. Perhaps the most interesting change is that the game doesn't feel like you are rushing to high level to start the "real" game. In GD, the "real" game starts at level 1. It encourages a lot of exploration as you find special altars scattered throughout the world that when activated gives you access to special powers called "devotions". These are represented as constellations (similar to Skyrim) and there are dozens such constellations each having some 5 powers. Again you have a lot of customization options.
A short addendum: I recently discovered that Grim Dawn has a very active mod community. I installed the necromancer mod: awesome. ARPG fans can't go wrong with getting this game.

Where to start? Firstly, it detracts from the main gameplay component of the entire series: real-time combat. I don't like turn-based games and generally they are boring and slow. In a gaming world of this generation, do we really need a turn-based game that previously was real-time based? Divine Divinity was awesome, and so was Divinity II; but this game was an absolute disappointment. It is far from being given a review and I urge Larian Studios not to develop another turn-based game and move forward with the storyline and develop a real-time action-rpg which is on par with modern RPGs such as Torchlight 2 and Diablo 3. To get the best of both worlds, a system whereby you can pause the game and emuulate a turn-based experience or just having a real-time action game would be of proven merit. Overall, I'd give this game a 6/10 for GFX; 3/10 for gameplay; 5/10 for story.

The game has a lot of potential, but the question turned me away from being able to progress any further than 2 hours. It's just really clunky and confusing. The last thing that made me not want to play any more is the actual battle system keys. They're just weird. It's not like a standard MMO. They have weird key combinations for your abilities like CTRL+Right Click and Shift+R or Tab+E, etc. I couldn't get past it. If that doesn't bother you and you can get past it, I think you'll enjoy it. If you're looking for a standard MMO, I don't believe you'll enjoy Black Desert Online.

Someone needed to say this. No game is more RAM intensive than D:OS. Even with minimum system requirements, and streaming textures turned off (something which is a no-no in any case), I encountered 30+ minute load times, extreme lagg, and an inablity to even get past the first village.  On a system which fits the minimum system requirements, this is a no-no, and a sign that the engine is not optimized past the point of the frankenstein monster.
I eventually had to uninstall this 40 Gb behemoth, hoping to come back to it with a beefier rig.
On to the gameplay: environmental interactions were already done by Bioshock (a terrible game, IMO, in contrast to System Shock 2); nothing stands out about the setting--just more generic, cliched fantasy; choices seemed binary and forced, though more branching than Bioware--thank God!
In other words, nothing stands out as completely original. If you've played the original two Fallouts, you already have an idea what choice-and-consequence can do, and the game was an attempt at a retro-fallback, one which succeeded brilliantly in design, and flawed in execution, simply due to a poorly implemented and refined engine.
I could not make it much past the first-town, thanks to the excessive lag, but if you enjoy the sense of a turn-based RPG with artificial rather than emergent choices, but with the one-trick-pony of an emergent design to spellcasting, once again done by Bio♥♥♥♥e; this game may appeal to you--so long as you enjoy tripe and usual fantasy. Otherwise, it's a bruiser, but also a misser; if Larian had spent as much time nailing their engine as good gameplay, not only would they have a winner, they'd have a contender against other similar turn-based games like Shadowrun and Grimrock.
I have seen much better looking game functioning on a third the system requirements of Divinity: Original Sin.
Which tells you something about their design team. What good is a good game without a proper implementation?
Next time, when you advertise minimum system requirements, make sure the game runs on minimum. No lag.
Then you won't have to worry about poor reviews, like this one.
To nail the camel: my rig exceeds, not only meets, the basic requirements--which makes this even worse.
I still experience lag, and slowdown, even with streaming textures turned off in the .ini. And that was simply to get the unoptomized mess running... Good luck!

Black Desert Online probably has the best graphics among all MMORPGs. It does kind of feel like playing skyrim with those visual mods installed. The combat system actually feels like an action game, better than most similar games I've played so far. And the character editor is absolutely top notch. However, the game has some flaws that could be a dealbreaker for many people:
1. Lack of cosmetics variety. I leveled my first character to level 52, and I've been wearing the same armor for at least 40 levels. All free armors look very similar. If you want your charactor look a bit more fancy, you have to buy those costumes with REAL MONEY. The same thing also apply to your horse and house. There's no free way to make yourself look fancy.
2. No fast travel. The map is huge. Sometimes you literally have to sit back and wait 10+ minutes for your horse to auto run you from point A to B.
3. No free pets. I never owned a pet, and I don't know how helpful they are in combat. But why not make some pet that I can buy with in game currency that I earned?
4. Repetitive missions. Well, this is pretty common among all MMORPGs right?
So, if you're someone who love MMORPG, you'll like this game. If you're looking for an RPG with great story and gameplay that never gets boring, Black desert online is not for you.

I love this game more than any MMO I've ever played but I really can't give it a positive review for several reasons. The game is very strong in the professions you can do, anywhere from gathering to trading, to even sailing the high seas to hunt whales! The game is huge and is completely open world. You can make your own empire and focus on ship building, or you can go on to become the leader of a massive trading company while your workers make all the goods for you. The possibilities of the game are endless... but... let’s talk about the multiplayer aspect. It is so limited... I hardly could call this a MMO, but would rather call it "Single player Online." Why? Cause there is so little you can do to help out your guild or friends outside of pvp and knowledge. This game severally lacks a trading system so you can help your friend build that awesome galleon to sail the seas or to help them get a piece of gear they may have accidently got. There is almost no trading outside of the broken marketplace. Market prices are set which is nice but what grinds my gears is the lack of giving a friend the item you want to get them. There is a bidding system but it seems to be completely run by a trash RNG system like most of the game. On top of that the more and more I try to get items I want on the marketplace the more and more I believe there are bot programs which auto buy things when an item goes up. I can sit there for hours and not get a single item I want just because another person/bot is able to get it in less than a second, even if it takes me a few seconds to try and get an item. There is a boat in this game that takes weeks of work to get but you can't have friends help you out just cause any form of trading is non-existent... This game is a Single player game! This game is fantastic. It immerses you into the world of Game of Thrones just as well as the show does. And while the story itself is incredibly different from the books or the show, it doesn't harm the original books in any way. Or at least, in my opinion. The non-original characters in this game, such as Jon, Tyrion, Ramsey or Daenarys, are spot on with the way they're written in the books or portrayed in the show. There is no deviation. So the characters involved are well written, which helps with the immersion.
I've played up until the end of Episode 4 now. Can't wait for episode 5 to be released! The game itself focuses primarily on tough decisions in tense situations on a timer. And the timer isn't long. 3-5 seconds at best. In most cases,  it doesn't even give you enough time to read the full answer, so be prepared to skim the answers and make a selection fast. There is some combat in the game, but it's few and far between and extremely easy. Like tapping buttons at a certain time. And I've noticed that the timers on the buttons aren't specific and a lot of times, if you miss something, the game will perform it for you. This doens't always happen, but it has happened a few times for me when distracted by a barking dog or attempting to eat and play at the same time. haha.
There are several different stories happening all at the same time. The kicker is that each story is different, but your decisions on one character directly affect another character's story. For example WITHOUT SPOILERS, if you were to go to the store and purchase the last loaf of bread, the customer after wanting that bread is going to be directly affected by your decision to buy that loaf. Crazy example, but I had to pick something not game related.
WIth that said, you are going to have to remember some of the decisions you made on one character when making decisions on another. If your decisions conflict, there could be trouble. And perhaps even better than any of this is the fact the game is incredibly gripping. The climatic points in the game's story leave you on the edge of your seat just as much as the books have done. Or the show at its peak points in a season. Sometimes after a decision, I find myself immediately regretting the decision I've made based on what happened as a result. But by then, it's too late to change your answer! I stick with what I've got, mostly because in the real world, you can't go back on most of the decisions once they're made. Furthermore, some of these decisions are incredibly puzzling, but again, you're only given so much time to answer. Sometimes you'll be forced to please another character. Other times, you'll be stuck in the same room with two characters you have dealings with and be forced to choose between one or the other, which will negatively impact one story line while positively impacting another. The fact that you absolutely cannot make everyone happy makes this game believable. And the idea that you cannot win the game in that reguard makes it that much more fun. You'll never be bored!
In any case, I highly recommend this game. I'm glad I picked it up and I look forward to the last 2 episodes, as well as playnig more A Telltale Games Series games.

One of the best things about this game is that it weaves characters, settings, and plots from the TV series into a completely new storyline. This game unfolds in such a way so the player/viewer understands the importance of actions and dialogue that occur between scenes of the GoT TV series.

The only downside to this game is the occasional bug with loading, freezing and saving the game, all things that are not detrimental to distract from the overall experiene. Another thing to note is that this game relies on keyboard and mouse commands, so I suggest you keep your fingers ready to press away those buttons and most definitely use a mouse over a trackpad if you are able.

tl:dr version:- an enjoyable and beautiful looking game that combines metroidvania style levels with jrpg style combat though it start to feel dull and repetitive towards the end.
Full version:
This game sees you play as Aurora, a young Austrian princess who wakes up in a strange land called Lemuria and must try and find a way to get back to her father with the help of some friends who join her along the way. The gameplay is interesting as it combines metroidvania style levels with jrpg style combat and its actually a good combination. It also has a greats setting in Lemuria and is a visually beautiful game.
Good points:
- the game looks beautiful and the animation is like something from a fairytale book which fits the game really well. Lemuria makes for a great setting as well with its strange and varied inhabitants and locations
- i quite liked the combat in this game. You can see enemies moving around the levels and bumping into them initiates combat. A type of active battle system with a progress bar is used, where the key is to interrupt your enemies attack during the casting phase or avoiding having your attacks being interrupted.  On top of this a firefly you control can be hovered over an enemy to slow theirprogress to their next attack, hover over allies to heal them as well as picking up hp and mp boosts. This lends a tactical approach to battles
-the soundtrack for this game is quite nice and really adds to the games atmosphere
Bad points:
- the games story is a bit dull which is a shame. The characters all speak in rhyming lines which kind of limits story development and gets annoying after a while. Given Lemuria seems like an interesting place it feels like a missed oppurtunity to not have an interesting story to go with it.
- the game does start to get a bit repetitive towards the end. There is a new game + mode but after playing the game once i didnt feel like i wanted to go through it again.

Considering I have all the achievements and have spent over 70 hours in the world of Neptunia, I figure I should share my experience. I knew nothing about the Hyperdimension Neptunia franchise until one fateful afternoon when I had nothing better to do. I stumbled upon the store page of this game, Re;birth1, and bought it in the summer sale of 2015. This is my first experience with the series and my fourth or fifth JRPG, so take my opinions with a grain of salt, as always.
Hyperdimension Neptunia is a turn-based JRPG that was developed by Compile Heart and its parent company Idea Factory, released on PS3 in 2010. In regions outside of Japan, it was flooded with negative reviews, criticizing its terrible music, nonsensical plot, bland and unlikable characters, painful performance issues, and tedious gameplay. Despite this, the game sold enough to warrant two more games, mk2 and Victory.
The franchise then grew to include spinoffs such as Hyperdevotion Noire (a Fire Emblem style SRPG) and Producing Perfection (an idol sim) on the Vita, and enhanced remakes of the PS3 trilogy titled Re;birth 1, 2, and 3. All 3 remakes are available on the Playstation Vita and Steam for about $30 each. (At the time of this review, Re;birth 3 has not been released on Steam, but is available on the Vita.)
There are numerous DLC content packs for Re;birth 1 and 2, none of which are necessary to enjoy the game. The Additional Content packs add exactly what is advertised: additional content such as raising the level cap past 99, a few more dungeons and more loot to obtain. There are also additional party members you can buy. They are quite powerful, and can make the game more of a cakewalk than it already is, so buy at your own discretion.
Compile Heart develops numerous other RPGs, such as Omega Quintet on the PS4, and Fairy Fencer F on PS3 and Steam. While their games are not very well received by critics, they do have a certain charm that gamers, including myself, enjoy.
Hyperdimension Neptunia Re;birth1 (and the rest of the series) is a parody of the video game industry in the seventh generation of consoles (PS3, Xbox 360, Wii). The world is called Gamindustri, and has four Lands representing the major game companies: Planeptune (Sega), Lastation (Sony PlayStation), Leanbox (Microsoft Xbox 360), and Lowee (Nintendo Wii). Each Land is ruled by a goddess called a CPU (Console Patron Unit), all of whom are recruitable party members. The protagonist, Neptune, is based off of a cancelled Sega console by the same name. There are support characters who represent major figures in the industry as well as influential game series, such as Falcom (Nihon Falcom, the developers of Ys), Tekken, MarvelousAQL, and various others.
The story starts in the middle of the Console War. Each CPU is fighting for dominance over Gamindustri. Nobody is winning, so a mysterious voice advises them to rally against the weakest link, Purple Heart. She is defeated by her enemies, transforms into her normal form and falls from the sky, crashing in her city. A girl named Compa (representing Compile Heart) sees this and goes to help her. Upon recovering, Neptune develops amnesia and cannot remember why she fell, nor what she was fighting for. She asks Compa to assist her in recovering her memory, and the story goes from there.
The story is relatively light-hearted, with plenty of jokes, references, parodies, and jabs sprinkled into the serious stuff. Neptune's happy-go-lucky personality elevates the mood, as well as the relationships of the CPUs. Throughout the game, Neptune breaks the fourth wall, stating that she is the protagonist, the story was changed with the remake, and so on. It's a linear story with 2 endings, one neutral and one good. To achieve the good (or  "true") ending, one must fulfill a certain requirement, which may take some time, but it's not ridiculous like some other games. I promise it is worth it. The plot may be predictable and bland at times, but what do you expect with a JRPG? It's meant to be fun and fluffy.
A large portion of the game is spent reading on screen text in a visual novel format. Character sprites will appear to indicate who is speaking, with light animation. You can choose to skip through the text if desired, or replay spoken lines. The entirety of the exposition is told in these segments, so unless you are on your second playthrough, I would advise reading them.
Outside of reading, the game consists of exploring various small dungeons and fighting enemies in a turn based system. In combat, you can have a maximum of 3 party members. There are 3 styles of attacking: Rush (lots of hits to build up super moves), Power (straight damage), and Break (to wear down the enemy's guard, useful for bosses). Outside of attacking physically, one can use SP skills (spells), consumable items, and initiate an EXE attack (an extremely powerful series of attacks). The CPUs can transform into their HDD form (Hard Drive Divinity) which increases their damage output and resilience at the cost of some mana points per turn. As with any RPG, there are status ailments such as Poison, Paralysis, Skillseal, and Virus (which stops a CPU from transforming). The rest of the mechanics are standard JRPG fare, so I won't go into that.
New to the Re;birth series is the Plan system and the Lily Rank system. Plans are a form of recipes for items, dungeons, modifications to dungeons, and various gameplay modifiers. As the player gathers materials and ingredients, they can activate these plans at the cost of MB (Megami Bytes, the game's form of resources). The player gains more MB through story events and New Game Plus. The Lily Rank system is an interesting one. Party members can either be placed in the Front or Back positions. The members in front are actively engaging in battle, while the members in the back provide buffs and assist attacks depending on their relationship. The more battles one completes, the higher the rank between two characters will be, unlocking more positive effects. Some of the more powerful EXE attacks are done between Front and Back partners with a certain Lily Rank.
Some characters can only be unlocked through Plans. Each CPU (with the exception of Green Heart, the CPU of Leanbox) has a Candidate, or a younger sister type character. Some of the best weapons and armor can only be crafted through Plans, as well as dungeons that contain the materials for the aforementioned weapons and armor. There are countless (and I really mean
accessories and outfits one can adorn the characters with, which is where the niche appeal of the game lies. There is a place called the Colosseum where one can fight increasingly difficult monsters for currency, weapons, and items.
The art style is clean and polished. Characters have distinct looks, the backgrounds are gorgeous and wallpaper-worthy, animations and effects are impressive for what they are, and the interface is attractive and easy to navigate. The soundtrack is comprised of themes from mk2 and Victory, with a few brand new remixes specially composed for Re;birth1. My favourite track is the battle theme of certain bosses, One Two Three. It happens to be composed by none other than Nobuo Uematsu and his band, the Earthbound Papas. The rest of the soundtrack is composed by Keiji Kaneko. It's a wonderful blend of light hearted techno and electronica.
I highly enjoyed my time with Hyperdimension Neptunia Re;birth1. If I didn't, I would not have gotten all the achievements and done multiple playthroughs. If you are looking for a fun, humorous, satirical representation of the gaming industry, look no further. And for the love of God,

Everlasting Summer is a visual novel from russian developer Soviet Games. The story follows a 25-year-old man named Semyon who lives in a big city of today's Russia. One winter evening our protagonist decides to go to his university reunion. He jumps into old LIAZ model bus with a number 410 and suddenly falls asleep only to wake up inside a completely different Icarus bus. But this isn't the biggest mystery. After Semyon steps out, he finds himself in front of the gate leading to the Sovyonok pioneer camp with no trace of winter, but a warm and sunny summer. Somehow Semyon traveled to mid-1980's Soviet Union, reverted to his 18-year-old self and is now surrounded by some attractive pioneer girls. As you try to solve the mystery of such events and find the way to leave this place for good, you also start developing various relationships with camps' inhabitants. Maybe the camp isn't as bad as it seems? It's up to you to find out the truth and decide the route you are going to take.
The game features at least 10 hours of visual novel style gameplay with 13 different endings that forms a single story. The soundtrack consists of over 60 different tracks, ranging from calm and chilling ambience to heavy russian metal. The art style for backgrounds, CG's and sprites definitely shows how much work has been up in this project and may make you ask yourself why is this game free, some may say, that it's better than AAA products on the market even. The developers really hit all the high notes with this and I wish all the best to the Soviet Games with their upcoming release of "Love, Money, Rock'n'Roll".

Vertical gameplay means you can approach any situation from almost any angle
Decent variety of weapons
Coop is fun as hell.
Cons:
Movement while falling is kinda broken, if you're falling straight down with no forward movement, and you tap forward once as quickly as you can, you'll sling shot forward at 45 degrees for the remainder of the fall, and cannot slow down.
Objective prompts fail to update from time to time.
-Potential Spoilers ahead-
The final mission, at one point you drop into a sewer and have to kill a screamer, as soon as that happens you start getting chased by lots and lots of volatiles, and have to run a gauntlet to get out to the exit. Inventory is managed in real time, so if you don't know this is coming and you don't have flares equipped, its very hard to find the time to equip them. Also; if you die during this sequence you're brought back to the start just after you killed the screamer, and aren't able to get a couple seconds to change your inventory.
If you use a bunch of resources (like ammo) but fail an objective and get reset to checkpoint, you do not get your resources back. Couple this with objective prompts failing as listed above, and you can spend 10 minutes in an area killing off zombies that never stop spawning, use up 80% of your ammo, eventually die, respawn and have 20% of your ammo left.
The final boss fight was a QTE. The games first and only QTE... rather than using direction to tell you what button to press, they use the actual key. if you don't know off hand what direction corresponds to wasd, or worse, if you use RDFG like me, then you're in for quite a bit of rage. A simple arrow on screen would have completely resolved the control issues, but that doesn't excuse a QTE final boss. The player didn't carve a path through hundreds of zombies and humans to get to the one-handed boss, be unable to do anything than press the 'win' keys.
The cons put a horrible finish to an otherwise fantastic game. Unfortunately, they're negative points that I cannot reconcile with.

Although the game itself is pretty unique, good-looking, great soundtrack and has a nicely crafted SP experience, this game is really all focused on multiplayer. Unfortunately, as it currently is, i can not recommend it. Aside from the fairly cranky pathfinding units have, the Goo faction is completely broken. (also fundamentally, so a few nerfs here and there probably will not resolve the issue) They will force a non-goo player into complete defense, leaving the map pretty much safe to move its units anywhere. The Goo's opponent will not be able to scout out, which gives the Goo immense power. As they are a very mobile faction (their 'mother' Goo can be moved to anywhere on the map) you have no idea where they are, and scouting would probably mean instant defeat.
They also have all units right off the bat availible to build, so similair-power artillery to the Human and Beta faction, which generally takes some time before they can get it, availible right away.
With the Goo being able to traverse any terrain that would otherwise be impassable, an artillery piece can be set near the enemy's base and blow it all up - and there's nothing you can do to stop it. Having flying scouting units availible works well, but by the time you'll have them, you're already in deep and your base already under siege for a few minutes. Proteans (which spawn low level Goo units) are too fast to kite, and slow any enemy target once it is in range to attack. All you need to do is to place it right in front of an enemy factory, and any unit that will be built will be instantly destroyed. If you manage to kill the protean anyway, it can spawn its units just shortly before dying. The spawned units hp will not be lowered, so start at full health. Basically, for every unit they have, they pack double the punch for the price of one.
These are just a few things of a larger problem. If you have no to little interest in competitive RTS, prefer single-player or laid-back skirmishes, by all means, try Grey Goo. For everyone else remotely interested in a fair, competitive RTS, do NOT buy this game in its current state.

Grey Goo is a game that brings us back to the classical RTS playstyle with slower gameplay and base building orientation.
This game is basically a mix between C&C games, Universe At War: Earth Assault and Earth 2160. If you come at this game with an open mind you will enjoy it imensily. If you expect everything to be exactly as in C&C then you will be heavily dissapointed.
This is a real throwback to what RTS games once were about and I hope that will be again.
The UI in this game is one of the most non intrusive I have seen in any RTS game to date. The campaign is challenging on hard but passable. The missions are designed very good and provide a very long singleplayer experience. I would say that you can get easily 15-20 hours out of it. Skirmish offers quite a good AI that really knows how to counter players moves. The ressource in this game the so called Catalyst is mined on Catalyst/Veins fields by Extractors which are replenishible like Tiberium fields in C&C games.
The three faction are really distinctive. The Humans although a full turtling faction are capable of carrying out early rushes to disturb enemy eco production. What you need to realise is that base buildings in this game are hard to destroy so you have ample time to rebuild some of your forces that get destroyed. This game is not like SC2 just about how you Micro. Its about how secure your supply lines are and how secure your production is. So it does not matter if you loose your army since you can field another one in do time. Basically its a macro game. Humans are very adaptible when it comes to base defenses since they can teleport any building to any place on the conduit lines.
Betas as a faction are quite adaptive and offer a nice mix between a turtling and offense faction. They may look similar in playstle to Humans but they do offer faster counterattack options. And the Hand of Ruk rocks.
Goos really are a faction that is made for the fans of Micro management. It is important to note that Goos need some time before they can produce enough force but when they do then you will surely get a nice fight.
Also just to point out that the Map Editor is already included in the game since some people think that its not there. Its in the games Steam folder (PgPublicTerrainEditor).
Anyway I recommend the game to any UaW, C&C and Earth series fans but as said this is a new game that includes a lot of different concepts so you need to be open minded to it.

I love this game more than any MMO I've ever played but I really can't give it a positive review for several reasons. The game is very strong in the professions you can do, anywhere from gathering to trading, to even sailing the high seas to hunt whales! The game is huge and is completely open world. You can make your own empire and focus on ship building, or you can go on to become the leader of a massive trading company while your workers make all the goods for you. The possibilities of the game are endless... but... let’s talk about the multiplayer aspect. It is so limited... I hardly could call this a MMO, but would rather call it "Single player Online." Why? Cause there is so little you can do to help out your guild or friends outside of pvp and knowledge. This game severally lacks a trading system so you can help your friend build that awesome galleon to sail the seas or to help them get a piece of gear they may have accidently got. There is almost no trading outside of the broken marketplace. Market prices are set which is nice but what grinds my gears is the lack of giving a friend the item you want to get them. There is a bidding system but it seems to be completely run by a trash RNG system like most of the game. On top of that the more and more I try to get items I want on the marketplace the more and more I believe there are bot programs which auto buy things when an item goes up. I can sit there for hours and not get a single item I want just because another person/bot is able to get it in less than a second, even if it takes me a few seconds to try and get an item. There is a boat in this game that takes weeks of work to get but you can't have friends help you out just cause any form of trading is non-existent... This game is a Single player game! If you like the idea of running with a few mates and building a guild up outside of pvp then this game isn't for you sadly. Most of the guild will be focused around pvp and only that. Though I really enjoy this game it has things that hurt itself more than it benefits. This game has zero gold spammers because of the mechanics that stop the selling, but is taking away strong features in a MMO worth fighting them? Work needs to be done to prevent gold sellers, but don't just take away major features.

(IHOG)
Options include separate sliders for Music, Sound & Voice, custom cursor, fullscreen/Windowed, maintain aspect ratio, and the ability to change your difficulty level at any time.  There are three difficulties to choose from, each clearly defined on the selection page.
The first HOS we had was highly-interactive, with things to find and place in the scene in order to find more items.  Sadly, there were only three of these in the game, with the rest of the HOS being your standard, slightly-interactive fare, and each of which being visited twice.
There IS a mis-click penalty - even in Casual Mode - but you have to click pretty rapidly for it to come up.
The artwork is gorgeous, with many of the scenes having a moment or two with no HUD present -- Perfect for people like myself who love taking screenshots!
There are four orchestral pieces, all of which are lovely, and which can be saved on your computer in the EXTRAS portion.  Some of the voices are really professionally-done, and the rest are pretty good.  Sound effects were well-picked and non-invasive.
The save-your-sister storyline is nothing new, but I really enjoyed the way the devs incorporated well-known fairy tale characters into the mix.  The protagonists were likeable, and we had a companion for a good portion of the game.
There is one collectible - squirrel tokens - which we use to upgrade our pet's home.
Everything wraps up nicely, but there's juuuust a bit of ambiguity to suggest the storyline for another game.
The extra gameplay takes place immediately after the ending of the main game, and was just as enjoyable as the main game, and with 15 locations to visit - some of them brand new, some of them revisited but... changed.
This second Living Legends installment is a solid, beautiful and entertaining hidden object game that will likely take you between four and six hours to complete, depending on your style of gameplay.  I definitely enjoyed myself, and recommend it to my fellow IHOG fans.

The game follows House Forrester, like in the books and the TV series the story is told over a number of different characters. I enjoy the story, the houses of Forrester and Whitehills are everything you would imagine in the Game of Thrones universe. There is a nice selection of characters from the TV show voiced by their actors as well to make the game even more fun.
I have played it on both XBox and Steam and found it much easier to play on Steam using my keyboard, the reactions can be a bit slow but seem to be much faster on here then the XBox.
I like that you have a little bit of freedom with the characters but in the end it very much does end up the same way no matter what you pick. I have played the game through three times and no matter what you decide to do it tends to force the game in the direction its going which isn't bad but can be quite annoying on second or third playthroughs.
The characters are all interesting, the story is engaging and the look of it all is very much Game of Thrones. I personally don't think you have to know anything about Game of Thrones to play the game and enjoy it as I had read the first and second book, seen the first series and found the game much more enjoyable then either the book or TV series (though Ramsey Snows character made me hunt out my friends DVDs and marathon the show to see what he was like in the TV Series.)
Even though there are a lot of action scenes, especially in later episode when Asher Forrester shows up, it very much is a story heavy game and depending on the options you pick you can be sat for a long time being told a lot of information.
I'd recommend the game. It is engaging and you can replay it at least once to pick up information in different areas that you might have missed the first time.

The lack of game time is because I sadly encountered the launcher error. I was able to play the game by following the alternate solution that the devs provided. I think I spent a good 7 hours for both of them combined! As everyone might have figured, Frozen Fear collection is actually a duology of two HOGs, each with their own collector's edition, and bonus gameplay and content.
I recommend playing Ice Rose first since it's the older of the two. Even though I think Frozen Beauty could stand alone by itself, it's considered a 'sequel' to Ice Rose due to the reoccurring characters and identical theme.
Despite the launcher not working, it didn't hamper my enthusiasm for these games at all. They were absolutely enjoyable, I'd definitely say they even top some Artifex titles in terms of content and quality.
Pros:
> Surprisingly somewhat well-animated 3D character models?
> Beautiful graphics and backgrounds, especially when you reach the ruined castle!
> Very fun puzzles
> I love that the protag was funny and kind of tired of the bull she had to go through, her clues were really useful in terms of directing me to the next thing
> Enjoyable music
> Bonus chapter was fun!
Cons:
> No map, or fast-travel--- I was a fool and had the tendency to go up and down the very slow elevator because I missed something
> Basically backtracking hell because of the lack of a map
> A bit of pixel hunting in terms of some objects
> The story was a little dry but it got very, very interesting at the end
I have to say I enjoyed this one immensely. It felt very much like a very concluded fairy tale. There were plenty of different puzzles and HOs were simple enough that it didn't drive me up the wall. It was chocful of content. It was... just really pleasant compared to a lot of HOGs out there right now.
Pros:
> It was just really beautiful, there's TONS of places and things to look at
> The puzzles were entertaining and lovely to look at
> The protag for this one is just as sassy and funny, I loved how she complained about why there were so many missing pieces to the statues and the like
> Fast-travel map with action indicators (I feel so much at peace when I know I've looked in every nook and cranny)
> A little side quest hunt for coins to upgrade your pet squirrel's home
> You get to name the squirrel!
> TONS of locations so there's only a fair bit of backtracking, but they make sure that HOs appear next to when you come back to open another puzzle
> Lots of achievements to do
> Built-in strategy guide!
> Bonus chapter was really fun and was a lovely addition, it had its own locations and unique puzzles
Cons:
> The character models are really unattractive, I wish they worked on this more and maybe I would have loved this game a lot more too (especially the 3 deceased princesses)
> There's a slight quality drop to maybe 2 HO scenes, it was very apparent that the images were low quality, stretched out, and blurry that they stood out uncomfortably compared to the rest of the HOs
> Not a lot of variety in the music, and quite immemorable
Overall, I'd say this was a really, good refreshing purchase for me. It's worth every penny for the entertainment value it provided. I was more than happy to play Frozen Beauty twice to finish up all the achievements. I'm a little bummed out about the broken launcher but I'm willing to forgive it just for the quality of the games themself. Hopefully, they'll come back to this and fix the launcher.

With one mediocre and one rather enjoyable game packed into one, the Living Legends duology offers plenty enough for any hidden object gamer, especially if they prefer stories based on traditional fairy tales.
Ice Rose is a perfect example of how good graphics do not make a game. Theoretically, this one is supposed to be a hidden object adaptation of the Snow Queen tale, but in practise, it is one of those HOGs where the story is only present at the beginning and at the end, with the rest filled by repetitive, plotless tasks.
To the game’s credit, these tasks are at least enjoyable. The puzzles are fun and the hidden object scenes are comfortably challenging, so even with the lack of story, it is pleasurably playable.
While Ice Rose promised a “to be continued”, Frozen Beauty is actually a completely standalone game, based on the tale of Snow White. Actually based on, because this time around we get a proper story, completed with voice-acted cut-scenes. (As for the plot, well… it is Snow White.)
Game design inherited most elements from Ice Rose, meaning the puzzles and hidden object scenes retained their good quality and challenge. Sadly, they also retained their number, despite the game being much longer, so Frozen Beauty feels more “thin” in terms of content. At least it has a good map system to eliminate boring backtracking.
